en: Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati. Oṃ! Even those people who possess no merit whatsoever attain fortune instantaneously by meditating upon the pair of lotus-feet of this glorious one. I always worship this Lord, the husband of Māhiṣmatī, the progenitor of the *atyādi* [lineage].

*(Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a hymn or invocation. The term "amum" refers to the aforementioned deity; "māhiṣmatyāḥ patim" identifies him as the lord of the city of Māhiṣmatī; and "atyādi-jananaṃ" likely refers to his role as the progenitor of a specific lineage or class of beings.)*
Though I am not a traveler upon the path of the words of Śiva, nor one who knows their intent,
nor even one who can resolve my long-standing doubts instantly,
nevertheless, may the grace of the venerable Bhāskararāya [carry me] across the ocean of this Tantra with his mercies.

May this *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi* not become a source of ridicule for you; for from that ocean of love, the twice-born [author], there has arisen this work. What desired object is there not obtainable here through the grace of Kṛtavīrya’s son, the Lord of Speech (*Śāradātilaka*)?
Numerous commentaries on the *Kāvyasaṃjīvanī* are already in circulation;

nevertheless, let the wise who discern the essence render this labor of mine meaningful. Now, in order to uplift virtuous people who are submerged in the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, [the author], having assumed a form endowed with excellence...
Having considered that although the various methods were taught by the Blessed Lord Śiva, they were extremely difficult to understand due to their cryptic intent and even more so to practice,
he determined that very same purpose— establishing it as a single form through the harmonization of various tantras— and [expounded it] for the sake of ease.
Desiring to compose this new treatise in words that are easy to understand, the venerable Lakṣmaṇa—

having performed an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) for the destruction of the host of obstacles that hinder the completion of the work— binds [the following] to the instruction of his disciples, beginning with the words "eternal" (*nitya*), etc., [and continuing] without ceasing.
The connection [of the word] consists in the form of an operation conducive to the non-existence of the undesired, which pervades the meaning of "not having a second.

Since even a permanent non-existence exists, it is well-established among all people that its status as a sustainer is due to its being the cause for the cognition of existence; thus, it possesses causality with respect to the operation. The undesired...

Cessation (*nivṛtti*), however, is not a part of that [non-existence], because cessation, being of the nature of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), is dependent upon a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); and where the counter-positive has not even come into existence due to the absence of its own causes, [cessation] is unestablished there.
Furthermore, non-arising (*anutpāda*) in the form of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is also not a part of that [non-existence]. Why? Because it is not... [the counter-positive].

In a case where [the object] is not yet produced, there is a lack of evidence for its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Thus, the state of being the locus of the cognition generated by one's own sentence—which constitutes the status of being the "intended" (*uddeśyatva*)—is occupied by the student as the person addressed (*saṃbodhya*). Consequently, the property of residing in the meaning of the accusative case following the pronoun *yuṣmad* (which denotes the student) does not subsist in any part of the [verb's] meaning.

The word "bhāve" (in the case of existence) [is used] because, in the case of a connection with the undesired (*aniṣṭānvaya*), if the undesired were not established for a particular individual (*vyakti*), there would be an impossibility of its connection; therefore, by saying "bhāve," it is indicated that in some cases the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is indeed established as possessing the undesired. [Objection: But at the beginning of this treatise, what occasion is there for this greatness (*mahas*), by which [this topic] is introduced?
Regarding the statement that one should contemplate this [deity] rather than merely remembering Gaṇapati, the destroyer of obstacles to composition, or Sarasvatī, the presiding deity of speech,
he says "vācām" and so forth: "Is that splendor known as Sarasvatī now the object of memory?"

He says "it is not real" and so forth; "eternal bliss" (*nityānanda*) and so on is an epithet of the Great One (*mahaḥ*), meaning that whose own nature or form is eternal bliss. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss. [The term] "bliss" (*ānanda*) is used with the suffix *matup* (possessive), hence it is not in the neuter gender.
There is no contingency of difference [between the self and bliss] because bliss is related to it through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Alternatively,

since there is eternal bliss unmixed with suffering, and since bodies are of such a nature, and since saṃsāra— being beginningless and thus indivisible— is continuously [connected] to those very [bodies] at every moment.

The meaning is that this entire world is pervaded by that splendor consisting of fifty syllables— letters that are flowing and manifest— which, like the *kṣa* sound [in the word] *krādi*, are not counted as separate due to being conjunct consonants (*saṃyuktākṣara*) and thus lacking independent significance. For from the *Kāvya* and other [Vedic texts], immediately upon hearing them, there arises unsurpassed...
Joy arises for the audience from hearing sentences such as those of the Vedānta, and for some, through that sequence, there occurs an excellence of bliss consisting of liberation; thus,
phonemes possess this causality with respect to all words, such as "jar" and "cloth," as well as their respective meanings.

Now, some maintain that the pervasion of phonemes over the meaning of words occurs in some way— either by being conveyed through words designated for specific individuals or by being conveyed through pronominal words; however, another maintains that it is *śabdabrahman* alone that is all-pervasive,
while yet another [maintains] that it is the consciousness internal to individual souls (*jīvātman*).
One says that the world is pervasive, while another says that the one who wears the crescent moon (Śiva) is pervasive;
thus, these three views would contradict your own position. To this, he says "In sound," and so forth.
In this way, there is a distinction only in the words, but not in the meaning of what is named—this is the [conclusion of] the three views.
The intention is that our view is indeed contradictory;

for since Saṃkarṣaṇa is Keśava himself due to being a distinct manifestation (mūrti-bheda) of him, the syllable *au* is prescribed for the placement (nyāsa) of the Saṃkarṣaṇa-form along with the fourteenth vowel (*au*) in the Keśava-nyāsa and other such rites.

*Triśāhakāraḥ*: that in which the night (*niśā*) is accompanied by the letter *a*; this is a qualifying attribute of the Great One (*mahat*). "The abode of the half-moon and the lotuses" refers to the *Hauṃ* syllable;
by this, the seed-syllable of the Prāsāda (*Oṃ*) is extracted. In this same manner, other seed-syllables are also to be understood according to the meaning of the text.

What has been stated by the author of the *Itipadārthādarśa* is incorrect, as it results in a forced (kliṣṭa) interpretation; for even regarding a forced meaning, the author’s intention does not reside there, such that—due to the impossibility of that [literal sense]—one would necessarily have to resort to an implied meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) which is otherwise prohibited. Now, [if one asks], "Is it not the eastern direction?"...
If one recites this [text] during the three junctions of the day for six months while having the senses subdued, and so forth—
reaching up to twenty-seven days with twenty-one recitations of the *kavaca* (armour)—
how can you be intent on refuting the difficult explanations of others?

If you say, "This is a mere activity," you are mistaken. We do not strive here to display our own scholarship; rather, we follow the path of commentary for the sake of the practical applications mentioned in the scriptures. How should those "wish-fulfilling cows" (Kāmadhenus) spoken of by the Sage be employed, and by what ritual procedure is their accomplishment achieved?

In brief, because of the requirement to conform to the statements of the Daityas and others, there would arise the fallacy of expressing what is not intended to be conveyed by the words of the *Kavaca*, since even a grammatical application (*prayoga*) not taught therein would be presented in the *Saṃhitā*. Furthermore, his sovereignty over speech arises from his being composed of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*).

Some say that at the beginning of a work, one should remember the seed-syllable *vāgbhava* (AIM), which is divine, whose abode is the moon, and which has a bindu upon its head; they say this for the purpose of protection (*avyāt*). However, this interpretation is not strained, for [the effect] such as a jar is produced by potters and others who possess well-established causal agency in the world.

What is the use of accepting a superfluous greatness through the accomplishment of an effect? If it is argued that its existence is not established by its being the agent of the earth and so forth, we say no;

for since he is admitted to be devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), agency is impossible. Furthermore, if it is argued that agency is attributed to him due to a connection with some power (*śakti*), [we respond...]

If you say that the agent (*kartṛ*) in that case is merely her power (*tacchakti*), then she herself will also be the agent of the composition of your book, the granting of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), the removal of obstacles, and so forth;
therefore, with the intention that her recollection is absolutely necessary for these purposes, he says: "Within her... and so on.

Even in this laughter, the reason is this very same one: that although this Supreme Brahman lacks the status of being a cause, it will nevertheless be taught as the cause for transmigrating beings. Now, let it be granted that the Great Supreme Brahman, together with its powers (*śakti*), is worthy of being remembered; however, [the opponent objects: but that...

[Objection: "Meditation on the Lord is not easily attainable. [Response: If you say that it is easily attainable through the instructional words of some guru, then, because such a person is supremely beneficial, meditation upon him alone is necessary; with this intention, he says "saṃsāra... and so forth, beginning with the means to achieve what is desired.

Since the knowledge of one's own [work] cannot serve as a cause for activity in general— whether in the form of worldly activity in general or otherwise— without the apprehension that it is a means to achieve one's desired end, the activity of students toward reading and so forth of this book would not be possible; therefore, the fruit [of the work] is the knowledge of the meaning of one's own book.
He does not show [the meaning] by means of a single tantra among all the tantras, such as the *Sāramañjarī* and others; for if one were to show only a single tantra from among the various tantras,
in some cases the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) of that single tantra would be shown, in some cases the literal meaning of the words (*padārtha*), and in some cases only the required portions.

Furthermore, the meaning cannot be determined [merely by individual texts]; rather, it is the specific meaning established through the unity of purpose (*ekavākyatā*) of all systems (*sarvatantra*), provided that such a core essence is possible, and not the various sentence-meanings as if they were independent or optional prescriptions. By this, it is not the case here that there is only one system...

The author of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* has stated that even though the subject matter is not dependent on others and is not contradicted [by scripture], it is not a meaning newly fabricated by one's own imagination (*svakapolakalpita*), since the purpose of his own work is shown by this very verse beginning with "eternal bliss" (*nityānanda*); however, that is not correct.

Consequently, because such a meaning would not be clearly understood, and because [the statement] "I shall state the essence" and so forth would result in a lack of interest (*vairasya*), one might ask:

"What is that essence which is to be propounded here in this treatise? In response to this expectation, he states the entire subject matter of his own work in brief, beginning with "The word and the object," and so on. As for that which...

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that [the author of the *Sārasamuccaya*] shows the subject matter (*abhidheya*), purpose (*prayojana*), relationship (*saṃbandha*), and the qualified audience (*adhikārin*)— which serve as the causes for the listener’s engagement— by means of the two verses beginning with "The essence" (*sāram*). However,
even though the entire subject matter stated therein is established by each individual verse beginning with "That is the essence" (*tat tu sāram*), [the following applies].

Since the second verse must be required as a further elaboration of this very [first verse], the two verses may somehow be construed as a single syntactical unit; however, I shall not do so because of the discordance between the two verbal expressions such as "I shall speak" (*vakṣyāmi*) and so forth. Thus, there is no single syntactical unity for the two verses.

Because there would be a lack of aesthetic flavor (*avairasya*) due to the predominance of actions such as "he will speak" (*vakṣyati*), and because there would arise the fault of a grammatical mismatch (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*)— namely, that the connection [of the words] would be with "I" (*mama*) in the sense that "I shall speak such a work, the *Śāradātilaka*, in which the methods of worship for those [deities], as well as the causes of Dharma and so forth, are described"— [the author intends something else].

The phrase "for the sake of dispelling the mental distress of disciples regarding other objects" and so forth is an adjective specifically qualifying this very treatise (*grantha*), as well as its excellence for the attainment of knowledge.
Now, it has been established that the treatise itself is the cause for [the attainment of] dharma, artha, and so on; why then [is it called] a *stotra* (hymn)?

Regarding whether [the result arises] from the mere recitation of the text, or from the knowledge of its meaning, or rather from the performance of the actions prescribed therein, he says "śabda... and so forth. Thus, through the presentation of the injunctions by the mantras, there is the knowledge of them; from that, their performance; and from that, the accomplishment of the desired goal—this is the sequence.

The meaning is that the knowledge of this treatise (*tyāgrantha*) is a means to achieve the desired goal; therefore, it must certainly be studied at the outset. Furthermore, even regarding the injunction for obtaining the mantra, the status of being a "mantra-injunction" is not intended [to be primary];
thus, the injunction for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*), which is encompassed by the introductory verse (*pratijñāśloka*), is included here.
There is no harm even in the word *tipāda*. *Śāra* means independent (*svatantra*), and its state is *śāratva*, which is independence;
she who bestows that is *Śāradā*. Her *tilaka* is her ornament.
By this, it is stated through its etymological significance that this very work is to be accepted above all others; it is the *tilaka* of Sarasvatī.

It should be understood that this [state] is superior with respect to all bonds (*grantha*). Now, he begins to describe the creation of the parts as reached by the order of enumeration, starting with the words "nirguṇa" and so forth. This description of creation is necessary; otherwise, it would be impossible [to understand] the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other practices that are about to be explained.

Because the destruction of each respective cause and the production of each respective effect from that cause are difficult to discern, the term "eternal" (*sanātana*) avoids the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, it is "other" (*anya*) in the sense of not being comprised within *prakṛti*; the qualities (*guṇas*) are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and it is distinct from their inclusion.

The statements regarding the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) and qualified (*saguṇa*) nature [of the Supreme] are due to the Supreme Brahman having entered into specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*). It is precisely these aforementioned qualities, when fallen into such states, that are designated by the terms *prakṛti*, *avidyā*, and *kalā*.
Thus, within the two-fold Supreme Brahman, it is the second [the qualified one]...

The power (*śakti*) that has arisen through the inequality of the *guṇas* is the gross state known as *prakṛti*; yet it is indeed *prakṛti*. Thus, when the *guṇas* exist in a state of equilibrium in their subtle condition, they are synonymous with *prakṛti*, *avidyā*, and *kalā*. From Brahman, there arise those [entities] characterized by them.

The essential meaning is that *śakti*—which is a synonym for *guṇa* when it has attained a particular gross state—is born; the word "was" (*āsīt*) here means "manifested. As it is said in the *Yavīyānhitā*: "By the will of Śiva, the *parā-śakti* attains oneness with the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*)."

Therefore, by the statement that "first, from that [source], oil [arises] from sesame seeds and so forth," it is refuted as to how one could maintain that Śakti is produced from Brahman who is already endowed with Śakti; for the distinction between the [unmanifested] Moon (Śaśin) and [the manifested] has been established, given its state of possessing all parts (sakalatva).

The capacity for creation and other attributes of the Supreme Brahman does not fall away; however, because others are swallowed up by ignorance (*avidyā*), their sovereignty is lost—this is the intended meaning. From that *Śakti*, the *Nāda* and the *Bindu* arise.

These are indeed specific states, just as clay receives various designations such as "potsherd," "potsherd-fragment," "jar," or "water-jar. That which consists of supreme power (*paraśaktimaya*), consisting of Śiva’s power (*śivaśaktimaya*), and designated as the *sāktādvaita* Brahman, is the *bindu* itself; furthermore, it is produced again from the previously mentioned *bindu* and *nāda*.

By means of the two [states] that have not yet become manifest, he establishes the threefold nature of the *bindu* and others by applying his own modes of differentiation. In this context, the *bindu*, having attained a transcendent state (*parāvasthā*) distinct from the subtle and gross states, is indeed Śiva himself.

The *nāda*, having entered a subtle state, is thus impossible to utter; however, when it has entered a gross state and serves as the cause, it is indeed the aforementioned *bindu* that is designated by the term "seed" (*bīja*). Alternatively, the phrase "consisting of the supreme power" (*para-śakti-maya*) also merely indicates its particular state.

The term *śaktipada* refers to the gross state (*sthūlāvasthā*), because that which has previously been established as *śakti* is precisely what has now reached the gross state; thereafter, there is the state non-different from the Supreme (*parābhinnāvasthā*) and the subtle state (*sūkṣmāvasthā*) within the supreme state (*parāvasthā*). It is only in this way that the significance of these specific distinctions is maintained.

He states the nature of the divisions with the words beginning "the *bindu*," etc. Although [the *bindu*] was previously produced as the substratum (*dharmin*) of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), it is not mentioned prior to the relationship consisting of sound (*nāda*); this is for the sake of avoiding monotony. The "conjunction" (*samavāya*) is a relationship characterized by the state of the agitated and the agitator, which is a fabrication of one's own imagination.
In order to dispel doubt, [the text] begins with "all" (*sarva*) and so forth, and "Raudrī" and so forth;

these, being internal to the sound-creation (*śabdasṛṣṭi*), sequentially attain the status of the names Rudra and the others, in the form of the Obstructress (*nirodhikā*), the Half-moon (*ardhendu*), and the Bindu.
And these are also designated by the terms Knowledge-power (*jñānaśakti*), Will-power (*icchāśakti*), and Action-power (*kriyāśakti*).

The statement beginning with "From Sadāśiva, Īśvara arises, and from him the emergence of Rudra" will be explained with the intention of referring to the creation of objects (*arthasṛṣṭi*); therefore, there is no contradiction between the preceding and subsequent passages.
[It arises] from that which is being divided—that is, from the second [principle], the Supreme (*parā*), which has been differentiated into three forms; or rather, from Him...

Therefore, three divisions have been stated from that which is the root of men, the *parārdhavid* (the knower of the supreme limit), which was first mentioned and not subsequently; whose nature (*ātman*) is unmanifest (*avyakta*), being undifferentiated by specific attributes such as color and so forth— Śaṅkara, the master of all scriptures, has described him as such.

Vārya and others employ the term *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman) [to refer to the eternal word]. However, some say that it is the internal *sphoṭa*, which consists of both word and meaning, that is to be designated by the term *śabdabrahman*. Others, however, maintain that it is the word-*sphoṭa* awakened by the apprehension of the final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding phonemes.

Regarding the two views that the suffixes beginning with *ṭā* (the case endings) and the word *eva* are the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), he refutes both of them with the words "not so" (*na hi*). The "establishment" (*siddhi*) of those two—the word and its meaning—is the establishment of their being denotable by the term "Word-Brahman. The point is this: the referent of the word "Brahman" consists of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), whereas those two [the suffixes and the particle] are insentient (*jaḍa*). Consciousness...

The author's intended meaning is that the word "nyam" (the phoneme *n*), distinguished by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each preceding phoneme and manifested by the consciousness of all living beings within the final phoneme, attains the status of the category of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) as the revealer of the meaning of the entire sentence; for this very reason, it is called *sphoṭa*.
It should not be considered an unjustified assumption that [the Word-Brahman],
having reached and attained the Kuṇḍalinī situated within the bodies of living beings— primarily humans—
and subsequently piercing the gates of the throat, palate, and so forth, manifests the phonemes such as *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and others through those openings.

Having thus explained the creation of mantras— the subject matter of the present treatise— which assumes various forms through distinctions such as prose (*gadya*) and verse (*padya*), he now begins to describe the creation of meaning (*artha-sṛṣṭi*) in order to state the meaning of the mantras and the creation of their respective deities, starting with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.
As for the statement made by the author of the *Harṣadīpikā*— that the commencement of the creation of objects proceeds from that Unmanifest which is the root cause,

just as [creation] proceeds from Āditi, whereas this [present passage] is a restatement of the previously mentioned sequence of the creation of sound (which has now reached its conclusion) for the sake of immediate comprehension— that is not correct.

Since even [the status of] *dāśivā* and so forth would constitute an object (*artha*), it would be impossible to prevent their creation from being classified as the "creation of objects" (*arthasṛṣṭi*).
Otherwise, Agni and Rudra would not even attain the status of being objects due to their enumeration.
Furthermore, since the sequence has not been previously stated, it is impossible for this to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it. Thus, [the objection is refuted]. Śaṃ. [End of commentary].
O, from the proximity of the Supreme Brahman— which consists of the collection of meanings and categories previously described—

He performs His functions by resorting to *kalā* alone, and not through independence; thus, due to this performance of a single function, there is a metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of being of that same nature to Time (*kāla*) as well, regarding the birth of the world.

By these two qualifiers, the two following doubts regarding Śambhu—who is of the nature of the Nirguṇa Brahman—are dispelled: first, how can there be agency for one who is not composed of [any other] essence; and second, how could there ever be the production of anything whatsoever at any time [if he were not its cause]. By the phrase "being without a separate companion," the statement that he is of that very nature is expressed. Thus, both doubts are removed by this pair of qualifiers.

However, because it consists of the *bindu* and functions as the cause of the *bindu* through its specific state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*), it is designated as the "cause" by metaphorical attribution (*kāraṇopacāra*) to the effect. Furthermore, the purpose of taking this [Śiva] as the material cause is precisely that Śambhu’s status as the instigator (*prayojakatva*) of Sadāśiva occurs by means of the *bindu*; this has already been indicated by the phrase "the witness of the world."

The performer of the fivefold cosmic functions consisting of creation, maintenance, destruction, restraint, and grace— some, however, having already stated that the creation of sound was mentioned previously, have thereby also stated the production of the seed-syllable of Māyā;
thereafter, he describes the birth of Sadāśiva with the words beginning with "atha," [starting] from the letter *ha* of Śambhu.

"Kāla" means fire (*agni*), insofar as it is that which causes destruction; the term "time" (*kālatva*) is used because fire exists at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) as the destroyer of all things. It is like a kinsman (*bandhu*) because, by being contained within the single seed-syllable, it brings about [the manifestation].
Having thus manifested the letter *Ha*, the state of Kāmakalā is attained.
Having analyzed the term *kalāpada* as being followed by the fourth vowel (*ī*), which is the actual object [of the mantra],
and having applied it as an adjective to Śambhu— meaning "He in whom [the *kalā*] resides"— the extraction of the complete *māyāvīja* (AIM) has been performed.
As for the statement that the half-moon of Time (*kālārddhendu*) is the self (*ātman*) and the fourth vowel, this was made by the author of the *Padārthādarśa*.

That which was stated is incorrect; for if that were the case, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "of Śambhu" ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyant*), and the natural sense of the root text would be violated. Alternatively, the meaning is that Sadāśiva was born from the letter *ha*, from the letter *ra*, from the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and from the fourth vowel (*caturthasvara*). *Mā*... [text fragment].

If you say that the attainment of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) occurs through mutual conjunction via completion and so forth— whether it be "let it be" or "let it not be"— then those who claim that the lack of syntactic coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in such passages as "the knower, the Self, the eternal," etc., results in an unavoidable lack of elegance in the text, are [refuted] by the very surface of the words.

The intention is this: for Rudra and the others, who are objects of the misconception that they are established merely by similarity [to the Lord], the aforementioned sequence of the meaning of the verses applies; however, in the case of the creation of sound (*śabda-sṛṣṭi*), a different sequence has been stated, which does not pertain to the primary meaning. Now, regarding the specific meaning...

He begins to describe the creation of the elements with the words "mūla" and so forth: from the root, that is, from the supreme reality which is the root of all creation, [proceed] the unmanifest [principles], denoted by the term *parabrahman*,
which are not manifested through specific attributes such as color and the like— by these specific [attributes].
By the statement "the unmanifest self became sound," the sound (arava) has been shown;
from that which was modified and intent upon manifesting creation, the three qualities— sattva and the others—
and the four internal organs consisting of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (citta), [emerged] at that time.

Its nature as such is stated by means of metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the effect to the cause, because it produces that [effect]. This very thing is designated as the *buddhi-tattva* in the Śaiva Āgamas. In order to establish the distinction and differentiation of creation—namely, the creation of the Vaikārika deities and so forth—the threefold nature of the *ahaṃkāra* is taught due to the diversity of its causes.

The sense is that the diversity of effects arises from the threefold nature [of the cause]. Vaikārika, taijasa, and bhūtādi are, respectively, of the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Pracetā is Varuṇa; Upendra is... [the rest of the sentence is missing from the source text].
What is a specific form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa? What is a specific form of Brahmā?

Regarding this, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* has stated that the term "ten" (*daśa*) is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). In his view, the word "ten" would otherwise result in a sense of redundancy (*vairasya*). [The ten] faculties (*indriyāṇi*) are the cognitive faculties (*jñānendriyāṇi*) and the active faculties (*karmendriyāṇi*).
The mind is the eleventh; these eleven sense organs have as their presiding deities Agni and the others in sequence, while the Moon is the presiding deity of the mind. As it has been stated:
"Agni and the others, beginning with Vaikārika, are remembered as the eleven presiding deities of the sense organs, along with the Moon."

Regarding the phrase *vāste parikīrtitāḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthika*) to [the term] beginning with *bhūta*. Thus, there is a connection here specifically with the fourth quarter [of the verse] beginning with *tanmātra*. Accordingly, from the *ahaṃkāra* named *bhūtādi*, first arises the *śabdatanmātra*, and from that, space (*ākāśa*).
From that very same *ahaṃkāra*, through the quality of *tamas*, there arose touch; from space (*ākāśa*) conjoined with touch, air (*vāyu*) arose.

Then, from that same *ahaṃkāra*, form (*rūpa*) arose; from air conjoined with form, fire (*tejas*) arose. Then, from that same *ahaṃkāra*, through the quality of *rajas*, taste (*rasa*) arose; from fire conjoined with taste, water (*jala*) arose. Then, from that—
Therefore, the implied meaning is that from *ahaṃkāra* alone comes smell, and from water accompanied by smell comes earth; thus,
it should not be argued that there is a contradiction in stating that *ahaṃkāra* alone is the cause of the five elements,
because [the former] acts as the cause for each subsequent element through the medium of the production of its respective *tanmātra*.

Because it has been stated thus: "That which was said occurs through the conjunction with the sequence of the *tanmātras*. The meaning is that the elements (*bhūtas*) arise one after another through their connection with the *tanmātras*—namely, the *ahaṃkāra* and the elements produced from it—in accordance with the sequence. Furthermore, from the word "sequence," it follows [that they arise] from the *ahaṃkāra* accompanied by touch, sound, and so forth.

There is no consequence of the production of space and so forth being understood [from the text]. He explains this very point with the words beginning "From sound" (śabdāt) and so on. "Clear" (accham) means transparent (svaccham), that is to say, white (śvetam). "Distinct" (viśadam) means white.
"Each based on its own substrate" (ekaikādhārataḥ) means having as their substrates their respective preceding elements which constitute their causes.
As it has been stated: "In space, air, fire, water, and earth—these being situated therein—is the earth.

Thus, sound and the other [qualities] are, respectively, the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the elements beginning with space. Alternatively, they exist as the substrates of each successive element, characterized by the qualities of their own respective preceding elements.

The meaning is that [each element] possesses one more quality than the preceding one. As it was stated by Īśāna: "Space has sound as its sole quality; wind has the qualities of sound and touch; earth is known to have three qualities through sound, touch, and form;
water has four qualities through the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste; [and fire has five qualities through] sound, touch, form... [and so forth].

Intending the Sāṃkhya doctrine that "earth possesses five qualities through [the addition of] color, taste, and smell," he describes the circles of the elements in this context, beginning with the verse starting with *vṛttam*. Regarding the sun and space: if one were to mark six dots along the circumference of the circle, then for the wind...

The maṇḍala should be a triangle with its apex pointing upwards; for it is seen in another tantra that "that is the fire-maṇḍala by means of the corners of Indra, Rākṣasa, and Vāyu. Regarding the phrase "svastika" and so forth, the meaning is that one should extend the lines at the junctions of the triangle and form the shape of a svastika there. Svasti.
The meaning is that one should draw two lines intersecting at right angles to form four faces facing each other,
then draw a line in the shape of a half-moon starting from the middle of two [adjacent] sides, and then create two lotuses on both sides of that; however,
some say that after drawing an eight-petaled lotus, one should place half-moons at the tips of its petals.

Others say that "one should fashion" means one should draw a half-moon and within it a lotus; they explain the meaning as follows: upon the square lines themselves, in the directions starting from the east, eight *vajras* are to be placed. A *vajra* consists of two lines joined to each other, having three faces due to being oriented toward one another.
The meaning is as follows: by "colors" (varṇaiḥ) are meant the colors of the elements to be described; by "names" (nāmāni) are meant the mantras to be described.

Furthermore, whichever element has a mandala to be drawn according to one's desire, the colors of that element and the mantra of that element must be drawn within that elemental mandala. [This concerns] the elements.

Regarding the statement that "the kalās beginning with *nivṛtti* are the producers": if it is asked, "Since the cause for the production of the elements (*bhūta*) has already been stated, why is a cause for production being stated again now?", we reply:
we do not say that each individual [kalā], such as sound (*śabda*) and so forth, is the sole cause; rather, [we maintain that they act in combination].

There is no fault whatsoever in [the view] that it is indeed conjoined with auxiliary causes such as *kalā* and so forth; for, according to the analysis of the compound *nādadeha* (whose body is sound), the *bindu* is of such a nature, and thus the meaning of the passage beginning with "from *nāda*" is that [the *bindu*] is produced from *kalā*. [The term] *nṝṇām* refers to those who are qualified for the present scripture.

Since it is necessary for the generation of detachment—and thereby the arising of the inclination toward the worship of the Lord—to correctly describe the origin of these [elements] primarily, he states their origin in the verse beginning with "teṣu" and so forth. Now, one might ask: how can it be consistent that there is "only a single drop," and at what time?
Since offspring such as Cidvitra and others are also produced, a distinction in the *bindu* (the seminal point) is necessary according to the distinction in the offspring;

regarding this, he says "both," etc. By way of sequence, due to the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) governed by destiny (*daiva*), the phrase "both" and so forth is an elliptical expression referring specifically to human beings.

Previously, because [the act] occurs before the commencement [of menstruation] and because offspring are generally impossible at that time, it was stated that both [types of offspring] have human beings as their object; however, if one were to think that the seed alone is the cause of the embryo, then there would be no disparity such that sometimes a son and sometimes a daughter is born.
In our view, it is precisely the discrepancy in the number of *bindus* that must be accepted as the cause of that discrepancy;
regarding this, he says "rajodhika" and so forth. That there are twenty-two *mātrās* of *rajas* and fourteen *mātrās* of *śukra*, however, is merely natural and not [the result of] an excess.
Because of this, since the menstrual flow (*rajas*) is superior to all other [constituents], there is the possibility of a female child (*kanyā*).

Thus, when the portion of the menstrual flow exceeds twenty-four [days] and the portion of semen (*śukra*) is less than fourteen [days], a female child is born; likewise, when the semen is in excess, a male child (*putra*) is born.
Regarding the statement by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* that "there is nothing at all defective in birth, since it consists of both [semen and blood],
yet when the *saura* [fire-element] is predominant, one gradually becomes a woman," and so forth— this is not correct; for [birth] arises from the union of semen and blood.

Since the nature of being composed of both [elements] is already understood from the word *dityau*, this [separate mention of] "upādāna" (material cause) would result in redundancy; therefore, by the word "kramāt" (in succession), the following is intended: that very drop (*bindu*), having been separated from the wind, produces many offspring—this statement of yours is also what I have stated.
It is established only in this manner, and not by the interpretation you have stated;

for that which is the supreme secret is as follows: when the two essences, semen and blood, having come together and merged within, a single drop is produced, and that subsequently becomes the embryo.

The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* has stated that [the embryo] enters by itself; however, that too is not tenable, because it would result in a lack of consistency with the phrase "in due order" (*kramāt*). Furthermore, if the connection were "by way of sequence, consisting of both," then even at the time of emerging from the father, it would have been of a single nature, yet having entered the womb, it becomes... [the text here is fragmentary].

Although it might be intended that the *bindu*, having become of a dual nature through its connection with the nasal (*ṇita*), attains unity when combined and thus enters the womb, nevertheless, because there is no account of the birth of twins,
this would result in a deficiency on the part of the author; therefore, this objection is of no consequence.

He establishes the continued existence of Śyāvadanta with the words beginning with "pūrva" (former): those karmas consisting of merit and demerit that produce the experience of pleasure and pain were accumulated in a previous birth;
and in accordance with them, there is *yama*, which consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and acts as their auxiliary.

Being bound by the noose of the hand-form [of Māra], one is characterized by such restrictive determinations as: "this much alone is pleasure, this much alone is suffering, this much alone is life; or rather, this much alone is the performance of auspicious karma, and this much alone is the performance of inauspicious karma," and so forth.

Because of the multiplicity of selves, it should not be thought that a single self— though beginningless— attains the state of a *jīva* by possessing a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) that produces experience through the limitation of a body born from a drop (*bindu*),
nor that the self is produced from a drop; for bliss is changeless.

In that same way, this *jīva*, having encountered and become joined with the *doṣas* (humors) and the *dūṣyas* (tissues), manifests through its own sense organs when they are unaltered; however, when it encounters these *doṣas* and others in an altered state, it arises with impaired sense organs and does not remain possessed of its original, complete senses.

With this intention, he says "by defects" and so forth. He defines the meaning of the word *tatva* (reality) as it occurs in the phrase "having entered into reality" with the words beginning "knowledge" and ending with "those who know reality.
Although the excretion of urine and so forth is also his function, nevertheless, that [is not the primary point].

The intention [of the author] is this: what is the primary function of that which is deaf? Otherwise, why would even the articulation of sounds by the tongue not be considered its function? The word "ātmani" (in the self) implies "the grasper" as the ellipsis. He explains the fourfold nature of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself with the verse beginning with "manas," etc.
The mind consists of conceptualization and discursive thought; the intellect (buddhi) determines all objects of existence;

the ego (ahaṃkāra) is endowed with the conceit of being a knower; and the consciousness (citta) is free from conceptual construction. Regarding this momentary state, it is said in another Tantra: "This power is declared to be the supreme, having the nature of the individual soul (jīva)."

When performing thought-constructions (*saṃkalpa*) and conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), it becomes the mind (*manas*); when assuming the form of discernment (*buddhi*), it effects the determination of all states of being; when enriched with the conceit "I am the knower," it is the aggregate of ego (*ahaṃkāra*);
and when its nature is free from conceptualization, it is considered to be the very essence of consciousness (*citta*).
Just as a single dancer is perceived in many ways, so too the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is perceived differently according to its function:
when it performs the mental deliberation of the Self, it is called the mind (manas); when it discerns the objects for the Self, it is called the intellect (buddhi);
when it manifests the qualities of the Self, it is called the ego (ahaṃkāra); and when it reveals knowledge...
Then that mind is designated by the term "śayati" (it lies). Since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has four states, its fourfold nature is stated;
however, the intention is that this does not refer to a fourfold nature of its essential form (*svarūpa*). Some say that [the four states] are named by the words beginning with "daśa" (ten), etc.

Among those included within the *raṃtatva* [category], for some there are the *tanmātras*; the word "and" (*ca*) connects with the subsequent phrase "the modifications" (*vikṛtayaḥ*). By the word "and," the inclusion of the primal causes (*prakṛtis*) is intended. Their status as modifications (*vikāratā*) is due to their being eternally of the nature of effects. With respect to each subsequent element, each preceding one is a cause, and thus a primal cause (*prakṛti*).

Because each preceding element serves as the material cause (*prakṛti*) for each subsequent one, and each subsequent element exists as a modification (*vikṛti*) relative to each preceding one, they possess the nature of being both material causes and modifications. Furthermore, the term "elements" (*bhūta*) refers here specifically to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), because the word is applied metaphorically to the effects in order to denote their causes. As for the [gross] elements...

Because they are enumerated among the evolutes as being effects of *vaikṛta* [ego], there the designation "evolutes" (*vikāra*) applies to the organs of action, the organs of knowledge, the mind, and the five elements beginning with earth— these having reached the number sixteen—
as well as to the eight consisting of the five elements, ego, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the Great Principle (*mahat*).

The seven categories that are both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and transformation (*vikṛti*) are the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—beginning with sound—as well as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). The twenty-five principles (*tattva*) consist of these seven, plus the ten sense organs, the ten objects of the senses, and the five gross elements; as they say: "The [five] gross elements..."
By the statement, "The wise know the twenty-five principles (tattvas) as enumerated by the senses, their objects, and so forth," [the author] expresses his own disagreement with that view.

For in his own system, the wise know the principles to be the five gross elements, the subtle elements (tanmātras), the sense organs, the mind, ego (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), and primordial matter (pradhāna). Thus it is concluded.

The principles have already been enumerated; one should now return to the subject at hand, which was mentioned incidentally. [An objection is raised: "If the body were produced from semen and blood (*śukra-śoṇita*), then the well-known doctrine that it consists of fire and water (*agni-soma-ātmaka*) would be contradicted. To this, he says: "Fire... What is the reason?

In response to the doubt that this is inconsistent, he says: "The wise one. Therein, the white [element] is of the nature of fire (*agni*), and the red is composed of the moon (*soma*). In this scripture, the right side is sometimes designated by the term "fire" and sometimes by the term "sun"; for the function of light is twofold.
Because it is stated in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā* that "the body consists of fire and consists of water," there arises the doubt:

"In which part of the body, which consists of Agni and Soma, does each reside? In response to this, he says "the right side" (*dakṣiṇāṃśe*), and so forth. Furthermore, in response to the doubt as to where on the right side it resides, he says "in the *da* [sound]," and so forth.

When the channels (*nāḍī*) of fire and sun have ceased, the moon resides in the left channel (*vamanā*); this is the answer to be given. Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the designation of that channel is and how many such channels there are, he says "the channels" (*nāḍīḥ*), etc., regarding the three primary channels mentioned.

Having stated the names of the intermediate channels (*mavāntara*), he states the names of the remaining seven channels with the verse beginning "gāṃ dhārī" and so forth. In response to the inquiry as to the number of the channels known as *puṇyā*—which were indicated by the phrase "ten principal ones"—he says, "the channels are infinite. They are infinite.
Because they have entered within the sacrificial fire, they cannot be counted, yet they are not devoid of number;
some vessels (śirāḥ) face downward, some face upward, and others extend horizontally,
and there are more than half a million of them, while the channels (nāḍī) measure three hundred thousand.

Since it is impossible to provide an explanation for the literal meaning as it stands— because that would result in contradictions with such texts as the *Nādi*— the word "five" refers to the six chakras known as Mūlādhāra,

Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā, which are located in the perineum, the navel, the heart, the throat, the palate, and the space between the eyebrows respectively. These are what is being described.

These same five joints (parva) extend from the lower knot (adhograṃthi) up to the upper knot (ūrdhvagraṃthi); thus, although there are six knots, there is no contradiction. [This refers to] those characterized as previously stated—such as "prāṇa in the heart" and "apāna in the anus"—and which will be described hereafter.

This wind named *prāṇa* is distinct from the nine other winds; it pervades the entire body—the whole physical frame—of a person through those six aforementioned channels (*nāḍīs*). Furthermore, there is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "the corrupters" (*doṣās*) and "the things to be corrupted" (*dūṣyās*).
[The functions of these winds are: the burner (*bhrājaka*), the colorer (*rañjaka*), the moistener (*kledaka*), and likewise the unctuous (*snehana*).
Dhāraka, Vandhaka, Drāvaka as the seventh, Vyāpaka, Pāvaka, and Śleṣmaka as the tenth;
these names of the fire mentioned in other tantras should be kept in mind. This is necessary for the description of the waves of the present vital breath (prāṇa).
In connection with what must be done, he speaks also of the two bodies of the self, beginning with the words "hunger" (*vubhukṣā*) and so forth.
A "wave" (*ūrmi*) is a particular state conducive to the production of a specific kind of affliction.
Does it [the wave] produce the body of the offspring without distinction, by means of the drop consisting of semen and blood?

He states that [the world] is produced from the elements beginning with earth by means of the passage starting with "stādyasthi" (bones, etc.). The intended meaning demonstrated up to the point where it says "thus the origin of men is declared" is as follows: [it refers to] specific individual souls who have attained the state of being a living being (*jīvabhāva*) in accordance with their prior karma, and whose essential nature has been shown. Furthermore, [it refers to those] following the particularities of the self that have entered into the condition of a living soul in conformity with previous actions.

The meaning is that he had departed, acting as a mirror for the objects of perception, thinking "it is thus," with his hands raised above his ears, having blocked his auditory passages while seated upon his mother's back, meditating upon the means to liberation;
as they say: "He who has blocked the openings of his ears with his hands raised above them."

"Remembering various births and the torments previously experienced, and contemplating the means to liberation, he proceeds, intent upon practice"—thus they say. However, this is not the meaning, because the word *itthambhūta* refers back to the very meaning previously stated; otherwise, [the word] "practice" (*abhyāsa*)...

The traditionalists (*saṃpradāyikāḥ*) maintain that since it is possible for even one who has completely renounced [the world] to have that as their purpose, how could there be such a renunciation? Furthermore, the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even [after] the mother" (*mātaram api*) is to be construed with the time of emergence following the completion of the experience of the pains of the womb over the course of time; and thus, his own...

The meaning is that he who causes even his mother to suffer (keśayati) due to his hair (keśa). According to the tenth [chapter], or rather the ninth, following the general rule of Yājñavalkya and others, [the fetus] has a compressed body and contracted limbs; "in order to weep" refers to the state of dwelling in the womb and so forth.
With the thought, "Alas, alas! O Radiance! I must act in this way once more; forgive me," and so forth, as he desires to weep, a certain effort arises within himself.
Then, through that effort, an activity occurs in the wind at the *mūlādhāra*. By that activity, at the *mūlā*—

In the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), which is delimited by the stream [of manifestation], a certain state arises as a particular condition; that very state is named "Parā. When that same state has entered the subtle body (vaikhari) and reached the heart, it receives the designation "Madhyamā."
When it reaches the locations of the throat, mouth, and so forth, it bestows upon the servant the name *vaikharī*.

As it has been said: "That state which first arises from the *mūlādhāra* is called *parā*; thereafter, when it resides in the heart, associated with the intellect (*buddhi*), it is called *paśyantī* on its path; and when it reaches the middle [of the body], it is called *madhyamā*."
When a living being desires to utter speech, it is bound to the *suṣumṇā* nerve;

from that, impelled by the vital air (*pavana*), the conjunction of phonemes (*varṇa-saṃyuti*) arises. Thus, since the production of phonemes occurs in this manner, the intention is that the production of mantras—which consist of specific phonemes—has indeed already taken place.

He explains the manner in which the mantra arises: the grammatical connection is that immediately after the production of the body (*śarīra*), she, whose nature is consciousness (*caitanya*), gives birth to the world consisting of mantras. This indicates that even though she is the agent therein, she requires the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of Brahman.

"Thou art in the presence of Śiva," and so forth; the state of bliss (*ānandapada*) is either direct or indirect, and it is the supreme [state] that causes bliss for all the senses. Likewise, among eternal things—such as space (*ākāśa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so on—as accepted by the Naiyāyikas, [it is the supreme] among the eternal blisses of the senses.
The meaning is: "from whom" (yasyāḥ sakāśāt) refers to that from whose proximity there is the impelling and arising of these qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas.
By this, its beginninglessness is stated. Alternatively, it may be a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "eternal" (*nitya*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*).
By this, its nature as the bestower of liberation, which consists of eternal bliss, is stated.

The compound *nityānandā* is either a *bahuvrīhi* containing another *bahuvrīhi*, or a *karmadhāraya*. By this, her nature as the Supreme Brahman is taught. As for the word *āsādya*, it is followed by the word *sthitā* (situated) to complete the sense; and as for *śivavasannidhiḥ*, it means a "proper treasure" (*samīcīnanidhi*) residing in Śiva.

The performance of the ritual purpose for certain [deities] has been demonstrated in the *Padārthadarśa*; since both of these are impossible for any other meaning, it is characterized here as a certain supreme power (*parā śakti*), and this very power is what was stated when it was said: "It is twofold by that division."

"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—thus my nature is divided eightfold. But know, O mighty-armed one, that there is another, higher nature of Mine, which is the life-force by which this world is sustained. Thus [He spoke] directly.

The sense is that this [nature] can be known in its true state (*yāthātathya*) by those [ordinary people] alone as being contrary to its own form, and not by yogis. In the *ādhāra*—that is, in the cavity of the *mūlādhāra* or in the lotus of the heart—it is perceived as dancing, not as standing still; for "dancing" is indeed its state of manifestation.

The meaning is "no. Although [the Self] is luminous in all beings, there is a distinction in that it possesses a manifestation in the form of specific actions, such as the manifestation of sound and so forth. Just as a whorl situated in the middle of a conch shell remains fixed according to the sequence of its spirals, so too does the subtle [Self] remain situated.

She whose nature consists of atoms subtler than the *tryasareṇu* (the triad of dust motes), who is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), and who cannot be delimited by any measure; she whose abode is threefold—consisting of heaven, earth, and the netherworld (*svar-bhū-pātāla*), or consisting of the forms of the moon, sun, and fire; and whose meaning is composed of the letters of the five elements, as indicated by the passage beginning with "forty-two," and so forth.

The meaning of "fifty" has been explained. In the *mūlādhāra*, she exists as a single channel (*nāḍī*) coiled like a serpent. There, awakened by Śiva—the Supreme Deity, the Universal Self, and the nature of the Supreme Brahman—she is impelled with enthusiasm for the purpose of generating the universe.
When one intends to produce substances well-known as individual units by accepting a specific movement of air (*yātayā-vāyu*),
a single-fold multiplication consisting of a single enclosure (*saṃvaraṇa*) is performed;
when one intends to produce substances well-known in forms such as pairs and so forth, [a two-fold multiplication is performed].

The meaning of *ākhaṇḍala* is that by performing the concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*) through the numbers three and so forth, one accomplishes those respective numbers of objects. The seed-syllable of the Vedas is the *praṇava*; the seed-syllable of Vāsudeva is extracted as the seed-syllable of Gopāla; [and] Śrī-Puruṣottama, which is Śrī-yukta-Puruṣottama, is the *śakti*.

Through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference from the progenitor (the Creator), that which is intended here is indeed the seed-potency of Puruṣottama; this is also stated in the seventeenth [chapter]: "He who is embraced by Dharā, adorned with the moon of Māyā, known here as Puruṣottama, that god whose form is like the god of love."

In the *Padārthādarśa*, it is stated that "trā" is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) and constitutes the meaning of the word; however, that is incorrect because it would contradict the venerable *Padāsaura* and result in redundancy with the root text's phrase "manobhava" (the mind-born one).
Furthermore, other [syllables] such as the moon-seed (*candra-bīja*) and others represent the two supreme selves (*parātmānau*), while the syllable "haṃsa" denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Although the *Arthaveda* (Atharvaveda) also exists with the syllables "ka" and "ha," nevertheless, because the sacrifice is accomplished through the three categories of ritual acts consisting of the *Hautra*, *Ādhvaryava*, and *Audgātra*, it is stated here that there are only three Vedas by virtue of their being conducive [to the sacrifice]; for this very reason, it is said: "This triple knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) is the sacrifice."
The three worlds consist of heaven, earth, and the netherworld; the three abodes consist of the sun, fire, and the moon;

and the three classes (varṇas) consist of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m* which constitute the syllable *praṇava*. Alternatively, by virtue of their utility for the Vedas, the word "classes" (*varṇa*) following the word "Vedas" refers to the three twice-born castes (*dvijāti*).

Or it denotes the three powers—consisting of the power of lordship (*prabhu-śakti*), the power of energy (*utsāha-śakti*), and the power of counsel (*mantra-śakti*)—or the three forms of Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī; or the three modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*) consisting of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts, or agriculture, animal husbandry, and trade; or otherwise, [the three humors] phlegm, wind, and bile.

The triad of defects consisting of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*; the fourfold group of principles beginning with the *ātmatattva*, *vidyātattva*, *śivatattva*, and all the *sarvatattvas* along with the *devītattvas*; the triad of *sūkṣmā*, *aparā*, *paśyantī*, and *vaikharī*—the first term of which is to be understood as "mine"; and the [sites] such as Udyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa.

The four seats (*pīṭha*) consisting of form are intended by each of the first syllables, beginning with *uje* and so forth. The taming deities (*damaka*) and others, as well as the five forms (*pañcamūrti*) of Maheśvara—the Great Lord Mahādeva—are to be described in the eighteenth chapter. The six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) are five... [text ends]...
The six cakras located in the *mūlādhāra* and other centers are to be spoken of as the support (*ādhāra*).
The seven worlds— named *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, *svar*, *mahaḥ*, *janaḥ*, *tapaḥ*, and *satyam*—
are the fuel (*samidh*) for the planets, such as the *arka*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, and so forth, belonging to the planets.
Relying on a particular philosophical view regarding the nature of the seven [planets], the teacher Varāhamihira has stated:

"Indeed, this head of the Asura, though severed, was not abandoned by its vital breaths due to the excellence of its tasting the nectar; thus it did not attain the state of being a planet. This is endowed with eight groups of eight [verses].

The eight seats culminate in the sixty-four seats; the qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth— alternatively, the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā* are distinct qualities, while compassion (*dayā*), forbearance (*kṣamā*), freedom from envy (*anasūyā*), purity (*śauca*), absence of deceit (*māyā-śūnyatā*), modesty (*māṅgalya*), truthfulness (*satya*), and contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) are the eight qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇāḥ*).

"Of the virtuous" (satām) refers to those possessing the characteristics already described; "elephants and so forth" (nāgādigajāḥ) refers to the classes of beings such as the *avighna* to be mentioned later, or serpents; the "eight limbs of yoga" (yogāṅgāni), beginning with *yama*, which will be explained in the final chapter;
the "principles of power" (*śaktitattvāni*), beginning with the Primordial Power (*ādiśakti*), the Resonance (*nāda*), the Point (*bindu*), and the Duality (*dvi*).

The third point (*bindu*), *nīda*, the seed-syllable, Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmeśvarī, and the nine previously mentioned; the mandala known as Navanābha; the ten principles of power (*śakti-tattva*) beginning with Nivṛtti;
the five times (*pañcakāla*); the point (*bindu*), the digit (*kalā*), the resonance (*nāda*), the power (*śakti*), and Sadāśiva—these are other [aspects].

"Such" refers to: that which is multiplied thirteenfold, such as the Viśvedevas and others; that which is multiplied fourteenfold, such as the Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva-Gopāla mantra, Śakra, Bhuvana, and so forth; that which is multiplied fifteenfold, such as the Nityās, Śūlinī, the lunar days (tithis), and so forth; and that which is multiplied sixteenfold, such as the Cakra-mantra.

The *trasvarakalā* and others multiplied seventeenfold; the *tārāvidyā* and others multiplied eighteenfold; the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of Kṛṣṇa, Vāmana, Añjaneya, and Agni and others multiplied nineteenfold; the *kṛṣṇadharāmantra* and others multiplied twentyfold; and the *ratnadhāromā* and others multiplied twenty-onefold.
The mantra of Īśvaraśrīrājarājeśvara and others, multiplied twenty-one times;

the mantra of Aṭṭahāsabhairava and others, multiplied twenty-two times; and the mantra of Sumukhī, the sovereign of Kṛṣṇātra, and others, multiplied twenty-three times—[these belong to] Ālayuśyāmā Puruṣottama.

Since mantras and so forth are produced in this manner throughout the vision of various creations from one *parārdha* to another *parārdha*, it is impossible to describe all those entities; therefore, their abandonment is necessary.
When it is required to describe any particular entity as primary according to one's own will, [there are] thirteen [categories].

Intending to show what fault there would be even in abandoning the categories of the two [the self and the non-self], or what deficiency there would be, he sets aside those [categories] and states his own preferred [system] as being primary, beginning with the words "catur" and so on.
The meaning is: that whose nature (ātman) is the reality (tattva) of the twenty-four; that is, one who possesses twenty-four qualities (guṇin).

Thirdly, although the first quarter-verse of the intended *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, beginning with "tryambakam," consists of seven syllables, nevertheless, according to the *Chandaḥsūtra* rule stating that "for the sake of maintaining the *anuṣṭubh* meter, [syllables] such as 'i' and so forth are added to complete the quarter-verse," it is [treated as such].

The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* maintains that the mantra consists of eight syllables because it is traditionally recited as such; however, this is not correct, for since the line beginning with *urvārukam* contains nine syllables, the total would exceed thirty-two syllables, which results in a contradiction. Furthermore, the *lavaṇa-mantra* begins with *lavaṇāmbhasi*, etc., in the root text (*mūla*) at the *mūlādhāra*.

Multiplied by forty-two, that Kuṇḍalinī gives birth to the garland of letters consisting of forty-two [sounds], beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Sa'. He explains the mode of production for all the letters with the words "Śaktim" and so forth; it is indeed Consciousness itself, permeated by the quality of *sattva*.

That very state of the supreme space (*paramākāśa*), which is denoted by the term *śakti*, when permeated by *rajas*, is the state of the syllable (*akṣara*) denoted by the word *dhvani*; that same [state], when permeated by *tamas*, is denoted by the word *nāda*;
and that same [state], when *tamas* predominates, is denoted by the term *nirodhikā*, while when *sattva* predominates, it is [denoted by the term *unmanī*].
When there is a union of the two, *sattva* and *tamas*, she alone is denoted by the term *bindu*. Having entered the *mūlādhāra*, she is indeed *bindu* and is designated as *parā*.
When she resides in other locations, she is designated by names such as *paśyantī* and so forth. As for that which...
It is stated in another Tantra that this very *bindu*, having moved to other locations, becomes known by names such as *Parā*.

Furthermore, in another Tantra it is said: "The supreme *nāda* called *Parā*, which has arisen in the *mūlādhāra* from the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) impelled by the power of one's own will (*svātmechāśakti*), moves upward."

That which has been brought here from its own locus (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) attains the name "Paśyantī" as it unfolds; likewise, moving gradually upward, conjoined with the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), it is called "Madhyamā" in the *Anāhata* [cakra].
Moving further upward from that same place, reaching the region of the throat in the *Viśuddha* [cakra], it becomes "Vaikharī."

Then, the letters arise in sequence from the head, the throat, the palate, the lips, and the teeth; likewise, they reside at the root and tip of the tongue and on its back, and proceed in order to the nose. Furthermore, the letters arise in sequence from the throat, the palate, the lips, the teeth, the upper lip, and both the throat and the lips, extending from the beginning up to the letter *kṣa*. *Ā* [is the final].

It is stated that among those [levels of speech], the state of the *akṣara* (the imperishable) is illustrated as being within *Dikṣāntarata*. Thus, because it occupies the first position, because it is the most excellent, because it is the state of supreme vibration (*parā-saṃspanda*), and because it bestows knowledge, the intellect (*buddhi*) is joined with the state of *Paśyantī*; that which is situated in the midst of this is *Madhyamā*, characterized by differentiation (*viśeṣa*).
It should be understood that it becomes *vaikharī* by manifesting through the state of *ṣeṇakharatva*.
The *kalās* are Nivṛtti and the others; the *rudras* are Śrīkaṇṭha and the others; and by the word "etcetera," Keśava and the others are included.
Of both [the moon and the fire], there is the *nirodhikā*; of the half-moon and the fire, because of their nature as Śiva, [there is the half-moon and the fire]. Śi... [text fragment]

Because of the nature of *varu* (the letter *va*) as being half a part and having the form of *śakti*, [the deity] consists of both Śiva and Śakti; for this reason— this word *tat* being supplied as an ellipsis, or rather, being connected with the preceding *iti*— since they are produced from fire (*vahni*), the moon (*indu*), and the sun (*arka*), he therefore possesses the essential nature of that triad.

The meaning is that they are not mentioned in either the effects or the causes. [She whose mother is Udyotamatī, who is virtuous and endowed with good qualities; whose father is named Māpati, a treasure-house of love;
whose birthplace is Pathakulabhū, the land of Kūrmmācala; and who has made Kṛtavīrya easy to approach...]

[This is] the first chapter, concerning Yama and others, in the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*, which has its seat in Vārāṇasī, the abode of the imperishable state. Now, [the author] demonstrates the manifestation of *vaikharī* speech once again by clarifying it through the passage beginning with "that," etc., [stating]: "Impelled by the vital air (*marut*), *paśyantī*..."
The phonemes (varṇas), having been brought to their respective positions and made ready for emergence, exit through the aperture of the Suṣumṇā;
they manifest sequentially through the organs such as the throat.
Having exited the apertures of the Suṣumṇā—having emerged from the Anāhata and Viśuddha cakras—among these aforementioned [states]...

Among the fifty phonemes (*varṇa*), those whose nature is the *tattvas* possess the essential form of the previously mentioned *tattvas*. Now, one might ask: how can the *sparśas* (consonants) partake of that same nature, given the discrepancy in number? For it has been stated that the *tattvas* consist of twenty-four in number, whereas the *sparśas* are twenty-five.

Regarding the statement that they become numbered because of the addition of the letter *ma*, it is said here: "Because of *ma*. Since the letter *ma* is the Puruṣa, therefore the twenty principles (*tattvas*) are [designated] as its self (*ātman*) by way of technical terminology; thus, there is a connection through the relationship of cause and effect.
Pervasiveness, however, applies by implication to those [consonants] beginning with *ya* that have not been assigned intermediate names.
"Sarga" (emission) refers to the vowels;
among these, the form consisting of *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* is the middle, because six vowels precede and six follow them, making these the middle ones.

Regarding what they say, "Thou art in Piṅgalā": when the prāṇa is situated in the right [nāḍī], then it is the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana); there, the five short vowels consisting of the five elements arise. When the prāṇa resorts to the left [nāḍī], then it would be the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa); [there] the five elements...

When the winds rise individually from the long vowels *dā* and so forth, entering their respective parts such as the south and others, at that moment the wind flows within the *suṣumṇā*; then, in sequence, the four neuter vowels arise. As for their fruit, it is the performance of actions according to the rising of the six vowels.
The *Pāraṇa* and other such rites yield fruit when performed during the rising of short vowels for those of cruel karma;

otherwise, as stated in other tantras, for others— such as those whose names begin with the letter *ka* and so forth— it is easily accomplished in any manner whatsoever, even for consonants without the conjunction of vowels.

The intention is that there is indeed pronunciation [of the consonants]. Precisely because the consonants, such as *ta* and so forth, are easily manifested by means of vowels (*ata eva svaraiḥ*), he teaches, as an incidental digression, the phonemes (*varṇān*) such as *ka* and so forth—the phonemes that have served their purpose in various places—beginning with *ta*. *Kā* [is the first of these].

From the word *raṇāt* (from the sound), those that are "dropped" (*viṃdutaḥ*) are those produced in succession; these are the five short vowels, and so forth. Alternatively, for each of the [consonant] groups beginning with *gha*, there is respectively one short vowel, one long vowel, and one each of the fourfold conjunct sounds (*saṃdhivarṇa*) ending in *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*.
The junctional color (sandhivarṇa) has entered [the system] with the intention of describing the final space (*ākāśa*);
since such a color is not present among the junctional colors of the five-fold [set], and in the absence of obtaining such a color, he says "ending in the bindu" (*vindvantāḥ*).
This refers to each one of the five groups beginning with *ka*, starting from the *ya*-group in reverse order.

The meaning is that each one of the letters— the retroflex *ṣakāra*, the letter preceding that (the retroflex *ṭakāra*), the letter following the retroflex *ṣakāra* (the dental *sakāra*), and the final letter of "Nṛsiṃha" (the vowel *i*)— attains the status of the letters of the *vāghvādi* group in sequence. [This refers to] the five short vowels, etc.

It should be understood that the thirty-eight *kalās*, beginning with Amṛtā, which are produced from the *mātṛkās* characterized by their specific forms and so forth through the distinction and non-distinction of the deities Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, abide within the spheres (*maṇḍalas*) of Soma and the others.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "Soma" and so forth should be understood as follows: [one might ask], "How can the thirty-eight *kalās* arise from the fifty *mātṛkās*? To this he says: "From *ka* and *bhā*, etc.
Thus, from the two letters in the form of *ka* and *bhā*, the twelve *kalās* of the Sun [arise].

The sense is that there is no discrepancy in the number [of syllables] because of this. The word *vahā* is connected separately with both *havya* and *vaha*. From the letter *a*, which constitutes the first part of the prefix *pra*, the thirteen kalās beginning with *Sṛṣṭi* were produced by Brahmā.

They are called "progenitors" because Brahman is denoted by the syllable *jha*; and just as the non-difference between cause and effect is employed [by authorities], so too are sentences used by the learned through the metaphorical identification of the signifier and the signified. From the syllable *u* comes Viṣṇu.
The same method demonstrated in the passage beginning with "notpannā" [should be understood] here as well.

Regarding the two *kalās* named *sūkṣmāmṛtā* and *jñānāmṛtā*, which are specific names of the *pareti* [kalā], he says [in the section on] *nyāsa* that the application of these *kalās* everywhere is not according to the aforementioned sequence alone.

By the words beginning with "tu" (but), it is indicated that the worship of the conch and other items— distinct from the [other] nyāsas— should be performed according to the sequence previously stated in the *Sukhaṇṭharava*, and not as the vowels and kalās mentioned earlier. Now, from the fifty phonemes, [the deities] together with their śaktis and dhyānas are produced.

Having taught the two types [of deities], beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and others, as well as Keśava and others, he begins to teach the divisions of mantras starting with the words "mātrikā" and so forth.
Mantras, which have attained a twofold division through the distinction between *mantra* and *vidyā*, are each further threefold in sequence.

It should be understood that these [forms] primarily serve as the basis for the accomplishment of the three types of rites— subjugation (vaśya), pacification (śānti), and killing (māraṇa). Regarding the mantra of the Supreme Brahman, which is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda) and devoid of attributes (nirguṇa), its various modes of meditation appear in the forms of male, female, and neuter.
This conceptualization reveals that nothing whatsoever is unarisen.

As for what was stated regarding the nature of the mantras as being composed of Agni and Soma—that was not intended to mean that a single mantra possesses both natures; rather, some mantras belong to Agni and others to Soma.

With the intention of saying "you," he says "vahni" and so forth: the last [letter] is *kṣa*, *vi* is *ha*, and these four syllables are found abundantly in those mantras which are fiery (*āgneya*). *Indu* is the bindu (*m*), *sa* is the syllable of immortality (*amṛtākṣara*), and *va* is [the letter *va*].
This mantra, possessing two additional syllables, is gentle (*saumya*); it should be employed sequentially for both cruel and gentle rites.
He states that when this mantra is applied at its own respective time of awakening, it bestows its own specific fruit, but not even when applied at another time.

Regarding the passage beginning with "āgneyā" and so forth, here in all cases, being *āgneya* (fiery) or *saumya* (lunar) is not determined solely by the aforementioned characteristics; rather, as stated in the *Nārāyaṇī*: "An *āgneya* mantra would generally be *saumya* if it is endowed with 'namaḥ' at the end, and likewise a *saumya* mantra would be *āgneya* if it is endowed with 'phaṭ' at the end."
It should be understood that this is due solely to the distinction of the specific [mantra] employed; furthermore, another distinction is mentioned in another tantra:

"One should conquer the two mantras known as Āgneya and Saumya at the beginning and end of the [two] halves of the stars. This is the meaning: of the *tārās* (stars), which are the *nakṣatras*, the first two parts of the *Āgneyas* are [the first half], and the last... is the second half.

The two parts of the tail and the final two degrees of the gentle (saumya) lunar mansions are submerged; the first two degrees constitute the tail. Therein, the Āgneya mantras should be recited only upon the first two degrees of the Āgneya lunar mansion which have become the head, and not on the part of the tail which has become the rear. This is likewise for the Saumya [lunar mansion].

Regarding the necessity of recitation (*japa*) even when one’s own realization is not yet mature, another method has been taught in another Tantra: "One should diligently recite the letters beginning with *la* and ending with *ya*, along with the bindu (*anusvāra*), and again those same letters with the visarga (*visarjanīya*), and finally the letter *kṣa* alone. This is what is called *janīya*.
"Having recited [the mantra] in this way, this mantra, though unawakened, grants the swift accomplishment of one's goals.

To the objection that it is illogical for "all" to bestow the fruit—given that all mantras are reportedly afflicted by defects such as being "cut" (chinnatva) and so forth, and are thus swallowed up by these flaws—the response is: "True."
It has been stated that [the tree] does not yield fruit because it is severed and so forth; however, this applies only to one who is ignorant of these defects.

On the contrary, the knower—by employing any one of the three methods to be described hereafter to effect the removal of those defects—will certainly attain the root. Thus says the author of the *Uttara*.
In response to the inquiry— "Having understood these defects,
such as 'broken' (chinna) and so forth, what are those defects of being 'broken' and the like, and what are their characteristics?"—
the author demonstrates the defects of being broken and so forth along with their definitions by means of the verse beginning with "chinna," etc., in due order.
This seed-syllable *yā-yam-ity-ā-ni-laṃ*, when seen together with the mantra, is known as "Chinna" (the Severed);
