the word "bīja" (seed) recurs again, and the term "nirupadrava-bīja" (unafflicted seed) refers to the names of the Māyā-bīja:
Mālinī, Śivavallarī, Vātāvartti, and Śivāvāṇī.

According to the *Śaivasamaya-saṃketa*, "Jaṃ" is the power *Kuṇḍalinī*; it refers to the seed-syllable of *Māyā* (*Hrīm*), which is further qualified by being "overcome by vowels. The terms "three," "four," and so forth, also recur; thus, when combined in the beginning, middle, and end positions of the mantra, there are three, four, or [more].

If the seed-syllable of Māyā (h) is found to be occupied by any one of the five other vowels—the second, fourth, sixth, twelfth, or fourteenth—it is designated as "severed" (chinna); both of these characteristics are indeed accepted as such. When it is occupied by both of these...

Some, however, hold that the word *vāyu* itself is intended here as the root, based on the natural sense of the term; for since the rule "the consonant alone is *anila*" would otherwise necessitate its inclusion,
the phrase "occupied by a vowel" (*svarākāntam*) implies it must be occupied by any vowel whatsoever.
The meaning is that it is not merely a consonant alone. Is it then not to be grasped when joined with *ka* and so forth?
No; he says "joined. Is it then not to be grasped in a form such as *ya* when separated from *ka* and so forth?
It is indeed to be grasped; he says "and separated," taking the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*) as the basis.

There is no need for the repetition of words such as *bīja*, which are established by their own inherent force (*svarasasiddha*) in the root text, because that would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Furthermore, there is no fault even if definitions established in other systems (*tantrāntara*) are not included here; for it is not the case that every meaning stated in those various places must necessarily be negated here by these definitions.

They say it can be subsumed; however, if there is a great insistence on the repetition of the words "seed" (*bīja*) and so forth as being connected only to the subsequent application of the phrase "overcome by vowels" (*svarākāntam*), then it indeed results in a different definition: namely, that for which [the seed-syllable] occurs at the beginning, middle, and end of the mantra.

The Vāyu-bīja (ya) is seen as fourfold, fivefold, twofold, or as the "Single Hero" (ekavīra) accompanied by vowels; this mantra is proclaimed to be "severed" (chedita). There is also a corroboration from another Tantra:
"The Single Hero is *hraḥ*; when combined at the beginning, middle, and end, [the syllable] *laṃ* occurs in each instance."
A mantra is called "obstructed" (*niruddha*) when it contains the pair of seed-syllables *la* and *mi* within the word *satva*. In another tantra, [it is said]:
"O Dear One, that mantra which is joined with *vajra* is proclaimed as 'obstructed' (*niruddha*)—first in two ways, then in three ways in the middle, and again in two ways at the end.
If you ask how this is so according to its definition, what [is the reason]?

It should be understood that another system is not intended here as one that causes a fault in the other systems; rather, when there is contradiction, an option (*vikalpa*) is assumed, when there is no contradiction, a combination (*samuccaya*), when there is deficiency, a supplement (*kṛtsna*), and when there is excess, primacy (*mukhyatā*) is assumed. The threefold nature consists of the letters *ha*, *ra*, and *ka*.

The combined sixty vowels and bindus constitute the sound *phreṃkāra*. This characteristic applies even when one is missing from among the four beginning with *māyā*, and not only when all are collectively absent; that is, where the *māyā* seed-syllable is not present, or where there is the triad of principles (*tritattva*), or the sound itself, or the "Abode of Śrī" (*śrīgṛha*).
This mantra is proclaimed to be devoid of power because of the hearing of the letter *vā* in another tantra;

however, in the phrase "or indeed the goad (*aṅkuśa*)," the word *vā* signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*). This is in agreement with another tantra, which states: "The seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) is in the middle of *naya*, *māyā* at the beginning, and the goad at the end, [ending] with *parāṅmukhī*."
The letter *da* is joined with the *indu* (the nasal bindu), and the letter *ha* is likewise joined with the *indu*;
this is a collective application [of the bindu] at the beginning, end, and middle.

"That which has neither the void (*śūnya*) joined with the *bindu* at the beginning and end, nor in the middle, is not the seed-syllable of life (*jīvabīja*); he who possesses such a syllable is declared deaf," so it is said in another Tantra.

By hearing the form of the Revā [mantra], they have explained that the syllable *sa*—which is the seed-syllable of the individual soul (*jīvabīja*) with the nasal drop (*bindu*)—is preceded by the letter *ṭha*; thus, they have refuted the claim that this constitutes the primary "moon-footed" (*maulimindu-pada*) mantra.
However, this is rejected because it is not corroborated by other Tantras; for although it is not the case that one Tantra must necessarily agree with another Tantra...
It does not become a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it is spoken by God; rather, it is so by its own independence.

And thus, even in cases where there is no correspondence with reality, there will be doubt regarding its meaning; therefore, enough with relying on correspondence. Nevertheless, when there is doubt regarding the meaning, recourse to that [correspondence] is necessary.

Otherwise, if its lack of authority were based on being rooted in a different scriptural tradition (*anyathāśruti*), there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate another scripture as its own source; even if its authority were independent, there would still be a mutual contradiction regarding the various performances of those respective rites with respect to a single class of result.

Since it is impossible to state that there is a cause for fear [of contradiction], there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate a difference in nature (*vaijātya*) among the results;

therefore, as long as the systems maintain a single meaning according to the natural sense of the words, one should proceed accordingly. If, however, that [single meaning] is in any way impossible, then...

It should be understood that there is no other recourse for those who lack discrimination; thus, the meaning is that a mantra is "with *dhīḥ*" (*sadhīḥ*) if the seed-syllable *haṃ* or *saṃ* exists in any one of its positions—at the beginning, middle, or end.
Now, [one might ask: what of a mantra devoid of either of these aforementioned seed-syllables?

If it is argued that one should simply say "the other is the seed" (*nyobīja*), for there is no location other than the beginning, middle, or end where such a restriction would be necessary to exclude [other seeds], we reply: True; however, the presence of a seed other than those [three] in these three locations is highly commendable.

The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* maintains that this was stated for the purpose of making this known; however, it appears to me that in mantras consisting of eleven, thirteen, or more syllables, where two, three,
or more syllables follow [the initial portion], that particular seed-syllable (*bīja*) is indeed implied even if not explicitly stated, for its position has not been specified.
It is not included within any of the other positions, because "middle-ness" (madhyatva) is impossible there, just as it is impossible for the beginning or the end;
rather, middle-ness is only possible there after the fifth letter and so forth—for this reason, the division into three parts is made. [The letter] *ha* is the sun (*arka*).

The authors of the *Padārthādarśa*, the scholars Rāmacandra Paṇḍita, stated that because the principle of the Sun (*arka-tattva*) is assigned among the principles of the *Rauvaiṣṇava-bṛhat-tattva-nyāsa* by means of the letter *ha* and so forth; however, following the opinion of the Teacher [Abhinavagupta] that "the letter *ma* is the Puruṣa and the Sun," the hidden meaning is that the Sun is the letter *sa*.
The authors of the *Tattvadīpikā* and *Harṣakaumudī* stated: "That [mantra] is like the moon;

likewise, that mantra in which the three eyes—consisting of the letters *ra*, *ma*, and *sa*, representing fire, the sun, and the moon respectively—are absent is called 'eyeless,' and it results in miseries such as poverty."
The three [planets] cause grief from the death of a son and so forth, as well as obstacles and diseases;
when one is missing, it causes suffering (repha-hīna); when the Sun is missing, it causes grief;
when the Moon is missing, it causes disease; and when two are missing, it shall bestow both of those respective fruits according to their own sequence.

And this mantra would be defective (kāṇa) if it consisted of only one, two, three, or more syllables; therefore, he says "five" to show that the entire mantra has been thus made. He defines the "stake" (kīlita) with the words beginning with "ādi" and so forth: "Haṃsa" is its essential nature; the Prāsāda is "Hauṃ"; the Vāgbhava is "Aiṃ"; and the letter "Ha".

"Vindu-mān" is an epithet for the individual soul (*jīva*). That *jīva* (the letter *o*) is joined with the *vindu* (the nasal dot) in such a manner that, when combined, the letter *au* is established. Thus, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) results as "vam hraum. "Rāva" refers to the letter *phre*. It consists of four parts (*catuṣkala*). *Ha*.
Some say that the syllables *kā-ra-re-pha*, the sixth vowel (*ū*), and the bindu are joined together;

others, however, say that the fourth vowel alone constitutes the four-count (*catuṣkala*) word-meaning. Some maintain that the nature of the mantra is *māyā* (the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī), *bhuvaneśī-vījaṃ*, and *namāmi*, with the word *namaḥ* being the final part.
The meaning is that among these eight, where even one is absent, it is "bolted" (*kīlita*);

however, a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*) is not intended here. [That state] is joined with the ninth vowel, mounted upon the *jīva*, and possessed of the nasal bindu; for whomsoever the Self is not seen, what indeed is the use of the fourfold group?
"Laḥ, the temple, vāgbhava, haṃsa, and māyā are not seen; they declare that [the mantra] is pinned down at its beginning,
middle, and end"— this is because it is observed in the Piṅgalāmata that the vowel 'u' (the ninth vowel) is not counted among the vowels for neuter [mantras].
Regarding this, it is explained in that very [text]: "The sound *daṃ* is the self; *ātmāhaḥ* is *rāvaḥ*; *phreṃ* has four *kalās*; *lohrūṃ* is likewise.

Between the *phaṭ* of the weapon (*astra*) and the *la* of Indra (*puraṃdara*), there is one [syllable] at the head and two of either of those two at the end, which is found in the middle of whichever mantra [is concerned].
If the Śakra-bīja (Hūṃ) occurs once in the middle and twice at the end, it is "paralyzed" (staṃbhita);
this is stated according to the consensus of other tantras. Furthermore, in another tantra it is said:
"That mantra at the end of which the Great Weapon (Mahāstra) is seen twice, thrice, eight times, or sixteen times, is paralyzed."

The mantra was proclaimed by Śrīśa; however, Harṣakaumudīkṛt, having fabricated a reading for the root text stating that "the mantra should be together with the vidyā," [asks]: "Is it that for this mantra divided into three parts, there is neither [the vidyā] in the middle nor the two weapons at the end? Or rather...
Once Indra was struck down in the middle; they consider this to be the root meaning of "sa-stambhiti" (the paralysis).

However, the contradiction with other tantras written by [the author] himself is evident; we do not know how they can possibly tolerate it. At the beginning, by those situated at the head... sapra... [text fragment].

Based on the observation of other tantras stating, "Where the mantra is ignited by the winds of the seed-syllables *bhūḥ* and *yāvaka*, that [mantra] is declared to be burnt by the *māyā*," and because there is the risk of falling into the fabrication of various scriptural authorities (*śruti*) and so forth due to contradictions with other tantras,
it is far better [to follow the interpretation] of the word *mūrddha* itself.

The forced construction of a different meaning— [the phrase] "kaṭkarṇākarṇita" (heard from ear to ear)— is stated as a definition of a "burnt" [mantra] in another treatise (*tantrāntara*). By this it is meant that a mantra given to many is not to be imparted by disciples, nor should a single [mantra] be received by two, three, or more disciples at the time of its reception.

The meaning is as follows: it is intimated by the word *sahagrāhya* ("to be grasped together") that [the mantra] consists of two; that is, from among certain syllables numbering two or more, wherever an *astra* (weapon-mantra) is seen, there the mantra shall have the name of that *astra*.
At the beginning (*mukhe*), i.e., at the start, is *Śiva*, which is the letter *ha* with the bindu (*hakāraḥ sabinduḥ*). *Śakti*...

Regarding the letter *sakāra* (sa), some say that *śiva* is the *bindu*, while *śakti* is the *visarga*; however, this is not correct because the *bindu* and *visarga* cannot occur within mantras or similar contexts. The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* states that [the letter] is joined with another phoneme (*varṇāntarayukta*), and that *śakti* is the goddess Bhuvaneśī, who is the fourth vowel (*e*).
Someone [objects]: "If one of the three initial positions possesses two *m* sounds, then four phonemes would be possible across the three positions;
for instance, in the case of the seed-syllable *kūrcabīja*, *kro-dhā-hūṃ*, there is the third letter of the *tavarga* (*d*) between *krodha* and *hūṃ*."
There is no conceptualization regarding the state of stability; at the end, there is the conjunction of the two syllables *mūrdha* and *padārtha*;
the two words *hṛdaye* and *madhyebhyaḥ* [are placed] in the heart; the word *vaṣaṭ* is at the beginning of the head;
and the word *vauṣaṭ* is in the middle—such is the Netra-mantra, which is likewise differentiated by its own mantra.

Some say it should be *saṃjñaḥ*. Others, however, having recited "from the two at the beginning" (*bhyo dvayaṃ pramukhe*) and "the six-pointed weapon in the middle" (*ṣaḍastraṃ vamadhyi*), state that the word "from the two at the beginning" (*bhyo bhyo iti*) refers to the head (*śīrṣe*) and the end;
this is the *śikhā-mantra*. In the middle is the weapon (*astraṃ*), consisting of the syllables *ha*, *ra*, and the *visarga* (*hū*).
They declare that he in whom these three letters exist is "divided" (bhinna).

When two [mantras] of *haṃsa*-color are joined together, or when one of them contains the *āyāta* mantra, there would be a *suṣupta* (deep sleep) mantra. To the question, "Is it the case that all [mantras] are like that?", he says:
"consisting of three syllables" (*trivarṇa*). That is, where there is a pentad of *phaṭ*-sounds at the beginning, it is a *saphaṭkārapañcaka*.

The analysis of the compound is "eight [syllables] plus two times seven" (*dviḥ-sapta-adhikāni aṣṭau*), meaning "ten syllables where there is an addition of twice seven," and not "ten syllables where there is an addition of seven. If it were the latter, the result would be a *mantra* of exactly seventeen syllables; however, eighteen syllables are desired, whether for the *vidyā* or otherwise.

According to the statement in another Tantra, "If the Vāma mantra consists of eighteen syllables preceded by five *phaṭ*s, it is called *madonmatta*," the number seven is obtained through the seven words of the Vararuci-Saṅketana which will be described later; [this occurs] after the seven words.
Through the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the *kāra*, the number one is obtained; the analysis of the compound is "that in which there are more than seven and ten syllables.

Furthermore, by the aforementioned method, the term "seven-word" refers to the number eight, while the term "seven-word" refers to thirteen and the term "ten-word" refers to five, thus yielding the stated number.

Likewise, when the attainment of eleven syllables plus eight [is reached], others ask: "How many remain? Similarly, regarding the phrase "occurring at the place of pause five times," the connection with the word "not likewise" (*na tadvat*) is as follows: the application of four squares in the three initial positions is according to the stated method.
Vasūpapāda states in the *Harṣakaumudī* that the presence of seventeen syllables is a defining characteristic even in the deficient [meter];
however, this is not accepted in the *Padārthādarśa*. In another tantra, on the other hand, it is called "deluded" (*bhrānta*):
"A mantra consisting of eighteen syllables, joined with four *astras* at the beginning, the end, and in the middle."
The illustrious Bhairava spoke to the deluded one, saying: "Having stated that [the mantra] consists of eighteen syllables, you have shown liberation for them;

thus, you yourself have spoken in this very same way, which results in a contradiction between your earlier and later texts. Furthermore, in our own system, even regarding the definition of one intoxicated by pride (*madonmatta*), it is not as it is literally heard."

It should not be said that there are eighteen syllables [plus] seven, for if one were to say this, it would result in an inconsistency with the statement: "Whether it be the Vidyā or the Mantra, if it consists of eighteen syllables," and so forth, regarding the granting of accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Nor can it be claimed that the portion beginning with "it should be preceded by five *phaṭ*s" is intended as a citation from another authoritative source (*sammati*).

If that were the case, it would follow that the root [text] contradicts other treatises (*tantrāntara*); for if the two [cases] of "fainted" and "whose vigor is destroyed," falling between [the categories], do not follow from that [root], then a separation (*vyavadhāna*) would result, leading to a lack of consistency with the root; whereas if they do follow, then since you have not stated them in another work, there would be a deficiency.

There is no merit in this [objection]: that by not following the root-text (*maula-pada*) and instead completing it through supplementation, there would be a lack of aesthetic harmony (*asaurasya*) and an absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*). For, provided they exceed eighteen or nineteen syllables, [the mantras] are combined with the seed-syllables of *praṇava*, *māyā*, and *aṅkuśa*.

Because they are joined with those [defects], they become subordinate; now, he states at length that these are merely differences in name caused by specific numbers and do not exist as distinct entities in reality, beginning with the words "seven syllables" (*saptavarṇa*) and so forth. Although it would have been more appropriate to begin the treatment starting from one syllable due to its primacy, [the author] necessarily [proceeds] with the inclusion [of the subsequent categories].

Because it is to be given (*deyatvāt*), the author of the treatise has accepted that the priority of the stages beginning with childhood alone is what determines the sequence; [the meter] consists of four hundred syllables— that is,
one hundred and four syllables— and by the rule "four hundred [syllables] starting from the first," it receives the designation *ativṛddha*.

Furthermore, because a designation (*saṃjñitva*) cannot exist for that which lacks the cognition (*saṃjñā*) of being "increased" (*vṛddha*), there would arise a contradiction with other tantras which state: "That which consists of thirty syllables, a hundred syllables, sixty-four syllables, or even four hundred syllables above that is called 'increased' (*vṛddha*). Moreover, although [the category] *ativṛddha* (excessively increased) follows immediately after *vṛddha*, [this sequence would be disrupted].
Although it would have been appropriate to state [the definition] without the intervention of other characteristics, nevertheless,
immediately after the mention of "excessive" (*ativṛddha*), the mention of "afflicted" (*pīḍita*) alone was intended; and since completion (*samāpti*) itself was intended immediately thereafter,
that [definition] was stated at the end of all the characteristics.
The mantra is: *naṃ kṛtaṃ nistriṃśa ghātaka*, whose heart is [this];
*namaḥ* is the head (*śiras*), *svāhā* the crest (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ* the armor (*varman*), and *huṃ* the *śivaḥ ahaṃ śaktiḥ saḥ*.
Furthermore, at the end of this mantra, the words *namaḥ* and *svāhā* should not be present, nor should there be *vaṣaṭ* or *huṃ* in the middle.

The syllables *kārī*, *kiṃvā*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* should not be present; likewise, the syllables *haṃ* and *sa* should not be found anywhere. This means that this mantra is "seedless" (*nirbīja*). As it has been said: "At the end of the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon, or alternatively, [the mantra] consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti."
The King of Mantras consisting of the syllables *ṛṇau naḥ toyasya* is proclaimed as the *Nirvīja* (seedless) form for all rites;
it is held to be [the mantra] in these positions—at the beginning, middle, and end—characterized by being seedless.
Even in the absence of the initial position, due to the use of the plural number (*bahuvacanāt*), it applies even when separated by what precedes it.

The reference [to them] has been indicated; it is universally established that pronouns refer to what is present in the mind. Although, among those named "wrath caused by number" (*saṃkhyākṛtadoṣa*), the inclusion of those named "wrath caused by the persistence of the seed" (*bījasthitikṛtaroṣa*) would have made the text more consistent, nevertheless—
These are the three varieties of the *pinavākṣara* (the long-syllabled [mantra]). Among them, through its conjunction with the fixed *praṇava*, it is designated as *nistriṃśa*;

through the absence of the six-limbed mantras beginning with the heart, it is "seedless" (*nirbīja*); and through the conjunction of *phaṭ* and *ṣaṭ*, it is named *siddhi*. This appears to be the fundamental intention of the author.

As for those who say that this designation [of the *mūlamantra*] must follow the order of the enumeration (*uddeśa*), they, in turn, should be asked: "What is the reason for expressing it in that way within the sentence of the enumeration itself? It has been stated in some places that there are four syllables (*catur-varṇa*) and four seeds (*catur-bīja*), while the absence of the *dhruva* (the *praṇava*) is mentioned as an excess; in other places, the *dhruva* is absent...
[The meter] is established by four or six seeds (bījas), or by the sight of the tawny-haired (piṅgala) one with matted locks;

however, the fact that it consists of six and a half syllables and so forth must be explained by accepting that the consonant in forms such as "sthi" and "na," which possess a thousand arms, constitutes a half-syllable. It has eleven phonemes (arṇas).
There are four mantras known as *dṛpta* (proud/arrogant), consisting of twenty-three syllables and twenty-five syllables.
Although at the time of enumeration it was stated that the *atidṛpta* (exceedingly proud) consists of twenty-four syllables,
they know that mantra to be either eleven syllables, or twenty-three syllables— which is half of half a hundred— or indeed twenty-four syllables.

In the *Maṇtramuktāvalī* it is likewise stated: "In the case of a prefix (*upasarga*), the meaning [of the root] need not be intended; rather, fear should be associated with it. For there is no rule that a prefix must intend the mastery (*aiśvarya*) [of the action]. As it has been said:
'One [prefix] subverts the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), another follows it, and yet another qualifies it.'"
The commentator [states]: "Another [term] is employed in the sense of 'to overcome' (*abhibhavati*) and 'to subdue' (*praṇibhavati*)," and so forth;

these are the examples (*nyudāharaṇāni*). In the introductory sentence which indicates the subject matter (*lakṣya*), only the word *atidṛpta* is seen, and it does not refer to the meaning [of the root], but rather to the technical name (*saṃjñā*). For indeed... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete].

It is appropriate to refer to him by names such as Jñānadatta or Atiyajñadatta; he composed various unseen compositions and an incomparable work titled *Añjakara*. Thus, the verse by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa is addressed [to him], for those [names] are not etymological (*yaugika*) based on a formal derivation (*yoga*).

Therefore, in this defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), the term *dṛpta* (arrogant), though employed for the sake of metrical conformity, actually refers to the *atidṛpta* (excessively arrogant). For even the excessively arrogant is one who is characterized by the common property (*sāmānyadharma*) of arrogance; however, the general category of the "arrogant" cannot be designated by the term *atidṛpta*.

By not acting otherwise than that, it is implied that this very [method] is what is designated by the term *dṛpta* (pride/arrogance) in another tantra; this is what we maintain. The analysis of the compound is: "that in which there is one letter less than thirty," meaning twenty-nine letters. *Ekonatriṃśad-varṇa*.

Thus, up to the thirty-nine-syllable mantra and the thirty-seven-syllable mantra, there shall be those designated as having an excess syllable (*atirikta*). Starting from the forty-syllable mantra up to the sixty-three-syllable mantra, there are twenty-four mantras; all of these consist of thirty syllables.
The thirty-three syllables and the twenty-six mantras each shall be known as "with modesty" (*savrīḍa*).
[Regarding the term] "that which has sixty-five as its first [syllable]," this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the type where the qualities are not included in the designation (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
This is because another tantra is seen to state that there are one hundred minus one, namely sixty-five plus [fifty-four], up to ninety-nine. Thus...

Thus, the thirty-four mantras beginning with the mantra of sixty-six syllables (*itivābhinna-padamūrdhe*) and ending with the mantra of ninety-nine syllables are designated as *sthānabhraṣṭa* (displaced from their proper place). These include those consisting of one hundred syllables, one hundred and fifty syllables, and two hundred syllables.

The six mantras consisting of ninety-two syllables, ninety-one syllables, and three hundred syllables are known as *sneha* (oils). The grammatical connection is that "by whatever number" refers to the specific count of those mantras, such as one hundred and so forth. Those [mantras] exceeding four hundred syllables, however, are *ativṛddha* (excessively increased).
Beginning from *Ramā* and ending with *Sahasrākṣara*, there are six hundred and one mantras.
Although *Nisteha* is mentioned after *Ativṛddha*,
the sequence is set aside in accordance with the enumeration of two hundred and so forth, as these precede four hundred and the rest.

According to the author of the *Gītiharpa-kaumudī*, there is not even a doubt that, based on the injunctive statement "one who is excessively greedy is devoid of oil" (*sātivṛddho nistehi*), it is understood that the state of being devoid of oil (*nisteha*) is primary and occurs first. Furthermore, regarding the applications such as those for pacification (*śānti*) and so forth, these are the five *daṇḍakas*.

The meaning is that all those [verses] which, having not attained a state of syntactic unity with others and so forth, exist in the form of hymns (*stotra*), become mantras designated as *iḍita*. Therefore, even if there is an increase in length due to the *daṇḍaka* and other such meters, there is no violation of the division [of the mantra]. As for that which consists of two thousand syllables and so on...

He stated "mantratām" [the state of being a mantra] as "two thousand," and so forth. Here, only the fact of having the number two thousand is intended; by this, there is the exclusion of those substrata (*dharmin*) that have fewer than that number, while there is the inclusion of substrata such as three thousand and so on, which are divided into many parts, each consisting of a hundred.
The meaning is that they do not become mantras; they should be employed as mantra-functions (*mantra-kṛtya*).

This is what is stated in the *Harṣakaumudī*. To this, the following must be said: how does it follow that they "do not become mantras"? If you say, "Because they are hymns (*stotra*)," then [we ask]: what of the hymns?

The meaning that "they are mantras because of the state of being 'namas'" is not easily established; for since only the characteristics of mantras such as *chinnādi* have been promised [to be discussed], stating this particular meaning would be unnecessary and would result in a lack of elegance in the text. Therefore, for us...
The view accepted in the *Padārthādarśa* is indeed more excellent. For the term "mantra" (*maṃtrapada*) is used even in a general sense;
thus, even in a mantra addressed to a deity wearing male attire, it may pertain to a female deity. In that case, the term "vidyā" (*vidyāpada*) applies, as stated in the root text: "Mantra is vidyā."

The classes of mantras are of two kinds by way of division: mantras are to be known as having male deities, while vidyās have female deities, and so forth. In response to the doubt as to what the word "mantra" refers to among these characteristics of defects, he states that it refers to mantra in its general sense. Mantras...

By the passage beginning with "etayathā" and ending with "kāmyakarmmasu," it is stated that there is no fault in the desireless meditation (*niṣkāmopāsanā*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "ityādi," the inclusion of defects such as those residing in the enemy's serpents and so forth is intended; [the term] "śatrupakṣe" means situated among the enemies, and "ṛṣyā" refers to the sages.

The characteristic of the "void of directions" (*diśūnya*) is as follows: the mantra of Jupiter and the other [planets] is presided over by their respective deities; the mantra of Venus and the others has as its name that which stands in the enemy faction—the synonym for the "opposing side" (*vipakṣastha*). This applies to any [mantra] whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*devatā*), and so forth, are not known.

Even in the tantric statement shown in the *Padārthādarśa*, "He who is abandoned by the seers (*ṛṣi*), deities (*devatā*), and meters (*chandas*) is [called] *bhujaṅga*," it is knowledge alone that must be understood as being included therein;
for one who has not been awakened by the seers, meters, deities, and so forth, Śiva is his seer.

The *chaṃdogāyatrī* is the deity; she herself is the Supreme Brahman. The vowels are the power (*śakti*), the consonants are the seed-syllables (*vīja*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the pin (*kīlaka*). According to the *Śaktisaṃgamatantra*, since a deficiency in the [standard] seers (*ṛṣi*) and other components is in every way impossible, that which has been shown hereafter [is as follows]:

He explains the method for avoiding those faults with the words beginning with "mantrān" (the mantras). By the phrase "ātmaniyojanam" (joining to oneself), he describes a different method of purification consisting of the meditation on the non-difference of the mantra from oneself. He further states "śodhayet" (one should purify) and so forth. Some, however, [regard] the previously mentioned fault...
If one should apply six types of corrupt mantras to oneself due to excessive faith, ignorance of the guru, and so forth,
or if one desires to apply or receive them, then he states the method beginning with "one should purify" (*śodhayet*);
thus, some interpret this passage as being devoted solely to this single method.

Having meditated on the Yonimudrā, characterized by the act of kissing, as it moves up and down from its origin in the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*, and having performed the retention of the breath (*vāyudhāraṇa*), purification occurs through the performance of a thousand recitations (*japa*). This is indeed the instruction of the Guru.
Even today, because the disciple has not yet formally received the mantra, the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) must still be performed by the preceptor as his duty; however,
if they have not been performed by the preceptor due to negligence or other causes, then the disciple himself may perform them after receiving the mantra.
It should be understood that this is the "Supreme Ramā" (Ramāvaredevī). As for the definition of the Yoni-mudrā:

having pressed the anus and the path of the *yoni* with the heel, one should draw the *apāna* upward; this is called *mūla-bandha*. By contracting the *yoni*, which is the space between the anus and the genitals, one performs the binding (*prabandha*).

Regarding the phrase "one should know," [the author] states "by means of purificatory rites" (*saṃskāraiḥ*) and so forth, as a means of purification for those who are unable to perform the *yonimudrā* and other such practices. In the *Saṃhitā*, it says: "Alternatively, one should perform the consecration by means of the purificatory rites beginning with 'generation' (*janana*). Even a stone image that is defiled by the faults of the twice-born becomes perfected."

From the *Yogaratnāvalī* and other sources, it is stated that the atoms (*aṇavaḥ*) are to be known as being corrupted by such defects; therefore, the sequence for the destruction of those defects is now proclaimed:
birth (*janana*), animation (*jīvana*), awakening (*bodha*), striking (*tāḍana*), purification (*nirmalīkṛti*), and nourishment (*āpyāyatā*).

"By means of the seven limbs of the *ṣekauca* rite, the mantras, when purified along with their respective times (*sakālāḥ*), certainly become the granters of all desires. By this, the doubt as to what proof exists for the capacity to destroy the aforementioned defects is dispelled; and thus, regarding the root word *nityasya* [in the phrase] "the bestower of success" (*siddhidāyinī*).
The meaning is that they bring about success by means of removing the faults previously mentioned.

Having worshipped the *Mātṛkā-kamala* (the lotus of the alphabet) on birch bark— described in the chapter on the *Mātṛkā*— with saffron and water, one should [inscribe] one's own respective mantra on another place, such as birch bark, using saffron and so forth.
By means of the *khaṇena* (momentary) rite, the consecration (*jananasaṃskāra*) is produced within each respective mantra; thus, the mantra becomes free from defects.

This same principle should be applied to the other consecrations as well. However, some [teachers] maintain that by merely writing out the *mātṛkā* and extracting the syllables of the mantra, the "life" (*jīvana*) of the mantra is secured. This is the *mātṛkā*.
Some say that after having drawn the lotus of letters (*varṇābja*), its generation occurs through its extraction;
the specific instruction is that one should recite the extracted syllables a hundred times.
This is because of the statement of the Teacher (*ācārya*): "Having drawn the lotus of letters, one should extract the syllables of the mantra and recite them a hundred times."
The specific substances for writing [the mantra] are prescribed according to the difference in deities in the *Gautamīya*:

"Saffron for the Śakti-saṃskāra, sandalwood for the Vaiṣṇava, and ashes are declared for the Śaiva in the writing of the Mātṛkā-mantra. Regarding the phrase "separated by the Praṇava," it means that the Praṇava comes first.

First the mantra-syllable, then the *praṇava* (Oṃ); then again the mantra-syllable, then again the *praṇava*; then again the mantra-syllable, then again the *praṇava*, and so on in this sequence until the completion of all the syllables of the mantra—this constitutes one hundred repetitions of the recitation for the sake of longevity.

The name is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); it is said that the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is the seed. One should apply that [seed] at the end of the name, having placed it with an intervening syllable; for some say this because it is stated in the *Yogaratnāvalī* that "this mantra is empowered by the seed. [One should write it] on birch bark or similar materials.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "the mantra-syllables" (*mantravarṇān*) and so forth is as follows: having written the mantra using substances such as saffron or yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), one should strike each of those mantra-syllables one hundred times each with water from a *vaṃdana* vessel or with flowers while uttering the wind-seed syllable (*yāṃ*). This is done with the syllable ending in *yāṃ* accompanied by the *anusvāra*.

Having written the entire mantra on birch bark or similar material with saffron and the like using red ink, one should strike each syllable of the mantra individually with red karavīra flowers; this indeed is the "awakening" (bodhana). Regarding the number of red karavīra [flowers] corresponding to the syllables of the written mantra...

This awakening has been stated [by the author] because of the preceptor’s words, "One should strike with the fire-seed (RAUM)," as taught in the *Svatantra*. Thus, according to the method of mantras characterized by Vaiṣṇava and other attributes found in the mantra to be bestowed,
one should fashion a lotus with saffron and other substances upon birch bark or similar material, including its pericarp.

Having written each individual syllable of the mantra using a pen made from a *mālatī* bud that has not yet opened, one should sprinkle each syllable with a fresh leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, reciting: "I consecrate the [number]th syllable of such-and-such mantra; *namaḥ*. Thus...

If one performs the consecration by reciting each [mantra] one hundred and eight times, ending with the essential form "I consecrate the nine syllables of the five-syllable Śaiva mantra," then this is the consecration-saṃskāra; as it is said in the *Nijatantra*:
One should consecrate [the disciple] with the *dinamārga* and other [mantras], as well as with the sprouts of the *piṣpala* tree;

likewise, the mantra written on birch bark should be recited one hundred and eight times during the consecration. Furthermore, using jasmine buds, one should place the seed-syllable (*aṇu*) upon the pericarp, and with pure leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, the syllables of that mantra [should be applied].
One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the prescribed [number of] drops, according to the procedure established for one's own specific Tantra.

Regarding the placement of the mantra upon the pericarp (karṇikā) with the *kalikās*: it occurs by writing the syllables of the mantra upon the pericarp using a stylus made of *kalikā*. Thus it is done within the mantras.

Innate defects (*sahajadoṣa*) such as being broken (*chinna*) have already been described. Adventitious defects (*āgantukadoṣa*) arise from disrespect toward the Guru and others, and from revealing [the mantra] in an inappropriate place. Defects pertaining to *māyā* arise from reciting [the mantra] while in states such as passion (*kāma*) or anger (*krodha*). This very [defect] resides within the mantra.
Having mentally recited the threefold fundamental mantra and uttered "Oṃ Hraum," one says:

"I burn away the innate impurity of this mantra, Namaḥ. Again, having mentally recited the fundamental mantra and uttered "Oṃ Hraum," one recites the light-mantra (jyotirmantra) and [burns away] the adventitious impurity of this mantra.

Having uttered "nirdahāmi namaḥ," and again uttering as before up to the end of "māyāmalaṃ nirdahāmi namaḥ," the purification known as *vimalīkaraṇa* (cleansing) of the primary mantra should be performed.
Here, *tāra* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ); *vyoma* is the letter *ha*; *agni* is the letter *ra*; and *manu* is the fourteenth vowel (*au*).

The *daṇḍa* is the *anusvāra*; many [authorities] say that this refers to the *jyotir-mantra*, but in reality, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains it refers to the *mūla-mantra*. This is because it contradicts the *tantra* texts which state: "The replenishing (*āpyāyana*) should be performed by returning [the water] with *kuśa* grass and milk over which one has personally recited [the mantra]. Furthermore, the *jyotir-mantra* is [merely] a burner (*dāhaka*).

Furthermore, because being nourishing is contradictory to its inherent nature as [something] drying, the first position is not sound; nor is the second view superior, since there is no authority for purification by means of a purification when the mantra in question is itself that which is to be purified.
Therefore, because that word (*tat*) functions as a reference to what is present in the mind...

The meaning of "na" here is "iti avam," which signifies the seed-syllable of immortality (*amṛtabīja*). Indeed, the author of the *Harṣakaumudī* maintains that the nourishing nature of the seed-syllable of immortality is well-established. As for the question of how to resolve the contradiction with the previously mentioned mantra, some suggest that the consonant "s" is included as a constituent of the moon-seed-syllable (*caṃdrabīja*).
Because of the rule that "that which follows *ca* belongs to it," there is the exclusion of the third letter of the *pa*-group (*pha*).
Thus, by the arrival of the meaning "by means of the seed-syllable of nectar" (*amṛtabīja*), it appears that one [syllable] is obstructed.
Having first consecrated the *kuśa*-water one hundred and eight times with [the mantra], one should take that *kuśa*-water.

Having recited the complete mantra by pronouncing each individual syllable among those previously written, combined with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) according to one's own view or the nectar-seed (*amṛtabīja*) according to another view, one performs the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for each syllable in the manner of "I nourish this syllable of this mantra, *namaḥ*," and so forth; this indeed is the nourishment (*āpyāya*).
Regarding the refinement of the name (*nāman-saṃskāra*): for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should recite the complete mantra followed by the formula "I offer this mantra as a libation, *namaḥ*.

Alternatively, the libation may be performed over the previously written mantra, letter by letter, exactly one hundred and eight times. [The mantras] beginning with the *praṇava*, the *māyā-bīja*, and the *śrī-bīja*...
One should recite the mantra under discussion seven times; this is the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) known as *dīpana* (illumination).
Those who know the tradition maintain that one should recite it every day, for illumination must be performed daily.

Regarding the statement "having performed [the rites] according to the tradition" (*saṃpradāyena*), when the question arises as to what that tradition is, the purificatory rites have not been mentioned there.

The intention is that while *rāḥ* is employed in all mantras and is capable of bestowing fruits, it is only effective in certain ones and only when they are favorable to it; wishing to refute [the opponent's view] with what follows, he says "svatārā" and so forth, meaning that such consecrations (*saṃskāra*) as have been prescribed must be performed for such a mantra. In that regard:

Regarding the threefold favorability toward Tārā, beginning with the verse "Birth-favorability" (*janmasampad*) and so forth: one favorability is by means of the consideration of birth; the second is by means of the consideration of the friendship of the *yoni*; and the third is by means of the consideration of the friendship of the *gaṇa*.
Among these, the first favorability must be explained; although it exists in the root text, [the author] has not yet done so because of the names of the mantra and the practitioner, and so on.

Since that [calculation] depends upon the knowledge of the flowing asterisms (*kṣaranakṣatra*), whichever asterism belongs to whichever letter must necessarily be determined; therefore, he says "mostly" (*prāya*) and so forth. Here, the numbers are to be known from the letters belonging to the *ka*, *ṭa*, and *pa* groups, while zero (*śūnya*) is to be understood from the letters *na* and *bha*.

"It is stated that [the letters] are pronounced with their own respective sounds" (*thāsvarakevalakathitam*); this is the convention accepted by the Tantrikas regarding the *Śivatāṇḍava* and other systems.
The meaning is as follows: the *ka*-group and *va*-group each consist of nine letters; the *pa*-group consists of five letters; the *ya*-group ends with *ha* and consists of eight letters;
and the *kra*-group and so forth are "conjoined letters" (*yuktākṣara*), which are "compound syllables" (*piṇḍa*); among these, the last...
The intended cognition of the numbers two and one is derived precisely from the syllables *ma* and *ka*, and so forth;

however, by means of the syllables *na* and *bha*, and by the tenth letters of the *ta*-group and *ka*-group respectively, the number ten obtained according to the aforementioned sequence is not to be taken, but rather zero (*śūnya*). Likewise, there is the single syllable *a* alone, and so on.
Indeed, even by those [consonants], only the void (śūnya) is to be grasped; however, it is the number one, three, and so forth.

Thus, in this context, from the letter *ra* situated at the end of the group of consonants (*piṇḍa*), the number two is understood; whereas from the letter *la*, which represents the number one, the number three is understood, and so on.
And thus, the meaning is as follows: from the letters beginning with *a*, which represent the numbers one, two, and so forth...

The vowels that follow in sequence are differentiated according to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) beginning with Aśvinī and are shown by means of division; for example, the two syllables *ā* and *ai* belong to Aśvinī, the single syllable *ī* belongs to Bharaṇī,
and the three syllables *ī*, *ū*, and *ū* belong to Kṛttikā, as indicated by this [verse] beginning with "āi."

The single syllable *kṣa* is the moving star, possessing a stainless form, which is indeed the form of Nṛsiṃha. According to the statement in another Tantra, "The two letters *vi* and *du*, with the *visarga*, are situated in the portion of Aśleṣā (*vapuṣṇu*)," it follows that this [syllable] ends in the letter *kṣa*; thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has *kṣa* as its end. Furthermore, the letter *kṣa* belongs to the constellation Uttarabhādrapadā, while the letter *ṣa* belongs to the letter *kṣa*.
Because it serves as a constituent part and indicates that [deity], it has been said: "From that, the letter *kṣa* was born;
Nṛsiṃha is its presiding deity; he, moreover, went to the supreme state along with the six *ṣaṣahas*.
Thus, for practitioners (sādhakas) whose names begin with 'Anantātmārāma' and so forth, [the path] leads to Ananta."

For the mantras beginning with "Maḥ Ānandabhairavāya namaḥ," the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is Aśvinī; thus, there is no compatibility between this mantra and its practitioner. However, for the mantra "Indirāyai namaḥ," the lunar mansion is Bharaṇī; thus, there is compatibility between this mantra and its practitioner, such as Ananta and others.
This very same [rule] should be inferred by oneself for what follows; however, regarding the anusvāra and visarga which occur in sequence,

he provides an exception when they occur in the portion beginning with "kha," stating that although it is impossible for the bindu and visarga— which are at the end of vowels— to be considered the first letter of a word, the mention of them as constellations (*nakṣatra*) is not applicable here.
Nevertheless, because the placement (*nyāsa*) of those respective letters along with their corresponding asterisms is sometimes employed for a specific purpose,

and for the sake of that application, it is said— starting with "janma" and so forth— that once the respective asterisms for those respective letters have been established in this manner, [the author] speaks [the following] in order to examine [factors] such as favorability (*anukūlya*). First, *ja*...

Furthermore, prosperity and the like resulting from a name are not truly fruitful; for even the birth of one who has been born is impossible without death, and thus [the name] is indeed defective. As it has been said: "The eighth, ninth, and twelfth houses are auspicious even when situated in pairs;
the others are not auspicious—this should be understood by those skilled therein."
The second [type of] favorability is as follows: A horse is declared for Aśvinī and Anurādhā;
a buffalo for Svātī and Hasta; a lion for Citrā and Śatabhiṣaj;
an elephant for Bharaṇī and Revatī; a ram for Puṣya and Kṛttikā; and a monkey for Karṇa (Śravaṇa) and Mṛgaśīrṣa.
Likewise, the mongoose is [the deity] of the two Viśākhās and Abhijit; the snake of Anurādhā and Mṛgaśiras; the deer of Jyeṣṭhā and Maitra (Anurādhā);
the dog of Mūla and Ārdrā; the cat of Āśleṣā and Svāti; the rat of the two Maghās; and the tiger of Dvīśa (Śatabhiṣaj) and Citrā.
There is mutual great enmity between the goat (Aja) and the elephant (Gaja), and between the ram (Meṣa) and the buffalo (Mahiṣa).

The goat (Aja) has Pūrvabhādrapadā as its birth sign; the water-beast (Ambu-pa) [the crocodile] has Pūrvāṣāḍhā as its birth sign; the mouse (Mūṣaka) has Pūrvaphālgunī as its birth sign; and the sheep (Eḍuka) has Rohiṇī as its birth sign. The noble one (Ārya) [the horse]...
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Uttaraphalgunī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Uttarabhadrapadā, the third [triad] beginning with Śatabhiṣaj, the three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Svāti, Aśvinī,
Revatī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Anurādhā, Punarvasu, and Śravaṇa— these, along with the two Devas and the two Ādityas, are divine; while the remaining ones are Rākṣasa.

If [the planets] are in the midst of their own respective groups, there will be supreme affection between gods and humans; this is declared to be middling. If they belong to the groups of Asuras and humans, death itself is ordained.
And if they belong to the groups of Danavas and gods, there is absolute enmity—thus says the author of the Padārthādarśa.
In those [circumstances], one's own family becomes the stars of one's own qualities, while another's family becomes the calculation of another's group;

thus it is said that the investigation of *kula* and *akula* is indeed the investigation of the *gaṇa*. Others, however, describe this investigation differently, as follows: [the elements] wind, fire, earth...
The letters beginning with *lā*,

*kā*, *śi*, and so forth, which were previously mentioned as being rooted in the elements (*bhūta-varṇa-mūla*), are the initial letters of the mantras for practitioners if they belong to a single element.

Then, those belonging to one's own family (*kulavarṇa*) would be [the same], while those belonging to other beings would be of non-family color (*akulavarṇa*). However, for one desiring to bestow a mantra that has been purified according to the distinctions of one's own family and so forth, [there is a rule] regarding the name of the practitioner of the mantra (*manu-sādhaka-nāman*).

For those whose speech begins with the vowels *u* and *au*, the attainment of their desired object occurs through their own kinsmen; success is proclaimed when it is through a friend, death and disease when through an enemy, and nothing significant when through a neutral party.
For the classes beginning with the Kṣatriya (Pārthiva), their own names denote their respective families; however, for the Pārthiva [class], its own...

For a syllable born of water, the syllable born of earth is said to be its friend; the one born of fire is its enemy; and the one born of wind is neutral. For a syllable born of fire, the one born of wind is its friend; the one born of earth is its enemy; and the one born of water is neutral. For a syllable born of wind, the one born of earth is its friend; the one born of fire is its enemy; and the one born of water is neutral. For a syllable born of earth, the one born of water is its friend; the one born of fire is its enemy; and the one born of wind is neutral. For a syllable born of ether, all are neutral. Thus is the relationship of friends, enemies, and neutrals among the elements determined by their origin.

An enemy of the water-born color is said to be a friend of the earth-born color; the wind-born color is a friend of the fire-born color. The earth-born color is the enemy of the water-born color, while the water-born is neutral. For the four [elements] beginning with earth, space is...
In order to determine the compatibility of the *rāśis* (zodiacal signs) for those who are always together, there is here a specific *rāśi* assignment for the *varṇas* (castes);

however, it is not as in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), where a *rāśi* such as Aries and so forth is determined by constellations (*nakṣatra*) such as Citrā and the like, plus a quarter. With this intention, [the author] introduces the *rāśis*.

He states the various types [of mantras] with the words beginning "vāla" and so forth. By the words "vālam" and so forth, numbers such as four and three are expressed; thus, the resulting meaning is that a mantra, a practitioner, or a *jāti* (class) is to be known as having four vowels (*a, i, u, ṛ*) as its primary elements, and likewise [having] six consonants (*ś, ṣ, s, h, l, kṣ*). The letters beginning with *śa* are... [lāṃ].

These [letters] are indeed five-fold for the sign of Virgo (*kanyārāśi*), and not for the sign of Pisces (*mīnarāśi*) which is assigned to the vowel-group; as it is stated in another Tantra: "O excellent lady, Aries consists of four vowels, Taurus of three letters, and the third sign [Virgo] likewise of three letters in sequence."

O Dear One, when the Sun is in Leo, there is a heap of gravel; O Maheśvarī, from the letters *a*, *aḥ*, and the *śa*-group, a virtuous girl is born. From the *ka*-group comes Libra, and from the *ca*-group, Scorpio. From the *ṭa*-group comes Sagittarius, and from the *ta*-group, Capricorn. The *pa*-group corresponds to Aquarius.

O lady with the gait of an elephant, embrace the signs [of the zodiac] beginning with Aries; together with the four starting from that, there shall be the sign of Cancer, and Pisces shall be the twelfth.
Thus, O lady with the gait of an elephant, the purification of the signs has been described.
By counting from the practitioner's sign up to the sign of the mantra, one arrives at a number such as one, two, and so forth.
He states the results of the zodiac signs, beginning with "lagna" and so forth: even when they occupy a single sign, it is indeed auspicious. As it is said:
"The first, fifth, and ninth houses are remembered as kinsmen; the second, sixth, and tenth are likewise servants;
the third, seventh, and eleventh are honored; but the twelfth, eighth, and fourth are destroyers."
One should investigate the birth sign and the zodiacal wheel according to the [astrological] system; it is not by name alone that this is to be determined.
The meaning of the word *śiti* has been established in the *Harṣakaumudī* according to the previous method.

Furthermore, Jupiter, the preceptor of the gods, likewise [favors] those practitioners belonging to the signs of Aries and Scorpio,
which have Mars as their lord; for such practitioners,
the reception of mantras belonging to the signs of Sagittarius and Pisces, which have Jupiter as their lord, is auspicious, provided that the lords of the two signs are mutual friends.
It should be understood that the favorability of the sign (*rāśyanukūlya*)— as indicated by the verse beginning with *tvāditirītyā*— is twofold,
while the favorability of the house (*koṣṭhānukūlya*) is fivefold, due to the divisions of the *akadhahā*,
*kaḍama*, the four-housed wheel, the six-pada wheel, and the wealth wheel (*dhanacakra*). Among these, first is the [four-housed] wheel.

By means of the verse beginning with "muddharati catasṛbhiḥ" and so forth, one should produce a square consisting of four compartments by means of five lines each extending east-west and five lines each extending north-south, intersecting one another; therein, in due order, the letter *a*...
The letters of the days are to be written as follows: first, having inscribed the vowels *a*, *ā*, *i*, and the fourth vowel (*u*) in each of the first four squares,
then having inscribed the fifth vowel (*ū*) and so forth in the second and second [square], and then the ninth vowel (*ṛ*) in the third and third [square].

Then, having written the vowels from the thirteenth to the sixteenth in each of the fourth [groups] starting from the east, and having written the consonants beginning with *ka* and *kha* in the aforementioned directions, the *Siddhādicakra* is completed;
he describes the method for knowing one’s own favorable [position] therein with the verse beginning "one's own name" (*svanāma*) and so forth.

In the *Ktāvalī*, the wise one should write the letters sequentially according to their origin from the alphabet into the squares numbered by the directions (10), Rudra (11), the nine (9), the eyes (2), the Yugas (4), the quarters (10), the seasons (6), the Aṣṭas (8), the sixteen (16), the fourteen (14), the Bhūtas (5), the Pātālas (7), and the Viśvas (13). Thus it is written.
The *nakrama* is thus comprised: having first written the initial [consonant] in each of the four groups starting from the first, and subsequently in the second,
third, and fourth [groups], one should then write the vowels in sequence for all the groups, beginning with the letter *ca*.
One should count from the box corresponding to the first letter of one's own name—which has been written according to the sequence—up to the box corresponding to the first letter of the mantra.
Among those, the first is the *siddha* (accomplished) box, the second is the *sādhya* (to-be-accomplished) box, and the third is the *su*... [box].
The "Siddha-group" (siddhakoṣṭha) is the fourth group; that very group in which one's own name resides is the Siddha-group, its associated tetrad is the Siddha-tetrad (siddhacatuṣka).
The second is the Sādhya-tetrad (sādhyacatuṣka), and the third is the Susiddha-tetrad (susiddhacatuṣka), and that...
The fourth group of four arises; in each of these four groups, in the first square joined with the letter known as the *sādhaka*, there is the name *siddha-siddha*;
in the second, the name *siddha-sādhya*, and so on, according to the squares occupied by their respective names, [this applies] to the second group of four.

Starting from the first square of the *ṣka* [group] and proceeding in a clockwise direction, one attains the names of the enemy (*ari*), the well-accomplished (*susiddha*), the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*), the accomplished (*siddha*),
and the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*). In the third group of four squares, starting from the first square, the "well-accomplished" (*susiddha*) is reached by one's own name.

The names *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *siddhāri* arise from such a tetrad; furthermore, the fourth [tetrad] from that [first] consists of the names *ari-siddha*, *ari-sādhya*, *ari-susiddha*, and *ari-ari*. In all these tetrads, the name of the practitioner occupies the square [at the beginning].

In those squares occupied by any of the properties of being first, second, third, or fourth, one should follow that firstness and so forth, rather than starting from the northeast (Īśāna) square and so on. Among them, the established letters (*siddha-varṇas*) are beneficial, whereas the letters to be accomplished (*sādhya-varṇas*) are...

A servant is beneficial only to that master who causes him pleasure, not to everyone; likewise, even a well-mastered syllable, through effort such as recitation (*japa*), is beneficial only to one's own servant [the practitioner], not to everyone. A perfectly perfected syllable—

A supporter, such as a father and so forth, supports his dependents, such as a son and so forth, even without regard for whether they possess double the qualities or none at all; thus, by the words beginning with "siddhārṇā," he demonstrates the result—that one becomes an enemy of those who are enemies. Although [the word] *siddhidaḥ* means "one who grants success,"...

Although the result has already been stated by [the verse beginning with] "tyādi," nevertheless, since the application of the letters *va*, *ndha*, *ka*, and so forth is observed in relation to fire (*agni*), it should be understood that this is merely a technical designation (*saṃjñāmātra*) presented here for that purpose.
Furthermore, there is another distinction: the first [number] is to be purified by the first, and the second by the second.

When the consonants (*vyañjana*) are with the vowels (*svara*), or the vowels are likewise with the consonants, or when the letters of the names of the Manus or of the trees are uneven, then one should begin the mantra and employ it until it becomes even. Regarding the results there, such as *siddha-siddha* and so forth—

A *Siddha-Siddha* [mantra] is effective as stated; a *Siddha-Sādhya* becomes effective through double the recitation (*japa*); a *Siddha-Susiddha* through half the recitation; and a *Siddha-Ari* (enemy) destroys one's kinsmen. A *Sādhya-Siddha* is achieved through double the recitation; a *Sādhya-Sādhya* is useless; and a *Sādhya-Susiddha* is achieved through triple the recitation.

The *dhyāri* (enemy of the *susiddha*) kills those born of the lineage; the *siddha* kills through the recitation of the *ūrdhva*; the *sādhya* [kills] from one superior in qualities; the *susiddha* [kills] from the planets and deities; and the *ari* (enemy) becomes a killer of kinsmen. The *arisiddha* kills the son, while the *arisādhya* kills the daughters. The *tatsu*... [text ends].

The Siddha, Stūpa, Patnīghna, Arya, Ari, Sādhaka, Apahiti, and Dvitīya— these are favorable for the Koṣṭhas. In the *Ratnāvalī*, regarding the twelve-spoked wheel or the "Cakra of Speech," one should write the letters from the beginning to the end, excluding the *Kūṭa* and *Caṇḍa* [syllables], starting from the east as far as the letter *I*.
One should write the vowels and the numbers beginning with one (1) in order starting from the east; thus the mantra becomes clearly manifest as fourfold: Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Ari.
A mantra is Siddha by [the sum of] nine, one, and five; Sādhya by six, ten, and two; a friend (Mitra) by three, seven, and eleven; and an enemy (Ari) by four...
"By twelve [lines], it is the enemy"— this is the third [step]. As before,
having made a square of four compartments by means of three lines extending east-west and three lines extending north-south, one should place all [the letters] there in a single sequence.

Having written the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ha* in the squares of the alphabet grid (*mātṛkā*), one should count the *siddha* and other [categories] starting from the square containing the first letter of one's own name and continuing up to the square containing the first letter of the mantra.
For it is said in another Tantra: "The collection of Mātṛkā letters begins with *a* and ends with *ha*."

One should arrange each letter in sequence within four squares; one should count them in order as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, or *vairin*. Whichever letters arise there from the name or the mantra—thus, for example, having drawn the six-padded wheel (*ṣaṭpadacakram*) in the fourth [section].
One should write the letters beginning with *a* and so forth, one by one, on the petals starting from the east;
one should investigate [the result] beginning from whichever petal contains the first letter of one's own name.
In the first [case], there is misfortune; in the second, the destruction of prosperity; but in the third, the acquisition of wealth.
In the fourth [cell] there is loss of wealth; in the fifth, conflict with kinsmen; in the sixth, one becomes full of doubt;

and in the seventh, total destruction. However, where the writing of the first letter for Ṛtuparṇa and others is absent, having placed that [name] in another square, one should begin the second letter [from there].

The investigation into these very [matters] must be pursued; this is the secret. Regarding those wheels (*cakras*), the fifth is now to be investigated, and that too exists in various forms. Among them, one form is as follows: one should draw seventy lines horizontally and twelve vertically.

Furthermore, when it is done in this way, sixty-six *koṣṭhas* (cells) are produced. Then, the letters beginning with *sa*, *dha*, *ya*, *ka*, *ta*, *ta*, *na*, *ga*, *bha*, *bhi*, *no*, *na*, and *ga*—these, along with the five long vowels (*ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*) added at the beginning, should be placed below them in sequence. Then, the letters beginning with *ka*, *a*, *ṭa*, *ya*, *va*, and *ka* follow in order.

The letters *ṇa*, *ṭa*, *pha*, *ha*, *a*, *ntya* (the final letter of each group), *kā*, *kha*, *ra*, *ma*, *na*, *ra*, *ā*, *kī*, *na*, *bho*, *bhokāḥ*, *sā*, *dhakāṃ*, *kakāḥ*— having separated these letters from here and there in the form of divine condiments (*suravyañjana*),
one should make them into one's own heap of numbers and then divide by eight; the remaining number is according to the previous method.

If there is a deficiency in the mantra resulting from the remainder of the sum of the mantra's syllables, that mantra is to be known as "not to be accepted" (*anādeya*); if there is an excess, it is "to be accepted" (*ādeya*); but if they are equal, the mantra is "equal" (*sama*). This should be understood as the auspicious or inauspicious result.
Another method is as follows: one should count starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra.

The numerical value of the name is declared to be the remainder after the sum of the letters of the mantra has been multiplied by three and divided by seven. In this manner, having counted from the first letter of the mantra up to the initial letter of the name,
one multiplies by three, divides by seven, and the resulting quotient is the numerical value of the mantra.
The learned one has declared it to be as before, ending with "vanitārṇataḥ" (the number of letters in the name). An alternative method is as follows:

having separated the letters of the mantra into vowels and consonants, one should double them and join them with the letters of the practitioner's name; the total mass of the mantra is then divided by eight such [groups]. This is the first [method].
If it is subtracted in reverse, that is declared to be the "heap of names" (nāmarāśi). Whether it is in debt (ṛṇita) or in credit (dhanita), it is proclaimed here as before.
However, starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, having divided [the total] by three and multiplied by the vowels, the remainder is other than that.
The author of the *Padārthadarśa* states that the statement from the *Parīkṣitakamititāntra-rāja* also has the same meaning as the medium method previously mentioned; here,
in the process of forming the heap (*rāśi*), there is no inversion where one multiplies by seven and then divides by three.

In the *Mitimanoramā*, it is stated that one should observe the characteristic defined as: "He who sleeps in the treasure-house named *Nidhi* yet remains awake. Even when such [planets] are numerous, this investigation should be performed by taking into account the color corresponding to the birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*) and its quarter (*pāda*).
Even if one does not know the birthplace of Janmanakṛta, the conduct of his father should be accepted; or, if there is a plurality of such fathers, only the first one [is authoritative].

Like the beloved of the chest (the Earth), like the speed of the wind, like the boon of the Lord of Beings (Śiva), like the universe, like the sacrificial exclamation Vaṣaṭ, like the seat of consciousness, like the trembling of Vāsudeva, and like the speech of the Earth—[so is this].
The indeclinable *veti* and so forth; *āryotaḥ*; *asyāḥ*; *vṛndāraka-kratu-vadāyaka*;
the garments of the host of bards (*vandivṛnda*); the great enemies, the trees, and the rays; the wounds of the learned (*vidvad-vraṇau*);
Varuṇa, nourishment (*vṛṃhaṇa*), awakening, the creator (*vedhas*), kinsmen, destruction, warding off, bonds, and the Creator (*vedhāḥ*).
The fact that *ty* and so forth belong to the *pa*-class (*pavargīya*) and other such details should be understood from the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*, which is a source for investigation.

It is established by experience that even if a mantra is free from defects and favorable to the reciter, success is not attained through recitation at every location; rather, it is attained only in specific locations.
Regarding the desire for the specific locations, he says "the location of the lamps" and so forth:

"The letters from *ka* to *kṣa* are known as 'lamps'. This refers to the specific locations of these lamp-letters in places such as Kāśī; the location where the letter *ka* and the others reside is to be understood as their respective positions. Thus, the letter *ka* [is situated there].
He states the means for knowing the locations of the *rāśis* with the words beginning "pūrva" and so forth. This is an investigation of the *kūrma-cakra*;
it is not [to be practiced] in sacred fields such as Vārāṇasī and the like, but rather elsewhere—this is the intended meaning.
He says "puṇya" and so forth to explain that these locations are praised for the accomplishment of mantras. Alternatively:

Because there is an absence of authoritative means for investigating [the suitability of] places such as sacred fields (*puṇyakṣetra*) through the analysis of waves and curves, investigation must be performed even regarding those sacred fields and so forth.

In order to demonstrate a location that brings about immediate success (*sadyaḥsiddhi*) for the practice of mantra, [the author] says "sacred field" (*puṇya*) and so on; therefore, it is necessary to perform the practice of mantra.

Furthermore, the rules regarding food, such as "begging for alms" and so forth, should not have been mentioned here; for even the discussion of begging for alms is not relevant to the description of the *kūrma-cakra*. Regarding the human goals (*puruṣārtha*), [the text] should have dealt with the attainment of one, two, three, or all four of them—namely, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
The meaning is that they desire this very worship of the mantra; the intention is that it is indeed desirable for the sake of worldly goals (*daṃkāmyam*).

Nor should it be argued that it must be performed with absolute necessity because of scriptural injunctions such as "one who is uninitiated shall go to hell," for human birth is difficult to obtain, and even therein, noble birth within the families of one's father and mother is rare.
When the sharpness of the senses has been attained, while merit is present, and when a true guru stands before one—

if a person does not employ some means for their own upliftment, O wise one, there is no rescue for that evil-minded one from the ocean of hell which is so difficult to cross; such is the understanding derived from the words [of the scriptures] regarding hell itself.

Because there is no worship without initiation (*dīkṣā*)— since [worship] arises from awakening— and because, in the absence of the ritual application (*prayoga*) consisting of worship and so forth, one inevitably reaches hell due to previous cognitions and misdeeds,
there is no other evidence for a separate transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the case of non-initiation.
The intention is that all this accomplishment of mantras occurs upon obtaining a true guru;
otherwise, it is not possible. In response to the doubt as to what kind of guru must be served and what kind is not, he states the means for knowing that [the true guru].

Regarding the phrase "mātṛtītyādi" (beginning with "mother"): here, while possessing the essence of all scriptures—such as being of noble lineage and so forth—is useful by way of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), such knowledge is not beneficial by way of the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) without [the teacher's] own realization;

for [otherwise], he could not [instruct] the various mantras, meditations, twilight worship, recitation (*japa*), and so forth, which constitute the limbs of the disciple’s own spiritual practice (*sādhana*).

Doubt regarding what ought to be done can be dispelled; moreover, devotion to the welfare of others is beneficial only through a visible means, for it is impossible to reveal specific mantric conventions for the sake of removing another's suffering unless one is already established in such [a capacity].
Because it is impossible to pose questions regarding that which has already been destroyed, one should infer for oneself [the remaining cases] based on its state of tranquility and so forth.

Furthermore, there are five types of things to be avoided: by virtue of their connection to specific places, their specific characteristics, their specific states, their specific associations, and their incapacity for specific effects. Among these, the first [type] is as follows:

Those born in Karṇāṭaka, Aṅga, Kāmarūpa, Marudeśa, and other regions— whether possessing a second limb, having an excess of limbs, lacking limbs, having matted hair, or being shaven-headed; those born in Karṇāṭaka, Aṅga, Kāmarūpa, Marudeśa, and other regions— whether possessing a second limb, having an excess of limbs, lacking limbs, having matted hair, or being shaven-headed.

The first group consists of those excluded from the stages of life (*āśrama*) and so forth; the second group consists of those who are neither too old nor too young, nor lame, nor emaciated, and so forth; the third group consists of the father, grandfather, brother, the younger sibling, one who has gone to the enemy's side, the husband, the son, women, and so forth; and the fourth group consists of those residing with a disciple.

The fifth [category] consists of those who violate the rules of conduct (*śayāchedinaḥ*). Now, one might ask: "After the performance of the *gurukaraṇa* rite, how should one proceed when the fault of that [act] or the fault of the mantra is known? To this, it is said that in such cases, the *uṣṇāga* rite must be performed there. In all these matters, the authoritative sources should be consulted in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*.

Regarding that which must be personally examined by the teacher—the disciple who desires the instruction of the mantra—it is asked whether such a person should be accepted in its entirety or not; he says "the disciple," and so forth. Here too, as before, the application by way of visible and invisible results should be inferred as possible, since a visible result may occur.
Since it is improper to postulate an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) when a visible cause is available, if—

by some means— an unworthiness were to be perceived through an extraordinary mode of connection via an unseen factor, even in one who has been examined for a year according to the rule "for one year," then he should be abandoned immediately thereafter.

The rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be performed; however, when one recognizes a fault that is useful through a visible means—such as the absence of benefit to the guru—expiation need not be performed. Instead, with a tranquil mind, one should provide a proper response, dispel any doubts regarding it, and act out of a desire for their welfare.
O Lord, it is a secret that one who acts according to their own will, even if they are prone to error, does not incur fault—
[this was said] by him whose mother is the virtuous Udyotamatī,
whose father is Māpati, whose birthplace is the land of Paṭṭana known as Premanidhi, whose place of origin is Mount Kūrma, and who made the worship of Sūpāsya his practice.
In the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*, the second chapter, titled "The Abhyudita," concerning Vārāṇasī, the abode of the feet of the Unfallen One (*acyuta*), has arisen. Therein,
the necessity of performing initiation (*dīkṣā*) through the examination of the guru and the disciple, as well as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for that purpose, has been stated.

He begins to demonstrate that lack of distinction with the words "tat-tu" (but that). Now, if it is argued that by the very statement "then it is a limb," it has already been said that the fruit of initiation prescribed in this manner does not arise, and therefore passages such as "by which [it is] done" need not even be commenced—do not say so; for there is a distinction in its own exclusion (*svavyatireka*).

Even though the absence of the effect when the instigator is absent has been stated, it is necessary to mention that specific part [of the definition] in order to demonstrate the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)— namely, that "when this exists, that exists"— for it is taught that the determination of causality occurs through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Now, let it be so.

The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*), such as worship and the like, first produce a "limited transcendental result" (*apūrva*); then, together with the primary act (*pradhānakarma*) consisting of initiation (*dīkṣā*), they produce a "supreme transcendental result" (*paramāpūrva*), from which the fruit [of liberation] arises.
Therefore, how is it that by the words "by what" (*yena*) and so forth, the subsidiary act is stated to be the cause of the fruit of initiation?

If it is argued that the fruit is produced by the principal apūrvas arising solely from the principal action, assisted by the subsidiary apūrvas (kalikāpūrva), and not by the principal apūrva itself—[then we reply: if that were true, the fruit would be something other than the primary goal such as heaven or liberation; what then? [It is not so.]

Having produced [the mental image], one should offer the oblation (*bali*), as it is said: "one should offer the *bali*. This meaning of the word *bali*—referring to worship and so forth—is essential. As it is stated in the *Kapila-pañcarātra*: "All the gods... [and so on].

One should worship those deities residing in the site with grain-offerings; by that, they will either turn back or depart, saying, "Do not [obstruct] us by the command of Mādhava. Furthermore, elsewhere, those among them who are averse to worship would destroy the merits performed by others and their evil deeds as well; likewise in other houses.

"The deities of the site (vāstudevatāḥ) are worshipped with the ritual instruments of the directions; otherwise, everything there would become empty, struck down by Rākṣasas and others. Thus it is said. "According to the stated measurement" means according to the measure of one cubit as prescribed in the Śilpaśāstras; or else, "according to the stated measurement" means according to the square shape of the site (vāstu).

The thread for the square shape of the *puruṣa* should also be laid out in that same manner; the sense is that the squareness of the form must not be destroyed. As for the method of arranging the sixty-four squares: although previously it was stated that a single line measuring one cubit (*hasta*) should be drawn extending from east to west... Having made a mark in the center, one should draw a single line connected to it extending from south to north;
