having made marks in the four corners, one should apply strings connected to them.
In this way, the accomplishment of the four-square maṇḍala is achieved; thereafter, in each individual square, there are lines.

Two lines should be drawn extending from east to west and two lines extending from south to north; one line should be drawn from the northeast (Īśāna) to the southwest (Nairṛtya), and a second from the southeast (Āgneya) to the northwest (Vāyavya). In this way, sixteen squares are established. Thus, by performing this in each of the four [sections], sixty-four [squares] are formed.
It can be stated that the perfection of the squares is achieved in this manner:
by drawing lines extending east-west and north-south, intersecting the aforementioned lines, sixty-four squares are produced; this is accomplished by means of the diagonal thread (*karṇasūtra*).
Although there are various ways of counting based on the number of tastes (*rasa*) or the number of those [tastes],
he demonstrates the rule for that specific method with the words beginning "tanmadhyam" (*the middle of that*).
Having fixed a mark by taking the middle portion of the line from east to west, one should [draw] around it, extending from east to west.

From the *mūtra* line, two fish-marks—one on each of the northern and southern portions—should be made, one at each location. Between those two, a thread situated at the central mark should be drawn so as to extend from south to north. Having laid down threads at these three marked locations...

The resultant meaning is that one should draw a line extending from the west to the east. Regarding the phrase "by two and two," one should mark a point in the northeast using a cord of half the length of the cord spanning the east-west line, held at the eastern end of that east-west line;
likewise, [one should mark] with that same half-length cord held at the eastern end of the east-west line.
One should mark the southeast corner with the eastern thread; likewise,
having made a mark in the northwest with the thread situated at the western end of that same dimension, one should again make a mark in the southwest in the same manner,
using the two fire-points (agni) formed by the eastern and northern threads.

Having formed a crocodile (*makara*) at the southeast corner consisting of two lines, using the two fire-points (*agni*)— namely, the eastern line’s fire-point and the southern line’s fire-point— one forms a crocodile consisting of two lines at the south-eastern corner, using the two fire-points— namely,
the southern line’s fire-point and the western line’s fire-point.
The meaning is that, having formed a makara at the point of intersection of the two lines from the two corners of the southwest (nairṛta),
one should form a makara at the northwest (vāyavya) corner by means of the two lines from the two corners of the west and the northeast (uttara); it is merely a mark.

The intersection of two lines is a fish; from there, having placed the tip of the thread in the middle of the fish situated on the previously mentioned southern side, one should draw a line extending to the southeast (āgneya) crocodile. With that same thread, joined with the tip of the southwest (nairṛtya) crocodile, one should draw a second line.
In this very manner, having fixed the end of the thread in the middle of the fish-mark situated on the northern side as previously described,

one should again [draw] the third line from that same point toward the north-facing makara-head located at the northeast (īśāna) corner by means of the thread positioned at the fire (agni) corner of the fish-mark.

One should draw the fourth line by joining them together; likewise, two lines should be drawn starting from the northeast mark (īśāna-cihna) to the eastern mark, and starting from the southeast mark (āgneya-cihna) to the eastern mark.
Which.
Having drawn from the northwest makara to the southwest makara, one should draw two lines each up to the western mark;
thus he says, "of the fish. There, regarding the meaning accomplished by this method in the form of the intersection of the two lines situated at the four corners, he further states:

With the words beginning with *turu-asram*, he teaches such lines in order to indicate that the drawing of the lines connecting the pairs of corners is necessary for the construction of the sixty-four squares;
[he does so] by means of the directions starting from Īśāna, so that there may be sixty-four sections (*pada*).

If it were merely stated that "one should divide in this manner," there might arise the error of drawing six lines each extending east-west and north-south, intersecting one another; therefore, it is stated as it is. And thus, this is the final meaning:
Having formed eight squares by means of the diagonal line from the northeast to the southwest and the diagonal line from the southeast to the northwest of a square composed of four squares,
one should [proceed] with the horizontal line situated between the east and south, and the south and west...

Having drawn four lines by means of the aforementioned thread situated at the southwest corner, the aforementioned thread situated at the northwest corner, and the aforementioned thread situated at the northeast corner,
one shall obtain sixteen squares; thus [is the method for] the two primary diagonal threads.

In those [squares] where there are two sets of four intersections, one should draw another four diagonal lines across the four corner squares; then, by dropping two lines from east to west through the fish-figures produced in their centers, sixteen squares are thereby formed. Thus it is said.
The authors of the *Padārthādarśa* have stated that once the four intersection-points (*saṃpāta*) have been produced by means of two initial threads,
one should likewise place two other threads extending east-west and two threads extending north-south above those two intersection-points.

Regarding the statement by the authors of the *Harṣadīpikā* that "sixteen squares [are produced] when bent," both views should be explained by supplying the word "others" (*aparāṇi*). According to the previous method,
this refers to the four intersections of the circles formed by the four squares produced in that manner, as well as their respective eastern and western [sides].
Since only thirty-two squares are produced when two lines are drawn, this [number] is actually based on not counting the squares resulting from the falling of the diagonal threads;
thus, even in the root text, the mention of sixty-four squares is consistent.

It should be understood that otherwise it would result in a lack of connection. Thus, having prepared the square mandala consisting of thirty-two squares, one should [draw] the four diagonal lines (karṇasūtra) previously given within those four squares located at the corners in the center of them.

One should then divide [the space] with threads; subsequently, having drawn two lines extending east-west that meet at the two points of intersection located at the corners of the square, one should likewise draw two lines extending north-south meeting those same two points of intersection. In this manner, there are seventy-two squares.
Then, from that established perfection, one should apply two lines extending east-west and two lines extending north-south at the internal intersection,
as before. When this is done, by the application of the east-west line itself, [the south-north direction is established].
Through the gift of nine necklaces of pearls and through the gift of sixty-four earrings, those innumerable chambers became complete;
even when counting them, they would amount to one hundred and four in number.
Having fixed a point slightly more than thirteen and one-quarter finger-breadths from the middle of the north-south line (*cittu-pūrvapaścimāyatasūtra*),
and having drawn a semicircle to the north from the tip of the east-west line (*prācīsūtra*), one should likewise [proceed] from the western tip according to the stated measurement.
One should draw a semicircle toward the western portion; likewise, two semicircles toward the south.

Then, between the two "fish" (matsya) formed by the southern and northern portions, one should lay a cord extending from south to north with the previously mentioned measurement. Thereafter, one should place the starting point of the cord at the tip of the eastern cord.

Having fixed the midpoint of the eastern sūtra onto the measuring-sūtra so that it touches the point of intersection of the southern and eastern lines, one should draw a semicircle extending from the northeast (Īśāna) to the southeast (Agneya). Likewise, having fixed the starting point of the northern sūtra at the aforementioned intersection, one should draw [the other semicircle] from the northeast (Īśāna) to the northwest (Vāyu).

When this has been done up to the end of the *yūpa*, a fish-figure is produced at the intersection of the two half-circular lines in the northeast; that [fish] is generated by its two tips—the eastern and northern ones—by means of those two [lines] ending in fire (*agni*), which is the connection to the root text. Then, having placed a thread on the western tip, [one proceeds] to the east.

Having drawn a semicircle on the northwest side, one should place the starting point of the thread with its tip facing south; as before, when another semicircle is drawn connected to the intersection at the center, two fish-figures (*matsya*) arise in the southeast and southwest directions.
In this view, the two methods for forming the fish-figures are indeed synonymous.

Then they say that the giving of the thread and so forth is exactly as before; the word *samāhita* (composed/attentive) in the phrase "having placed the ear-thread" (*karṇasūtraṃ samāhita*) applies to all seven [steps], beginning with "one should lay down the thread extending from east to west," since these seven action-words require an agent. The agent is [the one who] acts.
Regarding the phrase "it should be a square because of the desire for such a construction," there is no connection with that [previous rule].
He states the application of these squares starting with the words "the Brāhmaṇa" and so forth; in the four central squares—which constitute the square located in the middle—along with the triangles.

In the eight compartments, having wiped them clean so that they are of a single form, [the remainder is] "in the eight-petaled lotus drawn there"—this is the sense. One should properly worship Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus (the remainder is "in the eight-petaled lotus drawn there"), in the very center; one should cause Brahmā to reside in the lotus.

It should be understood that because other *tantras* show three [sets of] threads (*tricataṃtra*), the act of worshipping (*pūjayet*) alone implies the worship of the seat (*pīṭhapūjā*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth;

therefore, the reliance on the word "concentrated" (*samāhita*) by those who compose the *Padārthādarśa* for the sake of obtaining those [elements] is indeed useless. This applies to the phrase "in the four directions" (*dikcatuṣkeṣu*).
Without a specific statement to the contrary, no preceptor performs worship out of the prescribed order;
thus, the phrase "in the four cells" applies everywhere up to the Mahīdhara [cell].
Furthermore, the instruction "one should cleanse with a single form" applies everywhere, as does the case of the Brahmakoṣṭha.

Having wiped away the four lines that divide the four squares situated within the eastern group of four squares embraced by the diagonal threads of the *lagna* (ascendant) and the *koṇa* (angles), and having unified them,
one should worship Āryā; likewise, in the four squares situated on the right, one should likewise unify them for Vivasvat.
One should worship Mitra by unifying the four squares connected to the west, and Mahīdhara by unifying the four squares connected to the north; thus five deities have been worshipped.
Then, one should worship Karṇa, who is situated in the four corners starting from the southeast and connected to the Brahma-square.
In the half-cells divided by the lines of the diagram, there are pairs of pairs; therein, according to the downward sequence,
having worshipped Savitṛ or Sāvitra in each single pair of cells, one should worship Śakra in the upper half-cell located in the southwest (nairṛtya),
and Dvaṃdvajaya in the pair of half-cells situated below that, in the northwest (vāyavya).
Having worshipped Rudra in the upper half-cell and Rudrajaya in the pair of half-cells below it,
one should worship Āpa in the pair of cells located in the northeast (īśāna) and Āpavatsaka in the pair of half-cells below that; thus [it is said] "in the pairs of corner-cells."

In the rule "the cleaning of the *raṇeka* and the *karṇasūtra* should be understood as occurring at the middle and the first and last points," since there is an expectation of the *karṇasūtra*, its cleaning is not appropriate; with this intention, it was stated that [it occurs] "in the two pairs of corner squares. Just like the *karṇasūtra* situated in the Brahmā-square, [so too is it] in the Āgneya...
Even when the lines drawn by a single cord through the diagonal squares are erased, there is no deficiency;
rather, it is because of the utility of those lines that run through the corner squares by means of a single cord.
Thus, according to the view of the authors of the *Padārthadarśa* and the *Harṣadīpikā*, who speak in this manner... [the text continues].

The *lagragrantha* (the "clinging thread") attains its integrity; however, others maintain that the worship of Sāvitrī and the others is established by the inherent nature of the root [mantra] through repetition in pairs of half-cells (*ardhakoṣṭha*). Otherwise, they say that one should simply state [the worship occurs] in pairs of corner-cells (*koṇakoṣṭha*).
Now, is it not the case that the worship of Sāvitrī and the others proceeds in an upward-and-downward sequence?

If it is asked what its measure is: consider that one should worship Sāvitra there, having relied upon Dhātṛ and Vahni and having placed three feet below; in the foot known as Rāma, between Vidhi and Sāvitra, one should worship Savitṛ in those three feet; here and even further on, whatever is here...

The phrase beginning with "yam" refers to the interior of the maṇḍala; [it denotes] the space between the directions of Brahmā—also known as Dhātṛ—and Agni, specifically the eastern star of Sāvitra. Between Brahma and Sāvitra, only the word "savitre" is included within the category of what is to be grasped in this context; the same applies to Agni.
Having relied upon the father and the brother and having placed the first three steps below, one should worship the highly fortunate Indra in the step known as *loka*.
Likewise, Indrajaya is to be worshipped between Brahmā and Śakra;
the father is Nirṛti, and Īśa is Rudra—this is the Rudra of that victory.

Dāsaka, Marīci, and Ārpyaka are known as his fathers; the lord of the Rākṣasas is Pāpa, because of the definition given right there starting with "Pāparoga. Likewise, having resorted to Vāyu and Dhātṛ, and having placed three feet below, one should worship the god Rudra there in the world-foot (bhuvana-pada).
Likewise, between Īśa and Vedhas, there is that Jaya in three quarters; since Īśa means Rudra according to the previously stated convention which is followed here as well, "tajjaya" means Rudrajaya.
Similarly, one should worship Āya situated well in the three quarters in the northeast (Īśānī), and then Apavatsa.

In the middle of the *dha* syllable, one should offer *āpavatsa* at the three joints; likewise, for Soma and Savitṛ, red flowers in the square below the southeast corner, and in the square below that,
one should give *kuśa*-water to Savitṛ and yellow rice to Indra in the square below the southwest corner.
One should offer cooked food to Indra in the northeast; to Rudra below that, ghee-cooked food;

and in the lower part of the northwest corner, one should offer meat from a red goat for the Rudra-recitation. Furthermore, in the southwest corner, water is offered, and likewise in its corresponding level, [the offerings are] as before.

Regarding the term *karṇasūtra*: starting from the southeast corner (*āgneya*) and extending up to the Brahma-square, there are three by three corner-squares; the diagonal line (*karṇasūtra*) that falls through their center—within the squares situated to the north and south of that [line], [one writes] "Śarva" and "Guha," and so on, in pairs.

The meaning is that one should worship the eight deities ending with Pūtanā in a double sequence. Regarding the lines drawn in the nine squares, how is it consistent for the author of the *Mūla* to state this, given that you have previously established [the arrangement] up to the central square (*brahmakoṣṭha*) in all the corner cells?
It should not be said [that this is redundant], because such a statement is possible even by taking the "ear-thread" (*karṇasūtra*) as referring to what occurred in the past;
furthermore, it is also possible to say "in both corners and squares," etc.
For the purpose of excluding certain other squares, one must follow the intended meaning (*tātparya*), etc., regarding the ear-thread.

Because it is the same [in application] according to the words of the Sūtra: "sārddhādyaṃta" and so forth; that is, those which exist together with "arddhādyaṃta"—meaning "half-beginning-and-end" (arddha + ādi + anta)—namely, with the two terms "arddhādya" and "arddhānta," are "sārddhādyaṃta"; and those words which are "sārddhādyaṃta" are "sārddhādyaṃtapada. In these [words].

The meaning is that one should worship these thirty-two deities who are about to be mentioned, in groups of eight. First, when the grid has been halved by the diagonal line from corner to corner, Īśāna resides in the half-square situated near the eastern side of the northeast (Īśāna) square; thereafter, in the six squares [following], Parjanya, Jayanta, and Śakra...

The six [deities] beginning with Kratu, Bhāskara, Satya, and Vṛṣa, when halved, are to be worshipped in the intermediate space (antarikṣa) within the half-cells situated near the eastern side of the fiery cell (āgneyakoṣṭha). Then, starting from the half-cell of the fiery corner (agnikoṣṭha) and extending to the half-cell of the southwestern corner (nairṛtyakoṣṭha),
the eight deities beginning with Agni and ending with Mṛga are to be worshipped in the eight cells.

Then, starting from the second half-cell of the southwest (nairṛtya) compartment up to the first half-cell of the northwest (vāyavya) compartment, the eight deities beginning with Nirṛti, the gatekeeper, and ending with Roga should be worshipped. Then, [starting] from the second [half-cell] of the northwest compartment...

The meaning is that the eight deities beginning with Vāyu and ending with Āditya are to be worshipped, starting from the middle square and extending to the first middle square in the northeast; [this is done] with five powders—
white, red, yellow, black, and green— consisting of rice flour, safflower powder, turmeric powder, and so forth.

He states with the words beginning "of the aforementioned" that one should fill the lotuses drawn in the respective locations of the deities with the [substances] to be described hereafter, and there worship those respective deities; furthermore, the method for coloring the lotuses is also to be described later, as it applies to every lotus.
In the *Karaṇa*, it is stated that the station of Brahmā should be filled with reddish dust (*aruṇarajas*), the station of Yama with black dust (*kṛṣṇarajas*),
the station of Īśa with white dust (*śvetarajas*), and the station of Indra with yellow dust (*pītarajas*); thus,
one should fill each respective square in accordance with the colors and other attributes of those particular deities.
With this intention, he said: "Of those mentioned," [meaning] that even the names of the intermediate verses were not grasped.
It appears that Harṣadīpita also accepted this position;
for he stated, beginning with "O Brahmin, the offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) is not for you," that the bali-offering should be made to the Ānantas by means of these mantras.
Then, starting with "atha" and so forth, [he explains] that this is for these fifty-three deities.
Thus, he describes the method for constructing the pavilion on the ground of the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtabhūmi*) with the words beginning "in the lunar mansion" (*nakṣatra*),

and so forth: in lunar mansions such as Aśvinī that are favorable to the practitioner (*sādhya*), such as a disciple, and likewise in zodiac signs such as Aries (*meṣa*) that are of the same nature, and on days such as Sunday (*ravivāra*) that are likewise of the same nature.

The meaning is that one should begin the construction of the Maṇḍapa on a day distinct from Reṣa, Śubha, Rikta, and so forth; and its favorability is twofold: by being in accordance with what is stated in the Jyotiḥśāstra and other sciences, and by the avoidance of prohibited lunar days such as those at birth, the eighth lunar mansion (tārā), the eighth zodiac sign (rāśi), and the current day of the week (vāra).

The second [type of] [lunar day], due to the deficiency of its lunar date and other factors, is to be inferred by oneself; the first, however, is stated in the *Rājamārtaṇḍa*: "When the Sun, the two [asterisms] Rohiṇī and Mṛgaśiras, Hasta, Svāti, Uttarā [Phalgunī], Pūṣā (Puṣya), Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Anurādhā, and the Wind (Svātī) are pure and endowed with auspicious stars..."

The sages declare that on days of the gentle planets, in yogas free from malefic influences, on lunar days devoid of *riktās*, and on days excluding *viṣṭi*, the undertaking of building a house and other such works is auspicious. [The asterisms are: the two Ādityas (Punarvasu), Puṣya, both Citrās, and Maitra (Anurādhā). Tvaṣṭṛ is the deity of the Asura.

Due to the absence of *vata* (wind), being pure—meaning free from conjunction with malefic planets—and being joined with auspicious stars (*sutārā*), as well as being devoid of unfavorable lunar mansions (*tārākṣasa*), portents (*utpāta*), *vajra*, and so forth;
in a yoga distinct from those [inauspicious ones] and characterized by forms such as *ānanda*, *siddhi*, and *śubha*; and on the fourth and ninth days known as *rikta*.

On the fourteenth day, on days other than those [specific ones], on the lunar days (tithis) known as Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā, and on a day free from the *karaṇa* named Bhadrā in the form of Viṣṭi—the inclusion of these six other *karaṇas* has been made. As for the zodiac signs (*rāśis*), they are stated in another work: "Destruction... [text ends].
Astrologers declare that in the signs of Capricorn, Aquarius, and Cancer, there is success in undertakings; in Aries, Libra, and Sagittarius, there is procrastination;
in Virgo, Taurus, and Gemini, there is the certain attainment of wealth;
and in Aquarius, Leo, and Taurus, there is success. (Note: *alikulīrau* refers to Scorpio and Cancer.)

The *dhaṭa*, the balance (*tulā*), the *saṣomīna* [the fish-ritual], the *kalaśa*, and the *kumbha*—these are the methods of purification according to the *Prayogasāra*. Having fashioned a cavity in the ground one span (*vitasti*) wide, one should place that earth within it; when those [other substances] have been added, it becomes auspicious provided they are equal in quantity.
One should know the middling [type] among those that are deficient; it is called the lowest. Having thus examined with effort, one should avoid inferior ground.
In the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra* it is said: "Cracked ground causes death; saline soil destroys wealth; ground with hidden thorns (or stakes) constantly gives rise to affliction; poisonous [ground]..."

Likewise, earth that flows toward the northeast causes fear from enemies; earth flowing toward the east certainly bestows wealth upon the builder; earth flowing toward the north grants boons; and earth flowing toward the southeast brings about enmity, death, and disease. In any other direction than these, the flow of earth [is auspicious].

This ground is undesirable for the builder; thus, according to the *Mahākāpila-pañcarātra*, in the manner of extracting the "thorn" (*śalya*) at the commencement of constructing a temple or similar structure, the practitioner should touch the limbs [of the site], and the wise man should place a firm "thorn" within the body of the *vāstu* deity at that point. Wherever...

It is implied that the absence of a "thorn" (śalya) in the *Ṛṣākaraṇa* [nakṣatra] must be ascertained; thus it is said by implication: "If a man scratches his head, one should extract the thorn from the head; a thorn should be known to exist there if, while digging three cubits [deep], fire, burning, disease, or loss of wealth occurs."

If a thorn is produced [in the body], one should extract it with effort if one desires success for oneself. If the *ūrūka* (thigh) is itching, one should indicate an iron mortar; if it remains for two cubits (*hasta*), it bestows longevity, but if it is extracted, it brings death. If the *ūrūka* is itching, one should indicate bell-metal (*kāṃsya*).

If one scratches with one hand, there will be a sting [from a thorn] and the loss of reputation due to a wicked wife; if scratching both hands, one should predict a skeleton-thorn (kaṅkāla-śalya). If scratching with three hands, there will be a fire-sting, pain in the thighs, and death; if scratching the back, it indicates a shoulder-thorn (bāhu-śalya).
If [the patient] scratches with one hand, it indicates a foreign object; if the feet are itching, it portends the death of the master;

if the hand is itching, one should diagnose a splinter as the foreign object; if [the itch] persists for half a cubit, it causes punishment by the king and the like; and if the belly is itching, one should point to a stone as the foreign object.
If one scratches the knee with a measurement of two cubits,
one should predict a splinter of ash; according to your stated characteristics,
there will be a burn from fire, mental anguish, affliction, suffering, and fear.
"One should extract the thorn from such karma. By digging down to the water's edge, or by digging even a single cubit (*hasta*), the extraction of all thorns occurs;
as it is said: "While being dug, until the water [is reached], the fault of the thorn is destroyed," [digging] five cubits deep.

For the sake of pacifying the defects of the "thorn" (śalya), one should first extract the thorn and then fill it up level; this examination, however, extends as far as the area measured by the *nivartana*, and a *daṇḍa* should be ten cubits (*hasta*) long, while a *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas*.
Regarding the term *ratna*, those learned in the tradition maintain it means "further examination from above.
There is also another method for purifying the ground mentioned in another tantra: "The earth that is white is considered Brāhmaṇī;
the earth that is red is considered Kṣatriyā; the yellow one should be known as Vaiśyā; and the black one is proclaimed as Śūdrā."
Likewise, the Brāhmaṇī soil has the scent of ghee; the Kṣatriyā is made fragrant with blood—blood meaning *rudhira*;

the Vaiśyā should have the scent of alkaline matter (*kṣāra*); and the Śūdrā has the scent of raw flesh (*viḍ*). Likewise, the Brāhmaṇī ground is sweet; the Kṣatriyā is known to be astringent (*kaṣāya*); the Vaiśyā should be understood as sour (*amla*); and the Śūdrā ground is pungent (*kaṭuka*). Furthermore, the Brāhmaṇī soil is endowed with *kuśa* grass, while the Kṣatriyā...

If [the earth] is filled with arrows, filled with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass, and filled with various weeds belonging to the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, then regarding that state, it is said: white, reddish, yellow, and black [soils] are recommended for the Brāhmaṇas and the others [in order]. That which has a scent equal to clarified butter (*ājya*), blood, alkaline salt (*kṣāra*), or wine—meaning that it is likewise recommended for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras respectively. Furthermore, that which is sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent is also [recommended].

"Excellence for the Brahmins and others," as before; having thus conducted an examination by means of form, taste, and smell, he demonstrates excellence through connection with other substances such as *kuśa* grass and so forth: "that which is prepared with *kuśa*, *śara*, *kāśa*, and *dūrvā* grasses"—here too [the same applies].

As before, it is prescribed that for the four castes beginning with the Brahmins, [the ground] should be excellent in sequence; "dūrvā" (durva grass) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for places abounding in various types of grass. Now, if one asks: in the case of a collection of various characteristics, does she possess the status of a Brahmin woman, or rather the status of a Kṣatriya woman and so forth?
"You are mistaken; for we do not employ a definition of caste (*jāti*) such that a confusion of castes would result.

Rather, we use such a mere designation for the purpose of designating a ground suitable for the castes of Brāhmaṇas and so forth. Thus, when two or three definitions coincide, [one is designated] as a Brāhmaṇa..."

In that regard, there would be a loss of the desire for accomplishment due to the lack of conformity to two or three [of the] castes. However, in the Gautama Saṃhitā, it is stated that land is to be accepted as common to all castes simply by virtue of its being Brahmin-owned (*brāhmaṇī*), for the sake of accomplishing all goals; thus, it is not [limited] to the Kṣatriya.

"O Sage, she who bestows the three kingdoms, who produces wealth and grain, and who is not censured as being of the Vaiśya or Śūdra class—having thus understood this, one should examine the ground: it should be auspiciously sloping toward the east and north, free of thorns, covered with *śatāvarī* grass, and well-saturated with water. While [the ground] is being filled...
Furthermore, that earth which is auspicious when more than a *khārī* in measure, where a heap of flowers does not wither,
where a lamp does not go out, and where water does not evaporate quickly—
that earth is common to all castes (*varṇas*). Thus it is said.

The meaning is: "having caused the *puṇyāhavācana* (the recitation for an auspicious day) to be performed through a Brāhmaṇa"—that is, having performed that specific rite known as *puṇyāhavācana*. Regarding the question of how one should perform this [construction] mentioned in the phrase "one should construct," he says "with five," etc., because the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.

Because there is no difference [in this regard], it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "Now we shall describe the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) as declared by Brahmā; it is remembered as being of three kinds according to superior, middling, and inferior measurements.
Now, a pavilion made with five cubits is the smallest, while one made with seven [cubits] is the middling.
The meaning of the root text must be stated as "he [is] praised by those nine," because a word's natural power lies precisely in its capacity to convey that meaning;
however, that is not possible, since the author of the root text himself has stated that Agni is to be described as being within the nine pits (*kuṇḍa*). Furthermore, those [pits] are also three...

For even in the case of the most excellent [shrines] equipped with three girdles and so forth, it is impossible for them to be accommodated within a pavilion of nine cubits, as there would be no space for the seating places of the Hotṛ and other priests.

If it is argued that there is a great contradiction between the earlier and later texts regarding the fifth enclosure (mekhalā) being far away from the middle and lower pavilions (maṇḍapa), as well as the [mention of] the *pakṣa* and *pratyāśeti*, then here the author of the *Padārthādarśa* [states]: "Combined with five and seven... [and so forth].
The smallest pavilion consists of twelve hands; the middle pavilion is formed by five and nine, totaling fourteen hands;
and the largest is formed by seven and nine, totaling sixteen hands. Thus it is said.

This meaning is consistent with other tantras; as it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra* and other works: "Alternatively, a pavilion twelve cubits in width is known as the smallest (*kaniṣṭha*); likewise, a pavilion of sixteen cubits shall be the best (*uttama*) here. It is also stated elsewhere regarding the smallest, middling, and largest [dimensions].

The authors of the *Haṣadīpikā* state that the pavilions (maṇḍapas) should begin with a width of one cubit and increase by two cubits for each subsequent one, such that all remaining pavilions are auspicious; however, they explain that the word "interval" (*antara*) refers to the altar (*vedi*),
which will be described as being constructed from one-third of the pavilion's width.

The meaning is that one should construct a pavilion whose middle portion, in the form of an altar (*vedi*), has an interval measured at five cubits; likewise for the fire-altar (*agni*). Furthermore, the smallest [pavilion] is fifteen cubits, and the middling is twenty-one cubits.
It is said that the altar (*vedi*) should be made with a third of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), which results in it being twenty-seven cubits for the best [size]; others, however, do not accept this,
stating that the best measurement is either twenty-four cubits or twenty cubits.
In the scriptural passage you have cited—beginning with "That which is sixteen cubits, or twelve cubits, is declared to be the medium;
that which is eight or ten [cubits] is called the lowest"—such a measurement is not mentioned; therefore, it does not accord with other tantras.

This pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be square; its measurement is square according to the Kātyāyana Sūtra, which states that "other [dimensions] may be as directed. The height of the pavilion should follow either twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) from the ground or one cubit (hasta). As it is stated in the Siddhānta:

In the *Mahākapiḷapañcarātra*, the site for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is said to be one *sthala* (unit) high, measuring twelve *aṅgulas*; its height should be one cubit (*hasta*), perfectly level and very beautiful.
Furthermore, these pavilions are not to be used simultaneously because they serve a single purpose; there is only one [pavilion] required.

Nor is there an option (*vikalpa*), because of the principle that things which serve the same purpose cannot be employed simultaneously, and because there is an absence of equal effort and expenditure [in both cases]; rather, there is a relationship of primary and secondary alternatives (*mukhyānukalpa*). Thus, according to such statements as "The capable [should follow] the first alternative," it is only for one who is unable to perform the first [alternative] that [the secondary follows] subsequently.

By this, it should be understood that the doubt raised by the author of the *Padārthādarśa*— namely, that since the goal is accomplished even in the smallest pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), there would be no performance of the medium and largest pavilions— is also refuted; for where the status of "best," "smallest," and so forth exists...

Since the distinction between the heavy and light [syllables] has been stated there by means of a non-laryngeal sound (*nakaṇṭharava*), one should determine the relative degree of the fruit (*phalatāratamya*) right there; and having thus fallen into the removal of the objection regarding impossibility, it must be understood by oneself that even through this [principle], "because it is a part of the same conceptualization as the Vedic text" (*arthādvāk kalpanaikadeśatvāt*), conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is also a part of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Because it accepts [the status of] being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*), and so forth; thus [it has been] stated that it is "joined with sixteen pillars.

Regarding that, in order to dispel the expectation as to at which location and how many of what kind are situated, [the author] states "four [are] by way of... and so forth. Among those sixteen pillars...

The meaning is that four pillars, each eight cubits long, should be placed in the four corners of the pavilion— beginning from the southeast— in the manner to be described for the altar (*vedi*) situated in the center;
one should install pillars whose nature corresponds to the Vedas in the corners of the altar, starting from the southeast.
Because it is seen in other tantras that [the sequence] must proceed exactly in this order, in other cases as well— such as when erecting a pillar,
laying a stone foundation, or joining threads and stakes— the commencement of the rite for preparing the pit by digging begins with the fire-god (Agni).
Regarding the passage beginning with "eight cubits" and so forth, up to sixteen cubits...

With reference to the pavilion (maṇḍapa), it is stated in the Pañcarātra: "The pillars, numbering five times the number of the Vedas [twenty], should be half the height of the pavilion and provided with finials. Regarding the word "on both sides" (abhitah), there are two pillars for each door; thus, at the doors of the four directions, there are eight pillars. In the four [corners]...

The meaning is that one should place twelve pillars around each of these [mandapas]. All of these [pillars] are indeed five cubits (hasta) each; by this, it is stated that the height of the twelve pillars is one-third of the mandapa's [dimensions], according to the *Harṣadīpikā*.

Although all of this is intended for the lowest type of pavilion (*adhamamaṇḍapa*), since that lowest pavilion measures fifteen cubits (*hasta*) and the middle pillars are to be installed at half that dimension, it would be more appropriate to state that they measure seven and a half cubits, rather than eight.

Even so, because the difference is slight, it is designated in that manner; nor is this slight difference itself a defect, for the method shown in the *Padārthadarśa* is accepted as the basis here. This being so, [the objection] that "there is not even a slight difference" is likewise [refuted].

Nevertheless, even in the case of external pillars being five cubits in height, the acceptance of the third part of the pavilion [as their base] is unavoidable, because the slight discrepancy [in measurement] is difficult to avoid; for in this matter, that slight discrepancy does not exist, as the third part of a pavilion five cubits lower than five [cubits] is itself five [cubits].
It should be understood that [the pillars] originate from the gods Hasti, Stambha, Īśu, Saura, and Deva.
They are "without flaws," meaning devoid of defects; "firm" (dṛḍhāḥ); and "straight" (ṛjavaḥ), meaning free from curvature. As it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"One should make the pillars fashioned from wood firm, straight, and even."

For the work of pillars, bamboo, *vakra*, or *kramuka* from sacrificial trees should be used; other pure trees may also be employed, but no other species of plants. Likewise, a pillar that is pierced by thorns, naturally dried up, crooked, grown from an old site, or produced from an inauspicious location must be rejected.
Regarding the phrase "one-fifth of that": for whichever pillar—whether it be eight cubits or five cubits in height—one must perform the digging;
having divided that [pillar] into five parts, one should bury the fifth part in the ground, while the four parts remain above ground as the height.
The meaning is "they should be. "On all sides of that" means on all sides of that pavilion;

the word "except for the doors" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the absence of coconut leaves and such, one should cover it with mats. As it is said: "Having covered [the pavilion] with excellent mats for the sake of victory... (Vijayā-maṇḍapa).
Likewise, one should decorate the pavilion (maṇḍapa) on all sides with branches of the Ārdrā tree;

by the words beginning with "at the doors" (dvāreṣu), he demonstrates the erection of the archway pillars (toraṇastambha). By this much, one should construct four doors from the fifth part [of the measurement]; according to the Pañcarātra, it should be the smallest [size].

The gate for the medium and superior [mandalas] increases by four finger-breadths. Thus, for the gates in the east and other directions respectively, one should fix the pillars of the archways (toraṇa) made from Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vararūpa (Śirīṣa) milky trees;
having a height of seven cubits, one should bury them with a fifth part [of that height]. Five...

One should place a portion of earth upon the ground; this is the rule common to all, according to the statement in the Śilpaśāstra. Regarding the sequence: the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees should be established in their own directions starting from the east, or alternatively, in reverse order from the end.

The meaning of the fourth quarter is as follows: first, a banyan tree (*vaṭa*) should be placed in the location of the *plakṣa*, and subsequently, a *plakṣa* tree should be placed in the location of the banyan. Furthermore, an archway (*toraṇa*) made of *nyagrodha* wood is prescribed for the east, one of *udumbara* for the south, one produced from *aśvattha* for the west, and an archway of *plakṣa* for the north.

In accordance with the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, the first alternative is established; for it is seen there, in agreement with that very text, that "the Plakṣa tree was produced in the south and the Nyagrodha in the north. Furthermore, in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*, it is stated that the gods are stationed in the form of arches (*toraṇa*) at the sacrifice.
In the pavilion, for the purpose of destroying obstacles and for protection, one should place trees:
a *nyagrodha* in the east, an *udumbara* in the south, a *pippala* in the west, and a *plakṣa* in the north;
furthermore, a very beautiful tree should be placed in the east, and the *Ṛgveda* and other [Vedas] in the southeast.

One should place the one named Subhadra in the south with the mantra "tritaṃ iṣetva," and the one named Sukarman in the west with the Sāmaveda and others; one should place Suhotra in the north with the mantra "śanno devī," and [the one named] Sāma with the Ṛgveda and others using the mantra "agnim īle."
Regarding what was stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī* concerning the mantra beginning with "agnāyāhi":
"One should install the eastern arch with the mantra 'agnimīle'; one should install the southern arch with the mantra 'iṣetvorje';
and [one should install] the western [arch] with the mantra 'agnāyāhi'."
One should place the northern arch with the mantra "veśanaṃ śanno devī" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.4.45.2).
Furthermore, this placement of the arches should be made one cubit outside the doors of the pavilion;
for it is seen in another mantra that [the placement] is at a distance of one cubit from the exterior of the pavilion doors, according to the sequence of the directions.

"One should cause these doors to be made for each direction of the mandapa using branches of the Nyagrodha, Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Raśā trees"— this is the statement from the *Vāstuśāstra*. However, while the arches (*toraṇas*) are designated as "doors" by implication, they possess the nature of doors only in proximity to the actual doors.
Because they are being constructed [from wood], this [designation] for these milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) is figurative.
Regarding the specific rule when none of these are available, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "In the absence of one of these, there should be the *śamī* tree;
in its absence, the *jaṃbu*, *khadira*, *sāra*, *tāla*, or *toraṇa* tree is prescribed."

"Those [arches] with seven cubits" refers to the intention regarding the supreme pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); however, for the middling and inferior [pavilions], he says "separately, separately," meaning they are distinct according to the different types of pavilions.
Thus, in that case, the height of the archway pillars (*toraṇastambha*) is six cubits for the middling and five cubits for the inferior.
The meaning is that these [dimensions] are to be accepted as the standard measure.

The circumference (pariṇāha) or width of those arch-pillars (toraṇastambha) should be made ten finger-breadths (aṅgula). Above the pair of arch-pillars, there should be a horizontal plank measuring three finger-breadths for the purpose of mounting the trident (triśūla).

In some places, it is provided together with a middle section; its measurement is stated by the words beginning with "tiryak" (horizontally), etc. This means that according to the vertical measurement of the pillars for the archway (*toraṇa*) of the lowest pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), which is two and a half cubits (*sārdhadvihasta*), there are five [parts] for the pillars of the archway of the lowest pavilion.

The path following the *Padārthādarśa* holds that [the width] was previously stated; however, according to the author of the *Harṣadīpikā*, by means of a measurement equal to half the size of the archway (*toraṇa*) of the excellent pavilion (*maṇḍapī*), which was described as being seven cubits high,
the horizontal [width] consists of three and a half cubits.

Regarding the length of the cross-beams (phalaka), they say that for each archway (toraṇa) in the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), the length of the respective horizontal beam of that archway is equal to half the height of its pillar; this is the meaning established by the inherent force of the root text. The use of the plural "śūlāni" (pillars/pegs) refers to each individual archway.
Since four tridents are completed by means of making one trident for each of the four gates, the use of the singular form "toraṇam" (archway) is justified with reference to the genus; therefore,
one trident should be fashioned upon each horizontal beam of every archway.

The fruit [of this] is that it should be made from wood for the arch (toraṇa) measuring nine fingers; furthermore, whatever trident (triśūla) is upon the arch, that too should be understood as being made of that same wood. Therein, three fingers' breadth is the insertion within the cavity. Thus it is stated in the Kriyā[pāda].

"Tridents with hands extend throughout their entirety"; thus, having constructed the arches (toraṇas) in this manner, one should place three voids (śūnyas) above. The length of the trident is one finger-breadth (aṅgula), and its width is one-fourth of that.
Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "The tridents are upon the fillet (paṭṭikā) in the middle portion between the two fires."
In the Piṅgalāmata, it is stated that the door-frames should be marked with tridents at their tops;

the central prong should be straight, while the two side-prongs should be slightly curved. Both of these are designated as being one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in width, and they should be fixed such that they extend for the length of a cubit (hasta). This refers to the three-pronged trident used in the construction of the [door] trident.
With the intention of forming a collection of parts (*yarūpa-samudāya*), one should fix nine new finger-breadths (*navanava-aṅgula*) for each trident-prong (*śūla*),

and having fashioned the other two as the central season-element (*madhyastha-ṛtubhūta*), one should achieve a total measure of twenty-seven finger-breadths for the collection; then, having inserted a hole of three finger-breadths, the remainder is twenty-four finger-breadths.
The statement that "each single trident, when combined, measures one cubit (hastamātra) in its bulbous base (gulātmaka)" refers to the heart [of the trident];

and although it is to be inserted into a hole measuring only one finger-breadth (ekāṅgulamātra), the expression "one should plant it three finger-breadths deep" intends to refer to the aggregate [of the parts]. Furthermore, the word "cubit" (hasta) is used even for the crown [of the trident].

The author of the *Mevavyākhyeya* (Padārthādarśaka) also adopted this very position; and Harṣadīkṣita states that for all tridents, the base portion entering the cavity [of the pedestal] is one cubit less than the total height. However, this is intended for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śaivas; in the case of Vaiṣṇavas, however—

The specific detail is as follows: on the tops of the arches (*toraṇas*), one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus by means of a twelve-part division starting from the east in clockwise order;

these [symbols] should be made of the same wood as those [arches]. On the tops of those arches, [the symbols] should be made of the wood of the arches, with a length equal to the twelfth part of the arch, consisting of the conch, discus, and so forth.

The meaning is that it is to be placed in the directions starting from the east and south, following the sequence of the directions. This very point is the authority for the tridents also being made of *toraṇa* wood; for according to the maxim that "as far as the material is concerned, [the rule] is based on scriptural statement," there is a scriptural statement regarding the production of [the trident] for the purpose of making the conch and so forth.

It should not be said that there is a lack of authoritative evidence for the application of the trident; rather, because one adopts a prescribed method in another location based on one's own inclination, disregarding the lack of restriction [in the original], it is precisely appropriate that there be a restriction. Regarding the phrase "in the directions," the characteristic of the banner is stated at the end of the Tantra: "The banners are five cubits long."
In length and breadth they should be two cubits (*dvihastaka*), and the staff should be ten cubits; one should place them in the ten directions.

According to the *Kriyāsāra*, one should decorate the exterior with banners ten cubits long, and in the eight directions starting from the east, one should sequentially establish eight banners. Of these...

The width of the middle [section] should be two cubits, equal to the width of the wheel; one should fashion the pinnacle and the tail to be half that width. Upon these, one should depict—in due order and according to rule—an elephant, a goat, a buffalo, a lion, a fish, a deer, a horse, and a bull in the center of the banner. Now...

"One should depict on the banners the eight elephants of the quarters, with Airāvata at their head, along with the aforementioned minerals and according to their characteristics. Thus, the installation of the banners is essential; O Brahmin, if the pavilion is devoid of banners, then all the worship, fire-offerings, and other rites shall be in vain.

Just as whatever recitation (japa) and other rites are performed by the wise perish for the owner of the field without protection, and just as a temple perishes entirely without a banner, so too do the cruel Viṣṇupāriṣadas known as the Kūṣmāṇḍas and others seize the worship and other offerings.

Because the *Ahiśīrṣa-pañcarātra* states, "One who himself does not have the banner," and so forth, and because it is heard that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for failing to do so, the word "banner" (*dhvaja*) is also indicative of a "flag" (*patākā*).
Thus, [the text says]: "The Guru should cause a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) to be constructed, joined with flags and banners."
The definition of these [banners] has been stated by Somaśambhu based on the *Siddhāntaśekhara* and other texts:
"The banners (*patākā*) should be seven cubits long and twenty finger-breadths wide;
the staffs (*daṇḍa*) for the banners should be ten cubits long and fixed at the fifth part [of their length]; the banners are [to be adorned] with perfumes and flowers."

"Endowed with" means they are fixed in the ground at a depth equal to one-fifth of their own height; these are the weapons of the guardians of the directions themselves, as they are inscribed upon the banners of those very deities' mounts. And "canopy" (*vitāna*) is a synonym for *candrātapa* (a circular shade).
One should collect items such as the wrapping of the pillars of the pavilion with *ādinādu* silk cloths, as well as *dūrvā* grass garlands strung on threads;
as it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Abounding with garlands of mango sprouts, adorned with canopies, and covered with variegated cloths."
One should construct a pavilion adorned with rows of pillars, various kinds of fruits, edible offerings, mirrors, and chowries,
as well as bells, hanging garlands, and so forth;
for it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra* that there is no fault regarding the dimensions of the pavilion being either less or more than prescribed.

If the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is crooked in shape due to the [faulty] means of construction, or if it is too large or too small, it will bring about the death of the performer; thus, he teaches the method of constructing the altar (vedī) in the middle of the pavilion with the verse beginning "tantribhāga" and so forth, regarding that pavilion.

The meaning is that one should construct a square altar (*vedi*) at the middle portion, which is the third part of the central line. Then, one should determine the lines of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) as threefold;
according to another tantra, the sacrificial altar (*vidikā*) is said to be in its middle part, proceeding in order from the east and so forth.
"From the agreement [of the sources], 'elevated by one *aratni*' means it is one cubit (*hasta*) high;
as stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
'Elevated by one cubit and wide on all sides by four cubits'; and in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: 'With bricks, with clay...'"
One who desires the accomplishment of the ritual should fashion [the altar] resembling the palm of a hand or the belly, with the height of a *rājahastra*.

A *rājahastra* is a cubit measured from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. According to the *Kriyāsāra*, having made the pavilion one-third [of the required size], [one should perform the rites] in the central portion.
The sacrificial altar (vedī) should be one cubit in measure, elevated, square, and level on all sides.

It should be made firm with either baked or unbaked bricks; such an altar is best. In the absence of those, it may even be made of clay, provided it is smooth and free from the marks of a wheel's rim.

Regarding the phrase "resembling the belly of a crab," since the term *aratni* is employed by Kātyāyana and others, it is likewise stated here. Furthermore, in the *Kādima-tantra*, after defining the finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), it is said: "By four of those [finger-breadths] there is a fist (*muṣṭi*); a span (*vitasti*) is made by three [of those]."
"By eight [units] it would be an *aratni*; by two of those, O Śivā, it would be a *brahma* on both sides.

To the question, "What is to be done after this has been made known? he says, "For the mandala," meaning for the purpose of constructing the *sarvatobhadra* and other mandalas that will be described there.

If it is asked, "What is the fruit of that [altar] as well?"—no; for the fruit of that is precisely the worship of the chosen deity upon it, which will be described later. Even if there is a deficiency or excess in the altar (*vedikā*), a fault is stated in that very same place: "That which is crooked, low on the sides, or depressed in the middle..."

Having thus described the construction of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) along with its ancillaries— [a pavilion] which is beautiful in six ways, free from defects in measurement, and which destroys the karma of the one who performs it through this much of a discourse—
one now describes another rite called *Aṅkurārpaṇa* (the offering of sprouts), which is auspicious for all virtuous undertakings.

He explains what is to be undertaken for the sake of excellence with the words "prāgeva" (beforehand) and so forth: one should perform the rite called *aṅkurārpaṇa* (the offering of sprouts) on the seventh day prior to the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*), counting from that point; what is this [rite] other than a subsidiary part?
He says "for the sake of all prosperity" (*sarvasaṃpattyai*) to indicate that its non-performance does not obstruct the primary fruit.
Thus, the sense is that by non-performance there is a deficiency in the constituent parts (*aṅga-vaikalya*), whereas by performance there is an excellence of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya-atiśaya*).
This will be explained in the seventh [chapter] regarding the subsequent fortnights.
The definition stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* is as follows: "In the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), ritual bathing (*snāpana*),
and likewise in festivals (*utsava*), in the rite of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) for the sake of pacification (*śānti*),
in marriage (*vivāha*), and in the binding of the sacred thread (*mauñjibandhana*), the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) must be performed in all auspicious rites."

The sowing of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should take place on the ninth, seventh, fifth, or third day prior to the day of the rite; or it may be performed immediately (*sadyas*) on the very day of the auspicious observance such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), for it is said that "the sacrifice of the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura-yajña*) should be performed right there."

According to the statement in the *Kapila-pañcarātra*, this offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should be performed on the day prior to the day of one's own ritual practice, preceded by the *nāndī-śrāddha* and having fasted; as it is stated in another *tantra*: "The Guru, being pure, [should perform it] seven days before the initiation."

On the day preceding the fast, one should perform the auspicious sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha, and the recitation of the Svasti-mantras; indeed, one should carry out all these according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra on that very day of fasting which serves as the preliminary for the sowing of seeds.
In response to the inquiry as to where this rite is to be performed, he says "in the pavilion" (*maṇḍape*) and so forth:

in the northern part of the previously described pavilion, one should construct a long rectangular enclosure (*gūḍhā*), ten cubits in length according to measurement, extending east-west, and five cubits in width.

The meaning is that one should construct a hall (*śālā*) enclosed by walls and so forth, protected from the wind, with a door on the south side. A hall measuring twenty cubits in length and ten cubits in width, characterized by the aforementioned definitions, is the best type of hall.

Since they are not useful for the present context, the authors of the *Padārthadarśana* and others have adopted the middle position here; however, others maintain that the highest position is indeed that which pertains to those who possess the capacity (*samartha*),
for the connection with the fruit occurs only for those who are capable, and not for others.

In that case, for those who are incapable [of attaining the goal] through the middle path, it is taught by the Omniscient Ones that even for those incapable there, [the result] comes from the lower path alone. Likewise, in the absence of a purpose, how could those who are capable obtain the fruit from another [inferior] position? It would not be so.

We understand that if the phrase "the middle hall" (*madhyamā śālā*) is intended as a distinction from the "great hall" (*mahatī śālā*), then the enumeration [of the halls] is purposeful and consistent with reason. However, if—
as is perceived according to the literal hearing— this is merely a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of the hall, then even so, [the same applies].
It has been stated that "one should consider it possible to do so"; now, he describes the manner of constructing that hall (*śālā*) with the words beginning "five cubits" (*pañcahasta*), etc.
In the middle portion of the hall, one cord (*sūtra*) measuring five cubits should be stretched from east to west.
Then, having left a space of twelve finger-breadths on each side,
one should place two lines on the right flank; thereafter, having likewise set aside an interval of twelve finger-breadths on the left flank as well, one should place two lines there.
Then, intersecting those five lines, one should leave an interval of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) between each and, by laying down eleven lines at intervals of two cubits (hastas) each,
one should draw eleven lines; thus, there will be forty squares.
The meaning is "they become. He states the subsequent procedure:
"one should sweep," which connects to "one should sweep four paths in the form of a row";
the words "on the ground" (*vāhyasthā*) are to be supplied as the remainder. Thus, one should first [sweep] one path consisting of four squares from the east.
Having cleared the outer pathway by marking eight squares on the south, four squares on the west, and eight squares on the north, one should then, within the remaining four sets of four squares,
mark the fourth and fifth rows on both sides of the central set of four squares.

One should erase those two paths consisting of two squares situated on the two sides—the eastern and western portions—of the central [square]. By this, three groups of four [squares] remain, separated by each individual path; such is the meaning. Those squares...
Having quickly reached the station of Īśāna with white, yellow, reddish-brown,
and white powders and conquered [the directions], one should color the paths (vīthīs) all around with dark-colored powder;
however, all the boundary lines (sīmā-rekhās) must be made white— thus says the Harṣadīpikā.

The author, who reveals the meaning of the words, has not intended here a sequence beginning with the North (Iśāna) and so forth by means of the wise term "crest" (*mauli*); rather, the filling [of the mandala] is to be done with white, yellow, red, and black powders according to the sequence starting from the northwest (*vāyavya*), southeast (*āgneya*), southwest (*nairṛtya*), and northeast (*aiśāna*).

They say that [the sequence] beginning with fire (Agni) and ending with Śarvāntaka is indicated by the syllables *rī*, *ya*, *mi*, and *ti*—namely yellow, reddish, white, and black respectively—for each successive step, in accordance with the statement of the Teacher (*ācārya*). Furthermore, due to their dark-green color from green dust, the shallow bowls (*śarāva*) placed upon the offering vessels (*pālikā*) are indeed somewhat... [thick/tall].

The three types of vessels (*pālikā*) and so forth, joined with three mouths and five faces, are what is denoted by the term "five-faced" (*pañcamukhī*). Regarding the phrase "in fourfold order," the meaning is that each of the three—beginning with the *pālikā*—should consist of four units. The *pālikā* is the embodiment of Viṣṇu, while the five-faced vessel is the embodiment of Śiva.
By stating "Rāva is of the nature of Brahmā," the Ācārya has indicated that their worship should be performed;
however, in the root text, the sequence of Brahmā and Śiva was not intended to be expressed.
Thus, it is stated in the Sārasvata Tantra regarding the white sacrificial threads: "One should write Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Vidhi [Brahmā] upon the white threads."
Regarding the height of these three vessels, beginning with the *pālikā*,

the measurements are sixteen, twelve, and eight *aṅgulas* respectively; however, there is no fault if these measurements cannot be obtained, and one may employ the *pālikā* and the others according to whatever measurement is available.
According to the *Diti-siddhānta-śekhara*, having washed the auspicious [threads] and purified them by that washing,
one should [place] a triple-threaded cord (*triguṇa-sūtra*) upon the *darbha* grass;
as will be described later, starting from the west, thus forming a row in the western four squares.

The meaning is that one should place a set of four glass vessels (kāca) in the middle group of four, a set of four five-faced [vessels] in the eastern group of four, and a set of four arrow-cups (śarāva) in the [remaining] group; therein, within each individual group of four,
the placement of the vessels follows the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneya), neither by one's own whim nor according to mere convention.

According to the statement in the *Prayogasāra*, "One should place the vessels individually in the four [corners] starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending with the southeast (Agni)," one should place them in the west and the east,
and then in the directions beginning from the west.
Since authorities sometimes accept the mention of a name by means of a single part of that name— as seen in such expressions as "the seat beginning with u,
jā, p, ū, k, etc."— and since it has been accepted even by [the author] himself [in the passage] "one should place the vessels in the west and so forth,
and in the southeast and so forth," [this is established].

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that even from the very root, this meaning emerges; by the word "maulena" (by the root), the status of being a preceptor (*deśika*) is indicated. According to the sequence of placement, one should perform the filling, removal of seeds, and so forth; "karīṣam" refers to dried cow dung.
The filling should be performed everywhere by first using cow-dung powder, then sand, and then earth; this earth should not be any ordinary kind,
but rather [earth] accompanied by festivities such as dance and song, and [conveyed] by elephants, chariots, horses, and so forth.

Having gone to the bank of a river, the shore of a lake, or near a flower garden, one should sweep a pure patch of ground there with *darbha* grass, sprinkle it with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and worship the earth by means of the *namas-mantra*,
preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, honoring it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having dug the ground with that spade and taken earth with the mantra "Vāmadeva," she placed it in a bronze vessel, purified it with the Astra-mantra, covered it with a cloth,
brought it near the pavilion, circumambulated it, and entered therein.

In that case, only such clay should be taken; the authority for this is to be understood from the *Siddhāntaśekhara* and other sources. One who knows the method of purification should wash it with the nine-fold nectar-seed mantra (*amṛtabīja*) and the water-seed mantra (*sudhāvīja*), preceded by washing with water.

The washing consists of using milk and the juices of the *kaṇḍu* plant; having thus washed those seeds with water and milk, as stated in the *Sārasvata-tantra*, they should be consecrated (*abhimantrita*) with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*). Since no specific number for the recitation is mentioned, [the standard count applies].

This is the scope of the statement from the *Kapila-pañcarātra*: "One should recite the *Vāja-peya* [mantra] eight thousand times, omitting the unaccented syllables. The five sounds are the mṛdaṅga, the paṭaha, the hand-drum (*āḍambara*), the mouth-instrument (*mukhavādya*), and the conch (*śaṅkha*). One should offer these; thus, all ten [elements] will be described hereafter.

The meaning is that, having unified [the grains] at night, one should pour them into those vessels while facing either east or north, using the root mantra. As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Facing either east or north, one should sow all the seeds with the primary seed-mantra."

In the sequence beginning with Nipālikā, Soma is the lord of the seeds; therefore, one should offer them at night. Even according to the opinion of Sārasvata, because the seeds and the deities possess splendor during the night, for that reason the Guru [should perform the rite] at night with the seeds.

The phrase "he should sow whatever [seeds]" indicates the types of seeds with the words beginning with "rice" (*śāli*); *śāli* refers to winter grains; *śyāmāka* refers to millet, well-known in the vernacular as *sāṃvā*; and *āḍhakī* refers to the pigeon pea, well known as *arahar̤ī*.

Niṣpāva is another synonym for vallā and śiṃvā; Rāmacandra states that niṣpāva refers to rājamāṣa. However, the author of the Padārthādarśa maintains that this [identification] is not appropriate, based on the scriptural injunction: "One should avoid niṣpāvas and rājamāṣas when the deity has fallen asleep."
In the opinion of Sārasvata, the worship of the deities for each seed is prescribed as follows: Skanda in *priyaṅgu*, Vāyu in *niṣpāva*, Agni in *kulattha*, Nirṛti in *āḍhakī*, Soma in *mudga*,
Vaivasvata (Yama) in sesame, Prajāpati in śāli rice, and Nara in mustard seeds.
"One should worship him on the twelfth day, and on the fourteenth day, O Daughter of the Mountain, one should worship Varuṇa.

Thus, beginning from the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), the worship of Soma must also be performed daily until the day of the *adhivāsana* concludes; one should constantly worship Soma until the end of the *adhivāsana* day.

Regarding the statement, "When the sixth day has arrived, the Guru should cause the Soma to be removed," the term "adhivāsa-day" refers to the primary day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) for initiation (*dīkṣā*). However, in the phrase "starting from the adhivāsa-day," that same term refers to the day of installing the *pālikā* vessels and so forth.
Thereafter, with the words "hariḥ śadbhiḥ," one performs the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*). Regarding the sprinkling preceded by mantras, the mantra is found in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Obeisance, obeisance to Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, to Śiva, to the foremost of all worlds, to the eternal one. [Then] the scattering...

"By means of this mantra, one should cause rain to fall daily upon the crops mixed with turmeric powder"— this is connected with the subsequent phrase "one should cause rain to fall" by means of this mantra; the modification [of the mantra] is clearly stated in the root text as being by the root mantra itself.
In the *Padārthādarśa*, this meaning is stated by the word "deśika" (the instructor);
it has been declared by the [author] that for the three types of vessels—
namely those known as *pāpālikā*, *mukhī*, and *śarāva*— which have been thoroughly washed with fresh [materials], [the ritual is performed] starting from the east.
The syntactical connection is: "One should offer the *bali* at night with a razor. He states the *bali-mantra* beginning with "with the *praṇava* and so forth":

first the *praṇava*, then the word "lotus" (*padma*), then "nightly *bali*," and then the names of the lords of the first, second, and subsequent nights, ending in the dative case (*caturthyanta*). *Bhū*.

The meaning is that the word "namaḥ" follows forms such as "tebhyaḥ" (to them) and so forth; thus, the mantras are finalized as "oṃ bhūtebhyo namaḥ" (Oṃ, salutation to the spirits) and "oṃ pitṛbhyo namaḥ" (Oṃ, salutation to the ancestors),
and this is precisely the intended meaning agreed upon by both the author of the *Darśadīpikā* and the author of the *Padārthādarśa*.

They cite the mantras as "stu oṃ namo bhūtebhyaḥ" and "oṃ namaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ. However, this designation [of them as *mantra*s] is contrary to the root definition, because the word *namaḥ* is understood only when there is another name [following it]; it is not the case that those [words] which end with *namaḥ* [are mantras].
We shall resort to a *tripada-bahu-vrīhi* compound so that the meaning stated by you may be understood;

however, [the phrase] "with words ending in *namaḥ*" refers specifically to a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Thus, when it is stated that the name-words end with the word *namaḥ*, what remains [to be said] is that for the name-words, *namaḥ* occurs at the beginning.

It should be stated that [the mantra] consists of the insertion of the word "praveśa" (entry) as the condition; for if that were the case, one would have to say "with those beginning with *praṇava*," or "with those ending with *praṇava*," or "with those ending with *namaḥ*.
However, the phrase "with those beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*" constitutes a distinct alternative formulation.
One should cause [the disciple] to enter; this mantra, beginning with "Kiṃcitāra" and ending with "Hṛdaya," consists of its own syllables.

Since it has been explained that the nature of the mantra of Durgā and others is likewise [composed of] these syllables, what else could there be here regarding the utterances of the doors other than the reality of the *namaḥ* ending?

We understand that the statement from another tantra has been presented here by Dāmanajñāna for the sake of corroboration, so that it may be appropriate to introduce a new subject matter even in this context. He speaks of the lords of the signs and so forth;
he states the nine powerful substances for the seven nights as follows:

By the phrase "lāja, sesame," and so forth, it is established that the *bhūtabali* consists of six substances, namely parched grain (*lāja*) and the others together with cooked rice; for this reason, this group of six is called the "offering to the elements" (*bhūtakūra*). These six are: parched grain, sesame, black gram flour, curd, sugar, and [the sixth].
Regarding the offering known as *trāṇibhūtakūra*:

one should offer a bali to the elephants by mixing parched rice flour (*saktu*) with coconut water, which is its natural accompaniment; alternatively, one may use rice paste (*taṇḍulapiṣṭa*). In the absence of coconut water, [one may use] coconut [water].
Having moistened the *tastha*-globule with water, the joining should be performed there.

"Unbroken" means whole grains of rice; this is the concluded meaning. For each individual vessel, in the eastern direction during the preceding night, twelve offerings (*bali*) are to be given by means of the offering to the spirits (*bhūta*).
On the second night, twelve offerings (*bali*) should not be omitted for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) from the vessels toward the southern direction;

on the third night, twelve offerings should be given to the *yakṣas* in the south-western direction (*nairṛtya-diś*), and so forth, which one should infer for oneself; [then] Tvaṣṭṛ and the other ten [deities].

An offering (bali) should be presented to the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) every night. Furthermore, the inspection of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) must not be performed by anyone other than the Guru. One should never look at the sprouts once they have grown; rather, the disciple may enter [the area] only upon the command of the Preceptor (ācārya).

Based on such statements as, "One should cause them to be well-concealed by covering them with cloths with great care," there is also another specific detail in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "For the sake of the prosperity of the patron, one should examine the sprouts; they should be properly grown upwards, exceedingly tender, and white."

One should avoid those that are smoke-colored, incomplete, excessively curved, dark, or humpbacked, for they are inauspicious. A black cloud brings lack of rain; one with a smoky appearance causes strife; an incomplete one brings the destruction of people; and a dark (śyāma) one brings famine.

If a sprout emerges slantwise, it becomes disease; likewise, if it is crooked, there is fear of enemies. When an inauspicious sprout has arisen, one should perform a propitiatory *homa*; one should offer oblations one thousand and eight times with the root mantra, or one hundred times with the Aghora-weapon mantra or the Astra-mantra.

Regarding the term "hasrakam" (a thousandfold): the author of the root text will later describe the application (*viniyoga*) of these sprouts as being in the form of their placement in the four directions. This concludes the procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*).
Now, demonstrating the application of the previously mentioned pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), [the author] indicates the locations of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*):

Having first laid out the thread all around, starting from the previously described altar up to the top of the pavilion, one should divide that thread into three parts; then, in the middle part, one should construct eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east in successive order, while one part shall serve as the altar (vedi).

One who has approached nearby—that is, one situated near the edge of the pavilion—should be abandoned [as an officiant]. A learned man (*vidvān*) is one possessing knowledge of the procedure for constructing a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), including its girdle (*mekhalā*), the womb (*yoni*), and so forth. He states the names of the pits beginning with "quadrangular" (*caturasra*) and so on; [this refers to] the nine pits, the placement of the deity, and the act of the performer.
He restricts the location of the preceptor’s sacrificial pit (ācāryakuṇḍa), designated by the word *padābhilayya*, as being in the middle;

that is, between Gaurīpati and Mahendra, in the northeast and east. Now, following the order of enumeration, he demonstrates the method of constructing the eight pits (*kuṇḍa*) as well, beginning with the square (*caturasra*).

The meaning is that, by [the words] beginning with "mityādi," this [mandala] attains the status of being one of these nine, and thus it does not deserve a separate exposition. There are three pavilions (*maṇḍapa*); among them, the first is the smallest (*kaniṣṭha*) at twelve cubits (*kara*). The central portion there, measuring four cubits, is equal to the altar (*vedi*).

On both sides of that [central part], there is one part each; when that part, consisting of four cubits, is further divided into three parts, each results in being one cubit and eight *aṅgulas*. Therein, having discarded the first and last parts, [the measurement] rests upon the middle one.
The construction of the square and other types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) should be performed by dividing [the space] into thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

The second [measurement], consisting of fourteen cubits (*hasta*), is the middle one. Therein, the third part, situated in the center, measures four cubits plus sixteen finger-breadths and is occupied by the altar (*vedi*).
On each side, there is one part; in the case of making the parts situated on the outside of the altar— which measures four cubits plus sixteen finger-breadths—
there are three parts on each side, each measuring one cubit plus thirteen finger-breadths plus a little less than three barley-corns.

The divisions have been concluded; therein, having set aside the first and last portions, the construction of the quadrangular and other types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) is performed within the middle portion, which measures thirty-seven *aṅgulas* plus slightly less than three *yavas*. The third [type], measuring sixteen *karas*, is the best; therein, the third portion...

The area occupied by the altar (vedi) measures five cubits plus eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas). On each side of this, there is also a portion measuring five cubits plus eight finger-breadths; this portion situated outside the altar is to be divided into three parts.
There are three portions, each measuring forty-two and five-eighths finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length; having excluded the first and last [portions],
one should construct the square and other types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around the middle portion of that same measurement.
