If one wishes to construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in a particular direction, that respective pit shall be located in the second of nine divisions from that specific direction; thus it is concluded. Furthermore, for each individual ninth division, [the location] is relative to the preceding pavilion (maṇḍapa).

It is slightly more than five finger-breadths, with an increase in each subsequent stage. Regarding that, he says "as before" because the arrangement of the square foundation is neither less nor more than the arrangement of the maṇḍala;
even though [the altar] is specifically characterized by the aforementioned ridges, the womb, and so forth, the kuṇḍa...

Although it is not merely a square, the statement is made thus by resorting to its future status as a *kuṇḍa*. By the passage beginning with "twenty-four," he defines the cubit (*hasta*) as that which enters into the definition of the square *kuṇḍa*;
the meaning is that the accomplishment of its essential form [is measured] by twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

The meaning is that it has twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) as its object, or rather, it has twenty-four finger-breadths as its referent; or else, the meaning is that twenty-four finger-breadths are another synonym for it.
In any case, a cubit (*hasta*) consists of twenty-four in number of finger-breadths.

If this definition of the hand were to be complete, it would require a knowledge of the fingers that constitute it; therefore, he states the definition of the finger beginning with the words "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*). Here, "the agent" refers to the disciple or the patron (*yajamāna*), and not the teacher (*guru*) in this context.

[Objection: What would be the status of the agent (*kartṛ*)? Since it has been stated that the agency of all the activities performed up to this point resides in the *guru* (preceptor) alone, [the sacrificer cannot be the agent]. [Response: This is not so, because Kātyāyana states: "In the acts of giving, reciting, undertaking, choosing, and measuring, one should regard the sacrificer as the agent."

The claim that this statement refers exclusively to the Smārta [tradition] because the Sūtra prescribes the measurement of the hands, fingers, and so forth specifically with reference to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), is an excessive assertion; for this statement,
which was composed to satisfy the requirements of the context, applies everywhere.

Because of the propriety of the sacrifice (*yitumaucityāt*), it has been stated that the measurements of the fist and the finger are not fixed for anything whatsoever; furthermore, because it is clearly stated in the *Gautamīya* that "the sacrificial act (*yajamāna*) must be performed by the patron (*yajamāna*) alone, and never by anyone else," the word "all that" (*tatsarvam*) is understood as the remainder here, referring to the patron.

The word "of him" (*asya*) here is connected [to the preceding]; thus, the meaning of the term *aṅgula* is the length of the middle joint belonging to the middle finger of the right hand of the disciple or the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Regarding the measurement of the *aṅgula*, there is an alternative calculation based on barley grains (*yava*) and so forth.

Since it is impossible to perform calculations such as one-third of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) without [defining its size], he demonstrates that the *aṅgula* consists of eight barley-corns (*yava*), stating: "constructed from eight barley-corns.
Thus, the *mātrāṅgula* is the name for a finger-breadth measured by the length of a joint.

The meaning is this: the designation "measurement-finger" (*mānāṅgula*) for what is fashioned from barley is a distinction created by the conceptualization [of the term], not a distinction created by a difference in the thing designated (*saṃjñin*); thus it is "differentiated by that. As for the barley grains, they are thick and closely joined to one another, like the bellies of mice.
Having placed it upon the chest, one should define the measure of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) according to the length of the central thread.
O fair-complexioned lady, having made eight large folds that are joined to the belly, one should drop a thread through their middle; by means of that, one should establish the finger-breadth.

From the observation of the Tirudrayāmala, since the reading "the finger-measure (aṅgula) is the same in both cases" is identical in both places, it is stated that the designation for the measurement of the fingers is the same in both modes; thus, the application of these two is likewise equal.

The intention is that [the ritual] is established through the oral tradition of the Guru and so forth. He now demonstrates the *yonikuṇḍa* (womb-pit), which follows the order of the enumeration, with the words beginning "made square" (*caturasrīkṛtam*), etc.;
for by stating that it has a square as its fundamental form, [he shows how it is prepared] just as in the case of a square pit.

The area of the ground becomes five hundred and seventy finger-breadths (aṅgulas); it is thus implied that this same calculation must be applied to all the other types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) which are modifications of that [square]. In reality, however, having first constructed a square, the arrangement of the other pits is described.

By that [statement], its being of that very nature is to be established, but not the fact that it yields a result for a field neither less nor greater; for such is what the author of the root-text intended, since the author of the root-text himself will later state the difference in the results of the fields. "In five ways" refers to the one-cubit [measure].

In a fivefold division, each part consists of four *aṅgulas* plus slightly more than six *pada*s; here, the authors of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* state that in a square field divided fivefold, one should place a fifth part in front— that is, from the east, toward the east.

One should increase it by the measurement of the marked point; then, starting from the center of the western line, one should fashion a semicircle by rotating a thread toward the southern end of the north-south line. Thereafter, starting again from the center of the western line, [one proceeds] toward the north...
By rotating the cord from the northern end of the *kṣiṇarekhā* (the line of destruction) [to the center], one should fashion another semicircle.
The "corner-position" (*koṇapada*) refers to the opposite end of the northern and southern lines;
according to the measure of half of a half, one should thus create two circles of half-of-a-half dimensions.
Since there is a traditional teaching (āmnāna) that two circles should be drawn— one as described and another likewise—

it is explained that one should first draw a thread starting from the half-circle line on the right, extending eastward to the mark that has been increased, and then [proceed] from the half-circle line on the north...
The meaning is that one should draw another [semi-circle] reaching as far as the previously increased mark; or alternatively,

having drawn a semi-circle starting from the center of the western line toward the corner— that is, toward the southwest— one should again [draw it] starting from the end of the center of the western line toward the northwest.

One should fashion half of the dance-pattern (nṛttārddha); starting from the tip of the thread of this half-vyavṛtta, one should apply two threads extending as far as the previous mark—thus they say the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) becomes beautiful like a womb (yonibha). However, the authors of the Harṣadīpikā [state that it should be] with a fifth part...
Having extended the eastern sūtra as previously described, one should then increase it; subsequently, from the two corners situated at the west,
one should mark off half-measures along the horizontal lines produced by the Nairṛta and Vāyavya corners— specifically,
half of a fifth part (the tenth part) in one corner.
One should increase the half of the fifth part of the other corner by a tenth part;

then, using the measurement of that increased corner, one should fashion a semicircle by rotating from the northwest corner toward the western limit of the eastern thread. One should do the same for the other [semicircle] as well.
From the extended southwest corner, one should draw another semicircle extending as far as the western end;
then, from the two extended corners of the northwest and southwest, one should drop two lines reaching as far as the ends of the extended eastern cord. In this manner, the *yoni-kuṇḍa* is formed.
The authors of the *Padārthādarśa* say that one should place the previously mentioned fifth part of the measure in the northern portion of the line running from east to west, thereby extending it;
then, by means of a measurement equal to half of half the diagonal, one should rotate [the compass] according to the measure of the corner. Thus it is said.

The term "half-foot" (*ardhapada*) refers to the point where the corner-line intersects with the middle of the two ear-lines; this is the second half-foot, located at the junction of the second ear-line within the pair of other squares,
because that ear-line is large.

Half of that [measurement] becomes the measure for the [other] half; from that measurement, one should rotate a thread by means of the corner-measure so as to join it with the corner. As for the method: having placed the end of the thread at the point where the two diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) intersect, which form a circle measuring only one square (koṣṭha).

From the tip of the transverse thread situated at the center, which is connected to the eastern end of the east-west thread, one should rotate the tip of the thread extending to the southern end of the north-south thread so as to touch that corner; one should likewise rotate another [thread] in the same manner— thus says the root text.

This is the meaning: thereafter, having placed the beginning of the thread at the point where two ear-threads intersect— each measuring only one square and situated to the west— one should [draw] from the tip of the middle horizontal thread,
which is connected to the western thread, toward the south, so that it touches the corner.

One should rotate the tip of the cord from the tip of the cord that has emerged upwards until it reaches the tip of the cord [already drawn]. Then, from the shoulder-mark at the tip of the semi-circle situated on both sides—which was just now produced—one should drop two cords, extending up to the tip of the cord to the north. Thus.

The pit becomes like a wounded womb; this is the intended meaning: a square field is adorned with diagonal lines drawn from Īśāna to Nairṛta and from Agni to Vāyu, as well as vertical and horizontal lines running south-north and east-west.
From the tip of the eastern line to the southern line,
having given a small interval for the ear-line that touches only one square— thereby dividing the great ear with a thread—
from the tip of the western line to the southern line, [one should likewise give] an interval touching only one square.
One should draw another ear-line intersecting the great ear-line;
then, one [triangle] faces downward and the other faces upward, resulting in a triangle—so they say. In all these views, the area of the square field remains equal.
It should be understood that this pertains to the construction of the *ardhacandra* (half-moon) pond.

By the passage beginning with "having made it square" (*caturasrīkṛta*), he demonstrates the method of arranging the half-moon pond: as before, having divided the central line of the square into ten parts, one should discard one-tenth part from the north.
Having set aside one part plus a tenth part from the south, and having made a mark on the northern side of the fire-altar, one should lay down a chord in the form of a bowstring across the marks.
Then, from that measurement— the measurement of the diameter through its center— one should rotate [the compass] toward the north and south.

By means of a cord measuring nineteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) increased by slightly more than two barley-corns (*yava*), that is to say, equal to the diameter of the cord at the midpoint between the two marks;
the method for this is as follows: at the point of intersection of the chord-cord and the middle-cord, the cord—

Having fixed the compass at the upper part, one should rotate it starting from the mark made there, taking one end of the chord-string as the pivot until reaching the second end; then, starting again from that same mark, one should rotate it once more. When done in this manner, a semicircle is formed.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is established facing north; as stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Now the half-moon is described: it is for the south, auspicious for killing; that which faces north is likewise [for other purposes]. This is the path shown in the *Padārthādarśa* by Harṣadīkṣita.
Having made the area square, one should divide the thread situated in the middle of the field— one cubit or more— in ten parts; then, having set aside one-tenth part below in the western direction,
one should place the second tenth part above in the eastern direction.
Having marked the point where the portion to be discarded has been removed from the previous [end],
one should apply a cord in the shape of a bowstring (jyā) as a transverse line; likewise,
by the measurement of a cord situated between the two points where a tenth part has been discarded above and below that [mark], [one should draw] the bowstring.
From the center, one should rotate a semicircle that touches both ends of the chord toward the western direction;
thus, they say this pit (kuṇḍa) becomes bow-shaped in the west and half-moon-shaped in the east, joined with a chord. In both of these two views, [the area] is four...

It should be understood that the area of the triangular *kuṇḍa* results in an area equal to the product of the length of the side and the height. By the verse beginning with "caturdhā" (fourfold), he demonstrates the method for constructing the triangular *kuṇḍa*: when the square-shaped field is divided into four parts along its central line...
When the division into parts has been made, one should place and extend a fourth part on each side of the transverse west-line;
from that measurement of a fourth part, one should mark a line in front, in the eastern portion relative to the central line.

One should make a mark; then one should lay down two threads. The method for this is as follows: taking the two marks on the sides of the westward thread that runs crosswise, one should extend the westward thread up to those points—this is one extension—and [the other] toward the southwest corner.
One should draw a thread from the mark placed at the tip of the middle line as far as [the center], which is the second;

and one should draw a thread from the mark placed at the tip of the middle line starting from the increased north-west corner (vāyavya) as far as the thread located at the south-east corner (nairṛtya), which is the third.

Thus, a triangular pit (*tryasri-kuṇḍa*), which is another synonym for a triangular pit (*trikoṇa-kuṇḍa*), is formed with its apex pointing upward and facing east; and whereas it was stated by you that one should not draw a pair of lines at the base, it follows instead that three lines are to be followed, as per the root [text].
It must be stated that the discussion regarding the avoidance of error should be addressed as follows:

since it has already been largely explained that one should place the thread on both sides of the western line immediately after marking [the center], the subsequent placement of the two-finger-width thread is performed precisely by disregarding that [previous instruction].

Some explain the meaning as follows: "Because the author himself has provided the title, the mention of the three sūtras indicates the group of topics to be treated; thus, everything is faultless. However, others do not accept this, [arguing that] the area of the field here is measured by finger-breadths equal to the sky, the Vedas, and the arrows (1440).
Furthermore, the area of a perfect square field would measure six, seven, or five [units],
because a deficiency of thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) results here;
moreover, equality among the three sides is not possible here, for [the sides] consist of thirty-six finger-breadths.
The base (bhūmi) is a horizontal line measuring twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
because it has been increased by six finger-breadths on each side from the original square line which serves as its basis; however, the two sides (bhuja) are the lines of the surrounding triangle.

The square root of the sum of the squares of those two [measures], which are thirty-five finger-breadths each—the vertical distance from the ground—is obtained as being exactly thirty-five finger-breadths by way of the diagonal (karṇa).
This is its meaning: having performed the squaring of those two, namely the half of the ground and the vertical distance...

Having multiplied the number eighteen by eighteen with the increased [value], one obtains the resulting figure; this is the square of the half of the base area under consideration. Then, by multiplying thirty—the length of the suspended cord—by thirty, one obtains its square. When these two are added together, the resulting figure is obtained.
The number obtained by the method of bringing the square root to the base becomes the hypotenuse and the measure of the side;
thus, there arises the contingency of the equality of the three sides being destroyed, since even the line on the ground is treated as a side. Others, however, [divide it] in four ways.
Having increased, as before, each of the two sides of the westward horizontal line by one-fourth of the divided area— which measures six finger-breadths—
one obtains a measurement of thirty-six finger-breadths from that point of increase; with that measurement, [one proceeds].

In front, that is, in the east; the procedure there is as follows: having fixed the beginning of a thirty-six-finger thread on one of the increased sides, one should make a mark at the point where it extends from the tip of the eastern thread (prācīsūtra) to its limit, and then... [the rest of the sentence continues].
One should lay down three threads measuring thirty-six finger-breadths each; in this way, equality among the three sides is achieved.
Furthermore, by adding four *yavas* combined on both sides according to the described nature, equality of the area of the resulting figure is also attained.

Thus, this meaning can be established even from the root text itself; for by the intended method, the term *kṣetra* (field) refers not only to its own primary sense, but also to the finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) that constitute the central thread measuring twenty-four finger-breadths,
as it is intended to signify even that which constitutes a fourth part thereof.

They say that this is because the meaning— that an increase of six finger-breadths on both sides, corresponding to one-fourth of a field measuring two by two yavas, must be performed— is established with ease.
He now describes the method for constructing a circular *kuṇḍa* (fire-pit) with the verse beginning "eighteen parts," etc.

As before, having divided the central line of the square field into eighteen parts, one should extend the eighteenth part outward along any line; then, from the center, one should rotate [the cord] around that mark to form a circle.

The meaning is that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) becomes circular in shape. Regarding the term "anuttama" (unsurpassed), it means there is nothing superior to it; this is its praise. Here, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* and the author of the *Harṣadīpikā* maintain that the area of the field (kṣetraphala) is less than eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
When divided into eighteen parts, one part exceeding a third of an *aṅgula* becomes the eighteenth part; thus, in the construction of the circle,
there are five hundred and two *aṅgulas*, plus eight [parts].
In a circular *kuṇḍa* derived from a square *kuṇḍa*, there is a reduction of fifty-six and four and a half *aṅgulas* from the area of the square field; thus,
the area of the circular *kuṇḍa* is less than that of the square field.

Since it is required that the measurement of the original material (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) be equal, the reading "one part should be placed outside the sixteen-part field" must be supplied in the root text. This being the case, [the dimension] is thirteen and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
They say that it becomes half of the *nivyāsa* (the perimeter), which results in equality with the area of the field;
others, however, say that having passed beyond eight parts— that is, eighteen—
such is the twenty-fourth part of the fifth sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), known as the circular one.
In such a field consisting of three fingers, which is square and composed of central lines,
one part— consisting of sixteen parts— is to be extended outward;
for among the twenty-four parts, eight parts are internal, leaving only the sixteen parts remaining.

Thus, they say that for the purpose of concealing the secret meaning [of the mantra], it is as in the case of "prāpalopāt paṭuḥ prājye" and so forth. He describes the method of constructing the hexagonal *kuṇḍa* with the words beginning with "aṣṭadhā," etc.; the field is square, consisting of twenty-four [parts] in the form of the central line.

One should divide that which consists of one hundred finger-breadths into eight parts; here, the term "middle line" (*madhyasūtra*) refers to the horizontal line running from south to north, and not to the line extending from east to west, because it is stated in the root text [that the lines] are on the two sides (*pārśvayoḥ*). Regarding the east-west direction:
If that central sūtra is intended to be described, it should be stated as being above and below;

on both sides of the middle sūtra, in the portions of the southern and northern sūtras, one should set aside—that is, increase—by one part each, which is an eighth part consisting of three finger-breadths (tryaṅgula), moving outward. Then, from that point...
"By this measure, by that measure, increased by this measure, increased by that measure"—this means by the mark of the increase;

"from the middle" means from the center of the field; "on both sides" refers to the right side and the left side of the center of the line extending south and north which has been increased on both sides.

One should draw four fish figures intersecting one another, which constitute eight semicircles, in the space between the east and west directions—that is, at the top; this is known as the *tantraviddha* according to tradition.
This is the method for constructing it, and this very form is what is intended here.

The meaning is that it does not belong to another. The method for this is as follows: having placed the end of a fifteen-finger-breadth cord—marked at its northern end—at the center of the field, one should draw a semicircle in the space between the eastern and northern [sides], and then [place] that cord at the mark made at the northern end.

Having marked the center and drawn a circle, one should then draw a second circle with half the radius of the first; by this, one should produce a single fish-figure (*matsya*). By this means, a fish is established in the interval between the east and northeast directions.
In exactly the same way, from the center of the field, one should apply a cord of that same measure.

Having constructed a semicircle in the space between the east and southeast directions from the mark made to the south, and likewise having constructed a second semicircle intersecting the previously made semicircle from that same southern mark, a second fish-figure is thus established in the space between the east and southeast directions. The third [fish] is established in the same manner.
From the center of the eastern field,

using two semicircles that intersect each other starting from a mark made in the subsequent portion between the southwest and northwest directions, a third fish-figure is to be constructed; in this very same manner, [one is to be made] in the space between the west and southwest directions.

From the center of the entire field, having divided a semicircle with a radius equal to that [measure], one should mark the southern portion; immediately thereafter, having constructed a semicircle intersecting the eastern half, a fourth "fish" figure is formed. From the northern mark of that, [one proceeds] toward the northeast.

From the northern mark, extend the first thread as far as the fish at the interval between the northwest and the west; from the southern mark, extend the second thread as far as the fish at the interval between the east and the southeast;
and from the southern mark itself, extend the third thread to the west.

Having laid down the fourth thread as far as the north-western fish, one should lay down the fifth thread intersecting the two eastern fish, and the sixth thread intersecting the two western fish. Thus, by the intersection of these six threads, the hexagonal *kuṇḍa* is formed.

The meaning is that it should be laid out. It is stated likewise in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having made the field into eight parts, and having placed two parts on each of the two outer sides, one should lay them out equal from the center using that same measurement;
[thereby] the other four corners and two on the two sides [are formed]."

"One should lay down two [lines] in six [directions]; therein shall be that hexagonal sacrificial pit (*ṣaṭkoṇakuṇḍa*). Regarding this as well, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that equality of area (*kṣetraphala*) is not possible. He now describes the method for constructing the lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*), beginning with the words "made square" (*caturasrīkṛta*).

As before, having divided the middle line into eighteen parts, one should extend by some amount—slightly less than three *yavas* and more than one *aṅgula*—one of those parts outward at some point on the line; then, using that mark as the measurement, one should draw a circle all around. Thereafter, the diameter of the circle...

Dividing the sūtra into three parts, one should draw three circles by means of each part, one inside the other. The first circle, situated at the very center, is the pericarp (*karṇikā*); the second circle outside that is the location for the filaments (*kesara*); and the third circle outside that is the petals (*patra*).

Following the instructions for excavation beginning with "the location [should be] as large as the pit," one should establish the elevated central mound (*nābhi*)— which consists of the pericarp (*karṇikā*)— at a height equal to one-third of the diameter of the expanded field; the width of this one-cubit mound should be slightly less than that.
The [pedestal] is twenty-six finger-breadths [in height]; one-third of that is the location for the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus, which is slightly less than nine finger-breadths.
Therein, the width of the navel is four finger-breadths and its height is two finger-breadths. In that regard, one might ask: how high should the pericarp, measuring nine finger-breadths, be?

One should proceed without hesitation until the body reaches a height of four and a half finger-breadths according to the calculation of the threefold system (*trairāśika-gaṇanā*). Likewise, having left a space of four and a half finger-breadths for the ear-lobes (*karṇikā*) in the middle, one should excavate everything else; furthermore, one should also excavate the location of the *kesara* (filaments).

One should fashion it merely in the form of a filaments; this is the method for the performance regarding the petals. Regarding the production of the outer circle within the interior, the petals and so forth should be executed according to the method to be described for the root.
For instance, within the circle exceeding eighteen parts of the field...

That third circle is external to that [second] circle; the circle situated between them, which is internal, is called the second circle. There, having placed the beginning of a thread at the junction-mark where the thread located in one of the eight directions meets the second circle, [one should extend] the end of that thread to the third circle.

Having laid down the directional thread according to the prescribed procedure, one should fashion eight half-moons (ardhacandras) in the eight directions by measuring the space between the two circles drawn at both ends of that thread. When those half-moons are formed, junctions arise within them; in those junctions, eight threads [should be placed].
One should cause it to fall in this manner; thus, the division of the sixteen fields is produced.
Then, having constructed on one side a semicircle with a measurement equal to the length of the tips of the petals, one should likewise construct a semicircle on the second side, facing outward.

In the intervals between the petals, one should draw [lines] from both ends of the central sūtra toward the outer hand, reaching the corners at the tips of the petals; that is to say, one should form them like a half-moon (ardhaniśākara). By means of two semi-circles, the production of a single petal-tip occurs. Therein, by way of reasoning, the third and fourth...
Just as in the intervals between the petals, half is taken up and half is left out at the tips of the petals,
so it should be done; one should dig out the entire middle of the petal-tips,
while digging in such a way that the tips remain above in their original form— thus [one makes] an eight-petaled [lotus].
According to Kuṇḍabhava, Tīrthaharṣadīpika, and Padārthādarśa,

one should divide the central line of the site into twelve parts; having extended one-twelfth of that part outward somewhere along the line, one should then draw a circle around it for the pericarp and other parts.
In the phrase "not outside" (*nāṃbahiḥ*), the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*) is to be repeated, and "from the center" (*madhyāt*) is to be supplied as a remainder.
Thus, one should draw three circles outside the previously drawn circle from the central field; these are the locations for the corner-lines (*karṇikā*) and so forth. Outside is the previous field.

The essential meaning is as follows: having drawn the first circle according to the prescribed measurement, one should then draw three other circles within it starting from the center; thus, a set of four circles is to be produced. As stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having first drawn a circle as before, one should draw [the others] within that."

Having rotated the three sets of lines, one should fashion the shape of a lotus by means of the pericarp and so forth; the meaning of the root text is that whatever is the outermost circle is itself the circle at the tips of the petals.
In the previously mentioned circular *kuṇḍas*, a deficiency of eighteen *aṅgulas* was shown; however, in this case, it is even less than that.

Others, however, say that there is a deficiency here; they claim it is eighteen parts. In a field of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), an eighth part is two finger-breadths; ten such parts, along with twenty-four finger-breadths, constitute the [required] portion. Ten.
Half of the flesh is one finger (aṅgula), together with twelve minor-fingers (vyaṅgula);
all this combined measures fifty-two and a half fingers plus forty-eight minor-fingers. Having divided this and halved it, the resulting [measure] is...
Having extended a single thread outside the field by a measure of two *aṅgulas* plus fifty-six *aṅgulas* and twenty-four *prativyaṅgulas*, one should rotate it from that point to form a circle;
this becomes the boundary circle of that field. The remainder...

They consider the meaning of "ṣaṃ" to be as stated before. With the words "pūrvoktam" (as previously stated) and so forth, he demonstrates the method for constructing the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Here, the authors of the *Harṣadīpikā* explain that "pūrvoktam" refers to that which was previously mentioned as consisting of twenty-four parts, namely twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

One should divide that field situated [therein] into two parts; having divided it into two, one should make it so. Since there is no reason for omitting the first part when not mentioning three or four names, he specifies the division into two parts itself; its portion consists of two finger-breadths (aṅgulas).

One should place the flesh outside; however, in reality, one should divide the field into twelve parts by means of those twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) which constitute half of the twenty-four finger-breadths. "One should divide the field into twelve parts" is the intended meaning. One part of that consists of two finger-breadths.
Having placed [the cord] outside and extended it, one should make an inner square. Then,
from the corners of that inner square consisting of four compartments, taking half of twelve *aṅgulas*—
that is, six *aṅgulas* as the measure— one should [mark] six *aṅgulas* each.

Having made a mark at that location, one should establish eight marks in the four directions. Having laid four threads from each of those marks toward its respective cardinal point, one should achieve sixteen squares; in this very same manner, [one should do so] for the outer square as well.
One should make eight marks, each measuring seven finger-breadths (aṅgula) from the edge of the altar.

Then, starting from one mark among those eight, one should draw a line toward its own third mark, proceeding in such a manner that the eight corners of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) are formed. Each [line] should be drawn individually.

One should drop eight threads; wherever the intersection of the eight threads occurs, one should erase everything starting from that point toward the interior. They say that the accomplishment of the eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is achieved when the corners fall upon the positions of the marks—so says the author of the *Padārthādarśa*.

One should divide the previously mentioned central line of the previously mentioned square into twenty-four parts; having placed one part outside in the four directions, the meaning is that one should construct the exterior with a length and width of twenty-six *aṅgulas*. Here, the term "corner" (*koṇa*) refers to the corner-line (*koṇasūtra*).
Beyond that, the diagonal cord of the inner square is thirty-four finger-breadths less four *pūkas*; half of that is seventeen finger-breadths less two *pūkas*;
half of that is eight and a half finger-breadths less one *pūka*. This is the measurement of the outer [square].
From two corners of the square, one should mark [the center] from the space between them—specifically from the northeast and southeast corners;

likewise, one should mark from the southeast and southwest corners, the southwest and northwest corners, and the northwest and northeast corners. Then, one should draw eight lines toward the eight directions.
From giving [the gift], the accomplishment of the eight corners [is attained]. Regarding the method for laying out the lines therein:
at the two marks on the sides of the corners, four lines should be drawn in each direction between those two;
indeed, these are the lines between the two marks in the middle of the lines of the square in the four directions.

"Threads"—thus there are eight threads; since eight threads are possible therein, the statement "one should lay down eight threads" is made. By the phrase "according to rule" (*yathānyāyam*), this very same meaning is further indicated; such is the meaning understood from the root text, and not anything more excellent than that.
Others say that because there is no deficiency in the length of the arms,
and because the area of the field remains equal even when it is reduced by forty-four finger-breadths plus two barley-corns, [the shape is considered a square];
however, others [hold that] the term "corner" refers to the directions beginning with Agni (southeast), and so forth.
Next,
having made a mark at the position of the half of that [half] belonging to the square situated at the ends of the four lines— east, west, north, and south— which are connected to it,
one should [draw a line] from that very mark to the exterior edge of the square.

Having increased [the grid] as it ought to be, one should lay down four lines in each of the eight resulting squares located near oneself; since the four lines are already established by the previously drawn lines, there are eight [squares].

They say that [the area] is not established; now, the method for calculating the area of the aforementioned sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is written down. The method for constructing a regular square is easy to understand, as stated in the *Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa*: "A line measuring twice [the side] with two nooses..."

Having fashioned the *mārjāra-sūtra* (cat-line) according to the measurement of the width and length, and having fixed two pegs (*śaṅku*) at the corners designated as the "pullers" at the end of the half-extension from the field-limit, one should pull the first [line] toward the corner; thus it is said.
The meaning of the phrase "by exchange of ropes, there are two others at the ends" is as follows:
having doubled the measurement of the desired square field— whether old or new— one should cause a cord to be made according to that measure.
A cord is placed at both ends of the measuring-line such that it forms two loops;
then, for the purpose of placing [the cord] over the two stakes situated at the ends, two loops are formed.
Thereafter, from the ends—that is, from the extremities of the cord—there are three [measures] equal to the length of the foot.
Regarding the length: having set aside one quarter from among the four quarters that measure the length and the width, one should mark a cord measured by three-quarters;
from the end of that very cord, [one should mark] at a distance of two widths and one petal.
One should mark two points on a cord measuring half the width;

these two points, taken in sequence, are named the *karṣa* corners because of the drawing (*karṣaṇa*) [of the line] from them. A point made at three-quarters of the length is named the *karṣa*, and a point made at half the length is the *āyāmārddha*.

Because it effects the corners, it is called *kaḥ-koṇa* (the corner-maker). Hereafter, he establishes the square with the words "the two nooses" (*pāśau*). The two stakes situated in the eastern and western directions of the field—there, at both of those places, are the two nooses.

Having marked the first point, one should draw [the line] across the middle part of the field; having stretched a cord of the desired length over the established cardinal directions and intermediate points, one should drive stakes into the ground at those two marks. At those two driven stakes—

Having placed the noose of the end of the cord that has been twisted and holding the mark known as the "puller," one should pull the cord toward a corner so that it becomes equally drawn, just as the cord reaching both stakes would be equal when pulled along the line in one direction.

In the place of the corner-mark, a gnomon (śaṅku) is to be driven in—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. In this manner, another gnomon is to be driven in; that very same mark of attraction (karṣacihna), having been drawn toward another direction, [should be placed] in the location of the corner-mark.

"It is not the second; it is to be measured by Śaṅku. Having thus established two corners, one establishes the other two corners by "exchanging" (vini-mayāt); that is, by the exchange or reversal of the two ends of the cord.
Having reversed the two cords at their ends by holding them, and having performed the drawing from the previous mark as before, one should drive stakes into the positions of the corner marks;
thus, a perfect square is accomplished. Now, regarding the field...
We shall demonstrate the means for knowing the result in the *Līlāvatī*:

"The desired side of the [rectangle] with equal sides of four units is to be assumed; then, subtracting the squares of those [sides], the square of the diagonal is four times that [result]; its square root..."
The second side is the measure of the hearing; likewise, the product of the unequal ears is the clear result of the two exits.
In a figure with equal sides and four sides, it is the same when the hearing is equal; and in a figure with equal sides and four sides, it is likewise extended to those sides.

The meaning of "jakotighāti" is as follows: it refers to that which has four equal and identical arms, meaning four sides designated as "arms"; having determined the square of one of its "hearings," that is, the measure of one of its diagonals—its square.
Having performed the subtraction from the product of the arms multiplied by four according to the count of the [number of] squares not yet produced,
and having obtained the square root by means of the method for extracting the square root of a completed number,
that root is the measure of the second diagonal line.
If it were not so, then according to the method stated for equal quadrilateral fields,
from the mutual multiplication of those two [diagonals] which have unequal measures, and by dividing that product by two, the resulting quotient would clearly be the correct [area].

The area shall be the measure of the field's fruit; "in a level [field]" means in one that is equal in measure, where the two ears (the diagonal lines) are equal— meaning it is an equiquadrilateral— and even a quadrilateral with equal sides, having compressed and contracted the two angles.

The area (*māna*) of a drum-shaped figure is long; it does not follow that this same result applies there [in other cases]. Thus, in the *Samūṣruta*, the four-armed figure is specified as being "elongated" (*āyata*), meaning long and rectangular;
even in that case, the product of the two sides is the area.
The word "syāt" (it may be) is to be supplied. The hypotenuse (*bhuja*) is also the line forming the perimeter of the square at its corner;
as it has been stated, there is no difference in name between the side and the corner, but only a difference in designation, not a difference in essential nature.
Thus, the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is the entry of a straight thread-like line into the tips of the side and the corner.
That which is expressible by words is the "product" (*kṛti*), which is a synonym for the square (*varga*). Its essential nature is as follows:

a number produced by multiplying a quantity by itself is called a product; it is also designated by the name "square" in the tradition of calculation (*gaṇitāgama*). However, from the perspective of algebra (*samuddhidyātaḥ*), it is [defined differently].

In expressions such as "the square of the square" (*kṛtiḥ kṛtim dviguṇayet*), it is not merely by convention that the term "square" (*kṛti*) is applied to a number; rather, its definition is established through its actual derivation. As for the method of extracting the square root: having subtracted [the last digit] from the uneven [place], etc.

One should double the square of the quotient and add the square root; having subtracted this from the first odd number, one should set down twice the obtained quotient in a row. When dividing the even number, having subtracted the square of the next odd number, one should place the resulting quotient in the row. This [is repeated] for that...
The square root of a number is found by repeatedly performing the "placing of the digits" (*guṇanyāsa*) in rows; the result is the "fruit" (*phala*).
Having marked the odd and even digits of the number starting from the left—beginning with the first, second, and so on—with vertical and horizontal lines, one proceeds from the last odd digit...
From any given square number, whichever square number belonging to any series whatsoever is to be subtracted— that is,
it must be diminished by such a square number of that series—
such that from the resulting square, the first odd number of that series [is obtained].
Having reduced that [number] by one, having doubled that resulting root-form,

and having divided it— either the odd number situated to the right starting from the first, or the even number alone together with the previously remaining odd numbers— one takes and obtains the quotient.

Having stated that the previously mentioned form of the *kasyakṛti* (the square of the *kasya*)— as before, situated either at the beginning in its entirety from the middle position, or in a portion accompanied by the remaining equal parts (*samāṃśa*) from the front— is composed of odd numbers (*viṣamāṅka*),
one should subtract that odd number from the square of the quotient (*labdhakṛtya*) until it is reduced.

Having doubled the square root digit (*vargamūla-aṅka*), one should place it in the form of a row to the right of the previous square root digit. Of that quantity of digits placed in the row, the square root (*pada*)—also known as the "half" (*ardha*) or the "root" (*mūla*)—shall be designated as the "digit" (*aṅka*). Thus ends the section on the digits situated in the "thorn" (*śalya*).
Regarding the method for calculating the square root of the number 574, which consists of the digits 24 (i.e.,
2424): where the square of a four-digit number is sixteen digits,
the extraction of the root involves the final odd digits being sixteen units in form.

The square of the number must be subtracted; the square root of that remainder is the divisor (sevāṅka). Then, the square of that divisor is subtracted from the original number, and the square root of that result is again the divisor. Where many numbers remain, the same process is to be repeated.

He says regarding that [verse], beginning with "divided by the row" (*paṅktihṛte*), etc.: when the even number— which has arrived according to the previous method by means of the row-number (*paṅktyaṅka*)— is divided by the odd number remaining as the residue, then the square of the resulting number, according to the previously stated definition, is obtained.
Having first discarded the odd number from the right-hand side of the dividend,
one should perform the operation with the resulting quotient; that is, having subtracted that odd number from the dividend,
one should double the obtained result and place it in the row, as well as the quantity of the digits in that row.
"Reduced" means diminished by its own half; it becomes a "square" (pada). Furthermore, regarding the case where there is no complete exhaustion of the digits (sakalāṅka), he says: "Thus repeatedly.
The meaning is that this very method should be carried out until the digits of the square number are completely exhausted.
The method for determining the circumference from the diameter, and the diameter from the circumference, is stated in that very same [work]:
"The diameter multiplied by nine and divided by twenty-five is the subtle circumference;
or, when multiplied by twenty-two and divided by seven, it is the gross circumference suitable for practical use. This is its meaning.
The three terms *vyāsa*, *vistṛti*, and *viṣkambha* are synonyms for the diameter of the width situated at the center of a circle.
Thus, having multiplied the numerical measure of the circle's width by four hundred and twenty-seven,
the resulting figure is five hundred and thirty-two.
Dividing by the figure one thousand and one hundred, the resulting quotient shall be the measure of the circumference of the circle and so forth.

This is stated as the subtle (sūkṣma) measure; however, this is not suitable for practical use because it cannot be implemented due to its subtlety. Rather, in the measure of the diameter of the circle, [twenty-two...]

When the circumference multiplied by three is divided by seven, the resulting quotient shall be a rough approximation suitable for practical use. By this same method, the measure of the diameter may also be calculated from the measure of the circumference; for as the diameter of a circle [increases], so too does its circumference.
Just as [a circle] is accumulated or diminished,

so too the circumference becomes increased or diminished; since the increase and decrease of the diameter are established by direct perception through the increase and decrease of the circumference, it is entirely logical to derive its measurement from that measurement.
To calculate the area of a circle from its diameter: multiply the square of the diameter by ten and three;

the precise result is obtained when divided by five thousand. Alternatively, when multiplied by nine and divided by ten, it becomes the approximate result, which is suitable for practical use. [The square of the measure of the diameter...]

According to the method stated as "the area is derived from my knowledge," multiply the resulting figure by the number thirty-seven thousand three hundred and ninety-nine; then, divide the resulting product by five thousand. The quotient obtained shall be the precise area of the circular field. Vyā...

When the number with the vowel *sa* (i.e., 15) is multiplied by the eleventh digit (i.e., 11), and the resulting product is divided by the number fourteen, the quotient obtained will be the approximate measure of the area of the circle, suitable for practical use; this is the meaning. [This] is joined with the area of the triangular field.

In a scalene triangle, the sum of two sides multiplied by their difference and divided by the base, when placed in two locations and increased by the quotient divided by the base, shall be the two segments of the base.
The square root of the difference between the squares of the side and its own segment becomes the perpendicular. Half the base multiplied by the perpendicular is clearly the area of the triangle.

The meaning of this is as follows: in this triangle, according to the opinion of Svāti, the horizontal side is designated by the term "ground" (bhūmi); the remaining two sides are likewise designated as "arms" (bhuja).
A perpendicular line drawn from the vertex where those two arms meet down to the ground-line is...
The two portions designated as *vasu* (eight), which are situated on both sides at the point of intersection, are those segments of the ground known by the term *āvādhā*;
they are also referred to by the word *āvādhā*.
In a threefold field, when the measures of the two arms are added together, [the remainder] by their difference... [is obtained].
When the difference between the two arms is multiplied by that very number,
and the product is divided by the measure of the earth (the number representing the earth's size),
one should place the resulting quotient as the measure of the earth in two places; then, in one of those places, either subtract or add [the other value].
When the two sides are divided by the square root of the sum of the squares of the two numbers, the two resulting values placed on both sides shall constitute the two arms (sides) of the triangle;
the distinction here is that the smaller value is the shorter arm and the larger value is the longer arm. However, where there is no difference between the two numbers, there is only multiplication.

Something else remains to be performed: having squared the two values obtained from the current calculation of the *bhuja* (the sine) and the *ābādha* (the versed sine), one finds the difference between the resulting figures;
the square root of that remainder, calculated according to the stated method, will be the required value. By that, it is established.
The area of a triangular *kuṇḍa* and other such shapes shall be the measure of half the ground multiplied by the measure of the *vapra*.

Furthermore, this [calculation] serves to dispel doubts such as: "If the navel has a diameter of four *aṅgulas* and a height of two *aṅgulas*, then for that [nave] which has a length of six *aṅgulas*, what would its height be? and so forth.

The method of multiplying by the three types of application (upayoga) is now stated. It is called *pramāṇa* because by means of it, the fruit (*phala*) is measured (*mīyate*) according to one's desire (*icchā-vaśāt*). This is so because, as will be explained later, the attainment of the fruit occurs through division [by that measure]. Alternatively, it is so called because it is a superior (*prakṛṣṭa*) measurement (*māna*) in terms of its excellence as knowledge (*jñānatayā*).

That [measure] is to be established as having that measure, being based on the authority of knowledge, starting from four finger-breadths and so forth. Even if the aforementioned definition is pervaded by the method of distribution (*vyasta-vidhi*) regarding the measure, there is no fault; for our stated definition applies extensively even in that case. This is due to desire (*icchā*). Desire...
That which has a desired measure as its standard means, in other words, that which has a desired measure as its authority; it should be placed at the end of those six fingers and so forth.
Furthermore, the homogeneity (*sājātya*) between these two is by way of being "finger-length" (*aṅgula*) and so on.
The result is such that it is of the same class as the result one desires to know, just like the fruit of the *aupavāraka* tree. This is the point.

Since there is an absence of [the conditions for] being two-finger-breadths and so forth, one should place a dissimilar pair of squares in the middle. Then, having multiplied that middle number— which has become the result-figure— by an arbitrary form according to one's desire,
and having divided the resulting twelve by the first number consisting of four units as the measure, the quotient obtained is...

Who would desire to know the nature of the result? The meaning is that, in the case of a reversed operation (*vyasta-vyavahāra*), one must adopt the opposite procedure: division by the divisor and multiplication by the multiplier. In the inverse method, the age and price of living beings are derived from their values.

In the case of the price of living beings (jīvamūlya) and similar instances mentioned in the rule, "The division of the gold for the color [of the object] would be an inverse triple-proportion (trairāśika) of the quantities," the brief summary is as follows: three quantities are called *trirāśi*; the multiplication performed by them constitutes a *trairāśika*. Now, regarding the area of a field...
Regarding the illustration of the quadrilateral, which is another synonym for the four-armed [figure],
each of its four arms is twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long; when the two numbers twenty-four, representing those two adjacent arms, are multiplied together, the resulting figure is—
The area of a square fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit is equal to sixty-seven and a half *śara*s (twelve and a half digits).
Regarding the lotus-bud-shaped pit (*yoni-kuṇḍa*), there are three areas according to the *Padārthādarśa*:
one triangle at the top, and a triangle at the base; [the area] of the two semicircles situated at the corners is...

The other field is completed by the square; there, by multiplying half the area of the ground—measured at sixteen fingers plus forty-two fingers—as suspended, one obtains twelve forms, which result in a measurement of thirty-six fingers. Thus, two...
By multiplying half the base of the triangle— which measures twelve *aṅgulas*—
by the hanging perpendicular which is also twelve *aṅgulas*, the area of the field is measured as forty-eight *aṅgulas* (four times four).
For each semicircle, however, it is eight *aṅgulas* plus twenty-nine *vyaṅgulas*.

The diameter is established as sixteen fingers plus eight arrow-lengths (five fingers), totaling twenty-four fingers, by combining the two halves of the circumference. When the diameter is multiplied by the "Nanda-fire" (thirty-nine) [multiplier], the result is forty-six fingers plus sixty-four Nanda-bāhus (twenty-four fingers).

The circumference resulting from the calculation of the measured degrees is as follows: when the sky-arrows (50) and suns (12) are multiplied by the degrees (360), the measure of the triple-circumference (triparidhi) obtained is three hundred and fifty-five *aṅgulas*, eighteen *vyaṅgulas*, and fourteen *prativyaṅgulas*.
By means of this measurement of the circumference—
By multiplying the aforementioned one-fourth part of Vyāsapāda— consisting of fourteen, thirty, and two *aṅgulas* respectively—
by the measure of five *vy-aṅgulas*, there result two hundred and thirty-six *aṅgulas*, five *vy-aṅgulas*, and fifty [units].

In this case, there are two *aṅgulas*; [thus] in the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the width is thirty-eight *aṅgulas* and two *aṅgulas*.

[The area] is less than five *aṅgulas*, being less by two *aṅgulas* and fifty-four *pratyaṅgulas*, and thus the area of the square measuring one cubit (*hasta*) is reduced. In the half-moon, the width is thirty-eight *aṅgulas* and two *aṅgulas*.
The measurement of the perimeter there is twenty-four [units], which consists of one hundred and twenty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
thirty-eight half-finger-breadths (*vyaṅgula*), and fifteen quarter-finger-breadths (*prativyaṅgula*).
When this is multiplied by one-sixth of the diameter— which is nine finger-breadths and thirty-six half-finger-breadths— [the result is as follows].
The measurement is six, nine, eight, and eleven finger-breadths; seven finger-breadths, two [finger-breadths], and twelve sub-finger-breadths.
The area of this present half-circle *kuṇḍa* is five hundred and seventy-nine *dravyāṅgulas*,

Some maintain that when the triangle is suspended by its altitudes, the area of this field results in a value greater than the area of the original square field measured in twelve finger-breadths;
