The fruit of the *trapa* measures ninety-seven, twenty-five, and thirty-seven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), half-finger-breadths (*vyaṅgula*), and quarter-finger-breadths (*prativyaṅgula*) respectively. When suspended, each of these measures twelve finger-breadths,
fifty-nine half-finger-breadths, and twenty-five quarter-finger-breadths.

Measuring fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), half of that is seven and a half finger-breadths. This [measurement], multiplied by six and increased by two finger-breadths for each year, is equal to a number of finger-breadths measured by fire (three) and fire (three). By these [finger-breadths] consisting of four, eight, and five, the calculation of the area (kṣetraphala) has been declared by the wise.
"Māna" refers to the measurement of the diameter of the previously mentioned final lotus-field,
which is twenty-nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas), fifty-two half-finger-breadths (vyaṅgulas), and forty-eight sixteenth-parts of a finger-breadth (prativyaṅgulas).
The numerical value of its square is eight hundred and ninety-two [with a remainder of] forty-eight...
In that [measurement], the form consisting of forty and fifty-five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and so forth is not multiplied by nine or three; rather,
the numerical marks on the petals are twenty-eight, zero, six, zero, five, and three units of finger-breadths,
as well as nineteen and twenty-four finger-breadths.
When five thousand [square] *vyāṅgulas* are divided by twelve,

the result is twelve *vyāṅgulas*, fifty-nine *praty-aṅgulas*, and one hundred and eighty-one *prati-praty-aṅgulas*. Thus, the area of the field within the circle marking the boundary of the lotus-field (*padmakṣetra*) has been demonstrated.
This very same term "square" (*varga*) is also expressed by the word *vṛttāgra*.

Just as there is a square result for a circle of intermediate size, so too, if the diameter of that circle is twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), its square value is five hundred and seventy-six; when this is multiplied by nine (the "wealth-wealth-fire" number), [it yields the area].
The measure of his arms is 2512 units;
when this is divided by the mark of five thousand (5000), the resulting quotient is 452 fingers, 23 small-fingers (vyaṅgula), and 25 minute-fingers (prativyaṅgula). This is the measurement obtained.
The sum of that [area] and the area of the aforementioned field amounts to 1548 finger-breadths;
following that, it is joined with 420, and following that, it is joined with 240. This is the measure of half of this complete area.

It should be understood that the area of a complete lotus-shaped (*padmaka*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) consists of five hundred and seventy-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), forty-eight half-finger-breadths, and twelve fractional finger-breadths (*prativyaṅgula*).
In the case of an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsra*) pit, there are eight triangles; therein, [the divisions are] east, west, north...
On the right side of the *rad* [pedestal], there are four equilateral triangles with equal arms;

therein, the measure of the arm is thirteen fingers, the hanging [height] is thirty-nine fingers, and the measure of the base is nine fingers plus two fingers. The ground [measurement] is... [the text ends].
By multiplying the half-measure with the suspended cord, there are produced forty-three and a half finger-breadths; for each [of these],
one should mark a triangle in the intermediate directions of Agni (southeast), Nairṛti (southwest), Vāyu (northwest), and Īśāna (northeast).
There are three equal-sided triangles; the length of each side is fourteen *aṅgulas* and twenty *vy-aṅgulas*.
Here, the perpendicular height is thirteen *aṅgulas*, and the base measurement is eleven *aṅgulas* and fifty-nine *vy-aṅgulas*.
Fifty *prativyaṅgula*s; here too, by means of the hanging measurement, there are twenty-five *prativyaṅgula*s plus one *acintyaṅgula* for half the ground, which makes fifty-eight *vyaṅgula*s;
[thus] there are fifty-five *prativyaṅgula*s, which is the area of all eight [squares].
In the *Nāṃmīlana*, six, four, and five *aṅgulas* are [the measures]; in the *Giriveda*, two *aṅgulas*;
in the *Vyoma*, forty-sixth part of a *turyaṃśa* (quarter) is known as one *aṅgula*.
Thus, in the *Ātodya*, there is a difference of more or less by exactly four parts of two *aṅgulas*, as it has been stated in the *Jā...* [text].
When the sun has moved halfway across the sky, that minute particle of dust which is first seen is the primary measure of dimensions;
they call it a *trasareṇu*, and a *trasareṇu* should be understood as consisting of eight atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Eight *trasareṇus* make one *rathareṇu*; eight *rathareṇus* are defined as a *vālāgra* (the tip of a hair); eight *vālāgras* make one *likṣā*; eight *likṣās* are known as a *yūkā*; eight *yūkās* they call a *yava*; and eight *yavas* make one *aṅgula*. [This applies] from two *aṅgulas* onwards.

We shall explain the true nature [of the matter]: in all these positions, there is no difference in the equality of the area of the field; thus, the refutation is identical. As for what was stated by the proponent of that view—that "there is no fault here because of the presence of an interior [space] in a lotus-shaped field"—that is not correct, because of the statement regarding the specific [difference of] deficiency or excess.

If it is argued that there is no fault [in the objection] because the application is similar even in other instances where there is a greater interval, since it is impossible [to establish the connection], then why would one not also adopt another instance with an even greater interval, since that too would be impossible? Therefore,
these positions are merely imagined by one's own intellect and are not based on the original source.

It should be understood that this is the method approved by Lasa and others; for the method of the primary *kuṇḍa* has been refuted by the commentators on that [work], and thus the method of its construction according to another tradition is now stated as shown by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa in the *Tattvaviveka*. Here, there are sixty [units] per finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Sixty *saṃkhyas* are said to be one *vyaṅgula*; sixty *vyaṅgulas* constitute the length of a cubit (*bhuja*).
Furthermore, according to the technical terminology, this [cubit] is defined by forty-four *aṅgulas*.
This measurement is declared for sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) of one cubit in size, as well as for the width of the arm, in accordance with the rules.
It is instructed that the arms are twenty-four finger-breadths long, with each [section] being three finger-breadths;

the width is fifty-six finger-breadths, square in shape. The *nanda* ground consists of finger-breadths likewise measured by seasons and Vedas (sixty-four); the arms are two finger-breadths, with the earth-measure (one) for each finger-breadth.
In the Yoni-shaped Kuṇḍa, the diameter is two fingers;
in the circular Kuṇḍa, the diameter is seven fingers. In the semi-circular Kuṇḍa, the diameter is eight fingers increased by two fingers.
In the hexagonal Kuṇḍa, the diameter is declared to be ten fingers, measured by the same [unit] as that of Indra (the square). [The side length is] measured in fingers...
The dimensions for the lotus-shaped fire-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) are declared to be, in sequence, nine, three, five, eight, six, four, and eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and so forth;
and for the serpent-shaped pit (*bhujagakuṇḍa*), they are twenty-one, thirty-eight, and [thirty-eight] finger-breadths and so forth.
The width of the triangular [kuṇḍa] is said to be twenty-five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and so forth;

it should be thirty-six finger-breadths for the eight-armed [form], with a diameter of two finger-breadths, seven and a half finger-breadths, and likewise [other measures]. In the octagonal kuṇḍa, however, the arms should be of that same measure.

If the diameter is five or five-and-a-half finger-breadths (aṅgula), and the height is measured at eight finger-breadths, then the measurement for the diameter is said to be thirty-three finger-breadths. The method for its construction is as follows: a circular pit (vṛtta-kuṇḍa) is formed by revolving [the radius] half of its own diameter; this is what has been described for a circle of one cubit (hasta).

The meaning is that by placing the compass point (*karkaṭaka*) on the ground at half of its diameter and rotating it around, the accomplishment of a circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) is achieved. Likewise, regarding the "half-moon" (*ardhacandra*):
it is a segment of a circle whose diameter is half of [the full] diameter; that is, on a ground measuring half the extent of the diameter stated for the half-moon.

The meaning is that by placing a circle and rotating it around [the center], a half-moon-shaped pit known as the *ardhacandra* (half-moon) is formed, which is one-half of the circle. Likewise, in the case of pits with three, four, five, six, seven, or eight sides, one should first draw a circle with a radius equal to half the width; then, the respective divisions should be made equally, one by one.

Then, by means of the statement regarding the full chord (pūrṇajyā), there shall be as many lines as the number of sides of one's own respective fire-pit (kuṇḍa) within the circle. Having divided the circle into parts according to each side, one straight line should be drawn for each part.
This is what is meant: when a triangle is desired to be made, that circle is divided into three parts, and within those [parts], [the lines are drawn].

When one wishes to draw a square, having divided the circle into three parts, one should draw one equal line in each of the three parts; when drawing a hexagon, having divided the circle into six parts, one should draw six lines at the marks of division; and for an octagon, [one should divide it] into eight [parts].
The meaning is that by taking six lines marked with divisions of the drawn-out portions, and likewise elsewhere,

the shape of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) such as the triangular ones, which are full [of those lines], is thus determined. Similarly, having first made it equal to an equilateral triangle, one should make the yoni-pit (yonikuṇḍa) with three equal sides.

From this point, three lines should be drawn from the middle of the arm outward; or else, by rotating upward here, three half-circles should be drawn. From the center of one half-circle, two lines should be made toward the tips of those arms on both sides. Having attached the bow (arc) to them, the remainder, once the [extra] is removed, becomes the *yoni-kuṇḍa*.

"Resembling the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree"—this is the meaning: having established a *karkāṭaka* (a compass-like instrument) on a ground measured by half the span of Vyāsa, one should fashion a circle by revolving it around; then, by means of the method for constructing a triangle within that [circle], one should construct a mandala with three equal sides, and [perform] the three oblations.

Having marked a sign at the center of each [section] and having fixed a compass there, one should produce three semicircles spanning the tips of both arms; then, starting from the center of the circle situated to the north,
one should draw a single line on both sides that connects to the end-lines of both sides— this is the bow.
Having erased two parallel lines of equal form, what remains shall be the *yoni-kuṇḍa*.

Likewise, one should first draw an eight-sided figure (*aṣṭāsra*) as previously described using the diameter and the arms; then, from the point where the arm is divided by that segment, one should indeed draw a semicircle above the arm and upward from the arm.

Having drawn a square equal to that [original] on all sides, one should take a fourth part of it; then, from the first and third divisions, two lines should be drawn to those two points. Equal to the segments of its sides, by means of those [lines], there shall be an eight-petaled pit known as the *padma*, which resembles a lotus.

The meaning of this is as follows: having constructed an octagonal mandala by means of the previously described method of drawing eight arms [radii] from the center according to the *Hemavṛtti*, one should then construct eight semicircles, numbering eight, all of equal size, on the outer portions of the arms, starting from the marks at the midpoints of those arms, using the measure of half an arm [radius]. These are the semicircles.

Each of the remaining sides should also be divided into four parts; in the first and third of these divisions, one should produce a fish-mark by measuring half the length of the respective arm from one end to the other end. The mouth of that fish—

Outside the great circle, one should draw two lines at the ends of the first and third divisions at the mouth of the fish; these two lines shall each be equal to half the measure of the [fish's] body. In this manner, one should perform all the procedures, beginning with the construction of the four divisions, for all eight semicircles.

It should be understood that because of its resemblance to a lotus, there is a pit named Padmakuṇḍa, which is like a lotus-pool. Regarding this, they say: Is the [Padmakuṇḍa] disregarded because the pits mentioned in the root text lack a surface area equal to their [stated] cubit-area, or is it due to a contradiction with the words of the root text?

Is it because of the absence of a root, or because another mode is possible? In that regard, it is not the fourth [alternative], for even when various modes are possible, the mode stated in the root text must necessarily be accepted due to the lack of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*) among them. Nor is it the third, for the root text is not unobserved...
Thus, such teachers deceive others by imposing meanings fabricated from their own imaginations;
otherwise, the meaning of every scripture would be unacceptable—what then to say of the *kuṇḍas*? Nor is the second [alternative] possible, for no one has ever written such a statement.

Because of that reality, you yourself have demonstrated that the statements of the *Kriyāsāra*, *Kāmika-siddhānta*, *Śekhara*, *Kalpa-kāra*, and others are mutually inconsistent and convey distinct and differing meanings; yet, by that very fact, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of all of them [is established].
Relying on the statements of these very [authorities] found in various places— such as the facing eastward and so forth,
as well as the *yonikuṇḍa* (womb-altar) and other matters propounded by Harṣadīkṣita and others—
how could there be any hostility toward the authoritative portions of the *Padārthadarśa*? For indeed, there is no contradiction here with direct perception.

If this scriptural statement (*kṣaśruti*) were perceived by anyone as being contradictory to this meaning, then, just as in the case of the Smṛti rule regarding the total wrapping [of the head], its lack of authority would be asserted; such is the word of Kanyākumāra.
Even the objection that the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is a rash act is untenable; for although the forms such as *kaleḥ* and *jhagiti*,

being contrary to direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*), lack authority, you ought not to treat the words of authors like Kalpa-writers as authoritative simply because they were intended to avoid taxing the intellect of students.

If it is argued that the gross measurement has been stated [in the scriptures] and that this is extremely censurable for them because it involves deceiving disciples with instructions on what ought not to be done—[we reply: nor is the first [alternative] tenable, since there is no harm [to the doctrine] by that much; and if it is asked, "In that case, let there be no relationship of cause and effect (prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva)," [we say] so be it—what does that matter?

Regarding the construction of that square: while it must be stated that there is some specific method for its formation, it is not a restrictive rule that this is the only method and no other exists here, since another method has also been mentioned previously.
If one asks, "How is it made with only one hand? [the answer follows].

There is no fault in proceeding with a square of one cubit (*ekahasta*) as it is indeed so; furthermore, the mention of the defects of deficiency or excess refers to methods other than those prescribed by the *Mūlakriyāsāra*, *Kāmika*, *Nūlpaka*, and others. Moreover, as for the Kamalākara mentioned by you:

Furthermore, since there is no criterion for selection (*vinigamanā-viraha*), who could prevent one from following yet another method that does not yield the fruit of the sacred field? In our own system, however, that which is stated in the Root Tantra and established by the tradition of the Guru must be accepted; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

In reality, since even that which is composed of *pūka* and so forth in the manner you described is impossible to pronounce, what need is there to mention that which is composed of *tryasareṇu*, *vyaṅgula*, *prativyaṅgula*, and so on? This is of no consequence; therefore, it is proper to adopt a gross measure that is suitable for common usage.

The moment of the *saṃkrānti* (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign) is so subtle that even when calculated by experts in mathematics, it is not suitable for performing rites such as ritual bathing or giving gifts; rather, [the rite is performed] during the preceding or succeeding *prahara* (three-hour period).
Likewise, although such a time can be known by mathematicians in this country as well, it cannot be precisely specified.

The intention of the authors of the root-text is that the construction of the *kuṇḍa* and other structures should be performed by relying solely on the gross measurement (*sthūlamāna*). Furthermore, according to such statements as "the means [for performing rites] in proximity to the *saṃkrāntis* are considered most meritorious," [the rite] is connected to a subtle time (*sūkṣmakāla*) in proximity [to the *saṃkrānti*].

If it is argued that, just as in the case of the "seizing of the channel" (*nāḍīgrahaṇa*), it is likewise necessary here to take up a location situated near a subtle location, we say: no. Precisely for the sake of attaining proximity to a subtle location, [the texts] speak of "more proximate" (*sannihitatarā*) and "most proximate" (*sannihitatamā*) locations across various tantras.

Having observed various scriptural injunctions, these should be established in sequence—referring to the possible and the impossible—as being directed toward the subtle and the gross; enough with excessive detail.
In the absence of skill in the craft, all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), such as those for the womb (yoni) and others, may indeed be square.

One should indeed make them circular, as it is stated in the *Māmnāyarahasya*: "One should make the fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) either square or circular. Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: "They should be square, or perhaps circular in some cases. However, the fire-pit for the Preceptor (*ācārya*) should be either square or circular.

It is definitely circular or square, situated between Indra (the East) and Īśa (the North), as stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "It should be circular or square in the middle position between Vṛṣa (the North-East) and Īśa. Furthermore, it does not belong to the class of *kuṇḍas* [meant for fire-sacrifices].
The method described in the root text is the best; in its absence, the alternative of five sacrificial pits (pañcakuṇḍī) should be followed as the middling option.
This is because it is stated in the *Āmnāyarahasya*: "Nine, five, or even one [pit] should be constructed, endowed with the proper characteristics.
Regarding the location of those five pits, it is stated in the *Nāradīya*: "Wherever a pit is prescribed..."

In that rite involving five [deities], the wise one should construct forty fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in the directions starting from the east— shaped like a Veda (rectangular), a weapon (triangular), a half-moon, and likewise circular and resembling a lotus— and he should cause a fifth pit to be made facing the direction of Īśa (the northeast), O twice-born one. This is a restatement of what was already established previously.

Regarding the specific details of the form, however, this is a novel injunction: even in the case of the five-pit (pañcakuṇḍa) arrangement, one who is incapable should follow the inferior single-pit (ekakuṇḍa) arrangement. Alternatively, as stated by the Teacher, there may be only one square pit in the northern direction, established according to the tradition; its placement is indeed in the north.

Or it should be performed in the west, or one should have it made in the north-western direction (the quarter of Śiva), according to the statement of Somaśambhu: "The wise man should have [it] made in the west.

And that [pit] should be either square or circular, and nothing else, because the *Kriyāsāra* states: "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) may be square, or it may be circular. Now, he states the measurement for the depth of the pits:

"Yāvān" means as much as the extent; the excavation should be of exactly that measure which is the length of the middle cord (*madhyasūtra*). Within that [area], whatever measurement is stated for the width of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), that same measurement is prescribed for its own [surrounding] area as well. Regarding this, they say: "by means of the girdle (*mekhalā*)."
This measurement of one *sahasrāṅgula* is to be followed; however, the digging should not be performed according to the dimensions of the width of the *mekhalā* (girdle) and *kuṇḍa*.

For it is stated in another Tantra that "one should dig to the measure of one cubit horizontally and upwards together with the *mekhalā*. This is also stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "The five-fold [Kuṇḍa] has three *mekhalās*..."
"Having ascertained the depth, one should dig downwards until it is complete"—thus says Viśvakarman.

Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The excavation of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) shall be equal in measure to its height, including the girdle (*mekhalā*). Regarding this, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* [comments]: [the pit should be dug] together with the girdle.
Because the girdle (*mekhalā*) serves as an ornament for the sacrificial post (*kuṇḍa*), it is not joined with those [other ornaments].

Nor should it be argued that, since it is an ornament, its occasional omission would entail a fault; for it is said: "A sacrifice devoid of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) causes the destruction of the sacrificer; death occurs when the girdle is severed."
Because of various scriptural injunctions such as these, and because it is heard that there is a transgression (pratyavāya) if one fails to perform it,

and because it is employed specifically for the accomplishment of the very nature of the sacrificial pit (khāta-hikuṇḍa), the girdle (mekhalā)— which is of the nature of an ornament— becomes an auxiliary (aṅga) that assists by way of immediate application (saṃnipatyopakāraka).
An auxiliary that assists from a distance (ārādupakāraka) [is otherwise].
It is endowed with a thousand [units] along with the *maṅgami* and the *nataya*. As it is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

"That which is dug out is equal to the wall; its status as a limb (*aṅgatva*) is proclaimed. It is distinguished by the girdles (*mekhalā*) and so forth through direct assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāra*). Furthermore, of the girdles, there are three, five, or two...

Since it does not follow from the enumeration of ten, there would also be a following [of that] due to the pain caused by its lack of conformity; furthermore, this contradicts both the statement of Viśvakarman— "the lower part should be nine finger-breadths, but the raised parts should be nine finger-breadths"— and the previously mentioned statement from the *Pratiṣṭhāsāra*.

Since it is clearly understood from the context that [the rules] refer to the three-fold girdle (*trimekhala*) and so forth, even general statements such as "together with the upper girdle" (*ūrdhvamekhalayā saha*) must be interpreted as referring specifically to the *kuṇḍas* with three-fold girdles and the like. As stated by the author of the Vārttika: "A general rule that is unclear... (is to be restricted by specific context).
It might be argued that there is a specific rule [to the contrary];
however, since there is no scriptural statement prescribing each individual girdle (*mekhalā*), and since the digging is accomplished even without a girdle, let it be so in all cases.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the measurement of the digging is performed without a girdle; [nevertheless], it is performed together with the girdle.

In a small-scale fire-oblation (*homa*) where fifty [grains] and so forth are prescribed, there is no purpose for exceeding that number; such is the established rule. However, where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts (*śruti-dvaidha*), both rules (*dharma*) apply. But in the case of a conflict between two Smṛti texts, the respective scope (*viṣaya*) for each must be determined separately.

Regarding the statement that [the measurements] are distinct, it is replied here: since there is a scriptural statement in some places regarding the necessity of a moat together with a girdle (*mekhalā*), why should it not be the same everywhere?
There is no evidence for such a discrepancy, given specific injunctions such as "the height of the five-fold girdle" and so forth.
Since the general rule is observed, and since the two items— the five and the three— are not intended as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*),
why should it not apply to all [the fires]? Therefore,
wherever there is an oblation performed by a single agent with a small measure, there it should be performed together with the girdle (*mekhalā*).

Since a larger measure is of no use, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that those scriptural injunctions regarding the performance of the sacrificial pit (*khāta*) without a girdle (*mekhalā*) refer specifically to cases where the oblation (*homa*) involves many measures and many performers. Now, he describes the nature of the girdles for the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).

The meaning is that just as the nature of the fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*)—beginning with the quadrangular (*caturasra*) womb-shape—is [defined], so too must the nature of the girdles (*mekhalās*) be fashioned accordingly.
"Threefold" refers to this superior option; the two-girdle option is middling; the single-girdle option is... [inferior].

Regarding the girdles (*mekhalā*), there are five, four, three, two, or even one, according to the *Yatīyasaṃhitā* statement; likewise, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) joined with the navel and the womb is best;
a pit with three girdles is middling; one with two girdles is inferior; and one with a single girdle is the lowest."

Regarding the term *mārga* (path), in some places the arrangement of the girdles (*mekhalā*) is stated: "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for a Brāhmaṇa has three girdles, that of a Kṣatriya has two girdles, and that of a Vaiśya has one girdle.

Thus, he describes the difference in the measurements of the girdles according to the difference in the dimensions of the pit, beginning with the words "in the measure of a fist" (*muṣṭimātre*), and so forth.
Since it will be stated later that "the kuṇḍas are one cubit [in diameter] and nine fingers [in depth] for the four fires," the venerable teachers have indicated that in all kuṇḍas,
the first mekhalā is one-sixth of the kuṇḍa's measure, the second is one-eighth,
and the third is one-twelfth. Thus says Mahākapi.

In the *Lalitapañcarātra*, it is clearly stated: "The first [line] is one-sixth of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), the second is remembered as one-eighth, and the third shall be one-twelfth. Therefore, here, the same should be done for the handful-measure vessel (*muṣṭipātra*);
"handful" (*muṣṭi*) means many handfuls, up to the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*), with the middle being even in the center.
In a sacrificial pit measuring twelve finger-breadths, the first girdle (mekhalā) should have both its height and width measuring two finger-breadths;
for the second, it is one-sixth [of the pit], which is also two finger-breadths; and for the third, it measures one and a half finger-breadths.
The compound *ekārddham* means "one and a half," being analyzed as *ekena sahitam arddham*.

Thus, the eighth part is indeed one and a half *aṅgulas*. Furthermore, the fact that it is a twelfth part, being equal to just three *aṅgulas*, is also clearly evident here at the very end; in this context, there are eighteen *aṅgulas*.
In this context, "gulma" is intended to mean three finger-breadths (*try-aṅgula*). It has been stated that the first [measurement] is the girdle (*mekhalā*), which is one-sixth part;
however, the final measurement here remains uncontradicted as being two and a quarter finger-breadths (*sapādadvyaṅgula*).
This is because, in this case, one *pada* refers to one part, whereas by two *padas*, it is two finger-breadths more.

Because the attainment of one-quarter (kaika-pāda) is possible, even the status of being one-eighth (aṣṭamāṃśatā) here is unimpeded. As for the third [line], it measures one and a half finger-breadths (mekhalā); since the word "finger" (aṅgula) here refers to a single finger-breadth, it signifies "half" through the etymological derivation of *ātma-kapada* as "one part of the self."
Because it is not obtained in that way by her [the shadow], here even the twelfth-part [of the shadow] is free from deception.
However, in the case of a single cubit (hasta), the measurement of four, three, and two fingers (*vedāgni-nayana*) for the first and subsequent girdles (*mekhalā*) is quite evident;
this is the path of those who follow the *Harṣadīpikā*. As for that which is with a quarter... [text ends].

The eighth part of a *yama* is one and a half *aṅgulas*, and the twelfth part is one *aṅgula*. Here, the omission of the quarter and half-parts by the Ācāryas was made because the difference is small; for those with excellent intellect, such as the disciples of the Ācāryas, merely seeing the general outline is sufficient, as they themselves [can understand] all the remaining details through their own wisdom.
What was stated by Harṣadīkṣita—that they take [the measurement] by inference—is merely a mockery resulting from his ignorance of their intended meaning (*tātparya*).
In reality, however, upon a thorough examination of the preceding, succeeding, and original texts, the measurement of the girdles (*mekhalā*) is established as one-sixth and so forth;
this is not the intended meaning of the root text, but rather that specific measurement.

We understand that the intention of the authors of the *Mūla* (the root text) is that the girdles (*mekhalā*) should not be made according to the nature described by others; however, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* takes the term "fist" (*muṣṭi*) to mean twenty-one finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
wherein the first [girdle] is two and a half finger-breadths plus five barley-corns (*yava*), and from that...
The third [measurement] is one and three-quarters *aṅgulas*; the *aratni* pit is likewise twenty-one *aṅgulas*.
However, by increasing the measurement by one *aṅgula* at a time, it becomes larger than the fist-pit (*muṣṭikuṇḍa*).
In that case, the first [measurement] is three and three-quarters *aṅgulas*, and from two *aṅgulas* plus six and a half barley-corns (*yava*)...

Those who say "two-third" (tṛtīya) meaning "two-thirds of two fingers" completely abandon the primary sense of the word; rather than considering such a total disregard for the root meaning, the method for making the girdle (*mekhalā*) as described in the *Harṣa-grantha* is more appropriate:
[it should be] one hand-span long and two fingers wide.
Starting from the neck, the first [tier] should be made with a height of one finger-breadth;

above that, the second should be three finger-breadths in height and seven finger-breadths in width; and above that, the third should be four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width.
This should be executed such that their [total] measure is four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively; this is the result of those [proportions].

Thus it is established: that which was previously brought forth as the earth, beginning with the girdle (mekhalā), consists of nine finger-breadths in height externally and four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width;
whereas the second [girdle] is five finger-breadths in height internally and three finger-breadths in height and three finger-breadths in width externally.
Regarding the measurement of the neck (*kaṇṭha*), it says "of the girdles" (*mekhalānām*):

the rim (*agni*) of the girdles, measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) on all sides internally, should be [one finger-breadth] around the neck of a one-cubit (*hasta*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). By this, the fourfold measurement of the pit is established.
It is implied by the phrase "the rim [is] twenty-four parts less," and it is clearly stated in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
"The neck (*kaṇṭha*) is proclaimed to be one twenty-fourth part. Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, regarding a *kuṇḍa* measuring one cubit (*hasta*), it says:
"One should make the neck one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) outside [the mouth]. For *kuṇḍas* of two cubits and larger, the same principle applies.

Regarding the increase of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) for each increment of the rim (*nemi*), he states the specific rule for when such an increase is required with the words "one should increase," and so forth:
according to the measurement of two fingers, one should increase that rim up to ten cubits (*hasta*) for other types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).
The sequence is as follows: by the verse beginning with "In a two-cubit [square] pit" (*kuṇḍe dvihaste*), he states the measurement of the girdles (*mekhalā*);
by the verse beginning with "The Hotṛ" (*hotuḥ*), he states the placement of the yoni;
and in the upper-middle portion of these girdles, in front of the Hotṛ—that is, in the eastern part—there is a horse.

By the statement "the womb [of the fire-pan] should be placed facing the Hotṛ," this is indicated: just as the altar (vedī) is positioned such that its back part faces the Hotṛ, who is either facing east or north,
so too [is the placement] relative to the western girdle (mekhalā) for some and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for others.
"The yoni should not be made above the southern girdle (*mekhalā*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*:

"The fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) are declared to be in the east, southeast, and south; the yoni faces north, while the remaining [pits] face east, or are positioned as desired for aesthetic appeal. This is also stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*. Furthermore, in the *Indrā...* [the text continues].
The *yoni* of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) dedicated to Agni and the others is situated facing north;
the *yoni* of those facing east is situated facing east; and for the others, it is situated between the east and northeast.
Soma and Śambhu also state: "The *yoni* of the fire-pits dedicated to Agni, Yama, and the others should face north, while that of the one facing east [should face] east."

Regarding the phrase "of all the remaining [fire-pits]": thus, while the eastern, southern, and western pits have their openings facing north, the northern pit has its opening facing east; the final meaning is that all other pits have their openings facing east. In a pit measuring one cubit, the six-fold [measurement] is by means of a fourth part of the width.

The length of the *yoni* should be four finger-breadths (in the form of four *aṅgulas*), while its width should follow the width of the *kuṇḍa* at one-sixth [of that], being two finger-breadths (in the form of two *aṅgulas*). This should be applied everywhere. As it is stated in another Tantra: "The fourth... [and so on].
The womb (yoni) should be shaped like a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), being long, wide, and high by six and twelve parts respectively;
its tip is one part of a skin (ajina). With this in mind, he says "six, four," and so forth.
Some, however, maintain that the length, width, and height are each twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula).

Regarding the construction of the *yoni*, as stated in the *Pañcarātra*: "One should fashion the *yoni* with a height of one *arka* (twelve) finger-breadths and a length equal to that; elsewhere it is also said that the *yoni* should be equal in height and length, or ten finger-breadths.

Having this in mind, he says "six, four, two finger-breadths," etc., [referring to] six... The meaning is that by the mutual addition of the numbers indicated by the three words [tri, pa, da], the number twelve is produced; thus they say. Regarding these two positions, the determination is according to their respective traditions.
By the phrase "one finger" (ekāṅgula), the yoni is [measured] by this twenty-fourth part of the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*.
In all [tantras], it is implied that "slightly downward-facing" means it has entered slightly into the *kuṇḍa*.

As it is stated in another tantra: "The girdle (*mekhalā*), joined with two pitchers and resembling a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, should be made so that it enters within the middle. Thus, it is twofold.
Regarding the measurement of the yoni at the front of the *stādikuṇḍas*, he says "one finger each" (*ekaikāṅgula-tu*).

For the others, from two cubits up to ten, it is "by an increment of two barleycorns" (*yavadvayakrameṇa*); that is, two barleycorns for two cubits, four barleycorns for three cubits, and six barleycorns for four cubits, and so on.

The meaning is "me" (mine). He teaches the application of the stalk (*nāla*); "starting from the base" (*sthalāt*) means that the stalk should extend from the base up to the *yoni*. By this it is stated that the stalk should be made attached to the outer girdle (*mekhalā*). [It should be] four finger-breadths in height and width, attached to the outer girdle.
The final meaning is that one should construct an altar and place the stalk upon it. Regarding the term "with a hole" (*saraṃdhrakam*):

having made a hole in the middle part for the purpose of spreading the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) over the middle girdle (*mekhalā*), the central portion of the *nyūha* should be filled with clay; this is what is taught by the insertion of the word "navel" (*nābhi*).

Regarding the phrase "of the fire-pits" (*ti kuṇḍānām*): the meaning is that one should fashion a navel for each fire-pit—whether in the shape of a lotus or in a form corresponding to the specific pit—and having fashioned it, one should place it within the excavation of the fire-pits; this is done by a Kṣatriya in the sun, using a limb of a living being as the navel.
Intending that the word *nābhi* is used in the masculine as well— on account of the rule stating "in both [genders]"—
the two qualifiers beginning with *sannibha* are taught by means of two masculine words.
The navel (*nābhi*) is two finger-breadths in height, depth, width, and breadth, and it is shaped like a clenched fist.
In the Arali-kuṇḍa, the navel is three finger-breadths in both height and width.

The meaning is that in a one-cubit [square] pit, the navel should be four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) high and four finger-breadths wide; in other pits, such as those of two or three cubits, the navel should be constructed by increasing it by two barley-grains (yavas) for each [increase in size]. This is the meaning of the phrase "by two barley-grains" and so forth. Regarding the *yonikuṇḍa*, it follows the general rule for pits.

By the words beginning with "yonim," he prohibits the *yoni* (the womb-shape) which would otherwise be obtained through the general procedure for the *kuṇḍa*, as well as the *nābhi* (navel) which would be obtained through the same general procedure; [he does so] by the words beginning with "nābheḥ" in order to effect the lotus-like shape of the navel. Regarding the phrase "one should make" (*kurvīta*), the word "partially" (*ekāṃśena*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Outside... [text truncated].

Some maintain that by the expression "by two words," it is already established by implication that [the action is performed] "by one part of that"; thus, they argue there is no need to supply the remainder of the sentence.
For according to the maxim that "a verbal expectancy is fulfilled only by a word," a word that conveys even an implied meaning must necessarily be supplied. However, this is the distinction:

Some maintain that filling in the gaps where the sense requires it does not detract from the original author's elegance, whereas in other cases it results merely in a loss of natural flow and consistency. He describes the arrangement of the *muṣṭi* and other types of sacrificial pits with the verse beginning "muṣṭi," and states an alternative view with the verse beginning "ekahasta."

With this one and a half verse, beginning with "sarva... and so forth, he states the specific application (*vyavasthā*) for square and other types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) according to the difference in the ritual purpose—whether concerning substances such as flowers, leaves, clarified butter (*ājya*), and the like, or concerning a *homa* performed by a single agent alone; [the term] *cheda* means destruction, that is to say, eradication (*uccāṭana*).
Because it causes mutual enmity among enemies, it indeed effects the destruction of their alliance;

thus, it is called "the destroyer of enemies" (*śatrukṣayakara*). Therefore, there is no tautology with the term "slaying" (*māraṇa*), nor is there any contradiction with the other [method] that will be described later. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "In the case of paralyzing, [one uses] the *aiṃḍī* [mantra]."

A quadrangular [mandala] is for the portion of Agni; a vulva-shaped one for the Moon; a half-moon for killing in the south; a triangle for causing hatred in the southwest; a circle for cooling in the west; a hexagon for eradication in the northwest; a lotus for prosperity in the north; and an eight-sided one in the northeast, which grants liberation. Now, [this applies] to Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.

If it is asked whether, in the case of a desire for sons and so forth, the shape of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should follow the [prescribed] color or rather the specific desire, [the answer is: in the case of daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) homas,
the scriptural injunction regarding the construction of the shape based on the color has already fulfilled its purpose.

In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), [the injunctions] are set aside by a statement that indicates a specific form while prioritizing a particular desire; and the injunctions regarding the *yonikuṇḍa* and other [methods], which have fulfilled their purpose when performed with the desire for a Kṣatriya son or the like, do not apply when there is a desire for a Brāhmaṇa son. Thus, [the rule applies] to the Brāhmaṇas.

It should not be argued that [the rules for other shapes] would be sublated by the very statement "it should be square," because there is no reason for such a preference (*vini-gamanā-viraha*). Rather, since the statement regarding the optional [shape] has already fulfilled its purpose in the case of one desiring a particular color, what need is there for it to be sublated by the statement specifying a particular color?
Since there is no means of determining [which specific rule applies] even in this case, the mention of a specific caste must therefore refer exclusively to non-desired [results].

This is because a statement regarding a specific desired result does not apply to the two types of obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites which are non-desired; thus, the statement regarding a specific desired result pertains to the desire of all castes.
Thus, let it be understood that this is the established rule.

These sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be made either of copper or of clay, as it has been said: "One should fashion [the pit] with copper endowed with the proper characteristics, or even with clay; a copper pit [should be cleaned] with acid, and one made of clay with cow-dung water. So it is said.

O bull among the immortals, one should thoroughly cleanse [the sacrificial pits] with a mixture of lime and water; for earthen pits, however, one should color the joints all around with red clay and rice-flour paste according to the prescribed measure. Thus, the measurement of the pits must be maintained exactly as it is, neither less nor more, and not according to one's own whim.
Regarding what was stated by Viśvakarman concerning excess in measurement and so forth: "If the excavation is excessive, there will be loss of cattle;

if deficient, loss of cows and wealth. If the *vakratuṇḍa* is present, there is suffering; if it is severed, death. If the girdle (*mekhalā*) is absent, there is grief; if it is excessive, there is destruction of progeny. [The wife...]"

"A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) devoid of the yoni is said to cause destruction; a pit lacking a neck is said to destroy one's progeny. Thus it is stated in the Jayadrathayāmala: "When the thread [measurement] is excessive, there is hatred from friends; when it is deficient, poverty occurs. When it lacks a neck, there will be skin disease; when the pit is deficient, there is non-attainment (asiddhi). When it is excessive...

If the waistband is too high, diseases increase; if it is too low, there will be loss of memory. If it is loose, torn, or full of gaps, there will be expulsion and public reproach. Thus [is described] the posterior part of the vulva.

Intending the single *kuṇḍa*, he states the alternative for the *kuṇḍa* with the words beginning "always" (*nityam*), etc. Furthermore, the alternative for the altar (*vedi*) is also mentioned in some places: "on the altar, or in a well, a metal vessel, or an auspicious earthenware one. Next is the method of constructing the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles used for the *homa*.

Rama said, beginning with "kathyete" (they are told): *Śrīparṇī* and *kāśmarī* are well-known by these names; *kṣīraśākhins* (milk-bearing trees) are those previously mentioned, such as the *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, and others. Having taken one of these, and having divided a measure of one cubit (*hasta*) into thirty-six parts, one should fashion the *sruva* ladle.
However, in that case, each individual part consists of five and one-third *yavas*.
Therein, the shaft (*daṇḍa*) is twenty parts from the base; the pedestal (*vedi*) is eight parts; its front is one part;
the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is seven parts; and the mouth (*mukha*) is [seven parts] according to the measurement of the smallest finger (*kaniṣṭhāṅguli*).
One should fashion the path for the exit of the clarified butter (ghṛta) in the form of a pipe (khepraṇālikā).
Its width should be one-third of the altar (vedi). The diameter (viṣkaṃbha) extends to the edge of the neck (kaṇṭha);
its opening (mukha) or tip is equal to the neck and has a width of one-third of the altar. [This applies to] the eight directions of the altar...

He states the rule for the placement [of the altar] with the words "in the middle of the altar" (*vedīmadhye*) and so forth. Two parts are comprised by the outer region of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) on all sides;
one part is comprised by the pit (*avaṭa*), which is a hole, and by the circular [enclosure] to be made around the outside of that pit; and [one part] at the opening.

The grammatical connection is as follows: "The girdle (mekhalā) should be [formed] by the measure of one upper part (ūrdhvāṃśa) from the top of the dome (dyu). Consequently, by that same upper part, the girdle is also obtained at the mouth (mukha); and that [girdle] should be made in a circular form.
By the remaining half-part, the arrangement of the beauty of the square (caturasra) should be fashioned around it. Ta.

One part is for the *thāka*, two parts for the *karṇikā*, one part for the *avaṭa*, two parts for the circle (*vṛtta*), and two parts for the petals (*dalāni*). One part is for the girdle (*mekhalā*), and one part is for the *śobhā*. Thus, eight parts have been utilized; the measurement for the *śobhā* portion is according to the *Mantramuktāvalī*.

"Whether it be the beauty of the presence of developed fingers, or even that which is variegated by good conduct"—in this context, the word *aṅgula* denotes a "part. In the phrase "with the staffs" (*daṇḍaiḥ*), because the topic under discussion is parts (*aṃśa*), it refers specifically to parts.
Thus, with three staff-like paths, there is a jar at the base of the staff; [and] with four parts... [the verse continues].

The mouth [of the staff] should be joined to the pot; according to the instruction "two pairs in the Kṛta and other ages," the meaning is that it should be made with two parts (aṃśas) of the three pairs. The *gaṇḍī* should be made in the shape of a bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*);
as Somaśambhu states: "At the base and at the tip of the staff, it should be like a *gaṇḍī* bracelet."

Because of that [calculation], eleven parts of the staff are taken by the two *kumbhas* and the two *gaṇḍīs*; thus, it is concluded that nine parts of the staff remain for the purpose of support. The circumference or width of the staff should be six parts; the girth of the staff is six *aṅgulas*.

Since it has been stated in the *Muktāvalī* that "the mantra is recited," and since it is prescribed that "the back portion should be made in the shape of a tortoise with six parts," there is the opinion that the phrase "the thickness (*ānāha*) of the staff is said to be its length (*dīrghatva*)" refers to something entirely distinct; however, in that case, [the word] *ānāha* does not denote length.

Furthermore, because this contradicts the statement in the *Uktamuktāvalī*, and because there would be no expectation for a specific shape on the back portion when it is fashioned in the form of a tortoise, [the author] states "of the swan," etc., saying that one should fashion the shape of the mouth of this *sruk* ladle's back portion in the form of the mouth of either a swan, a horse, or a boar.

Having thus described the method of fashioning the *sruca* ladle, he now demonstrates the method of constructing the *sruva* spoon with the words beginning with "in the *sruca*," and so forth. Having divided one hand into thirty-six parts, the depth of the *sruva* was stated; therein, twelve parts are joined together [to form] four [units].

One should construct the *sruk* ladle with twenty-two parts; therein, the handle (*daṇḍa*) consists of twenty-two parts and the head (*śiras*) of two parts. Therein, the hollowing should be such that it holds exactly one *karṣa* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). In this regard, the *gaṇḍīpada* is superior to the *kumbha*; likewise, at the base and the tip, the opening should be as described previously.
The established meaning is that two pairs [of twigs] are to be used as bracelets;
the substitute for these two has been stated in another Tantra: "In the absence of those, the oblation is offered with two Palāśa leaves.
This is because of the Vedic revelation (Śruti) stating, "With two leaves," meaning with the middle leaves, or specifically, one offers with the middle leaf. For this very reason...

By the statement beginning with "one should feed [the guest] on a row of leaves other than those of the *madhyapātra* or *palāśa*," the prohibition of the *madhyapātra* leaf is established for the act of eating; however, because that [leaf] is prescribed for the oblation (*havana*), it is employed there. By the use of the dual number, the functional capacity of both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is indicated, as it is stated that they function as a pair.
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, it is stated that the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of metal and not of bronze or lead;

they may be fashioned from the wood of the *yajñadāma*, or from the leaves of the *vāta* tree, or from the *pippala*. O Sage, one should provide two beautiful *sruk* and *sruva* ladles made of *palāśa* leaves that are free of holes.

Regarding the statement "the fire-offering (homakarma) is performed with the leaves of the *śvasta* tree," the author now demonstrates the method for constructing one of the four types of mandalas, such as the *Sarvatobhadra*, located in the center of the pavilion upon the altar, beginning with the words "square" (*caturasra*) and continuing with "oriented from east to west" (*pūrvaparāyatābhiḥ*).
Having produced a square consisting of four compartments by means of three lines extending from south to north and three lines [extending from east to west],

one should then draw two diagonal lines (karṇasūtra)— one from the southeast to the northwest and one from the northeast to the southwest— and [draw] a single diagonal line in each of the four corners.
One should draw two lines intersecting at right angles, forming four fish-shaped figures from their intersection;

within these, one should draw two lines extending east-west and two extending north-south. In this way, sixteen squares are produced, which are also called *pahāni*. [The subsequent description concerns] the diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*).
The half-cells that are already established are here designated by the term "cell-arrangement" (*koṣṭhapradana*).
With the verse beginning with *pūrvavat* and so forth, he describes in one and a half verses the method for producing the sixty-four cells;
the meaning is as follows: in the four corner cells that have arrived... [the diagonal line].

Having given a thread for each individual [mark], one should place two threads as before at the four points where the intersections of the produced threads meet— one with its tip pointing east and one with its tip pointing south— at the west and the north;
then, having drawn the lines, one should [proceed] with the four fish-shaped marks in the intermediate compartments produced by the intersection of these threads.
Having laid down two threads from west to east with their tips pointing eastward, and two from south to north with their tips pointing northward, a line is drawn;
thus sixty-four squares are produced. By the words "as far as" (*yāvat*) and so forth, [the author] indicates the method for producing two hundred and fifty-six squares.

The meaning is that one should cast as many threads as are required to produce two hundred and fifty-six squares— using that very same method and in the manner previously described— upon the sixty-four-square mandala already prepared.

And thus it is concluded: having laid down four diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) in the four corners as before, one should lay down two threads—one directed eastward and one directed northward—upon the four fish-figures produced by those [diagonals]. In the fish-figures within the intervening squares produced by the intersection of these four threads, six...
From the west, one should drop six threads with their tips pointing eastward; from the north, six threads with their tips pointing southward.
When this is done, two hundred and fifty-six squares are produced.
He now demonstrates the application of these squares: thirty-six...
In the manner described by the verse beginning with "śata," having set aside five rows each on all sides starting from the middle and the exterior of the constructed field,
one should fashion a lotus with the thirty-six squares situated in the center; this is the boundary of the lotus consisting of thirty-six [squares].
The outer protection, consisting of eight parts and being square, applies to the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the altar (*vedikā*),

and the beautifications of the doors (*dvāra-śobhā*) and so forth; likewise, one should construct a pathway (*vīthikā*) outside the boundary of the lotus by means of two rows consisting of twenty-eight squares.

The meaning is that outside of that, one should construct four items— namely, the doors, the *śobhās*, the *upaśobhās*, and the corners— using the two remaining rows consisting of one hundred and twelve squares each. Then, with thirty-six squares, [one constructs] the center.

Regarding the method for arranging the lotus, he says: "Of the lotus-field," meaning of the lotus-field consisting of thirty-six squares (*koṣṭha*), one should place a single part—the twelfth part—around the outside; by that, two parts are abandoned on both sides.
Then, having set aside one-tenth part, two directional threads— one extending from east to west and one extending from south to north—
and two diagonal threads (also known as *karṇa-sūtras*), were established as previously laid out.
The lotus-field itself is divided into eight parts; these very lines become the central lines for the petals. The method for this is as follows:
having divided the six internal ten-part sections into six, one should [draw] the central lines starting from the center.

Having drawn one circle with two parts [of the radius], one should draw a second circle outside that with two parts, and a third circle outside that with two parts. The coloring of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and other elements— such as "the pericarp with yellow color," and so forth— is to be described by the author himself in the root text.
Desiring to dispel the inquiry as to what the locations such as the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and so forth are,

he now teaches the literal meaning of those terms regarding their locations and so on, beginning with the words "the first" (*ādyam*), by means of the phrase "by the portion that has been released" (*muktāṃśena*), which refers to the previously abandoned twelfth part.
The meaning is that the circle previously described will be completed by abandoning twelve parts;
however, it should be understood that the current mention of that [measurement] is solely for the purpose of acquainting one with the location. Regarding the word "vāhya" (external):
that which is the external circle, the third of them, the space between that [and the center]—by that measurement, [one should draw] the filaments at the tips of the filaments.
Having placed the tip of the cord at the center of the circle and having fixed its end according to the procedure to be described below,
one should draw lines in the shape of half-moons on both sides of the field-lines; having thus drawn them, one should place cords at the junctions of those half-moons.
The procedure for drawing [the petals] is as follows: having fixed the thread at the point where the circle of the whorl and the cardinal-direction thread intersect,
one should draw a half-moon on both sides of that cardinal-direction thread, touching the circle of the whorl and extending to its two points of contact with the circle of the petals.

Thus, when the four lines for the cardinal directions and the four lines for the corners have been drawn, eight half-moons are produced. If it is asked, "Why is it that various half-moons are not produced? [the answer is: because of the plural expression in the phrase, "placing the beginning of the thread on the tips of the filaments" (*kesarāgreṣu sūtrādiṃ nidhāya*).
O Goddess, take [the thread] from there, where the positions of the filaments situated within the eight-fold grid are located;
then, at the eight junctions formed by the mutual intersection of the two half-moons, apply a single thread between each pair of facing points. When this is done, it becomes an eight-petaled [lotus].

Thus, eight boundary lines arise; those two situated on both sides of the boundary line located in the lower portion of the junction are to be wiped away by the rays of the half-moon, whereby the accomplishment of the petal-shape is achieved. To form the tips of the petals, he constructs a fourth circle.

With the words beginning with "lāgra" (tip of the petal), one should construct a fourth circle using that measurement which consists of the twelve parts attached to the exterior of the tips of the petals; in the space between those, namely within the interval between the petal-tip circle and the central axis,
one should [draw] on both sides of that central axis, equally on all sides, the outer...

The wise one should draw [the petals] by placing the tips [of the threads] in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions; this is the syntactical connection. The method for that is as follows: having placed the tip of the thread and so forth at the junction-thread situated on both sides of the central thread of the petal within the space between the fourth circle, [one draws] from the center of the clear petal-circle.

The point where the lines from the tips of the petals and the center of the circle intersect must be touched by the outer hand; likewise, it should be performed with the outer hand so that the two ends of the threads face each other. It is precisely for this purpose that [the measurement] is made on the outer hand.

Not so; otherwise, when one thread is laid from the position of the joint-line to the tip of a petal, and another is drawn from the position of the joint-line to the tip [of the adjacent petal], the two tips would not face each other. Therefore, omitting the circle of the pericarp (karṇikā), [one should proceed as follows].
One should erase the three lines situated within the center of the lotus petals and so forth,

so that the eight-petaled lotus becomes pleasing to the eye. Regarding the method for constructing the filaments, he says "in the petal" and so forth, [referring to] that which is shown as being located at the junction of the pericarp and the surrounding area.

In the space between the boundary lines of the petals, on both sides of the central line of each petal, one should draw two filaments (kesara) at each location; their bases should touch the circle of the pericarp (karṇikā), and their slightly curved tips should face one another.

The meaning is that wherever the wheel is constructed, in all those places this very method applies; thus he says "this," referring to the previously mentioned establishment of the *vīthī* for the sake of the *pīṭha*, wherein he now describes the manner of arranging the limbs and members.
By the words "ha padāni" and so forth, [it is indicated that] for each corner cell of the pathway situated outside the lotus, as well as the two cells located on its two sides...
Thus, one should erase three squares at each corner; these shall be the legs of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
The remaining four squares in each direction shall be the body parts of the pedestal.
Regarding the application of the squares for the path (*vīthī*), he says: "The squares are the path," and so forth.

The meaning is that one should erase the two rows in such a way that there is no division of the rows, so that the two rows become one. It has been stated that the doors and so forth are to be made with the remaining two rows;
he explains that method beginning with the words "In the directions," etc., for the purpose of establishing the doors and so forth.
Between the two rows, for the sake of the four gates,

one should erase the two squares situated on both sides of the central line within the inner row, as well as the four squares situated on both sides of the central line within the outer row; thus, by means of six [squares] each...
"Each door [consists of] one [square]," meaning that by means of twenty-four squares, four doors are formed.
He describes the manner of the arrangement of the ornaments with the words beginning "by the squares," etc.:
the three squares situated on each side of the doors, located within the inner row, are on both sides of the doors.

Having cleared each of those individual outer-row squares, there shall be one ornamentation for every four squares; thus, with two on each side at every door and four doors, eight ornamentations are ultimately completed.

The meaning is as follows: having cleared away three by three outer-row squares starting from each square connected to the *śobhā* (beauty) located within the row, there shall be eight *upaśobhās* (subsidiary beauties), each consisting of four squares;
this is done by omitting six squares and so forth, leaving two... [and so on].

The purpose of stating "by four squares" (*tuḥkoṣṭakaiḥ*) and so forth is to indicate that the removal (*mārjana*) of those words joined in two rows of two— which are of those respective numbers— applies only to those situated in a single row;
this very indication occurs at the time of performing the meaning [of the verse] with the words "situated in the inner row" (*antarapaṅktistha*) and so on.
We have not made it entirely clear; he [the author] states the method for constructing the corners with the words "by the remaining," etc.
On both sides, three squares each located within the inner row and also three squares each located within the outer row are to be leveled, joined with the decorative borders (*upaśobhā*).
The meaning is that the four corners should each be made with six [lines].
To describe the colors for the purpose of pleasing the deities, he says "one should color," and so forth.
Regarding "with safflower" (*kusumbha*), it is stated in another source, the *Gautamīya*, that red is also said to be that which is joined with the dust of evening twilight (*doṣā-rajas*).

It is said by the wise that "doṣārajaḥ" refers to turmeric powder (*haridrā-cūrṇa*). According to the lexicographical definition, "pulāka" means chaff or husked grain; therefore, the powder made from that which is more than chaff is "kṛṣṇa-cūrṇa. The method for its preparation is as follows: from chaffed grains...
At the time of its burning, one should prepare a powder by sprinkling it with milk and other liquids and then filtering it through a cloth.
By the phrase "vitvādi" (beginning with *vitva*), the inclusion of other green leaves is intended. As stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The dust that has become dark and dark-leaved is declared to be for one's own rites. [End of quote] *Śyā*...
By the word "mapada," the green color is understood;
moreover, this coloring is necessary because the hearing of its fruit [is recorded] in the *Kapila-pañcarātra*, where it is stated:
"The earth is to be known as yellow, water is proclaimed to be white, fire is of red color, and air is dark blue."

It has been proclaimed [to you]. O great sage, the fifth [element], space (ākāśa), is black in color. O sinless one, I have declared that Rudra is the presiding deity (adhidevatā) of the white, Brahmā is the presiding deity of the red, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the yellow, Acyuta himself is the presiding deity of the black, and the Nāga is declared to be the presiding deity of the dark-blue.

White dust destroys the calamities caused by the planets; red dust destroys those arising from the hosts of pretas; black dust destroys the power of all asuras; yellow dust destroys the misfortunes of men; and green dust destroys the piśāca and rākṣasa afflictions. Therefore, especially during fire-offerings (homa), consecrations (abhiṣeka), and sacrifices, one should color the mandala with these [dusts].

For the sake of achieving satisfaction while dwelling [there], all the boundary lines (*sīmārekhā*) are indeed white, because they are mentioned without distinction. With the words "Alternatively" (*yadvā*) and so forth, up to the end of the phrase "the black-colored ones," he states another alternative. "Yellow indeed," and so forth; in the second position as well, it is just like the first position.
The meaning is that the pericarp of the *kṣe* [syllable] should be yellow; having concluded the alternative view, he states the matter at hand, which is common to both positions,
with the words "even by the yellow," etc., ending with "the wombs of the seats."

The term *garbhaka* refers to the location of the womb-corners (*garbhakoṇa*) because they contain a womb; the suffix *-a* is applied here according to the rule beginning with *arśas*. Its neuter gender is established by the word *kamala*. The meaning is that one should repeatedly recite [the mantra] while coloring the corners of the lotus-field with yellow or black pigment. One should color the legs of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with red powder and the body of the pedestal with white powder.

Then, one should conquer; furthermore, in the four pathways (vīthī), one should paint various kinds of wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpalatā) joined with fruits, flowers, and so forth, colored with various hues. One should color the doors with white powder, the secondary decorations (upaśobhā) with red powder, the corners (koṇa) with yellow powder, and [the main decorations] with black powder.
Then, one should draw three lines of squares around the perimeter of the maṇḍala using powders of white, red, and black colors in sequence; thus he says, "The feet shall be," and so forth.
This is common (*sādhāraṇa*), meaning common to all deities, and not of a distinct nature due to the divisions of Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, and so on.
This is the meaning of *pamiti*. He describes another mandala with the words "the earth [divided] into squares" (*caturasrām bhuvam*) and so forth.
As before, having constructed a mandala of sixteen squares, one should divide each individual square into three parts;
the final result is that the thread for the cardinal directions (east and so on) is divided twelvefold. Among those... in the west... [the text continues].

Having drawn eight threads extending from east to west across the six marks of division made by the four squares at the eastern end, and again having drawn eight threads extending from south to north across the six marks of division made by the four squares at the southern end;
One should draw the lines so that there are one hundred and forty-four squares;
therein, a lotus is formed with thirty-six squares, the construction of the pedestal (pīṭha) is by the outer row,
and in the two rows outside that, as before, there are four-fold beauties, the path (vīthī), and the secondary beauties (upaśobhā).

In this manner of meditation, by means of the remaining words—specifically one word situated within the inner row and five words situated in the outer rows—one should color those respective locations with five syllables using six squares, and likewise draw three lines outside the mandala. The mandala... [is completed].
Some call this "the Path" (*lam*), identifying it as the second variety of the *Sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala.
Regarding the nine-naveled (*navanābha*) maṇḍala, he says "in a square" (*caturasra*) and so forth:
having first drawn a square of the desired measurement and divided it into sixty-four squares as before, one should [proceed] within the four central squares.

One should fashion a lotus as before. In its eastern portion, one should establish a straight boundary line reaching to the edge of the maṇḍala, consisting of eight squares for a single path, and then erase [the excess]. In this same manner, one should also proceed in the southern, western, and northern parts relative to the central lotus.
One should erase each individual path consisting of eight times eight squares. When this is done, eight groups of four squares remain in the eight directions;
therein, one should draw lotuses in each of the four-square groups situated in the cardinal directions, and likewise in each of the square groups situated in the corners.

One should fashion the *svastika* (auspicious cross). The method for its construction is as follows: having divided each of the four corners into four squares, and having established the form of a *svastika* by drawing two sets of lines—one extending east-west and the other north-south—with intervals between them; thus it is accomplished.

One should erase it in such a way that this [result] occurs; herein is the instruction: having excluded the four square cells located at the corners along with their boundary lines from among the sixteen cells, one should erase all the remaining twelve cells so as to produce the form of a svastika.

Regarding the term *vatī*: according to the author of the *Padārthadarśa*, for each individual square situated within the four central squares, there is a group of four squares consisting of one corner square—starting from the southeast (āgneya) corner—and three squares situated to its north; these four squares constitute the defining unit of the corner (*koṇatva*).
One should erase the three squares starting from the southwest corner up to the eastern square;
if there is one square that has entered into the central group of four, it constitutes a set of four squares,
and one should erase another [set] starting from the northwest corner square up to the eastern one.
One should erase four squares: three squares defining the corner situated in the southern part starting from the square in the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa),
and one square defining the corner therein.
One should cleanse four groups of three squares.
They say that the accomplishment of the form of a swastika surrounded by ten [deities] results from both [traditions], since both possess scriptural authority;

thus, the arrangement is determined according to the lineage of the Guru. In the former view as well, the sequence of Śveta and the others begins with Īśāna starting from Śiva, beginning from the northeast (Īśāna).

If it is argued that because these [elements] lack substance (*sattva*) and roots (*mūla*), they possess no inherent auspiciousness (*svastikatva*), then let there be rather a figurative auspiciousness (*gauṇasvastikatva*) therein by virtue of their being constituent parts of the *svastika*. As for the remainder:
the coloring of the panels (*padāni*), the creation of the *kalpalatā* in the walkways (*vīthīṣu*), and white or other colored lines outside the mandala.

And by the passage beginning with "nacanābha" and ending with "sarvasiddhida," he concludes [the section], making it known that this very [method] is to be adopted in every instance where it will be stated in this work or in other works, saying "this is to be placed in the navel-mandala" and so forth, [granting] all accomplishments and fulfilling desires.

Although there are various differences, it is suggested that this [mandala] is neither divided nor undivided, and that it is not something to be followed in some places while being rejected in others; thus, he extracts the *pañcābjamaṇḍala* with the words beginning "this," etc. This is the nine-navel mandala, excluding the *svastika*, as previously stated.

The meaning is that even those four sets of four [lines] placed in the four corners of the navel-maṇḍala for the purpose of performing the svastika-arrangement must likewise be wiped away in this five-lotus maṇḍala. The determination of their respective domains has been stated in the *Prayogasāra* regarding the ritual vessels (*kalaśas*).

The supreme state, which resembles the luster of a fresh lotus, is as previously described. In the previously consecrated field, one should wipe clean the corner compartments that serve as the location for the svastikas, just as before.
The placement of the five jars is declared to be five lotuses; it is square.
In the middle of that place, one should draw a lotus; this is declared to be the "single jar" (ekakalaśa) rite, described as the "lotus with elephants" (sāvāraṇapada).

In response to the expectation of where each of these mandalas is to be employed for which specific ritual action, he says, beginning with "in initiation" (dīkṣāyām), and so forth. Here too, what is the role of the preceptor?
To address whether this is for the sake of establishing one's own view, or for the sake of honoring some existing deities independently, he says:

"for the purpose of worshipping the deity. Accordingly, having drawn the *sarvatobhadra* and other such mandalas upon the altar, [one should worship] one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) there, upon a lion-throne or similar seat.
The implied meaning is that worship and other such acts should be performed for her alone.

Desiring to dispel any suspicion regarding her lack of authority, he says "sarva" and so forth; for even though a matter follows a single system, it remains entirely acceptable because it is authoritative—certainly not otherwise.

The authority of even a single word uttered by the Blessed One does not depend upon awaiting the testimony of another; rather, its authority arises solely from its being rooted in the Śruti, because it was spoken by the Omniscient One.
Therefore, in those portions that contradict directly perceived Śruti, one must infer a corresponding root-Śruti.
If it is argued that [the scripture] lacks authority because it is impossible for conceptual construction to be unobstructed by the certainty of sublation, we say no;

for [scriptures state]: "One shall not harm any living beings," "One who practices sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," "One should take the Ṣoḍaśin cup in the Atirātra," and "One should not take the Ṣoḍaśin cup in the Atirātra."

Since various types of Śruti passages are observed whose meanings are mutually contradictory, and since there is no certainty of sublation (bādha) [of one by the other], there is no obstacle to such a conceptualization;
therefore, even for that which has attained authority according to the aforementioned method, [it remains authoritative] despite being contrary to Śruti.

The non-performance of what ought to be done must be remedied; nevertheless, since in some cases there may be uncertainty regarding the meaning of the words or the intended meaning of a single treatise, one must indeed follow another treatise—this is the intention behind the word "all" (*sarva*), and this is the summary. [Of whom...]

The third chapter, concerning the completion of the word [of the Lord], has reached its conclusion: [He] whose mother was the virtuous Dyotamati, whose father was named Māpati, a treasure-house of love; who was born in the lineage of Tipanthaka, whose birthplace was Kūrmācala; who made Vārāṇasī his residence, having well propitiated the feet of Acyuta through the valor of his penance.

In the *Arthacintāmaṇi*: For ministers who have attained their mantras, and even for teachers, that benefit which results in the attainment of the welfare of the disciple occurs only if the disciple’s reception of the mantra takes place according to the procedure to be described;
and that procedure cannot be understood without a formal exposition.

Beginning with the words "Now, therefore" (*athetyādinā*), he proceeds to demonstrate the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of those who have been awakened; however, the phrase "of the mantra-practitioners and disciples" (*maṃtriṇāṃ śiṣyāṇām*) is not the intended meaning.

For indeed, one becomes a counselor (*mantrin*) by the reception of counsel (*mantra*); there is no desire to know the means for that [counsel] beyond that [reception]. However, one who has learned a counsel from a book or similar source is not the referent of the term "counselor. Furthermore, even for one who has obtained a counsel through improper means, or who has attained the status of a counselor merely by that [improper] way, there is no attainment of welfare.

Some maintain that the root text beginning with "of the practitioners" (*mantriṇām*) is intended to convey the sense that [the initiation] occurs until the re-acceptance of the mantra is performed by means of the ritual of initiation; however, if the reading were *mantrāṇām*, it would not be so,
