because one would intend to express the connection of the genitive case-meaning with the referent of the word "initiation" (*dīkṣā*).

There is no inconsistency whatsoever. In this reading, the phrase "out of a desire for welfare" (hitakāmyayā) means for the sake of accomplishing what is desired by either the teacher, the disciple, or both.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *mantra* has been stated in another tantra as: "Manana is the thorough knowledge of the universe; trāṇa is protection from saṃsāra."

Because it accomplishes [the goal] through wealth, it is called *mantra*; as it is said elsewhere: "It is a *mantra* because of its secret instruction (*guptopadeśa*), and also because of its contemplation (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*). Regarding the meaning of the word *dīkṣā*, the root text states "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth; [it is so called] because, while bestowing divine gifts, it destroys sin.

The meaning is that the word *dīkṣā* is conventional (*rūḍhi*) with respect to a specific meaning; it is not, however, expressed by the etymological (*yaugika*) meaning of the word *dīkṣā*, because such a meaning is not understood even through the etymological analysis of its constituent parts (*avayavavyutpatti*). This is because the specific meaning is heard [in the text] due to the use of the instrumental suffix (*-kāriṇī*).
Some say that there is no over-extension [of the term] to *nanādu* and so forth; however, this is merely for the sake of defining such a specific meaning. Therefore, it is not redundant.
In reality, however, the passage beginning with "from that, he saw" (*tasmād īkṣata*) establishes that this [term] is indeed etymological (*yaugika*), and not merely conventional (*rūḍhi*).
The intended meaning is this: although there is a short vowel *i* in the root *yuj*, it is a part of the word;

and since the root *div* (to play/shine) possesses multiple meanings, it is used here in the sense of "taking" (*ādāna*) by means of the long vowel *ī*, thereby expressing divine knowledge (*divyajñāna*). Furthermore, because that [knowledge] leads to a state beyond that [world], it is a partial constituent of the verbal roots.
The letter *kṣa* is called "the giver" (*dāyin*); because it is a part of the word for destruction (*kṣaya*), it expresses the destruction of evil.
By the sense that "one becomes [liberated] through Soma," the word *arśādyavākṣāpada* expresses the meaning of being the cause of the destruction of evil.
Therefore, the previously mentioned meaning is obtained precisely through the etymological derivation of its constituent parts; this is the truth.

In accordance with the sequence of the locations, he first demonstrates initiation with the words beginning "the teacher" (*deśika*). He instructs—that is, he teaches—the mantras, the means for their accomplishment, and so forth; thus he is the "teacher" (*deśika*), the Guru. He should go, but not enter; he should enter within the right [channel].
Since entry [into the ritual space] is to be described by the words "with the feet," it is indicated that one should remain outside and perform the necessary rites—
beginning with the sipping of water (ācamana) and ending with the removal of obstacles— to make the purposeful work effective;
thus, one should speak [the mantras] preceded by the recitation of the qualities and names [of the deity], starting from the bathing place on the river.

Having gone from this pavilion to another place outside, and having saluted the Guru, one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), and the deities of the directions and time, one should contemplate all that is sinful along with the expiation performed, [reciting]: "Oṃ! Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla, and the five great elements—these nine are the witnesses of the good and evil deeds performed here."

Having recited the two mantra-ślokas beginning with "sākṣiṇo viṣṇo yad prākṛtaṃ vitta pāpākāntam amūmama tan niḥsāraya vittān me pāpaṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ te namaḥ," and having thus cast off sin, one should wash both hands and feet. O Ananta!

He states what is to be performed with the words beginning with "having sipped water" (ācamya) and so forth. By the phrase "according to the rule for morning duties and the like," the performance of the *saṃdhyā* and *tarpaṇa* is indicated;

and by the phrase "the rites of the forenoon," it is indicated that this follows the general rule for the purpose of sipping water (*ācamana*) situated between those two. Even in the general rule for the purpose of sipping water, both of these [the *saṃdhyā* and *tarpaṇa*] are not perceived.

Because it depends on specific ritual procedures (*pividhiviśeṣa*), the meaning is that one should sprinkle with "weapon-waters" (*astrāmbu*)—that is, with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*)—or alternatively, with water [consecrated] by the weapon-mantra; this refers to the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*), which is the worship of the eight presiding deities (*aṣṭadevatā*) of the door. He states the locations and names of these eight deities, beginning with the word "above" (*ūrdhva*).

Is this not intended for the *toraṇa* (archway) constructed from *udumbara* wood, which is the horizontal beam situated above the door-posts? For it is mentioned immediately after [the description of] that, and moreover, these deities of the doors reside specifically at the doors themselves.
The worship [is performed] at the arches, upon the lintels situated above the western door,
with *udumbara* wood.

Some say this is stated with the intention that it is for the purpose of the act of worship (*mevakāryya*). Others, however, state that "made of *udumbara*" is merely an indicative mark for any sacrificial wood in general, and that the quality of being made specifically of *udumbara* is not intended here; on that wood, one should place Vighneśa in the middle portion and [the other deities] in the southern portion.

Having worshipped Mahālakṣmī in the northern part and Sarasvatī [in the same], one should worship Vighneśa on the branch extending toward the southern direction, Kṣetreśa on the branch extending toward the northern direction, Gaṅgā beside Vighneśa, Yamunā beside Kṣetreśa, and the Weapon-deity (Astra-devatā) at the threshold; thus [are the] eight.
The worship of the door-deities should be performed at all three doorways; thereafter, the gatekeepers are to be honored, namely:
Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Bala, Prabala, Bhadra, Saṃjña, Prabhadra, and the Vaiṣṇavas; and he who is known as Nandi is Mahākāla.

Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣabha, the one named Bhṛṅgiriṭi, the one named Skanda, Pārvatīśa, and Caṇḍeśvara are the Śaiva [deities]; the eight Mothers are the Śākta; the four are the Traipuras, namely Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, and Gajānana. Laṃ...

Vodara, Cavikaṭa, and Vighnarāja as the seventh; Dhūmrarāja, Gaṇapati, Bhadra, Subhadra, Vala, and Pravala—these are the door-keepers of the East in sequence. Candrapracaṇḍa, Vapunarjaya, and Vijaya likewise shall be the door-keepers of the Sun; thus it is stated in the Tantrānta.
Having first worshipped the eight deities at the entrance gate— which is remembered as the *resthi*— on all sides,

one should approach and dispel the three types of obstacles (vighnas) categorized as celestial (*divya*), atmospheric (*antarikṣa*), and terrestrial (*bhauma*). In a Śrauta rite, one should cause the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) to enter through the eastern gate.

Regarding this, many hold that one enters here as well through the eastern gate, following the previous [rule]. Others, however, maintain that since entry through the western gate is prescribed for the pavilions of the *tulāpuruṣa* and other rites, one should enter here too through the western gate alone; for generally, facing east (*prāṅmukhatva*) is the rule for both obligatory and occasional rites.

Because the *Tikā* and other [commentaries] praise the worship as being performed through the western gate, there is a rule that one must enter by the western gate alone; furthermore, the rule is that one must first perform the ritual service (*saparyā*) for whichever deity’s [mandala] one enters. Having reached the western gate, preceded by three *tāla*-claps, one should open the door with the mantra beginning with "O Goddess, O Essence... (*oṃ devi sārasam...*).

Even though the Tantric statement cited by Grahodāhṛta is quite clear, we see no reason for the confusion regarding which deities of the entrance gate should be worshipped first by means of the *varṣakomudī* [or *varṣakautukī*] rite. Enough!

One should smell it but not touch it, because the weapon-deity (*astradevatā*) has been worshipped there. Furthermore, the mantra of the weapon-deity is the weapon-mantra associated with one's own chosen deity (*upāsyadevatā*), and not merely the syllable *phaṭ*; this authority has been described by us in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*.

One should enter and sit upon the *natyāsana* (theater-seat), because it must be mentioned first. Regarding the phrase "to the end of the four-way path" (*catuḥpathāntam*), what is intended here by the term "four-way path" is a portion of ground measuring one cubit outside the pavilion, where archways (*toraṇa*) have been erected. Thus says the mantra:

Having first inspected the pavilion, extending from the *ḍapāt* (the base of the pillar) up to the area outside the Brahma-thread, with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should then sprinkle it with the water for general purposes (*sāmānyārghyajala*) previously placed outside, using the five-fold [mantras], and strike it again with *kuśa* grass using the weapon mantra (*astramantra*). Let this be done.

One should perform the sprinkling with the *takavaca* mantra; however, according to the instruction of those who know the tradition (*saṃpradāya*), when no specific mantra is mentioned, one should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth with the mantra under discussion. By the word "wise" (*sudhīḥ*), it is indicated that in cases where no mantra is specified—such as when incense is offered within the mandala—one may use either the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) or the mantra [of the deity].

In the *Harṣakaumudī*, it is stated that "it should be thrown" (*dartavya*), whereas in the *Padārthādarśa*, it is stated that "incense-burning [should be performed] silently" (*tūṣṇīṃ dhūpanam*). This is not contradicted by the aforementioned general rule (*paribhāṣā*) of those very [texts]. It is further stated there that the word "the wise one" (*sudhīḥ*) connects with the subsequent verb "he should scatter" (*vikiret*); here too, since there is an expectancy for an agent, the connection of both [terms] is appropriate.

And the scattering of the offerings: "May those spirits who are departing, those spirits who are stationed upon the earth, and those spirits who create obstacles—may they vanish by the command of Śiva!
May the spirits and piśācas depart in all directions; may [this rite] proceed without opposition from anyone."

To indicate that [the ritual] is to be performed with the mantra consisting of two verses beginning with *aham karmasamārabhe*, he says "sudhīḥ" (the wise one). The seven substances, such as parched grain (*lāja*) and others, which have been placed inside, should be arranged exactly so; and in the northeast direction of the cleansed pavilion, a small hut (*vūṭī*) should be established.
Regarding those vessels such as conch shells known as *kṛtyasanālaṃvarddhanī*,

when they become empty due to the pouring out of water, one should place a specific vessel beneath them— one which is necessarily required to serve as a receptacle for the water to be poured back into those respective vessels.

One should obtain it; furthermore, regarding the consecration (*abhimantryana*) of a handful of *kadarbha* grass for the purpose of purification with the *Harṣakaumudī*, it is stated that this should be done seven times.

As for the authority on that point, it was stated by them [the commentators] as "seven recitations" (*saptajaptāni*), but that does not connect here because of the distance [in context] and because of the difference in grammatical case endings (*bhinnavibhaktikatva*). Bhi... [text fragment].

Furthermore, because the word *nava* (nine) and the two words *saptapada* (seven steps) and *astra* (weapon) are all situated within the middle of a compound, they cannot be construed with one another; nor does that number [of nine] apply merely to the phrase "recited over the weapon" (*astra-strajapta*), for according to the principle that "when a scriptural injunction has been performed once, its purpose is fulfilled," it applies to the entire act.
By logic, unity alone is perceived; therefore, it must be understood that no number other than one is taught regarding the objects [of the mandala].

The mandalas such as Sarvatobhadra and others have been described; furthermore, the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and so forth is additional to the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Other matters already stated and those yet to be stated constitute the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
One should enter even into sorcery (*jāda*); the method for that is as follows: in a *kūrma-cakra* consisting of nine compartments, one should seat oneself in whichever central compartment it may be;
in that compartment, [one should worship] Yakṣetrapāla, Anna, Vṛṣabha, Śaila, Rāja, Vāsuki, Arthakṛt, and Śa...

Having worshipped Kṛttikā, Padmayoni, and Mahāśaṅkha as they arrive in the sequence starting from the east and so forth, and having requested their permission and inspected that site, one should consecrate it with the four purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Then, beginning with Ācāraśakti and ending with Maṇivedī, one should worship the deities therein and [place] the *kaṃ*...
Having spread the *valādi* seat, one should sit down with the mantra "Pṛthvi" (O Earth). Thus it is said:

"Having worshipped Kṣetrapāla, then, by the command of Kṣetrapāla, one should consecrate the established seat with the four purificatory rites beginning with *vīkṣaṇa*. Having worshipped the *tvaṃtra*, the *pīṭha* [should be addressed] up to the *āvedya*."

One should enter [the seat] with the mantra beginning from *Ādhāraśakti* down to *Pṛthivī*. Regarding this, it should be understood that the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Me (the Self), the meter (*chandas*) is *Sutala*, and the deity (*devatā*) is *Pṛthivī*; this is for the purpose of sitting. The softness of the seat is for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), for a hard seat is not [conducive].

One whose mind is healthy is [qualified], for one whose mind is unwell has no authority over rites such as worship; nor is such a person capable of successfully carrying out those rites, even when provided with the complete collection of requisites for worship—such as mantras, yantras, conch shells, vessels, flowers, garments, and other offerings. In this regard, [one must be] perfectly...

"Samāhitajiteṃdriyaḥ" means one by whom the senses, such as the mind and others—which had been directed toward objects of pleasure like sacrificial ladles, sandalwood, and women, and which were thus conquered by following after them—have been withdrawn from those objects and concentrated; he is both "samāhitaḥ" (composed) and "jiteṃdriyaḥ" (one who has conquered his senses). Thus, he is "samāhitajiteṃdriyaḥ."
Furthermore, the internal consistency (*svārasya*) of the treatise—which explains the meaning of the term *karmadhāraya*—is established precisely according to our interpretation;

for it is stated therein that attachment to objects such as garlands and sandalwood paste for the sake of honor and so forth, followed by detachment from those very same things through the desire for one's own enjoyment, constitutes [the nature of the path]. Thus concludes the treatise.
By demonstrating the skill of speech of the performer, one should show the place for arranging the vessels;

and by means of the words "one should place," etc., all the materials required for worship— such as sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, cloth, flowers, garlands, and so forth— all such substances necessary for the rite, [should be placed] on one's own right side.

On the left side, there should be a water-pot for the purpose of placing the conch and for sipping water (ācamana), while on the back side, there should be a vessel for washing the hands and so forth; and on all sides around the lamps lit with ghee and other fuels,
one should place four mirrors, chowries, an umbrella, and fans in the order starting from the east.

In the four directions, one should also place the previously mentioned *kruddha* vessels; when there are many of them, they are arranged according to the order of sowing, and in this case, there is a repetition of the eastern direction.

Here, everything other than the *aṅkura* (germinating seeds) is constant; he now describes the subsequent task following the placement of the vessels even during worship, beginning with the words "with palms joined" (*kṛtāñjali*). This refers to the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*).

Regarding the placement of the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) both inside and outside those two [hands] on their two sides, it is stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā: "One should purify the hands with the weapon-mantra, according to the tradition. Thus, the mantra is placed both inside and outside the hands.

In another Tantra, it is stated: "The binding of the directions (*digbandha*) consists of the placement of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra-nyāsa*) in the ten directions with the *nārāca-mudrā*, wherein the index fingers are raised. The phrase "with the weapon-mantra" applies to all three [preceding actions].
Thus, having performed the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the weapon-mantra, [one proceeds] with the weapon-mantra...

The connection is that, having performed the binding of the directions with the *treṇī* mantra, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). If it is asked, "How is it established that [the action] has been performed?", take it from the word "having approached" (*samāsādya*).
If it is argued that this is actually a single word, what follows from that? For even if that were so... [text fragment ends].

There is no further connection to the intent [of the previous section]. By the words beginning with "tena" (by that), he demonstrates the fruit of that triad ending with the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).

By means of that rite of binding the directions, one should effect the protection of the preceptor on all sides, the radiance produced by which serves as the agent for the act of protection. [Now follows] the method for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

He demonstrates this with the words beginning "suṣumṇā" and so forth. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: being composed (*samāhitaḥ*), one should, by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā* and according to the prescribed method joined with yoga, unite the self (*ātman*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) through the mantra of consciousness (*cin-mantra*). Yoga is that which possesses yoga; it is appropriately stated for those who possess the yoga of the *arśas* class (those characterized by such spiritual practice).

The meaning is that it can be accomplished by them through the *cinmantra* (the consciousness-mantra), namely the *haṃsa* mantra. Having uttered "huṃ," one should raise the *kuṇḍalinī* from the *mūlādhāra*,
bring it to the heart, take the individual soul (*jīvātman*) situated there into its mouth, and [lead it] along the path of the *suṣumṇā*.

Having gone [there], one should unite [the self] with the Supreme Self situated in the *brahmarandhra* by means of the mantra "I am He" (*so'ham*) according to the system of another school, or by the mantra "I am this" (*ahaṃ so'smi*). This task is to be performed only by one who is extremely attentive, not by everyone; thus is the statement regarding being composed. [The phrase] "in the state of the seed-syllable" (*bījabhāve*)...

Even the principles beginning with earth, though in reverse order, exist as seeds— that is, by way of their own respective seed-syllables— within the cause of all beings, which is the ultimate cause of them all;
likewise, they reside within water, fire, and so forth, which are the respective causes of earth and the others.

There, the dissolution of all things culminates at the end of the path of dissolution. By the word "api" (also), it is stated that the dissolution of the phonemes (*varṇas*) is also to be contemplated; therein, *kṣam* dissolves into *haṃ*, *haṃ* into *laṃ*, *laṃ* into *kāraṃ*, *kāraṃ* into *saṃ*, *saṃ* into *ṣeṣaṃ*, *ṣeṣaṃ* into *śe*, *śe* into *varṇakaṃ*, *varṇakaṃ* into *vevaṃ*, *vevaṃ* into *laṃ*, and *laṃ* remains dissolved in the letter *ra*.

Having performed the *pūraka* (inhalation) with the wind seed-syllable *yaṃ*, one dries up the body and its sins by means of the wind arising therefrom; then, having performed the *kuṃbhaka* (retention) with the fire seed-syllable *raṃ*, one burns them with the fire arising therefrom; and finally, having performed the *recaka* (exhalation) with the wind seed-syllable *yaṃ*.

One should separate and remove that which consists of the ashes of the sinful person; one should indeed leave behind the ashes of the body. Then, having brought nectar by means of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, and having formed those ashes into a mass, one should again contemplate the arising of another body. Furthermore—

From oneself, in the sequence beginning with "from the Self comes space, from space comes air," one should bring those elements into their respective locations from the head down to the feet; then, having produced the phonemes in the manner previously described, one should recite the *haṃsa* mantra— "I am He"— as the *jīvātman*, thinking "I am the Divine Swan."

By the words beginning with "tat" (that), he demonstrates the meaning that one should bring the Kuṇḍalinī, which has emerged from the heart by means of the Name-mantra, and establish it in the Mūlādhāra; for by that very fire,
the capacity of all names to refer to the delimiting conditions of the objects they denote is indeed negated.

Even that which is included within a compound lacks the capacity for reflective awareness (*aparāmarśakatva*), because in such instances as "the non-pervasion of the property of the subject" (*avyāpyapakṣadharmmatva*), the reflective awareness of that non-pervasion and so forth is accepted; and furthermore,
[in cases where] there is no such reflective awareness, as in "this woman is the mother of my son" (*prajāvatīyam me tvam*) or "to him [is given] the funeral garment" (*tasmai daivikaṃ vastram*).
It should be understood that [the term] refers to the brother and others who constitute the delimiting factors (*avacchedaka*) of the meaning of the word *dauprajāvatī*.

Therefore, according to the method previously stated, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the subsequent ritual placements (*nyāsa*), and so forth; by interpreting the compound *nyāsādi* as a *bahuvrīhi*—meaning "that which has ritual placements and so forth"—one should first perform the ritual placements of the sages (*ṛṣi*) and other such elements, followed by the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

It has been stated that the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth must be performed; or rather, regarding the *nyāsa* and other rites—of which *nyāsa* will be described later—the head (*kaṃśiraḥ*) comes first, and this [rite of] *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and so forth is essential. If it were not so, then the entirety of the tantric scriptures would not be properly consistent.

We do not know how you could possibly teach subsequent rites or other rituals without first performing the *māmrālāṃca* and the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*; however, those who perceive the true nature of the categories [of reality], having performed *prāṇāyāma* according to rule with the root mantra, should perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and so forth with the mantra of the Divine Haṃsa.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Haṃ puruṣātmane namaḥ"—thus at the *mūlādhāra*;
"Saḥ prakṛtyātmane namaḥ"—thus at the head; and having pervaded [the body] with "Haṃsaḥ prakṛtipuruṣātmane namaḥ," one should [proceed].

Regarding the statement "the head of the *da* [syllable]" as the placement (*nyāsa*) of the divine Haṃsa, they explain that by means of the first [syllable], one performs the placement in the eastern direction and so forth, as well as the offering of that recitation and the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the day's recitation.
To this, it must be said: since the two actions [of recitation and resolve] are separated by the act of "one should perform" and "one should place," [the sequence is interrupted].

How can this [instruction] of Manu—"one should bring the *haṃsa* to the Supreme Self"—be connected with the phrase "without *prāṇāyāma* according to rule"? It would require dependence on another mantra, namely, "one should bring the lotus of the heart [to the Supreme Self]. Nor is it [possible] for that [offering] to be an offering of that [month], nor for it to be a dedication to that.
Then, at that time, one should praise one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) with hymns;
thus, having praised [the Lord], one should offer the ajapā [mantra] to Maheśāna— according to the *Cidvallī Tantra* and other such sources—
at the time of the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*), following the morning bath, the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), and so forth.

If it is asked: "Since there are scriptural injunctions such as 'One who is constantly devoid of the *saṃdhyā* is impure and unfit for all rites,' how can its performance take place prior to the *saṃdhyā* and other such duties? [The answer is: In that case, immediately after the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*), [one performs] the mantra of the Guru’s sandals (*gurupādukā*).

If it is argued that the gaze should be fixed even on forms such as recitation (*japa*), praise (*stava*), and reading (*pāṭha*) because of specific scriptural statements (*viśeṣavacana*) to that effect, then what is that specific statement here? [The answer is: having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) and so forth for oneself according to the method to be described later, one should perform each repetition (*āvṛtti*) for every ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*).

Having performed the recitation of the *praṇava* and the subsequent purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as *garbhādhāna* which are to be described, one should thereafter assign the *ṛṣis* of one’s own mantra to the head and other parts of the body.
Because of the general designation "of one's own mantra," this applies specifically to whichever mantra is the primary object of one's worship.

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* explains that by saying "he obtains it as a limb of the body," it is implied that one should then perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of that very mantra upon the [body] through touch and so forth;

and he further states that the phrase "the self endowed with the head" is intended to exclude the head and other parts of the deity [from being the locus of the placement]. However, this is not at all appropriate. Why? [Because...]

Since words such as "head" (mūrdhan) when uttered in conjunction with "Dāntarāsa" are conventionally established (*rūḍhatva*) only upon one's own head and so forth, by this [argument] the objection "this is for the purpose of distinguishing the disciple" is also refuted. The phrase "on the thumb and so forth" implies "according to the wording of the respective mantras. In reality, however, this is merely the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the yantra.

The connection [of the mantra] is characterized by the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*), as if it had entered into the limbs (*aṅga*). Thus, the meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras characterized by the limbs upon the thumb and other parts;
that is, with the limb-mantras consisting of the heart, head, crest, armor, and so forth, together with their respective seed-syllables (*sajāti*).
The third case ending is used because [the limbs] are characterized by being accompanied by such classes [of mantras] as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *huṃ*.

Thus, the meaning is that one should assign [the mantras] to the thumbs and other fingers in accordance with the mantras such as "rīṃ *namaḥ* to the heart" and "rīṃ *svāhā* to the head. Therefore, the weapon [mantra] is likewise...

The phrase *llayornyaset* (one should place on the two palms) is joined with the second case ending for the sake of clarity regarding the front and back; here too, the meaning is that one should place the mantra *raḥ astrāya phaṭ* on the palm and the back of the hand—the inclusion of the "back" being obtained by intending it as the outer surface. Alternatively, [the text] does not contain the mantra...

The phrase "by which there is no internal difference between the two" (*dhakayoḥ antaram bhedaḥ na yena*) is a qualification of the mantra-installation (*maṃtra-nyāsa*) for the sake of attaining the purpose of that installation; that very [qualification] is also to be supplied subsequently. Alternatively, it refers to the mantra itself, meaning "that in which there is no internal difference or distinction between the two" (*na vidyate antaram sādhaka-bhedaḥ yasmin*). That [mantra] is what is to be installed; this is the object (*karman*) in the phrase "one should install that."

Thus, one follows the mantra; by the placement (*nyāsa*) according to the words of the mantra, one becomes "placed" (*nyasta*). Consequently, there is no difficulty whatsoever regarding the requirement for completion and so forth. Even the author of the *Padārthādarśa* has made the word immediately following [the first half-verse] connect with the subsequent part. However, this much is the difference: that by them [the root-mantra]...

It should not be thought that this [verse] is intended merely as an indicator of the meaning—that the purification of the three previous [limbs] must be performed—because it is capable of conveying that very purpose. In fact, it has been stated that one should perform the placement of mantras (*mantra-nyāsa*);
thus, one should place the syllables of the mantra upon the thumbs and other fingers, the heart and other centers, and the head and other parts.

With the intention that this is called the "Mantra-Placement" (mantranyāsa), in order to clarify the very subject of mantra-placement, there are five and a half verses beginning with "the thumb" (aṅguṣṭha) and ending with "one should perform the placement" (nyāsam ācaret). By the phrase "other placements" (nyāsān anyān), he will describe only the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) and so forth.
The [mantras] of the Mānasas are not [to be recited].
Because it is currently impossible to state the placement of those syllables in their specific individual forms, they are indicated by means of a general term in the form "other placements.
Thus, in the phrase "one should place [them] on the thumbs and so forth," the object of the action (*karmapada*) refers to the syllables of the mantra.

The form [of the ritual] is that which follows from the meaning; the suffix "iti" is easily applied as a mantra. Thus, "itisukaraḥ" (thus easily performed)—nothing here is inconsistent. Regarding this, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* says:

with the limbs (*aṅgaiḥ*) and the mantras prescribed for each respective ritual manual (*kalpa*), having uttered the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) there, [one should say] "namas" to both thumbs at the head.
Having uttered the mantra, the application with the two index fingers is "svāhā" and so forth. As the Teachers have said:
"One should assign [the mantras] to the fingers in order, starting from the thumb, along with the limbs," they say this.
Here, it must be stated that after the heart and other limb-mantras, one should [assign them] with the two thumbs, ending in *namaḥ*.

What authority is stated for this practice? It cannot be the root text (*mūlavacana*), because that does not convey such a meaning; nor can it be the statement of the Teacher (*ācāryavacana*), because that also stands on the same footing as the root text;
nor can it be the ritual manual (*yantra*), because the placement (*nyāsa*) therein is indicated by the use of the dative case and the suffix *namaḥ*.

It cannot be argued that such a rule is unnecessary because it would otherwise lead to the undesirable consequence of [the mantra] "aḥ lalāṭāya namaḥ" and "āḥ mukhavṛttāya namaḥ" also being applicable; for even though such usage has been observed by certain authors of *paddhatis*, there is still a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for it. Nor can it be said that... [text fragment ends].

Nor [is it so] because of contradiction with the primary texts (*agrantha*), for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of applying such formulas as "namas to the heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*) and "namas to the heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*) during the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) upon the heart and other locations; this is because, according to your own position, the first [occurrence of the word "heart"] refers to the limb-mantra itself, while the second refers to the locus of the placement.

Since even fear has its own purpose, it is not intended that the formula "to the heart, obeisance" (hṛdayāya namaḥ) should be applied immediately after each of those mantra-syllables during the nyāsa on the thumbs and other fingers; nor is that [application] correct, because those [syllables] do not have that [specific application] as their meaning.

The term "heart" (hṛdaya) need not denote a specific part of the heart belonging either to the object of worship or to the worshipper; rather, it refers to a particular deity within the body of that respective deity to be worshipped, who is included among the deities presiding over the vital breaths (prāṇa). Thus, there is no lack of syntactic connection whatsoever.

There is no such doubt that for some there are five limbs and for others six limbs; rather, this status of having more limbs would be established by way of a staff (daṇḍa). For neither the object of worship nor the worshiper is eyeless, whereby the state of being devoid of the mantra of the eyes would be easily established.
Therefore, the mention of the mantras for the armor (*kavaca*) and weapons (*astra*) is appropriately consistent;
for even that [mention] is not the name of any specific limb (*aṅga*) by which the status of those mantras as "limb-mantras" (*aṅgamantra*) could be established.
For this very reason, their worship in the filaments (*kesara*) and so forth, as well as their location in the southeast (*āgneya*) and other directions, does not occur.

Since these [deities] have not departed from their bodies, external worship would be appropriate; for just as the offering of handfuls of flowers for the sake of *sakalīkaraṇa* is performed upon the body of the Blessed One, so too does that worship become manifest within it. Therefore, the weapons are distinct.

Even their assumption of female attire and so forth is easily explained; for it is not logically tenable that the limbs and body parts themselves possess such a nature [as to be inherently female], and as for the specific statement— "Salutation to the two thumbs with *namaḥ hrīṃ*, salutation to the two index fingers with *hrīṃ*..."— its intended meaning remains undetermined even today.

Then, "Oṃ hrāṃ namo to the middle fingers," "Oṃ hrīṃ namo to the nameless (ring) fingers," "Oṃ hrauṃ namo to the little fingers," and "Oṃ hraḥ namo to the backs of the palms"— this recitation has been cited as the authoritative evidence by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* regarding the application [of the mantra] with the words "Oṃ hrāṃ namo to the thumbs."

Furthermore, that [position] regarding the single-syllable seed-mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī being merely a limb-assignment (*aṅganyāsa*) lacks proof, because it contradicts numerous authoritative root-texts such as the *Jñānārṇava* and other works by reliable authors such as Rāmopādhyāya, Kāśī Vyāsa, and others.
Since it is impossible to state that [the mantra] is directed toward all the limbs of the deity,

the statement from the *Gautama-saṃhitā*— beginning with "One should say *namaḥ* to the *Cakra* with the two thumbs, *svāhā* to the *Viacakra* with the two index fingers," and so forth— is intended for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands (*kara-nyāsa*), not for the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*).
Having begun with the statement, "The placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs [is] likewise proclaimed," it is said:
"O Teacher, having first recited the *āsanamantra*, one should then perform the five-limbed rite (*pañcāṅga*) with the mantra of one's own limb [mantras], beginning with:
'To the Discus, Svāhā! Salutation to the Heart! To the Discus that is the Destroyer of Asuras...'"
Yaḥ svāhā astrāya.

Because the mantras for the five-limbed placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) are taught separately up to the end [of the mantra] with "phaṭ," it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is no application of the thumbs and other fingers in the mantras for the limb-placement;
the author of the *Harṣakaumudī* also shows partiality toward the method stated by us.
This has been explained by us at length for those whose minds are overflowing with devotion.

Having performed the *aṅguṣṭhādi-nyāsa* (the ritual placement of mantras on the fingers and body), and having struck three claps (*tāla*) with both hands with palms extended, one should perform the piercing of the directions starting from the east using the *astra-mantra* with snapping sounds (*choṭikā*).
Having performed [the ritual] three times, the placement of the heart-mantra and the others (hṛdayādinyāsa) should be practiced; thus he says "one should do," etc.

The word "ca" (and) indicates that just as the limb-mantras were placed on the thumbs and other fingers, so too are they to be placed on the heart and other parts. Furthermore, for this reason as well, the limbs must have an identical sequence.

For those who follow the previously stated meaning in order to perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras in both cases, the contradiction with this very root text is evident even to the authors of the *Padārthadarśa*. As for the statement that [the word] "by those of the same class" (*sajātībhiḥ*) is connected to what follows, [it refers to] the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) by those of the same class.

Regarding the statement "one should place [the mantras] in the heart and so forth," the author of the *Padārthādarśa* has provided an interpretation that is incorrect. This is because, since the mantras such as *namaḥ* and *svāhā* are not connected with the preceding [seed-syllables], it would follow that even the previously mentioned practical application (*prayoga*) could not be established. Furthermore, [your position] is far removed from the [intended] meaning.
Because there would be the consequence of [the ritual] belonging to Sūrya, because the *aṅga-mantras* of those belonging to the same class (*sajāti*) are not connected [to it],
and because this entire root-text is linked specifically with that which belongs to Sūrya, such an effort [to apply others] would be redundant.
Now, some hold that the *aṅga-mantras* of the same class [end] with "Oṃ" followed by the name of each respective limb.

Those very [mantras] are employed as "Hṛdayāya namaḥ," "Śirase namaḥ," and so forth. One might ask: "Is that intended here in exactly the same way? No; he says "hṛdaya" etc., and "vahnivallabhā svāhā netratrayāya. But surely Rāmopādhyāya stated that the word for the eyes consists of three syllables (*netrāya*).

If it is asked, "What is the status of the statement from the *Nārada-pañcarātra* that was cited? [the answer is: although the phrase "to discharge the three debts" (*ṛṇatrayāya*) serves as the basis for the ritual application, it cannot possibly have Viṣṇu as its specific object.
Thus, in a context where a single deity has two eyes, the ritual application remains general for all deities when no specific qualification is stated.

In that case, there would be no room for the statement "of the horse" (*aśvasya*); however, in reality, the root meaning is as follows: when the word *yadā*—which consists of three syllables (*ya*, *dā*, *ya*)—and the word *vauṣaṭ* constitute the *netra-mantra* (the eye-mantra), then [it applies]. Nor is this a general rule regarding the deity.
This [term] would not have the status of being an object [of perception], for no one accepts the usage "netrāya" (to the eye) even when referring to a specific deity possessing two eyes;
and the usage "netrāya" can be applied to one with three eyes just as it can to one with two eyes. Nor is this the root [source] for Śiva and others who possess three eyes.

It should not be assumed that this [mandapa] has as its object only the general [deities], such as Śiva and others, and not Viṣṇu and others; for it was previously stated that the mandapa is intended for the general class of deities. This is because the mantras of the general class of deities...

Since it was promised that *dharvā* would be discussed, there would be a contradiction [otherwise]; therefore, one should understand that even in that context, the word *śūla* refers by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) to either the *śūla* or the *śaṅkha*. Now, for one who has exactly five limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*), the practitioner [should employ] the mantras of the five limbs.

How should the placement (*nyāsa*) of one's own six limbs and so forth upon the heart and other locations be performed? In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether there should be a repetition of a single mantra or the omission of a single limb; what is to be done here? To this question, regarding the position of omission, [the rule] applies: "In the case of *anta-lopa* (elision at the end), there is either elision or a vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*). Thus, by this logic, the hand... [is to be treated].
In response to the doubt that [the ritual] might consist merely of the striking of the palm, he says "five" and so forth. It should not be argued:
"How could the function of the mantra for the eye-limb (*netrāṅga-mantra*), consisting of the inspection of the water in the conch and so on, occur there?
For it is simply the mantra that has attained the status of a subsequent [limb], namely the mantra "vauṣaṭ to the eye."

In such a case, because the mantra of the eye has already been consecrated as a limb (of the deity), one might wonder: "Where the limb-mantras have not been extracted independently, with which mantras should the ritual application of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and so forth be performed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By its own [mantra]"—that is, by the principal root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) itself.

The meaning is as follows: for the purpose of performing the mental worship of the self-sacrifice (*ātmayāga*), it is necessary to conceive of the seat (*pīṭha*) by means of the installation of the deities of the seat upon one's own body; he demonstrates that procedure with the words beginning "one should conceive" (*kalpayet*), the syntactical connection being that one should conceive the seat in sequence by means of Dharma and the other [Tattvas].

The meaning is that the placement (nyāsa) of Dharma and the others, as reached through the sequence, should be performed by following the order of the placement of the deities beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Ratnapīṭha in the locations starting from the Mūlādhāra up to the heart;
by the word "O Teacher" (deśika), [the sequence] begins from the right shoulder and proceeds to the right thigh.

It has been stated that the placement (*nyāsa*) must be performed up to the limit, according to the instruction found in another *tantra*. Now, one might ask: "Even if it is so in that other *tantra*, how can such a restriction be established here, given that in this very *tantra* the root text is consistent even with the placement starting from the left shoulder and ending at the right shoulder? To this, he says: "Vi... [The text continues].

The meaning is that one who possesses the synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of the initial letters (*lādyavādi*) and so forth, according to the direction explained for the unity of the two systems (*tantradvayaikavākyatva*).

Regarding the phrase "the first letter of the names" (*nāmādyakṣara*), it refers to those [letters] such as *kaṃbha* and so forth, or *ya* and so forth, which are at the beginning of the parts of the names of their respective *kalās*, whose essential natures (*svarūpa*) are *tāpinī* and so forth. *Yamādi* means "beginning with *ya*. *Āmādi* means "beginning with *ā*."

The meaning is that they are preceded by three syllables; the implied sense is that those respective syllables should be placed before the *kalās* in a heated temple or similar location. In the same way, it is precisely by being preceded by the initial syllable of the name, and here, for names beginning with *satva* and so forth, the first syllable of the word begins with the letter *sa*.

By that [intention], since the state of having a *bindu* (the nasal dot) is intended to be applied to both, the practical application results in such formulations as "kaṃ bhaṃ tapinyai namaḥ" and so forth,
as well as "amṛtāyai namaḥ" and so forth, and "dhūmrārciṣe namaḥ saṃ sattvāya namaḥ" and so forth; or else, [the *bindu*] is to be brought down [from the subsequent position] to the preceding name.

Regarding the passage beginning with "dyakṣarā," it is stated in the *Itipadārthādarśa* that the phrase "tathaiva" means: "just as there is the placement [nyāsa] of the infinite [ananta] and other [mantras] one above the other, so too [is this case]. Furthermore, it is said therein that because the word ending in the feminine accusative plural appears in the recitation of the words (*padapāṭha*), a connection [to what follows] is expected.

The secret intended by the reading of the preceding words ending in the masculine dual accusative case is that, through the aforementioned method of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*),
once the body is established as being composed of the sacred seats, it follows by implication that the sacred seat is likewise composed of the body.

Intending that [the vessel] as such, one should place the mudrās—which will be described specifically in their respective Kalpas—within the triangular fire-mandala upon a support; "with a conch" is an adjective for the vessel, and with one's own mudrā, namely the *sannirodhana* (sealing) mudrā; if this much is not possible here, [one may use] a single [vessel].

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that this may be done in a single vessel, or one should arrange the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and so forth in a single vessel, based on the words of the Tantras. This is incorrect, because both a specific vessel for the *viśeṣārghya* and a general vessel for the *sāmānyārghya* are indispensable; [therefore] there is only one vessel...
If Maheśvara were not present in person, the meanings of the mantras would become fruitless;

for as the *Navaratna Tantra* states: "They would be [merely] words at every step. For this very reason, setting aside the phrase "all of it," the specific names such as *pādya* and so forth have been employed.

Regarding the phrase "with flowers and so forth" (*puṣpādyaiḥ*): this means with flowers when they are available, and with *akṣatas* (unbroken grains) when they are not. As for the author of the *Padārthādarśa*, who interprets it as "the first part of the flower is fragrance," and because of the plural number [in *puṣpādyaiḥ*] as referring to flowers, unbroken grains, and so on, he maintains that the meaning is "one should worship with fragrances, unbroken grains, flowers, and so forth."

That has already been stated; since the plural suffix merely indicates plurality residing in the meaning of the base itself, it is impossible for it to bring about the acquisition of *akṣatā* (unhusked grains) and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the plural suffix itself denotes "flower," because no such grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) exists. As for [the word] *puṣpā*...

As for the claim that "the inclusion of 'fragrance' (*gandha*) and so forth serves a specific purpose," even that is not correct, because it would entail the necessity of searching for other things such as "indifference" (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, regarding the objection that if "fragrance and so forth" were stated, there would be the undesirable consequence of including "unbroken rice" (*akṣata*) and the like,
and therefore it was not stated in that way— that too is not correct, because [fragrance] does not apply to unbroken rice and such things.
If it is asked, "Since there is no evidence for the desirability of the *Nāmasaṃgraha*, what is the authority for this compendium?"—

understand that the general scripture on worship itself is the authority. Immediately following that, he describes the mental worship (*mānasapūjā*) of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) with the word "in that" (*tasmin*), referring to the body worshipped according to the previously mentioned method.
Having worshipped the Supreme Deity upon the seat with all the services beginning with the food offering (naivedya),

one should meditate on oneself as having the form of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadeva). Then, having offered five handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali) to one’s own head and other parts five times, and having worshipped [the deity] again with the services remaining after the food offering, [one should offer the remainder].

One should perform the mental worship—including mental recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), waving of lights (*nīrājana*), and the offering of food (*naivedya*)—in the manner taught by one's own guru. However, according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*, in the verse beginning with "the supreme deity" (*paradevatām*), it is stated that this is performed "with offerings such as fragrance and so forth, excluding the food-offering" (*vinā naivedyaṃ gandhādyair upacāraiḥ*). And thus...

They say that even for the Blessed One, no food offering (naivedya) should be given during this mental worship. To this, it must be asked: according to all schools of thought, since there is an interruption by only a single verse consisting of a handful of flowers offered toward the bodies of the worshippers, how [is it possible]?

Likewise, there would be a logical consistency [in this view], because offerings (naivedya) are seen in various tantras such as the *Sudarśana-saṃhitā* regarding the mental worship of the Lord; how then could the omission of offerings be justified here?
Therefore, wherever there is the fivefold handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali-pañcaka), for that alone is there no offering.

It should be understood that the status of being the object of the act of worship has been stated by the words beginning with "tyādi. By the phrase "ananyadhīḥ" (with undistracted mind), the form that serves as the basis for one's own worthiness of worship is shown to consist in the contemplation of identity (*abhedabhāvanā*) with one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). [The term] "not other" means a cognition of the form: "I am not different from my chosen deity."

As for what was stated by the author of the *Padārthadarśa*— namely, that "this [is] for the sake of the welfare of those who have departed" and that "by this, it is said that [the offering] reaches the third state"—
that is impossible to establish even for Brahmā on the basis of the original scriptural words. Furthermore,
it has been intimated that even mental incense and lamps are included within the category of the specific ritual items (*viśeṣapadārtha*).

Because it is impossible for "remainder-ness" (*śeṣatva*) to apply there, since the phrase "by means of those [substances] such as fragrance" (*tena tadayita-gandhādyaiḥ*) serves precisely as a subsumer of that [fragrance]; nor is it the case that in the phrase "by means of fragrance and so forth" (*gandhādyaiḥ*), only perceptible fragrance and the like are intended and not mental [fragrance], for thus the status of being a remainder is indeed possible for the two mental [offerings], namely incense and lamps.

This must indeed be stated: if that were so, then since odors and other such things are also required therein, and since it is appropriate [to include] everything, there would be the consequence of deficiency on your part due to not counting those among the remaining categories;
for, being perceptible, there is no requirement at all for mental incense and the like among the remaining categories.

The objection that "counting is improper" is not a valid refutation, because it is possible to resolve it by stating that both types of worship are intended; thus, he begins to describe the external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*),
which consists of the offering of ritual services (*upacārārpaṇā*) beginning with the worship of the *dharmas* and ending with the worship of the Self (*ātmapūjā*).
Because it depends upon the ultimate goal (*arthāntala*), he begins to describe the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*) with the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth.

Immediately after the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), one should perform the worship of the mandala—such as the *sarvatobhadra*—drawn upon the sacrificial ground (*vedi*) with perfumes and other offerings; then, having filled its pericarp (*karṇikā*) with rice (*śāli*), one should [fill] the rice-grains...

Having poured rice and other offerings upon the blades of grass, one should spread *darbha* grass there and place upon it a *grāsa* consisting of twenty-seven *darbha* blades tied together in the form of a braid; this is called the *viṣṭara*. Having placed it there, one [should perform the worship] beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti* and so forth.
The collective meaning is that one should worship the deities of the directions; having worshipped those beginning with Dharma in the four corners starting from the southeast—
Dharma and the others being, in order, the specific forms of bull, lion, human, and elephant, and possessing the colors red, dark blue, white, and yellow— one should complete the worship.

In the four directions starting from the east, one should worship such [deities] as Adharma and the rest, and then worship the lotus. "Not from the east" (*naḥ pūrvāt*): by those words beginning with *adharma*, which are preceded by "not" (*naḥ*), the objects in the form of Adharma and so forth are indicated. Herein: "Salutation to the Root of Bliss" (*ānandakandāya namaḥ*).
Many desire the usage *savinnālāmanam* and so forth, on the grounds that such an expression is fruitful as a description of the actual nature of the bulbous root (*kanda*) and stalk (*nāla*).
However, since there is no evidence for such a usage, one should employ only forms such as *kandāyanam*. Others [disagree].

As for the question, "Why would one not accept the description of the *thā*, *dharma*, and so forth as being the seat (*pīṭha*), body (*gātra*), seat-base (*pīṭhapāda*), and so on?", the experts in logic [reply]: regarding the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), the words "solar orb" (*sūryamaṇḍala*) and the others are joined respectively, one by one, to the preceding parts consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.

Having performed the worship of the solar and other mandalas according to the sequence beginning with "having made the solar orb," and so forth, one should worship their respective digits (kalās) in the manner previously described; this is the summarized meaning. [The term] "consisting of the three qualities" refers to those whose nature is sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Some say that one should wrap the jar all around with a three-stranded thread made of spun cotton so that it becomes seamless, and then place it within a *kūrca* (bundle of grass); this is the meaning. Others, however, hold that *nīrañjam* is an adjective for the jar, while *madhye tu chaṃ* [refers to] the interior.
They say it was taken up merely out of deference; [they claim] it is "without gaps" (*nīraṃdhra*) and its limbs are covered by a triple-stranded thread.

They should be asked: "Why was the knot not mentioned? Why was the aesthetic essence (*saurasya*) not produced? Furthermore, there is no disagreement among any schools of thought regarding the inversion of words (*padavaiparyya*); thus, the critique offered by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* is [invalid].

It must be stated that "that very [thing]" (tameva), for even in your own view, this defect remains as it was; for by saying "the enveloped" (*āveṣṭitam*) instead of "the enveloped-and-enveloped" (*āveṣṭitaveṣṭitam*), there arises the understanding that what is intended is precisely that which is completely enveloped— or rather, that the word *aṅga* itself refers to all the constituent parts.
The phrase "for the purpose of delimiting" (*avacchedetaveṣṭanetātparyyagrāhakam*) serves to indicate the intended meaning; otherwise, even if only some part [of the vessel] were wrapped,
since the wrapping of some part of the *kalaśī* would still be accomplished, the purpose of the scriptural injunction would be fulfilled by that much alone— so say others, according to certain views.
There is no contradiction with the *Yajñasaṃhitā*, for its own text states: "It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;

strewn with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*); honored with *kuśa* grass and sprouts of *dūrvā*; encircled at the neck with a white thread; and covered with a pair of new cloths. In that regard, [the rule applies] to the delimitation of all its limbs.

Others say: "How is it that being enveloped by threads (*tantu*) does not contradict the state of being clothed (*vastra*)? Still others maintain that the word *aṅga* refers to specific parts such as the feet and the neck; thus, there is no redundancy [in the description], for while [the body] is enveloped by a pair of garments supplied [by the threads], it remains without any gaps due to the thread elsewhere.

The *kalaśa* (vessel) is to be made; that is to say, it must be wrapped with a thread by cutting off all parts except for the neck. In this way, the objection—"Why was it not stated that it should be 'without holes' (*nīraṃdhra*) or 'with closed limbs' (*saṃvṛtāṅga*)?"—is resolved, and they state that there is no contradiction with the aforementioned *Saṃhitā*.

Having filled the *kalaśa* with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) or with the decoction of the milky sap of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, and *rūpa* trees— or alternatively, having filled another conch placed to the east with the decoction water of the milky trees— one should [apply] the eight fragrances according to the mantras to be recited later.
Having stirred [the contents] there, preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, one should worship the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon;

then, having worshipped the fifty digits born of the letters previously mentioned, the consecrated decoction-water contained in the conch (śaṅkha) should be poured into the pitcher (kalaśa). Thus he says, beginning with "In the conch," regarding the powers (śakti).

The word *ātman* (self) in such passages does not refer to one's own self (*sva-ātman*), but rather to that which belongs to one's own (*svīya-ātman*). Thus, the "eightfold fragrance" (*gandhāṣṭaka*) consists of that which has power (*śakti*) and the rest as its own nature (*ātmaka*). In this way, the compound is ultimately resolved as a *bahuvrīhi*: "that in which the self of power and the rest [is found]," or "that in which there is the state of belonging to the self of power and the rest. Regarding power and the rest...

The author of the *Padārthadarśa* states that although the nature of the *śakti* (potency) and so forth is distinct from its possessor, and there is no actual identity between them, they are metaphorically designated as being "of that nature" (*tadātman*) because they produce pleasure for that possessor; this is well known in the Kanyakubja dialect as *coraḥ bhaṭi cūri* and *karvūra*.
Dhava is *kapikacchū*; raktacandana is well-known; hrīvera is *vālaka* and *sitica*; sevyaka is *uśīra*; tamāla is synonymous with sugandhi and samudra;
prasiraja is a specific blue-colored tree; jala is *hrīvera* itself; and kuśīta is *raktacandana*.

These eight ingredients in equal parts constitute the *sauragandhāṣṭaka* (the eight-fragrance group of the sun). In the *Ṛgbhāskara*, it is prescribed that *sevyaka*, *kuṅkuma*, *kuṣṭha*, *hrīvera*, *agaru*, *candana*, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and *mura* are known as the *sauragandhāṣṭaka*. Here, *mura* is a synonym for *coraka*; this is the *gaṇeśagandhāṣṭaka*.
In the *Māpirudrayāmala*, it is stated that saffron, uśīra, māṃsī, musk, agaru,

excellent sandalwood, mustā, and red sandalwood are designated as the "eight-fold fragrance" (*aṣṭagaṃdha*) for the pervasive Lord Mahāgaṇapati; thus, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath).

Regarding the phrase "tat-tatra-tatra" mentioned there, he states the requirement for that mantra as follows: "pāśādi" means that at the end of a mantra consisting of three syllables—namely, those whose nature consists of the *pāśa* seed, the *māyā* seed, and the *aṅkuśa* seed—the word "amuṣya" (of such-and-such) should be placed; this applies to the reading "at the end of the three-syllable [mantra]."

Even if there is some slight discrepancy in this mantra to be recited here—just as in the case of the *tusugamukta* or the *ardhaśūla*—it causes no harm; for it is universally accepted that when another tantra provides a definitive meaning, it takes precedence over an optional meaning. Thus says the author of the *Padārthādarśa*.

Regarding the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* (the noose) and so forth, they say that by the inclusion of "self" (*ātman*), "living being" (*jīva*), and "thread" (*tantu*), the seed-syllables to be mentioned later—such as *re*, *la*, and so on—are also to be understood as included; thus, there is no difference here from the mantra for the installation of vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) which will be mentioned later. This refers to the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa*.

Regarding the reading *nmāṃte*, even if one were to assume it means "at the beginning of a three-syllable word such as *pāśa*," etc., such a reading is not found, nor can it be postulated because it would result in a metrical defect (*chaṃdobhaṅga*). Furthermore, there is no authority for abandoning the text as it is heard; nor is it a single syntactical unit dependent on what precedes or follows.

This is not so; for since this mantra, which accords with the *Sudarśana-saṃhitā* and other texts, results in a single unified meaning through its necessity for all [the rites], it must be accepted that the purport of the source text is the same in both cases. Therefore, this objection amounts to nothing.

Let it proceed: having reached the number eight through the conjunction of the letters *ta*, *da*, *ka*, and *ra* in three parts, it culminates in the supreme mantra *ātmapadaṃ haṃsi*. Likewise, because the eight syllables beginning with *ya* and ending with *ma* are intended to be the *ātma-mantra* at the end, the preceding and following mantras form a single syntactical unit.

Some say that one should perform [the installation] for them as well; however, that too should be rejected due to the absence of any purpose. It is not appropriate for offspring. The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* also states that one should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the deity everywhere by means of this very [mantra]; but he will state the specific [details] for the sake of worship in the root text itself.
Having said this, he indicated that there is no connection with the supreme seed-syllables (*paramādivīja*) in the present context;

furthermore, he explained the reading as "at the end of the syllable" (*akṣarasyānte*). Moreover, if the complete *prāṇamantra* about to be described were intended here, he would have stated it as such at this very point.

The meaning of "amuṣya" (of such-and-such) is that the word ending in the genitive case of whichever [object]—be it the yantra of the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*)—one intends to perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* for, should be inserted here. The term "leading" (*nayana*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the word "eye" (*cakṣus*), which is a synonym for leading; this is solely for the sake of the meter.

Likewise, the statement of the Teacher—“Because of obstruction, [the senses] are taught as such; they are the makers of the perception of objects, and similarly speech and mind are seen, as well as the sense of smell together with its vital breath”—is presented as a supporting corroboration for the stated meaning. Similarly, having uttered speech and mind, that which follows...

The statement "having perceived [them]" (*nihāyāt*) has also been shown to be their [i.e., Padmapādācārya’s] own word; for neither of these two statements indicates the entry of the term "eye" (*cakṣus*), nor is the mention of speech and mind intended to include the eye, ear, and nose.
Thus says Padmapādācārya.

It should not be said that the very fact that the commentary on the words of the Teacher (Ācārya) explains the word "eye" (*cakṣus*) as indicating the word "vision" (*dṛk*) is the authority for that [interpretation],
and that the citation of the Teacher's words is for that purpose alone;
for there is the possibility that the word "eye" itself occasionally indicates even non-visual perception (*anayanopalakṣakatā*).

Because there would be no basis for determining [which specific term to choose], and since the word *nyana* is also seen in works such as the *Śivatāṇḍavasaṃhitā*, it is impossible to adopt only one particular position; for this very reason,
the undesirable consequence of inserting words such as *dṛk* or *locana* also arises.

Since that [specific mantra] is not found in the statements regarding the extraction of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), yet even the term *nayanapada*— just like the term *cakṣuḥpada*— is found in many root-tantras (*mūlatantra*),
it is impossible even for Brahmā to determine which one of them is the correct one; thus, there is uncertainty.

Indeed, it should be reflected upon in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*: since this very word is traditionally recited as such in its root [text], it is proper that it alone constitutes a mantra; there is no evidence for the status of a mantra in a version composed of different words inserted in its place, because such a version is of human origin.
If it is argued that the mantra "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi), which is heard in the archetype (prakṛti),

must have its word "to Agni" (agnaye) modified to "to Sūrya" (sūryāya) in the ectype (vikṛti) where Sūrya is the deity— on the grounds of the rule that mantras serve to illuminate the meaning of the ritual act to be performed— then let it be so.

The status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) belongs to [the word] *syāt*; however, because specific names such as "king" (*rājan*) and so forth are infinite, it is impossible to enumerate them all. Therefore, for the purpose of conveying the specific meanings of "king" and the like, this [word *syāt*] does not possess, by its own nature, the capacity to convey them in the form of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
It indicates that only those specific words which are unfit for ordinary usage are fit for ritual application;
therefore, it should be understood that even names such as *ajā* and others possess the status of *mantra* precisely because they are primarily found in the Vedic tradition (*āmnāna*).
The phrase "breath-words" (*prāṇapadāni*) intends here the nature of being a word (*pada*) in its essential form, namely that of a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), [as indicated by] the case ending.
In cases where no specific number is mentioned, the nominative case alone is appropriate for the sake of grammatical correctness;
furthermore, because the verbal form "tiṣṭhantu" (let them stand) requires a nominative ending,
the plural number is indeed appropriate there as well, given that a dvandva compound of speech and the other [organs] is observed.
"Mitighrāṇaprāṇāḥ"—this is the extraction [of the mantra] as established by Mūlākṛt through the path of sound (*adhvan*).
"Caṣakaṃ śarāvaḥ sa ca kalaśadhātūtthaḥ chāyāyām":

this refers to the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) situated above the cup (*caṣaka*), which is determined to be the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree, [the cup] itself being produced from the element of the jar (*kalaśa*) within the shadow.
It should be understood that [the Lord] has arrived for the sake of providing shade.

Having established the form of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) by means of the root mantra (mūlamantra) upon a substratum for worship— such as a yantra, a śāligrāma stone, or the like— and having placed it within that jar above the cup (caṣaka), or having merely visualized it there, and having performed the invocation (āvāhana) therein, the practitioner [should worship] the deity of the mantra at hand.

The circular meaning is that the Guru, possessing the respective mantras required for each worship, should perform the worship; however, by the word "mantrin" (the mantra-knower), it is implied that in the initiation of a single deity, or in the initiation of the five abodes (*pañcāyatana*),
one should install the central jar for the sake of the deity intended as primary, starting from the northeast (*īśa*) and so forth.

One should place another set of four jars in the four intermediate directions; for it has been stated by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* that "in whichever direction there is the installation of whichever deity, there too should be a jar. However, in that case, you must admit the subordination of one or the other.
Thus, let the initiation-vessel (dīkṣā-kuṇḍikā) belong to the principal deity alone, and not to the others;

for the traditionalists maintain that the worship of the other deities is performed by means of the arghya-vessel of the principal deity itself. Nor [is it necessary] to perform this rite of the vessel (kalaśa-vidhi) repeatedly, whether once or many times, as has been stated.

It must be explained how the statement of the Teacher beginning with "with jars" (*kuṃbhaiḥ*)— which I have cited as authority for the position of five jars— is consistent; [the answer is that] for one who is unable to perform the worship of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa-devatā*) for their own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), that worship may be performed within a single jar.

Furthermore, since the ritual of that many jars must be described according to the number of one's own chosen deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) even for one who is capable [of performing more], it is stated as "many" because there is no fixed rule regarding the number of enclosures for different chosen deities; on the contrary,
this is [only] true in your own view.

It is restricted because, in the case of a single initiation (*ekadīkṣā*), it is established that there is only one [initiate], whereas in the case of the initiation of the five abodes (*pañcāyatanadīkṣā*), there are five; for if it were otherwise, the incongruity would arise that a single statement indicating two optional alternatives would apply to only one person. Nor is there an option of restriction (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) intended here.

It must be stated that this cannot be so; for since a word that establishes either a single deity or five deities is difficult to find there, even Brahmā himself could not effect such a meaning. Furthermore, because only five jars are required, the integrity of the term "one" (eka) would be compromised.

Now, intending that worship of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) should be performed upon the images and other objects placed within the water-jars (kalaśa) and the cups (caṣaka), he describes that procedure beginning with the words "on the trident" (śūle na) and so forth: "the lotus of the Mātṛkās which has been meditated upon in the collection of flowers held in the hand..."
From the respective sacred sites (*trasvasthāna*) of the various deities— such as Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others—

which are well-known places like Mathurā and so forth, that light which has traveled toward the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) by way of the *suṣumṇā* path through the sequence of the six chakras, [is brought] by means of the nostril passage...

Having joined [the deity] who has departed, one should cast [it] into the image and so forth; this indeed is what is called "invocation" (āvāhana). However, those authorities who teach that the solar disc or one's own heart is the locus [of the deity] should, for the sake of those deities whose specific locus is not well-known, apply themselves to that [locus] according to the oral tradition of the Guru.
The determination of the inheritance and the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the deity] whole), which consists of praying for the deity’s presence through the completeness of its limbs;
and that which consists of praying for the perfection of the worship that might have fallen short due to a deficiency in the ritual services, one-pointedness, and so forth— if these are complete.

Even then, the ritual act (*kṛtya*) would be directed toward him; for from that mantra, through the attainment of completeness by avoiding the aversion that might otherwise arise due to incompleteness, there is understood to be a prayer for one who is indeed already facing [the deity]. By this, since the act of making [the deity] face [the practitioner] (*abhimukhīkaraṇa*) is not separately mentioned, [the purpose is fulfilled].

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that the deficiency regarding the root *saktamūla* has been avoided, and it is indicated that the subsequent term (*anaṃtara*) serves to bring [the subject] directly before one’s eyes. However, since it is recited immediately after *saṃnirodha* in another *tantra*, how can it be established as being denoted by the term "subsequent" (*anaṃtara*)? In some way...
*Āvāhana* is the request for the deity to come there, or the request for the deity to face [the practitioner], or the request for the deity to arrive.
*Sthāpana* is the request for the deity to remain, or the request for the deity to be present within an image or other object.

*Saṃnidhāpana* is the request for the deity to be present face-to-face, or the request for the deity to accept the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), or the prayer that the mind be focused on nothing else.

The fourth is the prayer for [the deity’s] stability; likewise, the fifth is the prayer for the removal of faults committed through deficiencies in the ritual services (*upacāra*) and so forth, up until the completion of the worship; and *sakalīkaraṇa* is the prayer for the deity to remain in its complete form, which is performed by [placing the syllables] beginning with *puṣka* upon the limbs of the deity.
From the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*):

*avaguṇṭhana* is the prayer for being beyond the range of unworthy vision; *amṛtīkaraṇa* is the prayer for abiding in the fullness of bliss; and *paramīkaraṇa* is [the prayer] regarding all transgressions.

Regarding the request for forbearance mentioned in the *Siddhāntasāra*: when the reality (*tattva*) is already fully present within oneself, that state of being favorably disposed toward it with reverence during acts such as worship is called "invocation" (*āvāhana*).
Once Śiva has been invoked, the continuous stabilization of him within the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) is [the next stage].

The establishment of the deity in the designated place, the offering of devotion, and the performance of worship— when these are being carried out, the capacity of the Lord to accept them and bestow grace and so forth is here called His "proximity" (*sāṃnidhya*). Indeed, that proximity of Śiva which exists until the completion of the worship is said to be the "confinement" (*saṃnirodha*) of this omnipresent Lord.

With the nine mudrās beginning with the *piśakti* and ending with the *svāgata*, one should remain composed and attentive; however, if one is inattentive, one may even perform the display of the respective mudrās and the recitation of the mantras for those respective rites out of their proper sequence, provided that both are nonetheless performed.

The intended meaning is that they are simultaneous. As for what the author of the *Padārthādarśa* stated—that by the word "concentrated" (*samāhita*), one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā, encapsulated by the root [syllable], within their respective locations in this very body—that is based on great recklessness, for such a... [text fragment ends].
Even by means of a thousand [other methods], such a goal cannot be attained through any other sequence; thus,
there is no possibility of the fault of redundancy with the root text to be stated later, beginning with "one should follow," because immediately after that,
one should contemplate the rays of the Lord— one's own chosen deity— who consists of a mass of light.

One should meditate upon those very rays of light that have gone to their respective locations as being ultimately established in the form of the presiding deities and their peer deities who serve as the guardians of the [five] sites; in the case of the worship of the deities of the five shrines (*pañcāyatanadevatā*), one should perform for them all the rites such as invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth within their respective images and other receptacles.

In this case, the *padārthānusamaya* method—whereby one performs the invocation (*āvāhana*) for each deity individually and then performs the installation (*sthāpana*) for the next, and so forth—is not to be adopted. Rather, one should follow the *krama-anusamaya* (sequential) method, performing the invocation and subsequent rites for one deity and then doing the same for the next; the same applies to the worship (*pūjana*).

Because of the statement, "Having offered a handful of flowers to the principal deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and others shall take place," worship indeed consists of the offering of services according to one's capacity; and because of the aforementioned scriptural authority, the order of worship begins with Gaṇeśa. Since Gaṇeśa alone holds the position of primacy, [the circumambulation] begins with the Sun.

Since it is stated in the *Kṣiṇye-nagaṇeśa* that "if one is a leader, one should perform the worship of Sūrya and the others," the sequence for their installation is given in another Tantra: "When Śambhu is in the middle, [place] Hari, Nara, Hara, Bhūdevī, and Harī;
in Hari, Śaṅkara, Bhāsyā, Nāgasutā, Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Ajā, and Vi..."

"Those established by the Dravidas—such as Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Rāvaṇa, Lambodara, Jaṅghārī, Āryeṇā, Śaṅkara, and Bhāgavata—which grant great happiness, are elsewhere said to be the sources of destruction;
for it is said: 'There is no auspiciousness from the middle of the Nāgara [style], nor from the Śaṅgara, Maheśvara, Śūla, or Śaṅga.'"
