The syntactical connection is: "Denāśaṅgara, Nānāśaṅbha, Sūci, and Dika are to be worshipped"; that is, they are to be worshipped in the intermediate directions (vidiś) starting from the center. Having first performed the worship in the center for the one previously mentioned who has been made the primary deity, one should subsequently perform the second and subsequent worships in the intermediate directions according to the sequence starting from the northeast (Īśāna).
[The claim that] Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, Ravi, Gaṇeśa, Devī, Bhavānī, and Sūrya are to be worshipped contradicts the previously cited statement, because it is stated that the worship begins with Gaṇeśa;
thus, the word "to be worshipped" (pūjyāḥ) here means "to be established" (sthāpyāḥ). [Objection: But otherwise...

Regarding the statement that "the sequence of installation is thus seen" and "these [deities] are to be placed separately," as it is said in another *tantra*: "Having worshipped Hari in the center, one should place Gaṇeśa, Pārvatī, and Śarva;
Gaṇeśa in the middle, Śarva in the north-east, Ravi and Viṣṇu in the south-east, and then Ravi, Vighna, Āja, and Śakti."
If it is argued that Śiva, Śakti, Īśa, Vighna, and Ravi are in the center, and Viṣṇu, Hara, Sūrya, Bhāsyā, Śivā, Acyuta, and Ahi are placed starting from the southeast corner (Āgneya) and so on—
let it not be so; for in terms of their respective fruits, those various positions ultimately result in being equal.

With Hari, Gaṇeśa, Naga, Gajā, Śarva, and Śambhu, [the deities] should be placed starting from the front; when Gaṇeśvara and Śivaghna are in the middle, my verse, which explains the sequence for the worship of both locations, is as follows: "In the center, one should worship Atyanta-Śakti, Vighna, Ravi, Hari, and Giri."
In the [eight] groups, starting from the east and proceeding through the cardinal and intermediate directions, there are Sūrya, Śrī, Maheśa, and Parvatasutā;
in the southeast and so forth, there are Vighna, Rameśa, Śakti, and Giriśa.

In the sequence of installation and worship, this [rite] for the chowries is prescribed according to the tantric rules by means of the *sudhā-mantra*. Regarding the phrase "by the *sudhā-mantra*," authoritative scholars maintain that it means "by the mantra *sudhā*" itself;
however, the authors of the *Padārthādarśa* and others follow the interpretation that it refers to the *amṛta-bīja*, namely the syllable *vaṃ*.

Since [the mantras] such as *stumu dhetyātamanaṃ mukhe* have been rejected by the *Uḍḍāmara* and other authorities due to the certainty that they refer to individual words (*padaparatā*), one must, in all *utsarga* mantras, accept only those instances where the word *namaḥ* follows a term signifying renunciation (*tyāga*),
such as *pādyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ* and *arghyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*.

The application of *sudhā*, *svāhā*, and so forth in the *nivedana-mantra* and in the *madhuparka*, *ācamanīya*, and other [offerings] is the heart [of the ritual]. Now, is it being said here that this is something unprecedented—that the *nivedana-mantra* is distinct from the *utsarga-mantra*? True; for whatever is given, such as clothing or ornaments, [the respective mantra must be used].
Having uttered the deity of those [offerings], such as gold and so forth, having performed the sprinkling and worship, and having released them,

one should announce [the offering] with the root mantra or by each individual name; this is indeed unprecedented for those who do not perceive the secrets of the *Yoginītantra* and other scriptures, and it is explained in greater detail for those who know the tradition.

And this has been established in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī* regarding the passage beginning with "jātī-lavaṅga" (cloves and nutmeg) and so forth: in the absence of those specific substances, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) alone are to be used for the sprinkling. Furthermore, the recollection [of the deity] is essential, as it is said elsewhere: "In the absence of those substances, one should cast rice grains while recollecting [the deity]. Likewise, in another place, regarding the absence of substances...

"Cleaned rice grains should be offered as auspicious [offerings] according to the sequence of the ritual placement (nyāsa). This means that in whichever part of the body a particular letter of the Mātṛkā is to be placed, one should worship one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) in that specific bodily limb, using the Mātṛkā syllable associated with that deity, encased within the mantra.

The meaning is "he shall conquer. Regarding the phrase "the limbs and so forth," this refers to those deities who are the primary attendants of equal status to the principal deity—such as Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and others for Śrī Rāma;
and Dattātreya, Hanumān, Kanakaprabhā, and others for the illustrious Rājarājeśvara.

In the root-mantra of the goddess to be described hereafter, which consists of eleven syllables, one should place Saṃskṛta-vāṇī and Prākṛta-vāṇī on the right and left sides respectively. Now, if it is asked: "What is the procedure for a deity for whom no subordinate deities of equal status have been specified? [The answer follows:]...

These [rules] belong to this very system (naya), and for that reason alone, the adoption of this general injunction is necessary; otherwise, the doubt as to whether the worship of such deities should or should not be performed—and if it should be performed, when—would never be resolved. However, in a case where there is an exception to that...

The doubt that there is no such thing as "aṅga" (limb/member) [in this context] is dispelled by the statement beginning with "from the limbs up to the world-protectors" (*aṅgādilokapālāntam*), since it is stated that the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*) are to be mentioned immediately hereafter; thus, the objection that the mention [of them] would be disconnected is refuted. However, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* [notes that] even here, the word "limbs" (*aṅga*)...

This intention is precisely that one should worship the deities of the limb-enclosures (*aṅgāvaraṇa*) and so forth; having offered incense and flowers to the principal deity, one should then perform the offering of incense, lamps, and so on after having worshipped the deities of the limb-enclosures.
Regarding the statement "one should worship the limbs and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the specific deities of each respective enclosure.

Although it is not to be spoken of as existing or non-existing in its own respective conceptualization (*kalpa*), since it is appropriate to speak of the general enclosures (*sāmānyāvaraṇa*)— such as the limbs (*aṅga*) and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*)— in accordance with the general conceptualization, [the author] reveals the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) in order to state the placement, the locations, and the applications of those two.

Furthermore, they say that he gathers [the deities] again, beginning with the limbs (aṅga) and ending with the world-protectors (lokapāla). Here, this occurs to me: if that is so, why was the expectation regarding their respective positions not satisfied in the first instance by the phrase "beginning with the limbs" (*aṅgādīn*), or why does it not arise later?
One must state the reason why the desire for [other] mantras is reawakened and then brought to cessation;

however, in our view, one’s own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) is the primary [deity], while the deities of the enclosures such as the Vahni and others— whether regarded as being on the same level as that deity or as its constituent limbs or as its body—
are considered subordinate.

Having first honored [the deity] with perfumes, offerings, food, and all the ritual services (upacāra) according to the prescribed equality, and having worshipped them fully, asked for forgiveness, and received permission, one should subsequently worship the deities of the limbs (aṅga) and the other enclosures (āvaraṇa).
Since there is a desire for their specific locations and so forth at that very time, their determination [is undertaken] right then; thus, there is nothing [inconsistent].

On the contrary, it would follow that according to your own view there is a deficiency (nyūnatva) because the worship of the deities who are equal to Pradhāna—established in other tantras—is not mentioned here; for this very reason, [it is said]: "Therefore, as is dear to Dattātreya, [one should worship] with incense, lamps, and so forth."

Having worshipped the limbs with the [five] limbs (*aṅga*) and those endowed with power (*śakti*) upon the petals, and so forth—according to the ritual procedures taught in the *Kāmyakalpa*, *Uḍḍāma*, and other tantras—any contradiction that might arise is resolved for you, as it is contained within this very [system]; this is the general direction.
These two, red and white, have been taught. These...

"One should not worship Durgā with *dūrvā* grass, nor Gaṇādhipa with *tulasī*, nor worship the Sun with *vilva* leaves, nor worship Hari with *arka* or *unmatta* flowers," and so forth; what is thus prohibited must not be used again.
This is stated by the words "not above" (*nopari*), which serves as an illustration for the removal of the previous day's offerings (*nirmālya*).

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Vidvallī Tantra* that what must necessarily be avoided is as follows: "One afflicted by thirst, one who has stepped on a leaf, a maiden who is menstruating, and a deity with faded garlands destroy previously accumulated merit.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, having removed whatever remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*), one should offer a handful of flowers."

The wise one, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for worship (*arghya*), as well as water for rinsing the mouth, should give a tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) and offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and give beautiful, pure clothing; by the word "the Preceptor" (*deśika*), it is understood that the offering of incense and other items should be performed with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and so forth. Thus [says] Jñānavān.

It has been stated that the offering of the *nīvi* follows immediately after that; however, as for the statement in the *Padārthādarśa* that the worship of the bell is declared by the mantra "O Guide" (*deśika*), I do not understand how this meaning can be obtained, since there is not even the presence of the bell as the subject matter in the current context.
Regarding the statement that one should offer incense while ringing the bell—which has been worshipped with the *argha-ghaṇṭā* mantra—using the left hand, this is what was asserted by them;

however, even that is not correct, because the meaning "one should offer incense" (*dhūpayet*) is simply impossible [in that context]. If it were possible, it would belong to you alone, as in the passage beginning with "O Teacher! (*deśika*).

The text would be contradicted because it is stated that "one should offer incense for the worship with the Ghaṇṭā-mantra. Furthermore, it should be understood that the offering of incense preceded by the ringing of the bell and so forth is indeed the presentation of the incense-oblation (naivedya), and not merely the discarding of the incense; [the word] "nīcaiḥ" means below the navel.
Regarding the high eye-region (uccairnetradeśa), there is this specific rule: ghee lamps should be placed to the right and oil lamps to the left;
likewise, if the wick is white, it should be placed to the right, and if red, it should be placed to the left. Thus, with a red wick for the ghee lamp and a white wick for the oil lamp...

If it is asked, "In which part of the lamp should [the wick] be placed?"—it is not so; for when there is no separate perceiver (adhyakṣa) for the oil distinct from the perceiver of the wick, the conformity to the oil must necessarily depend upon the form residing in the wick. Thus, "the minister should inform" refers to the act of informing.
"O Hara, being pleased with this offering, accept it"—this refers to one who possesses the mantra consisting of sixteen syllables.

This is because, in the absence of such a mantra, it is impossible to perform the offering due to ignorance of the mantra that serves as the instrument for the offering. As for the word "mantrī," it refers to one who [wields] the weapon...

Regarding the statement by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* that "one should sprinkle the offering (naivedya) as an act of worship," that is merely a general assertion, because it does not provide the specific meaning required here; otherwise, one would have to follow his entire stated procedure, such as "having protected [the offering] with the Vakramudrā, one sprinkles the oblation (havis) with the Vāyu-bīja," and so forth.
Since it would be possible to indicate that [point] by the word "syāt," its non-mention would result in a deficiency at that very moment;

moreover, since it would be possible to indicate all the various meanings to be explained hereafter by this very [word], the subsequent root-text (*mūla*) would also be rendered purposeless. This much alone [is indicated] by this [word].

If it could not be indicated otherwise, then in your view it would have to be determined by scriptural authority (*śruti*); however, in that system, the inherent power of the words (*śabda-svārasya*) alone is the determinant, so this [objection] is of no consequence.
"Upadaṃśa" refers to a side-dish or condiment eaten together with the meal, as well as a portion of the food offering (*naivedya*), which one who eats the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa-bhojin*) consumes.
Having given everything to the *bhyoda* [deities], one should take what remains in the form of grace with cupped hands and set it aside elsewhere;

for although it cannot be given again to those who eat leftovers because there is no longer one's own ownership over the substance offered to the deity, nevertheless, what is intended here is a gift in the form of a final disposal (*pratipatti*), and thus there is no fault.
Thus it has been stated in another Tantra: Viṣataṣeṇā is said to belong to Hari; Caṇḍeśvarī to Umāpati; Vikartanī to Vikaṭatuṇḍa; Gaṇeśitṛ to Caṇḍāṃśu; and Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī is said to belong to Śakti.

It is stated that one should dissolve [the deity] into all these during the performance of every ritual service (upacāra), including the consumption of remnants (ucchiṣṭabhojana). All ritual services are thus prescribed.

The meaning is that the worship is not restricted solely to the Lord (Prabhu), nor even exclusively to the deities of equal rank with the Lord as established by the initial words [of the text], but rather it extends to those deities as well as to the deities of their respective enclosures (*āvaraṇa*). What, then, are these enclosure-deities?
Even during intervals between [other] times, one should perform the worship of the Lord.

The word "also" (api) indicates a meaning that is in agreement with other tantras; furthermore, the meaning stated in the *Padārthādarśa*— that water should be offered at intervals even during the worship of the presiding deities (*āvaraṇadevatā*)—
would only be obtained if [the rule] were [applied to] the half-verse beginning with "limbs and so forth" (*aṅgādīti*).
The half-verse "naṃtaraṃ tatratatra" would [then] exist, and there would also be an internal connection (*antarā*) for the honorifics (*upacārāṇām*).
Furthermore, the reading "taretareti" and the subsequent ellipsis (*anuṣaṅgi*) of "api tā tatratatra" and so forth is not more tenable;
for there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) regarding the reason for the ellipsis of "api," nor is there any intended meaning (*tātparya*).

The status of being a grasper [is established] because it is described as having another purpose; nor should it be said that this is not the intended meaning as we maintain it, for if one were to interpret the stated meaning otherwise against its own natural sense (*svārasya*), there would result a violation of the fundamental natural sense of the source text.
This concerns the worship prior to each veil (*pratyāvaraṇa*).
One should worship those [deities] as Śrī and Īśa; this is because it would result in a contradiction with the meaning stated in the *Saṃhitā* and other texts. This is what should be reflected upon.

Regarding the location of the deities of the limbs (*aṅga*) and the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), he states: "In the filaments" (*kesareṣu*), etc.; the remainder of the sense is that this applies to places other than those specifically prescribed. Therefore, the limbs are indeed located in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

There is no harm even in the worship of the *Śrīrājarājeśvarī* winds [in these directions]. By the phrase "starting from the corner" (*koṇādītyādinā*), the inclusion of the South-West (*Nairṛtya*), West (*Vāyu*), North-East (*Īśāna*), and so forth is intended. This too is occasional; for that reason, it is stated in the *Śrīrājarājeśvarī* [tantra] that "the Heart and the others are in the corners of the East-North, the South-West, and the North-West."

There is no contradiction with the statement of the *Īśvarakalpa*. However, those who have not seen the original text of the *Padārtha* maintain that these two positions are established based on the secret tradition (*guhasampradāya*). To me, however, it appears that in the *Padyadevatākalpa*, the specific direction mentioned corresponds to that particular deity.

In the same way, this application is fixed; however, where nothing has been stated, let the rule remain exactly as it is. Thus, by appending "namas" at the end for the worship of the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and others, the word "namas" should be inserted after "hṛdayāya namaḥ," while the word "svāhā" should be used again in the fire-oblation (*homa*).

"It should be offered with the head [of the mantra], 'svāhā svāhā'; at the end of the mantra is the wife of Fire (Svāhā). Know that she, who is the very embodiment of the mantra, is mentioned as the second part of the oblation (homa). In the same way, know her to be present in the libation (tarpaṇa) for you. Furthermore, the Heart-mantra is the second [part] of the Śakti-saṃ..."

It has been stated in the *Bhaktiviveka* that [the rule] follows from the statement in the *Gama-tantra*; therefore, the usage consisting of the single word "namaḥ" (such as in *hṛdayāya namaḥ*) was rejected by him as not being a designation of the actual referent (*padārtha*). Furthermore, the application of the feminine suffix *strī* is not universal, as there are forms such as *puruṣākṛti*.

Since it is understood from the *Saṃhitās* and other sources— beginning with "They are to be meditated upon" (*dhyeyāḥ*)— that the deities who are the limbs (*aṅgadevatās*) of the venerable Rājarājeśvara and others possess human forms, and since at the end [of the ritual] the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) as prescribed in their respective *kalpas* is performed,
this too is generally the case; therefore, [the procedure] follows from the deities of the final enclosure of the venerable Rājarājeśvara.

Even when worshipping the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) at the very beginning, there is no fault; or rather, it should be understood that the fact that they constitute the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) at the end—starting from the outer *bhūpura* and ending with the world-protectors following the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth—has already been stated by this very [text].
By the statement "one should worship the world-protectors," [the sequence] beginning with "Oṃ Indra, namaḥ" and so forth [is indicated].

The application [of the rule] has been reached; regarding that, he states the distinction starting with "mūla": those words which express the deity intended as primary at that time, among which the word *ariṣṭa* (or a similar term) has entered at the end—that is, those words which convey that [deity].
The specific epithets of the guardians of the three worlds (*tilokapāla*), the weapons such as the vajra and others which are their types,

and the words for their presiding deities such as Suratejas and so forth— those [epithets] which have entered into or are contained within the sentences that express them; by that [means], they are also its qualifiers.

The application "namas śrīviṣṇupāriṣadāya asāyudhāya asurādhipāya indrāya" and so forth is not appropriate, because this specific usage has been established by another system (tantra) as being something entirely different; furthermore,
this present tantra contains ambiguous meanings, and thus there is no certainty [regarding its application].

Furthermore, regarding this root-text, does it refer to the individual words (*padaparatva*) or to the meaning (*arthaparatva*)? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of inserting only the words "he" (*saḥ*) and so forth;
moreover, if one were to employ only the term "with reference to the genus" (*jātyadhipetya*), the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajet*) would fail to be syntactically connected.

Furthermore, by extension, even the usage "śrīviṣṇupāriṣadāya" (to the attendant of Śrī Viṣṇu) would not be obtained at the end [of a mantra], because such a word only conveys the performance of worship for one who has already achieved their purpose; thus, it serves as an illustration regarding the understanding of the usage of such a statement.

Because it is [otherwise] soft, this passage is explained in a different manner as follows: Now, it was stated that "one should sacrifice to the world-protectors" (lokapālas). Is that because they are on an equal footing with the principal deities, or is it by way of a subordinate repetition (āvṛti)? Not the first, for their worship is merely a subsidiary part (aṅga) and so forth.

In order to dispel the doubt that the final [deity] is not obtained from the region because it is not mentioned in the Kalpa and because there would be no possibility of obtaining its worship, he says— intending that the worship of the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) must be followed precisely as they exist in their third form as attendants (pāriṣada)— as follows:

In the word *mūla*, there is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant; therefore, the meaning is "those who are endowed with the status of being attendants" (*pāriṣadatva*). Alternatively, it means "those to whom the term *pāriṣada* is attached" (*anvita*) or "followed" (*anugata*). By this, it is understood that these [beings] are to be worshipped by virtue of their status as attendants. In the phrase beginning with *hetīḥ* (weapons) and so forth, the abstract state is likewise [intended].
The [description of] the hand-gestures (*mudrā*) and so forth is as before.

This designation is for the purpose of meditation, or rather, it is intended to indicate that the meaning of this [mantra] may be inserted into the ritual application-mantra (*prayogavākya*) by means of any word whatsoever.
As for "to you, O Vajra, whose crown is marked with a vajra, together with your weapons, together with your vehicle... [and so on].
"Salutation to the illustrious attendant of Viṣṇu, who possesses the power of a river-iron [body]. This is the application [of the mantra].

Just as in the worship of Indra and others, so too in the worship of the thunderbolt (vajra) and other weapons should it be understood; they are to be worshipped outside, joined with their own well-marked crowns and the collection of their respective weapons and gestures of fearlessness.
The author of the *Padārthādarśa* stated that this is based on the statement of the Teacher (Ācārya), "pāṇipadyā-"; however,
since there is no other evidence [to support it], it is impossible for such a usage to be obtained whether this statement refers to either the word (*pada*) or its meaning (*padārtha*), or to both.
The application beginning with "Obeisance to Vajrāyana" and so forth, which is equal to the forest [of scriptures], is indeed excellent.

As it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "The mantrin should worship those very weapons, joined with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), preceded by *Tāra* (Om), situated in their respective directions, beginning with the Vajra."

[The weapons] are the mace, staff, sword, noose, goad, club, then the trident, discus, and lotus— these are the weapons in sequence for Śiva. Regarding "Yama" and so forth, the essential point here is that there is no arbitrary insertion of words into these various mantras for the worship of these world-protectors (lokapālas) during their ritual application.

Because of that same consequence, there is no inclusion of names mentioned in human-authored texts, as those too are exceedingly numerous; nor is there inclusion of names mentioned in tantras for the same reason, since they are likewise many and have already fulfilled their purpose through the very prescriptions for worshiping their respective objects by means of those specific words.

Because Saturn lacks the quality of being a restrainer (*yāmakatva*), its ritual application is now described: first the seed-syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), then "to Indra," then "to the lord of such-and-such [direction]," followed by "with weapons" (*sāyudhāya*), "with vehicles" (*savāhanāya*), and "to him" (*tasmai*).
Then "on the day" (*vārāya*), "with power" (*saśaktaye*), then "Kāya," and finally the word "Uru" (*uru*) and "Pārṣada."

This mantra, ending with *dāyanamaḥ*, is remembered as the mantra for the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*). In place of the word "Indrāya," one should utter the words "Vahni" (Fire) and so forth; in place of the initial word "amuka," the wise person should utter the respective classes [of beings] in order.
Before the attendants (*pārṣada*), at the appropriate place, one should place one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and so on. Thus [ends the section on] the *dī*.

Just as in the case of the *pakalpīya*, *hṛdayāmalaka*, and so forth, whatever the specific terminology of a particular Tantra, those names recited in that Tantra alone must be employed in practice and no others.
Thus, one should include the words *varuṇa*, *soma*, and so on, which are not seen [in other systems] within that context.
We do not know how the usages of those who composed works such as the *Padārthādarśa* and the *Harṣakaumudī* attain authority. If that is so, then listen to which names are included therein:
Indra, Vahni, Pitṛpati, Nirṛti, and Jaleśvara.
"Vāyu, Vidhu, likewise Īśāna, and then Brahmā— accept these in this sequence.
Having thus performed the worship of the Lord with the sixteen and other offerings,
and after the previously commenced worship has been concluded, once again, when the perfumes and flowers have first been offered, one should then pray to the limbs [of the deity].

Having seen that [the worship] was performed with offerings for the horse (araṇapūjā), and having completed it by worshipping with services such as incense, lamps, and food offerings (dhūpa-dīpa-naivedya), the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is to be performed; this is the meaning. Alternatively, he states what must be done immediately after the worship of the world-protectors (lokapāla) with the word "evam" (thus).

The phrase "one's own chosen deity" (*sveṣṭadeva*) is understood from the context; the meaning of *tat* (that) is "having worshipped" (*saṃpūjya*), as this is obtained immediately following [the previous mention]. Any suggestion that this [worship] might be superfluous or lack purpose is set aside, because it is described precisely for the sake of its specific function. And thus... [nai...]
The established meaning is that one should worship with the five services (pañcopacāra) on the sacrificial altar;
for one who accepts the worship of the principal deity at the conclusion of each of the enclosures (āvaraṇas) by means of these services,
there is the rule from another Tantra stating, "At the end of the worship of each enclosure, one should worship Śrīśa," and so forth.

It should be understood that there will be a partiality [toward this view] because it has been stated— with the intent that even for one unable to perform the worship at the end of the other enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), it is nonetheless absolutely necessary at the end of the *tarpaṇa*— that the worship of the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*) is performed at the very end, according to the root text (*mūlagrantha*). This is the daily [practice].

He describes the procedure in detail, beginning with the words "Then the Guru," and so forth: having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on the right side of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), having kindled the fire there, and having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—such as *vīkṣaṇa* and others—to be described later; and having invoked the Lord (*prabhu*) therein, [one performs] the oblation known as *vaiśvadeva*.

Regarding the statement by Padārthādarśakṛt that "whatever sacraments such as *garbhādhāna* (conception) and so forth are to be performed, they must all be performed," and his claim that "rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) exist within the daily oblation (*nityahoma*)," this assertion is contrary to the *Saṃhitā*. Furthermore, regarding the act of performing a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*)...

Since it has been stated by that very [author] that "having bowed and having praised, one should perform the daily *homa*," that too is not [correct], because this is not a daily *homa*; for in the *Saṃhitās* and other texts, after the description of the previously mentioned *homas*, one observes [the sequence] beginning with "immediately thereafter, the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnyādhāna*) and so forth. Therefore, [this is] the *Harṣakaumudī*.
The ritual known as *vaiśvadeva*, performed daily by one who has been initiated (*dīkṛta*), has been briefly described by the Ācāryas;
and since the author of the ritual manual (*kalpakṛt*), having mentioned only the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) in the *smārta* *vaiśvadeva*,
stated that the procedure for that rite applies here as well, the statement regarding the application of a common ritual rule (*bahutaṃtra-vidhi*) is inappropriate.

Having spoken thus, immediately thereafter, one should offer the *bali* to all the attendants (*pārṣada*) of the presiding deity with the mantra "Oṃ adodevatāyāḥ sarvapārṣadebhyo baliṃ namaḥ," using the remaining materials from the *vaiśvadeva* offering along with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, flowers, and so forth, in front [of the deity] and proceeding clockwise around the four directions at every step.
Having thus stated that the offering (*bali*) should be given, he says "the offering" (*balim*); thereafter,
following the presentation of the offering, this word— denoting immediate succession—

refers to the action performed by the deity whose essence is the external light that has emerged [from the mouth], which has as its object the face of the deity, and which follows the sequence previously described beginning with the giving of water, the feeding, ending with the giving of water for rinsing the mouth, and the emergence of the splendor.

Let those with true aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdayas) alone understand that there is no capacity for awakening the ritual acts ending with the offering of the portion to be known (nairvedya-aṃśa), which has Viśvaksena and others as the recipients, within the [rite of] entry (praveśa). Now, we do not say that its meaning is this; rather, it is the act of satisfying [the deities] by means of the offering of the oblation (bali-dāna).

If it is argued that [the word *iti*] serves as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) by showing that the act of offering the oblation (*nivedya*) is connected with the act of sprinkling (*udvartana*) through these intervening items, we say no; for its purpose is fulfilled simply by indicating immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and it is incapable of restricting the intended meaning in that specific way. If, however...

If the reading were *kīryate*, then because it would convey [the meaning] with very little effort, it would be appropriate to render that [reading], which otherwise lacks purpose, meaningful by determining its intended sense (*tātparya*) in that way. A *karkarī* is a specific type of vessel provided with a spout.
Having placed the collection of scattered items (vikira) in a heap toward the northeast direction,

one should fill it with water and worship the deity of the weapon (*astra-devatā*) therein. The two verses beginning with "hemavastra" and the four beginning with "siṃhastha" are adjectives qualifying the deity of the weapon.
Rising from his seat and sitting upon a firm posture (*sthirāsana*), the Guru took up that *karkarī* once more; then,
proclaiming the command of the gods and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) with water poured from its mouth,
he circumambulated the inner altar (*antaravedī*) by way of the inner enclosure (*antaḥmaṇḍala*) while reciting the *astra-mantra*.

Reciting the mantra as before, one should again establish [the fire]; having worshipped the Astra-deity therein and having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites beginning with *vīkṣaṇa*, one should cook the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) in the consecrated fire— this is the syntactical connection and the meaning— and then one should consume it.
It should be the size of one-third of a grain of rice, measured by three morsels, or the measure of eight morsels, while avoiding contact with the teeth.

Having placed [the water] in a cup made of *pālāśa* leaves or, as some say, in one made of *pippala* leaves, the practitioner of mantra should unite it with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). It should be used for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) with pure, filtered water; this is the specific rule stated by Somaśambhu and should be followed.
"With the Heart" means consecrated by one's own respective Heart-mantra, [held] from the middle of the thumb to the fingers of the outstretched hand.

"Up to the measure of a *tāla*": its definition is stated in another tantra: "The wise say that a *tāla* is the space between the thumb and the middle finger of one's own hand when it is extended. Regarding "according to the rule": [it means] on one's own left side, in a direction other than those prohibited, at the prescribed distance.
The meaning is: "without transgressing the procedure prescribed in other tantras, which consists of the preliminary act of throwing [the tooth-stick].

According to the *Prayogasāra*: "Having cleansed the teeth and having cut this tooth-stick—which has been consecrated with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and is produced from a milky tree or similar source—one should throw it on the ground with the left hand."

Having washed this [mudrā], one should cast it toward the directions starting from the east, including below and above. In its respective locations, beginning with the southeast (Agni), the results are proclaimed in order as follows: increase, suffering, death, loss of wealth, peace, disease, wealth, happiness, increase, supreme misery, and so forth. Thus it is stated in another Tantra; and elsewhere also, in the west...
The conjunction (pāta) with Mūla, Uttara-rudra, or Indrāṇī is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious. The syntactical connection is as follows:

where a *sarvatobhadra* or similar mandala has been drawn upon the altar (*vedi*), the Guru, having spread darbha grass there, should sleep together with the disciple. Now, what is the procedure if there is no space on the altar?
If it be argued thus, there is no fault, for the spreading [of the grass] should be performed on a spot near that [altar];
thus, according to Padārthādarśakṛt, the word "on the altar" (*vedyām*) expresses proximity as the sense of the locative case.
As for the phrase "he should lie down," this is a restatement of what is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga-prāpta*); and furthermore, in dreams, neither auspicious nor...

In the morning, the Guru should question the disciple regarding what was seen [in the dream]; he should declare it auspicious if it is auspicious, and if it is inauspicious, he should perform one hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra. Thus, the procedure for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the disciple has been declared in due order; otherwise, it would be contradicted and disturbed, and the performance would become mediocre, while if it remains unseen [or unaccomplished], it would be inferior.

Regarding the statement from the *Kapila-pañcarātra*, "Having seen a dream at night while lying on a bed of *darbha* grass, one should report it," there is no hope whatsoever for its consistency with the *Saura* [tradition],
because the perception [of the dream] and the reporting [of it] are clearly obtained elsewhere. This is what should be said regarding the perception and the reporting.

In the case of the two [methods], when one has not seen [a dream] out of respect for the formal procedure (*vidhāna*), the mere reporting of it at the final word is not prohibited by other statements; however, regarding dreams seen while asleep when no such procedure was performed, only the fruit is described, as there is a lack of authoritative means (*māna*) for the procedure of sleep, and thus it is merely worldly (*laukika*).
In brief, this is because the status of being subject to an injunction is accepted only with respect to those portions not already established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
[The son] whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī,
whose father was Māpati, who was born in the family of Premanivīti, and whose birthplace was Kūrmācala...
From him who was the abode of Vārāṇasī, whose valor was manifested through the Sūpāsya [mantra], and who attained the station of Acyuta,
this *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi* was produced by Dita, who is like a mass of oceans.

"Fire-generation" (*agnijananam*) means the generation of fire characterized by a specific power (*śakti*), whose nature consists in the offering of the respective fruits of oblations as prescribed in the *tantra*. [The author] thus makes a promise for the sake of the disciple’s attention, stating that he will describe such a ritual (*karman*) which is yet to be explained.

Even if fire were to arise without [the rubbing of] wood, there would be no harm; however, in order to dispel the suspicion that this lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*), he says "In that [tantra]," and so forth. To the objection, "In that case, since this matter is obtained from that very root-tantra (*mūlatantra*), what is the purpose of beginning this new work (*apūrva-grantha*)," he replies with "All," and so forth.

The sense is that when one observes various different systems (tantras), a great affliction arises; however, since such a purpose is achieved even by observing each individual system, this [present work] is not useless. Regarding what was stated as "properly consecrated" (*vidhivat-saṃskṛte*), in response to the inquiry as to what the procedure (*vidhi*) is and what the consecration (*saṃskāra*) consists of, he says: "the eight... (*aṣṭā...*)
Regarding the passage beginning with "ten," etc., since the word "according to rule" (*yathāvidhi*) occurs in proximity to "entering with one foot," it connects with *kuṇḍe* (in the pit).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by the path of the scripture" (*śāstravartmanā*), because of its proximity to the word "refined" (*saṃskṛte*), there arises the expectation: "What is that scriptural path? In response to this, the connection is simply with the passage beginning with "eighteen," etc.; there is no other distinction.

If it is argued that even regarding the fruit [of the rite], if it were not thus [performed] according to the path of the scriptures and properly consecrated in the preceptor’s sacrificial pit (*ācāryakuṇḍa*), then the *Padārthādarśa* commentary would be contradicted— what of it? For by the inclusion of either one of the two terms, "the path of the scriptures" (*śāstravartma*) or "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), that which was intended is already expressed.
Because the meaning is already understood, it would follow that the inclusion of either one of those terms is redundant; therefore, that [is not the case].

Since there is no specific door [for this], he says "In that [tantra]" and so forth, to explain whether these purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) are to be adopted even for the rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. The first purificatory rite is the inspection of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).
The second is the sprinkling of the pit with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). With the weapon-mantra...
Striking with the *śakti* weapon is the third; sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with the *kavaca* mantra is the fourth.
This is the distinction between *prokṣaṇa* and *abhyukṣaṇa*: the former is performed with the tips of the upturned hands, while the latter is performed with the hands joined in a fist.
Service (*sevana*) is the ninth consecration (*saṃskāra*); although it is indeed just a form of sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*), such is the commentary.

Thus, it has been explained that the saṃskāras are eighteen because they apply to distinct substrates (dharmin) according to their enumeration; however, a doubt arises as to whether this is due to a difference in the time of their performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) resulting in a difference in individual instances (*vyakti*), or whether "cultivation" (*sevā*) consists in [the application] across all parts (*avayava*). This must be resolved accordingly.
The sprinkling with water is not [the same as] the other [acts], for a distinction must be conceived based on some limitation;
the slight digging of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *astra-mantra* is the fifth [act]; the removal of earth from the pit with the *astra-mantra* alone is the sixth;
and the leveling of uneven hollows in the pit with other earth using the *hṛdaya-mantra* [is the seventh].

The seventh consecration is filling [the pit]; the eighth is bringing it near the site of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of the *astra* mantra; the ninth consecration is sprinkling it with water; the tenth consecration is digging the pit by means of the *hetimantra*, that is, the *astra* mantra; and the eleventh is sweeping it with the *varma* mantra.

The twelfth [purification] is the smearing with cow-dung while reciting the Kavaca mantra; the thirteenth purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is the conceptualization of its form through the Kavaca mantra itself, and the visualization of it as having the nature of the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon. Others, however, maintain that one should understand the form of the pit to be that of Prakṛti.

Since it must be stated that the "supreme body" (paramaṃ vapuḥ) is indeed composed of the root-nature (mūla-prakṛti), its being constituted of the five elements is logical; therefore, the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of those very *kalās* is appropriate. Thus, in this context, the conceptualization of the form of the *kalās* refers specifically to the contemplation of those *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti*, and not otherwise.

They say that one should not invent irrelevant matters or fabricate unmentioned details; rather, one should not invent parts not mentioned and irrelevant to the context. According to the three sūtras, the girdling of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is also performed with the Kavaca mantra alone;
this is the fourteenth [section]. The worship of the pit is performed with the Hṛdaya mantra.

The fifteenth [step] is the worship with *naṃ*; the sixteenth is the "vajrification" (*vajrīkaraṇa*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), which is the contemplation of firmness like a vajra. With the mantra *namaḥ* (the heart-mantra) and blades of *kuśa* grass, one should prepare a path in the four directions; this is indicated by the statement, "one should make a crossroads."
The sixteenth [chapter]: The rite called Akṣapāṭana; the opening of the sense-faculties by means of the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*); the final consecration.
Some say that because they wander at night (*kṣapā*), they are *kṣapāṭanā* Rākṣasas;
that which prevents them from wandering at night is the rite named Akṣapāṭana. And so it is said: "Hum."

They say that one should effect the warding off of Rākṣasas who have arrived for the performance of the rite by means of the *vacam* mantra. Regarding one who is unable to perform [the rite] with so many consecrations (*saṃskāra*), he says "or else" (*athavā*). However, if one possesses the capacity, one following the concise method does not achieve the desired result.

For it is said: "The master who, while entitled to ascend the primary ladder, does not proceed by means of the secondary ladder, does not obtain the fruit thereof. The word *tisraḥ* (three) refers to the three [steps] starting from the west and ending at the east, and likewise the three starting from the south and ending at the north.

The meaning is that lines intersecting the previously drawn lines must be made; three lines, each measuring one *prādeśa*, should be drawn according to the tradition. There is also another specific detail mentioned in the *Sauśamaṇī Tantra*: "One should draw [the lines] with their tips pointing east, situated toward the north, beginning from the south."
"One should draw [the mandala] starting from the west and ending at the east while standing in the west"—this alternative view he will state with the words "or else," and so forth.

By means of the *upacāras*, that is, the services of desire (*kāmopacāras*), which are well-known in the *Kāmaśāstra* such as massaging, kissing the lower lip, and so on; together with Vāgīśvara, [one should worship] the limbs...
The realized meaning is as follows: if sexual intercourse becomes playful through the pressing of the breasts, kissing, and so forth, then there is the birth of excellent offspring;
however, if it is otherwise, then there is the opposite result—this is the sense shown by the words of those who know the *viparīta-riti* (the reverse method).

"One should worship with offerings" (*upacāraiḥ pūjayet*) does not mean that one should worship by obtaining [all] the ritual services (*upacāra*); rather, it is more appropriate to understand it as "one should worship with whatever services are available. Furthermore, regarding the singular form in the phrase "the Goddess Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, and Umā," this indicates that in a single initiation (*dīkṣā*), only one [of these goddesses] should be invoked, and not all of them.
This is for the sake of indication.
Therefore, in the *brahmadīkṣā* [initiation of Brahmā], Sarasvatī; in the *viṣṇudīkṣā*, Lakṣmī;
in the *śivadīkṣā*, Pārvatī—who is conventionally designated by the term *Īśvarī*; and in the initiations of Gaṇeśa and Sūrya, [the respective goddesses]... [are to be understood].

[She is] denoted by the term *Iśvarī* through the yoga of the suffix *ktin*, conjoined with *Vāgīśvara*. Here too, "speech" (*vāk*) refers to *Kavāṇī*; furthermore, because the long vowel *ī* in *Lakṣmī* is conventionally established as referring to Lakṣmī herself, that which follows is the name *Īkārīśvarī*, where the word *Īśvarī* is a part [of the compound]. And she is according to the previously mentioned method.

The five powers of the five abodes— namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, and Sūrya— who possess the two-fold power of passion (rajas) and the power of Brahman (brahma-śakti), have all arrived here. The singular number used for each of them is to be understood as before, signifying that they act as lords over their respective domains.
Regarding the term *śivabīja*, here too it is not a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, but rather a *karmadhāraya*;

that is to say, "Śiva" means the fourfold auspiciousness (*śubha-catuṣṭaya*). For this very reason, the defect associated with a *tatpuruṣa*—characterized by the necessity of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth—is refuted, since a seed that is defective cannot produce offspring.

Because it is well known from the medical treatises (*vaidya-śāstra*) that even when intercourse occurs on the first day or other such days of the fertile period (*ṛtumatī*), a son who is auspicious and long-lived does not result; therefore, one should delight a woman who is beautiful— possessing qualities such as being called "a lotus" (*nīlendīvarā*) and so forth— which brings about such desirable traits.

It should not be argued that the inclusion here of other goddesses or other gods is fruitless; for if this Kalpa were restricted to a single deity, it would result in a contradiction with the root text, which concerns the general category of deities. Such is the concealment of this secret.
It should be understood that this has been explained in a strained manner, as in the case of [the grammatical rule] *prāyo 'lopaḥ* and so forth;

for this very reason, there are statements in the *Saṃhitās* and other texts regarding the union with Lakṣmī, such as: "One should contemplate the fire produced therein by the Lord Nārāyaṇa through union with Lakṣmī, who is in her menses, by means of the vulgar act (*grāmyadharma*)."

One should indeed offer oblations in the Vaiṣṇava fire using a vessel made of bell-metal or similar material, covered by another vessel; having thus prepared the fire produced from sūryakrāntā and other substances,
one should, in the southwest direction, designate it as the portion belonging to the Kravyādas (flesh-eaters) while reciting the Astra-mantra.

The meaning is that one should discard that foremost charcoal and consecrate the remaining fire with the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*). The "Vaibudha" fire is the fire originating from the *bindu*; since the *bindu* consists of the nature of Agni and Soma, it is possible for the fire to arise from it. The "Bhauma" [fire] is the fire of the earth.

The general designation "of the deity and the goddess" refers to the fire situated before the one under discussion; this indicates our previously stated position. By the phrase beginning with "having performed the ritual sipping of water" (*ācamana*), the inclusion of perfumes, flowers, and so forth is intended. At the end of the essential form "Cit Piṅgala," there are the two words "hane" and the word "daha."

Having uttered the two words "dvayampaveti," the mantra whose nature begins with "sarvajña" and so forth was previously proclaimed by Manu in the first verse with the words "by this [mantra]" and so on; the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that "this is that very mantra" which was described by the general property of being a *mantra*. And there is the kindling of the fire.
One should kindle the fire with the mouth alone, using [fans such as] a *nāsūrya* or a fan; for it is said, "From the mouth, Agni was born.

This prohibition applies to worldly fire, as it is established by the tantric statements cited in the *Sudhārṇava* and other works, beginning with: "Therefore, [it does not apply] to the non-worldly [fire]," and so forth. Regarding the body of the self...

Regarding the statement "one should perform the placement" (*nyaset*), when the question arises as to whether this is done for each individual limb starting from the head, or by way of pervading [the whole body], he says "in the *liṅga*" and so forth; [this means] everywhere, that is, by delimiting all the limbs.
Here, the placement of the final [syllable] is performed on the eye, which is distinct [from the others]; [and] the placement of *Vahurūpā* is performed in a low tone (*upāṃśu*).
In that [rite], the placement (nyāsa) on all limbs, including the genitals, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes,
is performed in sequence. According to the statement, "The goddess of many forms resides on all limbs,
ending with the *nityasēdā*," the author of the root-text [performs it] in reverse order on the tongue for the final and penultimate [syllables].

The naming [of these] is for the sake of ease in extracting the mantras of the tongues; otherwise, there would be no brevity in words such as "and so forth" (sādy-ādi). Furthermore, the placement (nyāsa) of the tongues occurs through the placement of their respective mantras, yet it is not known which mantras those are. Thus [the question arises].
Regarding the [mantra] for destruction, he says "vahni" and so forth; by counting in reverse order from the letter *sa* to the end of the alphabet, these letters— namely *va*, *hi*, *na*, *ra*, *ka*,
*ra*, *du*, *ra*, *ya*, *ka*, *ra*, *i*, *śa*, and the sixth vowel (*ū*)— when joined together, each one individually...
Seven sparks arise from the fire.

The tongues attain the status of mantras in due order; "distinction of qualities" (*guṇabheda*) refers to the differentiation of the *guṇas*, such as *sāttvika* and so forth. This means [the distinction] regarding specific actions—namely, *sāttvika* action, *rājasa* action, and *tāmasa* action. In the phrase "in optional action" (*kāmyakarmaṇi*), [the *rājasa* is implied].

The word "jase" (for [the sake of] victory) is the remainder [of the sense]. By the words "jātibhiḥ," "hṛdayāyanam," and so forth; and by the compound "tārāgnaye," which is a dvandva of the two words "tārā" and "agnaye"; then, there is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "those for whom the words 'tārā' and 'agnaye' are at the beginning. Now, one might object: how can the word "tārā" be construed with the word "pada"?

If that were the case, then in the expression *tārāgnaye* (to Tārā-Agni), following the compound *tārā ca agnaye ca*, there ought to be a *karmadhāraya* [compound] such as *tārāgnaye* (to the Agni who is Tārā); furthermore, this would result in the undesirable consequence of employing the word *tāra* [as a separate term]. [The phrase] *vahnimūrtayaḥ* refers to those who represent the forms of Fire (*vahnimūrti*).

Therefore, there is no contradiction even when words such as *jātavedas* and others are preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) despite their being [proper] names; thus, the practical application results in such forms as "Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Jātavedas. First, regarding the seat (*āsana*), within one's own body...

The meaning is as follows: having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities starting from the forest frog (*vanmaṇḍūka*) up to the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), and having likewise placed the seat-powers (*pīṭhaśakti*) of the Fire-god (*vahni*);

then, having mentally offered a seat (*āsana*) to the Fire-god by means of one's own self; one should meditate upon the form (*mūrti*) of the Fire-god therein—[meditating on him] holding his desired boon-mudrā and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*). After this meditation... [the rest of the sentence follows].

The meaning is "ram. Thus, the sequence is obtained as follows: after meditation (dhyāna), there is the sprinkling (pariṣecana); then the strewing of darbha grass (paristaraṇa); then the casting of the enclosing sticks (paridhi-prakṣepa); then the worship of Brahmā and others therein;
and finally, the worship of the meditated fire in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). However, according to the author of the Padārthādarśa, it is as follows: [the sequence]...

Thus, they say that the meaning is "having worshipped the fire within one's own heart by means of the sequence of internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). Indeed, this is not understood from the words [of the text] themselves; rather, it is understood from the very beginning of the meditation (*dhyāna*) on the fire, as the meditation on the fire is established as being primary. Furthermore, the mantra for the worship of the fire follows later.

Because it is so stated, how can there be worship [of the intermediate directions]? Since those enclosures (paridhi) are threefold—belonging to the southern, western, and northern directions—the worship is performed only for that triad. Therefore, the intermediate directions (vidiśā) are not included here; rather, the worship takes place in the center, within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
By the very mention [of "in the center"], the worship of the deities of the pedestal (pīṭha) beginning with Maṇḍūka is implied;
thus, when the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been worshipped with the mantras ending with those of the Maṇḍūka-pīṭha,
the author of the *Padārthādarśa* explains that such a meaning is somehow obtained.
Even in the absence of an explicit statement, there would still be an indication (*lakṣaṇa*), for such a meaning has already been established by us previously. Thus,
in the six corners starting from the southeast (*īśāna*) and ending with the southwest (*yukkoṇa*), one should worship the six tongues, excluding the remaining ones.

The meaning is that she is to be worshipped as Bahurūpā in the center. According to the statement of Somaśambhu, "Hiraṇyā and the others are situated in Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Gocara; these six tongues of fire follow in sequence, while Bahurūpā is in the middle," she is indeed in the center. Furthermore, [it is said] "in the middle" (pare tu madhye).

How could that which was first taken up be placed at the end? Or how would there not be a lack of elegance in the text? If such were the intention, why was it not stated that [the worship] should be in the center as well as in the six corners? Therefore, the worship of the tongue is first performed in the center, and thereafter in the corners.

The path beginning with "ṇeṣi" is indeed the one agreed upon by the texts; however, the statements of Somaśambhu and others refer to alternative views and are to be settled according to the respective traditions of one's own gurus. Regarding the distinction of rites, the arrangement of the tongues of the deities to be worshipped in the center has been stated in another Tantra: "Then, in the middle of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), she..."

The white [syllable] is praised for subduing the tongue, for gold, for worldly activities, for paralyzing, and so forth; the yellow is praised for causing internal hatred, and so forth; the red is indeed for killing; the black is for great power; here, by the best of the wise, it is for pacification; and the deep-red interior is for driving away (uccāṭana). It is said thus.

The meaning is that one should worship the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) in the sequence of placement starting from the east and so on, upon the *darbha* grasses situated on the directions, while saying: "O you of many forms, may auspicious things always abide in the center and in the directions.
As it has been said: "In the center and in the six corners [one worships] with the tongues, and also in the filaments (*kesara*) with the limbs (*aṅga*)."

"Then, having consecrated it with the mantras, one should worship the lords of the directions in order, starting from the east, upon the *darbha* grass resting on the girdle (*mekhalā*) by means of the eight forms (*mūrti*) in sequence. From this, the underlying intent of the root text is understood to be that an eight-petaled lotus outside the hexagon must necessarily be made for the purpose of worshipping the eight forms; otherwise [the ritual would be incomplete].
Regarding the statement "How could it be said that there is no overlap (*adaleṣu*)?", the objection raised by Harṣaka is refuted.

By showing the meaning of the words through the unity of the previously cited statements, the primary sense of the term *adaleṣu* is established as referring to the *darbha* grasses resting upon the girdle (*mekhalā*). Thus, [the phrase] "in the absence of leaves" (*adaleṣu*) is explained.

Since it is impossible for the phrase "in the Didigdalas" to imply such eight petals through a definitive interpretation of its meaning, and because, in reality, an eight-petaled lotus is necessary in accordance with the mention of "in the filaments" (kesareṣu),
it is more appropriate that the worship of the Mūrtis be performed upon the petals.

In the *Harṣadīpikā* treatise, it appears that the worship of the Guardians of the Quarters (*dikpāla*) consists merely of [offering] *darbha* grass placed upon the girdle; for this very reason, in the *Śiṣṭakalpa*, after having drawn a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus within a square fire-altar (*vahnikoṣṭha*),
one writes the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) in the center of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

The phrase "one should mark" (*mārcayet*) is clearly seen [in the texts]; the term "illusion" (*māyā*) is an elliptical designation for the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the respective deities and their powers (*śakti*).
For this very reason, it is observed in various tantras that in the Vaiṣṇava fire, *ra* is the seed-syllable.
As for the ritual act (*padārtha*) of worshipping the forms (*mūrti*) in the well-known directions starting with the East...

Regarding this, what was stated by Darśakṛt— that it is appropriate [to follow the conventional direction] because everywhere worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) is performed according to the technical convention (*pāribhāṣika*), and there is no evidence to sublate that here— is incorrect; nor is there sublation by the aforementioned specific statement,
because in that statement the words "east" and so forth are indeed present, and thus it refers to the technical sense.

Nor can it be established by logical necessity (*upapatti*), because the mere syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the words "lords of the directions" (*dikpatīn*) would still not suffice to establish the intended meaning; for in the worship of Dharma and others, the practice has been exactly the same in the east, and according to such scriptural statements as "the Indra and others [should be placed] between the worshipper and the worshipped, each according to their own [direction]," the presence of Indra and the rest is required.

It should be understood that the inclusion of the term "established" (*siddha*) for the eastern direction is accepted by all; he describes the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the words beginning with "behind" (*paścāt*), according to the sequence: the meaning is that one should cleanse the tips of the *darbha* grasses with the tips [of the blades], the middle parts with the middle parts, and the roots with the roots, using fire. He now describes the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*).
With the words "ha ājya" and so forth, by means of the water of the weapon (*astra-vāri*) accompanied by the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*),

and having sprinkled [it] with that water preceded by the recitation of the weapon-mantra; with the thumb and ring finger (or thumb and little finger), six times— thus praising [the deities] beginning with Tāpana and the others.

Having observed that there are six purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *tāmisra*, one might raise the objection that since the four purificatory rites of clarified butter (*ājya*)— which precede its casting into the vessel (*ājyasthālī*)— are indeed distinct,
there would be eighteen purificatory rites as declared in the Śaiva Āgamas. However, this is not so.

If it is asked how the lack of contradiction with other *tantras*—as seen in the *Padārthādarśa*, which states "eight [times] with clarified butter using the *sruva* ladle"—is to be resolved, do not say so; for this is consistent with the *Vāyavīya Saṃhitā*, which says: "Having placed the mantra [on the fire], one should display the mudrā known as the 'Cow' (*dhenu*) over the clarified butter in the vessel."

There is no fault in this, for it is taught that prior to the casting of the ghee, two additional consecrations must be performed upon the ghee: first, the consecration (*abhimantryana*) with the root mantra, and second, the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*). This is because the manner of casting the ghee to be offered depends upon specific particulars.
Intending this, the author of the *Mūla* stated "having placed" (*vinikṣipya*) after having omitted "having cast down" (*avikṣipya*).
However, for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, there is the taking up, heating, wiping, heating again,
the placement of one's chosen deity and their power consisting of Śiva and Śakti, and the forming of the triple-thread (*trisūtrīkaraṇa*).

There is no fault even in that location [of the vessel], as it consists of the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—namely, the wrapping of the neck with a cloth, worship, and its placement based on one's own right side. This is stated in the Śaiva Āgama:
"Having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, either facing upwards or downwards in sequence..."

Having heated the three darbha blades in the fire, one should touch them with honey at their roots and tips; having heated them again thirty times, one should cast the kuśas face-down into the fire. One should place the śakti on the sruva and the śambhu on the sruk, wrapped around the necks with three threads and honored with flowers and other offerings, while reciting the vadya-mantra.

One should place the blades of kuśa grass upon the three [blades] above, to one's own right. Then follows the throwing of darbha grass into the fire; that is the rite of disposal (*pratipatti-karman*), and it is not a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for anyone. Regarding the non-mention of this in the root text, it should be reconciled by the method of another tantra. *Heti* refers to the remnant of the substance offered in the oblation.

While standing with the *sruva* ladle, during each oblation (*āhuti*) as the homa is being performed with this *sruva*, not everything without exception should be poured into the fire; rather, it is taught that "without exception" refers to the root portion of the *vyāhṛti* words, which refers to the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. These are stated in another treatise (*tantra*) as follows: [the text continues].
As shown by the venerable Ārādhava Bhaṭṭas: *Oṃ bhūr agnaye ca pṛthivyai ca mahate ca svāhā;
oṃ bhuvo vāyave cāntarikṣāya ca mahate ca svāhā; oṃ svar ādityāya ca dive ca mahate ca svāhā; oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaś candramase ca nakṣatrebhyaś ca...*

"From the *gbhyaśca svāhā* [mantra], likewise the naming": the meaning is that when a fire-oblation (*homa*) is prescribed for the purpose of mantra-initiation (*mantradīkṣā*), preparatory rites (*purascaraṇa*), and so forth, one should perform a naming (*nāma*) corresponding to that; likewise, in the Śaiva initiation and other rites, [the fires are named] "Śivāgni" and "Mṛtyuñjayāgni."
The established meaning is that in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], the name to be established is either "Rbhubhairavāgni" or "Viṣṇvagni"; in the Śrīrā [tradition], it is "Śrīragni" or "Kṛṣṇāgni";
and in initiations beginning with the Śākta, it is "Śaktyagni" and so forth, or "Tripurāgni," "Tārāgni," and so on. This is the final conclusion.

The two ancestors previously mentioned are for the fire; immediately after this, while standing, one should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) by dipping them once at their roots and tips into the clarified butter and sacrifice them. Thereafter, the oblation (homa) for the tongues of fire, the limbs, and the presiding deities should be performed with their respective mantras; such is the inherent meaning of the root text.

The path has indeed been established, as if by the moonlight of joy. Following the description of all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with *garbhādhāna*, he states another purificatory rite: "With fuel-sticks," etc.

There should be five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) ten fingers long, produced from trees suitable for the sacrificial enclosure (*paridhi*); in their absence, they may be produced from the *aśvattha* tree or others.

One should offer the fuel-sticks—whose roots and tips are smeared with ghee, which have not been eaten by insects or other pests, and which still possess their bark—standing silently, one by one. Here, since the Teacher has not specified whether one should stand or sit, we have stated "standing" in accordance with Kātyāyana; thus, standing, [one offers] the *samidh*...

The authors of the *Padārthādarśa* have taught that [the term "immediately following"] is defined as such because it is used everywhere; furthermore, they connect [this definition] even to the phrase "the naming [of the fire] immediately following. The meaning of "immediately following" (*anantaram*) here is [the performance of] the five-fold oblation of fuel-sticks (*samidh-homa*) which is about to be described.

Having removed the [impurity of] *nālāpanayana* for a moment and purified the *sūtaka*, one should then give a name to the fire according to the names of the deities, such as Nārāyaṇāgni, Kṛṣṇāgni, Durgāgni, and so forth. Then,
having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the fires of the two parents, the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the *vaulā* (or *jātakarma*) should be performed.
Therefore, the sequence beginning with the extraction of the tongue, followed by the offering of charcoal, foot-washing, and so forth—starting with "Oṃ"—is indeed more appropriate.

As it is stated in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*: "Having performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) for the newborn immediately upon birth in this manner, one should then extract the umbilical cord and purify the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) by means of the auspicious fire."

Having performed the dismissal of the parents preceded by oblations with the names of the days and months, and having performed the sacraments beginning with the tonsure (*caula*) and initiation (*upanayana*), and ending with marriage— according to the *Śaivāgama*— one should then offer five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire for the removal of the "reed" (*nāla*) defect. Thus it is said.

Regarding the statement, "They say [the offerings] are soaked in ghee on the *temūla*," this must be said: although this point is established in other treatises (*tantra*), it is not established in the primary source (*mūla*). For, from the words "tataḥ śca" onwards, the *mūla* prescribes both the dismissal of the ancestors (*pitṛvisarjana*) and the oblation of fuel-sticks (*samid-dhoma*) immediately after all the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*).

Since these two [meanings] are understood as having attained a sequential priority and posteriority, one should not argue that this meaning is derived from the root by means of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) at the end, through a reversal of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*);
for if that were so, then since all the Tantras could potentially form a single coherent discourse (*ekavākyatā*), [there would be no distinction between them].

"In this way, one should not divide [the offerings] among the various deities," thus it is said. Following the sequence as stated in the section on worship according to the rules, the knower of mantras— one who knows the mantras for the *homa* and other rites— should offer one oblation (*āhuti*) to each deity individually, even when the mantras begin with the *praṇava*.

He who knows that there is no *praṇava* (*oṃ*) within [the mantra], yet at the end of the mantra—on the occasion of the *homa* sacrifice—there is again the ending with *svāhā*, is a knower of mantras; and he who, being such, has perfected the *mantra* for the *homa* through *puraścaraṇa* and other means, is the greatest of mantra-knowers. By him [should it be offered]: *oṃ svasti pūrṇāya śirase svāhā*.
It is stated that the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with the thirteen-syllable mantras beginning with "Hā Svāhā" and so forth; furthermore,

by the phrase "according to rule," it serves as a reminder that the homa-mantra must end with "Svāhā," and by the phrase "versed in mantras," it is stated that the guardians of the quarters and their respective weapons are to be included.
In the *Padārthādarśa*, it is stated that since such a meaning is possible from that [text],
one should perform some slight modification in the *homa* mantra; however, this refers to the forms (*mūrti*) which are subordinate (*aṅga-bhūta*) rather than primary (*pradhāna-bhūta*),
meaning, in short, the forms of the deities of the *āvaraṇa*.
And the deities of the enclosure, the deities of the limbs, the deities of the forms, and the world-protectors.
All those ending with the *dastra* deities are well-known; they are to be worshipped prior to the limbs (*aṅga*) and the coverings (*āvaraṇa*).

Even though some are not mentioned by name among other deities and are crooked (*jihyā*), they are included under the term "limb-forms" (*aṅgamūrti*) according to the previously stated meaning. Therefore, there is nothing inconsistent in their separate mention.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the preceptor, with a restrained mind, having placed the clarified butter (*ājya*) four times into the *sruc* ladle which is held steady by the *sruva* spoon, and while standing, should offer it into the fire with the mantra of Agni ending in "vauṣaṭ," having covered the *sruc* with the *sruva*. However, one who is inattentive should not place its root at the navel.
With his eyes fixed on the tip of the ring-finger, he should bring the base of those two [fingers] between the left breast;

otherwise, he would be unable to perform the ritual procedure as stated in other Tantras. Therefore, regarding the phrase "with effort" (*yateta*) and so forth, one should not be deluded into thinking that this [instruction] is specifically qualified for the desire for prosperity (*saṃpat-kāmanā*). What [is it then]? It applies generally.

The intended meaning is that this [rite] must necessarily be performed for the purpose of consecrating the fire, even though it does not bring about a specific result; or rather, its purpose is for the sake of the consecration of the fire; or else, "for the sake of the result" means in a proper place, namely, in the fire. And thus, regarding the flame of the fire...

In the previous view, the word "in fire" (*agnau*) would be meaningful only for the purpose of providing a substantive (*viśeṣya*) for the phrase "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*); however, since the desired object is already obtained by the word "therein" (*atraiva*), the word "in fire" would serve no further purpose. [This applies] to Vighneśvara by means of the mantra beginning with "daśa."

This also applies here; thus, having divided the twenty-eight-syllable mantra of Mahāgaṇapati into ten parts, one should offer ten oblations. Among those, the first oblation is with the first seed-syllable (*vīja*), the second with the first and second together, and the third with the second and third together.
The fourth [syllable] is formed from the third and fourth; the fifth from the fourth and fifth;
the sixth from the fifth and sixth; the seventh with five syllables as "gaṇapataye";
the eighth with five syllables as "varavarada"; and the ninth with five syllables as "sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya."

The tenth [verse] becomes [the same as] the first by means of the seven [syllables] beginning with *svāhā*; or else, by one [syllable] it becomes the first, by the first and second [syllables] the second, by the first, second, and third [syllables] the third, and by the first, second, third, and fourth [syllables] the fourth;
in this very manner, even further on, each preceding one [is repeated].
The inclusion of the color black (kala-varṇa) can be understood from the root text as being for the subsequent [rite];
therefore, it is established in another treatise that the oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) should be performed in their entirety.
As stated in the *Gaṇeśavimarśinī*: "First, with the Mahāgaṇeśa mantra..."

O Goddess of the Gods, having offered ten times with the six seed-syllables beginning with *Tārā* and others, distinguished by five-colored substances, one should then offer four times with the entire [mantra] in that same manner; thus, they are consecrated by the eighteen previously mentioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*).

Because of the provision of the qualification "in the consecrated [kuṇḍas]" within the phrase "of the consecrated kuṇḍa," and because of the general designation "the fire" (agni), the consecrations belong to the kuṇḍa alone;
these are to be performed by means of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) through its circular form, and that very consecrated fire is then to be carried forward into the other kuṇḍas.

This is indicated by the term *atevasamāhita*, meaning one by whom the fire has been properly established (*āhita*) and maintained (*saṃsthāpita*) according to the prescribed rite. Thus, because it was established once according to the ritual procedure, there is no further need for consecration (*saṃskāra*). However, as for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), [they must perform it] in their respective sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).

Having first worshipped with perfumes and other offerings the mantra-deity along with its limbs (aṅga) and surrounding deities (āvaraṇa)— which had been previously invoked by the preceptor (ācārya) or the disciple— they offered oblations of clarified butter twenty-five times while reciting the root mantra (mūlamantra). As for the preceptor, since he had already performed the homa in his own fire-pit, he did not perform it again.

By the passage beginning with "ha ṛtvij" and so forth, it was previously established in the preceding chapter that [the substance] was made into three portions along with clarified butter (*ājya*) for Varuṇa; among those, one portion was offered to the deity,
and it was stated that the second portion was to be offered as a sacrifice— this very act is the *homa*.
Now, it has been taught that the third portion [of the sacrificial food] should be eaten by the preceptor together with his disciple; this is what was stated.

Regarding this, the authors of the *Padārthādarśa* maintain—by supplementing the text with the word "by the officiating priests" (*ṛtvigbhiḥ*)—that the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the other fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) is also to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). However, we... [the text breaks off].
Because the word *tvij* is seen immediately preceding it, because of the weight of the [grammatical] completion, and because there is no evidence for another meaning,

it is the Preceptor (*ācārya*)— who is established by the context— who alone performs the consecration of the other fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). Therefore, the consecration of the pit is performed by one agent, while the consecration of the fire is performed by another.

We reply that this very inequality has been removed by our acceptance of the fact that the Ācārya alone is the sanctifier of both. By the word "morning" (*prātaḥ*), it is stated that the *homa* performed up to this point is the duty of the day of consecration (*adhivāsana*) itself; however, the morning duties [beginning with] clarified butter (*ghṛta*)...

In the phrase "they should offer the *vitasti-homa* and so forth," the previously mentioned preceptor (*ācārya*) and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) assume the status of agents; however, in the act of bringing [the materials] and so on, the preceptor alone is the agent.
Having gone outside the pavilion and caused [the participants] to drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), [he proceeds] to the south.

One should enter again through the same door; as it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having drunk the *pañcagavya* as prescribed, and having vomited according to the ritual rule, one should then cause [the disciple] to enter the sacrificial site by way of the southern door. That consciousness—the consciousness residing in the disciple—is [to be drawn] from the disciple's heart through the *vahni-nāḍī*.
