Having drawn forth consciousness by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one should unite it with one's own heart through the path of the central channel (*suṣumnā*).

As it has been said: "Taking that consciousness situated in the heart, which has the form of a shimmering star, one should establish it in one's own heart by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*. Furthermore, there is the triad [of mudrās]. Now, as for the lower...

If it is argued that it would be more appropriate to say "the sixfold" rather than "this triad" and "another triad," it is replied: such a statement was made with the intention of indicating their twofold nature by resorting to the opposing attributes of being verbal (*śābda*) and being objective (*ārtha*). Among them, three are verbal and three are objective.

According to the statement in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*, "samīritāḥ" (are impelled), and based on the group of five kalās mentioned in the second chapter beginning with "nivṛttiḥ sapratiṣṭhā syāt," this very group of five kalās is called the *kalādhā*. Furthermore, the *tattvādhā* is fivefold: the *śivatattvādhā*, the *viṣṇutattvādhā*, the *mitratattvādhā*, and [the others] beginning with *prakṛti*.

"Having transcended the reality of *tita*, one runs toward the reality of the three feet. Because of this initial instruction, [the author] demonstrates by means of the passage beginning with "Śiviti" those things denoted by the term "the state of Śiva" (*śivatattva*).
Among those, the five pure [principles] are devoid of the three impurities (*mala*): the individual (*āṇava*), the karmic (*kārmaṇa*), and the illusory (*māyīya*). Among these, the *āṇava*...
The self-reflection (*vimarśa*) of Sadāśiva in his own abode is the merit-bestowing *kārmaṇa* [body];

the cognition of inference (*pramiti-pratīti*) is the *māyīya* [body]. The notion of "I" regarding the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth is the perception of the Self as the *māyīya*. The seven principles beginning with *māyā* and ending with *puruṣa* are both pure and impure causes.

Because they are devoid of the three impurities (*mala*), these are pure; whereas because they possess the three impurities as their effects, those [others] are impure. Primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the state of equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇa*). The five organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) are the eyes and so forth;
the five organs of action (*karmendriya*) are speech and so forth; and the five... [objects].

The meaning is that the five subtle elements (tanmātras), such as smell and so forth, and the five gross elements (bhūtas), such as earth and so forth— these twenty-four being pure in themselves— when combined together with the [remaining] twelve, constitute the thirty-six Śaiva principles (tattvas) as declared in the Śiva scriptures. However, in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, there are thirty-two.
The *Tattva-nikathita* states that there is one heart-lotus, a triad of splendors, and three—the Fire, Moon, and Sun; Vāsudeva and the others—namely Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
Mitra, who is the Sun; and the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) taught in the *Tantra*.

In the Tantra, the principles (tattvas) are said to be derived from the tenfold power (śakti). Śiva is sevenfold as the support of the three-fold principles: Vidyā, Svayam, and Ātman. This is due to the distinction that the three are Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, which comprise all principles. Furthermore, some maintain that the "three steps" (tripada) refer to the supreme Praṇava.

Others say that "prior" and "subsequent" refer to the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), which consists of fourteen worlds. According to the *Padārthadarśaka*, these are fivefold, distinguished as ethereal (*ākāśa*), airy (*vāyavya*), fiery (*taijasa*), watery (*āpya*), and earthly (*pārthiva*). The letters from *a* to *kṣa* are themselves what is denoted by the term "path of letters" (*varṇādhvan*). [The author] says: "the sacrificial ladle" (*sruvam*).

The path of words (*pada-adhvā*) consists of those very *taṃ* and *tiṅ* suffixes. Now, he explains the method for purifying the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-śodhana*) with the verse beginning "pada" and so forth:

one should meditate on the path of kalās (*kalā-adhvā*) at the feet of the disciple, the path of worlds (*bhuvana-adhvā*) at his *liṅga*, and the path of worlds at his navel; this [purification] is differentiated by the various types of initiation (*dīkṣā*). At the end of the differentiation...
Having meditated upon the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) in his heart, the path of words (padādhvan) on his forehead, and the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) in his power (ṛddhi), the Guru,

while touching that disciple at the respective locations below with a tuft of hair (kūrca) possessing the characteristics as previously described, [recites] in his own sacrificial pit: "Oṃ, I purify the path of kalās of this person, svāhā."
Having offered eight oblations of sesame seeds with the *hetimantra*, one should contemplate the dissolution of the path of the kalās into the principles (*tattvas*).

In the same way, having purified the transgression and contemplated the dissolution of the path of mantras and the path of words, one should recite the mantra: "Oṃ, I purify the mantra-path of such-and-such; svāhā!"
Having offered eight oblations with the *treṇa* mantra, one should contemplate that "Oṃ, the path of mantras of such-and-such [the disciple] has merged into Śiva, O Supreme Śiva.

Then, from that Śiva, one should again contemplate [the elements] as having arisen through the sequence of the path of mantras up to the end of the path of kalās. By this, the purification of the lower [levels] and the purification of the body are accomplished, because...

Regarding the body composed of the [six] paths (*adhvan*) as described in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*: the *Śāntyatīta-kalā* is its head; *Śānti* is its face and hair; *Nivṛtti* constitutes its knees, shanks, and feet; the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is its hands;
the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) is its flesh and blood; the letters (*varṇa*) are its sinews; and the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) is its marrow.

Then, having understood that the body consists of the elements of earth, bone, and water, one should withdraw the consciousness from it oneself and re-establish it in the heart of the disciple. Having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the deity invoked into the fire into the ritual pitcher (*kumbha*),
one should again perform the *vyāhṛti-homa*, as well as the oblations for the tongues, limbs, and the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).

Having arranged the couch and sprinkled water around it, the preceptor, having dismissed the fire from his own self, should cast the *paristaraṇa* darbha grass and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire. This is indicated because, while burning is prescribed for occasional rites (*naimittika*), it is not applicable elsewhere; yet since it is prohibited in the case of daily rites (*nitya*), this specific instruction is made clear.
By the word "datra" (therein), even that which is performed with desire (*kāmya*) is intended, because it is also included by reason of its being characterized by desire.
The two rites [are not separate], because following the sequence of the sacrifice to the Self (*ātmayāga*),
the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth are to be performed as before, according to the previously described method of the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
Having performed the rites up to the conclusion of the sacrifice (*yāgānta-karma*) according to the rules— preceded by the dismissal of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā-visarjana*)— one should,

after first offering water to both [the disciple and] the chosen deity, recollect the place and time, record the name, clan (*gotra*), and so forth, and [state] the name of the disciple in the dative case.

Having written [the name] and having also stated the desire in the manner beginning with "for the sake of attaining the grace of such-and-such deity," one should, preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I bestow the mantra of such-and-such deity," [offer it] into the water from among the three types of resolves— bodily, vocal, and mental.

Since [the goal] is obtained in some way through the contemplation of that which exists as dependent, he describes the duty of the disciple with the words beginning "of the Guru" (*guror ityādinā*). Regarding the initiation consisting of phonemes (*varṇamayī-dīkṣā*):

having withdrawn the phonemes located in their respective places within the body of the disciple into their own respective causes, and having also withdrawn the consciousness (*caitanya*), [he proceeds].
Furthermore, having produced everything from its own respective causes and established the fitness [of the disciple],

[the author], intending that the instruction of the mantra alone is what remains for the disciple, begins to describe the initiation consisting of the phonemes (*varṇamayī-dīkṣā*), which follows in sequence, starting with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth, up to "in those respective locations" (*tattat-sthāne*) and so forth.
The disciple should sequentially join the syllable *laṃ* with the face, *haṃ* with the heart, *kṣaṃ* with the ears, *ṣe* with the feet, and *ṣaṃ* with the hands;

likewise, he should join the phoneme (*varṇa*), the location (*sthāna*), and the consciousness (*caitanya*) within the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thereafter, [he should contemplate] all phonemes as having arisen from the Supreme Self.

Having meditated upon the locus (*sthāna*), the state of being a deity (*devatābhāva*) is attained; thus, he becomes one who has achieved realization through the Command (*ājñāsiddha*). Following that, there is the instruction on the mantra (*maṃtropadeśa*). Here too, the entire collection of ritual acts (*kriyākalāpa*) ending with the bath (*snāna*) must be followed.
Some, however, say that this [instruction] is again [to be performed] as before; such is the extent [of it].

The meaning of "the gods must be made [present] here" is intended for the smooth flow of the text; furthermore, no more has been shown here than what was already indicated by the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. Regarding the initiation known as *Kalāvatī*, it begins from the sole of the disciple's foot up to the knee; that is the *Nivṛtti-kalā*, and it is the station of Brahmā.

One should place the *nivṛtti-kalā* within Brahmā; that [Brahmā] within the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* situated from the knees to the navel; that [pratiṣṭhā-kalā] within Viṣṇu; and Viṣṇu within Rudra. One should place [Rudra] within the *vidyā-kalā*, which occupies the space from the navel to the throat; and that [vidyā-kalā] within Rudra. One should place Rudra [within Īśvara].
One should dissolve Īśvara into Īśvarī, who resides between the eyebrows and extends to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), abiding in the state of Sadāśiva;
then one should dissolve her into Śāntyatītā.
From Sadāśiva comes Śāntyatītā, from that Īśvara, from that Śānti, from that Rudra, from that Vidyā, and from that Viṣṇu.

Then, having produced [the stages] in sequence as *Pratiṣṭhā*, then *Brahman*, and then *Nivṛtti*, the instruction of the mantra occurs; thus he says with the words beginning "Then, Kalāvatī... and so forth. He promises to describe the initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of piercing (*vedha*) with the words beginning "That" (*tat*), referring to that which is within the body of the disciple.

The connection is as follows: one should meditate upon the Śakti within the triangle situated there in the four-petalled lotus located at the *mūlādhāra*. Although it was previously stated that she possesses various forms even in the *mūla*, nevertheless, because she is connected to the three entities of the primary creation in the form of the three Vedas, [she is described thus].
The *thokti* consists of the six cakras.
The six centers known as Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā consist of the letters *ha* and *kṣa*,

the bindu, and the essence of Śiva. Within the bindu— which is synonymous with Śiva— and within the *kalā* which is the seed-syllable synonymous with Śakti, there occurs the union of that *kalā* and the power of Śiva.

Since it has been stated in the root [text] that the *bindu* is of the nature of Śiva, the *bīja* is of the nature of Śakti, and *nāda* is their mutual union (*samavāya*), and so forth; therefore, even *nāda* is of the nature of the cause,
being the state of equilibrium (*samatāvasthā*) of Supreme Śiva when He is intent on emission (*sṛṣṭyunmukha*), which is also known by the synonym "the end" (*anta*).

One should join that state [of the breath] which has gone there into the state called *unmanī*, which is free from *māyā*. Then, having joined that state as well into the face of the Moon (*caṇdramukha*),
and subsequently into the cave-mouth (*guhavaktra*), one should unite the power *Kuṇḍalinī* with the Self within the state of the Supreme Śiva, O Sovereign Goddess.

The meaning is that one should perform the instruction of the mantra by generating those [syllables] in this manner, joining them according to the sequence of repetition (*punarukta*). Furthermore, this entire fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed after ascertaining the location of the fire upon the ground, and not otherwise. The method for ascertaining that is found in the *Vrahmayāmala* and the *Dhṛti*.

Having combined the lunar day (tithi), the weekday (vāra), the seven continents (saptadvīpa), and the four ages (caturyuga), one should divide by three, O son; by the remainder, [the result is determined]: with one, he dwells in heaven; with two, in the netherworld (pātāla); and with zero, the mortal world (martyaloka) shall be so—thus dwells Pāvaka. This is the portent regarding the heavenly realm.

If [the remainder] is in Pātāla (the underworld), there is loss of wealth; if it is in Vahni (fire/the netherworld), there is the attainment of desired results through oblations and the like in the mortal world. Having combined the number of the two planets with the number of the *prakṛti* (which consists of twenty-nine units starting from *dhṛti*), one divides the resulting total by three; the result is determined by the remainder.

In the *Muhūrtacintāmaṇi*, it is stated that for the sake of happiness, one should perform a fire-sacrifice (*homa*) on the first day of the bright fortnight starting from the new moon, provided the lunar date plus the weekday, when divided by ten, leaves a remainder of three, eight, or eleven; however, if the remainder is two, there is destruction of the lord of life, both in heaven and on earth. This is taught as the desired [time] beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight.

The meaning of that [verse] regarding the "mouth of the planet" (grahamukha) is as follows: having counted up to the lunar day (tithi), adding one more to that number, and further combining it with the number of the weekday starting from Sunday (ravi), when this resulting total is divided by four, one should declare the result based on the remainder.

One should count from the day the oblation was offered up to the current day (including both) according to the *Urudrayāmala*; when that total is divided by three, the resulting quotient indicates the number of planets [elapsed].
Among them, the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Saturn, the Moon, and Mars are to be known as the respective lords of those days.
The sequence is Jupiter, Rāhu, and Ketu. However, if there is a remainder, one should add the obtained number by one.
This is the meaning: having counted up to the end of the asterism (nakṣatra) of that day, whatever the resulting number may be, divide it by three; in the first [division], [the result is] three.

In whichever lunar mansion (nakṣatra) the first planet is located, by the method of adding three for the second [planet] and so on up to nine for the ninth, the ninth [mansion] is obtained. However, if [the planet] is in the fourth, fifth, and so forth, then that is the lunar mansion of the day; even if the lunar mansion of the day has a remainder, the quotient is obtained.

One should add the number represented by the asterism (such as *ṛkṣa* and so forth) together with the number of the remaining [digits] starting from five, as a single unit; one should know that the number thus obtained and uttered refers to only one planet,
and not to another planet based on the remaining digits.
The fruit of this has been stated in that very place: "Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon are declared auspicious for gentle rites;

however, they are wicked for cruel rites. Indeed, the offering of wicked ones is not desired even in the offering of bricks to the non-wicked. In reality, however, [this applies] to the fire-dwelling auspicious planets."

There is no deliberation regarding the number of oblations (*āhuti*) because this *homa* lacks primacy as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Since the primary *homa* requires a specific time, the scriptural injunctions concerning that [primary] time apply; however, in the case of a subordinate element, the requirement for time is satisfied by the very time of the primary rite.

It appears that the fact that the learned (śiṣṭas) do not require the purity of the time for the prescribed homa in rites such as initiation (upanayana), marriage, and expiatory offerings (prāyaścitta) is consistent with the author of the root-text (mūlakṛt) having disregarded it; this suggests that [the rule] pertains to those who possess a specific desire for that [result].

He undertakes to state the measure of the substances for the oblations to be performed with the words beginning with "Now" (*atha*); the sense is that by defining the manner of the oblation, the definition of the quantity of the remembered oblation-substances is not to be neglected. And [the measure is] a *karṣa*.
A fourth part [of a pala] is a *karṣa*. Two *karṣas* are a *śukti*. A *karṣa* is the measure of an *akṣa*, a *prasṛti*, and two *palas*.
[These measures] are equivalent to a handful, equivalent to a fruit, half a mouthful, or eighty *rītīkās*.

A *rvāruka* (bottle-gourd) fruit, a *karkaṭī* (cucumber) fruit, a *culuka* (a handful), a *pāṇitala* (the palm of the hand)—meaning a *karṣa*—is the measure for *pura* (resin) and *guggulu*. A *vadara* (jujube) fruit, which is eighty *guñjās*, is the measure for *hiṅgu* (asafoetida). For *candana* (sandalwood), *aguru* (aloe-wood), *karpūra* (camphor), and so forth, the measure is one *viṃcā-phala* (a small fruit). *Kuṃ*... [text truncated]

The *Mantradarpaṇa* states that the measures for musk, deer-musk, sandalwood, and camphor are equal to a *caṇaka* (a chickpea). However, this is merely a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*). Now, while the measurement for substances to be offered with the hand has been stated, it remains incomplete; but regarding the *sruva* ladle and substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to be offered [with it], [the measure is as follows]:
If it is argued that there is no requirement for a specific measure because the *sruva* ladle is traditionally prescribed as having a hole that holds only one *karṣa*, [we reply:
True; however, since honey, curd, and so forth are taken by the ladle, while milk and similar liquids are light, it is stated that [the ladle] has a capacity of one *śukti*.
Therefore, it is possible for honey and other substances to remain in the *sruva* even when they exceed one *karṣa*.

In accordance with the requirement for ghee and other such substances, one performs the offering by drawing up [the liquid] from them; however, for milk and the like, the oblation may be performed using leaf-cups and similar vessels. Alternatively, it is not a fault that the oblation is indicated even by means of a handful (culuka) in the case of obligatory rites. Now, [one might object]:...

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the statement "one should offer sixteen barley grains," as well as with the statements "sesame seeds are said to be half a handful" and "mustard seeds are considered to be one karṣa," [the answer is] no; for these are intended as alternative options (*anukalpa*) for small quantities. In reality, however, regarding the substance for the *homa*...
The determination of the size of the cavities at the mouths of the *sruva* and other ladles depends solely on that which is explicitly stated as the measure;

it is not appropriate to calculate a deficiency or excess in the quantity of the substance by considering the cavities and so forth, which are merely subordinate parts. Furthermore, the primary term "taking a karṣa" was stated specifically with reference to clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

It should be understood that even in the context of the materials for the *homa*, because they are required as things to be taken up (*upādeya*) and are necessarily required in all *homas*, it was stated in accordance with that very requirement. Furthermore, the definition of the *karṣa* and so forth is stated in another *tantra*: "Ten *guñjās* make one *māṣa*; four *māṣas* make one *śāṇa*; two [śāṇas]..."

A *ṇaudhaṭaka* is equal to two *kolīs*, and a *kolī* is equal to two *avadaras*. Two *daṃkṣaṇas* make one *pāṇitala-karṣa*; a *suvarṇa* is a *kavalagraha*. A *pikṣu* is equal to two *viḍālapadakas*, and a *tiṃduka* is equal to two *ukṣas*. Two *śuktis* make one *aṣṭamikā*, and two of those make one *pala*. Four *aṣṭamikās* make one *vilva*, which is the measure of a handful (*muṣṭi*).
Two *kuñca* and two *pala* make one *prasṛti*. Thus, "within the mouth" refers to the characteristics of the mouth and so forth as described elsewhere:
"Fire with smoke should be known as the head, and smokeless fire as the eyes;
the flame becomes the ear when thin, and the nose when it is stuck to wood; where the fire blazes like a flame..."
That face should be understood there as resembling pure crystal, measuring one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in size;
by the word "Vipaścit," this is prohibited only in the case of desiring another [person],
whereas in the case of desiring success against one's own adversary through sorcery and the like, the oblation into those respective limbs is permitted.
Since it has been stated that each respective limb [of the fire] performs its specific function, this is what is implied.
For the sake of knowing future auspicious and inauspicious events, the color, smell, and other qualities of the fire must be examined.
In response to the inquiry as to which specific color and so forth indicate what particular result, he says "svarṇa" (gold), etc. Now, however—

Regarding such ill-omened birds, he states with the words beginning "twenty-five" that even the initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself must not be abandoned. This is because, according to the principle that "the occasional rite (*naimittika*) repeats for every occasion (*nimitta*)," there is a repetition of twenty-five oblations (*āhuti*) for each individual ill omen. Thus, [it is said] "various," etc.
It is your opinion that [the self] must indeed be abandoned when faults arise.

This [work] was born from him whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī, whose father was named Premanidhi, whose ancestral land was Pañchakula, whose birthplace was Kūrmmācala, who made the feet of Acyuta his refuge,
and whose place of residence was Vārāṇasī; it consists of ten thousand verses.
In the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*, [the section on] the letter *ṭa*.

Now, having stated that the mantras for initiation (dīkṣā) must be performed according to this specific procedure (itikartavyatā), there may arise the doubt: "Since the mantras themselves are unknown, this laborious effort to define their ancillaries is useless. To dispel this doubt, [the author] now [presents] the mantras for the deities of the five abodes (pañcāyatana).
All of these should indeed be recounted as things to be adopted, according to one's own inclination and according to what is favorable to oneself.

In that regard, because it must necessarily be employed in the worship of all mantras (*sakalamantra*), and because it is primary as being composed of the various phonemes that constitute all mantras,
[the author] states that the triad of nectars— the *Praṇava*, the Goddess *Mātṛkā*, and *Hṛllekhā*— is the illuminator (*dīpana*) of all mantras. Thus says Bha[skararāya].

Based on the words of Gauḍapāda, Śiva, and other Tantric authorities, and because it serves as an illuminator for other mantras, he promises to first describe the Mātṛkā-mantra itself, which is necessarily required, beginning with the words "Now" (atha) and so forth;
[he says] "in which," meaning in which [Mātṛkā], once perceived... [the rest of the sentence follows].

It should not be argued that it is improper to state [the absence of the reason] by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since it is more appropriate to state such things as "this becomes awakened" by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*); for this has already been effectively stated by way of positive concomitance through the very words "awakening the universe" (*viśvabodha*). Thus, [there is] both positive and negative concomitance...
It is implied that when there is a distinction in awakening through these two [methods], this very meditation (*upāsanā*) is the cause;

therefore, those who desire knowledge should by all means strive in this regard. The fifty-one letters, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣa*, [are located] on the body, the forehead-joint, the face, and the circle...
The meaning is: "Sarasvatī who possesses body parts such as eyes and so forth. By this, it is also suggested that the phonemes (*varṇas*) themselves constitute the nature of the mantra.
Furthermore, one might ask: why has no extraction of a mantra (*mantroddhāra*) been performed here, as is done in other *mantra-kalpas*? This [is the point of] inquiry.

It should be understood that [the sequence] is "kā-vyā-ha-tī-kṛ-te. The seven, eight, nine, and ten [letters] are the four neuter vowels; one short vowel occurs first, and one long vowel follows it subsequently.
Between these two, there is one [consonant group] in order: the *ka*-group (*kādivarga*). At the end of the long [vowel], [there is the word] "hṛdayāya" (to the heart).

The limb-mantras beginning with *namaḥ* should be extracted in this manner; thus he says, starting with *aklība* and so forth. In the phrase "by the six groups" (*ṣaḍvargakaiḥ*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The six limbs are the six limb-mantras joined with their respective *jāti*-suffixes, such as *hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *śirase svāhā*, and so on.

The mantras beginning with "raḥ svāhā" and so forth, joined in sequence at the end, are to be applied in the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the six limbs— starting with the thumb and so forth, as well as the heart and so forth. Thus,
one should employ them with mantras such as the thirteen-syllable one beginning with "aṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ."

The ultimate meaning is that the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is to be performed; however, the interpretation that "six limbs" refers to the six *nyāsas* themselves is untenable, because although the application of generic categories (*jāti*) is possible within mantras, it is impossible in the sense of a ritual placement (*nyāsa*). One should [visualize] the *mudrā*, namely the *jñānamudrā*, and the book of knowledge (*vidyāpustaka*) held by that [deity].

From the forehead (*lalāṭa*) to the mouth (*āsya*), the term "mouth" (*āsya-pada*) refers to the vowels; alternatively, it is used figuratively for the tongue due to its connection with being located within the mouth. Immediately following this, the author of the root text will provide the visarga by the phrase "the letter *ra* [is] on the tongue. As for the remaining [consonants], there is the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *hal*s (consonants) in the heart.

From the phrase "tpūrvam" (preceded by *t*), it is understood that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed by sequentially touching each pair— hands, feet, belly, and face— and then from the heart up to the right hand, and from the heart up to the left hand; here, the "heart" refers to that which is on the right shoulder and chest.

The left shoulder belongs to *ka*, the right hand to *ku*, the left hand to *lla*, the right foot to *śa*, the left foot to *ṣa*, the belly to *ha*, the face to *la*, and the throat to *kṣa*—thus it should be meditated upon. Regarding the number for the *puraścaraṇa* recitation, he says: "One should recite that [mantra] according to that number. *La*.

The meaning is that it should be performed as many times as there are syllables (*mātṛkā*). Thus, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* letters upon one's own body once, the recitation (*japa*) of the *mātṛkā* should be performed; then again the placement, and again the recitation. Having thus meditated upon that very form consisting of the fifty letters within one's own body, one should place them in sequence upon the previously mentioned locations.

Because of the statement, "One should constantly recite the letters [of the alphabet] fifty times until the number reaches one hundred thousand," the meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is that of being characterized; this [instrumental] connects with the referent of the word *lipi* (letters). This is intended merely as a formal enumeration of the nature [of the practice], and not as something applicable to the daily recitation (*puraścaraṇa-japa*).

This [offering] is intended to establish the number [of oblations], as otherwise it would result in the requirement of many years. Regarding the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*)—defined by the statement "milk, honey, and ghee are remembered as the three sweets"—some desire sugar in place of milk; others say jaggery (*guḍa*) should be used in that place, as praised by the gods (*gīrvāṇendra*). [This is for] the *homa*.

In order to specify a particular substance, even when mentioning that alone, one must not forget other auxiliary elements obtained from general injunctions. Regarding the phrase "one should worship" (*yajet*), since there is an expectancy for a locus,
he describes the worship-yantra with the words beginning with "space" (*vyoma*) as an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp and filaments, and outside of that...
Having protected the city of the Ṛbhus, with the intention that what is obtained through the general procedure and the general scripture therein should be understood from the common treatises,
only the specific details have been shown: the ether, the fire, Indra,
the letter *au*, the nature of the vowel, and the sound to be placed upon the tongue.

This entire creation, having merged together into the state of a single seed-syllable, resides within the pericarp; the vowels are arranged two by two among the filaments, while the eight groups of consonants beginning with the *ka*-group are on the petals. In the four directions, the syllables *laṃ*, *ga*, *li*, and *ṭa* revolve around the letter *va*. This is the *Lāṅgalī-ṭakā*.

Having turned back, one should draw [the diagram] in the four corners of the square up to the pericarp (*karṇikā*), up to the filaments (*kesara*), up to the three groups (*trivarga*), and up to the circle (*vṛtta*);
these four are the specific attributes of the lotus. Here, on this diagram produced in this manner, one should worship Sarasvatī, who consists of the phonemes (*varṇātmikā*). The phonemes...
One should offer the seat (*āsana*) or pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the mantra *bjaneti mātṛkāyogapīṭhāyanam iti*;

the word "preceded by worship" (*pūjanapūrvakam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. In that context, it is intended that worship is the instrument (*karaṇatva*) of that [offering]; some hold that the phrase *varṇābjapada* refers to the term *mātṛkāyogapīṭha*.

The intention of some is as follows: having first placed the seed-syllable *stauḥ*—which consists of the aforementioned syllables for the worship of the letters (*varṇa-pūjā*)—within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus that constitutes the previously mentioned yantra of the letters, and having preceded [the rite] with that same seed-syllable, one should employ the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*), namely: "O Lotus-throne of all powers" (*sarva-śakti-kamalāsana*).
Regarding the root text beginning with "paratvaṃ varṇābja," they state that immediately following is the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇa*).

In response to the inquiry as to what the powers (*śakti*) of those eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*) are, he will later say "Vyāpinī" and so forth. For the term "vajra-pada" generally refers to the seat (*pīṭha*) or the locus of the mantra (*yantra-pada*) of all the deities.

Outside the *bhūpura* (enclosure) of the yantra, in the four directions, one should draw specific marks consisting of six and three forms respectively, which are mutually connected and facing one another; this refers to the first term [of the mantra]. Furthermore, this should include the tridents (*triśūla*) situated at the corners of that yantra, for their worship is certainly intended as well.
Since it is not logical to ask "why does he not perform the *kiṃhivacana*?", [the author] says "with the weapons of the world-protectors" (*lokapālāyudhaiḥ*).

If only this much were stated, there would be the undesirable consequence of including the bow of Viṣṇu and others; therefore, the qualifying phrase "with the thunderbolt and so forth" (*vajrādyaiḥ*) is added.
For in the ritual placement of creation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*), there is meditation according to the prescribed rule upon the fifty [letters].

Since it has already been stated by the verse beginning with "llipibhiḥ" (by means of the scripts) and so forth, the resonance (*dhvani*) is taught there separately; the "worship" (*abhyarcana*) refers to the stability of the *mātṛkā*, and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the worship of the seven enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) beginning with the limbs (*aṅgas*) is included. If, on the other hand, by the very term "worship of the words" (*padārcana*), the worship of both is intended, even then it is not [contradictory].

Because the *vidveṣa* [mantra] and others are to be employed for the worship of the yantra, some here maintain that there is the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* from the letter *a* to *ṭa*, the *sthiti-nyāsa* from *u* to *kṣa*,
and that the twenty-eight letters ending in *ṭa* possess the visarga and the bindu.
They say that even the "both" (ubhaya) status of the letters beginning with *ḍa* applies only to the twenty-three consonants;
when both [the sṛṣṭi and saṃhāra sequences] are combined, this constitutes the complete Mātṛkā-nyāsa.

For this very reason, they maintain that the natural sense of the root text—namely, the phrase "beginning with the letter ḍa"—is justified, because the letters ending in *ṭa* are indeed placed according to the path of creation (*sṛṣṭi-vartman*) alone.
In that regard, one should place each syllable encased by the seed-syllable, or the seed-syllable itself enclosed by the syllables, in the locations of the Mātṛkā;

for the statement "the tenfold emanation is proclaimed" contradicts the Saṃhitā, since the natural implication of that text is that the placement of all syllables follows the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). This is because the word *varṇa* [in the verse] refers to the individual phonemes.

If [the word] were intended to denote that alone, there would be the consequence of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), because otherwise it would be impossible to prevent the application of other colors; for indeed, from the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), the understanding of pots consisting solely of five substances,
or pots consisting solely of blue color and so forth, is not possible without *lakṣaṇā*.

However, the fact that the *saṃhāra* [cycle] begins with *kṣa* and the *sthiti* [cycle] begins with *ḍa*—as established by specific scriptural statements—cannot be refuted by anyone; this is intended merely to convey that understanding. Therefore, it does not establish that the previously mentioned *sṛṣṭi*-nyāsa ends in *ṭa*.

This is the meditation on the Lord of the Universe, whose nature is consciousness, who has entered within; preceded by the external visualization of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) through the manifold variety of the grasped and the grasper, it is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Having meditated upon the state of total interpenetration of the entire universe within the Supreme Self, this ritual placement is the "placement of stability" (*sthitinyāsa*), which is a purification (*saṃskāra*).
Having meditated upon one's own connection with the Supreme Self through the state of being nothing but *Ramā* (the Goddess), the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution-assignment) is now described.

Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that [this] is merely the assignment of the vowels from *ā* to *ḷ*, etc., and the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*, etc.? Furthermore, because it is not pervasive in the case of mantra-assignments and the like, and because it consists only of the assignment of letters starting from *pa* and so forth for the deity..."
The assumption of a general body is indeed established [by the mere fact of its existence]; thus, the arrangement of forms such as *it* and *ivarṇa* would be redundant.
Nevertheless, for the sake of establishing the specific parts, that [general body] is accepted first.
There is no authoritative rule that the assumption of a general limb must come first, followed by the assumption of specific limbs.

Nor is there a fixed rule that the withdrawal of the specific must precede the withdrawal of the general; nor should it be argued that the withdrawal of the specific is redundant because [the specific] is already withdrawn by the withdrawal of the general,
for the sequence of the withdrawal of the specific is also established by the specific scriptural statement.
Since these [deities] must be kept in mind, these *nyāsas* are preceded by the internal *mātṛkā-nyāsa*;
for it is stated in the injunction: "Having performed the internal *nyāsa* in this manner, one should resort to the external *nyāsa*.
The method for that is found correctly in the *Kalāpatrāmbuja* chapter of the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*.
One should place the vowels at the throat; the letters beginning with *ka* on the twelve petals of the heart;
the ten letters on the ten-petalled lotus of the navel; the six letters on the six-petalled lotus at the base of the *liṅga*;
then one should place the four letters on the four-petalled wheel of the foundation (*ādhāra-cakra*); and finally, the two letters on the two-petalled lotus between the eyebrows.
"One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the alphabet ending with *rukṣā*," as shown in the *Tantrasāra*. In another tantra, it is stated:

"Uttering each letter individually from the *mūlādhāra* to the head, ending with *namaḥ*, this is proclaimed as the internal (*āntara*) placement. Regarding these two alternatives, [the placement of] Śakti...

The author of the *Tantrasāra*, maintaining the perspective that Viṣṇu is the supreme reality, describes the final arrangement; he teaches the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *kalāmātṛkā* with the words beginning "Tāra" and so forth. From the five components of the *praṇava*—consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*—the creation [proceeds].
Although *nāda* is the final [element], it was previously stated in the root text that the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*, which arise from it, occurs first;
however, here, because of the observation that they arise from the *tāra*, [the order] follows the sequence [of the vowels]. Thus, [the *kalās*] are... the *akāra*.

In response to the doubt—"Since it appears that the installation (*nyāsa*) of the primordial energies (*kalās*), such as *Sṛṣṭi* and the rest, should come first, how can this statement be free from the contradiction of preceding and following?"—he says:
"Beginning with the phonemes (*vārṇādyāḥ*)," which means beginning with the letter *a* (*akārādyāḥ*) because of its being the first to present itself; thus it is.

The sense is that [the letters] such as *vidhvasta*, *nivṛtti*, and so forth, are precisely those that should be placed [there]. Thus, the sequence of the *kalās* arises from the sequence of the phonemes (*varṇa*) alone, and not from the sequence of the parts of the *praṇava*; this is the intended meaning. By using the term "conjoined" (*saṃyuktāḥ*) instead of "properly joined" (*yuktāḥ*), it is implied that first the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) [is placed].
Yoga is intended [here]; by the very mention of the suffix *-namaḥ*, the state of ending in the dative case is implied.

By that, the usage *oṃ aṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ* and so forth is indicated. "Guṇa" means the noose; "śubhra" (white) is an adjective qualifying the skull (*kapāla*). "Dara" means a conch shell. There are ten hands and five faces.
This Sarasvatī, who has three eyes and a face with protruding fangs, is the Mother of the Kalās (Kalāmātṛkā).

He now demonstrates the Nyāsa of the Śrīkaṇṭhādi Mātṛkā, beginning with the phrase "preceded by the third" (*tārtīyapūrvām*). This refers to the letter *ra*, which is conjoined with the third vowel—the visarga (*visarga*)—and the fourteenth vowel (*au*), and is mutually embraced by them.

The *hi*, *tau*, *ru*, *kā*, *ra*, and *sa* [syllables] are the third seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhairavī in the twelfth chapter, because it is to be spoken in that manner. Regarding the phrase "joined with Rudras," the Rudras are Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, joined with the Śaktis such as Pūrṇodarī and so forth; as will be explained later, here too [it is joined] by means of the seed-syllable.
Since there would also be an inclusion of the letter *k* (as in *ktau*), the specific mention of *hasa* is made here; this refers to the root letter.
Regarding the arrangement of the letters beginning with *ya*, he states the distinction: "because of being like the elements" (*dhātuvat*).
The seven [constituents] are: bone, skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and semen. These are the seven primary elements (*dhātu*).

The meaning is that, having thus combined "ṇaḥ śaktiḥ," "ātman nṛsiṃhasya," and "asau ātma krodham," the application of the ten [elements] beginning with the skin (tvak) and so forth should be performed in the Nyāsa known as Yādinyāsa. Now, if this is so, at the end of the accomplishment of the entire mantra, the word "ātmani" [is used].

If it is argued that [the method] should be understood from the *Prayogoneta-tantra*, what follows from this? For the practice must be followed exactly as it appears in other tantras. However, the author of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* is insistent that the practice of the letter-nyāsa of "kṣa" should be taken exactly as it is heard in the text: "the Self."
It causes that very life-force and even anger to rest within the Self; such [an interpretation] would contradict the aforementioned Tantras.

If it is argued: "But how can there be a reference [to Rudra] when the word 'Rudra' does not appear previously?"—if one says, "The phrase 'united with Rudra' (rudrasaṃyutām) does indeed exist previously," [we reply: no, for that [compound] is a third-case *tatpuruṣa*.
If it is argued that [the property] is not a delimitor of the word-meaning because it has entered into a compound, do not say so;

for we observe such usage as *avyāpyavṛtti-pakṣadharmma-tattvāvahita* and so forth. Furthermore, in the view that [the pronoun] refers to what is present in the mind (*buddhistha-parāmarśaka*), there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the mutual [exclusion].
The remainder [of the phrase] is that [the letters] *ha* and *sa* are joined together with the *bindu*.
Therefore, the resulting application is as follows: *hsāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hsīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth.
This demonstrates the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* beginning with Keśava and others, starting with *smarādyām*.

In this context, having brought forth such applications as "Obeisance to Keśava joined with Kīrti" (*dinā atra kīrtiyuktakeśavāya namaḥ*), "Obeisance to Kīrti joined with Keśava" (*yuktakeśavāya namaḥ*),
"Obeisance to Keśava, obeisance to Kīrti" (*keśavāya namaḥ kīttyai namaḥ*), "Obeisance to both Kīrti and Keśava" (*kīrtikeśavābhyāṃ namaḥ*),
and "Obeisance to both Keśava and Kīrti" (*keśavakīrtibhyāṃ namaḥ*), one should employ the word *yukta* (joined).
Due to the absence of a valid means of proof (*pramāṇābhāva*), because of the contingency of a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) when combined with words such as *saha* and so forth,
and because of the resulting intervention (*vyavadhāna*) of Keśava and others by the mention of the mother, the grandmother, and the co-wife,

[the rule] would apply the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*) in both instances based on the first, second, and fourth usages. Thus, there is no valid means of proof to establish [the desired result] in both cases.

Having refuted the third application by means of the occurrence of a contradiction with the unity of the deities understood from the verses on the *nābha* meditation, the authors of the *Padārthādarśa* accept the fifth application;
this same method applies even to the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā-nyāsa in the *Agastisaṃhitā*.

In accordance with the Gautama Saṃhitā, we accept that the third alternative alone is correct, being devoid of the word *namaḥ* at the beginning of the compound; however, for the sake of metrical requirements (*chandaḥ*), when the expression *keśavakīrtibhyāṃ namaḥ* must be employed,
it should be stated as *keśavāya tataḥ kīrttyai kāntyai ca*.

To claim that [the sequence] beginning with "rāyaṇāya cetyādi" was taught [by the author] is based on sheer audacity; furthermore, if one resorts to [altering] the meter for the sake of conformity, then from "viṣṇave dhṛtyai" onwards it would follow:
"namo śūrāya ramāyai puruṣottamāya vasudhāyai baline parājitāyai vṛṣā... [and so on].

In various places, such as the passage beginning with "yatsandhyāya enam," it is explained that he does not rely upon that [view]. In our own system, however, disregard for that [view] is appropriate because it conforms to the desired applications. Furthermore:
"The syllable *oṃ*, the seed-syllable *māra*, and likewise the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*), as well as the one God..."

The sequence is as follows: first the Śakti (AIM), then the Kāmabīja (KLĪM) according to the same order, then a letter of the Mātṛkā, or Keśava, or Kīrti, ending with "Namaḥ"; this should be installed again.
Thus, even from the Gautama-saṃhitā and other sources, it is determined that the forms must end in the singular number.

How could it not refute the application [of the rule] stated by you? This very statement is the authority for the singular application of the word *namaḥ*; this same authority is also what brings about the dative case in both instances. And if, even when the authority establishing the dative case is firm, there is a single deityhood (*ekadaivatya*), then...

Even then, there is no fault on our part; however, in the third alternative, the word "namaḥ" twice is not accepted, because we observe [the rule] that there is only one "namaḥ. Thus, the practical application results in such forms as "oṃ klīṃ keśavāya kīrtyai namaḥ," and so forth, even where Keśava and the others appear.
One should place [the letters] beginning with *yu* and *ta* along with *kīrti* and so forth; even in that case, this same method applies.

In practice, for the sake of obtaining both [results], there is no authority for their insertion by means of mentioning words such as *yuta*. By this very direction, the mantras for the placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha and others should also be understood.

These [details] are to be performed; for, in the absence of a specific statement, there is the maxim that "what has been determined in one place regarding a common [rule] should be applied elsewhere as well. This has been further clarified by us in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*. Now, he states the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* beginning with the [vowels] starting with *yā*, preceded by *Śakti*.

One should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with mantras such as *hrāṃ hrīṃ hraum*, which are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Māyā and Śakti; thus he says "long [vowels]," and so forth. Regarding the *jayavaṭī* (victory-garland) rosary, he describes the assignment of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*) preceded by the *śrī-bīja* with the words beginning "one should assign," using the aforementioned *śrī-bīja*.

He describes the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* beginning with the seed-syllable of Smara (Klīṃ) with the words "smarādyām" and so forth. He describes the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* beginning with the three seed-syllables with the words "śakti" and so forth. As previously stated, the *saṃmohana* [mantra] consists of the three—*śakti*, *śrī*, and *kāma*.
Thus: *hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *śrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *klīṃ* [śikhāyai vaṣaṭ].

The placement (nyāsa) upon the six limbs is to be performed with the six-limbed mantras as follows: "To the crest, vaṣaṭ! Hrīṃ kaca vāya huṃ śrīṃ! To the three eyes, vauṣaṭ! Klīṃ! To the weapon, phaṭ!
Thus it is said that [the nyāsa] must be performed.
He describes the *Prapañcayāga* preceded by the *Nyāsa* of the *Mātṛkā* of the *Prapañca* with the words beginning "Prapañca...":

in the *Praṇava* (Oṃ) is the power (*śakti*) of the Vedas and so forth; the seed-syllable of *māyā* is "A"; the two-syllabled mantra "A-jayā-aham" is the mantra of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); and the mantra "So'ham" is the *Tāra* (the syllable Om) placed at the beginning of each letter.

Those mantras such as *oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ svāhā* and others, which consist of nine syllables, have been shown to be placed on the locations beginning with the forehead (*lalāṭa*). When it was stated "by the five mantras," the inclusion of *praṇava* (oṃ) and the rest would follow; therefore, [the author specifies] "by those beginning with *svāhā*," and so forth.

Since the mere mention of *nam* would include the *mātṛkā* beginning with *a*, in order to exclude that, it says "pañca" (five). However, this does not refer to the fifth mantra within the eight-syllable mantra, because it is taught as being merely *nam*. Thus it has been said: "Taking each one of the *anūn* in reverse order."

Having performed the *pañcāṅga-nyāsa* with the *yate* mantra, it follows that the *ṣaṣṭāṅga-nyāsa* should be performed using the four syllables "Hari Hara" preceded by the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) "Astrāya Phaṭ. In this context, the placement of the *ṣaṣṭāṅga-mantra* in other mantras involves first clapping the palms.
"What is to be done here? There is nothing; rather, [one should perform] the binding of the ten directions with snaps of the fingers," he says.

Regarding "the weapon" (*astra*): after performing the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five-limbed mantras on the little finger, the eyes, and so forth, one should in reality further effect the weapon-mantra (*astra*) with the syllables of Hari and Hara. Further...

Furthermore, one should form the *bandha* with the ten syllables of Hari and Hara; this is precisely the meaning [intended] here. This is indeed the path followed by the authors of the *Padārthadarśa* as well. Others, however, hold that the letter *ha* and the letter *ra*, along with the final vowel (*u*) and the third vowel (*i*), constitute the meaning of the word "Hari" (*hari-padārtha*); while the letters *ha* and *ra* constitute the meaning of the word "Hara" (*hara-padārtha*).

They say that the placement of the weapons (astranyāsa) is performed with the syllables *iti-hri-he-iti*. Since these syllables are of the nature of the five elements, it follows by implication that the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, are of the nature of the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya).
Thus, the organs of knowledge, such as fire and the other four elements, constitute the body.

The intention is that the sacrifice of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-yāga*) is accomplished precisely through the oblation of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), as well as the letters and the locations (*sthāna*) which are themselves of the nature of the phenomenal world. Furthermore, this is the method of reversal (*viloma-nyāsa*);
it is indeed different from the previously mentioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*), for the former was performed according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*). Thus it is said.

The mind should first perform the meditation on the dissolution of each preceding letter, such as *va*, into the mouth and other organs which serve as the places of articulation (*sthāna*) for each succeeding letter, such as *kṣa*;

this should be preceded by the recollection of the words that will be explained hereafter. Furthermore, one should meditate on the dissolution of those preceding places of articulation, such as the stomach, into their own respective preceding locations.

The authors of the *Padārthadarśa* state that the recitation of the syllables in reverse order (*viloma*), preceded by the visualization of the nine syllables, constitutes the constituent element (*padārtha*) of the rite and is not a separate fire-oblation (*homa*). Furthermore, they hold that the mention of the "organs of cognition" (*jñānendriya*) is merely illustrative; thus, it includes the ten organs of cognition beginning with space (*ākāśa*).

The organs of action have the nature of the color of air (vāyu-varṇa); the objects of the senses have the nature of fire (agni-varṇa); and the ten vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, have their own respective natures. Thus, this entire phenomenal world (prapañca) is composed of that alone; even the body is composed of the elements (bhūtamaya). In this way, [one should contemplate] the ten colors of earth and so forth as before.

Having recited each one individually starting from the feet up to the end of the *jānu*, one should assign the letters of water (*jala*) from the knees to the navel, and likewise up to the end of space (*ākāśa*).
Then, beginning again from the letter of space down to the earth, one should assign those letters ending at the feet; thereafter, [one should assign] the syllable *ca* and its presiding deity.
Meditating on the mantra "I offer this into the abode within the presiding deity;

svāhā," and reciting the mantra beginning with "Oṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ svāhā," they say that one should perform the nyāsa in reverse order, starting from the heart. In that regard, in reverse order: Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ...

One should gaze at the letters from *a* onwards, ending with *ā*, in reverse order at their respective locations, according to the sequence beginning with "saḥ so'haṃ svāhā" and "oṃ hrīṃ laṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ svāhā," such that each preceding letter is placed upon each succeeding letter,
and each preceding letter's location is placed upon each succeeding letter's location.

Mentally recollecting the mantra beginning with "I offer into the mouth, which is the locus of the *ras* [taste] element, which is the *vala* [skin/surface], delimited by that locus, svāhā," and so forth; then, at the end, while recollecting the mantra "I offer the letter *a*, that locus, and the forehead into the Supreme Brahman, svāhā," one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
This indeed is the non-elaborated sacrifice (*aprapañca-yāga*), as well as the placement of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*). For those who are established up to this point,

there is the ten-fold placement of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*), consisting of the ten groups beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, Keśava, Māyā, the Śrī-bīja, Kāmā, and the three bījas, which correspond to the powers of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

He states that all these ritual elements— from the *prapañca-mātṛkā-nyāsa* up to the *prapañca-yāga*— are to be applied to all mantras by means of the passage beginning with "having performed the placement" (*nyasya*), etc.; the phrase "according to rule" (*yathānyāyam*) refers to all forms of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

The meaning is that, by one's own capacity or according to the available opportunity, a devotee of a particular deity must certainly perform the nyāsa of that specific Mātṛkā, either alone or accompanied by the Kevala-mātṛkā-nyāsa. Hereafter, he describes the applications of the Mātṛkā-mantra, beginning with the words "With substances," etc., up to "tadidam pary-."
The worship of the Mātṛkā-mantra is twofold, primarily distinguished as principal or as a subsidiary limb.

Among these, when it is principal, one must perform the worship of whichever one of the previously mentioned mantras is primary on a daily basis; for that [worship], the bathing, twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), libations (tarpaṇa), Vaiśvadeva offerings, and so forth, are likewise required.
Following the aforementioned accomplishment (*siddhi*), the practice (*prayoga*) to be described by that very [author] is also to be undertaken as an ancillary (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, the worship (*upāsana*) of all *mātṛkā*s is indeed indispensable, because it is heard in scripture that there is a fault (*doṣa*) in the worship of mantras without the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*). Thus, the *mātṛkā* mantra also possesses the status of a mantra.

Since the worship of even one among them is necessarily accompanied by the renunciation (nyāsa) of all the others, it is indeed essential; thus, by the word "by these" (*amībhiḥ*), there is the qualification of plurality as presented by the pronoun, but not [the requirement] for each individual one. For this very reason...
Although the requirement [of the sacrifice] is satisfied by the statement "one should offer with clarified butter," the further mention of "with these" is purposeful;
for its result is the removal of the misconception that they are to be offered individually.
However, according to the author of the *Padārthadarśa*, the oblation is performed with the substances mentioned for each one respectively. This is a *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication).

They say that the number [eight] is for the purpose of completing the oblation of all substances, and not by means of each one individually; however, others say that there is an option (*vikalpa*) among the eight substances, just as in the cases of "he offers with rice" (*vrīhibhir juhoti*) or "he offers with barley" (*yavair vā juhoti*). In that regard, there is no simultaneous connection of two [substances] within a single verbal meaning, because it would result in two separate sentences (*vākya-dvaya*).

A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is appropriate when there is the hearing of the word "and" (*ca*) or the hearing of the word "or" (*vā*); however, in this case, since there is no hearing of the word "or" regarding the two [terms] within a single verbal sense qualified by plurality, there is a great disparity. This has been resolved; thus, by that means, even from half [a statement], one obtains the other half, as in the case of a mantra.

The author of the *Padārthadarśa* has stated that [the measure] may be doubled or even halved in accordance with other tantras; however, that is not correct. For even if there were a thousand other tantras, it would be impossible to derive such a meaning from this word in its root form.
If, on the other hand, the meaning stated by me is somehow...
It is said that this work, which is to be composed through the effort of explaining it and by means of the excellence of its harmony with other tantras,
shall not become unacceptable; in that case, one part—
meaning that part which is abandoned or not intended— must be made [the subject], because one part is already present.

If even one part of half of that very half is not to be taken, then we ask: what would remain when there is the loss of half of a half? We say: even in the case of the destruction of small [components] and so forth, a number smaller than that must be followed; this he states with the words beginning "by these," etc., ending in "two pillars."
Stambhana (paralysis), vaśīkaraṇa (subjugation), uccāṭana (eradication), bhrama (delusion), and māraṇa (killing), as well as disease—these are remembered as "minor" (kṣudra).

Some maintain that this term "minor" is a technical designation (*paribhāṣita-kṣudra-pada*). Non-utterance of the mantra-syllables according to the instruction, or acting contrary to the proper procedure—this is the fruit [obtained] from such a mantra.

The cognition that "it will not come to be" is non-comprehension (*apratipatti*). The result of acting contrary [to the prescribed method] is a disorder (*vikāra*), such as affliction by wind (*vāta*) or diseases like leprosy (*kuṣṭa*); for the second [type], madness (*unmāda*) and so forth are cited.
This *homa* has been illustrated; it is performed with one thousand repetitions of the *arka* [mantra], or at the very least, twenty-five thousand repetitions.

In the case of a small [obstacle] through half a hundred thousand repetitions (*lakṣārdha*), and in the case of a great [obstacle] through a hundred thousand repetitions (*lakṣāvṛtti*), as well as in their modifications,

the previously mentioned *homa* performed with the eight substances has been stated; it quickly, without delay, utterly destroys [the obstacle] through the revolution of births— thus says the *Padārthadarśa*.

They say that by performing the recitation one thousand times, the *kṛta* [mantra] becomes a *homa* (oblation), and it destroys the transformations (*vikāra*) of those who have been smeared with collyrium. However, this is not the *homa* cited [in the root text], for it says, "One should pacify [the afflictions] by reciting the *ravi* [mantra] one thousand times.

If you argue that this is the intended meaning based on the corroboration of other sources (*tantrāntara*), then even for one who considers such things, the root text has already provided its own citation.

If it is argued that this [is stated] in another tantra— this being a supplement to the ellipsis— and that we explain the meaning of the oblation (homa) cited in another tantra as "it destroys the modification," then, because there would be no reason for disregarding what has been performed a thousand times,
the application [of the rule] elsewhere would not occur.

Furthermore, by providing such a definition of the *vahni* (fire-altar) yourself, you have rendered the passage free of expectancy; however, the root text itself suffers from a lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*) in that it anticipates another treatise (*tantrāntara*).
Yet, even that other treatise can be reconciled by you as being intended for those with lesser desires.
The same rule applies to both light syllables and heavy syllables.

One should offer oblations with these [mantras] one hundred thousand times; however, in the introduction concerning the meaning of the root [mantra], having considered whether the task is small or great, the homa should be performed as double or quadruple that amount.
Alternatively, one should offer twelve thousand, or double that, or quadruple that. Thus it is said.

When [the result] is extremely small, it should be understood that one may perform even one hundred repetitions starting from one; the practitioner (mantrin) should offer oblations after observing each respective modification through an increase of one, two, three, or four hundred, according to the statement in another tantra beginning with "he should offer," taking into account the gravity or lightness of the task to be accomplished.
This is because one observes [the rule] beginning with "having seen the appropriate measure," and so forth, from the examination of your own treatise; such is the direction.

With these eight substances accompanied by the *trimadhu* (the three sweets), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "subjugation and so forth" includes attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). According to the *Saṃhitā*, there is considered to be a single procedure for both attraction and subjugation.

Because [the substances] are seen to be pure—meaning unmixed with other previously mentioned substances—and furthermore, because mixing is determined in the previously mentioned applications, if this were not the case, the term "pure" (*śuddhaiḥ*) would not need to be employed here; nor is this [term] intended for the purpose of excluding hair, gravel, and the like. Therefore, these are indeed the constituent items.
Regarding the phrase "having made [the materials] pure six times," it should be stated that this means having removed the refuse and purified them through direct observation;

otherwise, there would be the fault of deficiency (*anyūnatā*) because such purity was required previously as well, yet it was not mentioned there. Now, if it is argued that purity in that case follows from the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) alone...

If it is argued that [the word *dṛśam*] has been encountered [in the text], then does the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) not apply here merely by virtue of your command? Or, if it is held that words such as *hi* must necessarily be employed for the sake of filling the meter, then why, having omitted those, is a "pure" word (*śuddha-pada*)— which serves no further purpose— employed here?

If it is asked, "Why is this so?", then what more need we say to you, who, despite assuming the role of a commentator, have failed to provide even a single word regarding the lack of elegance in the root text?

Even though the term "lakṣa" (one hundred thousand) is understood by way of textual continuity (*anuvṛtti*), the explicit mention of "lakṣa" again [indicates] its repetition in places not explicitly stated.

The purpose [of the suffix] is to exclude the notion of mere attainment; thus, by intending to express a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) between the two verbal roots—namely, "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*) and "one would attain" (*prāpnuyāt*)—the meaning is: "having sacrificed, one would attain. This is equivalent even if one supplies the correlative pronouns *yaḥ* and *saḥ*, as in: "He who sacrifices, he would attain"; for the result is the same. [One should prepare] a pill from salts...

The connection is that one should offer oblations with these [substances]. Regarding the plural "with salts" (*lavaṇaiḥ*), it is appropriate to take as many varieties of salt as are available—such as sea salt, rock salt, and soot salt—because there is no word for "all" (*sarva*); therefore, there is no authority for taking every single variety.

Because the plural number here is meaningful through its application to the three [types of] divine conduct, by this the *Harṣakaumudī* text stating "with the five salts" is refuted; for on the palm-leaf fragments,
they are placed individually one by one in separate sections, not in groups of two, three, or more.

It is established in all systems of thought (*sarvatantra-siddha*) that when a person desiring various specific fruits is unable to perform the *homa* themselves, it must be performed through the agency of a Brahmin; and in that case,
a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given to that very Brahmin, because by means of that gift, the *homa* is as good as performed by him.

Since one would otherwise not share in the fruit of the sacrifice, and since a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is necessary even for a self-performed homa to ensure its completeness, he says "a thousand," etc., because there is a requirement for it even in that case;
and by saying "and half," this indicates that the direct [method] is a secondary alternative (anukalpa). Thus it is said.
Even though it is impossible to establish a fixed rule based on the distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable,

the phrase "according to his capacity" (*śaktitaḥ*) should be explained as referring to the purpose of reaching [the prescribed amount] even by means of half a *niṣka* or other portions; for others, however, maintain that it refers to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of one *niṣka* or its half.

Regarding the option of either taking or not taking the *ṣoḍaśī* cup, they say it is not an arbitrary choice, but rather a regulated option determined by one's capacity or its absence; thus they say, "according to capacity. In the phrase "at the time of drinking," the words "in the month of Ārka" are to be supplied as the remainder; [the ritual] is performed at the time of drinking and does not cease.

"By this, even a fool who is proud of his own poetic compositions attains supreme perfection," according to the words of the Ācārya. Regarding the phrase "the juice of *brāhmī*," the instruction here is as follows:
[one should take] two *pala*s of ghee from a single-colored cow whose calf is still living, measured at one *prastha*.
To this, one should add four times as much *śvetavacā* decoction, four times as much *brāhmī* juice,

and four times as much milk from a single-colored cow whose calf is living; having combined these and added water equal to four times that total amount, the cooking should be performed while preceded by the recitation (*japa*) of the *Mātṛkā-mantra*.
Having ascertained that the ghee has reached the state of *asamapāka* according to the method of the Vedya-śāstra, one should remove it from the fire and allow it to cool. Then,

having purified it with a cloth and placed it in a clean vessel, one should meditate upon the Mātṛkā-pīṭha in its center and worship the Mātṛkā along with her limbs (*aṅga*) and enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) according to the prescribed rite, [reciting] ten thousand times.

Having consecrated [the substance] with the Yāmātṛkā mantra, one should place it in a secluded spot. Then, one should drink it every morning for a year according to its true nature; by that, the aforementioned fruit shall be attained.
With the words beginning "vrāhmīm," he describes another application and states the procedure for the consecration (abhiṣeka). Pū... [text continues]

By the words "as previously stated" (*pūrvoktam*) and so forth, it refers to the previously mentioned *mātṛkā-pūjā-yantra*, specifically that spoken on the occasion of the *mātṛkā-pūjā*. The word "man" (*nara*) is not intended to be restrictive in gender;
for another tantra states: "Even a barren woman, by worshipping this, gives birth to an excellent son who is the abode of various virtues."
He describes another application for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the words beginning "in the previously mentioned maṇḍala," etc.;
the connection is that [the substances] should be "deposited" in due order. Because the central flask is primary—since it is the locus of the principal deity—it is taken up first, and so forth.
The author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that one should place a pearl in the central jar,
a ruby (*māṇikya*) in the eastern jar according to the technical definition, lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) in the southeast jar, and so forth; however,
in other traditions, all nine gems are placed in every jar.

Because the act of depositing is seen in this very context, and because it is seen here as well that "the nine jewels [are to be placed] in those jars," the insertion of all nine jewels into each single [jar] is understood.
Due to the proximity of the phrase "in due order" (*yathākramāt*), it is appropriate to connect the word "stated" (*uktāni*) with this very point; however, [the reading] "navara... [is not].

One must also ward off the expectation as to whether the placement of these [suffixes] occurs simultaneously, or according to one's whim, or in a sequence of priority and posteriority, or some other order; for that purpose,
we maintain that the phrase "according to the sequence" (*yathākramāt*) and so forth is appropriate, starting from *vṛṣā* and the like.
"In the pitchers of the directions" (*dikṣu kumbheṣu*)—these are locative cases in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). "The groups," etc.:
the mantras of the eight groups consisting of the letters *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *a* are the worship-mantras (*pūjāmantra*).

They are "joined" (*yutāḥ*), meaning they are connected by the relationship of being the worship to be performed subsequent to the worship of one's own [deity] (*svakaraṇaka-pūjottarakālānuṣṭheya-pūjā-kartṛtva-sambandhena*). Those [mantras].

The meaning of the result is that the worship of the groups (*varga-pūjā*) and the worship of the Pervasive Goddesses (*vyāpinī* and others) in their respective forms as specific powers (*śakti*) are performed with those aforementioned mantras. Some maintain that the groups themselves are the mantras. By the repetition of the word "hundred" (*śata*), meaning "more than one hundred" (*sāgram aṣṭottaraṃ śatam*), he instructed [the disciples] to recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for each jar (*kuṃbha*).

The meaning is that one should sprinkle [the deity] with the jars ending in the east according to the reverse order— namely, by the sequence starting from Īśāna, North, Vāyu, and so on— and finally sprinkle [him] with the central jar at the end. Furthermore, this consecration occurs after the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), not before.

Thus he said, "having given the sacrificial fee. He states another application beginning with "afflicted by fever," and he states yet another application beginning with "the splendor of another. One should meditate upon the thousand-petaled lotus above the *brahmarandhra*, the abode of the Supreme Self, as being filled with the nectar flowing from it like the full moon; [therein] one should [meditate upon] the *mātṛkā*.

The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra]. He describes the application of the *mudrikā* (finger-ring) with the words beginning with "saumyā" and so forth: according to the number of syllables of the vowels, there are sixteen parts of silver; according to the number of syllables of the consonants, there are twenty-five parts; and according to the number of syllables of this [mantra], there are ten parts.
These are the sixteen, twenty-five, and ten parts respectively for the *mudrikā*.
Having kept in mind the purpose of [demonstrating] the *sphuṭa* (manifestation) of lead, silver, gold, and copper, he says "the vowels and the first letter," and so forth.
Alternatively, the letters of the classes (*varga-varṇa*), numbering twenty-four, which are on both sides of the letter 'ma'— which is of the nature of Śiva— are produced from the twelve *kalās*.

By those [terms], the number twelve is understood as being of that very form; thus, there result exactly twelve parts of gold (*hemabhāga*). As for the statement from the Śaiva Āgama, "Of copper, silver, and gold, by twelve, sixteen, and one," that too indicates the number through a transposed order.

It should be understood that this concludes the previously mentioned meaning. First, they were not combined and were not joined with one another; later, when they were joined together with the assistance of the *mudrā* (seal), they were conceived as being united.
Regarding the nine-planet *mudrā*, he says "one should divide," etc., [describing] the division by means of the *mudrā*.

By the verse beginning with "vāha aṣṭau," it is stated that the first eight letters of the vowels belong to the Sun; then eight [consonants] belong to the Moon; the *ka*-group belongs to Mars (also known by the synonym Raktā); the *ca*-group belongs to Mercury; the *ṭa*-group belongs to Jupiter; the *ta*-group belongs to Venus; and the *pa*-group [belongs to Saturn].

The *ya*-group of four letters belongs to Maṇḍasparśana; the *ṣa*-group of six syllables belongs to Rāhu, the deity of the serpent; and for Ketu, there are the rubies (*māṇikya*) and other gems corresponding to their respective deities in sequence. As for the five [groups], although they are pervasive, they are not [exhausted] by the vowels (*pratyāhāra*).

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that the *ya*-group (*yavarga*) consists of five letters; however, it is not correct to claim that the *ya*-group contains four letters, as this would contradict the *Śivatāṇḍava* and other authorities. Furthermore, if this division into groups were not intended, how else could the group [of consonants] consist of sixteen letters?
Just as in the case of expressions such as "the dance of Śiva" (*śivatāṇḍava*), where even though the group [of letters] has attained a single status,
the division into "eight and eight" is consistent; likewise,
although the *ya*-group consists of four letters, only five letters beginning with *ya* are to be taken by Rāhu.

Thus it is said; nevertheless, what is the proof for the fact that the letters [beginning with] *ra* have Rāhu as their presiding deity? That should be cited. However, this proof establishes that only the *ya*-class (*yavarga*) has that deity, and not any others, because of the statement in the hymn (*sūkta*) concerning the *ya*-class within the four classes of letters.

He describes the *dhāraṇā-yantra*, which is authoritative as the deity of the five-colored [maṇḍala], beginning with the words "by the third," etc. By the third seed-syllable of Bhairavī, namely *hsrauṃḥ*, it is characterized as having a radiant pericarp (*karṇikā*). The vowels are placed two by two on the filaments (*kesara*), and on the petals...

The groups of consonants are *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *la*. Among them, the *ya*-group consists of four letters, the *śa*-group also consists of four letters, the *la*-group consists of two letters, and it should be understood that the remaining [groups] consist of five letters each.
He states the distinction from the previously mentioned worship diagram (*pūjā-yantra*) with the words beginning "Tāra" and so forth; [this refers to] Tārādhī.

The letter *va* has the color of a dog (*śvavarṇa*), and the letter *va* has the color of water (*vāri-varṇa*). The meaning is that their wheel should be drawn by revolving in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*).

As for the statement "shining in the two directions and corners," because of the reason [given] that it refers to the directions and corners, [it applies] to the intermediate directions and the corners.
In that same way, one should write the syllable *va* in the intermediate directions and at the corners of the triangle;
this means that this yantra is indeed non-different from the worship-yantra.

As for the statement that "one should wear [this] yantra," it is not appropriate there, because this yantra is intended for the worship of the body of letters (*varṇatanu*) which destroys all diseases.

Because the extraction of the yantra from the first half of the final quarter of the verse— *ghnadhṛtam iti*— itself accomplishes all desired objectives, it would follow that composing another verse would be redundant. Furthermore, the word *vipada* is not appropriately joined with the meanings of "direction" (*dik*) and "corner" (*koṇa*), as these meanings are already expressed by the two words *dik* and *koṇa*.

The construction of the words beginning with "vātārādhīśvara" as qualifying "vanaśobhita-yantram" (the forest-adorned yantra) is consistent with your reasoning. Furthermore, the difference between the two types of worship-yantras will arise solely from the difference in the seed-syllables (*bīja*) to be written in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). For there is no collection of letters [forming a name] such as "vyoma" (ether), "indu" (moon), or "rasa" (taste).
