Thus, although this is the third seed-syllable, there is no fault whatsoever even in the view that the mantra consists of the syllables *ā*, *kāśa*, *bhṛgu*, *vahni*, and *stha*, ending with the *visarga* (*ḥ*) as will be described by its definition;
for another refutation has already been provided there. This is the summary.

The sixth chapter, which completes that [work], was born for the lineage of Dhītipaṃtha, whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī, whose father was Māpati, whose birthplace was Kūrmāvala, who was born from the noble Kṛtavīrya, whose venerable abode was Vārāṇasī, and who attained the state of the Immortal.

In the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*, intending to demonstrate the *bhūtalipi* mantra— which is a specific form of the *mātṛkā*— the author makes a formal promise (*pratijñā*) beginning with "Now," etc., in order to secure the attention of the disciple; and that attention, moreover, cannot be secured without making [the disciple] grasp that [the practice] is a means to achieve his desired goal.

Regarding the passage beginning with "duṣkaram ity ato yām prāpya," the author of the *Padārthadarśaka* says that the word "atha" refers to the script (lipi). Others, however, say that by the word "atha," the mantra is being proclaimed.
Furthermore, they explain that the meaning of "atha atheti" is "atha, etc.," and by the word "ādi" (etcetera), the extraction (*uddhāra*) of that mantra is indicated.
If it is argued that the verse is also being cited [as authority], by what inconsistency do you, O venerable teacher, set aside the initial citation and then provide such an explanation?
We do not understand why you quote the mantra "pañce" and so forth, and then the subsequent portion of the text follows right there.
It would be redundant, because the passage beginning with "five" and so forth has already been cited previously. Furthermore,

as for the claim that there is an application (*viniyoga*) by means of the phrase "all desires," that too lacks intrinsic force (*svārasya*), since the application is stated only after the mention of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details.

It should not be argued that there is a deficiency [in the text] due to the failure to state the nine applications because they are already established; for it is possible to indicate the application through the very examples shown for the fire-mantra. This is evident from the root text: "He who serves the deity Śrībhūtalipi is filled with auspicious sons, wealth, and grain."

Because it is easy to understand, he extracts the mantra previously promised as something to be examined first, beginning with the words "five" (*pañca*) and so forth. Here, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* are the short vowels; *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* are the diphthongs (*saṃdhi-varṇa*). In this context as well, the final, the first, the second, the fourth, and the middle [of each group] are short vowels according to their respective order.

Some maintain that the nature of the elements beginning with space (ākāśa) is to be understood from the final vowel in the conjunct consonants (*saṃdhi-varṇa*), due to their transposition; thus, they claim there is consistency with the second chapter. However, in reality, the vowels are indeed [the letters] starting with *ā*, and the first group of five [consonants] corresponds respectively to space and the other elements.

The *saṃdhi-varṇa* (conjunct consonant) of the final letter of the earth (*bhū*) following the sequence of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth does not exist at all; this is accepted as there is no disagreement regarding the vowels (*svara*), whereas in the case of the consonants (*vyañjana*), there is indeed unity of statement—such is the traditional path. [Thus: *vyoma*, *haḥ*, *iraḥ*, *vāyuḥ*, *tena*, *makāraḥ*, *a*.

Regarding the sequence of letters in the *gniraḥjalaṃvaḥvarālaḥ*, it is not by the order of the consonant groups (*varga*) that the letters of the *na*-group are taken here, but rather by a specific sequence.
In response to the question of what that sequence is, he says "the last," and so forth.
The three letters following the *va* (i.e., *va*, *ra*, and *la*) are the "moon-like" (*candramas*) letters. [Objection: But is this not already established?
In the *Īśvara-tāṇḍava-ādi-tantra*, fifty [letters] are enumerated as being like the Ṛbhus;

furthermore, in the root text itself, they are shown to be included within the long vowels and so forth, such as "the five short [vowels] and the five long [vowels]. To the question, "How then can these letters constitute the Bhūtalipi? he says: "dvi... [and so on].

The meaning is that [the mantra] beginning with "tvāriṃśat" and so forth is distinct from the collection of those phonemes. To dispel the doubt as to how there can be such a distinction here when the *bhūtalipi* is described in another tantra as consisting of nine groups (*varga*s), [the author states] that it consists of nine groups...

He establishes the *tāmasī* [nature] with the words "āyaṃvara" and so forth. Here, "aśceva aṃvarārṇaḥ" is a *dvandva* compound meaning the letter *ha*. Thus, the *a*-group (*avarga*) consisting of five syllables is the first, and the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) consisting of four syllables is the second.
By the phrase "ha-vargaḥ vyoma rāgnijaladhare," it is stated that the *ha*-group consists of five syllables.

The third is the *ṅa*-group, the fourth is the *bha*-group, the fifth is the *ṇa*-group, the sixth is the *ta*-group, the seventh is the *ma*-group—these five each consist of five letters—and the ninth is the *śa*-group consisting of three syllables; this is the established meaning. Now, is the *bhūtalipi* (elemental script) composed of elemental letters?

Having thus refuted [the objection] regarding Śaṅkara by means of a specific line of reasoning, he says "vyoma" and so forth in order to state it explicitly; this has already been explained in meaning. Alternatively, one might object: "But surely it is more appropriate for the letters beginning with *ya*, which are recited after the letter *ma*, to belong to the ninth class (*varga*), since the letter *ma*..."

Furthermore, because the letter *ha* belongs to the third group (*varga*), and its placement follows the order of recitation, there arises a twofold doubt: whether that group consists of only one letter, or whether other letters are also constituents of it. To dispel this doubt, he says: "In the void... (*vyome*).

And likewise, by the phrase "thus the group of *ha* letters (*havarga*), consisting of five colors, is obtained separately as the ninth," it is stated that this meaning is not merely a product of one's own imagination, but is established by the ancient Trika tradition; for it has been taught that the elements [arise] from the letters of the nine groups.

Regarding the statement that the first letters of each of the nine groups, beginning with *vyoma* (space) and so forth, consist respectively of the elements starting with space (*ākāśa*), this was stated by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* in order to express their elemental nature; however, that is not correct, because [the text] states: "This is declared to be the *bhūtalipi* (elemental script)."

Furthermore, because it would result in redundancy if the meaning were thus obtained, and because it would follow that the *ha*-group would not be extracted from the *kṛti* [set] consisting of however many letters; for is the status of the second group as a "five-element syllable" (*pañcabhūtalipi*)— given that it consists of four syllables— to be established by repeating the final letter, or otherwise?

Regarding the doubt that one should practice [the mantra] devoid of the letters of its own elemental class— since the ninth class consists of three syllables, and thus there might likewise be a doubt regarding the elements water and earth—
the second resolution is intended, and he says "the second," etc., concerning the nine classes.

By the words beginning with "Virañci," the name-god (nāmadhidevatā) declares that all the world-protectors (lokapālas), such as Indra and others, are intended to be considered as a single deity by virtue of being the lords of the directions (diggīśvara). Furthermore,
there is a triad of deities consisting of the power of action (kriyāśakti), the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), and the power of will (icchāśakti).

The meaning is that by combining them in this way, they become the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) of the nine groups. However, according to the *Padārthadarśa*, the four lords of the directions (*digīśvara*) are intended here, and the triad of powers (*śakti*) repeated three times brings the total to nine. Thus, Viriñci and the others, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa... [and so forth].
The nine ending with *ṇa* are the deities, and the nine powers (*śaktis*) are the deities of those [letters].
Regarding the first group, they say that there is a pair of deities: Viriñci and Kriyā-śakti; likewise, for the letter *a*, there is also a pair of deities.
Since this is in agreement with other tantras, this interpretation, though laborious, is indeed logical.
Since this [view] is based on the root text of the *Saurasamhitā*, it should indeed be disregarded. However, Harṣakaumudī states:
"First is Will (icchā), then Knowledge (jñāna), then Action (kriyā); thereafter Kāminī, Kāmadāyinī, Ratī, Ratipriyā, Ānandā, and the ninth is Unmanī. And so forth.

Regarding the inclusion of the power of *kta*, the venerable teachers (the *guru-caraṇas*) have stated that there is a transposition of the three [powers] therein, which constitutes the sequence of *kāminī* and the others; however, this is not established in the root doctrine (*mūla-siddhānta*), because it is impossible to include *icchā* and the others by means of the word "beginning" (*ādi*). If it were said that "the beginning of action" is meant, then [the objection remains].

Since a summary beginning with "raṃ" and so forth is impossible, one should infer for oneself that the heart is assigned by the *ha*-group together with the generic mantra "to the heart," and the head by the *ha*-group ending in "svāhā to the head," and so on.
When it is stated "by the six groups," this includes the initial groups such as *ka* and the others.

By the maxim of "elision of what is internal" (*antāllopitinyāya*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of abandoning the final letters of the *namaḥ* and the consonant groups; therefore, setting that aside, these are specifically mentioned. Regarding the locations: in the *liṅga*, it is the region between the genitals and the anus; in the *adhiṣṭhāna*, it is the region at the base of the genitals; and in the *vindu*, it is the space between the eyebrows, according to some.

In the nine support-cakras (ādhāra-cakras) characterized by forms such as "Śānta," "Śakti-aṅka," "above the Śānta," "Śiva," and "Brahmarandhra," one should deposit the nine letters— consisting of four from the *ava* group and five from the *ca* group—
according to the prescribed method and sequence: namely, *oṃ aṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ ī namaḥ*, and so forth.

One should place the aforementioned *he* and *va* in the upper, eastern, southern, northern, western, and rear regions of one's own face, starting from the upper part; [this applies] to the letters *ro*, *ya*, and *tsvi*. Here, by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the locations such as the stomach (*jaṭhara*) and so forth are also to be included, and likewise in the hands.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that one should place the five groups (*pañcavarga*) in the feet, the abdomen, and so forth. Regarding the sequence therein, from "in front" (*agre*) up to "at the back" (*pṛṣṭhe*), if taken according to the literal text, there would be the consequence of placing the five groups in the arms and feet; [therefore, the intended meaning is] to place the five groups in the feet, the abdomen, and so forth.

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that the fault of "indirect indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) does not apply here because, while there is an expectancy for the word "fire" (*agni*) in the phrase "that which is...

(*yat svit...*), there is no such expectancy for the stomach and so forth, as it has been clearly stated. However, this does not reflect the true intent of the root text (*mūla*), because the second half of the verse beginning with "in the stomach" (*jaṭhare*) is separated [from the first half].

The meaning of "two letters" (*dvau varṇau*) is the number twenty; for, since the letter *va* indicates the number four, when that number is multiplied by the number five indicated by the letter *ṇa*, the number twenty is obtained. Thus, [it refers to] the five groups (*varga*).
One should place the twenty letters obtained in sequence on the arms and feet;
as for the placement of the remaining letters, he will state it later with the words "in the belly" (*jaṭhare*) and so forth.
Therefore, when the placement of the complete five groups of consonants (*pañcavarga*) is intended, one should simply say "the five groups."

It should not be argued that the word "letters" (*varṇān*) was used so that there might be no confusion regarding a single placement by grouping them as the *na*-group and the *ta*-group; for in this case,
such confusion is already precluded by the very specification of the locations [of the letters] starting with "here" (*atra*) and so forth in the root text.
Because they cannot be licked, the four extremities consisting of the tips of the fingers and toes,
the four roots consisting of the two shoulders,
the two thighs, and the two hips, and the four regions near the roots— namely, the two elbows and the two knees— are [not to be eaten].

The term *tvāraḥ* refers to the four locations: the four regions near the tips of the fingers and toes (the first joints of the fingers and toes), the middle region [of the hands], the two wrists, and the two ankles;
thus, there are twenty locations [for the assignment of the letters] beginning with *ḍa*.

The meaning is that one should assign the letters from *śa* to *va* starting from the stomach and so forth, assign the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) to the secret place (*guhya*), and assign *śaṃ* to the heart and *saṃ* to the center of the eyebrows.
This nyāsa is of three kinds—creation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*)—due to their respective distinctions;
among these, in the case of creation, there is the presence of the visarga (*visarga-anatva*) for the letters arranged in their proper sequence.

It is as follows: in the state of maintenance (*sthiti*), one should adopt the presence of both *visarga* and *bindu* at the ends, as well as being preceded by the syllables of fire (*ra*) and so forth; whereas in the state of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), one should adopt the presence of *bindu* at the end and the reverse order (*lomya*) of the aforementioned mantra-syllables—thus he says [by means of] creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *lakṣa* by means of [the mantra] beginning with "m" and so forth; thus, the *bhūtalipi* mantra is as follows:

aṃ iṃ uṃ ṛṃ ḷṃ e aiṃ oṃ auṃ haṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ ḍaṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ taṃ thaṃ dhaṃ daṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ bhaṃ baṃ maṃ yaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ. These are the forty-two letters of creation (*sṛṣṭi*).

*Nyāsa* (ritual placement) consists of two types: *sthiti-nyāsa*, which begins from the base of support up to the center of the eyebrows, and *nyāsa*, which begins from the navel up to the private parts.

Having placed the syllable *u* at the navel and having placed the syllable *cha* at the private parts, this is the *nyāsa* beginning with *u* and ending with *sha*. The mantra for that is as follows: *ḍaṃḥ iṃḥ*.
*Ṛṃ, haṃ, ḷṃ, oṃ, aiṃ, auṃ, eṃ, eṃ, yaṃ, vaṃ, haṃ, laṃ, khaṃ, kaṃ, ghaṃ, ṅaṃ, gaṃ, chaṃ, caṃ, jhaṃ, bhaṃ, jaṃ, ṭaṃ, ṭhaṃ, ṇaṃ, ḍaṃ, thaṃ, taṃ,
dhaṃ, naṃ, daṃ, phaṃ, paṃ, bhaṃ, maṃ, vaṃ, saṃ, ṣaṃ, śaṃ.* Thus, these two mantras are recited here to eliminate confusion regarding the phonemes, [as found] in the *Śrīkaṇṭhī*.

First, there are the syllables *ṭha*, *kṣa*, *śa*, *ra*, *ga*, *na*, *da*, *pu*, *ra*, *ji*, *bha*, *nu*, *tri*, *bhū*, *śa*, and *kra* in sequence; then follow *vi*, *yat*, *ma*, *hat*, *atha*, *vo*, *ya*, *maha*, *t*, *a*, *tho*, *va*, *hnija*, *m*, *laṃ*, *bhūḥ*.
Then, according to the rule of the final letters of the consonant groups (*varga*s), one takes the letter *ka* (the first of the gutturals) and the letter *va* (the last of the labials).

The mantra that bears the syllables of the consonant groups (*ka-varga*, etc.)— beginning with *paraḥ-śrotra-akṣi-adri-prathama-navama-aviśva-bhāt-iṃdra-śarva-prāṃtya-agni-vāyu-vāri-tritaya-vara-ma-ka-bhūḥ* and ending with *dṛk-kṣoṇī-turya-vāṇa-jvalana-parimita-arṇa-abhṛgu-śveta-varṇa-u-śveta-ādyaḥ*— yields its fruit.

"For those of perfected intellect, at the time of the placement [of mantras], they remain there"—thus, the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution-arrangement) begins from the space between the eyebrows and ends at the region of the foundation (*ādhāra*). However, the locations [of the deities] differ according to the various types of *nyāsa*. Having performed the *nyāsa* once and having recited this mantra once, one performs the *nyāsa* again.
The meaning is that the placement (*nyāsa*) and recitation (*japa*) should be performed one hundred thousand times in this manner.
"As previously described" means on an eight-petalled lotus provided with a *bhūpura* (protective enclosure).
Here, all the powers (*śaktis*) are to be worshipped upon the petals themselves, arranged in an inner and outer sequence; therein, eight powers constitute one round, making sixteen [in total].

Then, one should worship the eight Śaktis with a double enclosure outside of that; then, thirty-two Śaktis with a fourfold enclosure outside of that; and then, sixty-four Śaktis with an eightfold enclosure outside of that. The four Śaktis beginning with AṂ VIKĀ are located on the petals of the eight-petaled lotus in the cardinal directions.

Regarding the phrase "one should worship in the four [directions] starting from the east," the author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that "Śrī" refers to the distinct power (*bhinnā śakti*). Therefore, the powers beginning with Aṃvikā constitute the five [powers]. In that context, after the worship of the limbs (*aṅga-pūjā*), the four [powers] beginning with Aṃvikā and ending with Śrī are to be worshipped in close proximity to the locations of those limbs.

The authors of the *Harṣakaumudī* state that the fifth [power], Śakti, should be worshipped in the three locations; however, this is not tenable because Śrī-Śakti is to be mentioned among the sixteen powers [of the Goddess] as will be explained later. Furthermore, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and their weapons are to be worshipped everywhere within the inner cities (*bhupura*), specifically under names such as Ambikā and so forth.

He restates [the point] in order to explain it further: "In different places," etc. For it is not the fact that the worship occurs in different locations that is the determining factor for there being different coverings (*āvaraṇa*); rather, it is merely the intention (*vivakṣā*) of the author of that [text].
However, the result is the repeated offering of the primary worship at the conclusion of each respective [section].

Regarding what was stated concerning the washing of the merit-maker (*puṇyakara*) and so forth— wherein the author of the *Padārthādarśa* says that outside of that [lotus] there is an eight-petaled one, then a sixteen-petaled one, and beyond that the earth-circle— we do not recognize his underlying intention regarding the thirty-two powers (*śakti*s) and their respective doubled powers.

If it is argued that the worship is performed by means of a sixteen-petaled lotus because of the disregard for the growth of the lotus in such and such a manner, then what offense has been committed by the eight-petaled [lotus],
such that another two lotuses with thirty-two petals and so forth must also be accepted there?
If it were argued that [this is so], even then it would not be correct, because there is no purpose in performing that [second] enclosure (*āvṛtti*).
For an enclosure does not constitute the status of being an object of worship (*pūjākarmatva*) by virtue of being a covering for the desired deity situated in the center from all sides;
since that has already been accomplished by the worship of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) alone, what need is there for a second enclosure and so forth outside of that?

If the sixteen powers beginning with the ninth [Navamī] are worshipped as being included within the first [sixteen] powers, then they would constitute a separate enclosure (āvaraṇa) due to the distinction of enclosures, and not an inclusion within the first; for it cannot be argued that such a rule is unestablished, since no such thing is observed in other mantras. However, this restriction is not a necessary factor.
Because it is the will of the Blessed One alone that serves as the cause for the distinction between the various types of concealment (āvaraṇa).

This is not something previously unobserved in other Tantras; for even after describing the worship of the hundred Śaktis of Kārtavīryārjuna and others in the ten directions, it is stated that there is only a single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa), despite the prescription for the worship of those bearing all weapons and so forth in the eight directions outside, as well as [the worship] in the filaments (kesara).

Having described the worship of Madavibhañjana and the others, and because even when the worship of Kṣemakari and so forth in those [directions] is mentioned, it is declared that there is only one enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*), therefore, in the system of three enclosures (*tryāvaraṇa*),
the worship of the Lokapālas and others outside [the first enclosure], as well as that of Vajra and the others, constitutes the single enclosure.

Furthermore, how could the locative case-ending (*saptamī*) in the phrase "on the previously mentioned seat" (*prāg-īrite pīṭhe*) be consistent? The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* maintains that the meaning is not "one should worship the previously mentioned Śakti-pīṭha mantras here as well," because by virtue of the word "here" (*itaḥ*), even Brahman can be made an object of worship.
In this [system], sixteen powers are to be worshipped on each of the eight petals in the sequence of four by four;
thirty-two in the sequence of eight by eight; and sixty-four powers are to be worshipped in the sequence of eight by eight.
Thus they present their own teacher’s doctrine. In the previous doctrine, there is one [power] with the limbs (aṅgas), and [the others] beginning with Aṃvikā.
Some also say that if the second [circle] were with the [goddesses] beginning with Karālī, the fourteenth with those beginning with Indra,

and the eighteenth with those beginning with Vajra, then the nineteenth would constitute the nineteenth enclosure; thus, they argue, the root text stating "there are eight enclosures" (aṣṭāvṛtiḥ) would be contradicted.

This [text] has indeed been corrupted; furthermore, we do not know by what specific statement this could be set aside— the fact that writing on the second leaf immediately after writing on the first leaf everywhere is established both by logic and by scriptural injunction— and one should write with an abundance of power through the repetition of powers.
It should be understood that [the scripture] is not incapable of providing instruction, nor does it contradict a matter already established;

this is the summary. "Auspicious" (*śubhā*) is an adjective qualifying power (*śakti*), not its name. *Daṇḍinī* and *Muṇḍinī* are derived from the meditative identification (*abhiṣyāna*) with the mantras *svadhā*, while *Māyā* is the designation of her name.
Although the reading "yasyāḥ sthitiḥ saṃhṛtiścaiva" is not traditional,

the reading "yasyāḥ sthitiḥ saṃsthitireva ca" is authoritative; thus, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* has maintained the reading "saṃhṛti," while in the *Harṣadīpikā*, the term "sure" refers to a single demoness.
She whose supreme solar line is non-dual is thus [described]; "supreme" (*parā*) is a specific name for *Śakti*.
Here, there are eight ending with *Māyā*, sixteen ending with *Skandamātā*, twenty-four ending with *Sṛṣṭi*, and thirty ending with *Paradevatā*—[these constitute] the Destroyer of Asuras.
There are forty Śaktis ending with Nityāntā, forty-eight ending with Gaganavegā,
fifty-six ending with Anaṅgakusumā, and sixty-four ending with Vāgīśī;
these are the Śaktis in the Harṣakaumudī, while Abhiṣyā and Saṃjñā are the independent Śaktis.

Others do not accept that it is a name, or rather that it is the name of another power; in their view, one must consider the method for preventing the addition of further names to a single power. Here too, although the *bhūtalipi* mantra has attained the status of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*), it is not the *mātṛkā* mantra.

One should perform the application of *kṣapa* (the *kṣapa*-practice). The yogi, by means of the central path—the *suṣumṇā*—should unite Kuṇḍalinī with the Supreme Abode, the Supreme Brahman, at the crown of the head;
then, meditating upon the nectar (*amṛta*) flowing therefrom, one should [fill] the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) down to the *mūlādhāra* with that nectar.
Having meditated upon the [mantra] that has been washed away, he who performs the *bhūtalipi-nyāsa* (the ritual placement of the letters of the alphabet) shall become like the Sun;

thus he demonstrates one application. Regarding the phrase "while [the deity] is asleep," it is not only this specific procedure for the diagrams (*yantra*) to be described hereafter, but there is also another general procedure applicable to all diagrams.

He says "it must be drawn" (*nusartavya*) by means of the passage beginning with "in the yantra" (*yantra*) and so forth. "Rites" (*karmāṇi*) refers to those rites to be accomplished through the respective elemental mantras;
he describes those very *yantras* by means of the passage beginning with "rich in the bindu" (*bindvāḍhya*) and so forth.
Here, in every case, first there is an eight-petaled lotus, outside of which is the mandala of the respective element, and outside of that is a circle.

Beyond those three, it should be known that there is the outer enclosure (bhūpura). That very thing is the sky (gagana) enriched with the bindu and joined with Śiva (the letter *i*), and joined with the letter *e*; thus, the word "jñānin" results.
Consequently, the extraction of the seven-syllable mantra culminates as: "O, O Jñānin, protect me! (*haṃ he jñānine namas*). This is the conclusion.

Having written the mantra in the pericarp, one should write the aforementioned letters—which are of the nature of space and related to that letter *ha*—on the eight petals, enclosing them with the letter *ha*. [Objection:
But where should the ninth [letter] be written?

He restates that doubt must be prevented by the maxim *antyalopa* (elision of the final letter) with the words "the remainder," and so forth; thus, having written one syllable enclosed within two *ha* letters at the end of the last petal, and having likewise written the second syllable in that same manner, six syllables are established.
The "true phonemes" (*bhūtavarṇāḥ*) are precisely those mentioned in this chapter, beginning with "the five short vowels, the five long [vowels]," and so forth;
for these alone possess immediate presence. For this very reason, the singular form "the remainder" (*śiṣṭam*) is used;
however, if one were to include what was previously stated, two syllables would remain as the "remainder," and thus that [singular usage] would be inconsistent.
It was not stated that "only what remains" [is intended] because otherwise,

by the inclusion of the previously mentioned vowels, the status of being "what remains" would indeed be possible there as well; for this very reason, it was stated in the *Bhūyastilaka* that "[the consonants] ending in *la*," since otherwise the quality of ending in *la* would have been obtained there by the aforementioned method alone.
In this case, all the letters, including the *bindu*, belong to the practitioner (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, according to the statement that "the letters which are the kinsmen of one such as Devadatta who is seized by poison are called the *dhava* [supporters] in the *Siddhārṇava*," one should also place on the leaf those very phonemes situated in the *siddha* square.
Alternatively, one should write [the letters] using the name of Devadatta or others by means of the syllables of the *bandha* (bond).

Here, the "friend" syllables of the initial letter 'da' and so forth are taken; these have been shown on the day of the *kula-akula-vivāra*. Furthermore, their state of being non-composite (*apuṭitatva*) is indicated by their being specified separately.
In Rohiṇī, during the Muhūrta of Rohiṇī, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, at the eighth part of the day and night—
specifically at a time measuring two ghaṭikās— this Muhūrta is not to be accepted in its entirety; rather,
it is that very [time] at which the rising of the sun occurs, [lasting] twelve [muhūrtas] every day.
The five *ghaṭikās* of the five elements constitute each zodiacal sign (*rāśi*).
Among them, the rising of the planets occurs; therein, the measure of the five *ghaṭikās* of a sign is as follows:
there, the first *ghaṭikā* belongs to air (*vāyu*), wherein Jupiter (*guru*) and Rāhu rise; the second belongs to fire (*vahni*), wherein Śukra [rises].

The third [level] from the earth belongs to Mars and Saturn; the fourth level from there belongs to Mercury and the Sun; the fifth level from there belongs to Saturn and the Moon; and the sixth level, the sky (*viyat*), is where the rising of all the planets occurs.
As it is stated in another Tantra: "One day consists of the period from Aries to Pisces."
The rising of the planets (grahodaya) is to be understood among these elements (bhūta) through ten signs (rāśi).
That is to say, within the specific elements existing at the time of birth, it occurs during the specific elemental minutes (ghaṭikā) situated within those respective signs.
Likewise, in each individual sign here, there are five elements; [the fifth being] wind (vāyu).

Fire, earth, water, space—this is the fifth; according to the respective order of all the signs (rāśis), the first nāḍī is of fire, the second nāḍī is considered to be of earth, the fourth is known as of water, and that fifth is remembered as belonging to space. Thus says Guru.
"Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, the Moon, and the Sun [are assigned] respectively to the four elements;
space (vyoman) is the soul of all. This means that this yantra should be constructed when Rāhu is situated in Rohiṇī;
this is established in the *Harṣakaumudī*. He now describes the Vāyavya yantra with the words "He who is two... and so forth.
It should be joined with the third vowel of the third group (the letter *u*), the crescent moon (*indu*), and the bindu;
it should be joined with the second [vowel] of the second group (the letter *i*), the twelfth vowel (the letter *au*), and the bindu—
thus forming the essential form *kopeśa*, joined with the dative case singular ending (*ai*), resulting in *piṃyaiṃkopeśāya*.

The extraction of the eight syllables of the *mitya* [mantra]: Having enclosed the letters of the wind-element mentioned in this chapter with the letter *ya*, one should write them upon the eight petals. This wind-mandala is indeed a circle marked with twenty-six lines. [This is performed] under the asterism Svāti, during the *muhūrta* of Svāti, and [the conjunction] Ārdrā.
The constellations Śleṣā, Anurādhā, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā,
Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, Mūla, Śatabhiṣaj, and the two Phālgunīs (Pūrvā and Uttarā)— these fifteen muhūrtas are auspicious by day; at night, they are half as many.

According to the observation that "Thā, Cā, Ṣṭau, Pūrva-bhādrapada, and so forth; Punarvasu, Kṣaṇa, Puṣya, Śruti, and the three beginning with Kara [constitute the muhūrtas]," the thirty-first muhūrta of a complete day and night is the Svāti-muhūrta; this is the time of Saturn's rising, occurring at the end of the [thirty-first] part.

The essential meaning is this: when the *muhūrta* of Svāti coincides with the rising of Saturn at the hour of the Cat (Caghaṭikā), this Vāyavya instrument should be drawn. Regarding the instrument of Fire, he says "the seed of Fire," which refers to two *rakāra*s.

One should sequentially join [the syllables] with *śravaṇa* (sa), *sadya* (ha), *ardhendubhi* (ī), *pañcama-svara* (u), *trayodaśa-svara* (o), and *bindu* (m). The forms are *kha-rauḥ-ro-pha-ḍit*, followed by *svarūpam-han-namaḥ*.
Regarding the letters of the *sādhya*, [the letters] are the nourishers (*poṣaka*) of the *siddha*-box; they are the well-accomplished ones (*susiddhaga*) residing in the *vāndhava* [box]. *Ghā*.

The meaning is that the letters situated in the "well-accomplished" (susiddha) squares—namely, the letters *ra*, *ka*, and *puṭita-vahni* (the letter *ra*) which is the form of fire (*vahnirūpa*), and the elemental letters (*bhūtavarṇa*)—should be written on the petals, according to the statement: "The servants residing in the enemy's square are those belonging to the square to be conquered. Furthermore, the "killer" letters are those letters located in the enemy's square; [these are to be placed] upon their cloth.
Regarding the statement "one should destroy with the fire-weapon," the remainder [of the instruction] is that this is done by burying that particular yantra.

He describes the water-yantra with the words beginning with "nāsa" and so forth: it is joined with the nose (the letter *na*), the seventh vowel (*u*), and the half-moon (*ardhendu*); thus, the letter *va* (which is the "water") is joined with the half-moon and the letter *ma* (the fourteenth vowel).

The syllable *ṅe* is to be joined; thus, the word *vidhuḥ* ending in the fourth case singular (*caturthī-ekavacana*) is [joined]. After the word *vidhu*, there is the word *bhuvai*, and then the word *namaḥ*. By that, the one-syllable mantra *vṛṃ vauṃ vidhave vidhubhuvane* is extracted. This belongs to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*).

Thus, here the conclusion of the eight Varuṇa syllables occurs precisely at the end of the eighth triangle; furthermore, there is the writing of the group of syllables belonging to the Vāndhava [deity] as it is obtained upon these petals according to the stated method. Therefore, nothing further has been mentioned here, as there are no additional syllables.
Just as in the case of [the mantra] beginning with "tśiṣṭamaṃtyeva," since there is an absence of even an eighth [letter] on this earth [of the yantra],
in response to the doubt as to what should be written on the eighth petal, he will state "the letters ending in 'la'. Thus,
having inscribed the letters corresponding to the elements of the earth (pṛthvī) up to the seventh petal, [he proceeds to the eighth].

The meaning will be that one should inscribe [the mantra] with the letter 'ma' added as a prefix, in the form of the color of the earth (yellow), as stated in the second chapter; thus, nothing is inconsistent.
When the planet Venus (Kāvya) rises during the auspicious moment (muhūrta) of the constellation Śatabhiṣaj, which belongs to Varuṇa... [kaviśu]... [text fragment].

The arising associated with that [mantra] should be as follows; here, he extracts the further yantra by means of the words beginning with "gaṇḍa" and so forth: *gaṇḍa* is the ninth vowel (*u*); *vasumatī* is the letter *la*;

between the two *gaṇḍas*, i.e., between the letters *ga* and *ka*, there are *ja* and *ga*, and *jaga* refers to the forms of the letters *ga* and *ja*; *luka* is their own form; and *nati* is *namaḥ*.

The word *śabdaḥ* [is followed by] *tena lāṅgagaja-gaṇḍalukena*; thus, the ten-syllable mantra is extracted. Here too, in order to prevent the delusion that—as was the case previously with the consonants (*samārṇānām*)—the letters should be written as the elements and the earth (*pṛthvī-bhūta-varṇatayā*) up to that point, [the author says] "lāṅgāni."

By enclosing all of these [syllables] with the letter *la*, three *la*s result at the final petal. This yantra was written on a clay vessel in the hour of *mṛdī* during the rising of Mercury; it is effective everywhere, not merely for the sake of distinguishing between light and heavy syllables, or what else? Sarva... [text ends].
Because it effects the immobilization of thieves, serpents, the movements of enemy armies, the speech of opponents, and so forth, all desires—

including sons, grandsons, and others not specifically mentioned here— are accomplished; therefore, he says "guhya" and so on, indicating that this [mantra] should be worshipped by those seeking their respective desires.

[Objection: "In that case, why does everyone not abandon everything else and apply themselves to this alone? To this he says, "more secret" (*guhyatarām*). The sense is that because the method of this mode of worship cannot be attained by all, they apply themselves elsewhere. By this much of the treatise [the point has been established].

The *mātṛkā* mantras, which constitute the fundamental nature of all mantras, have been fully concluded. Now, other mantras must be explained. In that regard, since it was introduced that the *mātṛkā* is the Goddess herself, and because it is necessary to first explain the goddess-mantras due to her being the source of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), [the following is stated].

Because she is of the same nature as Sarasvatī by virtue of being the power (śakti) of the Brahmā who is the speaker, he first states the various mantras of Sarasvatī beginning with "Atri," and so forth: "Atri, Daḥ, Varuṇa-saṃruddhaḥ,
joined with the letter 'va' at the beginning and the end, 'Dāgvādinī' as the essential form, 'vadvayam svā'..."

The letter *ha* is the tooth, and the letter *ca* is the moon; since both the letters *sa* and *va*, which denote the moon, are present here, *svāhā*—which is like a bee (*virepha*) for the sake of the bee—is also denoted by this term.
Thus, the ten-syllable mantra "O Goddess of Speech, *svāhā*" (*vadavāgvādini svāhā*) is extracted. Śravaṇa...

By that [method], the placement of each of the ten syllables individually in the ten locations, beginning with the head and ending with the anus, bears fruit as stated by Mātṛkā: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ*.

The meaning is that it is according to the sequence beginning with "Āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth. With the lotus of letters, using the seed-syllable *hsauḥ*, the ancients prescribe the union of the other eleven syllables as well, namely: "vāgvādinī-yoga-pīṭhāya namaḥ". These [mantras] follow.

Having manifested the *pada*s, the *mudrās* are explained; beginning with the word "hṛdaya," he teaches another method of recitation different from what was previously stated. "Aiṃ namo bhagavati vada vada vāgdevi svāhā"—this mantra consists of sixteen syllables and six *pada*s. Thus [begins] the *Vāgbhava*.
First is *namaḥ*, second is *bhagavati*, third is *vadavade* (the word repeated), fourth is *iti*, fifth is *vāgdevī*, and sixth is *svāhā*.
He then states another mantra beginning with *tārā* and so forth; although the vowel *u* is followed by a bindu (*ū*), it is indeed distinct.

Even though it has been thus indicated, since a mere moon cannot be delineated on its own, and some substratum must therefore be resorted to as its locus, it is logical to resort to the twelfth vowel, which is denoted by the word "lower lip" (adharapada) and is established by the preceding rule.

The seed-syllable of Tivāgbhava is extracted as *oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*; this eleven-syllable mantra is applied in sequence to the nine apertures consisting of the two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, the mouth, the genitals, and the anus. Thus, he demonstrates another mantra for the speech [deity].

By the word *spate* and so forth, [the author] indicates that the first element of the mantra is the seed-syllable (*vīja*) of Vāgbhava; furthermore, the term *amṛte* is a qualifier of the mantra, signifying that the vowel *ā* belonging to that word is connected with the letter *t* of the word *pate*.
To indicate this meaning, he says "consisting of eleven syllables" (*rudrasaṃkhyākṣara*). Now, if this is so...

If it is asked: "For what reason is it stated that the first mantra has eleven syllables, since there is no doubt regarding its composition even there? [The answer is: That very doubt exists there as well, because of the possibility of the misconception that the two terms *adhara* and *bindu* are independent; for the *bindu* is specifically...
Even if it were a mere practice (*cārya*), since it would be possible for the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā* to exist merely as placements upon the seed-syllable (*bīja*),
the statement "consisting of sixteen phonemes" would be unnecessary; therefore,
[the author] provides this [explanation] in order to dispel the delusion that the words "heart" (*hṛdaya*) and so forth refer merely to their own literal forms.
Because it must necessarily be adopted, even in cases such as "the lower lip is bitten" (*adhara-vindu*), it can be explained in this same manner;
likewise, in other instances as well, one should oneself infer some purpose for its adoption according to the rules, through the combination of generic types (*jāti*) and their respective *mudrās*.

When it is stated "by five feet," there might arise the confusion that the sequence of the five limbs begins from the word *vācaspate* (O Lord of Speech), as this would follow the order of the opening [of the hymn] composed by oneself. To prevent this, one should employ the third case ending in the phrase "by speech and so forth" (*vāgādyaiḥ*),
treating the limbs as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the action of "one should perform" (*kuryāt*), and the [hymn] itself as the object (*karman*).

By the word "according to rule" (*vidhivat*) used in conjunction with the entire preceding phrase, the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) has been declared. When the question arises as to how it should be performed, it is stated that it is done "with five words. If only this much were said, a doubt might arise as to how these five [words] constitute the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*); therefore, [the author] says...

Regarding the phrase "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), the author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that by this it is meant that the sixth limb [of the ritual] should be performed with the entire mantra, and that it is not explicitly mentioned for the sake of concealment. To this, the following must be said: for when the term "according to rule" is used in close conjunction with the word "limbs" (*aṅgāni*), [it refers to those specific components].

Furthermore, it is not understood that there is a rule for its performance, nor is it established by the force of the words that "it must be performed ending with the sixth [chapter] called Astra"; as for what was said— that by the injunction "one should perform the ancillaries" (kuryād aṅgāni), only the six ancillaries are obtained— that too is not correct.
Because it would follow that [the mantra] would pervade the life-span with the nine syllables ending in *gānimi* and *raṃti*, as is seen in the *Saṃhitā-dāpa* and other texts;

and because, in the passage "one should perform the six limbs with the six long-voweled *Muṇḍā-bījas*," it would follow that the word "six" (*ṣaṭ*) would be redundant in the *Yāmala* and other works. Therefore, [it is not so].
If it is argued that since the attainment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is possible by the word "gāni" alone, and that even in your own view the six-word phrase [beginning with] "ṣaṭ dīrgha" etc.
would be redundant once the attainment of the six limbs is established,
then even so, one should perform [the rite] as prescribed in the *Mātṛkā-prastāva* which states that the six limbs are to be enjoined.
The six limbs are performed in sequence by means of those seed-syllables (*bījas*) which are the twice-repeated introductory mantras of *Itibhuvaneśvarī*; and likewise,
the six limbs are performed in sequence by means of the root-mantra (*mūla*) of *Tripurā*, which begins with *Aṃ* and so forth, and is the very essence of the *Saurasamhitā*.

Because it would result in the redundancy of the word "five" (*pañca*); and as for what was said—that where there are five limbs, one should state only "the five limbs" and so forth—that too is not correct, since in the *Mahālakṣmī-mantra*, which possesses ten syllables, the limb-mantras are indeed taught even though they possess five limbs. Thus, the limbs [are established].

The summary is as follows: because it is stated in the root text [of the *Nārāyaṇīya*] that "one should first sacrifice," etc.; the paste (*kalka*) is one-eighth part of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with *brāhmī* juice; the *brāhmī* juice is four times the amount of the clarified butter; "consecrated" (*japta*) means seven times; and this should be done daily for three or five years, as stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*.

He who drinks at dawn the lukewarm decoction of *vrāhmī* juice mixed with tawny clarified butter (*kapilājya*), having first consecrated it with mantras, shall indeed retain in his memory what he has heard three times, even after five years; for that water is the syllable *Va*, wherein lies the bed of Viṣṇu.
Some say that by combining the second vowel (Ā), which is established as being conveyed by Ananta who lies upon Viṣṇu,

with the letter Ka— which is established either by the four-faced one (Brahmā) alone, devoid of vowel, or by the Vāgbhava seed-syllable established as "Ki"— the mantra "Ko" is formed. Thus it is said.

Others say that the mantra is a constituent part of the seed-mantra (*bījātmaka*). Others say it is not so; rather, the mantra is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, which is a constituent of the mantra. Since the bed situated upon the waters is Ananta, by him [is signified] the second vowel (*u*); by *kaṃ*, the head, [is signified] the first vowel (*a*). Thus, the essential nature is *A-u*. *A*.

Where there is a curved union of the letters *re* and *ka*, that is the simple combination of the vowels *a* and *e*, resulting in the eleventh vowel (*ai*). When this is joined with the second vowel produced from the first [vowel *a*] through their conjunction, the twelfth vowel (*o*) is produced. Thus, O Four-faced One, the head is formed.

When it was said by someone that "nāviṃdu" (nā + viṃdu) is the attainment of the seed-syllable *vāgbhava* (aiṃ), that is incorrect, because it would result in the redundancy of the word *tastha*; for the state of being "situated therein" (*tastha*) is already obtained from the word *śayana* itself.
[The second syllable is extracted as follows: *arghīśa* is the sixth vowel (*ī*), *vahni* is *ra*, and with that, *rū*—thus the second [syllable] is extracted. *Sadyo*.

*Kāra*, *ambu*, *vaḥ*, and *Bhṛgu*—by these, the third seed-syllable (*svauṃ*) is extracted. *Vyādya* refers to *Tāragvadha* (Cassia fistula), *Siṃduvāra* (Vitex negundo), *Nirguṇḍī* (Vitex negundo), and *Āmrāta*, which is well-known in the vernacular as *Āmāḍā*. *Taila* is the oil itself, manifest before one's eyes; it is praised by the learned as *Śāḍrīṣṭa*, *Śiṣṭa*, and *Śiḍāḍā*.
The meaning is that one should not sleep while holding betel (*tāmbūla*)—which is well known as such—in the mouth;
for it is stated in the *Smṛtis* regarding the commencement of sleep: "One should remove betel from the mouth. Therefore, there is no fault in consuming betel at night. [End of verse. *Akṣarāḍhāni*.

Thus, the meaning is that just as such leaves are protected even when they are of no further use, so too should this [work] be preserved. [He whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī, and whose father was named Māpati, a treasure-house of affection... pathaku... [Note: The final fragment appears to be a partial or corrupted title/colophon.]

The land of his birth was Labhū, the mountain Kūrma; his father was Kṛtavīrya; his place of residence was Vārāṇasī; and he reached the state of Acyuta. Thus ends the section on the Śabdārthacintāmaṇi. Having described the mantras possessing the power of creation, [the author now describes those] for the maintenance of the world.
With the words "Now," and so forth, he undertakes to state the mantras of Śaktibhūta-Mahālakṣmī;
for an exposition is fruitful only when it motivates the listeners to engage [with it],
and that motivation does not occur here because there is no apprehension of the means as being conducive to one's own desired goal.

Desiring to dispel the doubt that "this description is thus fruitless," he qualifies the mantra with the words "Śrī-saubhāgya" and so forth. Now, this might be so regarding the power of the mantra, provided that such power existed in its presiding deity; but that is not the case.

To dispel doubt, he qualifies the locus with the words "of which," and so forth. Although it might seem more appropriate to state the qualification of Śrī first— since she is the subject of the mantra and lacks primacy— nevertheless, it is the power of the mantra itself that accomplishes the task at hand, not [the deity].

It should be understood that even among certain mantras dedicated to a single deity, a specific power is observed in some; for instance, through the conjunction of these— *va* (the letter *śa*), *agni* (the letter *ra*),
the left eye (the fourth vowel *ī*), and *indu* (the *bindu*)— there arises the venerable *Vī*.

Having extracted that which occurs in the sentence denoting the *chaṃdas*, the second letter is *kūrma* (the tortoise), but not water; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the letter *śa*, the power (*śakti*) is the fourth vowel (*ī*), and there are six long vowels.

The meaning is: by means of the second, fourth, sixth, twelfth, fourteenth, and sixteenth vowels. Regarding the phrase "with three *kamala*, *tila*, and *bilva* fruits," some say that one should perform a thousand oblations using these three combined; however, the number of three hundred and thirty-three [oblations] is to be completed with those counted as a thousand.

Regarding their number, some say there is one oblation for each; others say it is by whatever number one desires; still others say that since three have been mentioned, one should offer a thousand for each, such that the oblation results in three thousand. However, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* says that by the three mentioned...
They explain that the oblation is performed by offering one thousand times for each individual mantra separately, and then again three thousand times collectively;
thus, the oblation results in a total of four thousand offerings.
However, the word "tu" (but/however) brings a natural elegance to this position [of the author].

The phrase "as in the case of the *tipura*" means that, as previously stated, the worship of the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*) should be performed upon the filaments (*kesara*). On those very petals and on the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should likewise [place] the Śaṅkha-nidhi to the right of the Goddess and the Padma-nidhi to her left.

Having worshipped these seven presiding deities of the enclosures— Dhaḥkaṃvukanidhi, Śaṅkhanidhi (the word order is reversed here for metrical reasons), Vasudhārā, and Vasumatī, who are their consorts— and having thoroughly perfected the mantra of Śrī, demonstrate the ritual applications.

By saying "thus he shall speak," and so forth, [it refers to] the fire of *aśoka*—that is, a fire kindled by *aśoka* wood; this should be understood in the same way for similar instances that follow. By "pure" is meant those things which are devoid of the nature of being saturated with the previously mentioned clarified butter (*ājya*). Although, in all cases, there is no oblation (*homa*) without clarified butter, [the term is used here in that specific sense].

It should be understood that this occurs because of the specific statement regarding "pure" (*śuddha*). However, the authors of the *Padārthādarśa* explain that it means having removed impurities such as hair and insects, washed them, and brought them to a state of purity;
they argue that since such purity is required everywhere, it is mentioned here specifically.
This has already been largely refuted by the statement beginning with "because there is no seed for its designation" (*tad-abhidhāna-bīja-abhāvāt*). Now, if it is argued that purity—

which is already established by general rules— is mentioned here again in order to indicate the non-application of those general rules, then [the same logic would apply to] breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and sipping water (*ācamana*).

If it is argued that "let even the direction be lost, let the loss of iron be accepted," then there would be a contradiction with the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Therefore, our stated meaning is the more reasonable one. Having increased the *vilva* tree in his own land by reciting the *Śrīsūkta*, he [should place] the three sweets on its eastern leaf.
Then, having prepared a heap of wood consisting of flowers and fruits grown on that [tree], and having performed oblations with its roots while surrounded by the preliminary rules within the maṇḍala,
one whose self is purified shall somehow behold the form of Ramā;
thus, by this other ritual application from another Tantra, misfortune shall never again exist in that family.

The meaning is this: A Brāhmaṇa, on his own land, should cause a *vilva* tree to grow by means of water poured with the recitation of the *Śrīsūkta*; he should also mutter the *Śrīsūkta* while touching the *vilva*. Then, with six substances—leaves, flowers, fruits, sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), horn-shavings (*śṛṅgabher̤a*), and roots—sprinkled with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), [he should perform the offering].

The summary is that by performing oblations in sequence, the aforementioned results will be attained; this applies to those beginning with one million (*niyuta*) and one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), because it has already been established with examples that such terms refer back to the objects included in the preceding compound. He states another mantra, beginning with "Vāgbhava," etc.
The seed-syllable of Śrī is the consort of Viṣṇu; the seed-syllable of Kāma is that of the one whose banner is the makara.

Having completed a hundred thousand recitations at the end [of the mantra], the sense is that one should not rely on the daily performance of *homa* (fire-ritual). A thousand of those is a "thousand suns" (*bhānusahasra*); "by its procedure" means by its worship.
The meaning is that the worship for removing those obscurations and so forth should also be performed according to the very same method previously described.

He states another mantra with the words beginning "dīrgha" and so on; here, the letter *a* is long, for this [letter] serves as a negation, and this negation is the cause of a long exhalation for both the giver and the requester.

The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* maintains that the letter *na* is indicated by the long syllable (*dīrghapada*) according to the *Vatīti-śāstra*. However, in reality, since the digit known as the "long" (*dīrghasaṃjñaka-kalā*) arises from the letter *na*, it possesses that designation; its designations are "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth, while its designations are indeed "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) and "maintenance" (*sthiti*).
It should be understood that [the mantra] arises from the letters *rā* and *te*. For the letter *ya*, its beginning is *ma* (Brahmā), *ka* (the Sun), and *ma* (Vasundharā);
at the end of the letter *va* is *la* (Cāṃtā). At the end of the letter *si* is the form of *na* (Svāhā, the beloved of Agni).
Thus, the ten-syllable mantra "namaḥ kamalavāsinyai svāhā" is extracted; this is the gift (*dāna*).
The granting of a boon is what is meant by the "boon-mudrā."

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "state of fearlessness" (*abhayapada*), and because their association is seen extensively, he extracts the thirteen-syllable mantra with the words beginning with "Vāgbhava. The third seed-syllable of Vālā is the third [syllable], or else it consists of the letter *ha* and *sa* joined together.
The third [syllable] of Bhairavī is to be taken as having this form: the letter *ra* (repha), the *visarga*, and the *bindu*, joined with four vowels.

Some, however, say that the third [syllable] of Bhairavī should be taken as being without the *ra*. All three of these positions are stated in the *Padārthādarśa* as the essential nature (*jagati svarūpam*).

The letter *Pārśva* (the letter *pha*) is set ablaze by the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*), conjoined with *Arghīśa* (the letter *sa*) and the sixth vowel (*ū*), and topped with *Bhṛgu* (the nasal bindu). That which has the *Tāra*—the *Praṇava* (*oṃ*)—as its first part attains such a state; the meaning is that the twelve-syllabled mantra becomes thirteen syllables. The *Praṇava* is the seed-syllable...

Having performed the purification of the hands by reciting the complete mantra beginning with "jaṃ tārtīyaṃśaktiḥ hastau" and so forth over each hand individually, one should assign the mantras as follows: *oṃ aiṃ namaḥ* to the two thumbs, *oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* to the two index fingers,
*oṃ śrīṃ namaḥ* to the two middle fingers, *oṃ klīṃ namaḥ* to the two ring fingers, and *oṃ hsauṃ namaḥ* to the two little fingers.

Having placed [the seed-syllables] on the two little fingers with "Oṃ jagatprasūtyai namaḥ," and having placed each of the seven syllables individually on both palms, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the complete mantra. Then,
in the same manner starting with "Oṃ aiṃ namaḥ," one should place the five seed-syllables on the head, the two eyes, the chest, and the...
Having sequentially placed these two syllables on the feet, one should mentally place the remaining seven syllables— *oṃ jaṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ gaṃ ta namaḥ*, *oṃ praṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ sūṃ namaḥ*,
*oṃ tyaiṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ naṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ maṃ namaḥ*—
respectively upon the skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, semen, and the mind; thus one should assign the [seven] constituents (*dhātu*).

Regarding the performance of the empty-consecration (*śūnyāseka*), this is the specific procedure: having meditated upon those elements with the mind, one should sprinkle [the water] with the heart-mantra.
Then, [one recites]: *oṃ ai jñānāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ aiśvaryāya śirase svāhā*;
*oṃ śrīṃ śaktyai śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *oṃ klīṃ balāya kavacāya*.

One should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the following six-limbed mantras: *oṃ hāṃ sauṃḥ vīryāya netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ jagatprasūtyai namaḥ*, *tejase*, and *astrāya phaṭ*. [Regarding the herbs: *nameru* is *rudrākṣa*; *lakuca* is called "bāhel" in the vernacular; and *suraparṇī*—of these, the words ending in the third case... [are used].

The word "adorned" (malamkṛtam) is connected here [to the following]. "Golden pavement" (hemakuṭṭimam) refers to a ground surface paved with gold. "Ateyoja" refers to water shining brightly; it is not a redundancy to mention "water" (ambu) again, as it refers to a specific fragrant substance, namely the musk (nābhi) of the deer called *kastūrī*. It does not refer to the musk of other types of deer.

The expression "the musk of Dāsāyaka" is used not merely to indicate that only that much was separated there, but rather to suggest that the musk-deer themselves were also present; alternatively, it may be a dvandva compound meaning "musk-deer and [their] navels," since the navel is naturally associated with them.
The result is the same even in both cases; likewise here, in the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha), this is the distinction:
immediately after the earth is the Ocean of Milk; in its center is the Jewel Island (ratnadvīpa); there is a grove; there a supreme lake;
there a pavilion (maṇḍapa); in its center a Pārijāta tree; beneath it, a jeweled lion-throne.

The word "sanam" (with sandalwood paste) is understood as being like other deities; [the offerings include] a crest-jewel, a necklace, a pearl necklace, and *paṭīra-paṅka*—that is, sandalwood paste. Then, after the *homa* performed with pure ghee according to the ten-part (*daśāṃśa*) proportion, when the *tarpaṇa* is performed according to the ten-part proportion of the *homa* numbering twelve *ayutas*:

To refute the claim that "twelve thousand [merits] are obtained by that," he says, "twenty thousand. For worship can indeed be performed by anyone even with a single offering; therefore, it is established that this [number] is intended for the attainment of worship consisting of sixteen offerings and so forth. Indeed, by means of the sixteen...

Having worshipped the Lord with services out of devotion and having again offered fragrance and flowers, one should pray to the Lord; according to such statements, the worship of the *āvaraṇas* (retinue) occurs only after the complete worship of the principal deity and those equal to the principal has been performed, once again offering fragrance and flowers.

It is an established tenet that the worship of Gaṇeśa follows after praying to Jñāna; however, this applies to Skanda only when there is a specific scriptural injunction. As for Gaṇeśa, his worship is ordained everywhere and awaits only a particular place or time, or else [is performed] otherwise.
On the right and left sides of our pericarp,
one should worship, in sequence, Jahnu’s daughter Gaṅgā and Sūrya’s daughter Yamunā; and right there, on the western side behind the Goddess, is Varuṇa.

In this *Śrī Rājarājeśvara Stavarāja*, the phrase "the one who abides facing the eastern direction" (*pūrvadigāta*)— referring to Kṣemaṅkarī Mahāśakti, who is adorned with red garlands and unguents and holds a parasol of pearls—
is explained as having the well-known meaning of "facing the east"; however, it actually refers to her being positioned behind the Lord.

It causes [the worshipper] to reach the conclusion in the western direction. Although it would be more logical to mention the deities to be worshipped on the pericarp (*karṇikā*) at the very beginning— just as in the case of the Son of Śaṅkara (Skanda)—
nevertheless, this is stated in this manner to indicate that this worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) occurs after the worship of the [main] deities, and not before.

Thus, it should be understood that Gaṇeśa and Kāmadeva hold a status equal to the primary deity, while all others— beginning with the limbs (aṅgas) who are worshipped thereafter— are merely part of the retinue (āvaraṇas). Then, outside the eight petals, in their respective directions starting from the east, the zodiac signs beginning with Aries (meṣa) and the nine planets (navagrahas) are to be worshipped.

They should be worshipped in their respective directions because there is no rule for abandoning those specific directions; nor is it improper to say that one should worship them "all around," for according to the Smṛti statement, "the Ketu has four colors and is in the northwest," some maintain that its worship should take place in the northwest (Vāyu).

In the four directions, starting from the east and each respective direction within that space, are the eight enclosures (āvaraṇas) of Mahālakṣmī: first, the limbs (aṅgas); second, Umā and others; third, Gaṅgā and others;
fourth, the zodiac signs (rāśis); fifth, the nine planets (navagrahas); sixth, the elephants of the directions (diggajas); seventh, [the guardians of the quarters].

The distinction is that the [deities] beginning with Drā are the eighth, starting with Vajra. Among those, the limbs (*aṅga*) are on the filaments (*kesara*) of the pedestal-diagram (*pīṭhayantra*); Umā and the others are on the eight petals of that same pedestal-diagram; and the triad beginning with Gaṅgā is on the pericarp (*karṇikā*) itself, in the southeast, northeast, and rear portions. From the eight-petaled [lotus],...
Inside the innermost line, the zodiac signs beginning with Aries from the east and so forth are to be worshipped; the procedure there is as follows:

having first worshipped Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer in the four directions starting from the east, one then worships Leo, Virgo, Libra, and Scorpio starting from the east, and then Sagittarius starting from the east.
One should worship the four signs beginning with Aries:

namely, Taurus and Aries in the direction of the gods (East); likewise, Cancer and Capricorn in the West; the two signs Gemini and Scorpio in the direction of Yama (South); and for the Moon, Leo and Aquarius; while for the Sun, they reside in the directions of Agni (Southeast), Asura (Southwest), Marut (Northwest), and Vāyu (Northeast).
The remaining [planets] are the Gemini, the Virgo woman, the bow, and the horse; thus, outside of that, the planets are situated in the eight directions starting from the east.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the east;
Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu are in the corners starting from the southeast."

Thus, the Sun is likewise in the eastern direction alone; the "elephants of the directions" (dig-ājāḥ) are also [situated] in their respective directions starting from the east, as they are well-known as the directional elephants of those specific points such as the east and so forth. However, for Indra and the others, it is simply a square (caturasra) as before.
Here, for the signs (rāśi) and the rest, ending with the elephants of the directions, it is just as it is for Indra and the others.

It should be understood that the worship of Apūrva and the others is performed according to established tradition; however, because Gaṇeśa and Kandarpa—being the sons of Śaṅkara and Puṣpadhanvan respectively—are equal in status to the Principal Deity (Pradhāna), they are not included among the *āvaraṇas* (enclosures).
At the end of each enclosure, there is the worship and libation (*tarpaṇa*) of Mahālakṣmī.
One should attend to the fruit of discernment, namely the washing of the hands and the offering of worship;
he demonstrates the application of these mantras with the words beginning "with dūrvā grass," etc.
She whose mouth has the form of a betel leaf and who has a red dot in the center is declared to be Lakṣmī, adorned with white flowers.

Regarding the number of mantra-recitations for the consecration of the ashes, the authors of the *Padārthādarśa* maintain that it consists of one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight recitations, as these numbers are most commonly encountered by learned scholars. Indeed,
the author of the root text does not explicitly state the specific number, as it is not interrupted by any other previously mentioned number.

Even the connection with the name does not alter the natural sense of the root. Having explained eleven ritual applications (*prayoga*) through this much of the treatise, he begins to describe the twelfth application, that of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), with the words "having performed," and so forth; yet the words do not mean "one who has [placed] nine squares within himself."
By the analysis of the compound *grahānnavapadetyātmāparyāyāntarasvarūpaṃ*— meaning "that whose nature consists of synonyms for the self such as 'the planets' and 'nine squares'"—

the author has here taken up the nine-petaled lotus mandala described in the third chapter; with this mantra, [the deity] is to be drawn upon its own pericarp by means of the Mahālakṣmī yantra to be described below.

It has been stated that one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) for that which is adorned and required according to the prescribed rule; regarding that, he states the answer to the inquiry as to what that rule is.

With the words "kalaśān" and so forth, having properly constructed nine lotuses according to the previously mentioned sequence of directions using gold weighing one hundred and sixty *ratikas*— bound together and joined by means of the nine gems—
and having written the *lakṣmī-yantra* again upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that [central lotus], it is to be placed in the central jar.
Having cast that [mixture] into it, one should then grind ten substances— sandalwood and the rest—
in equal parts and distribute them portion by portion, beginning from the central jar up to the northeast jar;
likewise, gems should also be placed in all [the jars], but not in the central jars.
If it is argued that the nine jewels must indeed be cast [into the fire] because it is traditionally taught that all jewels serve to consecrate the lotus as a qualification of the abundance of gems,
and because of the statement, "One should place these, which consecrate the jars, into the jars," [the response follows].

Regarding this, some hold the view that the capacity for producing specific fruits arises from the water in the *kalaśī* being conjoined with jewels; however, since that [capacity] can also arise from a single deposition [of the water],
it follows that even when it is simply stated that "jewels are present everywhere," it can still occur even without their further deposition.

Others say that there is no authority for its insertion [into the middle jar] because it was not mentioned [in the initial injunction]. However, others maintain that since it is observed that jewels are placed in all the jars, their insertion into the middle jar is likewise logical. Nor should it be argued that the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to everything except the middle jar, because the term "all" has the function of denoting every single item introduced at the outset.

Because the derivation [of the term *sarva*] is established from its initial application, and because it would follow that sandalwood and other substances would be placed into every intermediate jar; for it is not logically tenable to say that the single word *sarva* denotes the middle jar and does not denote it at the same time, nor can it be said that the word *sarvakuṃbheṣu* (in all jars) is understood as "even in those containing jewels" in this context.

It should not be said that "in this way" means "in the nine jars of the first [altar]" and "in the eight jars of the second"; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the particle *api* (also) being redundant in the phrase "the jewels also," since two properties are being conveyed regarding a single substratum (*dharmin*) denoted by a single word.
They declare that the *vādi* group is employed starting from the center in sequence up to the northeast (*īśāna*),
and likewise the *priyaṅgu* group; however,
in reality, the more excellent position is that every single substance should be placed into every single jar.

It should be stated that, since [the items] have been largely discarded, the addition of each of the five substances beginning with *dhātrī-phala* should be made into a single [mixture]; for even there, a one-to-one correspondence is not possible because their respective numbers are unequal—this is the truth. This same path applies to flowers and sprouts as well, by way of the *kuśa* grass.

Some maintain that the recitation should be performed three thousand times while maintaining a posture such that contact with all the jars occurs simultaneously; thus, the consecration of each individual jar should be performed three thousand times,
totaling twenty-seven thousand [recitations].

Others maintain that the recitation is completed according to the total number; this number for the consecration of all the jars is not for a single one. Thus, having divided the number three thousand into nine parts, the consecration of each individual jar is performed with a count of three hundred and thirty-three.
Some say that for each [deity], one thousand [offerings] should be made, with the number increased by one for each;
having first worshipped the Brahmins with auspicious, non-widowed women, and having satisfied them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and other gifts, [one should receive] their blessings.
It has been stated that [the deities] are otherwise in the six wombs; according to the sequence of their establishment, they follow the order starting from the East.
Here too, the worship follows the conventional terminology beginning with the East.
"Auspiciousness" (*bhadra*) means the absence of affliction for others, or the absence of affliction for those within the auspicious state (*śiva*), or alternatively, it refers to the body itself.
"Happiness" refers to that which is produced by health and so forth; "auspiciousness" (śiva) refers to the happiness derived from sons and so forth.
Since the terms *bhadra-pada* and *śiva-pada* are synonymous, one might suspect tautology; however, this is not the case here, as it is stated:
"The King [perceives] the extraction of the worship-mantra (*pūjā-mantra*)... and so on. Here, the first half [of the verse]...
Regarding those three qualifiers of the *yantra*, there is another statement: "one should draw a lotus outside of that.
In that context, there is another statement regarding two qualifiers of the lotus, beginning with "by the orb of the earth" (*dharā-vimba*) and so forth.
The "Veda-beginning" is the *praṇava* (OM); situated within that is the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya-nāma*), followed by the name of the desired object (*kāmyārtha*).

Relying on the opinion of the author of the *Padārthādarśa*, who teaches that the term "name of the object to be accomplished" (*sādhyasādhya-nāman*)— which follows the general rule for mantras and which includes other elements such as the name of the practitioner and the verbal action—
is not prohibited here, and whose meaning is that it signifies the name of the practitioner’s ritual action,
this [is stated] in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī*.
However, it is better to follow the manner explained below.

One should understand that the term *sādhya* refers to the deity, the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*), based on the observation of [texts] such as the *Śivatāṇḍava*, where the word *sādhya* is recognized as having both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings when applied to the deity; for otherwise, in the absence of an address to the deity, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*asvārasya*) of the word *kriyā* (action) and others being improperly applied.
And [it is] "joined with the three primordial seeds"—

this is a qualifier of the yantra— meaning it is endowed with each of the three seeds individually by cutting out the filaments four times in pairs. Thus, having previously written the Śrī-bīja, Śakti-bīja, and Kāma-bīja one by one up to the third [position], [one should proceed].

One should write [the syllables] from the fourth to the sixth, then again from the seventh to the ninth, and again from the tenth to the twelfth, repeating this cycle four times; or alternatively, one should first place the *śrī-bījas* in each of the four filaments, and then the four *māyās* in those from the fifth to the eighth.
Some maintain that [the sequence] concludes with the four *kāmās* from the ninth up to the final *vara*;
furthermore, they arrange them in pairs (*yugaśas*). Thus, in the first pericarp (*kiñjalka*) there are two seed-syllables (*bīja*) consisting of Śrī and Śakti;
in the second, those consisting of Śakti and Māra; in the third, those in the form of Māra and Śrī, and so on in this order.

They say that one should draw [the diagram] up to the completion of the twelve filaments (*kiñjalka*). However, the authors of the *Harṣakautūhala* state: "In the first filament, [one should place] the nature of Śrī-Śakti; in the second, the form of Śrī-Kāma;
in the third, the nature of Śakti-Kāma; and again in the fourth and subsequent [filaments], as before."

The authors of the *Padārthādarśa* state that the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) should be written by repeating them three or four times; however, they further state that after first writing the three *Śrī*-seed syllables once, then the two *Śakti* syllables, and then the two *Kāma* syllables—
thus having written them upon the six filaments— one should write them again in the same manner on the twelve petals.
One should worship with the twelve syllables excluding the *praṇava* (oṃ), which are related to the invited [deities].
Regarding the consonants, by not resorting to counting the letter *la* twice, there are thirty-four in number;
however, because of the instruction to write either *ha* or *kṣa* elsewhere, there are thirty-two in number. Furthermore, [the vowels] are *ūrva*.

By writing their squares in pairs, one by one, upon the filaments (kesara), or by rotating them as they are written, the completion of the sixteen filaments of the petals becomes possible. That which possesses sixteen petals—eight pairs of petals—is [the lotus]. Its own [filaments] exist individually. Thus, there are sixteen petals. That which has those is... [dha].

This yantra should be surrounded by two *bhūpura*s (enclosures) connected to each other, and it should be encircled by the mantra of Tvaritā— which will be described later— using the mantra ending with *vaṣaṭ*, having inserted the word *vaṣaṭ* at the end of the Tvaritā mantra; thus, it shall be completed by this mantra.

The encircling with the *bhūpura* (the protective perimeter) should be performed after it has been encircled by the *tvaritā*; the sequence [of these actions] is according to the requirements of the *chaṃda* (meter), according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. In the phrase "by the *tvaritā*" (*tvaritayā*), the meaning of the instrumental case is a qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) connected to the *yantra*; and that *yantra*, qualified by the meaning of such an instrumental ending, is what is encircled.

The experts in logic maintain that because there is a desire to express the connection with another category of meaning (*padārtha*) for the word "constant" (*nitya*), the conjunction with "swift" (*tvarita*) is first apprehended; therefore, it is logical that this [conjunction] alone should have primacy.
As for the case where, in the absence of mutual intermingling between the earth and the sky, the second square [of the diagram] is in the machine...
The author of the *Padārthādarśa* stated that "there would be no encircling of the *bhūpura* because it is already encircled by that [the *tvaritā*]," but that is not correct;

for in that case, since the encircling of the *tvaritā* itself occurs from both sides of the *bhūpura*, there is an absence of the encircling of the *yantra*, and thus the same fault remains for you as well. [Objection: But what about the *tvaritā*?

If it is argued that it is the very nature of the yantra itself, we say no; for I too could claim that everything up to the first enclosure (bhūpura) is the nature of the yantra. We accept, however, through the oral tradition (saṃpradāya), that these two are intermingled. Thus, first there is the twelve-petaled lotus, and then outside of that—
Outside of that, there is a sixteen-petalled [lotus], an eight-spoked [wheel], and a square; such is the nature of the lines of this yantra, which completely surrounds [the center].

"Sufferings" refers to those arising from fever and the like; "calamities" refers to those arising from kings, enemies, thieves, and so forth—this is the distinction. He states another mantra beginning with "śaṅkha," etc., starting with the seed-syllable of Śrī (Śrī-bīja).
