In those two, the three seed-syllables beginning with *yukta* and *māyā* are complete: the letter *ka*, the letter *ma*, and the letter *ka*; the letter *la* joined with the eleventh vowel, which is *bhaga*; *brahmā* is *ka*; *āditya* is *ma*;
the long lower lip is the letter *lā*; the nature of *li* is this: what is this *ya*-group?

Regarding this, he says "beginning with *kṣa*," and so forth. It should be explained as "the *kṣa*-class beginning with [a vowel] having a visarga in the middle" according to the reading *savisargamadhyakelas-kṣādiḥ*;
or, according to the reading *avisargamadhyakelas-kṣādiḥ*, it refers to the beginning of the nature of the *tulakṣe* [syllable].

The meaning is that the purpose is the same in both cases. The fruit is identical. "O Marutya," "O Bhagavati"—the meaning of these has already been stated. "Mahālakṣmi" is the essential form, ending in the vocative case. Thus: *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kamale kamalālaye prasīda prasīda śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mahālakṣmi*.

This mantra, consisting of twenty-seven syllables, concludes with the word *maḥ*. One should be pleased by that very word, as well as by the four-syllabled form *Mahālakṣmī*, which consists of four phonemes.
Indeed, the six words beginning with *kamale* should not be accepted merely according to the traditional recitation (*āmnāya*).

However, he says that they are "enclosed" (*saṃpuṭita*) by those three seed-syllables (*bīja*) which have entered at the beginning of the mantra, starting with the words "by these words," and so forth. Thus, the resulting application is as follows: *śrauṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kamale śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so on. [This is] Devīsahadevī.
The *madhuvrata* is the *bhṛṅgarāja* (clitoria ternatea), known in the colloquial language as *hāthājoḍī*.

*Haricandana* is yellow sandalwood (*pītacandana*). *Mālūra* is the *vilva* (wood-apple). By the phrase "with the juices of *niśā*" (*niśārasaiḥ*), it is implied that the *haridrā* (turmeric) used here should be freshly dug up at that time; [the juice] of dried [turmeric] is not intended.

Because it is possible [otherwise], there is no evidence for establishing that [the statement] depends on a connection with water, even though such a connection is not present; for this object is such that it is preceded by a smile,
is pleasing, and brings about the suffering of another.

There is no risk of violating the meaning of the scripture even by speaking harshly at that time— speech which causes unhappiness for one destined for a [lower] rebirth and appears unpleasant at that moment, much like the administration of bitter medicine. However, regarding the vows such as the Ekādaśī, co-sleeping with a young woman is indeed prohibited by the scripture, as it is prompted by passion.

To the objection that this would lead to a logical inconsistency (bhaṅga), he says "not otherwise" (nānyathā). For, since sleeping with women is already established by worldly attachment (rāga-prāpta), there is merely a prohibition against an old woman; the intended meaning is not to enjoin sleeping with a young woman. It is well known that one should praise a *droṇa* measure; [she is] like the goddess Śrī, Lakṣmī.
*Lī* is *viṣṇuvallabhā* (beloved of Viṣṇu), *viṣṇukrāntā* (striding of Viṣṇu), and *kanyādhṛtakumārī* (the maiden held by the Virgin).
By stating that devotion to Viṣṇu is also necessary for her worshipper, it is taught that we should follow the conduct of the Vaiṣṇavas here.

May that Mataṅga, whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī, whose father was named Premanidhi, who was born in the lineage of Paṃtha, whose birthplace was Kūrmāvala, who made the feet of Acyuta— worshipped by Kṛtavīrya— his object of supreme devotion,
and whose residence was Vārāṇasī, attain perfection.
In the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*:

Now, following the description of the power that is the agent of maintenance (*sthitikartṛśakti*), the mantras that are the power which is the agent of withdrawal (*saṃhārakartṛśakti*) are to be described.
Since there is a multiplicity of those powers, there is no fixed rule governing the sequence of their description.

In the context of the *vaprāsakti*, it is appropriate to mention first the power (*śakti*) named Bhuvaneśvarī; for she is the bestower of sovereignty over each and every level of existence (*bhuvana*), and not merely of the absence of suffering. Therefore, she is the Sovereign (*Īśvarī*). Having known her, [one attains this] through knowledge preceded by [her grace].

Even Brahmā and the others, though they possess the power to perform creation and other such acts, are objects of worship; how much more so, then, the lords of sages? What need is there to mention ordinary men? Or rather, even if one does not know [the Lord], why would one not worship Him? This is the sense of the verse. Indeed, they have attained some exalted and unsurpassed glory.

Intending to state the restrictive rule that "this very one becomes the most excellent among all the powers," he says "atha" and so forth. *Lakulīśa* is the letter *ha*; the "left eye" is the fourth vowel (*ī*); *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *ī* is the power (*śakti*). As it is stated in the tenth chapter: "The seed-syllable *haṃ* is the power of Īśa."

The application [of the letters] to the eight *rasas* (flavors) is as follows: the letter *sa* is used immediately; those beginning with it which follow in order—such as *o*, *e*, *u*, and so forth—are the short vowels (*hrasva*) that reside therein. Those whose initial elements are such root-seeds (*mūlabīja*) are the five beginning with *hṛllekhā*.

The application of the qualifiers is as follows: *viśeṣaṇaṃ* (the qualifier), *itthaṃ ca* (and thus), *hrīṃ hṛllekhāyai namaḥ*, *dreiṃ gaganāyai namaḥ*, *ūṃ raktāyai namaḥ*, *hriṃ karālikāyai namaḥ*, *hrūṃ mahoṣmāyai namaḥ*. As for the two neuter [syllables] that have arrived in the sequence, they are to be included within the short vowels; this is according to the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā*.

What was stated there by the Picu-kṛt is not correct; for one who knows the mantras, the vidyā should be divided and the *hṛllekhā* and other [syllables] should be deposited one by one, lest there be a contradiction with other tantras. Furthermore, the placement of the two feet of Mahoṣmā must be performed here simultaneously with the hand; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of repeating the mantra.

This [view] of the author of the *Tipadārthādarśa* should be disregarded because it contradicts the *Āvṛtti*, the *Aṅgayuga*, the *Iṣiti*, and the *Saṃhitā*. Those [energies] which possess a radiance (*prabhā*) that proceeds sequentially from the five elements (*bhūta*), beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*), are the "limbs" (*aṅgāni*). This was previously extracted [from the source].

The commentator [states] that now is the occasion for the performance of the *traṃ* mantra; for previously, the extraction (*uddhāra*) was not performed in its entirety, and had it been so, it would have been stated simply as "one should perform the placement of the limbs" (*aṅgāni vinyaset*).
In reality, however, the placement was previously performed with the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*), whereas now it is accompanied by the *jāti* (the syllable *phaṭ*).
This is to be understood as the fundamental purport of those limb-mantras (*tāṅga-mantra*). Thus, regarding "to Brahmā" and so forth:

*oṃ braṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ gāṃ gāyatryai namaḥ*—this is the placement (*nyāsa*) on the forehead. In the same manner for other locations; however, others [prefer] "salutation to Brahmā together with Gāyatrī," and so forth.

Others say that the *yoga* consists of the practice beginning with "Obeisance to Gāyatrī and Brahmā" and so forth. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra upon the mouth, one should then [place] the nine categories— beginning with the six pairs starting from Brahmā and ending with the two treasures and the root mantra— from the throat onwards.

"One should place [the mantra] in the locations," so he says with the words beginning with "vadan" and ending with "deśika. Some, however, claim that there are two locations for each of the breasts and the sides; they argue that the reading is not "etāni" (these), but rather "etām" (this).
Thus, one should place this root-vidyā in the nine locations beginning with the throat.
According to the tradition of the *Artha*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight Mothers— beginning with Brahmāṇī—
in the eight locations from the crown of the head (*parakaikakudi*) down to the heart;
she whose splendor is like that of the rising sun, the Lord of the World (*Bhuvaneśī*), [is worshipped] with the seed-syllable of space (*vyomabīja*) as Maheśānī.

Likewise, O Dear One, it is established in Kailāsa and other places; thus the sovereignty over the world of the Sun (Svarloka) is said to arise from the seed-syllable of Fire (Ra), through which gold and other things are produced in many ways.
By that [syllable], this world-sphere exists in the world; such is the established rule. Through the fourth vowel (Ū), Pātāla is [established], and Śeṣa is in the form [of the consonant].
The great circle of the earth is not supported by anything else; therefore, O Great Sovereign, she is the mistress even of Pātāla.
Thus, he describes the worship-yantra with the words beginning with "padmam" (the lotus): within is a hexagon, and outside of that is an eight-petaled lotus.
Above that, one should draw a single-lined circle; outside of that, a sixteen-petalled lotus;

and then a square with four doors—this being the general procedure for the yantra. Following this, preceded by the seed-mantra (*bīja*) and other elements of the present mantra, one should provide the seat, namely the *yogapīṭha* seat. Thus: *Oṃ hrīṃ*.
The mantra concludes as: *namaḥ bhuvaneśvarī-yoga-pīṭhāsanāya*.

With that very seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should worship the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the filaments (*kesara*) within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) itself, starting from the center and proceeding to the east and so forth. Thus he says, "in the previously mentioned [places]," followed by the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*).

Since the worship of those [deities] also takes place within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) itself— which is composed of six corners— the term "afterwards" (*paścāt*) is used rather than "outside" (*bahiḥ*) for the purpose of indicating merely their immediate succession; for if it were stated thus, the region outside the pericarp would be understood.

However, it must be understood that the statement "having bowed to the hexagon" is not intended to mean that the powers (śaktis) to be described later, such as Anaṅgakusumā and the others, are to be worshipped on the petals; for this will be explained immediately hereafter, and that would be inappropriate because the deities of the filaments (kesaras) are to be worshipped after the worship of the deities of the pericarp (karṇikā).
Immediately following that, having raised the objection that the procedure for the worship of the deities has already been extensively set forth,

he says, "The limbs" (*aṅgāni*). For likewise, since the worship of the deities of the filaments (*kesara*), who are the very nature of the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*), was already described previously, what is currently [being discussed] is specifically the worship of the deities.

There is no lack of propriety here; rather, by the power of the specific statement, the worship of the deity of the filaments (*kesara*) is mentioned even before the deity of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
By this, since the worship of the deities belonging to the filaments was already stated previously, there is no contradiction in that designation.
It has already been answered that this is not improper, because by the injunction for limb-worship (*aṅgapūjā*) in the passage "the limbs [are placed] on the filaments" (*aṅgāni kesareṣu*),

the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) would be sublated even in the context of worship; for first comes the placement of *Hṛllekhā* and the others who are equal in status to the principal deity, then the placement of the limbs (*aṅga*), and after that, the six couples (*mithunapaṭka*).

Thus, it is observed that for the two nidhis (treasures) which have not been [previously] assigned, the *hṛllekhā* and other nyāsas are seen [first]. Therefore, the *aṅganyāsa* (limb-assignment) before the *hṛllekhā* and others is not desired, as it would result in a contradiction with the sequence stated for worship (*pūjā*).
In a doubtful matter, one must resort to a method of applying a uniform sequence in both cases.
Because of this, there is an eightfold retinue consisting of Anaṅga, Rūpa, and the others.
The eight items, beginning with the cup for the one-eyed goddesses, are to be understood as being held in their hands in sequence;

furthermore, the two chowries are to be assigned one by one in order rather than both to a single goddess. Thus, there is no contradiction regarding the number eight. In this manner, by performing the aforementioned excellent worship (*pūjā*)... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
It is implied that even one who performs the mantra-observance for the worship of the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) incurs no sin;

for this very reason, it is well known that fools, women, children, the elderly, and others are [eligible] "knowers" (bodhas). Furthermore, the fourfold [principles] beginning with the jewel (ratna), the seat (maṇḍapa), dharma, and so forth, as well as the serpent, the lotus, the root-form (mūlamūrti), and their limbs (aṅgas)—these are to be worshipped.

By the statement "the worship of all others [is performed] through effort" and so forth, it is stated in the *Tantra* that the limbs (*aṅga*) themselves must necessarily be worshipped among the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*). Among the deities of the seat (*pīṭha-devatā*), there are exactly seven deities: the jewel pavilion (*ratnamaṇḍapa*), the four beginning with Dharma, and Anantakāla.

Regarding those for whom it is difficult to understand that only the auxiliary deities (*aṅgadevatā*) within the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) are to be worshipped, there is this procedure for the worship of women and others; even for those who understand well, when the occasion for an essential abbreviation arises, there should be no abandonment of any object whatsoever by one's own will, nor should there be an elision of the final [syllable] according to the maxim *antyalo-pi* (elision of the final).

Furthermore, having taken up the constituent elements (padārtha) according to the very direction previously stated, the meaning of that [practice] is established here as the remainder of the sense. Now, he states the application of these mantras with the words beginning with "the minister" (mantrī), etc.; "his wives" refers to the king's women; "ministers" refers to the king's counselors; [and this applies] during the performance of daily ablutions and so forth.

He describes one application in the form of the statement beginning with "twenty-five," etc., stating that whoever performs his own consecration with water consecrated by the mantra spoken in the number twenty-five shall partake in all fortunes; it is not merely the attainment of wisdom alone.

However, it is said that he shall also attain renown as the best among all poets by means of the verse beginning with "kavīnām" and so forth; this is accomplished through the number one hundred and eight as prescribed in other authoritative treatises,
consecrated by mantras, and applied to a twelve-finger-long effigy (puttalī).
In the *Rasasaṅgraha*, there is a specific distinction regarding the birth-ascendant: for the Moon, it is sixteen finger-breadths;

for the Sun, however, the measurement is according to the sun's [specific] size, and the determination therein shall be made by means of the Bhairava [method]. In the nine asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, the measurements are fourteen finger-breadths; in the [next] nine, they are twelve and a half; and in the [final] nine, they are thirteen and a half.
That [image] is thirteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in height, starting from the head;

there, the head is one-eighth [of the total], the chest is of that same measure, the abdomen is of that same measure, and the portion from the navel to the hips is also of that same measure. Then, by doubling that, the thighs are formed, and by doubling again, the shanks.

Regarding the direction: the instruction is that for the subjugation of men, one begins from the big toe of the right foot and proceeds to the big toe of the left foot; for the rite of subjugating women, one begins from the big toe of the left foot and proceeds to the big toe of the right foot. This [mantra] is to be recited while eating.

Having consecrated it one thousand and eight times with that same number of recitations, and having previously approached the King with the words "the king" and so forth— the meaning being that [the mantra] is dissolved ten thousand times— one should [employ] that *māyā* (the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī), which has been perfected through prior service and the like, together with the object of attainment (*sādhya*) and the syllables "Bho bho bhuva."
One should write "O Goddess, grant her an easy delivery" (*neśvari asyāḥ sukha-prasavaṃ kuru*) together with the syllables of the *sādhya* (the name of the woman) in this place;

this is to be written on the navel of a woman suffering from the pains of labor. However, if there is a strong possibility of giving birth to a son, it should be written with the ashes of *palāśa* wood; otherwise, it should be written with the ashes of *umā*.

Those who know the tradition say that a square [diagram] should be drawn; at that time—meaning at the time of the pangs of labor—it should be shown to the pregnant woman (the word "to her" being understood). She should give birth having experienced ease and not suffering;
it is not merely the cessation of pain, but rather this [showing of the diagram] results in an easy delivery. Thus it is said: "by seeing this..."

It is established that this is not without fruit. Regarding the yantras to be described for the purpose of the deity's desires, he first states the triple-folded yantra with the words "situated within Śakti. The phrase ending in "nāmāntam" (ending with the name) is an adjective qualifying the yantra.
"In the abode of Vahni" means in an upward-pointing triangle; this functions as a locative absolute.

The author of the *Ṭīkā* maintains that although it is a part of a compound (*vṛttaikadeśatva*), the elision of the *tva*-suffix occurs here in accordance with the usage of authoritative practitioners; thus, by accepting the elision of *tva* specifically within a qualified name, the intended meaning is obtained:
"the seed-syllable of power (*śaktivīja*) is in the center of the triangle, and within that [seed-syllable] is the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhyanāma*)."

The traditionalists (saṃpradāyavidaḥ) who have abandoned the useless proliferation of arguments maintain that the terms "sādhya" (the goal) and "sādhaka" (the means) are also indicative of the object to be accomplished and the agent of accomplishment respectively; furthermore, the word "sādhya" refers to the fruit (phala), and it is used in the accusative case, while the word "sādhaka" is used in the genitive case—
even when writing such instructions as "do this," it follows the general grammatical procedure.
"Even here, that which has not been attained [is not attained]."

According to the *Padārthādarśa*, although in reality it is stated that the term "sādhya" refers to the deity based on statements such as the *Śivatāṇḍava*, the term "sādhya" serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and so forth, according to both your own view and our own view,
regarding those who achieve the fruit and the like.

What would be inconsistent [in this view]? Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "action" (*karman*) in other systems—such as the statement that "actions are those which accomplish what is to be accomplished"—would not be necessary separately, because according to your own position, that [meaning] is already expressed by the word "the object to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) alone; for thus, the agent who is to be accomplished is the action (*karman*).
In the authoritative statement "that action and so forth," these two are mentioned separately; thus,
because there are three external corners at the tips of the outer triangle,
the symbolic writing of the three powers (*śakti*) is also implied by their very number, as each one is repeated by means of its respective power.

There is no possibility of an infinite regress regarding the nine powers and so forth; for, according to the maxim that "once a scriptural duty has been performed, it is as good as done," the use of the plural number is fulfilled by writing a single power in each of the individual corners,
and thus the effort of writing more is without basis.

The intention of the authors of the *Padārthādarśa*, who maintain that only the three capacities (*śakti*) are to be recorded here because [the other two] are purposeless efforts and are prohibited according to the principle of the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*— just as in the case of "one shall not harm any living beings"— is precisely this. It is not "in vain" (*vṛthā*).

It is also heard as a prohibition that one should not perform [more than three] actions; since the purpose of the plural number is to exclude a higher count, why would the prohibition not apply even to the preceding [lower numbers]? Therefore, just as there is no killing of four or more *piñjala* birds, so too there is no [performance of] four or more [actions] when the capacity for four or more exists.

Since even not writing [the syllable] is indeed prohibited, [the phrase] "again in the corners" (koṇagate punaḥ) means that in those very corners, delimited by the intermediate directions, it is joined with the letter *ī*—which is the fourth vowel accompanied by the bindu (*īṃ*).
This is an attribute of the yantra itself; and because there are three corners, this too is threefold.

Regarding the verse beginning with *vāraṃ kapola* and so forth: the two syllables *ha-re-ti*, which are without case endings (*nirvibhaktika*), are placed on the right side of the upper corner of the two triangles; likewise, those same two syllables are placed on the left side.
In this manner, they are written on the sides of both corners; thus, this writing is completed in three ways.

Regarding what was stated by someone that the two syllables "tu" and "hi" should be written as "vasitam," that is incorrect; for the author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that on each side of the corners there are the syllables "ha-rya" and "ha-rā," because otherwise a contradiction with that [text] would arise. On this point, the following must be said:

By which word, indeed, is it understood that this [word] follows the word *hari*? That must be stated; for even when three [words] are joined together after the word *hari*, its status as such does not disappear. Nor is it by the greatness of the word *arṇa*; for even when three [words] meet, its status as *arṇa* does not disappear. [The examples are] *harīti* and *hareti*.

If it were the case that, because such a sequence has been taught, a different sequence should not be adopted, then that would indeed be so; therefore, one should understand that the arrangement must follow the tradition exactly.
This is to be kept in mind by those who have applied their minds [to this matter]; here, the instrumental case in "kapolārppitaiḥ" is used in the sense of an instrument (upalakṣaṇe).

The meaning is that one should form a *yantra* surrounded by the four syllables *ma*, *ti*, *ya*, and *te*, combined with *ha-ri-ha-re-ti*— each joined with the vowel *rī* so as to attain five syllables— and further surrounded (*āvītam*) by the letters of the *mātṛkā*. As it has been said:

Furthermore, in the *Saṃhitā* it is said: "Between these two again, one should place the fourth [vowel] with the bindu; one should encircle it with letters and make a circle on the outside. Elsewhere also: "One should place the seed-syllable of Hari, the letters beginning with 'ha' and ending with the letter at the end of initiation (*dīkṣā*), on the outside. The seed-syllable is the fourth vowel together with the bindu.

Some, however, say that [the mantra] is surrounded by the six syllables "hariṃ īharaṃ ī," asserting that it consists of the letters of fire (ra), water (va), and fire (ra) placed in the middle. This contradicts the statement of Ācārya [Śaṅkara], who says, "by those which are equal.
Furthermore, the author of the *Sārasaṃgraha* states that after the four syllables "hari hare," there are the fourth vowel (ī) and...

They say that after this, the sequence has been shown by this writing; thus, it is established that what is written out of order does not lead to the attainment of the result. Furthermore, authoritative teachers instruct that one should first draw a circular line (*vṛttarekhā*) for the encircling (*veṣṭana*), and likewise, previously, the triangle...
From the inside out, there is space for one row each: in the first circle, the *hari-rītyata* [mantra] and so forth; in the second, the *mātṛkā*;

in the third, the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*. Then follows the drawing of the lines for the outer square. This concludes the description of the results, beginning with "saubhāgya" (good fortune) and so forth, as well as longevity (*āyuṣya*).
Having encircled [the diagram] with the *dhyāmā* and the *śakti*,

those who know the tradition understand that one should subjugate [the target] by means of the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra and the seed-syllable (*vīja*) of *śakti* for the sake of wealth, prosperity, fame, and victory; thus they teach the sixfold yantra.
By the words "the seed-syllable" (*śati vījam*) and so forth, the seed-syllable itself is introduced. Here, the locative sense is applied to the phrase "in the two fire-cities" (*vahnipuradvaye*).
The "two fire-cities" refers to two triangles joined together, which is to say, a hexagon. Thus, as before, [one should place it] in the pericarp.

The seed-syllable, with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth inserted within it, should first be surrounded five times by five *māyā* seeds; then, it should be surrounded five times by five *śrī* seeds; thereafter, an encircling with the *manmatha* seeds must be performed. Thus, one complete enclosure is formed by these fifteen seed-syllables.
The author of the *Padārthādarśa* stated that [the mantra] "resolves" (*ryavasyati*), but that is contradicted by the very root-text which has been shown;

for the teacher Padmapāda stated that there is one enclosure by means of the *māyā*-seed (*hrīm*) repeated five times. From this, it is understood that a single wrapping is complete. Hara... [text ends].

According to the statement of the Teacher, "Those [lines] which are fivefold on the outside, [forming] a circle around the *garbha*; outside that, the *śara*, the *māyā*, and the *kala-māyā*," it is clearly understood from the inclusion of the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*) that there are three enclosures (*veṣṭana*). Having drawn the fire-altar (*vahni*) thus enclosed, one should place the *Śakti* in the center.
One should employ [the seed-syllable] encircled by the letter *ṭha*, having written the *Śakti* five times on the outside;

likewise, outside of that, one should write the *Śrī-bīja* and the *Kāma-bīja*. This is in accordance with another Tantra which favors the position of three enclosures. Within the six-cornered figure (*ṣaṭkoṇa*) enclosed by the six flavors (*rasapuṭa*), [one should place] the *Sāmāka*.

The term *saviṃdu* means "possessing the bindu" (the nasal dot). Since it is "without self" (*anātmaka*)—meaning it cannot be uttered as such—it is joined with a visarga that resembles its own nature.

Thus, the resulting meaning is this: having written the three previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*) along with their bindus within the six corners, one should then write those same three seed-syllables in sequence, joined with a visarga. It is thus in this very [manner]...

The method of writing: In the upper portion, having reached the letter *ī*, one should write the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the three seed-syllables *vaṃ*, *ti*, and *sa* along with their *bindus* within the three corners. Then, proceeding clockwise, in the lower portion, having reached the letter *ra*, one should write the name of the object of practice (*sādhya*), the ritual action (*karman*), and *vaṃ* along with the *visarga* within the three corners.

It is said that one should write [the syllables] in the six corners of the outer [triangle]: in the upper portion, one should write the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) together with the *viṃdu* (bindu); these should be joined with the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). In the lower portion, those same syllables, however, should be joined with the *visarga* and endowed with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and the ritual action (*karman*).
"One should write" means that it should be joined with the names of the month (Āṣāḍha), the year (Amṛta), the goal (Sādhya), and the practitioner (Sādhaka).

"That which has the fourth vowel [I], the moon [I], and the bindu at its crest" is an adjective for the seed-syllable (*bīja*); the meaning is that the *yantra* is one in which such a seed-syllable is located. Thus it is explained by the tradition.
In this [yantra] as well, both sides should be marked with the two words "Hari Hare" as before;

its joints should be bound six times with the root-syllables (*bīja*); and it should be [further] adorned with the *lipis* (the letters of the alphabet) and the two houses of the earth (*bhūgṛha*), which are mutually intersecting.

The meaning is that one should write those two seed-syllables in the eight corners according to the following method: surrounded by two *bhūpura*s (enclosures), the *Ciṃtāmaṇi* seed-syllable in the *Īśāna* corner and the *Narasiṃha* seed-syllable in the eastern region, and so on for the other corners. As it has been said: "The syllables of Nṛsiṃha are placed in the directions of the earth, and the *Ciṃtāmaṇi* [in the others]."

Having written "Śritāsrika" there, one should draw tridents in the corners and joints; this is the specific instruction from the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. Furthermore, the teachers state that there are sixteen tridents on the outside. Thus, first [one draws] a hexagon, and inside it, three circles and a hexagon.

One circle is drawn first; then an eight-sided figure (octagon) in the form of two enclosures (*bhūpura*); outside that, another circle; and then a four-gated enclosure (*bhūpura*). This concludes the drawing of the lines. Regarding the twelve-fold yantra, it is said starting with "the seed-syllable," etc., that the house of *vasu* is a triangle, and twice that is six.
In the twelve corners of that [square], one should place the previously mentioned seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the seven *vyāhṛtis*—

namely, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *mahaḥ*, *janaḥ*, *tapaḥ*, and *satyam*— surrounding it with these in reverse order, as recited according to the traditional instruction, together with the root-mantra (*mūla*).

Thus, even when the desired result is not obtained, the practitioner should encircle [the object] with the seven vyāhṛtis in reverse order, according to the statements in the Saṃhitās and other texts; for there is no great lack of efficacy in the root mantra here, since the encirclement by the vyāhṛtis remains effective even when performed in the opposite direction.
Because of the possibility of attaining perfection, [there is] the removal of the evil associated with Durga and Durgā.

One should write the twelve *sulis* (triangles) in the corners of the three seeds; by means of pairs of letters from the well-known *Gāyatrī*, that is, by two syllables at a time from the *Gāyatrī* in reverse order (*prātilomya*). Thus, starting from the well-known eastern corner, one proceeds in reverse order along each side of every corner.

Having written two syllables and then another two syllables, twenty-four syllables will have been written within the twelve auspicious corners. Having written "vareṇiyam" instead of "vareṇyam" in that place, the completion of those syllables is achieved; thus, "outside" refers to the tips of the corners on the exterior.

The meaning is: that whose internal space (*vivaram*)—the intervening region—is bound by twelve powers (*śakti*) which are the seeds of *māyā*, delimited by specific locations. And the method of binding therein is as follows: everywhere, having circumambulated each respective seed with its own vowel and *repha* (the letter *r*), one leads it down beneath another, [skipping] every other seed.

One should bind them starting from the letter *ī*; however, those [lines] should be joined to one another at intervals of one, according to the words of the Ācāryas and others: "The inner [lines] are joined with the outer [lines], and the outer [lines] are joined with the inner [lines].
This same principle of being bound at intervals of one is also found in the *Mantramuktāvalī* and other such works.

The reasoning for this has been stated: by binding each individual *tara* (syllable), the binding of the seed-syllables situated in one's own *triṣṭubh* [mantra] is accomplished. Furthermore, the *triṣṭubh* mantra beginning with "jātavedase" and so forth will become clear in the twenty-second chapter; this encircling (*veṣṭana*) is also [to be performed].
Relying precisely on the reverse order, one should surround the outside of its corners and sides with the *mātṛkā* letters—
both in direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) order— in accordance with the statement of another *tantra*: "One should encircle it with the *mātṛkā*, both in direct and reverse order."

In accordance with the statement in the *Ritisaṃhitā*, he shows another yantra—beginning with "one should write" (*likhet*) and so forth—which serves as an equal commentary on the expansion of the mantra starting with "Dhara" (*dhareti*) and its sixfold multiplication. One should write [the letters] in the center, in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and in all six petals; however, this is the distinction: that it is specifically in the pericarp...
The inscription of the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth is prescribed elsewhere, whereas in this case it is written alone;

thus he describes another yantra with the words beginning with "six" (*ṣaḍ-*) and so on. Here, it appears that even within the six central triangles (*ṣaṭkoṇa*), there is an inscription of the *māyā* containing the name of the person to be accomplished at its beginning; indeed, that very [syllable] contains the person to be accomplished within it.

Because of this statement, some say that even in the previous yantra, one should write the *māyāvīja* (the seed-syllable of Māyā) containing the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and others within the seven locations.
He states another mantra with the words beginning "Vāgbhava," etc. With the word "madhyena" (in the middle), he describes the application (*prayoga*) together with the consort of Śambhu.
With the words beginning "hutvā" (having offered oblations), he describes the further application (*prayogāntara*).

If, despite being engaged in the performance of that [rite] with great intensity and strength, success is not attained on a single day, then the procedure should be performed three times. If there is still no success after three attempts, another repetition may be undertaken based on such scriptural statements as "the rite should be done with five lamps," and so forth; however, this [present case] is not for that purpose.

The sense of "geṇeti" is as follows: by performing *homa* with sesame seeds (*tila*) and rice (*taṇḍula*) mixed together, one shall attain the glory of sovereignty (*rājya-śrī*); this is the meaning. Having previously stated the seed-syllables (*vīja*) of Bhuvaneśvarī, he now states another mantra beginning with "vāgvīja," etc. [The word] "vāgbha... [refers to the Vāgbhava].

He states that the six-limbed nyāsa (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the *māyā* mantra joined at the beginning and end by the syllables *va-vī-jā-bhyāṃ*, and conjoined with the six long vowels.

Starting with the words "in the middle" (*madhyena*), he describes the meditation on the Mothers, which bestows gifts, boons, and the removal of fear— that is, the *abhaya-mudrā*— and their respective counts of twenty-four hundred thousand (*caturviṃśati-lakṣa*).
By the words beginning with "Bhairava," it is meant that each [deity] is mounted upon a single square in sequence.

This is to be meditated upon; for it has been stated that the eight Bhairavas, such as Asitāṅga and the others, are mounted upon the squares of the Bhairavas, and this is mentioned here for the sake of that knowledge, as they are useful in certain instances for the worship of Bhairava.

Many authors of the *Padārthadarśa* maintain that the statement "beginning with short vowels" (*hrasvādyāḥ*) is intended here to demonstrate, in this very context, the specific details regarding the mantras previously mentioned; however, others hold that the mention of Bhairava is for the purpose of establishing the practical application of the mantra *āṃ vrāhme namaḥ* to the one residing in the heart of Añjasa-tāṅga-Bhairava.

As for the claim that [the suffixes] beginning with *hrasva* are [included] by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), that is to be considered carefully; for the root [of the rule] can be construed otherwise, and there is no evidence for such an application [of the suffixes]. Furthermore, it would follow that forms such as *smeravaktrāyai* and *madālasāyai* would also fall within the scope of this application. Now, [if you object]: "But surely... [the text continues].

If it is argued that there is no insistence on the non-application of the portion that is useful, then what [is the point]? Is it not the case that those who have ascended to the lap of Bhairava do not apply themselves to meditation? Furthermore, even the vowels *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *o*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ*—namely, the first of the eight short vowels—attain the state of being an obscuration (*āvaraṇatā*) to Bhairava. Thus, the first of the eight short vowels, consisting of the forms *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *o*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ*, [functions in this way].

Having extracted the mantras of the Mothers beginning with *Ā, Ī, Ū, Ṛ, Ḷ, E, AI, O, AU*, and having performed their worship, one should extract the eight long vowels— *Ā, Ī, Ū, Ṝ, Ḷ, E, AI, O, AU*— and perform the worship of those Mother-mantras (*mātṛmantra*).
As for the claim that the nature of these two as obscurations (*āvaraṇatva*) is either distinct or one— that is another matter—

it has already been stated previously that it is the word of the Blessed One alone that establishes the distinction between obscurations; yet even that [claim] is [refuted] by demonstrating that the root text is more consistent when interpreted otherwise, as [Bhairava...]

Since there is no evidence for [the mantra] being a name-mantra (*nāmāvaraṇa*), he demonstrates that another mantra— the root mantra for the jar, bolt, and yantra which are to be described— beginning with "Ananta," etc.
In such statements as "the three-syllable [mantra] beginning with *pāśa* residing in the belly," the word "pāśa" and so forth [is used].

In order to establish the origin [of the mantra], he states the number of syllables of the mantra with the words beginning "pāśa," preceded by the recitation of the name of the first seed-syllable (*bīja*), for the purpose of dispelling the delusion that [the mantra] refers to the essential nature of Brahmā, Agni, and so forth. The word "with the seed" (*vījena*) means with the *māyā*-seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*) joined with the six long vowels; this is the implied meaning. Some...

The singular number [in the word *tuvījena*] is intended to indicate that each individual limb is to be assigned by means of one seed-syllable (*vīja*), or two, or all three; thus, this refers to the assignment of limbs by repeating the triad of seed-syllables twice, such that each limb is assigned by means of a single seed-syllable— this is the intended meaning.

Thus they say: "Hṛllekhā," and so forth. Here, the sixteen-petaled lotus on the outside is to be made; for the author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that there is no mention here of those [deities] who are to be worshipped at the navel. One should offer that thousand—that is, a thousand oblations of the *tattvas*—excellently, according to the procedure taught in the *tantra*.

One should offer oblations according to one’s own will, with that same number as previously established; [the result is] Vaiśravaṇa himself, possessing a Vaiśravaṇa-like prosperity neither deficient nor excessive— surely it would not be a prosperity less than that— or like the Sun-god, by virtue of having a chariot drawn by seven horses, or through his designation.

In response to the inquiry as to whether [he is so called] by means of all qualities such as being "attainable" (*llabhya*) and so forth, he says "by his splendor" (*tejasā*) and so on. Since the word *rāja* (king) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) to refer specifically to a protector of subjects distinguished by qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and thus the [status of] his wife would not be attained [by that term alone], he further says "his wife also" (*tatpatnīm api*) in order to establish it.

[The phrase] "with this mantra" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Now, he demonstrates the dhāraṇā-yantra named Ghaṭārgala for this mantra, beginning with the words "one should draw," etc. First, having produced an eight-cornered figure consisting of two squares as previously described, [one should draw] the lines situated within the eight corners.

One should extend all [the lines] straightly so that, like two lines joined together in the middle, they take on a shape similar to a small drum (*kṣudraduṇḍubhi*); having extended them such that there is a junction at the tips of the bolts (*argalāgra*), one should draw a single circle, and upon each of the eight sides, one [mark].
Just as the formation of the *koṣṭha* occurs, one should draw the intervening space within it;

the meaning is also stated in the *Padārthādarśa* treatise as "having fashioned two circles on both sides of the center of the *dundubhi*. Thereafter, from the outer circle, there are eight lines between the *dundubhis*.
Starting from two [lines], one should fashion eight petals with filaments resembling a bolt (argala),

and at the end of the three circles, one should draw a jar encircled by upward-facing and downward-facing lotuses; this is the method for constructing the body of the yantra, as stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*.

For the ultimate benefit, one should join the two circles by forming them into a hollowed pair; O Goddess, it becomes as beautiful to the eye and mind as an eight-cornered figure. Then, O Goddess, the practitioner should draw lines from the tips toward the eight directions, and with those two lines, he should fashion a beautiful, bolt-like shape at the base.

Then, one should form that [shape] at the front like the disc of the moon; then again, drawing it inward from within, the best of practitioners should draw an excellent circle as before. Then, in due order, he should clearly delineate a pair of eight squares (aṣṭakoṣṭha), as well as two sets of eight corners and beautiful crossbars (argalā).

Just as [the syllables] are clearly manifest, there, in the center, the root mantra of the entire sādhya—consisting of the three syllables beginning with *pāśa*—should be written. In the middle of the *māyā-bīja*, one should write the name of the sādhya as before. In the eight squares connected to the square, the *hṛdaya* [mantra]...
The eight syllables of the mantra beginning with *pāśa* (the noose) are to be written in the squares immediately following those of the limbs (*aṅga*).

In the eight squares following that, the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *kāminī* is to be written. On the bolts (*argala*), one should write the seed-syllables extracted starting with "apūrva" and so forth. In the pairs of intermediate squares, [the syllables] are arranged from top to bottom.
One should gradually write the sixteen syllables upon the sixteen squares on a copper plate.

Here too, the drawing of the protective circle (rakṣācakra) on the outside of the square with its four gates is not specifically mentioned because it is obtained from other general scriptures; nevertheless, it should not be forgotten, as it involves the writing there of the yantra, the Gāyatrī, the seed-syllables of the world-protectors (dikpāla), the maṇḍala, and their respective mantras.

Outside the original pitcher, one should draw a square with four doors and two inner circles; therein, even the mantra for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and its inscription must not be neglected, for this is not an ordinary yantra, such that it would be governed by the general procedure for ordinary yantras.

One should meditate on the mantra as reaching [the heart], situated within the pericarp of the navel. Here, the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth are to be indicated in the center.

In the four corner-cells starting from the southeast (āgneya), one should write the limbs beginning with the Heart and ending with the Vaśya-mantra. In the center of the pericarp, one should write the Eye (Netra), and in the four cardinal cells, the Weapon (Astra).

Having first written the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* (the noose) in the eight outer squares of the *khet*, one should then write the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *kāminī* in the eight outer squares. Regarding the phrase "beginning with *ava*" and so forth: the six [syllables] beginning with *ava* are *ā, ī, ī, u, ū, ṛ*.

The six vowels *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, and *aṃ*— these being of such a form— and likewise the four letters beginning with *la*, each joined with the aforementioned vowels, are those in which the "seat" (*āsana*) of the letter *ha*, representing space (*vyoman*), is established; such are the [syllables] preceded by Indra, Varuṇa, and the others.
In the sequence beginning from the west, according to the order of the three syllables by way of their qualities,

having formed two rows from [the first] two rows— and not merely in a single row— one should place each set of three syllables in a single row, starting from the eastern side and proceeding downward in order toward the northern direction.

Having written [the first three syllables] up to the end of the bolt on the right side, one should likewise write three syllables starting from the tip of the second bolt in the second row, extending as far as the circle;
these being (–) (–), namely *hrāṃ hūṃ hūṃ*. Then, of that [bolt], at the western bolt—

One should write the syllables *ma*, *pye*, *va*, *hrehraiṃ*, *hrauṃ*, *hrauṃ*, *huṃ*, and *haḥ* there, just as before, with three syllables in each of the two rows; this should also be understood for the eastern and southern [sections]. In this way, twelve syllables are written for the letter *hra*.

In that very same way, one should not write the vowels with the *su-bindu* (anusvāra) following the letter *ha* in the south-eastern, western, and northern directions; thereafter, one should write the six long vowels in the north-western intermediate direction following that;
then, in the southern direction, one should [write] the *ha* together with its *su-bindu* from the east onwards.

Having written the six vowels [starting with *a*] in the west, one should then write the six long vowels from north to south. Then, having written the six vowels including the nasal bindu of the syllable *hraḥ* in the southeast starting from the east, one should write the six long vowels in the northeast from that westward.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "Take the seed-syllable of Śakra (the letter *śa*), endowed with water (*va*), Brahmā (*la*), and the bindu and space (*ha*); join it with the vowels in sequence, excluding the neuter ones. O beautiful one, divide that single syllable twelvefold, and therein make four divisions. The twelve [syllables] beginning with the vowel-forms are devoid of the neuter ones."
Through the sequential union of the twelve vowels with a single seed-syllable, it becomes twelvefold;

by drawing lines for the eastern and western paths in the sequence of two rows of two, it is described as fourfold in its circular form. One should write the end of the petals in the directions starting from the top half in the correct order, with the first triad facing east as the primary direction.
"O beloved, one should draw [the second circle] to the north; then, to its south, [one should draw] the end of the circle starting from the east.

Thus, having drawn from the south up to the end of the bolt (argalā), and from the tip of the bolt to the north up to the end of the circle, there is a line on the western bolt. That third [circle] is described in the west.
One should draw [the lines] in the south-eastern portion; likewise, one should draw the fourth path-line there, and similarly draw it in the north.

Here, by the phrase "third" and so forth, as well as the words "likewise" and "similarly," the intention is that for each of the thirty-two seed-syllables, there are four parts (aṃśas) formed by three vowels each.

The sequence beginning with *vṛta* and so forth has been stated in the *Āgneya-purāṇa*: having first written [the letters] in the northern direction, one should subsequently write them starting from the west in the southern part. As it is said:
"Having left the earth [element], one should place the wind [element] there among the solar seeds (*arkabīja*); [this applies] to the three *argalās* of fire."
One should first draw the eastern [line]; likewise, from the west, one should draw this triad on the southern side.
Regarding the northwest bolt (vāyavyārgalā), having first drawn it from the west, one should subsequently draw it on the southern side from the east.
As it was stated regarding the northwest bolt, so should one draw it from the west first; then, in the northern portion, one should draw it from the east toward the south.

"One should draw the triad" means: on the southern bolt as well, having written the three seed-syllables starting from the north toward the east, one should write them starting from the west toward the east;
on the northern bolt, [starting] from the east...

In the northwestern direction, from west to east, having omitted the wind [seed-syllable], one should place Varuṇa where the sun [was mentioned]; the first triad in the south, the second in the east, and the third triad in the west;
then, for the northern bolt, there is a triad from east to west.
One should draw the fourth [line] from the east toward the southern part.
Regarding the bolt (argalā) in the southwest (nairṛtya), the beginning is in the east and the end is in the south; then, starting from the west toward the north, the drawing extends to the east.
Regarding the bolt in the northeast (īśāna), the beginning is in the north and the end is in the west.

The commencement is from the west toward the east. As it has been stated: having removed the vowel *ī* from the seed-syllables of the Sun (*arka*), one should insert the letter *ra* there. The practitioner should write the first *tri-kāma* (the three *kāmas*) and the subsequent *tri-kāma* upon the *argalā* (bolt) of the blood [mantra], from south to north in sequence; furthermore, the *śaiva-argalā* is likewise at the beginning and end.
From the southwest corner of the goddess [the diagram], extending to the very end of the west on all sides,
this is the *argalā* (bolt), which consists of sixteen syllables of the mantra— equivalent to eight pairs of letters— situated in the sixteen squares located below the intermediate space.
Then, one should write [the syllables] "aṃ, āṃ," and so forth, in the midst of the short and long vowels within the filaments (*kesara*).

The mantra of the Self (*ātma-mantra*) is of the form "haṃ si. [The seed-syllable of] Māyā is the fourth vowel. Thus, the seven-syllabled mantra beginning with "aṃ haṃ saḥ īṃ haṃsaḥ āṃ" should be written, as it has been said: "Haṃsaḥ pa..."

Having again written the syllable *haṃsa* adorned with the *daṃvāmanetra* (the eye of the dwarf, i.e., *i*) and the vowel *u*, one should inscribe the seven-syllabled mantra situated within a pair of vowels (*a* and *ā*), which thus becomes eightfold. Then, on its petals, having arranged three rows from bottom to top, one should write the original three-syllabled root-mantra.

Then, one should draw a path (vīthī) outside of that, forming a single enclosure with nooses (pāśa) and hooks (aṅkuśa). Having completed this for the full yantra, one should make a second enclosure outside of that using the *mātṛkā* in direct order (*anuloma*), and a third enclosure using the *mātṛkā* in reverse order (*pratiloma*). Thus it is said: "three times with nooses," and so forth.

Some say that there should be a threefold encirclement by the *pāśa* and *aṅkuśa* alone, two [encirclements] surrounded by the *mātṛkā*, and another outside of those; they say that this very thing should be encircled by the *pāśa* and *aṅkuśa* in a circular form on the outside, with the *mātṛkā* encirclement in the direct order (*anuloma*).

The statement that "in the same way, the wrapping with the Mātṛkās should be done in reverse order" is to be disregarded, as it contradicts other Tantras. The term "Ghaṭārgala" (the bolt of the jar) is an etymological designation derived from the drawing of the jar and the bolts; it [destroys] even the kings who serve as the support for all mortals.

To indicate the purpose of subjugating mortals—namely, "subjugation by means of poison"—the word *viṣeṇa* (by poison) connects with the phrase "he shall subjugate all mortals. However, according to the literal reading (*yathāśruta*), because the qualifying term is not displaced, it would be understood as "the lord of the earth" (*mahīpati*); and this is not appropriate.
Regarding the yogas for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), there is a specific method for easily subjugating kings;

however, as for other mortals who are not so easily subjugated, since the purpose—namely, the attraction of women for the sake of enjoyment—is achieved in some way or another, it is a matter of established fact (*apūrva*). Thus, there is a distinction in the attraction of women for the sake of enjoyment.

By the words "māha nīlapadaiḥ" and so forth, it is indicated that the time of application is seven days and so on, not the time of the result; otherwise, there would arise the expectation as to how long the term "constantly" (nityam) extends. By the phrase "smaravihvalām," it is shown that the attraction is not merely [of the body].
It is not merely that this [mantra] is accomplished, but rather that it also brings about enjoyment according to one's own desire;

thus, by the word "desired" (*vāñchitam*), it is stated that one should bring about even an impossible enjoyment. "Having written" (*vilikhya*) means having prepared the liquid substance with the pen employed.
In the writing of the *ṇa*-letter itself, a specific distinction must be intended for its composition.

Regarding that which has been established as being drenched with clarified butter (*ājya*) through the conjunction [of mantras], he states the internal difference beginning with "vajra" and so forth: within the two cities of fire (the hexagon), one should visualize the *māyā*—that is, the seed-syllable of the noose (*pāśabīja*)—bound by both the noose and the goad.

The meaning results as follows: one should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) three times, encapsulated by *kuśa* seeds; thus, when writing the *māyā* three times according to its qualities (*guṇaśas*), it possesses a threefold nature. Furthermore, the sense is that one should write that *māyā* three times between the *pāśa* and the *aṅkuśa*. This refers to the reading "on birch-bark" (*bhūrje*) or "in a lotus" (*saroje*).

May that [work] reach completion, which was composed by one whose mother was Udyotamatī, whose father was Satiguṇavatī, whose name was Māpati, who was born into the Paṃtha family, whose birthplace was Kūrmācala, who made Vārāṇasī his residence, and who took refuge in the feet of Acyuta, the Lord of Vācya, through well-practiced valor.

[In the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*, the chapter on *Toṅka*: Since the mantra of Tvaritā was previously taught as something to be written down, [the author], in response to the expectation for that, teaches its mantra with the words beginning "That," etc. And this being so, it follows immediately after the chapter on Mahālakṣmī.
It should not be said that this designation is improper because it has entered into those very two ends located at the edge of that section;
for the phrase "endowed with Śrī and Śaktimāra" is mentioned first right there,
and thus the definition of the seed-syllable of Śakti, which was stated first, is indeed primary.
The sense is that it is appropriate to compose [the mantra] in this manner. Then, following the *Bhuvaneśī* mantra,

by the phrase "bestowing fruit swiftly" (*tvarita-phaladāyinīm*), it is implied— rather than being based on mere conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone— that there is a *yoga-rūḍhi* (a combination of etymological and conventional meaning), since the quality of bestowing fruit swiftly is not found in other mantras.

Furthermore, because of the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the term *tvepi*, it will be explained as "swift" (*tvaritā*); this is indicated by the first quarter [of the verse], and thus there is such an application there. "Prosperity" (*ṛddhi*) is the letter *s*; for the digit known as prosperity (*ṛddhi-saṃjñaka-kakalā*) arises from the letter *s*. In that regard, when there is a conjunction of vowels (*svarasaṃyoga*), it is *khe*.

Thus, *kūrma* (the tortoise) is established as *ka*; with the letter *cha* at its end, joined with its portion, the eleventh vowel (*ī*), *che* is established. *Kṣa* is the form of the woman (*strī*). *Dīrghatanu* (long-bodied) is the covering (*chada*), which is the syllable *hūṃ*. *Saṃvarta* is the letter *kṣa*. Thus, *oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ khe cha che kṣaḥ strī hūṃ kṣe*.

The mantra "hrīṃ phaṭ," consisting of twelve syllables, has been extracted; here, the word "mantra" is to be understood as the remainder [of the phrase], and it also connects with the term "twelve-syllabled" (*dvādaśākṣara*) in that very context. The word "pair" (*yugma*) is used to indicate the attainment of two locations on the thighs, in the order from right to left; by that, the syllable is placed there.
Regarding the "placement of pairs" (*dvayanyāsa*): although there are two locations, such as the knees and so forth, the placement is performed by repeating each individual syllable.
Thus, it is established that the eleven syllables are placed sequentially upon the eleven locations. However, according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*, even the two *māyās* [are included].

By the phrase "deceived by illusion" (māyayāvarjitān), that [position] is refuted; thus, they say that the placement (nyāsa) of the ten vowels alone should be performed, while the placement of only a single vowel should be performed on the pair of thighs. This is not correct, as it would result in the pair of thighs being rendered meaningless.
Since there is a twofold division even regarding the locations such as the knees (*jānu*) and so forth, stating it as such in only one of those places would result in an inconsistency with the text.

It is possible that the statement was made in that manner to indicate that, according to our own view, the two locations belong only to the *ūrū* (thighs) and not to the knees and other parts. This interpretation is plausible.

By the word "māyayā" (by illusion), because of the singular number and its position as the first [word], only one illusion is perceived; thus, everything is faultless. However, in your view, even the singular number is more unsatisfactory, so this [objection] is of no consequence. By the entire compound, the twelve-syllable mantra...
By the word "only" (*eva*), as before, the exclusion of being devoid of *māyā* is established.
The ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the seven syllables beginning with *kūrma* and ending with *cakāra*.
In that regard, the subsequent limbs should be assigned by means of two syllables at a time, excluding each preceding pair.
Although by the phrase "each preceding [part]" (*pūrvapūrva*) and so forth, the abandonment of each preceding limb-mantra (*aṅgamantra*) appears to be indicated, this is not intended;

for it is intended that the limb-mantra consists of the successive adoption of one syllable at a time, through the abandonment of only the first syllable of each preceding part. Nevertheless, of the preceding...

The intended meaning of the phrase "devoid of the first [letter] of the preceding mantra" is that it refers to the very first syllable of the preceding mantra; however, since each subsequent [mantra] consists of only a single syllable,
it follows by implication that only one syllable is to be excluded from the first mantra, resulting in the retention of that single syllable.

Since only a single phoneme is required [for each position], it is understood from the subsequent [verses] that the third phoneme is effectively excluded by the two [preceding ones]. Although it would be more appropriate for the phrase "by the two" (*dvābhyām*) to qualify "being devoid of each preceding one," nevertheless, this is done out of consideration for the meter (*chandaḥ*).

Even that which is performed with specific distinctions such as the *kūrma* [mudrā] and so forth ultimately results in being characterized by those two alone; thus, for example, *vaṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *che kṣaḥ śirase svāhā*, and so forth, ending with *kṣe hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ*.
The authors of the *Harṣakaumudī* maintain that these six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) thus conclude.

However, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* states: "The first [syllable] of the Tortoise is *kha*; the plural number is used in the sense of 'beginning with' (*ādyartha*), meaning 'with *kha* and the others. With the seven syllables ending in *kṣa*, together with *phaṭ* and the *praṇava* (oṃ)."

Having extracted this very mantra consisting of nine syllables, the seventh group of letters beginning with the fourth [syllable] should consist of seven letters; by means of those, the limbs (aṅgas) should be made of two letters each—this is the instruction based on the statement in another Tantra. And thus: *khe ca* for the heart, *namaḥ*.

They say that the mantras for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) conclude as follows: *che śiraḥ svāhā*, *che kṣaḥ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *kṣaḥ strī kavacāya huṃ*, *strīṃ huṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *hūṃ kṣe astrāya phaṭ*. Furthermore, it has been stated previously that [this deity] is devoid of *māyā*.

The mother and father must be followed accordingly; likewise, regarding the sixth [syllable] "cakṣephaḍ," there is a distinction based on the previous tradition. As it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*, concerning the previously mentioned ten-syllable mantra, starting from the fourth syllable of the *vidyā* with seven [syllables].
Then, one should perform the assignment of the limbs (*aṅga*) using pairs of syllables in a sequence of six for both the hands and the limbs.
Thus: *che* and *kṣe* as a pair at the heart; then *kṣaḥ* and *strī* as a pair at the crest (*śikhā*);
*strī* and *hūṃ* as a pair for the armor (*kavaca*); likewise *huṃ* and *kṣe* as a pair for the eyes (*netra*). Having thus assigned them, [one proceeds] with *kṣe*.

Regarding the statement, "Phaṭ is proclaimed as the Astra," although the letter-assignment (varṇanyāsa) was mentioned immediately after the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), it should not be performed in that manner; rather, the letter-assignment must follow the six-limbed assignment. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the *Tantrarāja*, for that [work] states the same in its root text regarding the complete mantra.

Having stated the application (*viniyoga*) of the three syllables, it appears that the author intends to state the application of a few more syllables; with this in mind, he describes the meditation (*dhyāna*) beginning with the words "śyāmām" and so forth,
[connecting it] with the phrase "bearing the eight hoods that have reached the neck and other parts."
Among them, Ananta and Kulika were of the Brahmin caste and appeared in the form of earrings;

Sukīśa and Śaṅkhapāla were of the Kṣatriya caste and appeared in the form of bracelets (the latter being synonymous with *aṅgada*); Takṣaka and Mahāpadma were of the Vaiśya caste and appeared in the form of waist-bands; [and] Karkoṭaka and Padma...

The two [Nāgas] Nāna and Auśūdra are to be known as having attained the state of anklets; as it has been said: "O King, the Brāhmaṇas are adorned with snake-earrings, the Kṣatriyas with snake-armlets, the Vaiśyas with snake-belt-bands, and likewise the Śūdras with snake-anklets. Furthermore, Ananta and Kulika are declared to be the two Brāhmaṇas, possessing the color of fire. Thus, each [is assigned].
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are adorned with a thousand hoods and are to be known as Kṣatriyas of red complexion; Takṣaka and Mahāpadma are the two lords of serpents who are Vaiśyas;
and Padma and Karkoṭa are of blue complexion, possessing five hundred hoods upon their heads.

*Kauśūdrauphaṇātriṃśatakausitau* refers to one serpent in the form of a small bell (*kṣudraghaṇṭikā*) and another serpent in the form of a string (*guṇa*). When Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava, was performing austerities for the sake of the *pāśupata* weapon, [he encountered Śiva] in the form of a Kirāta.
At that time, Bhavānī also assumed the guise of a Kirāta woman;

she was dark-limbed, wore a crown made of peacock feathers, fashioned her own garments from leaves, her heavy breasts were adorned with a necklace of guñjā berries, and she was decorated with ornaments made of the eight nāgas and other beings. She was bestowed by Śiva.
Then, O Pāṇḍava Arjuna, that goddess was propitiated by him with the previously mentioned twelve-syllable mantra; therefore, he became the first proclaimer of that mantra among men.
Knowing the mantra, [he recited]: "Oṃ hrīṃ namo nitye svāhā"—this is the eight-syllable mantra. "Oṃ namaḥ... [and so forth].

The mantra consisting of twenty-nine syllables— *bhagavateśavarāya mahākirātarūpāya kaṅkāladharāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*— as well as the five-syllable *Śiva* mantra (*kiṃkara* mantra), are for the purpose of attaining knowledge of them; first, for one who worships this *vidyā*:

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that according to another Tantra, the recitation of the secondary mantras (*upamantra*) is prescribed at a one-hundredth part of the recitation of the primary mantra (*mukhyamantra*), such as the *Trasyajapa*. Regarding the passage beginning with "Hṛllekhā" and so forth,
here too the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is indeed eight-petalled, because there is an absence of a mantra for the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*) among those sixteen to be worshipped.
As it has been stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "One should draw an eight-petaled lotus and encircle it with the diagrams of fire and earth.
In the center, one should place the two Lords of the World (*Bhuvaneśānau*), and outside, one should surround them with the *Mātṛkā* letters.
This is declared to be the 'Wheel that Grants All Protection. Having invoked the Goddess therein, one should worship her with the ritual offerings (*upacāras*)."

The meaning is that by maintaining this worship mantra, "su-kalpitaiḥ" (well-prepared), it becomes a provider of protection against all [harm]. He extracts the seat mantra beginning with "saṃvarttaka," etc.; "kalā" indicates the half-moon and the bindu. "Vajradeha" is its essential nature; [the seed-syllable] is *kṣiṃ*.
Thus, the essential form [of the mantra] is as follows: the final letter *kṣa* should be joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the second vowel (*ā*), resulting in *kṣāṃ*.
The essential form for "to the five-faced one" (*pañcānana*) is the heart-mantra *namaḥ*. Likewise, the mantra is: *kṣaṃ huṃ haṃ vajradeha puru purukṣiṃ gulugulugarja garja huṃ huṃ kṣāṃ pañcānana*.
The thirty-syllable mantra for the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) has been extracted as "yanamaḥ" and so forth.

He now describes the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) with the words beginning "with the limbs" (*aṅgaiḥ*): one should worship the six limbs on the filaments in the east and other directions; then, on the filaments in the north (Kubera) and northeast (Īśāna), one should worship Praṇītā and Gāyatrī.

The meaning here is as follows: although there is a specific statement regarding the eyes, the worship of the filaments (*kesara*) is performed by the presiding deity of this [mandala] alone; thus, the distinction from the previous case is that the worship of the filaments is performed as a single unit according to the sequence obtained. Having worshipped the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*) on the filaments as before, once again—on the filaments...

The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* states that after worshipping the *praṇītā* vessel in eight ways within all [the petals], one should again worship Gāyatrī in the same manner. Regarding this, it says: "There, one should worship the eight [deities] on the pericarp;
the deities of the limbs starting with the East [should be worshipped] in the North-East; the *praṇītā* in the North, and Gāyatrī in the Northeast."

The phrase "contrary to other tantras" (yedititantrāntaraviruddham) refers to the weapons and ornaments of these [goddesses] being like those of the world-protectors (lokeśānām), such as Indra and the others; this is the meaning. This is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for their vehicles and colors; by that, [it includes] Airāvata and so forth, which have forms identical to Indra and the others.

It has been stated that the eight Śaktis—Vāhanā, Vajrā, and so forth, beginning with Āyudhā and Huṃkāryā—arise in sequence. Herein, there is a distinction: the first [syllable] begins with the letter *ka* (Kavaca), the second with the first letter [of the series], the seventh with the long vowel [corresponding to the first letter], and the eighth with the letter *ti*. Since all [of these] begin with the seed-syllable *Śrī*, [the mantra for the first Śakti is] *Śrīṃ Huṃkāryai*.

The mantras beginning with "Namaḥ śrīṃ khecarīyai nam" and so forth are concluded; some offer only the syllable "Śrīṃ" at the outset before the Goddess’s face. However, outside of these, on the exterior part of the door—that is, the door of the *bhūpura*—one should recite "Phaṭ kāryai nam".

Having worshipped Jayā and Vijayā respectively on the right and left sides as prescribed by the general scripture, Kiṅkara is to be worshipped outside the door; he recites his mantra beginning with "Kiṅkara," etc.: "O Kiṅkara, protect, protect, O swift one! (kiṅkarāya rakṣa rakṣa tvarite).

The mantra for the worship of the *kiṃkara* consists of eighteen syllables: *jñāsthirobhavahuṃphaṭ*. Regarding the meditation on the *kiṃkara*: his hair is black, dark-hued, coarse, and curly; he has hair upon his head—this is the visualization of the *kiṃkara*. Here, the Lord of the World (*lokeśāna*) is to be worshipped.

Since those very powers (śaktis), such as Hukārī and the others, possess that very nature [of the Goddess], it is therefore appropriate for them to bear those weapons and so forth; for this reason, some maintain that the worship of Indra and the other deities was not taught in the root text regarding Prakṛti. Others, however, hold that one should worship Indra and the others in female forms.

However, it is stated in the *Totalāmata*: "One should worship the lords of the directions in the form of women on the outer enclosure. Others, however, say that although the worship of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*) and so forth was not explicitly mentioned in the root text, it was already taught previously as a general rule and is therefore not prohibited here either.

Intending to state that forest-grown substances are recommended for the worship of this Goddess, he says "āraṇyaiḥ," which means "produced in the forest. He states the ritual applications with the words beginning with "yonau" and so forth;
here, in the application of the fire-oblation (*homa*) for this deity, elsewhere it is according to the distinction of specific desires.

The selection of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) such as the *turyasravra*, circular, lotus-shaped, or hexagonal is intended here for a specific deity through the adoption of one or another of these; the meaning is that it depends on the specific requirement.

"According to one's own wish" means: when there is a desire for the teacher’s rite, [one follows] the number of the teachers; when there is a desire for the disciple’s rite, [one follows] the number of the disciples.

The meaning is that the number of items to be taken should be small; as it is said in another Tantra: "The number of oblations may be a thousand, or a thousand plus three times ten thousand; the skillful practitioner should act after deliberating upon lightness or heaviness in the ritual. [The flowers] *mallikā* and *camelī* are [known] in the vernacular as...

The *siddhā* [mudrā] is prepared with rice-husks from threshing, *akṣa* fruits (*vibhītaka*), consecrated with this mantra, and combined with the remnants of oblations (*saṃpāta*) from previous fire-offerings; it is fashioned as a ring from equal parts of the three metals and, when worn, brings success.

It is said that [this mantra] destroys the fear of obstacles caused by unchaste women and others, beginning with the words "triloha" and so forth. Regarding the general procedure for drawing the yantra, the *Gāyatrī* [mantra] is obtained from another tantra as follows: one should extract the word "vidmahe" after the word "tvaritā," O Goddess, and [the word] "tūrṇim vidyām."

"Dhīmahi, that [we may] contemplate; tat naḥ devī pracodayāt—may the Goddess impel us. Thus he states the *dhāraṇa-mantra* for Gāyatrī and Tvaritā, which brings about their presence through recitation, beginning with the words "in the center" (*madhye*) and so forth:
"In the center of the lotus," that is, in the middle of the lotus, within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of ten sets of ten lotuses.

One should draw a lotus with ten petals, outside of which is a hexagon, and outside of that a square; there, in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should place the *māyā* seed-syllable (*vīja*), and within that seed-syllable, one's own desired object—the goal to be accomplished, such as a son, wealth, and so forth—along with the words "quickly grant! (*bhoh tvarite*).

The word for the deity of the *yantra* in its natural form, ending in the vocative case— by this it is implied that the word for the deity should be written in other *yantras* as well; and this is appropriate, otherwise the verb such as "do" (*kuru*) written in the *karṇikā* would remain expectant of a subject.
In the context of the *Hanumantra*,
he clearly instructed that one should write "protect, protect" (*rakṣa rakṣa*) for the sake of this lord; furthermore, according to the *Sudarśana-saṃhitā*,
one should write the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) along with the ritual action and other details, as stated in that *Saṃhitā*.

Regarding the two-footed [yantra], he states another yantra: "Tāre-huṃ. *Tāra* is the thirteenth vowel (Ū) with the bindu (ŪṂ). Having written the *praṇava* (OṂ) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should write the syllable *huṃ*—which is the form of the armor (*kavaca*)—within it; within that, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the desired object (*kāmanā*), and so forth, as well as the letters of the mantra and the two *māyās*.

Having performed the encirclement three times with the *māyā*-seed syllable (*hrīṃ*) devoid of the *tāra* (the *oṃ*), one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus below that and place a jar upon it. Inside that [jar], this yantra should be drawn; at the beginning of this yantra, on the lotus denoted by the word "mouth" (*mukha*), [one should draw]...

Because it is situated [there], there is no knowledge [of it]; thus, the internal and external arrangement of the names and the like of the armor-mantras (kavaca), which are to be accomplished through the ritual of visualization (saṃjñā), cannot be obtained without that which is established here.
He states another yantra with the words beginning "of the squares" (koṣṭhānām), which is oriented from east to west.
By drawing twelve lines extending both north-south and east-west, one hundred and twenty-one squares are produced. Therein,

having written the Praṇava (Oṃ) joined with the names of the practitioner, the object of practice, and so forth, in the central square, one should [write] the Praṇava in sequence starting from Īśāna (the northeast) toward Śiva (the center).

One should write the aforementioned root mantra—which has attained a state of ten syllables by being deprived of the seed-syllables *vaṃ* and *māyā* (*hrīṃ*)—twelve times. After reciting it forty-eight times repeatedly, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed; the pouring of the remnants (*saṃpāta*) therein has already been explained in this section.

Some say that in the case of *abhicāra* (malevolent rites), one should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) and so forth within the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Mṛtyuñjaya; in the case of *vaśya* (subjugation), within the seed-syllable of Māyā; and for the attainment of prosperity (*śrī*), within the seed-syllable of Śrī. Where, then, is the writing of the *praṇava* as stated in the root text [to be applied]?

If it is argued that this is the task to be performed, they must be asked: "Is it for the sake of the desire for liberation? If so, then since such a fruit would originate from this very yantra, one would have to search for other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); furthermore, this statement could even be explained as having another meaning. He mentions another yantra: "The eighty-one..."

By means of these [instructions], having drawn lines extending ten units east-west and ten units north-south, one should delineate eighty-one squares. Therein, in the central square, one should write the letter *ṭha* ending with *ṭha* (i.e., the entire ṭha-group), and in its center, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) and so forth. Then, [one proceeds] to the east, west, south, and north...
In the four squares located at the cardinal directions, one should write the four syllables *jūṃ*, *saḥ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *iti* four times in rotation. Then,
in the remaining sixty-four squares, one should draw the *Sarvatobhadra* [yantra] as described below.
Having written the Lakṣmī-mantra once in the sequence starting from Īśāna in the form of a *vaṃdha*,
