one should then write that same Lakṣmī-mantra again in the sequence starting from Nairṛtya.
Then, having erased the *phaṭ* of the weapon (*śastra*) in its place, it becomes manifest.
One should encircle [the area] in each of the four directions with the *Tvaritā* mantra, which has the nature of "Vaṣaṭ" manifested at its end, wrapping it one by one in every direction.

However, in the Yantra of the previously mentioned Lakṣmī as well, they say that one should omit *phaṭ* and instead insert *vaṣaṭ* in its place; thus, according to their view, the encirclement is performed with the *Tvaritā-vidyā* alone. In this system, the weapon-mantra (*astra*) is recited ending with *vaṣaṭ* at the beginning [of the mantra], whereas it was not so in the previous case.

The *travīja* must be questioned as before, for otherwise such a meaning would not be obtained; furthermore, its inclusion here would otherwise be purposeless. Therefore, having added the *vaṣaṭkāra* itself there, the wrapping must be performed with the complete mantra—this is the root of the author’s [position].
Then, one should encircle that which is to be worshipped while lying down with the syllable *vaṃ* accompanied by a bindu;
thereafter, one should encircle it with a jar joined to a lotus at its base.
Thus, for Tvaritā, the encircling is performed only by delimiting the four directions, not starting from the southeast (*āgneya*) and so forth.

Furthermore, by the letter *va* delimiting the intermediate directions (*vidig*), and by the letter *tu* delimiting all eight directions, the terms *vīta* and *pravīta* are mentioned here and there in order to indicate the decrease and increase [of the protective circle].
The fruit of this is also stated in another *tantra*: "The *yantra* held by Yama was indeed held by Brahmā."

By the power of this vidyā-yantra, even Śuṣṇa, Vṛtra, Bhairava, Hiraṇyakaśipu, and Guha—all these are brought to submissiveness. Likewise, having drawn it with a stylus on a flat wall or in a house, one should worship it; this is the supreme Anugraha-cakra (Wheel of Grace). All...
There, the group of family members became entirely subject to him and no longer capable of independent deliberation.

Thus, he teaches the *Śrīsāman* mantra, which was previously indicated as being written [on the body], beginning with "Śrīsāma" and so forth: the seed-syllable of Śrī without the nasal dot (*aviṃdu*), followed by Bhṛgu (the letter *b*) along with the long vowel *Ā*, and then the pair of *Aya* (the letters *a* and *ya*) together with the nasal dot (*sadi*).
Furthermore, each of those [syllables] is again associated with *dīrgha* (long) and *hrasva* (short) by virtue of their transposition;

and again, by virtue of the transposition of *jña*, *śiva*, *para*, and *kārya*, these become *māyā*, *lu*, *vidhi*, and *lubhujā*. Moreover, when these attain the state of inversion (*vilomatva*), they are established as having *śiva*, *jña*, and *āsa* at their head.

Having first drawn nine lines extending eastward and westward, as well as northward and southward, according to the sequence of the syllables *mukha-lu-satu-ryo-lo-rṇo-mī*— which are considered again in reverse order by way of inversion— and having thus described the method of drawing them in an upward direction, one should write [the letters] starting with "aśuddhatva" and so forth.

There are sixty-four squares; there, beginning from the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding in order, one should write the previously mentioned Śrī-mantra. Then, beginning again from the southwest (Nairṛtya) with the [squares] starting from the maiden (Kanyā), one should write that same Śrī-mantra once more. In the houses of the east and other directions, two by two, [the deities] Kriyā and the others [are placed].

From the *Jyotirnibandha*, it is stated that because the sign of Virgo (Kanyā) is situated in the southwest direction from the mountain (the starting point), the attainment of that [result] is obtained from the word "Kanyā. Regarding the phrase "swiftly" (*tvaritayā*), as before, it means "with the *vaṣaṭ* ending. This applies everywhere in the four directions within the four [circles] located in the center.

By the phrase "having written [the letters] in the squares" (*koṣṭheṣu likhitvā*), it is stated that the wise one has understood the general method previously mentioned. Having written the letter *ṭha*, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth within it; this refers to the sixteen-square diagram to be described below.
The meaning is that one should deposit [the mantras] according to the manner previously stated. He recites another mantra beginning with "Kavacam" and so forth:

"Ścaṇḍaś-cakāro-bhagavān-punaḥ-huṃ-ve-kṣaḥ"—this is the three-syllabled mantra. The grammatical connection is "sitāsyāt" (she whose mouth is white). [The rest of the mantra is: "daṃṣṭrākarālair-udara-ya... (with fangs formidable, O you of the belly...).

It should be understood that the Triśūla-mudrā (Trident Gesture) is formed by joining the little fingers with the four faces [of the hands] turned inward, while the remaining fingers are extended; thus it becomes terrifying in its appearance.
Regarding the phrase "there would be delusion," he describes another mechanical device (*yantra*): here, the purification leaf (*śodhapatra*) is [to be placed on] the *kṣeru*.

The meaning is that *drāstrī* consists of the letter *kṣa* at the beginning and end, with the letter *strī* (the vowel *ī*) in the middle as its essential form. Nṛsiṃha is rich in fortune (*bhaga*), and he is also a husband (*vedhū*) who is devoid of the moon (*śaśāṅka*). Furthermore, the letter *kṣa*, being rich in fortune and virtue, acts here as a necessary means for the attainment of women; thus, the man (*nara*) arises.
One who is not afflicted by obstacles is able to perform the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*) with repeated recitations.

He states the *Nityā* mantra consisting of three hundred thousand—that is, three lakhs—beginning with "Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ," etc. The fifteen-syllable mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ nityakline madadrave aiṃ hrīṃ svāhā*. It should be recited; therein, two...

The manner of taking up the phonemes beginning with *bhyām* and so forth— by the phrase "even without speech"— it is stated that the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) must be performed independently of speech;
this meaning is established in other Tantras.

Having meditated upon the island in the form of a triangle situated in the midst of the ocean of wine, one should assign the six limbs with one's own letters according to the number of cruel [planetary] portions of the night, and without speech; then, according to the instruction, one should again assign the limbs with speech alone.

The connection is as follows: having remembered the ruby pavilion on the island of Sminda, having visualized a jeweled lion-throne there, having meditated upon a lotus there, and having remembered a triangle within its pericarp, one should contemplate the Goddess therein; this applies even to the pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśakti) in other deities.
To dispel the delusion that the number [of powers] here should likewise be nine,
he points out the distinction that there are indeed four *pīṭha-śaktis* for the deity under discussion, and not nine; thus he says "four powers," or alternatively, "three powers."

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that this is in agreement with other tantras: "One should worship [the deities] beginning with Māheśvarī in the three corners starting from Īśāna; then in the center, in the northwest corner, and in the center starting from Īśāna, one should install these Śaktis. One should worship Guhyaśakti in the northwest (Vāyu).

Since the reading *ktimiti* is observed in the root manuscripts (*mūlapustakeṣu*), and because the alternative—namely, that worship pertains only to the northwest (*vāyavya*) corner or the abandonment [of others]—would not produce aesthetic satisfaction (*asaurasyādhāyakatvāt*), the author of the *Harṣakaumudī* states: "The worship of the secret power (*guhyaśakti*) is in the northwest (*vāyavye*). *Āṃ*. Vā. [End of quote].

The mantras for her worship should be inferred as follows: *māyāyai namaḥ*, *īṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*, *ūṃ raudryai namaḥ*, *aiṃ guhyaśaktyai namaḥ*. Some maintain that the specific epithets such as "the Enchantress" (*drāviṇī*) and so forth should also be mentioned; thus, [the mantra] would be *māyāyai drāviṇyai namaḥ* and so on.

They say that the following application is established: "Maḥ, salutation to Īṃ, the Joy-bestowing Jyeṣṭhā; Ūṃ, salutation to Kṣobhiṇī, the Fierce One. Thus, "Māyādyam" (beginning with Māyā) refers to the seat-mantra: "Hiṃ, salutation to the Lotus-seated One who possesses all powers," followed by "Hrīṃ, salutation to the Seat."

Some say the mantra is "Maḥ. The pair of initial vowels is "Ā" (ā-a); the pair of final vowels is "Aṃ" and "Aḥ" (aṃ-aḥ). The four neuter vowels are Ṛ, Ḷ, Ḹ, and ḹ. These eight, excluding the letter Ra, along with the eight vowels beginning with I (ī-ū), are respectively the Nityā goddesses and so forth.

There are no seed-mantras (bījamantra); likewise, by means of mantras such as "Iṃ Nityāyai namaḥ" and "Iṃ Subhadrāyai namaḥ," the deities beginning with Nityā are to be worshipped on the petals—this is the meaning to be understood from the phrase "beginning and ending" and so forth. On the other limbs, [she is] on the back, and with a quiver (niṣaṅga) or a case (tūṇīra), [there are] arrows.
Rich by virtue of their specific abodes, the seed-syllable of desire itself—*klīṃ* or *vāḥ*—is joined with the two additional letters *ha* and *ra* from among the five desires.
It is further endowed with these six vowels previously mentioned: *ai*, *au*, *svara* (*a*), *u*, and *e*. These are devoid of the pair of lips (*o*).
The ten vowels beginning with *ā* are joined with the syllable *ja* by the Four-faced One (Brahmā);

these sequentially become the seed-mantras (*bījamantra*) of Rati and the others. Likewise, on the eight petals surrounding [the center], the five Kāmas are worshipped with mantras such as *hrīṃ klīṃ anaṅgāya namaḥ*.

On both sides of each respective desire (*kāma*), the ten Śaktis are to be worshipped with the mantras: *Jaṃ Ratyai namaḥ* and *Jāṃ Viratyai namaḥ*. Thus, the four-faced Brahmā is obtained through that letter *ka*; likewise, *kaṃ*, *kāṃ*, and so forth, are indeed the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Rati and the others.
The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* states another mantra beginning with "Vāgbhava," etc.: *aiṃ klīṃ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā*.
This is a twelve-syllable mantra. Regarding the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth:
where the seer, meter, and other such details are not explicitly stated, [one should apply] the seer and so on because of its status as a highly perfected mantra.
Some say that because there is no purpose for a separate list (*ullekha*), the mention of those [sites] is merely descriptive;
others say that the *ṛṣis* and so forth are present there because they were mentioned immediately prior in the mantra.
Even though the *pīṭhas* have been mentioned in the passage beginning with "the *pīṭhas* described in the *Hṛllekhā*," the specific locations where those *pīṭhas* are situated are indicated here.
Regarding this, some maintain that his very own *darbha* grass and other implements should be taken; however,

[this is incorrect] because of the mantra previously extracted from the passage beginning with "the skull-bearer, the one with *kuśa* grass, the one with a skull filled with wine, or the one with a skull-cup," which states, "to him who possesses weapons, to him who possesses a vehicle," and so forth.
He states another mantra for the purpose of battle with the words beginning with "vāk" and so forth.
Having inserted the *māyī* seed-syllable in the place of the *kāma* seed-syllable, or else using the previously mentioned twelve-syllable mantra;
and here, in this worship of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), after the earth is [worshipped], there is a red ocean, above which is a red boat,
and therein is a lotus with twelve or ten petals— this is the remainder [of the description]— [and] the bow of Madana.

Having worshipped the eleven Śaktis, beginning with Hṛllekhā, upon the twelve petals due to the weight of her breasts from the burden of hunger and the excessive heaviness caused by their extreme height,
one should worship Kāma on the twelfth petal; [the goddesses] Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, and Vegavatī [are also to be worshipped].
Because of the statement in another tantra, "The Kāmas are remembered as these four," this meditation belongs specifically to the Śaktis;

thus, the word "Śaktis" is used to indicate that this is not for Smara. Otherwise, since it would have been possible for it to belong to the Śaktis by the very fact of being introduced [in that context], the term "Śaktis" would have served no further purpose.

If one should wish to perform the meditation on Smara, that which is taught in another Tantra should be followed. As for the worship of the Mothers (mātṛpūjā), it should be performed in the eight directions, starting from the front portion outside the twelve-petaled [lotus] and proceeding clockwise.
Here he states the mantra with three parts, beginning with "Śrī" and so forth. One should take a single betel-box (tāmbūlakaraṇḍaka) along with its lid (samuhuka).

Some say that there is merely the placement of ornaments, caskets, perfumes, and so forth. [The goddesses] Ghṛṇinī, Sūryā, Ādityā, and Prabhāvatī—these four, who are gentle and have two arms each—are positioned in the east, south, west, and north; in their right hands, each holds a fly-whisk and so forth, a set of four.

In the left hands of each [of these goddesses], the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) gesture is prescribed; for all of them, the hand is said to be weaponless, as it is stated that "the *vara* (boon-granting) gesture is common to both. As for the Dūtīs, another Tantra states:
"The Saumyā, Ghṛṇinī, Sūryā, Ādityā, and Prabhāvatī [are the Dūtīs] with palms joined in *añjali*."

The state of having joined palms (*añjali*) has been mentioned; this should be reconciled as being according to another tantra. Although pleasing the Guru is universally required, its mention here is for the purpose of emphasizing its necessity.
"Pūjā" means worship performed according to the prescribed rule. First, one should draw a hexagon.

The wise one should write the Vidyā in the center; by repetition, he should write it in sequence within the six corners of the hexagon. On the outside, he should skillfully fashion a square mandala adorned with four gates and embellished with long vowels, as stated in other Tantras.

The procedure for worship above the yantra should be disregarded; [the claim] that [the deities reside] on a seat fashioned from the *hṛllekhā* mantra within the six triangles starting from the southeast (āgneya) should also be disregarded because it contradicts the root text.
In the six triangles starting from the southeast, Lakṣmī and the others [are to be worshipped] in sequence.

The six deities ending with Rāṃ are to be worshipped; then, on the two sides, the previously mentioned Nidhis (Treasures) together with their consorts are to be worshipped. On the filaments (kesara), the limbs (aṅgas) are worshipped; on the petals, Brahmā and the others;
and in the eastern path of the square, Indra and the other [guardians], assuming the forms of their consorts as before. Outside of that—
In the second path, Vajra and the others indeed assume three forms;
for the fire [mandala], which is square and endowed with four doors, is constructed within the lines— thus,
one should not suspect that there are two paths here, nor is this [arrangement] intended for any particular deity in this context.
One should also reflect that this injunction of ours is intended solely for the purpose of recalling the general scriptural rule;
one should consider that the specific power known as "mounted on a horse" (aśvārūḍha) is the mantra,
as stated in the passage beginning with "pāśa," wherein the power enters into the interior of the noose and the goad.
The essence is the letter *ṭa*, followed by the letter *ṭha* (the eleventh vowel), resembling [the letter] with the third vowel; thus, the thirteen-syllable mantra is extracted as:
*Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Ehi Parameśvari Svāhā*.
[The phrase] "she, who is overwhelmed by the arrows of Smara, binds the practitioner with a noose" implies here that she binds him at the throat.
"Bind him with a noose at the throat"—this is seen in another tantra. Regarding the "five hundred thousand arrows," he says "having drawn," etc., for the purpose of describing the yantra.
Having made sixteen lines—five each running east-west and five running north-south—one obtains a sixteen-fold [grid].

The meaning is as follows: having produced the six [triangles] and having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the four central squares, one should write the twelve mantra-syllables—excluding the *praṇava*—starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and proceeding clockwise, after having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) at the end of that [central *praṇava*]. He states the *annapūrṇā* mantra beginning with "māyā" etc., ending with "hrīṃ na."

The mantra is "Oṃ bhagavati māheśvari annapūrṇe svāhā. Now, one might object: since the letter *ka* (k) is heard following the letter *a* (a), according to the grammatical rule *iko yaṇ aci*, it ought to be replaced by the letter *ya* (y); so how is it that this substitution is not made here? To this, he says: "seventy," etc., [meaning] likewise.
The fourfold [set] is said to be twelvefold.

The sense is that its inclusion here is determined even without a *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction), because otherwise there would be the contingency of contradicting the state of being perishable (*kṣaratva*).
Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Brahmā, its metre (*chandaḥ*) is Gāyatrī, its deity (*devatā*) is the goddess Annapūrṇā,
its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Māyā, its power (*śakti*) is Svāhā, and its successions are the abundance of food and the abundance of wealth.

Regarding the application [of the mantra] for meditation, recitation, and so forth, the commentator states that "by Māyā" means by [the syllable] joined with the six long vowels; "Śiva, adorned with the crescent moon, together with Śrī"—
by this it is shown that the practitioner's prosperity does not come from mere begging alone, but rather [from this practice].

For the sake of the increase of wealth, there is the increase of food; thus, having explained the mantra of Padmāvatī, he speaks of "Māyā" and so forth. Here too, the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other factors are exactly as previously stated. Regarding the optional mantra, he says "six-cornered" (*ṣaṭkoṇa*), meaning a six-cornered [diagram] consisting of two hundred thousand recitations.
In the *rṇikā*, having written the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in the portion of the letter *ra* and the name of the practitioner (*sādhakā*) in the portion of the letter *ī*,

and having written the word for the ritual action (*karmapada*) beneath it, one should write the remaining six syllables of the mantra clockwise in the six corners starting from its tip; outside of that, [within] two circles...
The meaning is that one should encircle [the mantra] with the letters of the Mātṛkā. He describes the *amaṭha* placement (*nyāsa*) with the words beginning "Tārām" and so forth.

For the *amaṭha* placement mantra, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Bṛhatī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), *Aṃ maṭa Śrī* is the deity (*devatā*), *Śrī* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *Klīṃ* is the power (*śakti*). It is used for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*) in this placement.

Having formed the resolve for the ritual application (*niyoga*), one should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with these mantras: *oṃ śrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *śrīkarī śirase svāhā*, *dhanakarī śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *dhānyakarī kavacāya huṃ*, *ṛddhikarī netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ*, and *puṣṭikarī astrāya phaṭ*.

Having visualized the goddess Bhāratī-Sarasvatī according to the method described in the seventh chapter, one should utter "Oṃ, obeisance to that Sarasvatī," or simply utter the *praṇava* alone, and perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the head. Then,
having visualized Bhuvaneśvarī according to the method described in the ninth chapter, [one should place] "Hrīṃ, [obeisance] to Bhuvaneśvarī."

One should place the seed-syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) on the forehead in the manner beginning with "nam" and so forth. Having performed the meditation on the Sun as will be described hereafter, one should place the syllable *aṃ* on the right eye, saying "namaḥ to Sūrya. Then, having meditated on Agni according to the method stated in the fifth chapter, one should [place the syllable] on the left eye, saying "namaḥ to Agni," and so forth.

One should place the syllable *tyāḥ* in the left eye; in the mouth, one should place the letters from *ṭa* to *ṇa* in a circular form, and the letter *ṭa*; and while meditating on the Moon according to the method to be described as "by the Moon" (*caṃdramasena*), one should meditate on Śrī according to the method stated in the eighth chapter, reciting: *śrīṃ śriyai namaḥ*.

One should place the *Śrī-bīja* on the tongue. Then, having performed meditation in this manner— "I worship the two elephants, who are like Lakṣmī and Gajendra, white as jasmine and the moon, fierce with rut from their temples, rich in the beauty of their shining trunks, and with gleaming tusks"— one should [offer] to one's own limbs.
One should place the form [of the deity] in the directions with "Namaḥ hāṃ gajāya namaḥ" and so forth, and on the right and left cheeks;

having first performed the cleansing of the face with the Kāma-bīja, one should then perform the recollection once of the remaining nine syllables of the ten-syllable mantra according to the previously stated method.
Having spoken thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*); however, there is this distinction:

not only should the *praṇava* be placed upon the head, but both the *praṇava* and the *vāgbhava* [bījas] should also be placed. It is desired that they be placed in the location of the visarga during the placement of the first vowel. Thus, "he who destroys the darkness" is *saṃ*.

By meditating on him as the destroyer of the body, he is the abode; by meditating on him in the form of the sun and fire, he is existence (*sattva*) as the destroyer of darkness; by placing him in the eyes in the form of the eyes, he is the existence of objects;
and by being the destroyer of doubt, he is the abode. Thus, he is indeed the form of the *bindu* and the letter *A*.
Because it effects the desired goal, the ten-syllable mantra is extracted even from the root *a* itself for the purpose of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

In another Tantra, the wise one should place the *praṇava*, *vāgbhava*, *māyā*, *maṃ*, *ṭhaṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *vaset*, *sudhīḥ*, *māraḥ*, and *vahnivadhūḥ*; this is declared to be the ten-syllable mantra, beginning with *aṃ* (or *jhaṃ*) and ending with *maṭhaḥ*.

Thus: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ aṃ ma ṭaṃ āṃ klīṃ svāhā*. According to the followers of the *Harṣakaumudī*, some [place this] on the head in the form of Vāṇī with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and on the forehead in the form of the power (Śakti) of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī). Furthermore, they place *raṃ* and *oṃ* in the eyes, and *ma* and *va* in the mouth.

The form *ṣṭanaṃṭāṃ* is for the Śrī [mudrā]; on the tongue is the Svarūpā; on the two hands are the forms of the elephant (*karirūpa*) joined with long vowels; having reversed them, they bestow beauty of face, fortune, sovereignty, fame, luster, and intelligence. According to this system, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letter *ma* situated in the sixteenth vowel is specifically designated as the *aṃmaṭanyāsa*. This is what is being defined here.
They say that the remaining portion concerning the cheeks, which have become the locus for the intoxication of youth, is already almost explained; such is the summary.

May that King Udyotamati— who has the virtuous Satī as his mother, whose father is named Māpati, who is born of the lineage of Paṃtha, whose birthplace is Kūrmāvala, who has made the feet of Acyuta his object of worship, and whose residence is Vārāṇasī— attain perfection. May he be praised.

In the *La-śabdārtha-cintāmaṇi*, since the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Durgā was previously mentioned as something to be written down, and there being a desire to know its specific form, he states the mantras of Durgā: "That," etc. "Seen" refers to wealth, sons, and so forth;
"unseen" refers to heaven and so forth. "Atri" is the letter *da*; "ear" is the fifth vowel (*u*); "again," *pu*...
Even Narapati Asauḍukāra, in his *Svargāvatī*, states that this is another seed-mantra (*bījāntara*) by virtue of its independence;

thus, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that there is a visarga at the end of the mantra under discussion. However, this is not tenable, for it does not follow from the root text regarding the extraction of the mantra currently under consideration.

Therefore, the master [Abhinavagupta] explains it as follows: the letter *ga*, accompanied by *ra* (the *rāsa*) and joined with *sa* (the *sarasa*), and followed by *u* (the *vāsu*), constitutes the fifth creation (*sarga*).
That letter *ga* undergoes doubling; when combined with the *repha* (the *ra*) and the *udatta* (the *uddhata*), and [joined] with *na* (the *neti*), everything becomes well-established.

Now, regarding the phrase "nanu asau," it refers to that which grasps three moras (*trimātra*), or rather, it refers to that which possesses a specific quality (*saviśeṣaṇa*); in either case, [it is so].
If you argue that [the word *pañca*] is merely a non-apprehender of the word *vidu*, then this is equally true in your own view as well;

however, in our view, this is like an axe—what recourse do you have in your position? If you say: "In this way, the word *bhūpa* is an apprehender of the number four, and the word *ya* is an apprehender of the number one; therefore, through their conjunction, there is the number five."

The understanding [of the compound] is as follows: from that [word *bhūyas*], by the suffix *yac* (forming *bhūyīya*), the meaning is "belonging to the fifth" (*pañcamavartin*). The word *asau* refers to Atri. Thus, what remains is the attainment of the mere syllable *tri*.
Alternatively, *asau* refers to Atri with his specific qualification; [the phrase] *bhūyaḥ punarapy atrividyaḥ triḥ* means "Atri, who possesses the threefold knowledge, again and yet again."

Since there is no third [syllable] in the syllable *duṃ*—for therein the letters *a*, *u*, and the *bindu* are joined—what immovable [third element] could there be in the absence of a third? That has been explained there; furthermore, regarding the word *bhūyaḥ*, its lack of propriety (*asaurasya*) lies in the fact that it is the repeated employment of what was already previously present. "Again" (*punar*)...

The first [syllable] is employed, but it is not present in that manner; such is the direction. The letter *ga* is the end of the fifth [group]; it is joined with the second vowel, which is the *Pratiṣṭhā*. That which has the twelfth vowel as its seat—that is, as its substratum—is the letter *ya*, together with the wind (*m*).

Thus, the eight-syllable mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Duṃ Durgāyai Namaḥ" is extracted; the seed-syllable "Duṃ" is associated with the Māyā-śakti (the syllable "Hrīṃ"). The six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the root-mantra joined with the six long vowels beginning with "Hrāṃ"—namely, Hrāṃ, Hrīṃ, and so forth—while being devoid of the word "Namaḥ. As follows: [Vi]...

It has been stated that by means of this [mantra] *dhīti*, the inclusion of *hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth within the supreme mantra must be performed; thus, the practical application results in *oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so on. Some, however, maintain that the application should be *hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth alone.

They say: "This [interpretation] contradicts the root text, because the root manual (*mūlagrantha*) shows that [the mantra] is recited with the *hrām* and others along with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "having fastened the armlets (*aṅgada*) and so forth upon the hands. Or, [it means]:
after the visualization (*dhyāna*), Durgā [is to be worshipped] with the weapons in the first two upper hands and in the last two lower hands.

For the display of the *mudrā*: having formed fists with both hands and placed the right over the left, joining them at the head—this is declared to be the *Durgā-mudrā*. One should [recite] eight hundred thousand (*vasulakṣa*) times; some say with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), that is, with rice boiled in milk. In the three short [syllables], one should...
Because they are present in all [the vowels], their nature is that of the *aiu* vowels; these nine syllables— *ā ī ū e ai o au aṃ aḥ*— being devoid of the four neuter vowels,
are each placed at the beginning of the nine syllables by means of the mantras of their respective names ending in the dative case, such as "to this power" (*imāyai prabhāyai*) and so forth.
One should worship the [eight] Kṛttikās with the formula: *Āṃ prabhāyai namaḥ*, *Īm māyāyai namaḥ*, and so forth; this is the application.
*Oṃ vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāyudhāya mahāsiṃhāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*—this nineteen-syllable mantra is the Siṃha-mantra. With that, the worship of the *pīṭha* (seat) should be performed using one's own name.

The meaning is: "those which have 'kṣa' as their first syllable" because it is present first by virtue of its own name; furthermore, the conjunction with the *bindu* (anusvāra) has been mentioned elsewhere, so let it be here as well, and thus the application is "oṃ jayāyai namaḥ" and so forth. "According to the rule" means beginning with the *śrī*-bīja (*śrīṃ*) for Śrī, and so on.

The meaning is that one should apply the procedure taught in other tantras, such as *tyuṃ* for longevity, *jādī* for victory over enemies, *ṇṛsiṃhādi* for desire, and so forth, according to the wish for a son. Furthermore, this seed-syllable (*bīja*) yoga should be understood as following the primary *māyā-bīja*. However, this must be noted: [the specific application varies].

Just as with the primary eight-syllable and other respective mantras, it is required that even the seed-syllables (bīja) to be deposited [in the vessel] be perfected through preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth; thus, by the phrase "hemādī" and so on, there is the inclusion of perfumes, sprouts, and other items to be deposited in the jar. This is indicated by the words "sthitān in the nine squares."
It is implied that one should draw the circle of the nine suns beneath this vase;
for even when enemies are destroyed by the sudden falling of thunderbolts and the like,
it is indeed a victory, yet it is not a supreme victory, as there is mutual conflict between the two armies with swords and other weapons.

Victory preceded by the act of striking is indeed victory; he says that this [victory] shall come from this practice. One might think that for one who is ill, freedom from disease could occur even through the abandonment of this body, and thus it would not be [attained] from this.

Through yoga, there may be the destruction of disease; however, it says "long-lived" (*dīrghāyuḥ*) precisely so that this does not conflict with the body. Similarly, for one who is afflicted and short-lived, even the acquisition of a wicked son—though in reality there is no son at all—may occur through this practice, yet it occurs as being characterized by qualities desired by oneself.

The best [of mantras] is the most excellent; thus he says "vara" (the boon). When the clarified butter (*ājya*) has been consumed and the ashes have been applied, it shall grant the aforementioned fruit. Regarding the yantra for the purpose of wearing, he says "in the middle," etc.;
having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center of the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus, therein...

Having written the seed-syllable *dhyai* and having written the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) within it, one should write the eight syllables of the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) on the petals in a clockwise direction starting from the front.
Then, having drawn three circles outside of that, one should protect the first enclosure (*vīthī*) with the *Jātavedas* mantra.
The meaning is that the drawing of the color for the mandala, which has become non-dual through being enveloped by pride (*māna*),
should be adopted according to the method of the substratum as obtained from the general treatises. Here, both previously and subsequently,
it is established by tradition that the drawings of the processional paths (*vīthī*) are to be drawn only upon the circular line (*vṛtta-rekhā*).
This must not be forgotten: the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra* in the third enclosure bestows sons upon pregnant women who desire a child, or rather,
by destroying the afflictions such as miscarriages that may occur for pregnant women, it grants the gift of a son.

The meaning is that even from obtaining a son who is short-lived or possesses bad qualities, there may still be the attainment of a son; thus, during the state of pregnancy, this [mantra] should be maintained so that it results in the superior attainment of a son,
preceded by the experience of its fruit— or rather, he states the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī.

With the words "bhāṃta" and so forth, there is an eight-syllable mantra: *Aśvetahṣaḥ mahiṣamardini svāhā*. Mārkaṇḍeya is the sage (*ṛṣi*); the meter (*chandas*) is *Prakṛti*; the deity (*devatā*) is Mahiṣāsuramardinī; "laṃ" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); "vasupriyā" is the power (*śakti*). Others, however, say... [the rest of the verse is truncated].

They know the sage to be Ka-vat-saṃ. He states the mantras for the limbs starting with "Mahiṣa... and so forth. Regarding the extraction of the mantras for the *śikhā* (crown) and *varma* (armor): one should recite the word "mahiṣa" in the accusative case at the beginning. Thus, [the mantra for the heart is]: *mahiṣa siṃhikaṃ huṃ phaṭ hṛdayāya namaḥ*. [The mantra for the armor is]: *mahiṣa śa...* [and so on].

With the root mantras in their respective order: *śeṣādhi huṃ phaṭ śirase svāhā*, "Make the buffalo bray, bray, huṃ phaṭ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*)," *mahiṣaṃ hanahana devi huṃ phaṭ huṃ to the armor (*kavaca*)," and *mahiṣasūdini huṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*.

The assignment of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) is concluded with [mantras] of ten, sixteen, and twelve syllables. He describes the meditation (*dhyāna*) starting with the words "Gāruḍa," etc. The weapons are placed in order on the right and left hands; the first and second [weapons] are on the arms, and below those, the third and fourth; further below those, the fifth and sixth.
Below that, in the right hand, is a trident; in the left, the *tarjanī-mudrā*.
When the index finger (*tarjanī*) is in the form of Kākinī and the remaining fingers are joined together, this is called the *tarjanī-mudrā*.
It should be understood according to the description stated as: "It bestows liberation upon both the speaker and the listener. Thus it is to be known.

It is stated in the Īśāna-saṃhitā: "The discus, the chain, the excellent Brahmā [the lotus], below that the sword and shield, and below those the arrow and bow; below that, the trident and the threatening gesture (tarjanī)—thus it is proclaimed. Since this was spoken immediately prior in the recitation of Durgā, it refers to long vowels (*dīrghasvara*). And thus: "Ādu... [and so forth].

The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* prescribes the usage as "ṛṃ gāyai namaḥ" and "īṃ varavarṇinyai namaḥ," and so forth. However, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) occurs when there is a long neuter dual ending or one of these three [vowels] followed by *tar*. This is because such an explanation is given in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*; and likewise, [the text reads] "ṛṃ kanaka... and so on.

The ritual application beginning with "Obeisance to Prabhā" and so forth is not established by your own doctrine; rather, it is far more excellent [according to our view]. What then? It is as follows.
They say, "Salutation to Prabhā," "Salutation to Kṛttikā," and so forth;
however, according to the inherent force (*svārasya*) of the root text, there is no contradiction with the previously stated meaning by those beginning with *ya* and ending with *ha*,
which are respectively the mantras for the wheels (*cakra*) and so on.
Thus it is to be deposited; therefore, the application [of the mantra] begins with "Obeisance to the Discus (Cakra)," "Obeisance to the Conch (Śaṅkha)," and so forth.
He states the mantra of Jayadurgā starting with "Tārā" and so on: "Rakta" is the letter *ra*; "Antya" is the letter *kṣa*;
"Ṭhāntareṇa" is the letter *ka*; and "Salocana" is joined with the third vowel (*i*). Likewise...

The ten-syllable mantra "cadurgedurgarakṣiṇi svāhā" has been extracted; "salocanam" is the qualifier for both [mantras], by which the syllables "kṣiṇī" are obtained from the mantra-text. [The mantra is: Oṃ (Tāra), the two "durgas," fire (Ra), the final letter (Ha) with the end of "ṭha" (Ṇa), and "sadṛkśi"—thus it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya Tantra.
Because the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotikā* has explained that the word "dṛk" (vision) is connected to both [the preceding and following terms],

and because the author of the *Itipadārthādarśa* has likewise explained it, here too [the mantra consists of]: the sage is Mārkaṇḍeya, the meter is Bṛhatī, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Oṃ (*praṇava*), the power (*śakti*) is Svāhā, and the weapon (*astra*) is the three-pronged trident (*triśikha-triśūla*).

Although acts such as *rppaṇa* (the offering) are necessary, the mention of "merely feeding" (*bhojana-mātra*) establishes that it is an indispensable requirement; for it has been stated: "O Dear One, even by the propitiation of Brahmins alone, a rite with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*) becomes complete with its ancillaries (*aṅga*). Thus, in every ritual application, the feeding of Brahmins is essential.

Although it is not strictly mandatory, this statement is made here to indicate the absolute necessity of consuming those respective foods when one is engaged in extremely fierce rites. He describes the practical applications of the eight-syllable mantra revealed by Durgā, beginning with the words "the mantra," and so forth.
Regarding "missiles" (*strāṇi*), these are weapons such as arrows; "bladed weapons" (*śastrāṇi*) are those such as swords.
He states the mantra of the trident-bearing Durgā beginning with "jala" and so forth: *jala jala śūlini duṣṭagraha huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is a fifteen-syllable mantra. Regarding the phrase "with five and ten" in the root text, [it refers to] five...

The meaning is "by the ten remaining [verses]. The seer (ṛṣi) is Dīrghatamas; the meter (chandaḥ) is Kakup; the deity (devatā) is Śūlinī; the seed-syllable (bīja) is *huṃ*; the power (śakti) is *svāhā*. He describes the mere placement of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) with the words beginning "O Durgā" (*durge*), and so forth. "O Durgā" is the essential form (*svarūpa*); "to the heart, *namaḥ*" is the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).

Similarly, in other cases, these five mantras should begin with the word *śūlini*. For whichever mantra the word *śūlini* is placed at the beginning, the syllable *huṃ phaṭ* should be added at its end.
Thus: *śūlini durge huṃ phaṭ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *śūlini varade huṃ phaṭ*.

*Śirase svāhā*, *śūlini vindhyavāsini huṃ phaṭ* for the crest (*śikhā*), *ṣaṭ*; *śūlini asuramardini yuddhapriye trāsaya trāsaya huṃ phaṭ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *śūlini devasiddhapūjite dina rakṣa rakṣa*.

The essential meaning is that the five-limbed ritual assignment (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*) must be performed with the five-limbed mantras: *hāyogeśvari huṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*. He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*): "Mounted upon... [and so on].
That which possesses streams of eyes is the *aparicakra*; the lotus-born is the conch; [the one] in the right...
Down to the level of her lower hands, her weapons are to be known in sequence: the sword, shield, and so forth.
She is served by four maidens named Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, and Kātyāyanī, who bear [the weapons] along with shields. [She is] the hundred thousand syllables, the letters of the mantra.

He states the application of the number equal to the *lakṣa* (one hundred thousand) with the words beginning "eighty-one" (*aṣṭottara*) and so forth: according to the observation of another tantra, one who desires a wife shall obtain her by offering *dūrvā* grass eighty-one times; likewise, by offering [oblations] eight hundred times, [the goal is attained], as seen in other tantras. [The term] *saṃpātājya* [refers to...]

The connection is that [the sword] was smeared and consecrated by this mantra; the *sampātārtha* oblation is performed five thousand times, while the recitation (*japa*) is ten thousand times. As it is stated in another Tantra: "Having invoked the deity into the sharp sword and worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, [one should perform the rite] in the clarified butter (*ājya*)."

One who knows the specific mantras should offer five thousand oblations according to the prescribed method; having been consecrated with the mantra and smeared with the residual ghee (*saṃpāta-ājya*),
he becomes capable of destroying enemy armies with his sword in hand, striking down mountain-like hosts of foes.
The mention of "yudha" (weapon) is an illustration [of other weapons as well], based on the teacher’s statement beginning with "the dagger,

the sword," and so forth. Regarding the *aśvattha* (holy fig tree), the number of oblations (*homa*) to be known here is twelve thousand, performed with *arka* (calotropis) fuel-sticks mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), or with *aśvattha* wood, or with very bright sesame seeds.
"One should offer oblations"— because this is seen in other tantras, one should meditate upon her as holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, being of a reddish hue,
binding the target with the noose and drawing him in with the goad.

The instruction is that one should perform the oblation to the Goddess alone; when such [an occasion] arises, having meditated upon oneself as the very form of the Goddess, one should mutter the mantra while touching the afflicted person—this is the connection. The singular number in "graha" (the seizing spirit) is not intended to be restrictive; one should contemplate these [spirits] as being seized at the head.

"By means of water from a *culluka* [ladle] consecrated with mantras glowing like flames, the reciter of mantras shall strike those with two arms and drooping eyes; in a mere moment, he shall cause all such *ṛ-grahas* who have entered [the victim] to depart.
As it is said, the method of liberation is as follows: between oneself and the patient, it is stated...

Having meditated on the form of Durgā, one should firmly grasp the three [fingers] starting from the little finger with the thumb, clench the fist, extend the index finger toward the side of the right ear, and rotate it very rapidly like a wheel;
by means of this *cakra-mudrā*, one should release [the obstruction]. Thus it is said: "Then, O King..."

Having meditated upon the goddess Umā, who is filled with her own weapons, even as she stands between a man, a self, and a sick person, the malevolent spirits (grahas) flee helplessly with their bodies shattered by means of the *ari-mudrā*.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "serpents, etc.," horses and other such creatures are included; the word "for oneself" (*ātmane*) is to be supplied [as the object], and thus for one's own self...
The connection [of the sentence] is that one should destroy poison while reciting the mantra with the mental conception of the deity as previously described.

Indeed, through a specific form of meditation characterized by the cognition of the deity, one will quickly destroy poison arising from snakes, rats, scorpions, and so forth, or that produced by spiders, mongooses, and moles.

And by the very sight of the Rāṇas, [I beheld] the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas, resembling the autumnal moon, her lotus-face radiant with a smile; holding in her lotus-hands a conch, a discus, and a pair of nectar-pitchers;
auspicious, sprinkling the bewildered Viṣama with nectar, adorned with white ornaments, and full of ambrosia.

"Thinking 'May the Goddess destroy the poison,' one should meditate on the Goddess even upon the tip of the arrow; having fixed the meditation on the Goddess upon the sharpened arrow and having recited this mantra that brings security (*kṣemakarī*), one should enter. The word "reciting" (*japan*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. As it has been said: "Having visualized oneself as the Māyā..."
Entering the enemy force while reciting the mantra, she who is endowed with a trident and noose swiftly seizes and destroys the weapons of the foe;
she nourishes awakening and is dark-complexioned,
massive-bodied, with eyes like blazing fire, holding a noose, a damaru drum, and a trident.
Holding a noose and a goad in her four hands, adorned with the lords of serpents,
and with her exceedingly long, great black hair spread all around, she, intent on a loud laugh, covered the army; thus was Durgā meditated upon by Vīra.

Having visualized the army of enemies in this manner—entering the enemy host while causing delusion among the foes—one shall remain personally unscarred from their grasping of weapons; such is the intention. "According to the rite" means joined with the name-mantra and the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*.

The meaning is that one should perform oblations while reciting [the mantra] joined with the *ullava* [syllables]. The term "enmity" (*vidveṣa*) is also an indication of separation, as it is said: "By means of enmity, two people become separated from one another.
She (Kālī) should be meditated upon by those clad in black garments and others as holding in her hands a pestle, a trident, and two skulls.

The specific visualization (*dhyāna*) as "the one who causes aversion to the embodied form" should be understood. Regarding the phrase "cow-dung from the sky," it means cow-dung that was caught in the atmosphere at the time of its emission;
this is because it is stated [in the source] that the cow-dung was not touched by the pot in the atmosphere. Water [is used] because...

Having meditated upon the noble Durgā with water in her hand and being serene, if one should go toward a village or a city, having recited the mantra and offered libations, he shall enter and obtain desirable food along with his circle of servants.
This is the meaning: here, having meditated on Durgā with water in her hand and having recited this mantra... [satisfied].
For a practitioner who goes to a village or a city along with his circle of attendants, there is the attainment of desired food for as long as he remains in that village or city;
since it is impossible to describe all the applications individually, he says "not many," etc.

Regarding the mantra of Vanadurgā, the syntactical connection is as follows: "Utthiṣṭa" and so forth, ending with the word "Puruṣi. The term "Pitāmaha" refers to the letter *ka*; it is joined with the third vowel (*i*), the moon (*bindu*), and the nasal dot (*bindu*). In the phrase "bhayaṃ ca," the word "ca" (and) is included within the mantra. Thus: "Utthiṣṭa puruṣi kiṃ... [What is this, O Puruṣi?]
"O Blessed One, protect me; fear has come upon me; whether it be possible or impossible, grant me refuge"—this is the mantra consisting of thirty-seven syllables.

The three syllables *vāta-n-me* are the *kīlakas* (stake-points) here; if, in their place, the three syllables *huṃ durgai* are inserted, and if previously the seed-syllables (*bījas*) of Pāśa, Māyā, Durgā, and Kavaca-Durgā were at the end of all mantras, then the seed-syllables of Durgā and Māyā are further added.
Now, this Vidyā, when ignited by the *Niṣkala* [mantra], becomes a bestower of immediate success (*sadyasiddhi*).

As it is stated in the *Īśānasaṃhitā*: "Having extracted the seed-syllable of Guṇa, then the word 'tiṣṭha', then having extracted 'Puruṣa' along with Brahmā, joined with Sūkṣma and provided with the *bindu*..."

One should utter the words "cārya racapiṣīti"; having spoken "bhayaṃ ca me sa mā bhāṣya," and likewise "tathā ca samupasthitam," having declared "yadi śakyam" and having uttered "aśakyam," having extracted the seed-syllable *ca* and saying "durge bhagavatī," one should extract [the syllable] "śamaya" and [utter] "iti."
One should utter the word "thāḥ svāhā. In this way, this Great Goddess Niṣkīlā bestows all accomplishments (siddhis).

At the end of the qualities [the mantra], one should extract Bhuvaneśānī and the seed-syllable (bīja) of Durgā. At the end of the armor (varman), having uttered one's own seed-syllable, one should then join the three previously mentioned seed-syllables in reverse order.
Then, when the fierce [mantra] has been ignited, it is "without a kīla" (niṣkīla) and bestows all accomplishments (siddhi).

Likewise, regarding the extraction of the *maula* [mantra], whether it is with a *kīla* or without a *kīla*, in this context, the mere state of being without a *kīla* is the quality [of the mantra]. When there is the addition of other syllables, such as the seed-syllable *dīpī* at the beginning of the *pāśa* and so forth, [it becomes without a *kīla*].

This [mantra] is to be known and meditated upon; here, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the fifth vowel with the nasal drop (*bindu*), "svāhā" is the power (*śakti*), and "duritau" is the seed-syllable—so say the teacher Padmapādācārya. He describes the ritual placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) starting with the words "on the feet," etc.;
there are four joints on each foot and four joints on each hand, thus making six...

There are ten locations: the six locations of the two sides, the two breasts, the two nostrils, the two cheeks, and the two eyes, which constitute twelve; and the nine locations consisting of the anus, the genitals, the *ādhāra*, the abdomen, the heart, the throat, the mouth, the middle of the forehead, and the top of the head, each being a single location. Thus, there are [twenty-one].
Having combined [the syllables], the placement of one letter each should be performed in the thirty locations of the sentient beings.

He describes the *aṅganyāsa* (limb-placement) with the words beginning "yadbhiḥ" and so forth: "O Puruṣa, arise! *Namaḥ* to the heart; do you sleep? *Svāhā* to the head; fear has come upon me, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*)."

The meaning is that the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the six limb-mantras: *yadi śakyam aśakyam vā kavacāya huṃ*, *tan me bhagavati netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *śamaya svāhā astrāya phaṭ*. [Furthermore,] the discus (*cakra*) is on the upper right hand, and the conch (*śaṅkha*) is on the upper left hand.
With the left hand below the *kṣa* [syllable], [one offers] the *abhaya* [mudrā]; with each single substance, ten thousand (*ayuta*) oblations are made.
When ten thousand oblations are performed for each of the four substances, the homa results in forty thousand. Some say this constitutes the "ten-fold portion" (*daśāṃśa*) homa.

Others, however, say that these substances may be taken optionally according to what is available, because there is an absence of words such as "or" (vā) that would indicate optionality or a secondary alternative; rather, some maintain that all four are to be offered together.
Regarding this, there is a yantra used for worship and retention.
It is stated in another Tantra: "A lotus with a six-cornered pericarp and eight petals along with filaments;

outside of that, one with twelve petals, then one with twenty-four petals; outside of that, two circles. In the center, the syllable *duṃ* joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*); in the pericarp, in the six corners, [the names of] Dāva, Durgā, and the six limbs; in the eight [petals]..."

One should write the syllables of the Durgā-mantra three times each upon twelve petals of a lotus that crushes the enemy of Mātṛ-mahiṣa; the remainder, however, should be written on the first petal. Furthermore, one should write pairs of syllables from the Mālā-mantra, which is in the Triṣṭubh meter, on each of the twenty-four petals.
In reverse order, outside of that, one should place the eight forms at the junctions; outside of that, in the first circle, one should place the eight weapons. Thus is the unsurpassed Durgā-yantra.
The meaning of this is: in the pericarp of the six-cornered [lotus], one should place the six syllables of the Durgā-bīja, namely "du" and "ma."
In the corners, the six-limbed mantras of the primary mantra; on the eight petals, the eight syllables of the Mahiṣamardinī mantra;
on the twelve petals, the syllables of the present mantra three times each;
outside of that, on the twenty-four petals, in pairs on each petal, [the vyāhṛtis] *oṃ bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ* and *jva*.
Having written the letters of the forty-eight-syllable mantra garland— *Lajjvalajvālāmālinī sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike varade jātavedase jvala jvala hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—
in reverse order, [one should write] two by two the syllables of the *triṣṭubh* mantras to be described hereafter.

Having written sequentially up to the end of the twentieth joint (*sandhi*), and having not written the remaining letters in the remaining joints, [one should worship] Durgā herself, the first circle, the Excellent Lady (*Varavarṇinī*), and Āryā, with one *kanaka*...
The second circle is to be encircled by mantras ending each with "namaḥ," such as *bhāyaikṛtikāyai*, *abhayadāyai*, *kanyāyai*, and *surūpāyai*;

and [further] by the eight [mantras] consisting of the words for the discus (*cakra*), conch (*śaṅkha*), sword (*khaḍga*), shield (*kheṭaka*), arrow (*bāṇa*), bow (*dhanus*), trident (*triśūla*), and skull-cup (*kapāla*), each [ending] with the dative case and *namaḥ*.

The phrase "he should surround them" means that, as before, one should perform the worship of the four [mantras] beginning with the Āgneya— namely the Heart and so forth— in front [of the central deity], and the worship of the Eye in the four directions and the Weapon-mantra on the filaments (*kesara*). As for the statement regarding the worship of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) within the pericarp (*karṇikā*), this refers to the sequence of ritual items (*padārtha*).
What was stated by Darśakṛt— that it is "as before"— is incorrect, because it would contradict the root text (*mūla*),

since that worship was previously prescribed specifically for the filaments (*kesara*). Nor are the filaments identical to the base of the petals (*patramūla*), such that because the worship of the Śakti is traditionally taught there, the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) would not be performed there.

It might be argued that [the term *kesara*] refers to the filaments, because the filaments and the base of the petals are distinct entities; for this very reason, the author of the *Harṣakaumudī* states in his usage: "The limbs are on the filaments, the Āryās and others are at the bases of the petals, the weapons such as the discus (*cakra*) and others are in the middle of the petals, and Brahmā and others are at the tips."
Regarding the subjugation of enemies, the attainment of longevity, and so forth, the visualization is otherwise as it has been stated:

for the crushing of enemies, one should visualize her with sixteen arms, resembling blazing fire, mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, and terrifying; however, for the complete destruction of enemies, one should visualize her with eight arms, dark-limbed, [trampling] the demon Mahiṣāsura.
One should contemplate him standing there, intent upon the accomplishment of longevity; he is the fire of time, the conflagration of dissolution;
with his right hands held upwards, he holds a skull-cup, a discus, a sword, an arrow, and a trident;
with his left hands held upwards, he holds a conch, a shield, a bow, and a skull—this is for the purpose of protection.

Dhyāna is included within this very procedure for recitation (japa) following the morning bath, which is designated as fourfold; for, with regard to the attainment of success through the recitation of the *ari* mantra and so forth,
it is inappropriate to assign only one count there, as it constitutes a subsidiary action (*aṅgakarma*) and because it has not been explicitly mentioned.

One should recite the mantra one thousand times for the attainment of the fruits of one's own actions; however, according to the statement in another Tantra, "For minor rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should recite ten thousand times. In such applications as these, [the name of] the planet, minor spirits, enemies, thieves, kings, and so forth, should be placed before both parts of the root mantra.

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that the mantra beginning with "daṃ prakṣipya agrahabhayaṃ me samupasthitam" (Having thrown this [into the fire], the fear of the planets has come upon me) is to be recited; for it is only where there is an impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) that the insertion of worldly words is appropriate, as when someone, upon hearing "iṣe tvā," [supplies a word] due to expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
The word *chinadmi* ("I cut") and others are rejected on the grounds that [the meaning] is not perceived as such;

however, in this case, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. For the word *bhaya* does not fail to denote the fear of seizing, hunger, and so forth. Furthermore, if the insertion of that word were intended, one would have simply said "fear of such-and-such."

"It appears as if [the sun] is shimmering; standing in the water, one should meditate upon the Goddess in the solar orb"—thus it is stated in another Tantra: "One should recite this mantra one hundred and eight times for this Durgā, who possesses radiant luster, who stands upon a lotus within the orb of the sun, who is red in color, well-adorned, and holds a conch, a discus, a lotus, and a vessel of treasure in her hands."
"Standing in water up to one's navel, self-restrained, one should recite the mantra for the sake of swift success.

Thus he states another application with the words beginning with "ten thousand" (*ayutam*): "One should perform ten thousand oblations (*homa*) with the best fuel-sticks (*samid-vara*) produced from the *vaṭa* tree, which have tips intact and are offered with their pointed ends facing upward, while the deity is worshipped."

Regarding the connection: some maintain that although it was already established by the word *arcita* ("worshipped"), it is restated here for the purpose of reminding; however, according to the natural sense of the root, the meaning is "this oblation is to be performed with fire kindled specifically by means of banyan wood (*vaṭa*) twigs," and he states another application [of this rule].
With the words beginning "apāmārga," [the author] refers to wild sesame seeds, commonly known as *jartila*.

With the words beginning "sahasra," he states another daily application; from the phrase "sārān" onwards, it means having taken pieces of wood—fragments of hard, pure trees such as the *khadira* and others.

When the fire has increased and reached a small [steady] state, one should perform oblations for seven days, beginning from any day, using the aforementioned mantra in accordance with one's own favorability. All the offerings should be mild and sweet; however, there is a specific detail in another Tantra regarding the Goddess who resembles a fresh *kundana* flower and holds a trident.
[He holds] a hand-drum, an arrow, a bow, and a pair of beautiful water-pots in his arms.
Having meditated upon Durgā as the supreme *dhātrī*— of massive body, with a terrifying face, and well-adorned—
one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) in the midst of each [verse] during rites for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*). If, however, it is for the rite of sugarcane,
one should contemplate the six-armed Goddess as holding two jars filled with the juice of sugarcane, as previously described.

The wise man, facing the western direction, should offer oblations of pure, refined wood-shavings mixed with ghee, reciting the mantra in reverse order for each syllable; this is another ritual application.
He states "in fever," etc., as follows: the specific distinction is that one should wave them with the left index finger; [these refer to] those fevers and so forth.

He describes another application with the words beginning "vidarbha" and so forth: having written two syllables of the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) on a birch bark leaf, followed by one syllable of the mantra, then two syllables of the name of that same person, then one syllable of the mantra, and then the syllables of the *sādhya*'s name again until the end, that leaf should be rolled up into a small ball.
Having reduced the potter to a mere tool, at the time of fashioning earthen vessels such as jars,
one should take the clay adhering to his hand and fashion from it an image twelve finger-breadths in height; then,
having inserted a pill of that [substance] into its heart and performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), [one should proceed].
For the practitioner who, having worshipped the image with incense, flowers, and other offerings,

places it upon a pedestal in front of himself below his own feet, recites [the mantra] one thousand and eight times daily without interruption during the evening twilight for a period of one fortnight; for that practitioner—

The meaning is that one becomes a true adept and a master of the senses. Having written this mantra—which contains the syllables known as the *sādhya*—upon a leaf, the practitioner of mantras should place it upon an image fashioned from the clay of a potter’s hand;
then, for seven days, he should recite it ten thousand times while facing [the image] with his heart fixed upon it.

If one recites [the mantra] eight hundred times during the three junctions of the day, that deity will certainly come under one's control; this is the meaning. Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should then distribute and write the syllables of the mantra upon the eight petals outside of it, using a thread [as a guide]. A potter...

Having fashioned an image from clay held in one's hand and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) for that deity, one should place it before oneself; by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day,
the person to be accomplished will certainly come under one's control— this is another ritual application.

Or, having worshipped a maṇḍala consisting of the svastika and other symbols, or on the seat of Bhuvaneśvarī covered with silk cloth, one should place thirty arrows there; having invoked and fully worshipped the Goddess therein,
and having likewise invoked and worshipped the Goddess in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered oblations thirty times with either sharp oil, half-leaf oil, or mustard oil,
one should pour the resulting consecrated oil (*saṃpātataila*) into those [arrows] and simultaneously touch thirty arrows. Then,
having recited the root mantra one million times (*niyuta*) according to the count of the targets, it is consecrated.
The collective meaning is this: those arrows, wrapped with red threads at their nocks, should be hurled at the enemy armies; by doing so, one shall cause the army to flee. As it has been said:
"When the *māyā* [syllable] is placed in the center of a *svastika* on a ritual seat (*pīṭha*), or even within a wheel, one should worship it according to the prescribed rule..."

Even when enveloped by subtle time and other factors, one should place thirty sharp, gold-feathered arrows; then, having invoked Kātyāyanī, one should worship her with excellent perfumes and other offerings in the triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) produced according to the previously mentioned sequence within the fire.

Having invoked her who has sixteen arms, and having worshipped her with sandalwood and other offerings, one should offer clarified butter mixed with white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*)—either a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand oblations. Then, with the residual drops obtained therefrom, one should anoint [the image]. Having dismissed the Goddess from that very place, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) the same number of times as the oblations, using blood.
One should wrap it firmly with thread near the nock;
by means of those arrows, when discharged by a skilled archer, the enemy host—though protected by Indra—will lose its senses and charge forward.
Such is this cruel rite performed with a *pratiloma* mantra, according to Padmapādācārya.
He also states another application with the words beginning "having recited," etc. A *kuḍava* is four *palas*. A *kulika* is a specific *muhūrta*, as stated in the *Ratnamālā*:
"By means of the Manu, Sun, directions, sky, seasons, Vedas, and fortnights, the *kulikas* arise during the day according to the twelve *muhūrtas*."
On the days of the Sun and other planets, during the nights of Nireka and others, there are seven muhūrtas beginning with Manu and so forth that sequentially become the *kulikas* by day;
however, at night, those same [periods] beginning with Maitra, reduced by one each, having reached thirteen muhūrtas, become the *kulikas*. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: others, however, explain the connection as "when the *kulika* of the enemy arises. Furthermore, they say that according to the analysis of the *Svara-śāstra*, this refers to the time when the *mṛti-svara* (death-sound) of the enemy occurs during the lunar day (*tithi*) and so forth. He states another application in the verse beginning with "by the army" (*senā*), etc.
The *kāraskara* is well known in the vernacular as *viṣatinduka* or *kuvelā*;
it should be employed here for the purpose of paralyzing (*saṃstambhana*). Furthermore, he who likewise offers a thousand oblations with *kāraskara* flowers shall effect the paralysis of an army.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the word *udiśya* (aiming at), in the case where it is to be completed [by a specific object], even if it is not explicitly stated, it should be understood that one should offer oblations with those flowers aiming at "stambhana" (paralysis). According to that view, however, by the offering of *kāraskara* leaves, the army shall turn back—that is, it shall withdraw from its own territory. This is the practical application (*prayoga*).
He states another method with the words beginning "aṅgāra" and so forth: on a Tuesday (Bhauma-vāra), during the tenth muhūrta called Kūlika,
one should take ashes consecrated one hundred and eight times with a mantra over the head of an enemy,
[visualizing] a black woman with a terrifying face adorned with serpents, and [apply] the powder of black pepper and fire...

One should meditate upon Mahādurgā, who is naked, whose arms are filled with piercing pain, and who is intent on uprooting, wandering, destroying, performing *kṛtyā*-rites, and pursuing [the enemy]—in accordance with the method stated in another Tantra.
Meditating thus on the Goddess, one should cast [the ritual materials]. He states another application, beginning with "mahat": *Mahad...* [and so forth].

By means of the dust from the foot— specifically the left foot— of that enemy, together with *kāraskara* leaves fallen by the force of the wind, there shall be the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of enemies through the performance of the oblation preceded by the aforementioned meditation. He states another application beginning with "kāraskara" and so forth, regarding the image.
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should fashion a wooden image measuring twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
ninety-six finger-breadths,
or twelve finger-breadths, using the "measure-finger" (*mātrāṅgula*) according to the sequence prescribed for those two rites. Thus it is said.
One should not be deluded into thinking that the twelve-finger-breadth [measurement] alone is primary because it was taught first;
rather,

it is primary for the purpose of avoiding the futility of those injunctions which would otherwise apply only to those [meditations] accomplished through excessive hardship, excessive wealth, or great exertion.
Since this [practice] is to be accepted, the word "one should cut" implies a number of one thousand and eight;
"limb by limb" means starting from the right thumb and ending at the left thumb.
In the same way, as in the case of fire and so forth, it refers to a thunderclap occurring through the falling of a tree or against a wall.

"An enemy is certainly destroyed quickly by a sword, water, fire, the bite of a serpent, a rutting elephant, a banyan tree, or by yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, or other causes"— from this traditional teaching [it follows that death occurs] within three days.

It is stated that there is no doubt that one dies before the practice on the fourteenth day, which follows the three [days] starting from the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at the time of the ritual application; thus, regarding the specific meditation for killing: "One should meditate upon Durgā, who is as black as the sky at the time of dissolution and adorned with serpents, holding a sharp sword..."

One should meditate on her as mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, holding a sharp sword in her right hand and, with her left hand, seizing the victim by the hair and dragging him away; this is for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
Thus he states another application, beginning with "unmattā" (the intoxicated one), wherein the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is established in this rite.

One should take the powder of *śatabhaṅgā* and fill a skull with it; Radhā, Nāśāvarī, and Durgā are to be meditated upon for the rite of intoxication. Regarding the other application beginning with "ulūka," etc., [it involves] the fat and blood of an owl and a crow.
By performing oblations at night after going to the forest with those belonging to both sides combined, the death of the enemy will occur.

He states another application beginning with "rātroḥ" (of the night): knowing the birth-constellation (*nakṣatra*) of the enemy, one should use a tree belonging to that constellation; if it is unknown, one should use a *kāraskara* tree. [One should fashion] a twelve-finger-long image of the enemy...
Having fashioned an image with a form identical to that of the enemy, and having established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) therein,

one should [use] poison (*viṣa*), *hālāhala*, *kuṣṭha*, and *marīca*; for it is stated in the lexicon that *śāmala* is known as *vallīja* and *ghoṣaṇa*, and thus it is specifically [to be understood] by its synonym *marīca*.
One should cast [the image] into very hot water in such a way that it is entirely submerged— so that there is contact with the water on all its limbs— and by doing so,
the aforementioned result will be attained. If, however, milk is used for that image, then one [should act] in this manner.
The meaning is that the fever shall be destroyed and not otherwise; he now states another application.

With the words "the threatening gesture" (*tarjanī*) and so forth, he states another application by means of the verse beginning with "sword" (*khaḍga*). Having taken up weapons and the like in order to destroy a well-armored enemy who is prepared to charge, there may be destruction through crushing, trampling, or even by means of [causing] him to fall; therefore, this is not a repetition of the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
It should be understood that these two methods— consisting of the specific meditation on holding weapons and so forth— are conceptualized solely according to one's desire for killing.
He states another application beginning with "the bow" (*cāpa*), etc., [describing] such a [state] running until the lower part of the knees...

Regarding that very [subject], he states another application which is required: "ānityaka" refers to a specific type of tree well-known by the name *paracchī* according to common parlance. He states another application:
"for protection," [meaning] with [the mantra] consecrated one thousand and eight times, five...
The meaning is that by smearing elephants with products of the cow, protection is attained.

He states another application in the passage beginning with "gavyājya" and so forth: having offered oblations one thousand and eight times daily with each of the eight substances—among which is the clarified butter of the cow—and [having fed] Brahmins...
Having fed more than two people daily according to one's capacity— by the force of the plural number—
and having satisfied the preceptor with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other offerings,
that king shall possess great prosperity consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth; [this applies] to the lowly ones regarding the killing or driving away performed by others.
There would be no suffering from [the acts of] striking, piercing, and so forth. He states another method with the words beginning "one should cause to be made" (*kārayet*):

having had the five weapons, such as the conch and others, fashioned by an artisan from a fruitful *palāśa* tree standing on Brahmin-owned land, one should immerse them in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

One should recite [the mantra] five thousand times while touching [the weapons]. This means that one should recite one thousand times for each individual weapon. Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with that same number of offerings, and having cast the remaining clarified butter (ājya) into them, one should perform their worship with their respective mantras as will be described hereafter.

Having extracted the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and touched them again as before, one should recite the mantra five thousand times. Then, having caused pits to be dug in the middle and in the four directions starting from the east,
one should pour the *pañcagavya* into those pits, beginning with the center, while playing the five musical instruments.
Having sounded the conch and other instruments from the center to the beginning, and having performed their worship as before,
one should fill the pits with sand and level the ground with clay; then,
at each respective spot, one should offer oblations to those various weapons and also to the guardians of the directions.

Having offered those respective oblations to the directions, having fed the Brahmins, having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to one's capacity, and having satisfied the poor and the helpless, this protection— wherever it is performed, whether in a village or a city—
therein increases the abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches.
The collective meaning is that they should not be cut every day. Also, in the *Īśānasaṃhitā*:

"Having cut a tree rich in fruit standing on the land of a twice-born, and having split it into five equal parts from the center, one should [fashion] from the portions in sequence the conch (*śaṅkha*), the sword (*nandaka*), and the discus (*cakra*)."

One should fashion a conch, the Kaumodakī mace, and a palm-tree staff, each measuring one *tāla* in height. One should place these in a vessel containing the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having established them upon a *svastika* diagram, one should worship them properly and recite the mantra five thousand times. Then, having offered oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in equal measure according to the prescribed rite, [one should perform the final rites] with the residual drops of the ghee.

Having smeared [the ground], the wise one should again mutter this mantra; having dug pits one cubit deep in the center, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions—though no specific detail has been mentioned there—one should worship the pedestal with the root mantra and install it. Having invoked Mahādurgā into those [pits] with faith...

One should recite [the mantra] while remaining in that state. Therein, having worshipped the deities of the seat (pīṭhadevatās) situated within the central hollow, one should place those weapons, such as the conch and so forth, there with the root mantra of the deity of the present mantra. Having invoked Mahādurgā, the deity of the present mantra, into the conch situated in the center, one should worship her.

The meaning is "he shall conquer. Likewise, one should construct a surrounding wall with the *astra-mantra* [using] the forms of the heated weapons, which possess the characteristics previously described for the directions; these "respective weapons" (*tattad-āyudhāni*) are the weapons of the deities under discussion, and those "respective forms" (*tattan-mūrtīḥ*) are the forms of the retinue of the deities under discussion.

The meaning is that, having worshipped in this manner according to the previous procedure, one should contemplate [the deity] all around the enclosure wall, with weapons placed in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions above them. In another Tantra it is said:
"Having contemplated Mukunda, whose hands hold a lotus, a conch, and a mace, as being inverted upon the sun-lotus..."
"One should mutter the mantra of the venerable Ṛṣi, which bestows all accomplishments"—

this is the meaning: for one who meditates upon Viṣṇu, four-armed and bearing the weapons known as the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, within the solar orb, and then mutters the previously mentioned Vanadurgā mantra, there is the accomplishment of all undertakings.
In the case of a mantra addressed to a male deity (*puruṣīti-sthale*), there may be a reversal of gender (*liṅga-vyatyāsa*)— that is,
the use of the masculine gender in place of the feminine— but the specific difference regarding the ritual action (*kāryya*) is as follows:
he demonstrates the desired yantra with the words beginning "the lotus" (*padmam*), which is a twelve-petaled lotus.

Having drawn [the lotus], one should write the Praṇava (Oṃ) in its pericarp; inside that, the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ); inside that, the Durgā-bīja (Druṃ); and inside that, having written the names of the person to be protected (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka) and so forth, one should write the twelve syllables of the Mahiṣamardinī mantra, two by two, upon the twelve petals in their respective directions.

Having completed the night by repeating [the mantra], one should write the letters of the present root-mantra in groups of three according to its qualities; having written the single remaining letter on the final petal,
one should then write the letters of the Mātṛkā within the space between two circles outside of that.
Having constructed one *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) with three lines and two *bhūpuras* with six lines,
