one should write within them the seed-syllables (*vīja*), the *yantras*, the *gāyatrī*, and so forth, as obtained from the general scriptures; or else, [one should write] that which is situated between the two *bhūpuras*.

It should be understood that the intended state of being situated between two outer walls (bhūpura) at the intermediate corners of the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as the possession of four gates— which is generally obtained for the *bhūpura*— is not to be negated by anyone.
As for what is stated in the *Harṣakaumudī* regarding the writing of the seed-syllable of Durgā after the seed-syllable of Māyā...

The claim that the *naṃ* (the syllable *nam*) must be accepted as the "seed" (*bīja*)— meaning it is capable, belongs to the capacity, and is related to the capacity— with the intention that this is the primary sense of the "root-seed" (*māyābīja*)— is inconsistent with the root [of the word]. For if such an intention were intended, one would have to say "the seed of capacity" (*śaktivīja*).

One might argue that the word *gapada* is redundant, since only the long seed-syllable with the visarga should be adopted here; however, that is not certain, because in the root [text] it is specifically stated that the seed-syllable of Durgā is indeed that which possesses the bindu (*savindu*). Furthermore, in the twelve-fold *yantra*, both he himself and others have likewise used the form with the bindu.
This is the summary: [The work] of him whose mother was Udyotamatī,
whose father was Guṇavatī, whose name was Māpati— a treasury of love—
and whose birthplace was the land of Paṭhakula, which is like Mount Kūrma, and who made Lord Vācya (Viṣṇu) his object of supreme worship.
The venerable Vārāṇasī-vāsabhuṣaṇa, a devotee of Maheśa, has reached the completion of this work,

the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*. Now, fearing that the deities might become enraged by the disclosure of this science (*vidyā*) which is intended to be kept strictly secret, as it will be explained hereafter, he seeks their forgiveness.

He does not praise wealth with the words beginning with "ajñāna" (ignorance), etc.; rather, the sense is that by the illumination of this knowledge, there will be benefit for my disciples as well as the fame of myself, and thus even the destruction of that ignorance—which is of the nature of an offense—will occur for me as well. How so? [The text continues: mataḥ katha...

There will be a description of this ignorance; otherwise, how could there not be anger among its practitioners toward one who provides such a description? Even in the case of a traditional description, the mantra-deity becomes powerless through the loss of the purificatory rite known as *gopana*.

Thinking, "In this way, by means of [the practice of] *nasya* and so forth, may I too succeed in crossing the ocean of anxiety," he qualifies [the object of worship] with the words beginning with "in saṃsāra" and ending with "the seed of bliss. Thus,
the intention is that when it is worshipped through such investigation and the like, it will most certainly bestow bliss.
By the phrase "it is inconceivable to you," it has been stated how it is possible to describe that which is beyond the reach of speech and mind;
this was said for the sake of motivating the listener. Having thus praised [the Goddess] with the words "knowing whom...
and so forth, and having asked for forgiveness for his transgression, he makes his formal promise (pratijānīte) with the words "the Tripurā-vidyā," as stated for the sake of motivating the listener.
Having thus understood [the situation] and praised her in this manner, he seeks forgiveness for his offense and makes a vow, saying "Tripurāṃ vidyām" (the mantra of Tripurā).

In the *Siddheśvarī Tantra*, the etymology of the word "Tripurā" is stated as follows: "Because she was worshipped in ancient times by the three cities"—that is, by the three deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna. She is thus called Tripurā because she was worshipped in the past by these three gods.

The name *Tripureti* was thus proclaimed by the gods. The word *pura* implies that in the past, at the beginning of creation and other such occasions, [the Lord] desired to perform various respective acts;

the sense is that [the Goddess] is so called because she grants the desire to perform those specific acts. Likewise, she is the sole bestower of sovereignty over the Siddhas and others, as well as the power to accomplish great and difficult tasks such as creation and so forth.

*Viyat* (ether) is *ha*; *Bhṛgu* is *sa*; *Hutāśa* (fire) is *ra*; the *Bhautika* (elemental) is *ai*; and *Indu* (the moon) is the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). Then, *Viyat* is *ha*; that which begins with it is *sa*; its own form (*svarūpa*) is *ka*;
*Indra* is *la*; *Agni* is *ra*; the left eye is long *e*; and the *bindu* (dot) constitutes the second [seed-syllable].

The letters *ha*, *sa*, and *ra*, along with the fourteen vowels, the *visarga*, and the *anusvāra*—these six constitute the third seed-syllable (*bīja*). These three seed-syllables are known respectively as *Vāgbhava* and the others. Now, in the second unprecedented [seed-syllable], there are five phonemes consisting of *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, and *ra*.

Because it consists of those five syllables, beginning with *janānām* and ending with *prathamītimayośca*, together with their respective vowels, it is said to be composed of five *kūṭas*. Regarding this three-seed-mantra (*trivījamantra*) consisting of five *kūṭas*, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Paṅkti is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Tripura...

The deity Bhairavī is the primordial seed-syllable (*bīja*), Śakti is the middle [syllable], and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the accomplishment of all desired goals. From the navel down to the feet is the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, the first seed-syllable;
thus, these designations are made solely for the sake of conventional usage regarding the hands, the left...

Having shown three types of nyāsa based on the observation of other tantras— namely, that the two palms are [assigned] to the left and right hands respectively, and the second [set] to the two eyes— he describes the fourth nyāsa, which consists of the nine-yoni (navayoni),
beginning with the words "karṇa" and so forth, using groups of three locations each to form a triangular shape.

The traditionalists maintain that for those who perform the ritual, there is a placement of the three seeds (*bīja*) one by one upon the womb (*yoni*), beginning with the left side; for it is observed everywhere that the previously mentioned placement begins with the left hand, and likewise, the worship begins from the left corner of the two conch shells (*śaṅkha*).

The term *kukṣi* refers to the elevated regions on the sides of the forehead; in some instances, it indicates the region of the navel, and in certain readings, the word *nābhau* (at the navel) is used instead. Therefore, the placement [of the syllables] is in the form of a vulva (*yoni*).
The *kūrpara* is the joint portion in the middle of the arm. The *dhvaja* is the penis (*liṅga*); [the term] *guhya* [refers to the secret place].

Since the *liṅga*— which is designated by the term "secret" (*guhya*) because it is conventionally established as the "secret region" (*gudapradeśa*), meaning the region that is not to be shown— is what was previously mentioned, he now describes the fifth [placement], that of Rati and the others,
with the words beginning with "mūla," etc., using the three seed-syllables (*bījas*) to be described in sequence for Rati and the rest.
The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* maintains that the placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed in the Mūlādhāra and other locations by means of [the syllables] joined with the *bhis* ending.
However, because the word "in reverse order" (*viloma*) is heard in the root text, there is a connection here with the third seed-syllable of Vālā and the second of Matobhavā;
thus, there is no requirement for these specific locations.

Because of the existence [of the word "sthāna"], there is an expectation for a subsequent location; since the word "sthāneṣu" is connected with what follows, it does not show the meaning of the word "tarati. For this is not logical: it has been stated that the middle occurrence of the word "sthāna" and so forth cannot connect with what follows because it would be contrary to the sequence, whereas its final occurrence can connect with what precedes it. This is difficult to maintain.

It cannot be argued that, by way of the context of *thāsaura*, this [rule] must also be connected with what follows for the sake of obtaining the position in reverse order (*viloma*); for if that were the case, one would have to consider that there is no authority for the reverse-order application of the *bāla* and *vīja* syllables. Nor is it the case that everything...

Even *lomya* is based on *rati*, because it relies solely upon the first seed-syllable of the first *rati*. It is stated in the scripture: "The seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*) is declared to be *vāgbhava*, while the final one, called *mohana*, is likewise proclaimed as the seed-syllable of *prīti*. Thus it has been said by me.

It must be stated that this is not a valid authority; for even if it were authoritative, it would have to be resolved as referring to an alternative position due to its contradiction with the source text, since neither the reverse nor the direct order of the *bālā* [mantra] is adopted here. He states the sixth placement (*ṣaṣṭanyāsa*) in the verse beginning with "amṛte."

The connection with the fourth quarter [of the verse] begins with *śī*; thus, *śī* is at the *bhrūmadhya* (between the eyebrows) in conjunction with the first *vālā* and the *amṛta* (nectar); *hṛdi* (in the heart) is *śī* in conjunction with the second *vālā* and *yoga*;
*mūlādhāre* (at the root-support) is *śī* in conjunction with the first *vālā* and *viśva*. At the *mūlādhāra*, it is *śī*.

The meaning is that the Source of the Universe (Viśvayoni), accompanied by the first [syllable] *re*, should be deposited. He describes the deposition of the seven forms (*sapta-mūrti-nyāsa*) with the words beginning with "of the ether" (*khasya*), etc.: Bhṛgu is *saḥ*; the sky is *haḥ*;
fire is *raḥ*. Those which begin with Sadyojāta and the others are thus five *hṛ*s in reverse order.

When the vowels *a*, *o*, *e*, *i*, and *u* are joined in sequence with the letter *s*, they become the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the five forms (*mūrtis*). Thus it is said: *Śrīṃ Īśānāya tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*.

The implied meaning is that one should assign the mantras beginning with "Oṃ śaetatpuruṣamakaradhvajāya namaḥ" to the head, face, and other parts [of the deity]. However, according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*, the seed-syllables for the five forms starting with Īśāna have already been stated; as for those of Manobhava and the others, there are five.
Since the seeds of Nāñca, Nitā, and the others are to be mentioned [later], they must be placed at the beginning;
therefore, they say that the application should be *oṃ īśānāya strīṃ manobhavāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
This is the view accepted by the Mūla[-tantra]; otherwise, [the sequence] would be like that of Īśa and the others, rather than Manobhava and the others.

Furthermore, since it is necessary to define the seed-syllables (*bīja*) right here, the failure to define them would result in a deficiency in the root text; however, in our view, although the mind-born [Kāmadeva] and others exist as independent beings due to their independence, for those who are accompanied by their forms (*mūrti*), this very seed-syllable [is what constitutes them].

There is no deficiency whatsoever in not stating this, as it was due to the intention of [protecting] sentient beings (*satvābhiprāya*). He states the eighth, the placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*), beginning with "that" (*tat*) and so forth: one should place those respective forms, preceded by the previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*), upon the five faces according to their desires. The ninth is the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).

The meaning is that one performs the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantras *hsrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hsrīṃ śirase*, and so forth, as indicated by the words "six" and so on. However, according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*, there is also the application of the six long vowels to this very second seed-syllable; furthermore, according to the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīm*) is also included here.

The six long vowels joined with the first [consonant] should be applied at the beginning; this refers to the seed-syllables (*bīja*) that constitute the mantras for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Since the phrase "by the first" (*ādyena*) functions as a qualifier for the specific seed-word described as being the second [syllable], it means "by that which is the first of the seed-mantras. Thus, *hrāṃ hsklāṃ* [is the heart mantra].

They say that the ritual application begins with "dayāya namaḥ" and "hrīṃ hsklīṃ śirase," and so forth. Since this is the intended meaning of the root text, according to the *Ādyamakriyā* system, one should employ only the first [mantra] joined with the six long vowels;
however, one should not employ the two [mantras] favored by you as the qualifier and the qualified.

One should insert another word within the interval; for if it is argued that the position [of the opponent] is based on a mere semblance of scripture inferred through the lineage of teachers, then the root text itself will restate that very same meaning. To illustrate: the term "ākāra" refers to a single part.

The term "ākāśapara" (following *ākāśa*) means following the letter *ha*, since the word *ākāśa* begins with *ha*; thus, the meaning is "preceded by the letter *ha*. Such are the three seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Furthermore, in the middle [of these], there is that which has this name, beginning with the sixth, the sixty-sixth long vowel, and the fourth short vowel.
The meaning is that it is joined with that which possesses the form of the six long vowels. The sixth [syllable] is excluded by the phrase "with the second seed-syllable in the other place.

Furthermore, the sequence beginning with "the six long [vowels]" must be repeated. For that which has its literal meaning as stated, there is a connection with the second seed-syllable obtained according to the aforementioned method; this is without qualification (*nirupadam*).

Although it is stated that the seed-word (*bījapada*) is indeed the *māyā*-seed (*hrīṃ*), nevertheless, since the phrase "six long [vowels]" (*ṣaḍdīrgha*) and so forth must be construed according to its literal meaning, what remains for the attainment of the sense you have described? Alternatively, the first word refers to the six long vowels beginning with *ā*, due to their association; and thus, by the *arśa* [affix].

The attainment of being "joined with that" (*tadyuktatva*) is achieved by resorting to the suffix *ādyac*. Furthermore, according to the maxim of the "lamp on the threshold," this [suffix] connects with both the first and last terms—namely, the seed-syllable (*padabīja*) joined with the six long vowels—to convey the aforementioned meaning. Thus, the secret is: "What remains when you employ [this method]?"
It appears that the author of the root text has provided this exposition using extremely cryptic terminology precisely because of its secret nature.
He now describes the tenth, the *bāṇanyāsa* (arrow-assignment), with the words beginning "the five arrows" (*pañcabāṇān*), and so forth.
In this regard, although in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* there is only the letter *me* at the end of the two feet of the goddess Rādrī...

It is recited thus: the first seed-syllable is known to be accompanied by Atri, Śo (Śiva), and the mouth [of Brahmā], together with Vahni (Fire), along with the staff (Daṇḍa), and indeed that very syllable is pervaded by the three forms (Trimūrti). The second is remembered as situated at the beginning of the face, mounted upon the King of Gods (Indra), with the left eye, and joined with the eastern face. Bha...
"Combined with the first of the single-unit [syllables], preceded by the Lord of the destruction of the half-svara of the six enemies of Vṛtra"—

this is the meaning: here, *atrīśa* (the letter *a*), *udaḥmukhavṛtta* (the letter *ā*), *vahni* (the letter *ra*), *araḥ* (the letter *da*), and *anusvāra*— these, when joined together, attained the state of the first seed-syllable (*bīja*).
If the fourth vowel (Ī), which is the seat of Yajñanara, is conjoined with Atri’s form (the letter *i*) at the end,
and all the remainder remains as before, then that is the second seed-syllable (*mukha*).
Because of its placement upon the mouth (*mukhe nyāsāt*), it stands within the middle of that [syllable].

The letter *ka* and the letter *kṣa* arise from the conjunction of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*. That which falls within them is the King of Gods (*devarāja*), *lu*, the left eye (*vāmekṣaṇa*), the fourth vowel (*caturthasvara*), the face (*vaktra*) which is the *visarga*, and the anusvāra preceding it; these are its [components]. When placed upon the mouth (*mukha*) of that [syllable], they form [the mantra].
The third seed-syllable is preceded by the letter *va*, which is the friend of the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*).

Then there is the letter *ṣṭa*, followed by *r* and *l*. The sixth vowel is the letter *ū*. This indicates the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the half-point (*bindu*). These, when joined together and attained the state of *lūṃ*, constitute the fourth seed-syllable, [belonging to] Gautama.

In the *Hitā*, it is stated that the fourth seed-syllable (*bīja*) ends with the fifth vowel; [the syllables] "thā" and "tu," joined with the letter "ra," and adorned with the "śa" of peace (*śānti*), joined with the bindu and nāda, are the two seed-syllables that enchant the three worlds (*trailokyamohana*). After that, the Kāma-seed-syllable (*kāmabīja*) is followed by Jalandharā.

That [seed-syllable] is conjoined with the fifth vowel, endowed with the *bindu* and the *nāda*. These are the seed-syllables: *vaṃ*, *te*, *va*, *caṃ*, *draḥ*, and *sa* (with *sarga*). The sixth is the left ear;
by the etymology "that from which the second vowel arises," this statement is also intended to refer to the fifth vowel.
The syllable *kyate* is *tu*, *ṃkaṃ* is *ja*, and *tvaṃ* is *va*. From that, the fourth is *sa*, and the preceding one is the *visarga*.
This is because in the *Mātṛkā* [alphabet], the *visarga* is recited before the letter *ka*. Thus, this is the fifth seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Nevertheless, according to those who have seen various Tantras, it may also be *ḍaḥ*.

It appears that for those who follow that [view], the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed with mantras ending in *ḍrāṃ* and *garbha*, such as: "Oṃ *ḍrāṃ* to Drāviṇī, namaḥ; Oṃ *ḍrīṃ* to Kṣobhiṇī, namaḥ," and so forth. Now, he describes the eleventh, the *Subhagā-dinyāsa*.

By the words "on the forehead" (*bhāle*) and so forth, a specific location situated in the middle of the face is indicated. By the phrase "according to the rule of the necklace" (*kaṇṭhikāvidhinā*), the meaning is that one should begin with the five stars (*pañcatārā*) as they are appropriately arranged from the start. By the word "to the practitioner" (*mantriṇe*), it is implied that this applies not only to the mantras beginning with the five stars and the *Subhaga* mantras, but to other mantras as well.

Having obtained the mantra from the mouth of a Śrī-guru according to the prescribed method of instruction on the mantras that constitute its limbs—mantras which are liberated from the defects of that [unauthorized] time—one must possess the status of being initiated by the mantra; for it is stated that the state of one who has merely learned the mantra through the inspection of books and such means does not accomplish the task. Thus [it is said in the] Vākya...
The seed-syllable *Vāgbhava* (AIM) is that which was spoken by Sarasvatī in the *Prastāva*; *Kāma* is well-known as having the characteristics of the *Kāmabīja* (KLĪM);
and here, the fourth is the *Strībīja* (HRĪM). These five seed-syllables are to be understood as denoted by the five *Tāra* words.
He now describes the twelfth [practice], the *Nyāsa* of ornaments (*bhūṣaṇanyāsa*). Regarding the *Nyāsa*:

By these and other [verses], the *bhūṣaṇanyāsa* (the ritual placement of ornaments) is described: it consists of meditating upon the very letters of the Mātṛkā as the ornaments of the Goddess and then performing their ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own limbs, beginning with the head.
In this context, according to the *Padārthādarśa*, the word "bhrū" (eyebrow) indicates a single location; thus, [the placement occurs] on the two rows of teeth.
In the *Harṣakaumudī*, it is stated that although two locations are intended by the term "eyebrows" (*bhrūpada*),
and although there are indeed two locations which constitute a pair (*yugala*) or a couple (*dvandva*),
the ancient authorities (*prācīna*) must be asked: why is it that [the ears] and so forth do not likewise possess the status of being two locations?

Since there is an equality of dual number in the case of the two cheeks (*gaṇḍau*), the two lips (*oṣṭhau*), and the two rows of teeth (*dantapaṅktī*), why is it that the last two have a single location while the others have two locations each? This is what the second [opponent] should be asked.
Furthermore, how is it that the locations beginning with the head and ending with the mouth are sixteen in number?

If it is argued that [the placement] must be established so that the placement of the sixteen vowels occurs there, you are mistaken; for even though the nose is one, the number sixteen cannot be obtained. Indeed, neither the nasal faculty nor its substrate is twofold; therefore, the *prāṇa* situated at the tip of the nose...
In the Nyāya-śāstra, there is a well-known maxim: "The ringing of the bell [is heard] by both ears.
Thus, the dual number is used everywhere for the ears and so forth, while the singular is used only for the nose, as in:
"The two ears have pervaded the three worlds; the eye is Puṇḍarīkākṣa; the nose is Guṇāka," and so on.

In the *Śrīrājarājeśvara-kavaca* and other such texts, where it is taught that there are two locations for the nose (*nāsikā*), one should understand that the word "nose" (*nāsikā*) is used there as a designation for the two nostrils (*tatpuṭa*). Thus, it should be kept in mind that the singular number is employed in the root text [of the mantra] by way of this designation. Therefore...
The nose has a single location.

Furthermore, because they are conveyed by words ending in the singular number, and because they occupy a single location, there is no difficulty whatsoever in establishing the number sixteen by including the head and so forth from the mouth onwards; nor is there any contradiction with the root text, on the contrary, [the singular]—
The direction is that the sweetness of the internal descent (*antaḥpātana*) of the pair at the end of the two nostrils (*nasya-yugala*) is indeed superior.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the twenty-seven letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ra* from the forehead (*vivuka*) down to the big toe of the foot; therein, [the placement] on the hands...

The claim that the referent of the term *tat* has two locations, as stated in the *Darśana* commentary on the word *tvaṃ*, is not tenable; for, just as in the case of "the base of the arm" (*dormūla*) and so forth,
there is no possibility of two locations because, despite being co-occurrent with it, the [term] lacks the dual ending even when situated in multiple places such as the palm and the back of the hand.
Even a minute distinction is discerned according to the maxim that "even a small forest is perceived through determination.

Now, when the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *a* are to be assigned to the toes and the thumbs, since no other letter remains [to be assigned], and by virtue of the force of the traditional teaching (*āmnāna*) that "afterwards, two [are assigned] to each," one [letter] alone [is assigned].

It should be placed on the head; for according to the maxim that "even the conceptualization of a single location [is acceptable], there may be elision at the end or an increase [in size]," its placement at the end is appropriate. Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that because of the similarity in height with the word *sthika*, two fingers are intended here, not the middle finger; this very point is the correct position.

Here, "concentration" (*samāhitatva*) is intended in the sense of attentiveness (*sāvadhānatva*), which consists of not forgetting the instruction regarding the positions and permutations of duality, unity, and so forth.

As for the placement of the remaining eight letters beginning with *va*, [the text mentions] "the waist" (*kāñcī*) and so on; in the region of the waist, one should place *ka* and *ca*. In the neck...
The letter *la* is on the wind [the left shoulder], the second *la* is at the base of the bracelet [on the left wrist], the *tāluva* (the letter *ta*) is in the heart,

*śa* is in the secret place, the final letter *kṣa* is on the two earrings, the head-sound (*mūrdhanya*) and the final labial (*daṃtyauṣa*)— the vowels *e* and *ka* (*e-ka*)— are respectively on the crown and the forehead, and the letter *ha* is on the crest; such is the distinction according to the Ṛṣi.
Even though the *dinyāsa* (deity-assignment) here is brief, it must be followed according to the general injunctions; thus,

after the general assignment (*sāmānyanyāsa*) such as the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the thirteen specific assignments (*viśeṣanyāsa*), beginning with the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣinyāsa*) and ending with the assignment of ornaments (*bhūṣaṇanyāsa*).

"One should meditate upon the Goddess," he says with the words beginning "thus" (*evam*), and so forth: she who has a garland of severed heads on her head is the *Vacchinnamuṇḍamālā*; her breasts are smeared with flowing blood;
in her two right hands she holds a rosary and a boon-granting gesture (*vara*), and in her two left hands a book and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).

Although the requirement for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed equal everywhere, nevertheless, he speaks again of "initiation" with the intention that one must strive in every way for the aforementioned type of initiation alone, and that one should not consider one's purpose fulfilled by mere instruction (*upadeśa*).

The attainment of the state of the Goddess as described in the Īśvarītantra—characterized by the specific mode mentioned for the excellence of what is to be attained—is achieved through the particular mode of practice prescribed therein, and not merely in any arbitrary way;
furthermore, this occurs after the attainment of that which is to be attained, and not prior to it. Its measure is twenty-four lakhs.

Regarding the statement "the lotus" (*padmam*) and so forth for the worship yantra: having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus, one should create two triangles within its pericarp—one with its apex downward and one with its apex upward—and by means of this method, having produced the nine-yoni (*navayoni*), one should draw a square outside of that; such is the meaning.
The reasoning is as follows: within the pericarp, one should leave aside a portion of the pericarp sufficient for three triangles at its western end;
then, having established [the remaining space], one should draw two [triangles] on each side of that eastern-pointing triangle, corresponding to the directions of Īśāna and Agni.
Having formed two triangles by the drawing of two perpendicular lines,

and having set aside a small portion of the base of the great triangle, one should draw two lines from the lower point of intersection of the side-triangle and the great triangle toward the south and north, [forming] two triangles.

Having formed another triangle from the point where the two [previous] triangles meet, extending westward as far as the middle portion of the great triangle, one should position the western apex such that its tip lies at the center of the middle triangle.
"One should make the interior of the triangle" means that, in reality, one should pierce the power (śakti) with the powerless (aśakti), and then enclose it again within the city of fire (vahnipura).

According to the statement in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, first one should draw a single śakti-line; having pierced that [line] in its middle portion with another line, one should draw the left and right lines joined to the tips of the northeast and southeast portions of the dividing line, [extending] to the western end of the first śakti.

From the western corner, by generating another corner within the western corner, one should fashion the second śakti. Then, starting from the eastern direction of the first śakti and preceded by the construction of corners, [one should fashion the lines] to the left and right, extending as far as the northwest and southwest.

Having drawn the eastern line upward and joined it with the western corner of the first triangle, one should construct the city of fire (vahni-pura) according to this method; thus, the practice of constructing the nine-yoni diagram is performed, wherein the triangle pointing downward is the Śakti and the triangle pointing upward is the city of fire.

Regarding the variations: some maintain that there should be two upward-pointing triangles and one downward-pointing triangle; thus, the arrangement of the nine *yoni*s should follow the previous method. Furthermore, tridents (*triśūla*) should be applied to all eight triangles, in accordance with the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*.
This [text] speaks of the purpose and extracts the *pīṭhamantra*, beginning with "vāgbhava" and so forth.

*Nā* is the nature of *lohita*; *paḥ* is *parā*, which is the nature of *śrīkaṇṭha*. *Aḥ* is the elongated form of the letter *ra*; *pai* is the nature of *parā*, and *apara* is the nature of *para*, yet it is joined with the vowel *ā*.

The *ha* and *sau* are the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) of the letter *a*. *Ha-sau* is the nature [of the mantra] always connected with Sadāśiva up to the end of Mahāpreta. *Aiṃ parāyai aparāyai parāparāyai hsauṃ sadāśivamahāpretapadmāsanāya namaḥ* consists of twenty-nine syllables.

The meaning is that the *komaṃtras* are those worthy of worship belonging to the *pīṭha*. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that one should worship the lineage of the venerable Gurus (*śrīgurukrama*) within the space between the eastern [mouth] and the central *yoni*. That [lineage] is threefold, distinguished as the Divine Current (*divyaugha*), the Siddha Current (*siddhaugha*), and the Human Current (*mānavaugha*). [It begins with] Paraprakāśānanda, Paramaśānanda, and so forth.
The first [lineage] is sixfold, consisting of Paramaśivānandakāma, Īśvarīnandakāma, Amṛtānandakāma, and so forth;
the five Siddha lineages are Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadānanda; while the Mānava lineage consists of one's own respective Guru, Paramaguru, and so on.

"One should worship the lineage of gurus on the northern part of the seat oneself"—this is the general rule that applies here in the performance [of the rite], since no specific rule is seen in this context.
By the mere statement "as declared in the Āgama," its authoritative status is asserted; for [the word] *āgata* [derives from] Śiva.
The mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) has proceeded from the mouth of Vāsudeva; therefore, it is called [the *Mata*].

By hearing this etymology, how could there be any suspicion of invalidity regarding those [scriptures] which are based on being accepted as composed by and approved by the faultless, omniscient Blessed One?

Regarding the statement "by means of the five *praṇavas*" due to their occurrence, he explains that state with the verse beginning with "Speech" (*vāk*) and so forth: the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbhava*), the seed-syllable of Māyā (*māyābīja*), the seed-syllable of Ramā (*ramābīja*), Vyoma (the letter *ha*), Sva (the letter *sa*), Ādi (the letter *ka*), Durgā (the letter *la*), Pārśva (the letter *va*), Antya (the letter *kṣa*), Agnistha (the letter *ra*), Jhiṇṭīśa (the letter *jha*), Indu (the letter *sa*), Turya (the letter *au*), Tāra (the syllable *oṃ*), and Jīva (the letter *ha*), which is the final [syllable] of the Yantra.
The extraction of these [mantras] is as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hkhphreṃ sauṃḥ*—these are the five *praṇavas*.

The salutation (*nati*) is the gesture of obeisance (*namaskāramudrā*), as before. Within the central triangle presided over by the principal Goddess Śrī, on the left side of the inner Goddess and to one's own right:
There, one should worship Bhāgerati on the right side of the Goddess and Prīti on her own left side;

having worshipped Manobhavā there in front of the Goddess, one should worship the limbs as before upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus outside, and in the center of the central *yoni*, in the four directions, and in front of the *candrāvalī*.

Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Nyā, one should worship the eight Śaktis beginning with Subhagā in the eight yonis starting from the east; having worshipped the [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī on the eight petals, one should worship Indra and the others in the first enclosure of the square, and Aśani and the others in the enclosure outside of that.

In that regard, having honored the flavors (*rasa*) and so forth as being equal in rank to the principal deity, and having made a formal request for the sake of the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), the deities of the six enclosures—beginning with the limbs (*aṅga*) and ending with the vajras—should be worshipped as before; this is the collective meaning. With milk-rice offerings...

The third section: [the addition of] "with ghee" (*saghṛtatvam*) everywhere; [and the herbs] *amṛtā*, *guḍūcī*, *girikarṇī*, *aparājitā*, *anulomā*, and so forth; at the end of the three seed-syllables (*trivīja*) of the root mantra, [one says] "bring [so-and-so] (*amukam*) under control" (*vaśamānaya*).

The meaning is that, having uttered the words of the *sādhya* beginning with "Oṃ" and so forth, one should again utter "svāhā" at the end of the three seed-syllables (*vīja*) of the root mantra in reverse order and perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*). The intended root [mantra] consists of the combined *paṭula*, salt, and *bilva* flowers; having applied the word "bhava" at the end of that, one should [offer] the flowers.

Because of the act of making [the flowers] into a paste (*ritikaraṇāt*), the oblation of both types of flowers cannot be accomplished by means of an oblation of only one of them; for in the case of [the injunctions] such as "with *kṛtamāla* flowers," "with *rājavṛkṣa* flowers," and "with *pāṭala* flowers," the qualification "fully blossomed" (*vikasitaiḥ*) indicates that the flowers themselves are understood to be the substance of the oblation.

He describes the application of *lakā* with the words "the two feet," and so forth. *Kapi* is red sandalwood; *cora* is *karvūra*, commonly known as *saṭī*. On the night of the fourteenth day, it should be ground by a maiden in a cremation ground—this is the specific detail.
It is well-prepared and consecrated with the root mantra for the purpose of wearing. *Maṃ*... [text ends]

He says "in the middle" and so forth. By means of the prescribed method for the worship yantra, one should first draw the yantra here as well—on birch bark or similar material—consisting of a nine-yoni [design] enriched with an eight-petaled lotus, outside of which are two circles, and further, two squares whose eight spokes are mutually intersecting. Having thus drawn it... [the rest of the sentence follows].

The seed-syllable *maṃ* is to be written in the central yoni; then, starting from its tip, the other seed-syllables, beginning with the second, are to be written in the surrounding yonis in a clockwise direction. Thus, by repeating the three-peak mantra (*trikūṭamantra*) three times, the nine yonis are completed. Here, regarding the phrase "the first [syllable] in the middle," it means the first syllable is in the middle, that is, in the central yoni.

Some maintain that the meaning is: "Just as the middle seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*) should be [the first], so too should the middle womb (*madhyayoni*) be the first"; others, however, hold that it means:
"Of the root mantra consisting of three seed-syllables, that which is the middle—the middle seed-syllable—that should be the first."

The meaning is that it should be as it was in the first [instance]. Thus, in the middle enclosure (*madhyayoni*), one should write the middle seed-syllable (*bīja*) first; then, in front of oneself (*svāgre*), the first [seed-syllable] first, and then the third—following this sequence one should write. However, in the second and subsequent enclosures, the writing of the seed-syllables follows the [original] order. There is no authority for abandoning the sequence.
According to the first opinion,

they say that since it is observed that one should write the seed-syllables such that the middle syllable is at the center of the nine-fold grid (*navayoni*), even in the second and subsequent rotations,
it is proper for the middle seed-syllable to come first, followed by the first and second [seed-syllables].

The phrase "the first [syllable] in the center" and so forth is not particularly restrictive; for in all yantras, it is established that the drawing of the yantra must begin from the central pericarp (*karṇikā*) and from the very first syllable of the mantra,
since no specific distinction is stated regarding the second seed-syllable.

Since writing [the mantra] on the pericarp (karṇikā) was not previously established, it appears that in the second opinion there is a specific statement [regarding it]; however, even here, the name of the practitioner, the object to be accomplished (sādhya), and so forth, must not be forgotten. Then, upon the eight petals, [one should write] the present root Gāyatrī.
One should write the letters of the alphabet in groups of three according to their sequence; outside of that, in the surrounding path (vīthī), the Mātṛkā letters are to be written.

Then, one should write the Kāma-bīja (Klīm) in the eight corners of the two Bhūpura squares. It should be understood that whatever remains is to be done here as well, following the general procedure for yantras.

He describes another yantra with the words beginning with "Kāmam" and so forth: having fashioned a hexagon, one should write the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and other details within its pericarp; then, having written the six seed-syllables at the tips of the six corners, one should [place them] upon the sixteen petals drawn outside of that.

Having written the seeds of desire (kāmabīja) one by one, one should surround them on the outside with the syllable *ha* accompanied by the bindu (*hūṃ*). This enclosure is formed by two lines creating a single path, just as before.
In this context, the seed of desire to be employed is specifically that which takes the form of the second seed-syllable of Bhairavī.

Even the author of the *Padārthadarśa* shows partiality toward this very position, which is well-known. Therefore, the instruction is that one should practice [the drawing] marked with vajras in the four corners and the eight directions.
He states another yantra with the words beginning "of fire" (*vahneḥ*), etc.: having first fashioned a hexagon, its diagonals—

One should write the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) upon the body, and within it, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and others. Then, one should write the first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), which is the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable of Bhairavī, within the six corners.
After that, having written the fourth *kāma-bīja*, namely "a mlam," six times at the junctions of the lines of the hexagon, [one should place] the outside of that.
One should enclose it with the "woman" (*strī*) seed-syllable. Here, the singular form "woman" (*strīm*) is intended;
thus, one should write a single long *strī* seed-syllable outside [the triangle], just as was done previously for the hexagon.

It is desired that what has been written should enter into the interior; as it is said, "one should cast all of this into the belly of Manobhava. However, the claim in the *Padārthādarśa* that Manobhava consists of the three female seed-syllables (*vīja*) while Vāgbhava is well-known [as the male] is erroneous. Regarding that...
Since it lacks the designation "manobhava," the name "fifth manobhava" would not be applicable;

furthermore, as for what the author of the *Harṣadīpikā* stated— that one should form two external coils and then encircle them within with the seed-syllable of the woman— that too is to be disregarded because it contradicts other authoritative tantras.

Regarding the phrase "yameva": because this [mantra] is extracted from the five seeds of desire (*kāma-bīja*) belonging to the Mind-born One (Kāmadeva), it is known as the "Five Mind-born" (*pañca-manobhava*). Furthermore, those Five Mind-born ones are extracted in another tantra as follows: "The fifth [vowel], conjoined with the end of *śu-vinaya*, together with the left eye, the wind, and *gu*."

The letter *ka* joined with *na* (kṇa), the sun-sound (*ra*) joined with the horse of Hari (Viṣṇu) and Viṣṇu’s sixth (the letter *u*), and then the letter *ta* joined with the enemy of Bala (Indra) and Bhṛgu (the letter *sa*). Upon their heads, the wise one placed crescent moons (*u*).
These, indeed, have been declared by me to be the five desires (*pañcakāma*). This is its meaning: *kaṃ*.
By "jala" (water), the letter *va* denoting it is indicated; from that comes the fifth letter, *ha*.

That [seed-syllable] is joined with the letter *ra* preceded by *śu*, with the letter at the end of "naya," with the second of the first eye, and with the vowel of the fourth eye which is denoted by the word for the second eye. This is the first seed-syllable, Māyāvī.
The letter *ja* is joined with this [letter *ma*], which is the first of the winds (*pavana*); therefore, the third quality is the letter *u*.

Joined with that, the hand is the letter *ka*; by the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letter *ka* at the base of the hand, the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) is extracted. The solar vowel is the letter *ai*. In this context, "here" (*iha*) refers to this [mantra].

Between the letters *ri* and *ha*, that is to say, excluding the four syllables [of the word *vinā*], there is an ornament at the end of those syllables; when combined with the number three, it becomes the seventh letter from the beginning, which is the letter *sa*. Viṣṇu is such a Hari who possesses this [letter *sa*] in his midst.
Thus, the first *kūṭa* (syllabic cluster) is extracted as *tisvarūpam itthaṃcahsrai*.

The sixth vowel is *ṣaḥ*; where there are the two letters *va* and *la* (*vahaṃtau valau*)—namely, the letter *va* and the letter *la*—such is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). By this, *lum* is fully extracted; *taraḥ* is the letter *ra* together with the letter *ta*.

The meaning is that "there is *raḥ* (the letter *r*) in this"; thus, it means Bhṛgu is joined with the letters *ta* and *ra*. That which has the fifth vowel (*u*) as its [final] syllable is "that which has the fourth vowel" (*turyasvara*), namely *bhṛguḥ*. By that, "strī" is extracted. Of these, the *vī*—
It arises from the offering of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) upon the *jatvaṃśiras* and the bindu indicated by it;

alternatively, since the placement (*nyāsa*) of *rati* and so forth preceded by the seed-syllable of *ālā* was previously mentioned, he extracts that mantra for the sake of understanding it, beginning with "the lower" (*adhara*), etc. The "lower" is the twelfth vowel (*au*).

The syllable *brahmā* (brā) is situated in *ka* (the letter *ka*), and the syllable *indra* (in) is situated in *lu* (the letter *la*). It is joined with the Moon (*śaśīyuti*), meaning it is joined with the Moon—the bindu—and the fourth vowel; thus, it is endowed with power (*śaktiyukta*), which means it is to be practiced by Brahmā. Because the letter *ī* is placed at the end of the word "Moon" (*śaśi*), it is joined with the letter *sa* and the visarga.

The third [syllable] consists of the fourteen vowels; its application is as follows: in another tantra, it is stated that one should recite ten thousand times over ghee cooked with *brāhmī*, *avākpuṣpī*, turmeric, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Then, a pregnant woman, by licking that [ghee], becomes a sovereign of speech through her intellect, omniscient, and possessed of exalted qualities.

It produces eye disease and leprosy; likewise, at the beginning of each day, during the eclipse of the moon and the sun, or even at night, those who recite this [Gāyatrī] from their mouths with their faces turned downward will have it emerge in the form of a great torrent— so it is stated in the Triśitīyantra regarding the Gāyatrī.

In the desire for that [mantra], he extracts it with the words beginning with "manmatham" (the mind-born). The word *manmatha* is extracted as the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). The second is the seed-syllable *dhīma hi*. Regarding the action expressed by the word, the accusative case is used.
Thus, the four [syllables] are: *klīṃ*, "O Goddess Tripurā, we know thee," "O Kāmeśvarī, we meditate upon thee," and "do thou impel us, O Kinnā."
Having completed the worship of one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), which consists of a hymn of praise and prayer in the *gāyatrī* meter of twenty-four syllables,

[the author] praises [the practice] with the words beginning "Brahmādayi" in order to emphasize that the worship of the Supreme Deity included within the five-shrine system (*pañcāyatana*) must be performed and not left incomplete; by this, it is shown that in the case of the *kāṇḍānusamaya* method, the worship is indeed [to be performed in this manner].

The *Padārthādarśa* author also adopted this very position, which was implied by the principle that one should proceed according to the sequence of the ritual acts (*padārthānusamaya*). [He states: "But you praise You who are subtle in form and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) with words of praise (*stuti*)—that is, with words that convey praise—is the praise of the quality-less."
Even they do not know that words such as "hair" have three parts; how much less can we?
Therefore, O Mother, abandon this subtle form and [reveal yourself].
We praise her who possesses a gross form, bearing saffron and other [ornaments];

we worship her alone. Regarding the word *tāra*: "The pure *tāra* is a pearl necklace (*hāra*), and *tāra* may also mean a pure pearl," according to the lexicon. As for the phrase "mutually" (*anyonya*): those who perform your worship [according to] other authentic scriptures...

Those of dull intellect, whose wealth of discernment has been utterly uprooted by the strife of refuting differences of opinion regarding the specific means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can they know Your true nature?
Or rather, [they may speak of You] as "Vāgbhava," based on the etymological derivation meaning "that from whose presence speech (*vāc*) arises."

The four states— *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*— which constitute the nature of *kuṇḍalinī* and are the supreme manifestations (*bhāva*), resort respectively to the locations of the base, the navel, the throat, and the mouth;
and through the organs such as the throat, they are directed toward specific meanings.

The meaning is that they utter words for the sake of what is not beneficial or for desired objects; having attained you—the wind of prāṇa and apāna, and the group of six enemies consisting of lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, as will be described in the final chapter—they effect creation in you alone. In you...

Having cultivated [the power of support], even a created world would dissolve; for there can be no stability without a support, and thus, by that [support], the stability of the creation is maintained—this is the sense. Some, however, say: "Having attained You, the creation was brought about by the Enemy of Manmatha (Śiva), and not by one attached to desire."

If it is argued that creation arises from both male and female, and that this is the established order (*maryādā*), they say: "It is you alone who establish that very order. From your own dwelling place, the *mūlādhāra*, [you ascend] to the royal capital of Śiva, situated in the *brahmarandhra*.

The thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, the other lotuses with four petals and so forth located in the places beginning with the *ādhāra* (the foundational center), and the *suṣumnā* path— wherein the essence of existence (*bhāva-sattā*) of both word and meaning resides;
she who shatters (*chinatti*), that is, cuts asunder (*khaṇḍayati*), the fruit of karma which is the "arrow" (*śara*) of the seven [lotuses], is thus called Śāradā, and so forth.

The intention is that, having offered praise and requested forgiveness, one should obtain permission and worship the host of supreme deities, beginning with Gaṇeśa, in their proper sequence. He extracts the Mātaṅgī mantra starting with "vāk" and so forth;
it ends with "namaḥ," and "tamaḥ" refers to the syllable *oṃ*. The letter *ka* is Brahmā, and the letter *ra* is Agni; its [the mantra's] seat...
The letter *na* is conjoined with *asthiti* (the state of non-existence), and such is the *netra* (eye); *hrasva* (short vowel) is *bhṛgu* (*ha*), and *sa* is *tu* (*sa*)—thus it is *sva*.
*A* is its own form, and *ravi* is the letter *ma*. Conjoined with *śiva* (*i*) and *kāra* (*ka*), it becomes *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo bhagavati śrīmātaṅgeśvari sarvajanamanohari*.

"O you who bring all kings under control, O you who bring all men and women under control, O you who bring all wicked beasts under control, O you who bring all beings under control, [bring] such-and-such a person in this world under my control, svāhā!"— thus [recited] eighty-eight times.

The Ṛṣi of this Kṣara-mantra is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the metre is Gāyatrī, the deity is Mātaṅgī, the seed-syllable (bīja) is *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), and the power (śakti) is Svāhā. The specific locations for its application are the throat, the region of the larynx (*tanmaṇi*), and the lower part of the neck (*gala*). It is stated that there are eighteen words [to be applied] in these parts.

In this regard, when the doubt arises as to whether a word (*pada*) consists merely of its phonetic form (*varṇa-mātra*), or whether it is a meaningful unit (*śakta-pada*), or perhaps one ending in a nominal suffix (*su-anta*), or one ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ-anta*), or finally each of those two types individually,
[the author] demonstrates the division of words concerning their own nature (*svarūpa*) by means of the passage beginning with "guṇa" and so forth. First...
The first [part] is with three *mikas*; the second with the *praṇava* (oṃ); the third with two [syllables], *namaḥ*; the fourth with four [syllables], *bhagavati*; the fifth with *śrīmātaṅgeśvari*;
the sixth with eight syllables, *sarvajanamanohari*; and the seventh with *sarvamukharājī*.

The seventh [chapter] is with six verses, titled "All-Face-Dyed"; the eighth is with seven verses, titled "Bringer of All Kings Under Control"; the ninth is with eight verses, titled "Bringer of All Women and Men Under Control"; and the tenth is with ten verses, titled "Bringer of All Evil Beasts Under Control."
The eleventh [syllable] is formed with ten [vowels]; the twelfth with eight, preceded by "sarvasattvavaśaṃkarī";
the thirteenth with four, preceded by "sarvalokamiti"; and the fourteenth is the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), such as "so-and-so," even if it consists of many syllables.

Because it is introduced by the three syllables "mukamiti," it is called "three-syllabled" (tryakṣara); with that very intention, the state of having eighty-eight syllables for the *Aṇu* [Tantra] was stated, including the additions of Jānakīvallabha, Rāma, and so forth.

There is no fault even if there is a deficiency of syllables; for instance, the fourteenth [is indicated] by three [syllables], the fifteenth by one, the sixteenth by two, the seventeenth by three as "ānaya," and the eighteenth by two as "svāhā. Pa...

The meaning is that it should be performed. According to the traditional teachers (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*), the third [mantra] consists of two [syllables] beginning with *namaḥ*, the sixteenth with two [syllables] beginning with *vaśa*, and the seventeenth with three [syllables] beginning with *mānaya*.
It is proper that the placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the root mantra should be done exactly as they stand.
The intention [of the author] is that, by the natural force (*svārasya*) of the original words, what was stated previously alone is appropriate;

this is the first arrangement of the words. Regarding the passage beginning with "Speech" (*vāk*), the applications such as *aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ ratyai mātaṅgyai namaḥ* and *aiṃ ratyai mātaṅgyai namaḥ* should be understood according to the differences in the traditions (*mata-bheda*).

The second [type of] nyāsa begins with *tira* and so forth; it is stated that the first letter of one's own name serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and its possession of the nasal drop (*bindu*) has been mentioned.
Therefore, the practical applications are such as: *Hṛllekhā-mātaṅgyai namaḥ*, etc. This is the third nyāsa. The fourth is the six-limbed nyāsa (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*): *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo bha...*

"Gavati-Śrīmātaṅgeśvari-sarvajanamanohari-hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth is the application there; by the phrase "beginning with one's own name" (*svanāmādīti*), the application such as "drāṃ śāviṇīmātaṅgyai namaḥ" and so on is indicated. This describes the fifth placement (*pañcamanyāsa*).

I shall now describe the sixth placement (*ṣaṣṭanyāsa*) with the words beginning "Manmatha" and so forth: starting from the left side of the body and extending to the right shoulder, one should sequentially place the eight Kāmas in all six locations on the face using the mantras such as *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ manmathamātaṅgyai namaḥ* and so on. This is the seventh placement (*saptamanyāsa*).
The phrase "samāhatatonyasya" and so forth means "in the locations such as the mouth, shoulders, and so on.

"Mantravit" means one who knows the mantras; that is, one who knows the mantras of Anaṅgakusumā and the others through the instruction of the Guru. By that [knowledge], the mantras of these [deities], beginning with the three seed-syllables and ending with Kāmātaṅgī, [are established].

By that which was indicated by the three [syllables], the application beginning with *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ anaṅgakusumā mātaṅgyai namaḥ* and so forth is established. He states the eighth placement (*nyāsa*) with the words beginning "they are to be placed" (*vinyastavyāḥ*), etc.; here too, the word *mātaṅgī* refers to those such as Śiva-śekhara-lakṣmī-bhūtā and others. In this mantra as well...

By the word "triṇi" (three), the attainment of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) mentioned previously is indicated; or, the phrase "beginning with the three seed-syllables" (*bījatrayādikāni*) applies throughout. Therefore, the practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ lakṣmībhatāryai namaḥ*, and so forth. Then, the ninth [step] is the placement of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra-nyāsa*) upon the head. This concludes the enclosure (*āvāra*).

The placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, occurs in these eight locations; here too, by way of recurrence, the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) are obtained. Thus, the practical application (*prayoga*) is: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ brāhmīmātaṅgyai namaḥ*, and so forth.
This is the tenth placement (*nyāsa*). In these same locations, there is also the placement of Asitāṅgabhairava and the others.

Here, as before, the application begins with *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ asitāṅgabhairavaṃ mānagye namaḥ* and so forth; this is the tenth nyāsa. Again, the placement of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) on the head is the twelfth. He describes the thirteenth nyāsa with the words beginning "on the foundation" (*ādhāra*).

These [powers], ending with *ityam*, constitute the single creative power (*kriyāśakti*) known as "Emission" (*sṛṣṭi*). One is called "The Single," one is "The Beautiful," and one is "The Embodiment of Bliss. Beginning from "One between the two eyebrows" up to the end of Śiva, ten locations should be understood, situated one above the other. And within these, starting from the Mūlādhāra and so forth, up to Śiva—

In the sixteen locations beginning with the left [nostril], the sixteen powers (śaktis) starting with Vāmā and ending with Navṛddhi should be installed. Regarding that, the applications are as follows: "Salutation to Vāmāmātangī," "Salutation to Jyeṣṭhamātangī," and so forth.
He describes the fourteenth installation with the words beginning with "on the head" (śira), etc. These...

One should install the aforementioned Mātaṅgī, beginning with the word "Mātaṅgī," then again Mahadādyā-Mātaṅgī, then again [the one] beginning with the word "Mahālakṣmī," and finally [the one] beginning with the word "Siddhalakṣmī. The application of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) is universal; likewise, the ending with "Mātaṅgī" is also universal.

"Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mātangī mātangī mātangyai namaḥ"— this is the first mantra, composed of three instances of the word *mātangī*. "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mahāmātangī mahāmātangī mahāmātangyai namaḥ"— this is the [second] *mātangī* mantra, formed by incorporating the additional word *mahā*.
The second [mantra] is composed of words: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mahālakṣmīmātaṅgīmātaṅgyai namaḥ*. This is the third: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ siddhilakṣmī*.

"Salutation to Lakṣmīmātaṅgīmātaṅgī"—this is the fourth [mantra]. In reality, however, it is understood from the root text that Mātaṅgī is preceded by "Mahāpadā" (i.e., Mahāpadamātaṅgī), ending with "Mahādā" (i.e., Mahādāntā), and not that "Mahāmātaṅgī" is the preceding word; thus, [the mantra is] Mahāmātaṅgī... [etc.]

"Obeisance to Mātaṅgī"—thus, this mantra should be understood as consisting of two instances of the word *mātaṅgī*, not three; this is the fifteenth nyāsa, the placement of the root mantra at the mūlādhāra. Furthermore, the sixteenth is the pervasive nyāsa (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) performed with the root mantra.

O Kūlikākeśa, even here one must not forget the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa which has attained the common process of darkness (tamas), the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal (saṃhāra) of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, the expansion of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa consisting of the kalās of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, and so forth.
The head of the group was bound— meaning fixed— by means of a *kalhāra*, a species of fragrant lotus;
some say it refers to a conch-shell ear-ornament (*tāṭaṅka*) fashioned from a conch, which had been brought there by a particular movement from this side or that.

Some say that the word *śaṅkhapada* refers to a specific kind of ornament made from conch shells, such as bracelets (*kaṅkaṇa*) and so forth; the word *tāla* means a palm leaf (*tāḍī*), and women fashion an ear-ornament (*karṇabhūṣaṇa*) from it; thus, they say she is "one whose [ear] leaf is accompanied by a conch."

Based on the memory of the *Trikāṇḍī* lexicon which states that *citraka*, *tilakantama*, *patra*, *tilaka*, *cittaka*, and *viśeṣaka* all refer to the same thing, he describes the worship diagram (*pūjā-yantra*) with the words beginning "tri-kona" and so forth:
first a downward-pointing triangle, above that a single circle, and then an eight-petaled lotus.
Then a circle; then again an eight-petalled lotus outside that circle; then outside that, a sixteen-petalled lotus; then outside that, a vajra-encircled square (bhūpura).
One should meditate on these three lotuses as having filaments. Vibhūti and the others are not the pedestal-shaktis (pīṭhaśakti) here.
The application [of the mantra] is "O Mother of Vibhūti, Taṅgyantā, enaṃ," and so forth.

"Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of all powers" (aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ) is the mantra for the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā). By the phrase "as before," it is stated that one begins from the northeast corner (rāmakoṇa); this refers to the worship of Rati and the others.
The mantras are indeed the nyāsa-mantras; therein, Rati and the others are in the middle of the triangle, while Hṛllekhā and the others are in the left corner and so forth within the triangle itself.
The limbs (aṅgas) are in the four directions starting from the east and in the center; then [the mantras] are on the filaments of the first eight petals. Then, tri-...
In the outer region starting from the corner marked with the *hṛllekhā* [mantra], there are five arrows in the four directions;
at the tips of the first eight petals are Anaṅgakusumā and the others; in the center are Brahmāṇī and the others;
at the front are Asitāṅga and the other Bhairavas; and on the petals of the sixteen-petaled lotus are Vāmā and the other sixteen [Śaktis].
In the four corners of the square, starting from the east, are Mātaṅgī and the others;

in the corners of the square, starting from the southeast (āgneya), are Vipreśā and the others. Outside this square is the *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) formed by three lines, as obtained according to the general scriptures.

The extracted meaning is as follows: Indra and the others are to be worshipped in the *thamavīthī* (the row of power), and Vajra and the others are to be worshipped in the row outside of that. Having prayed for permission to perform the worship of the deities equal in rank to the principal deity, such as Rati and Hṛllekhā, one proceeds with the worship of the twelve enclosures beginning with the limbs (*aṅga*).
At the conclusion of the worship of each enclosure, the washing of the hands, the offering of the first worship of the first enclosure, and so forth, are performed as before. Now,
having been instructed that a mantra accomplished in this manner is a means for achieving one's desired goal, there arises a desire to know the specific method therein.
The *mallikā*, *camelī*, *punāga*, and *kesara* flowers;

the *utpalas*, which are blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*); *lakṣmī*, which is the *tāmbūlākāravallī* vine; *kiṃśuka*, which is the *palāśa*; and *vañjula*, whose synonym is *veḍasa*; [the word] *kṛṣṭiḥ* means attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), all of it.

In this context of mantras mentioned previously, only that which has already been stated should be adopted, and not even that which is yet to be mentioned; for if it were so, then this [definition] would have been stated at the very end for the sake of the paribhāṣā, whereas its mention here in the middle is merely for the sake of the structural elegance of the treatise— this is how it should be understood.

*Trimadhura* consists of honey, ghee, and sugar, though some say it consists of honey, ghee, and curd. By the phrase "saffron and so forth," *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *karvūra*, and red sandalwood are likewise included.

The result of the combined offering of these eight fragrances ending with *śakti-gandhāṣṭaka* is the subjugation of the world. Furthermore, on the fourteenth day at night, one should apply a tilaka made from flour mixed with sugar and modakas, having consecrated it again with this mantra.

One should place those eight substances, beginning with sandalwood, as seeds ground with water in a bronze vessel and expose them to the heat of the sun; from that, the oil will certainly emerge, and not otherwise. By means of this method, one performs a homa with salt mixed with *nimba* oil for the sake of [subduing] enemies.

Nārāyaṇa conquered his enemies, the adversaries; the number of oblations (*homa*) mentioned therein has been stated generally previously. Having observed the requirements such as the materials and so forth, according to the rule that it should be performed once, [the rite] consisting of the *maṇḍala* and other forms is to be done a thousand times or ten thousand times, as no specific time limit is prescribed.

It is established by all authorities that where success is not achieved through a single application, the applications must be performed up to five times; this is proven for a practitioner who possesses a perfected mantra,
provided there is an abundance of materials according to their specific desire, up to the number five.

Having established that the Blessed One’s promise— that through yoga the fruit of one's own karma necessarily arises— is infallible, and having thus defined the ritual procedure for the Mātaṅgī-mantra up to its optional applications, [the author now provides] the primary hymn of praise for the purpose of expiating the offense incurred by revealing what was to be kept secret.

Having completed the worship of the deities of the directions (*ṣṭhāṃtapūjā*), he begins the hymn to Mātaṅgī in order to indicate that the performance of the worship of other deities, such as Gaṇeśa and others, has not yet been concluded. He says, "O Goddess...
The name of this hymn is *Ratnamālā*. Others [such as] Bṛhaspati and so forth...
It is implied that others such as Kuvera and the like should worship her alone for the sake of attaining their respective desired goals.

Regarding the Goddess Padmarājñī, since her sovereignty (*rājyasampat*) was not mentioned first, he speaks of that as well with the words beginning "vinamra... (bowing down), and so forth. By this, [the first]...
By the final word of this verse, [the author] indicates that Indra and others are to be understood as kings;

thus, the *Harṣakaumudī* is refuted. For the word *śrī* does not denote royal splendor (*rājyaśrī*) without the labor of defining its characteristics and so forth, whereas it does denote prosperity (*saṃpad*).
Out of mere weariness with debate, he asserts that [the Vedas] are not composed by fallible human beings; however,

this amounts to accepting what has been taught by the Naiyāyikas— namely, that the Blessed One is omniscient— on the grounds of such statements as "the incarnation as a fish spoke to the god" and so forth.
The word *pinakṣatiḥ* means "speaking," which here signifies "manifesting.

*Nidaṅguṃphāḥ* refers to compositions, namely the Vedas and the Āgamas. May she—who, step by step (*padāt padaṃ*), at every single word, fulfills the path by placing her own footprints upon it—delight and gladden [the heart].
Regarding the phrase "not having obtained" (*alabdha*): prior to "having obtained" (*labdhāni*), there was an absence of ornaments;

thus, those who have obtained ornaments are called *labdhabhūṣāḥ*. This means that they previously lacked ornaments and subsequently came to possess them. By their very nature, from birth onwards, they were already the locus for ornaments.

The meaning is that it is beautiful because a special ornament has been placed upon the lower lip, which has not yet received its decoration; it is as if the face were beautiful with a tilaka-mark placed on the lower lip rather than on the forehead. This is not merely a face, but rather the lower lip is what is truly beautiful, like a tilaka-mark.
This is the meaning; some say that the words "he attains supreme prosperity" (*parāṃ śriyam āpnoti*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis.
May that [work] which has Udyotamatī as its virtuous mother, Māpatinātha as its father, the Pañchakula lineage as its source, Kūrmmāvalī as its birthplace,
Sūpāsya and Kṛtavīrya as its ancestors, the feet of Acyuta as its goal, and Vārāṇasī as its seat of residence, bring fulfillment.
The Chapter on Magadhinīśa in the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*.

Now, having performed the primary worship (*mukhyapūjā*), the worship of others must be performed; for there is a statement in another Tantra stating that after offering a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the principal deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others should take place. This handful of flowers is intended as a prayer for the worship of the other deities. In that worship, Gaṇeśa—

The sequence for the deities follows from the previously mentioned scriptural statement; therefore, worship should be performed in a clockwise manner according to the order of installation prescribed by me. Thus, it follows that Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are to be worshipped in that sequence, and by that very order...

Intending to define Gaṇeśa by considering that even "form" (rūpaṇa) is applicable [to him], he says "atha" and so forth. This [mantra] beginning with the *praṇava* was spoken by the Teachers for the sake of engaging the listener;
it consists of four [syllables] and so on, or even in reverse order, beginning with *tārā* and joined with the *bindu*.

In the *Prayogasāra*, regarding the procedure for worship starting from the heart-mantra of Vighna, there is the application of the vowel *au*; likewise, the seed-syllable is joined with the moon (*u*) and *ra*, and similarly with the third [vowel]. Regarding the visualization, it begins with "having the hue of vermilion" (*siṃdūrābham*), and so forth, [describing] the goad in the upper left and right hands.

The lower pair [of hands] holds the *pāśa* and *aṅkuśa*; for those two, the *daṇḍa* and *vara* mudrās [are prescribed]. Four hundred thousand (*vedalakṣam*)—that is, four hundred thousand [repetitions] of this entire [mantra]—is intended for the Kṛta Yuga.

In the Kali age, the number prescribed for the Kalpa is multiplied by four for all mantras. In the Kṛta age, one should perform exactly what is prescribed for the Kalpa; in the Tretā, one should perform double that; and in the Dvāpara [double that again].
Because of statements in the Saṃhitās and other texts such as, "This is declared to be threefold for a Kālā," [the number] is fourfold;

therefore, after one hundred thousand (lakṣa) recitations for the deity, this too is a rule: by twenty lakṣas of recitation, one should perform the fire-oblation (havana) at a sacred ford or in a secluded forest; or alternatively, one may perform it separately at the conclusion of each lakṣa.

"One should perform the homa at the end of each hundred thousand [recitations]; this is the auspicious sequence," according to the Smṛti texts such as the Saṃhitā. Therefore, performing the homa at the end of each individual hundred thousand is more excellent. Here, the homa is performed with the eight substances combined, consisting of a sacrificial act characterized by a number equal to one-tenth [of the recitations].

Since all eight substances are connected by virtue of being performed simultaneously, each individual substance-act constitutes the oblation; it is not the case that the oblation consists of all eight substances together. As for what the author of the *Padārthadarśa* stated—that there would be no determination of the measure of the oblation—that is incorrect.

Since it has been stated that the measure of each individual substance-oblation applies to the root [text], it follows by implication that the measure of the oblations is determined by the quantity of substances combined; furthermore, regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya: "If one should sacrifice with rice, or with barley, or as prescribed by the scriptural text, or if one should sacrifice with mixed [grains]," etc.

It has been argued that by means of a single oblation of a mixed substance— which is distinguished by the act of *nyāsa* (deposition)— an oblation is effectively performed with each individual substance; however, even that is not correct, because in cases such as barley (*yava*) and rice (*vrīhi*),
the hearing of the word "or" (*vā*) establishes that the status of being the instrument of the oblation belongs to each substance independently of the others.

If it is argued that the status of being the meaning of the scripture is established because each individual substance is understood, we reply: since the particle *vā* is not heard in the present context, we do not know by what the independence (*nairapekṣya*) of the agent is expressed. Furthermore, if the understanding of the single letter *o* were to occur upon hearing the particle *vā*, then the employment of the particle *vā* itself would be redundant for the sake of the qualified [meaning].

Even if it were a different substance (*dravyāntara*), what loss would there be? For we do not favor the position that the oblation must consist of each individual substance; rather, you might say in our view that your oblation was not performed with any one of the substances such as molasses (*modaka*) and so forth, but rather with that which is distinguished by being a different substance as you intend.

This is not a refutation at all for one who maintains that there is an instrumental function (*karaṇatā*) consisting of eight substances. Furthermore, as for the citation of the statement from the *Gaṇeśavimarśinī*, "One should offer oblations separately with the eight substances smeared with the three sweets," that too is actually favorable to our position regarding [the efficacy of] combined [substances].

Because the eight substances participate simultaneously in a single action, there is no other distinct substance called "the eight substances," as there is a lack of evidence for such a thing; furthermore, if a new substance were produced merely from conjunction, it would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) by postulating multiple substances. Therefore, it is simply those respective substances that are conjoined.

In order to indicate that there are eight substances, the phrase "separately, separately" is used in connection with the substances; by this, the doubt as to what the measure of the oblation (*āhuti*) should be in a *homa* performed with eight substances is dispelled,
since the measure of the oblation for each of those substances, when combined into eight, constitutes that single oblation.

This is because [the deity] is obtained from the object itself by virtue of being the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); such is the direction. Having cleared away the refuse with pure materials and sprinkled [the site] slightly with water, one should perform the rite of the ground (*pīṭha*) starting from the root-mantra with the mantra: "Obeisance to the lotus-throned one who possesses all powers" (*sarvaśakti-kamalāsanāya namaḥ*).
This is the instruction. The primary worship is performed in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Immediately after that, prior to the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) and other enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), the worship of the lords of the hosts (*gaṇādhipa*) and others who are equal in rank to the principal deity must be performed in the four directions. As for the original statement, "from the limbs up to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*)," it refers to the deities of the enclosures mentioned previously; for [the category of] the hosts... [is not included therein].
The deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*) are located here at the feet [of the central deity]. By this same method, it should be understood elsewhere as well;
and because it is possible for them to extend from Gaṇeśa up to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), there is no fixed rule.
Thus, the claim by the authors of the *Padārthādarśa* that the root text is deficient is refuted. This concludes the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).

Since it is accepted that the status of being a *yāma* and so forth is strictly fixed, it would be more appropriate to accept that the status of ending with the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*) is merely conventional (*prāyika*), as there is no other recourse.
This is because [the deities] such as Indra and the others are understood to favor [beings] by first granting them a place on the ground.

In certain instances where there might be a deviation regarding that world-protector (Lokapāla), since the possibility exists of [Kārtavīryārjuna]— who is among the most venerable— being the one who received the power, it is possible to establish the inherent consistency of the entire root-text; thus,
thinking "one should satisfy him within," [the author] [mentions] Gaṇeśa.

Some prescribe the formula "ya-namaḥ," while others say the formula should be "gaṇeśaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ. Regarding the phrase "day by day" (*dinaśaḥ*), one should offer oblations with each of the materials, such as coconut and so forth, four hundred times every single day; thus, within the span of four days, [the total number of offerings] shall be complete.

When it is stated that "the practitioner shall perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the four substances in sequence," the oblation may be performed either out of order or with the substances combined; even in that case, the order of mention would not override the combination that is obtained through the [general] rule,
for the order of mention does not override a combination that is established by a prior direction.
On the contrary, some [scholars] maintain that the plural number used here in response to the mutual pairs serves as a proof;
furthermore, because the sequence is explicitly mentioned here, it is understood that there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) in the preceding case as well.

As for the taking of the eight substances according to availability, does this not imply that each individual substance is to be taken separately? Indeed, it is the inclusion of all substances that is intended.

The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* has stated that [the substance] is traditionally taught as being essential (*śyaka*), because otherwise, if either one of those substances were unavailable, it would follow that the act of oblation (*homakarman*) could not be accomplished at all; however, that is not correct, for even if the act of oblation were not accomplished, such a result is acceptable (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor does this [non-accomplishment] entail the incurrence of sin (*pratyavāya*).

Because there is an absence of evidence for its eternality— just as there is no proof for the eternality of the status of being an instrument— it should not be argued that this eternality persists even after initiation (*dīkṣā*), since the non-obligatory nature of the *puraścaraṇa* has been established with full scriptural authority in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī* regarding rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*).

Because the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary preparatory rite) is indispensable, and because it must be performed prior to optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), its etymological definition is as follows: it is called *puraścaraṇa* because it is to be practiced before (*puraḥ*) the main ritual. Even in the absence of the fire-oblation (*homa*), the completion of the rite is achieved by resorting to secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*) such as doubling the number of recitations (*japa*).

This is indeed possible; nor should it be said that my statement "according to what is available" (*yathālābham*) is merely for the sake of complying with optional rites (*kāmya*), because when there is no desire to perform an optional rite due to the absence of material resources— as indicated by the injunction "one should do what one is able"— there is no such requirement.
