There is no occasion for the conceptualization that "one may act according to what is available," because even for one who has begun the performance after procuring all the substances prescribed by the ritual injunction, a desire certainly arises when, unexpectedly,
one or more substances are lost: "What should be done?"— this is the case specifically regarding optional (*kāmya*) rites.
If it is argued that, according to the statement "some know of a substitute [only] after the commencement [of the rite]," this is not so;

for by the word "something" (kiñcit), it is implied that there is no primary status [for the substitute], but rather that in such a situation, the Blessed One [the Goddess] resides within the very limb of the optional performance—this being the meaning agreed upon by all. Thus it is suggested.

In the phrase "with sesame" (*nāt satilaiḥ*), where "with parched grains" (*lājaiḥ*) occurs, one should understand that the sequence beginning from the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) up to the end of the fourth day continues; this refers specifically to the four-day period.
By this, when there is an increase or decrease [in days], even if it is not exactly four days starting from the *pratipad*...
If the dative case-ending is not possible, then this application should not be followed; this is the implied meaning (*dhvani*).

[This] corroborates the statement that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the disputant. [The procedure involves using] an elephant's tusk—broken by an elephant, white as jasmine, or red sandalwood—or any one of these, for the meditation (*dhyāna*) of Gaṇeśa as described.
Having fashioned an image according to the prescribed proportions and having worshipped Gaṇeśa preceded by the invocation (āvāhana),

one should observe a fast while touching that image; beginning from that touch until liberation [from the vow], during a lunar eclipse, one should mutter this mantra and, upon the conclusion of the eclipse, place that image— which has been accompanied by the performance of oblations— upon the crest-lock (śikhā).
Carrying [the mantra], the practitioner should perform the recitation (*japa*) during disputes and the like; *mada* means "elephant.

Regarding the phrase "in direct order" (*anuloma*), the state of being situated in both direct and reverse order for a single seed-syllable ultimately results in its being situated in the middle. Thus, between these two seed-syllables, in this...

Having written the mantra *kaṃ vaśaṃ kuru* and so forth upon a vessel made of gold, silver, bell-metal, or other materials— having spread fresh butter within it— and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) for Vighneśvara therein, having worshipped him, and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with the root mantra, [one should perform the rite] at night.

The meaning is that if one performs [the rite] and eats [the substance], then the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) will certainly and quickly come under the control of that practitioner (*sādhaka*). Thus says the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* states that "ga" should be written at the beginning and "mi" at the end in reverse order; and this is indeed appropriate.

Otherwise, even for a teacher who knows that this mantra consists of a single syllable, how could his statement regarding its presence in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order be appropriate? [The seed-syllable *gaṃ*] should be placed in a pure vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or even clay, located to the south of those two.

Having spread out fresh butter, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus; in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should write the *gaṃ* seed-syllable facing two other [syllables] toward each other, and in its center, one should write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).
The letters of the practitioner’s name (*sādhaka*) should be interspersed with the *gam* seed-syllable, and the mantra should be enclosed by the *huṃ* seed-syllable.

Then, one should recite the auspicious *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra for the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) one thousand times, or a hundred times; having quickly recited it, the practitioner should certainly consume that fresh butter. He should practice in this manner for seven days, and by the power of the practitioner, the person to be accomplished will surely become submissive through wealth.

"By means of one's life-breaths and all one's possessions, he certainly becomes submissive"— this is the statement found in the *Śrī-Bhagavat-praṇīta-tad-ṛyāmala*, which reveals the specific distinction between writing the name of the person to be influenced (*sādhya*) and the recitation of the *prāṇamantra* and the *mūlamantra*.
Thus, facing one another, it is indeed in this direct order (*anuloma*).

That which was taught by the reversed words—that the root mantra (mūlamantra) should be recited one hundred and eight times—should be understood as following the natural order (*anupūrveṇa*) because of the minimal difference [in meaning]. However, regarding the instruction "having recited the root mantra," it should be understood that the requirement for a specific number is to be fulfilled by the number of one thousand mentioned in the *Tantras*. This is what must be kept in mind.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth in a transverse line like a row of eyelashes between those two [lines] on the hand—some say this is the case—this procedure should be performed with fresh butter;
"fresh butter" is an elliptical expression for cakes and the like, as seen in other Tantras which state, "if it is a cake. For seven days, starting from the first day of the bright fortnight...

Having begun [the discussion], it is more appropriate to accept that the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), which is present in the context (*prakaraṇa*), satisfies the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in a different manner than by depending on the removal of expectancy through another means;
therefore, one should adopt the optional yantra described in other systems, such as: "having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with its filaments..."
One should write the name together with the *vāgīśī* (the goddess of speech) joined by the *bindu* above it;
then, in the petals of the corners—namely, those of Agni, Īśa, Nairṛta, Anila, and Saumya—in sequence, one should write the letters of the respective *aṅga-mantras*.
Then, on the tips of the lotus petals, one should write the letters of the *mātṛkās*, the *śaktis*, and so forth; thereafter, outside of the lotus.

One should write the initial syllables of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions; the remaining [syllables] of the Mātṛkā should encircle it with both a noose and a goad. Having invoked the Lord of Devas into that [yantra], one should worship Vighna within the yantra. Having wrapped it in linen or other cloths, one should carry it around the neck or on the head. Into his hand...
"May the Goddess of Fortune (Lakṣmī) always reside upon my tongue, Vāṇī within my mind, and may Fame, ever increasing, abide there.
This is its meaning: first, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, then having drawn an eight-spoked [wheel] above that, then having drawn a sixteen-petalled [lotus] above that, and then a circle...

One should arrange three rows with contentment; there, having written the root mantra consisting of seed-syllables in the pericarp (karṇikā), and within that, starting from the base of the eastern petal, having written the names of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth, as well as the syllables of the eight forms and so on of the mantra for swift propitiation which is about to be described, [one should write] the eight-syllabled [mantra].

Having written the initial syllables of the names of the five limbs (*aṅga-pañcaka*) in sequence upon the petals of the corners beginning with the southeast and upon the petal in the northern direction,

one should write the first letters of the names of those Śaktis who are the forms of the Mothers (Brahmī and the others) at the tips of the petals of the first eight-petaled lotus; then, on the eight spokes situated outside of that—

Having written the initial syllables of the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with Indra and the others, in the directions starting from the east and proceeding in order, and having written the vowels (svaras) upon the sixteen petals, one should write the remaining letters of the alphabet (mātṛkā) from *ka* to *kṣa* in the first enclosure (*vīthī*) using the noose-mantra (*pāśabīja*), and the second enclosure using the hook-mantra (*aṅkuśabīja*).
"One should not encircle it with a third [line]," because the *gāyatrī* is to be written within the yantra;
thus, in another version of that [mantra], one should utter the word *vidmahe* at the end of the word *ekadaṃṣṭra*, then the word *vakratuṇḍa* with the dative case-ending (*ṅe*),
then the word *dhīmahi*, then the word *tanno vighnaḥ*, and finally the syllable *pra* followed by *vo*.

The wise one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the materials used for the fire-oblation (homa) and worship with this Gaṇeśa-Gāyatrī, which destroys all obstacles; it is the opinion of the virtuous that this [mantra] beginning with "gaṇapataye" is for that purpose. However, in the Sārasaṃgraha, it is stated that the writing on the leaves should be done with this Gāyatrī at the front of the [text].

The instruction for his procedure is as follows: one should write [the mantra] with fresh butter on a palm-leaf in the direct order; one should then envelop the seed-syllable named after the person to be accomplished who resides within the belly. Having established the Wind [element] and recited [the mantra] eight hundred times, one should silently consume this for seven days.

At night, having offered the *vaśīkaraṇa* [substance] to it, one should write two *gaṃ* syllables facing each other in the center of a hexagon within the pericarp; having written the names of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and so forth in the middle of the seed-syllable sections,
encircling them with the seed-syllables, and having written the six limbs (*aṅga*) in the six corners, then...

Having written the vowels twice in the filaments of the pericarp and the Gāyatrī three times in the petals, and having surrounded that with the consonants on the outside, and having further written the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in two lotuses,
one should recite "May the vital breaths and the foundation of the seat be established," and [proceed] with the seed-mantra.

Having consecrated [the substance] one hundred and eight times with the mantra, and having turned his face toward the direction of the person for whom the rite is intended, he should consume it himself in silence at midnight; this is the established rule according to our own tradition. Now, the *Mahāgaṇapati* mantra is extracted beginning with "Śrī-śakti," etc., starting from the well-known seed-syllable of Śrī.

The seed-syllable *bhu* (bhū), the fifth letter with the end [of the alphabet] (kṣa) joined by Indra (i) and the bindu, followed by the human vowel (u) and supported by the *pāśa* (pha); then the seed-syllable of obstacles (*vighna*) as previously extracted—the single-syllable mantra thus consists of these five seeds.
In the first mantra, "Varada" is used in the accusative case for the purpose of action; however, in the second mantra, it ends in the vocative.

According to the opinion of some, even the word *gaṇapati* should end in the vocative case and be in the singular; others, however, state that the word *śrīmahāgaṇapati* should end in the vocative and that the term *vaśam* is intended to be repeated (*vīpsita*).
It is precisely with this intention that [the text speaks of] the Great Gaṇa multiplied by thirty-two divisions.
The seed-syllable *Gaṃ* is said to be rooted in inference by Patañjali; *Svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).

According to the statement, "the sixth seed-syllable is *Dviṭha* (Ṭha), and the power is [the same]," one should utter the *praṇava*, *Kamalā* (Lm), *Māyā* (Hrīm), mounted upon *Bhuvaḥ*, then *Gaṇa*, and likewise *Manmatha* (Klīm). One should utter the first of Gaṇeśa’s [seed-syllables] as the sixth; these are the seed-syllables.

Having proclaimed those [mantras] with "svāhā," the mind would become empowered; however, those who follow the Rudrayāmala state that all six seed-syllables (bījas) are required. He extracts the mantras for the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with the words beginning with "six seed-syllables" (ṣaḍbīja), etc., situated within those six of his own seed-syllables previously mentioned.

The meaning is as follows: by means of the six long vowels joined in sequence with their own seed-syllables (bījas) in the form "ga" and so forth, which are accompanied by the intermediate [vowels]; and according to the rule, that is, for the purpose of attaining the accompaniment of the heart-mantra and the others, by the phrase "according to the ritual procedure," [one should perform] the mudrās of the six limbs and so forth.

It has been stated that for the purpose of battle, possessing knowledge of those [mantras] is most required; thus, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* concludes that the ritual application culminates in the sequence beginning with "Oṃ gāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ, śrīṃ gīṃ śirase svāhā," and so forth, ending with "Gaṃ gaḥ astrāya phaṭ. [The seed-syllables are: Oṃ, Śrāṃ, Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, Glauṃ.

The author of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* maintains that the practical application is indeed "Gaṃ Gaṅgā-hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth; for he argues that since the root text specifies the six seed-syllables (*bīja*) themselves as being primary, the primacy of each individual seed-syllable has not ascended to the level of authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*). Thus, [the mantra is] simply "Gaṃ Gaṅgī."

The six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with mantras beginning with "Om" and so forth. Indeed, there are many seed-syllables (*bīja*) belonging to one's own [deity]; however, as seen in another Tantra, it is stated: "These five seed-syllables of the Lord of Obstacles (*Vighneśituḥ*)—namely, *khāṃ*, *taṃ*, *sāṃ*, *viṣaṃ* (accompanied by the *bindu*), and the *bindu* alone—each bestow their respective fruits individually. Thus...

When the question arises as to which of one's own seed-syllables (*svabīja*) should be employed, the qualification "consisting of six seed-syllables" (*ṣaḍbījastha*) is traditionally taught. This indeed is the path that follows the natural force of the root text.
Had the first view been intended, it would have stated "as separate [syllables] such as Tārā and so forth. As for the second...
Some say that one should recite [the mantra] with the six seed-syllables ending in *matānumatauṣaṭ*, or with one's own seed-syllable (*svabījena*), or even with the self-seed-syllable (*svavījena*).
Others state that after the five seed-syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ),
the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed using the six seed-syllables starting with *gaṃ gīṃ*, etc., provided there is evidence for the mention of the seed-syllable twice.

Some others, however, following the *Rudrayāmala*, maintain that there is no [such] absence; they hold the view of the author of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* alone, stating: "The first seed-syllable of Gaṇapati should be joined with the six long vowels, and then conjoined with the six seed-syllables for the six limbs, beginning with the heart and ending with the crown. Thus they follow the *Rudrayāmala*.
In the center of the earth is the ocean of sugarcane juice; in its midst is an island made of the nine jewels;
in its center is the Pārijāta tree made of jewels; beneath it is the lotus of the Mothers;
within that is a hexagon, and within that a triangle, where the Great [Deity] resides.

"One should worship the Lord of Ganas"—this is the specific instruction. He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*): "With the face of a lordly elephant" means she whose face is like that of a lordly elephant; "whose left lap belongs to her beloved" means her left hand holds a lotus while her right performs an embrace.
Thus, Mahāgaṇapati has ten hands. In that regard—
Starting from the lower left hand up to the upper right hand,
there are the objects of a goad, a trident, a lotus, a conch, a water-lily, and tusks;
starting from the lower left hand up to the upper right hand, there are the objects of a grain-ear, a noose, and a wheel.
The *kṣudhanu* (small bow) and *bījapūra* fruits [are held]. For it is stated in the *Gaṇeśavimarśinī*:

"Beginning from the lower right hand and ending with the lower left hand, he holds in his right hands a mace (*gadā*), a trident (*śūla*), a lotus (*abja*), a *kahlāra* lily, and a venomous fang (*viṣāṇa*);
and in his left hands, a sprout of rice (*śālyagra*), a noose (*pāśa*), a discus (*cakra*), a sugarcane bow (*ikṣucāpa*), and an excellent *bījapūraka* fruit."
"Placing a jeweled pitcher playfully upon his lotus-foot which shines with tinkling anklets," and "the jeweled pitcher [is] on the tip of the trunk"— this is how it should be meditated upon.
[This concludes] the recitation of the mantra forty-four thousand times for the four hundred thousand repetitions of the *Lakṣmīpuraścaraṇa*.

The meaning is that one should satisfy [the deity] every day with the number four hundred and forty, as previously stated. The worship diagram (*pūjā-yantra*) consists of a downward-pointing triangle with an eight-petaled lotus possessing filaments above it; having worshipped the deity under discussion in the center of that triangle, [one should proceed].

Having worshipped the four pairs of deities, beginning with Mahālakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, in the four directions in order starting from the east, and having worshipped the five pairs of deities, beginning with Lakṣmī and Gaṇanātha, in front of the deity, one should [worship] the six [deities] beginning with Āmoda in the six corners in sequence.
Having worshipped Ṭakkaṃsa together with his own consort on the two sides, and having worshipped the treasure-deities Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi along with their respective consorts,

one should worship the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇas) beginning with the limbs (aṅgas). Here, the enclosures are of four kinds, distinguished by the limbs (aṅgas), the Mothers (mātṛs), the World-Protectors (lokapālas), and the weapons beginning with the Vajra (vajrādyāyudhas).

The distinction is that those ignited by another are equal in rank to the Pradhāna. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the root text to be cited later— which states that "the first enclosure belongs to the couples, the second to Ārāma and others who are naked (Digaṃvara), and the third to the limbs [of the Lord] such as the Sun and so forth"— because the enclosures begin precisely from the deities of the couples.

It should not be said that there is no counting of the deities of the *ṇa*-group; for since the deities of the *mithuna* (couple) and others are not mentioned there by way of direct instruction (*upadeśataḥ*), it is logical to state their "firstness" and so forth for the purpose of including those respective deities in their proper order within the worship. Indeed, the sequence of instruction does not apply there.

Regarding the extension [of the rule]: it should not be said that the term "repetition" (*āvṛtti*) is not applicable because the worship of the treasures (*nidhi-pūjā*) is to be excluded; for since the deity situated in the center is surrounded by those stationed in the four directions, its status as being "surrounded" (*āvṛtta*) is not lost. Furthermore, the mention of "being surrounded" refers to the central [deity].

Just as there is an enclosure for the deity, so too, within the temporal limits of the four ages (caturyuga) and so forth, worship for the sake of prayer is merely conventional; however, the intermediate [worship] is primary, consisting of libations (tarpaṇa), the first of the first offerings, the washing of hands, and so forth, which serves as the basis for the state of being an enclosure (āvaraṇatva).

Starting from the deity of the *gaha* (the house) and so forth, up to the *mūla*, the limbs (*aṅga*), and ending with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*)— according to the natural sense of what has been previously stated— the Boar (*potrī*) is Viṣṇu in his Vārāha incarnation,
and the Parrot (*śuka*) is a well-known specific type of bird; one should accomplish one's desired goals by means of substances prescribed for the respective *kalpas*.

Having stated that, regarding the requirement for a specific substance therein, he says "padmadi" and so forth. A "lord of men" (*narapati*) is one distinguished by qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the like; by virtue of his fitness, this refers to a Kṣatriya alone, since the Brāhmaṇa and Vaiśya castes were mentioned previously and subsequently, [it follows] that even one belonging to the middle caste is included.

Since it is appropriate that [the offering] be made with what is most excellent, he first describes the procedure for the *tarpaṇa* (libation) using lotuses— which are difficult to obtain but become great and most excellent flowers— using the word "previously" (*pūrva*) because they were easily available; then,
beginning with the words "each one," he states the application of the homa, starting with Mahāgaṇapati by means of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Having offered libations to Gaṇeśa four times with the mantra ending in "tiṃ tarpayāmi," and having performed the libation four times for each of the five [deities] beginning with Śrī and Śakti— each accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) and joined with their own beloved palaces and so forth—
at the conclusion of the libation for each couple, [one should perform] four...

Having gratified Gaṇeśa four times in the courtyard of the maṇḍala, and having pronounced the seed-syllable (bīja) of Gaṇeśa, one should gratify Āmoda and the others, together with their respective consorts, four times each; likewise, one should gratify Gaṇeśa himself four times, at the end of each [name]. Then, with the conch and the lotus, [one should worship] with their own names preceded by the syllable *sa-* (saṃ) and the nasal drop (*bindu*).
Having satiated [the deities] four times with the liquid seed-syllables (*kṣarabīja*) as before, one should likewise satisfy Gaṇeśa four times.

Thus, one hundred and eight satisfactions (*tarpaṇa*) are established. First, there are four for the principal deity; then twenty-five for the five pairs (*mithuna*) combined, including Āmoda and the others.

There are six pairs; for these, there are twenty-four libations (*tarpaṇas*), as well as twenty-four principal final libations for each of them. For the two treasures (*nidhi*), there are eight libations, and likewise eight principal final libations for each. This is the lowest sequence.
When it is understood that those beginning with Śrī— who possess the qualities of being beloved by their elements (*dātupriyānvita*) and are endowed with power (*śaktiyukta*)—
are to be propitiated as Śrīpati and others who are likewise joined with Śrī and other powers (*śakti*),
then [the number of deities] is two hundred and sixteen.

These are the propitiatory offerings (*tarpaṇa*); this is the middle course (*madhyama-pakṣa*). In that regard, having offered the root mantra four times, one should offer [the water] four times with the formula: *Śrīṃ, I propitiate Śrī together with the Lord of Śrī*;
and again, four times with the formula: *Śrīṃ Śrīṃ, I propitiate the Lord of Śrī together with Śrī*.

Thus, when each of the twenty-six deities is offered libations four times, there are one hundred and four libations in total; furthermore, the four primary libations performed at intervals among them also yield thirteen results, and their number is as follows.

Furthermore, the sequence is as follows: at the very end of all, there is a root-satisfactory offering (*mūla-tarpaṇa*) four times; this is the superior method, which consists of four hundred and forty-four tarpaṇas. The procedure for that is as follows: first, the root [mantra] four times... [end of fragment].

For each of the twenty-eight syllables of the *rpyamūlīya*, perform four offerings of libation (*tarpaṇa*) respectively; at the end of each syllable, as before, perform four sets of twenty-eight libations by means of the root-mantra (*mūla-tarpaṇa*), and again perform four libations with the root-mantra. Thus, combined, [there are] two hundred and twenty-eight...

Thus, those [specified] numbers of libations have been produced; then, following the previously stated middle method, two hundred and sixteen additional libations are added, so that when combined, the total number reaches the maximum stated amount. That is...

Thus it is said in the *Gaṇeśavimarśinī*: "I shall describe the propitiation (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of four cycles, which bestows all desired objects. In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, free from all disturbances, the practitioner (*mantrin*), having performed his ablutions and other rites, and endowed with the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) as before, should contemplate [the deity] in the middle of a pond while holding flowers."
Having meditated upon that lotus grove, and in its center a great lotus as radiant as the rising sun,
lofty, rich in fragrance, delightful, captivating, and freshly blossomed—
the knower of the previously mentioned mantra should [visualize] Mañcī at the end of a pure flight of silver stairs.
Having visualized [the deity] as having emerged from the solar disc and descended to reside in the center of the pericarp,
one should worship Mahāgaṇapati along with his retinue using manifest perfumes and flowers; then, as before, placing the lotus-like mouth [of the vessel].
Having meditated on a stream of jewels raining down upon the head of the Lord and upon the head of the preeminent practitioner,

one should first perform the libation (tarpaṇa) four times with water smeared with moon-fragrance (candracandana), saffron (kāśmīra), and musk (kastūrī) using the root mantra; then, [one should offer] five or six pairs [of couples] into the conch.
The practitioner of mantras should likewise satisfy the two Padmanidhis individually with their respective seed-syllables and other components ending in *svāhā*, four times each;

and as before, he should satisfy them separately with the root mantra four times. Combined, this constitutes one hundred and eight [offerings], which is the minimum procedure. Alternatively, [he may do so] with the root mantra and others used individually.
The wise one should satisfy Vāta with water as before, using the mantras according to the method prescribed for worship.
This is the middle procedure, which totals two hundred and sixteen [offerings].
Alternatively, having satisfied him four times with the root mantra (mūlamantra), one should offer with all the syllables of all the mantras, each ending with "svāhā."

Having first offered libations four times with the root mantra, one should then satisfy the couples; thereafter, one should satisfy them as before. This should be done collectively four hundred times.
Thus has the sequence for the elders been declared by the wise who are masters of the Āgamas.

Having thus satisfied [the deities] with the rivers and subsequently worshipped them with the aforementioned offerings, the wise one should request the desired boon and then perform the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the Prāṇa. One should always satisfy [the deities] in this manner from the mandala, and it shall become fruitful; even in times of drought, terrible fear, or kings and thieves...

In times of danger from celestial beings, during great fevers, in disputes, in the crisis of extreme poverty, and especially in all undertakings such as marriages and the like, a ruler of men with a tranquil mind should indeed perform this *tarpaṇa* (libation). Thus, Mahāgaṇeśvara is pleased, and there is great prosperity.

One should perform the extraction of the seed-syllable *bhūḥ* according to the rule beginning with "smṛti" (the letter *ga*), "māṃsa" (the letter *la*), and so forth. This is another application [of the mantra] for achieving desired results through other tantras.
One should write [the syllables] upon iron, palm leaves, or copper, using seven lines and four squares formed by intersecting lines.

Having invoked the deity to be accomplished according to the sequence of the *śūlaka* mantra, and having duly worshipped Gaṇeśvara, one should touch the wheel while reciting the mantra a thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, there shall be the attraction of women. [This is] the sevenfold four-line meter (*saptacatuṣkocchanda*), the right-hand path.
From north to south, there are seven squares formed by eight lines, and from east to west, four squares formed by five lines;

thus, there are twenty-eight squares. Having inscribed the letters of the mantra one by one into the squares, starting from the northeast corner and following the sequence of the lines, one should place them within the squares.
Having encircled [the name] with the letters of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and having completed the *yantra*, one should invoke Gaṇapati, worship him,

and recite the mantra over that *yantra* one thousand times clearly. Regarding the number of recitations, by means of the summarized [instructions], one should previously indicate the attraction of women during the morning twilight.
The meaning is "it shall not be. For the purpose of providing refuge, one should extract the mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and so forth.
First, there is a downward-facing triangle; above that, a hexagon;
above that, an eight-petaled lotus; and above that, four circular lines, each consisting of five [units].

Having fashioned three paths (vīthīs) with intervening spaces and, above them, two interlocking squares (bhūpuras) forming an eight-spoked figure, one should write the root seed-syllable *gam*— accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth— in the center of the triangle;
this should be encircled externally by the *praṇava* (oṃ), and outside of that...

Outside the corners, starting from the well-known eastern direction and proceeding clockwise through the four directions, one should write the single syllables of Lakṣmī, Māyā, Manmatha, and Bhūmi; then, having written the six seed-syllables beginning with Praṇava within the six corners,
one should [place] the previously mentioned six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*) on the outer junctions of the six corners.
Having written the mantra starting with *trāṃ*, having written the remaining twenty-one syllables three times each upon the seven petals,
and having written the remaining single syllable on the eighth petal,
one should worship the path with the letters of the Mātṛkā in forward order for the first [circle] and in reverse order for the second.

"One should fill the third [square] with a noose and a goad"— this statement regarding its downward orientation here, despite the upward orientation of the city of fire (analapura) elsewhere, follows authoritative texts such as the *Padārthādarśa*. However, the teacher Padmapāda [states that] for the remaining twenty-two syllables of the mantra...
The eight-word mantra named Śatasaṃkhyā consists of these eight words individually: "Gaṇapataye" is the first;
"Varada" is the second; "Varade" is the third; "Sarvajanaṃ" is the fourth; "me" is the fifth; "vaśam" is the sixth;
"ānaya" is the seventh; and "svāhā" is the eighth word. These are the eight [words].

Having drawn three rows on the petals and having encircled them individually with the *mātṛkā* letters, *pāśa*, and *aṅkuśa*, they say that one should write the *pāśa* and the *māyā* seed-syllables on the eight spokes in four turns; by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "guṇaśaśca," the second previously mentioned method is indicated; and by the word "learned" (*vidvān*), it means one who possesses knowledge.

Knowledge that possesses meaning is distinguished from meaningless phonemes; writing is that which causes the cognition of word-meanings, and since this writing occurs precisely through the writing of names, its essential nature is established.

Thus, even the second position is indeed accessible from the root text; this is the summary. There is another formal argument (*prayoga*). *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "prayogāṃtaraṃtaṃ". The translation reflects the available portion of the Sanskrit text.)*

In the interval, having offered perfume, flowers, incense, and an oblation to the white Arka, Apāmārga, and other plants grown upon the earth according to the *Siddhayoga* and other methods, and having prostrated on a Friday, Saturday, or Monday, one should say:
"O plant, for what purpose were you created upon this earth? We have now come here for the sake of accomplishing that very purpose."

Reciting the mantra "tiṣṭha tiṣṭha mahauṣadhe" three times and twelve times, one should generate the *siddhayoga* from the beginning with the root mantra without interruption. Having fashioned a ring from that and wrapped it [with thread], one should worship Gaṇeśvara within it; then, having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times, one should wear it on the finger.

If a wise person touches the tips of the hands of living beings with that hand, they will certainly and surely come under his control by that mere touch. Indeed, once living beings have fallen under his power, they will offer even their very lives as servants. On that seal-ring, the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati should be inscribed. *A* [end of fragment].
The meaning is that one should wear a ring consecrated with the mantra one thousand and eight times;
the rest is clear. He states the mantra of Virigaṇapati beginning with "māyā" and so forth:
*khadgīśo vaḥ pāvako raḥ hrīṃ vira vira gaṇapati varavarada sarvato...* (O Khadgīśa, protect us! O Pāvaka! Raḥ! Hrīṃ! O Vira, O Vira, O Gaṇapati, bestower of boons, [protect] from all sides...).

"Bring [him] under the power of my karma, svāhā!"—this is the mantra consisting of twenty-six syllables. Regarding the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), he says "the internal organ," etc. "The internal organ" consists of four [syllables];
likewise, "Gaṇapati" consists of four syllables, preceded by the *māyāvīja* (the seed-syllable of Māyā). [The mantra for] the heart is "to the heart, namas" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*).
The placement (*nyāsa*) of these [mantras] upon the heart and the thumbs has been explained; the same should be applied to the other fingers as well.

He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*) with the words beginning "having the luster of vermilion" (*siṃdūrābham*), etc.: in the right upper hand is the noose (*pāśa*), in the left the goad (*aṅkuśa*); below the right is a honey-filled skull-cup (*kapāla*), and below the left is the yoni placed [therein]. Thus he is four-armed; Puṣṭi is also four-armed.

Regarding the phrase "she whose two hands shine with two lotuses [held] by her upper right and left [hands]," this meaning can also be derived from the root [of the compound]. It should be meditated upon that there is an embrace of his beloved with the lower right [hand], and with the lower left [hand], there is the touching of the tip of his *liṅga*. Puṣka... [text ends].
The trunk of the elephant is well known as *raṃha-sti-hasta-agra-śuṇḍā*. Edibles (*bhakṣya*) include sweets such as *laḍḍūka*; foods (*bhojya*) include rice and the like;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), lickables (*lehya*) such as *rasālā* and suckables (*coṣya*) such as pieces of sugarcane are included.
He states the mantra of Śakti-Gaṇapati with the words beginning with "Śakti," etc.: *hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ gaṇapataye svāhā*.

The meaning is that one should perform the five-limbed assignment (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) ending with the eyes using the five [syllables] consisting of *māyā* (hrīṃ), its own seed-syllable, *māyā*, the seven-syllabled [mantra], and *svāhā*;

then, one should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the entire mantra. He describes the meditation (*dhyāna*) starting with "mukta" etc., [visualizing him] with an upward-pointing [trident]... in the right hand.

In his two left hands he holds a lotus and a noose; in the lower right hand is a jewel-pot, and in the lower left hand is the goddess seated upon him. Thus he has four arms, while the goddess has two. According to the description "the beauty of whose chest is enhanced by the lotus held in her right hand," she possesses a lotus in her right hand. Her left [hand]... [is empty].
[The mantra] "O you who touch the top of the banner of the great lord of sleep" is thus stated as another mantra for Gaṇapati:
"Oṃ hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ bring [him] under control svāhā. This is the eleven-syllable mantra.
It has been stated that the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the words of the mantra; anticipating the question of what those words are, he says:

With the phrase beginning with "by one," etc., the second alternative is that the offering consists of cakes alone, even without the addition of ghee, using the eleven-syllable mantra in its entirety. Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of ghee is mandatory based on general scriptural injunctions such as "the oblation is accompanied by ghee," because the cakes themselves are already cooked in ghee, and thus possess the quality of being associated with ghee.

Because it is bound [by a specific rule], the sublation of the general scripture by means of the specific statement composed with the negative particle (*na*) contained herein is intended, as before, like the ritual manual for the *Gaṇapati* mantra.
He demonstrates the *Kṣipraprasādana-Gaṇapati* mantra beginning with "saṃvarta," etc.; "saṃvarta" means destruction.

The syllable *kā* is the side, and the syllable *pa* is the heart; with the syllable *na*, it is the "quickly bestowing" [mantra]. Thus, the ten-syllable mantra is extracted. With the seed-syllable joined with the long vowels—that is, each joined with the six long vowels—and beginning with the syllable *svā*, he describes the visualization starting with the word *pāśa*. This will be explained hereafter.
"In the first of the two [syllables] above, and in the last of the two below; in the weapon and in that which is to be meditated upon—[these are] with the three sweets.

This is a qualification of the sesame seeds (*tila*). As for the statement "the *homa* with eight substances according to that system," since the bathing substances (*snāna*) are already included within the eight substances, their separate mention would result in redundancy.
It should not be said [that this is redundant], because since the combination of the three sweets is not otherwise established there, a tautology is impossible;

furthermore, the inclusion [of the three sweets] is purposeful as it serves to indicate that among the eight substances, sesame seeds (*tila*) hold such preeminence. This remains true even if the reading is *madhuratritayaiḥ*.

In this context, the term "the triad of sweet things" (*madhurāṇāṃ tritayam*) must be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound qualifying the sesame seeds themselves; for the Teacher has stated: "One should offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed [with other ingredients] and sprinkled with the three sweets. Furthermore, the upper portion situated inside the coconut shell constitutes the "clod of earth," while the outer husk represents the "skin."

"Alas, a portion of the body is called 'skin' (carma-pada) [in the previous rule]; it was previously stated that in the oblations one should first offer eight coconuts, and this [present statement] is for the purpose of setting aside that [rule]. By this method—that is, by the method of subjugating the earthen [linga] through the oblation of eight substances—he describes the ritual application of the satiation (tarpaṇa)."

By the words "at the beginning of the day" (*dinādi*) and so forth, [the author] prescribes that during the auspicious times at the start of the day, such as morning, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with pure water mixed with sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and other substances— since that practice was adopted in the previously cited *Gaṇeśavimarśinī*— and he describes the visualization (*dhyāna*) for this libation starting with the words "with the noose" (*pāśa*) and so forth, along with its stages.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: one should satisfy [the deity] by perceiving the reflection of the Lord of Day (the Sun) coming from the solar orb into the water, which is not turbid due to its silver-like clarity. Regarding the word "water" (*jala*), the previously cited authority is the *Gaṇeśavimarśinī*, which completes the missing portion [of the verse].
As for those who claim that this visualization (*dhyāna*) applies to all ritual applications (*prayoga*), that is incorrect.

Their measure should be sought; that libation which is to be performed upon the lotus situated in the water should be accomplished by offering a lotus flower from a lake or similar body of water onto the head of the Sadhya [deity] visualized within the water, while also understanding that he is being sprinkled with the nectar flowing from that mechanism. As it is said regarding the lotus from the *Bimba*:

Having approached the calf with silver stairs, holding water in vessels made of lotus leaves and bearing a creeper as a tooth-ornament along with a noose and a goad, he should place it before those [goddesses] who have accomplished their purpose; then,
sprinkling it daily with nectar flowing from the summit of that mountain, he should remember Gaṇapati and satisfy him with ambrosia.
Thus he states the Heramba mantra, beginning with "pañca" and so forth; this mantra consists of four syllables: *oṃ gūṃ namaḥ*.

He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*) starting with "mukta" and so forth: [the deity] is characterized by five faces in the form of elephant heads, colored with five colors—pearl and so on—applied from top to bottom using saffron (*dyusṛṇa*); and [he is mounted upon] Hari, which means a lion.

The form [of the deity] seated upon a lion has five faces, each with three eyes, and ten arms; her lower right and left hands display the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), while her upper right and left hands hold other objects and display the *vara* (boon) mudrā. This is the iconographic form to be worshipped there. Regarding the attainment of the *pīṭha-mantra*, as before, there is this specific distinction.

The meaning is that the worship of the *pīṭha* (sacred seat) should be performed with the seventeen-syllable mantra: *oṃ huṃ huṃ mahāsiṃhāya gāṃ heraṃbāsanāya namaḥ*. First of all, [the seat] should be [cleansed] everywhere with the seed-syllable of Vighna, namely the syllable *gaṃ*, which belongs to that very Vighna.
Because it is presided over by a deity, those who do not perceive the meaning of the words include the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantra of the archetype (*prakṛta*) within this very [mantra].

Regarding the phrase "on the sixth" and so forth, since no distinction is specified, the three lunar days belonging to both fortnights are intended. On the festival day—the full moon and the new moon—he states the *dhāraṇā*-yantra: "Abho..."
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus on birch bark with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), elephant musk, and saffron using the syllable *jam* and so forth,

one should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the present mantra, *gūm*, in its pericarp (*karṇikā*). Inside that, having written the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*), one should place the four limbs (*aṅga*) upon the filaments of the petals located in the corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*).
Having inscribed the *netra* (eye) in front of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and having inscribed the *astra* (weapon) fourfold upon the petals and filaments of the directions,

one should inscribe the syllables of the *mālā-mantra* to be described hereafter— seven for each— in the middle of the petals starting from the east in due order, up to the seventh petal; then, on the eighth [petal], the remaining six...

The meaning is that one should write the two syllables [ŚRĪM] and surround them with the *māyā-bīja* (Hrīṃ) on the outer path; then, on the second path outside of that, one should surround them with the palatal letter Śa together with the bindu. This is because the *Padārthādarśa* states: "There are two enclosures: by the power (*śakti*) and by the letter Śa. He now states the *mālā-mantra*: "By the power... [and so forth].

Thus, "one's own seed" refers to the seed of Heramba just mentioned; its connection is with the word "paralyze" (*staṃbhaya*), making two [syllables]. By the phrase "fifty-five syllables," it is understood that this is for the purpose of pacification (*śamanāya*); there is no sandhi (euphonic combination) between the vowel *a* [of *śamanāya*] and the *e* in *ehi*, because the reading itself is *ehyehi* as a compound through sandhi.

Indicating this, it resounds as follows: *hrīṃ kroṃ oṃ gūṃ namaḥ sarvavighnādhipāya sarvārthasiddhidāya sarvaduḥkhapraśamanāya ehyehi bhagavan sarvaṃ khādaya staṃbhaya staṃbhaya hrīṃ gūṃ namaḥ svāhā kroṃ hrīṃ*. Thus [is the mantra] five times five.
By stating that "this *mālāmantra* of the three syllables (*trivarṇaka*) should accomplish [the goal] through its application," its independence is also indicated;

furthermore, some maintain that this is said with the intention that even the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) possess the capacity to bring about the fruit by means of assisting the principal part (*aṅgin*). He then recites the *suvrahmaṇya* mantra, beginning with *tāre*.
The Lord of the Sword (Khaḍgīśvara) is "tyādi"; Kūrma is "caḥ"; Niḥsvara is "niḥ"; one devoid of the commonality of vowels is "ṇānta";
"staḥ" is the essential form of the earth; "nati" is the word "namaḥ". Here, through the sandhi of the letter *t* with the letter *b*, the letter *d* arises;
this is to be included within the mantra. Thus, the mantra for bowing to the Earth is "bhuve namaḥ".

If it is asked how this meaning emerges from the root text of the *Suvrāhmaṇyādhidevatāprayogasāra*, [the answer is: thus, because of the specific qualification "uttered" (*īrita*) and the technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) that "the numbers are the final syllables of the *piṇḍas*," the word "uttered" (*īrita*) signifies the number two. Likewise...

The meaning is that [the letter] has gone from its position in the second syllable to the end of the word; thus, its substitution by *da* is established by implication (*arthāt*), for the substitution by *da* cannot occur without being connected to the letter *bh*.
Even if such a connection were possible, the mention of its "being in the second" would be purposeless. In my view, however, the letter *da*...

It should be understood that this is intended precisely to indicate permission (*abhyanujñā*). And thus, the seven-syllable mantra *oṃ vacadbhuvena maḥ* is extracted. Regarding the meditation (*dhyāna*) with the fire-seed syllable *ra*, he says "sindūra" and so forth; [the placement is] on the first of the two raised [fingers] of the right hand and below that.

O Agnīdhra, that which is known as Tye Suvrahmaṇya is a specific form of Kārttikeya; he has one face and four arms. In his left hand there should be the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and in his right hand a lotus. A cock should be placed in his left hand, and a spear (*śakti*) in his right. This fire-born deity is thus described.

Based on the statement from the *Pañcarātra*, by the phrase "to the west of the fire-maṇḍala," it is taught that the worship of the deities of the seat (*pīṭhadevatā*) begins with Maṇḍūka and extends up to the fire-maṇḍala, and not only that, but also beyond it according to the prescribed rule.
By the words "in the filaments" (*kesareṣu*) and so forth, one should fully worship the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*) in the filaments.

Having worshipped Jaya and the others in the middle of the lotus petals, the commanders of the divine armies (deva-senāpati) and the others in the four directions starting from the east, and Śakti and the others in the four tips of the petals at the cardinal and intermediate points,
one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons in the two pathways of the outer enclosure wall (*bhūpura*) surrounding the lotus.
In this context, it should be understood that the offering of a portion of the *naivedya* is for the specific *gaṇa* named Dhūrta-sena.

Regarding the *kumāras*—those who are uninitiated (*anupanīta*) celibates (*brahmacārin*) who are well-known—the intention is that the worship of Gaṇeśa and his praise must be performed; with this in mind, he begins the praise with the words "Oṃkāram... and so forth.
The virtuous, being self-restrained, praise with their speech that which is the primordial of the Vedas; He who is expressed by the *oṃkāra*, the first of the Vedas,
and who is the very letter 'A' (akāra) that constitutes the beginning of the *oṃkāra*—
with his lotus-hand and the tip of his trunk, he [touches] the breasts of the Goddess from nearby, as it were, out of delusion.
The sense is that He is never defiled by the remnants of food at any time. The "course of time" refers to subjection to time. The "words of the authoritative ones" are the Vedas.
The "cause" is the one who sets [the world] in motion. The "ancient" is the Mahābhārata. The "abode" is the state to be described;
the "non-abode" is that which is beyond the range of perception, indivisible, and immeasurable. That indeed...

Because they perceive the common quality of fear in both Śiva and Śivā, [the Lord says: "O Śivā and Aśiva," regarding His own parents who have assumed various forms through their many divine sports (līlā). In reality, for those persons and scriptures, there is nothing else to be known or to be propounded other than You; therefore, that... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a verse from the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, specifically 10.87.24–25. The translation reflects the philosophical context of the passage.)

The meaning is that through various yogas— specific yogic practices performed at their respective times— even by yogis who have practiced many such yogas, you alone are the one to be attained through the liberation of *sāyujya*. Alternatively,
it means that you are attained by all through the connection with the time of their own respective deaths, according to their sequence.
The meaning is that even this [state] likewise undergoes dissolution. "Maugdhyam" (infancy/ignorance) refers to the assumption of a body;
for even this occurs merely as a sport (*līlayā*), since there is no possibility of such a state for that which has been previously described as being the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
"Naraḥ" is the nominative plural form of the word *nṛ*, whose radiance... [is such].

The mother of this [work] was the virtuous Matīsatī; his father was named Māpati, a treasure-house of love; his ancestral lineage was the Paṃthakula; his birthplace was Kūrmācala; he rendered the feet of Acyuta (Viṣṇu) easily accessible; his place of residence was Vārāṇasī; and thus the "Viśvapaṭala" [section], concerning the meaning of words, has reached completion.

In the *Cintāmaṇi*, it is stated that even the description of the worship of Gaṇeśa situated to the right [of the deity] must necessarily be accepted; likewise, the Sun is not [worshipped] merely in his form as the Sun. If that were so, it would follow that the Moon, Fire, and others would be excluded from the five-shrine (pañcāyatana) arrangement.

However, since [the sun] is indeed of the nature of a specific light common to the moon, fire, and so forth, and likewise Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others are [to be understood] only by way of their respective common forms, no distinction is thereby established. Thus, when any deity of light might have been proposed for definition, [the author specifies] the Sun—

Due to the predominance of mantras according to the "needle-and-anvil" maxim (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*), and because it is appropriate for the peaceful [mantras] to come first in relation to the fierce ones, and furthermore because the *akhyāna* Brahmins who are authorized in this scripture hold royal status,
he first explains the lunar mantras with the words beginning "Now it is said," and so forth.
The meaning of "the state of Khaḍgīśa" is that in which there is the station of the letter *va* belonging to Khaḍgīśa.

This six-syllable mantra is "svau somāya namaḥ. Some say it is with its own seed-syllable (*sva*) located at the beginning of the mantra; [others] say it is with the seed-syllable "sve. "Wealth" refers to a vessel of treasure, produced from a deer situated on the lap.

In the application [of the mantra], it is stated that the status of being a "most excellent practitioner" (*sādhakasattama*) must also be required; this is achieved through the aforementioned practice of the *vidyā* and *mantra*, which consists of recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and so forth, performed for ten parts (*daśāṃśa*) of the total count—wherein the basis (*āśraya*) is characterized by one million [recitations] and the characteristic of the flavor (*rasalakṣa*) is six hundred thousand. Thus, the excellence of the substratum is indicated as being characterized by these specific measures.

One should also perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *vidyā-mantra* ten times the number [of oblations] offered; "ending with Soma" means that when the seat (*pīṭha*) has been worshipped up to the limit of Soma, one should worship these [deities].

Then, having fully worshipped the lotus-seat with the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*), one should worship the Lord of Rohiṇī (*rohiṇīpati*); such is the syntactical connection. [This continues] until the end of the fire-mandala (*vahni-maṇḍala*).

The worship of the mandalas mentioned here is to be performed ending with the lunar mandala (somamaṇḍala); thus, the sense is that after first worshipping the solar and fiery mandalas, the worship of the lunar mandala comes at the end. However, some maintain that the deities of the pedestal (pīṭhadevatā) should be worshipped only up to the lunar mandala, but not in the fire.
Their worship must be performed; furthermore, the deities of the seats (*pīṭhadevatā*) have been mentioned by Pinākin [in other places].

In another tantra, they are stated as follows, in order starting from the east: Rākā, Kumudvatī, Nandā, Sudhā, Saṃbhāvinī, Kṣamā, Āpyāyanī, Candrikā, Hlādinī, and likewise Navamī. One should [worship] them in this sequence.

One should worship these three [deities] with extreme devotion; then, having worshipped the lotus-seat (āsana) with the seat-mantra, and once the pedestal (pīṭha) has been worshipped up to the moon, one should worship the Lord of Rohiṇī. Regarding their installation, this should be reconciled according to other tantras; elsewhere, among the deities, it is as follows: [text fragment].

They say that the non-demonstration of that [reality] in some place merely strengthens its own established non-existence. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "even when worshipped" (*pūjite 'pi*), it is intended to mean "ending with *soma*," so as to avoid any further expectancy;
whereas the reading "even when worshipped on a pedestal" (*pūjite pīṭhe*) implies worship preceded by the nine powers of the pedestal (*pīṭha-śakti*).

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* provides an account of the nine powers mentioned subsequently in the *Ktvā-tantra*; however, that [account] is not accepted as the root authority, for otherwise their manifestation would have already been established. He describes the worship of the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*) with the words beginning "the limbs in the filaments" (*kesareṣvaṅgadevatāḥ*), and so forth; [he states that] the deities of the limbs are in the filaments.

The meaning is that, having worshipped the eight Śaktis beginning with Rohiṇī and ending with Kalā within the petals, and having honored the planets starting from the solar orb (Sūryamaṇḍala) in order at the tips of the petals, one should worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and their weapons in the square outside of that; [the materials used] should be of the same color as oneself.

The meaning is that those whose seeds (*bīja*) consist of the initial syllables of their respective names—accompanied by the nasal bindu—and which are like garments (*vastra*) laid down; this refers to the phrase beginning with *sasvavarṇa*. He now describes the ritual application for offering the *arghya* on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).

By these and other [verses], until the time for offering the *arghya* during the portion of the night, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), even if not sitting [in a specific posture] by day, should prepare three square mandalas of cow-dung, facing east and west; therein, he should place a seat for his own sitting in the first [mandala], and the materials for worship on both sides of the middle one.

Having placed *grīṃ* [as the seed-syllable] and fashioned a white eight-petalled lotus, one should perform the worship of the Moon there as before; then, having placed a silver vessel for the *arghya* offering in front and filled it with cow’s milk,
one should consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the Moon-mantra and the Vidyā-mantra.

The wise one, meaning one who intends to offer the *arghya* to the Moon, should fill [the vessel] completely; that is, the wise one, knowing that the filling must be performed preceded by the recitation of the mantra in reverse order (*viloma*), should do so. As it has been said:
"Having placed the silver cup there, one should fill it with cow's [milk], reciting the mantra in reverse order."
There, the wise one should respectfully cast camphor, sandalwood, saffron, unbroken rice grains, *kuśa* grass knots,
barley, and these flowers— *kusuda*, blue lotus, golden *ketakī*, fresh jasmine, *campaka*, and *śatapatra*— as they may be available.
One should cast [the deity] forth and invite the All-pervading Lord from His own heart, which is like the orb of the moon;

thus invited, one should worship the Moon with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Since it is stated that "one who has fasted should offer the *arghya*," it is implied that eating thereafter is not prohibited. Thus it is established.
He extracts the previously indicated Vidyā-mantra with the words beginning "vidye" and so forth:
"vidye vidyāmālini candriṇi candramukhi svāhā"—this is the sixteen-syllable mantra.
He extracts the Sūrya-mantras with the words beginning "tāra" and so forth; "ghṛṇi" is its essential form (svarūpa).
The syllable *va* is the seat (*āsana*) of the "good" (*vasu*), meaning it is that wherein the station of the vowel-less fire (*agni*) resides; thus it is *marut*, the syllable *ya*.

The vowel *ā* is the meaning of the remaining word. *Atri* is the syllable *da*. *Manetṛ* is the syllable *tya* accompanied by the vowel *ī*; that which has this at its end is so described. *Oṃ ghṛṇiḥ cha*.

The term *vastuvastutvena* is a compound with the middle word elided (*madhyapadalopī samāsa*), meaning "by way of being the reality of the thing. Since it exists here, the suffix *aC* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. Furthermore, because the final member of the compound is used at the end of all vowels, it is followed by a *visarga*; and since that [final vowel] is at the end, there is either its elision (*antolopa*) or its lengthening (*vivṛddhi*). Thus it is said.

Just as *yādamta*, so too *tathācānta*—possessing the letter *a* and the *visarga*—means Atri; this should be understood as an epithet (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the context of the non-removal of the *visarga* according to the opinion of the *Padārthadarśa* and others who follow the previously stated meaning. *Oṃ ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityaḥ* is the eight-syllable mantra.
He states the mantras for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with "To Truth" (*satyāya*). For all these mantras, one should append the ten-syllable mantra "tejovālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā" at the end;
then, the ritual placement of the limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is to be performed with the mantras beginning with "To Truth," as follows: *satyāya tejovālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ*.

*Oṃ svāhā-hṛdayāya namaḥ; Oṃ brahmaṇe tejo-jvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā; śirase svāhā*—these and other such applications are established. He now describes the *pañcamūrti-nyāsa* with the words "one should install again," etc.: *Oṃ ādityāya namaḥ; aiṃ ravaye namaḥ; uṃ bhāmā*.
"Salutation to Venama, salutation to Ībhāsvara, salutation to Aṃsūrya"—such are the applications [of the mantra].

He describes the placement (nyāsa) of the arrows with the words beginning with "on the head" (mūrdha): "Oṃ oṃ namaḥ, oṃ ghṛṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṇiḥ namaḥ," and so forth. On the left and right upper [arms] are two red lotuses; beneath them...

For these two [deities], after granting the boon of fearlessness (*abhayavara*) and [the state of] being unslayable (*avadhya*), one should display the lotus-disk mudrā (*padmabiṃvamudrā*) before them; for it is stated in the *Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi*: "The lotus-disk mudrā is as previously described. The definition of that mudrā is as follows: having brought the two hands together facing each other, they are joined and raised upward.

One should join the thumbs within the hollow of the palms; this is the *Añjali-mudrā*. Having formed the hands in the shape of a lotus, one should hold the two middle fingers separated from each other; this is called the *Bimba-mudrā*. Thus it is said: "Eight hundred thousand [recitations] for the first preparation of the *pīṭha*."
Prior to the conceptualization of the deities of the *dharmādipīṭha*, one should worship from the *maṇḍūka* onwards up to the pedestal (*vedikā*)— that is to say,

before the worship of *dharma* and the others. Having worshipped the four [deities] beginning with *Prabhūta* in the cardinal directions and *Paramasukha* in the center, the worship of *dharma* and the others must indeed be performed following this.
Some say that because there is no authoritative evidence for renunciation [in this context], otherwise one would have simply said "in the place of dharma and so forth";

furthermore, since worship was previously prohibited, worship is now subsequently permitted. Others, however, cite another tantra stating: "One should arrange these on the seats with the heart-mantra in the center and at the intermediate directions."
They say that because these [entities] perform functions such as merit (*dharma*) through their very perception, it is their worship that is required and not the worship of merit itself;

furthermore, the worship of demerit (*adharma*) and so forth is universally accepted, since even they (the opponents) do not deny that its effects are produced by them. Here, the word "direction" (*dik*) refers to the intermediate directions (*vidiś*), for the cardinal directions themselves cannot be called "directions" [in this specific sense].

Because there is no [existence] of eightfoldness and so forth, as it would result in a contradiction regarding the directions; thus, the intended meaning is that one should worship them in the directions starting from the southeast (Āgneyī) and so on. Alternatively, one should worship the pure, essential, venerable, and supremely blissful Bhūtā in the three directions starting from the southeast, within the center of the seat of power (pīṭha-śakti).
Because of the statement "prior to" (*prāk*) up until the word "ācammeva," it is stated here that dharma and the others perform their respective functions;

for dharma and the rest were not previously mentioned as being applicable to the directions starting with the east. Regarding the term *aklība* (neuter): there are three short vowels (*i*, *u*, *ṛ*), four neuters (*ṛ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *o*), making seven vowels; [the term refers to those] distinct from these.
Having joined the nine vowels with the *bindu* (anusvāra) and the letter *repha* (the letter *r*), one should apply them at the beginning of the mantra.

These are the nine seed-syllables (*bīja*)—*te*, *naḥ*, *rāṃ*, *rīṃ*, *rūṃ*, *reṃ*, *raiṃ*, *raṃ*, *raḥ*—which correspond respectively to the nine throne-energies (*pīṭha-śakti*) beginning with Dīptā. Some, however, [advise] that in place of the phrase "joined with the *bindu* and fire," one should use the *bindu* [alone].
Considering "samanvitāni" to be the root reading, some say that the seed-syllables (*bījas*) consist solely of the nine vowels.
He extracts the *pīṭhamantra* with the words beginning with "vadet," etc.: "Obeisance to the Solar Yoga-pīṭha, whose nature is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva"—this is the nineteen-syllable *pīṭha[-mantra]*.

The seed-mantra is *khaṃ haṃ*; the other essential form is the eight-syllable mantra: *oṃ haṃ khakholkāya namaḥ*. With this mantra, one performs the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Sun into the image. Then, having worshipped the principal deity there with the sixteen primary offerings (*upacāras*) and others, one worships the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatās*) upon the filaments and the Ādityas upon the petals in the cardinal directions.

In the intermediate petals are Pūṣan and the others; in the [other] petals are the Mothers, Brāhmī and the rest. In the pericarp of the principal deity is Aruṇa. Outside, in the spaces between the petals, are the eight planets beginning with the Moon, as before.
In the square, Śakti and the others are to be worshipped. Their names, beginning with their respective initial letters and accompanied by the *bindu*, are the syllables [to be used].

The meaning is that one should understand these from the context where no specific distinction is mentioned; however, according to the author of the *Padārthadarśa*, the word "four" (*catasraḥ*) is connected with "powers" (*śaktayaḥ*). As for the five previously mentioned [deities] beginning with Āditya, their worship is performed in the four directions, and having performed the worship of Āditya in the center, one should perform the worship of Arka and the others...

They say that [the worship] should be concluded with the worship of the Rudras and others; however, in this view, how would the root text—"Āditya and the others on the petals of the directions"—be consistent, since you have taught that the worship of Āditya is in the center?
Nor can it be explained as a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the qualities of the members are understood), meaning "those of whom Āditya and the others are the first."

It should not be said that this [text] refers only to the group of four beginning with *vrīhi* (rice), because that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the worship of the Sun (*āditya*) would not be established. Nor should it be argued that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), on the grounds that the worship of him is already accomplished through the worship of the Principal Deity (*pradhāna*); for the worship of the Sun and the others is likewise already accomplished. Therefore, their...
Because there is no fault of repetition (*pitada*), since this [worship] enters into the mantra of Āditya himself, it is his worship alone that is performed through the *jātaka* and other rites.

Therefore, the statement in the *Padārthādarśa*— "there is no restrictive rule as to why the five-fold worship (*pañcasūka*) is offered"— is refuted, for the very syllables of the mantra serve as the restrictive rule.
Even if you were to say "Tvādi," nevertheless, because Sūrya has entered the mantra and is thus worshipped,

there would be the consequence of his worship being [incomplete]; and since the worship of one direction would result in the absence of a form (mūrti), and because the worship of the five forms everywhere for Agni is traditionally enjoined, this [objection] applies only when there is the worship of three forms alone.

Since it is impossible to commit an offense that one has not already committed, if you say, "But rather, having reconciled the root text, the position of the worship of the five forms (pañcamūrti) accepted by Padmapādācārya and others must be reconciled," then [the answer is: the original word "first" (ādau) refers to the limbs (aṅga). Worship...

The word "ye" (those) is not disconnected from what precedes it; for, because of the instruction on worship [given] previously and because of the general rule, it is possible to understand that worship comes first. Rather, it should be construed as: "first, in the four directions, Āditya and the others. And the word "ādi" (and so forth/first) refers specifically to the pericarp, which is the beginning of all.
Even there, because the principal deity has been worshipped in the center, that [space] in front of him is empty;

thus, having worshipped the Sun (Āditya) there and having fully worshipped the four [deities] beginning with Aruṇa in the four directions, know that the worship of the five forms (pañcamūrti-pūjā) is accomplished. According to the view of some, the worship of Aruṇa is performed with the [mantra of] Brāhmī.

In the place of the Mothers, one should worship the Mother named Mahālakṣmī, who is the last among the eight Mothers; for according to the words of the Teacher (Ācārya), the worship of the planets is not performed according to the well-known sequence,
but rather [the planets] beginning with Candra, Budha, Guru, and Bhārgava are placed in the four directions starting from the East, and [the remaining ones] in the four directions starting from Agni.

Kṣu, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the East; Candra, Jña, Guru, and Bhārgava in the corners starting from the Southeast (Āgneya); and Kuja, Maṃda, Ahi, and Ketu [in the remaining corners], according to the statement of another Tantra.
He describes the procedure for offering the *arghya* with the verse beginning with "dadyāt" and so forth: a circular mandala should be made with red sandalwood.

One should not perform [the rite] with the measure of a *prastha* as stated by the ancients; rather, since a *kuḍava* consists of four *palas* and a *prastha* consists of four *kuḍavas*, one should fill [the vessel] in reverse order,
while reciting the mantra, returning to the sequence and filling it with very pure [substances].

Based on the scriptural injunction (*ritivacanāt*), one should employ whatever is available from among the twelve items— namely red sandalwood, bamboo, *karavīra* flowers, *japā* flowers, and red substances such as saffron (*kuṅkuma*)—
according to the principle that "one should do what one is able to do," rather than waiting for a specific time when one might be able to obtain them all.
It should not be thought that this must be performed only when all [the materials] are obtained as desired;
for according to the statement of the Teacher (Ācārya): "Since devotion is to be joined with whatever is obtained, the rite of the Arghya is prescribed.

Having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) in that maṇḍala, [one should perform] the previously mentioned [worship] together with its limbs (sāṅga) in the established noble vessel (ārya-pātra).

After the recitation together with all the protective coverings (*āvaraṇas*), he states another mantra beginning with "ākāśam" and so forth: *hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ*. This mantra consists of these syllables. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is said to be Brahmā, or alternatively Bhṛgu; its meter (*chaṃdas*) is indeed Gāyatrī; and its deity (*devatā*) is Tīkṣṇadīpti.

The first seed-syllable is *dhiti* (dh) and the second is *śakti* (ś); these two are considered the beginning of *Tārā*, while the remainder is exactly as before. [The text] extracts the seed-syllable of Mārtaṇḍabhairava with the words "ākāśa" and so forth; within the thirteenth vowel of *Sadyojāta*, there is the fourteenth vowel, and likewise the letters *ha* and *ra*.

The *kārās* (the consonants *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*) are to be pronounced, joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), the nasal dot (*bindu*), and their respective *gurus* (the vowel *au*), according to the instruction of one's own teacher. Together with the fire (*ra*), the eye (*i*), and the moon (*u*), the letter *ṭha* at the end becomes the seed-syllable *biṃba*.
Thus, the root mantra is established as *phaṭ* followed by *dhriṃ*, *hrauṃ*, and *ddhriṃ*; this is preceded by the five [syllables] mentioned before.

The five forms beginning with Sūrya, joined respectively with the short vowels from *a* to *au*, and conjoined with the seed-syllable of Ārttaṇḍabhairava, should be deposited upon the middle finger, the index finger, the thumb, the ring finger, and the little finger, as well as upon the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet. [Thus it is] established.

He states with the words beginning "five" (*pañca*) that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart, head, crest, armor, and eyes using the seed-syllable joined with the first [vowel] and the long [vowels] respectively.

As for the phrase "ending with the eyes" (*netrāntāni*), it is intended merely to establish the correct sequence for the eyes which were obtained earlier [in the list], and not because they are placed in every single instance.

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* has stated: "Having likewise placed the *astra* at the end of the armor (*varma*), one should again place the *astra* and then place the *netra*. This is not correct, because there is no possibility here for the six long vowels to occur, as only the phrase "by that which is joined with the long [vowels]" (*dīrghayuktena*) is heard; furthermore, due to its prior presence, the *pañca-*... [is implied].

Since long vowels related to short vowels can arise instantaneously, it is understood that here the prescription of the five limbs for the mantra— including the eye— is established as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "one should abandon the eye of whichever [mantra] has five limbs. One should perform the limbs.

The knower of mantras should place [the seed-syllables] in the center with the syllable *ramā* (Śrī-bīja) enriched by the two vowels (*a* and *ā*), conjoined with the long [vowels], and sealed (*ākpuṭita*). The knower of the mantra should then apply the limbs (*aṅgas*) along with their respective *jātis* in the prescribed order. Thus, by the illustration provided, there is also the proclamation of the six long vowels for the word "pada."

That [interpretation] of theirs is not correct; for in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), since only the member-word (*aṅga-pada*) is seen, and in the absence of any specific distinction, it is more appropriate that this word refers specifically to the six members (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*). Thus, by following the respective order (*yathā-saṃkhya*), those mantras are obtained. However, the long word (*dīrgha-pada*) is intended to refer to the group of six long [syllables], whereas in the present context, it is said "ending with the eyes" (*netrāntāni*).

Since the term "limb" (*aṅga*) has already been restricted [to five] by this very [text], how could there be a state of being followed by six long vowels for it? On the contrary, the five-limbed [mantra] present in the context is indeed the sublater. The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* also accepted only the five-limbed alternative for the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjā*).

The claim that the worship of the ancillaries (*aṅga-pūjā*) is also implied by the word "thā" (in the phrase *thāpūrvam*) is not correct; for the worship of those ancillaries whose positions have already been determined by the definitive scriptures is merely restated here after first indicating their locations. Furthermore, it is precisely these definitive scriptures that establish that the term "ancillary" (*aṅga*) in this context refers to the ancillaries ending with the eye (*netrānta*).

When there is a desire for that specific location, it is "Īśāna," and thus, according to the specific statement, there is the worship of the two limbs beginning with Īśāna. Now, he states the *jayā* mantra with the words beginning with "viyat" and so forth;
for then, the first letter of the syllable *ha* is *ha*, which is joined together with the following one.

Intending that its unity is intended by virtue of being a collective (kṛtatvena), the singular number is used; thus, there is the attainment of usage such as *tena ha sāṃhasīm*. He states what is to be included by the word "etc. in the phrase "limbs, etc. (*aṅgādī*) with the words "the sacrifice," and so forth.
[He says] "rich in mantras" (*mantrāḍhyā*); [this refers to] having written the Ajapā mantra upon the pericarp of the lotus of the Mātṛkā.

The meaning is "having placed. By "one who has placed the mantra" (*nyastamantra*) is meant one by whom the *ajapā-mantra* has been placed—that is, meditated upon—therein. With the left hand, [one should act] with the two drops (*bindu*), which are the final seeds (*antyabīja*) consisting of the components of the final visarga, and which are to be meditated upon as being like two lunar orbs (*candrabiṃba*). Thereafter, the final seed...
The meaning is that one should contemplate the form of the letter *ha* as being inundated by a drop (*bindu*) flowing from the letter *ja*.
Regarding this, the specific detail mentioned in another tantra is as follows: sixty breaths (*prāṇas*) constitute one *nāḍī*;
six *prāṇas* are considered one *ghaṭikā*; sixty *nāḍīs* constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*); and this is the number for the recitation (*japa*).
O Lord of Devas, for practitioners of mantra, even without the formal recitation of the *japā* mantra, the recitation becomes an "Ajapa" (unstruck) recitation;
therefore, it is declared to be the cutter of the bonds of worldly existence. O Maheśānī, one should thus offer this recitation every day to Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, O Supreme Goddess.
To the individual self (jīvātman), and likewise to the supreme self (paramātman), one should offer six hundred, then again six thousand,
then six thousand, then a thousand,
then another thousand, and finally a thousand more, in sequence to the Guru; [and] in the foundation (ādhāra).
There, at the base of the *liṅga*, is a four-petalled lotus where the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) resides; at the root of the *liṅga* itself, Brahmā certainly dwells upon a six-petalled lotus.
In the navel, the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu) dwells upon a ten-petalled lotus;
in the heart, Śaṅkara dwells upon a twelve-petalled lotus; and in the throat, [he dwells] upon an eight-petalled lotus.

O Supreme Goddess, the individual soul (jīvātman) resides in the heart-lotus; the supreme soul (paramātman) resides in the lotus situated between the eyebrows; and the venerable Guru resides in the thousand-petaled lotus at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). One should offer the recitation (japa) to those who reside within these seven cakras.
O beloved, the Ajapā-Gāyatrī, which arises every day and night, is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.

By constantly chanting the Ajapā, rebirth no longer exists. By the mere resolution to practice it, a person is liberated from sins; there is no knowledge equal to this, nor is there any greater than this.
