Regarding the recitation of the *Dṛśo* mantra: "There has never been, nor will there ever be, a merit equal to this. Furthermore, the formal offering (*nivedana*) of this recitation should take place at the time of the morning rites; this was already mentioned in passing.
He states the *Agni-mantra* with the words beginning "Vyāhṛti," etc.; "Agni" is the essential form [of the mantra], and "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ... is the prefix.

"O Agni Jātavedas, bring hither [the gods]; accomplish all rites, Svāhā!"—this mantra consists of twenty-five syllables. Here, *praṇava* (Om) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). This deity has eight arms; therein, starting from the upper left, they hold the power (*śakti*), a handful of *kuśa* grass, a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
The mudrās— beginning from the right side— are the svastika, the specific weapon, the rosary, the *sruva* ladle, and the boon-granting (*vara*) mudrās. On the fourteenth day prior to the [full] moon,
the disciple, having received the mantra from the Guru, fasts on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra and [performs] twelve thousand [repetitions].

Having recited the mantra six times on the new moon day, and having fed the Brahmins with foods and other offerings that are predominantly sweet— meaning those characterized by an abundance of sweetness— and having satisfied them with sacrificial fees,
he himself brings six kinds of materials for the oblation, such as fuel-sticks of the *vaṭa* tree and so forth.

Having purified [the site], beginning from the first day (pratipad) and continuing for ten days, one should offer oblations eight hundred times each with six substances. Having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and so forth, one should satisfy Guha. As for the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās), they are exactly as previously mentioned; therefore, they are not set forth again here. Now, however... [text truncated]

Since the chosen deities (*iṣṭadevatā*) have already been mentioned, would there not be redundancy in their presentation once again? It would not be so. Agni Vaiśvānara is declared to be the one who is behind the back;

he is the consumer of oblations (*hutāśana*), the one whose path is the oblation (*hutavartman*), the knower of all beings (*jātavedas*), and furthermore, the bearer of oblations (*hutāvaha*). Furthermore...
Since other forms of Agni—such as Vāmukha and Saṃhājihva—are established in other tantras, this [repetition] is not intended to introduce yet another form;
rather, its purpose is to indicate that the eight forms previously mentioned constitute the complete set of eight. Thus, the repetition is meaningful.

If it is argued that there might be a deviation from another tantra, [the response is: while the eight forms (mūrtis) mentioned in other tantras are not included in these three utterances of the fire-mantra, here they are indeed these very ones. With their own seed-syllable *raṃ*, which is the seed-syllable of fire, the seat-mantra is:
*Raṃ vahniyogapīṭhāya namaḥ*. This is the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*).

Regarding the statement, "One should offer oblations daily, or on each lunar day (*pratipad*)," the *Padārthadarśa* has proposed an alternative interpretation. However, this is not tenable; for an option (*vikalpa*) is not appropriate between two things that require equal effort and entail equal expenditure.
Indeed, there is no such option here, as those two do not possess that nature. Therefore, first...
It should be understood that this alternative rite (*anukalpa*) has been handed down for the sake of favoring those who are incapable [of performing the primary rite].

Regarding the materials, the author of the *Hṛdaya-kaumudī* maintains that seventeen substances are required by taking all of the following milk-bearing trees: the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa*. Others, however, hold that there is only one [tree] to be used.

Rāmacandra, relying on the view that "milk-tree" (dugdhataru) refers to the material cause (upādāna), maintains that there are fourteen substances; however, by taking the term *aruṇotpala* to refer to both the red lotus (*raktakamala*) and the red water-lily (*raktakuvalaya*),
he asserts that there are fifteen substances, seven of which are the aforementioned fuel-sticks (*samidh*).

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that one should offer oblations daily, beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the end of the fortnight (*parva*), using fifteen substances— namely, seven flowers and one *dūrvā* grass—
with each substance individually, and not all combined; thus, with each single substance, [one should perform] one hundred and eight [oblations].

From a hundred-fold oblation (*śatasaṃkhyakahoma*), there results a repetition one hundred and eight times, equal to the number of [the syllables] of the *bhavya* [mantra]. He shows the mantra for the horse-fire (*turagāgni*) with the words beginning "uttiṣṭha" (*arise*, etc.).
Although the word "me" (*my*) is replaced by "mama" (*of me*) and so forth, even though it stands at the beginning of the verse, nevertheless—

There is no fault here, as it serves the purpose of mere sound through its form as an imitation. This mantra of twenty-four syllables—"uttiṣṭha puruṣa haripiṅgalalohitākṣa dehi me dehi dāpaya svāhā"—was proclaimed of old; Bhṛgu, Gāyatrī, and Agni are its seers (ṛṣis) respectively.

The five elements beginning with *dayaḥ* (water), the four instruments (*karaṇa*), "Arise, O Puruṣa, obeisance to the heart," and so forth— these applications were previously mentioned and stated immediately before. Now, he states the applications beginning with "In the morning" (*prātaḥ*) and so on, [referring to] the sun reflected in water.

The phrase "having conquered even the fear of death" connects with the preceding; however, due to the avoidance of breaking the meter (*chaṃdobhaṅga*), the word "fear" (*bhaya*) is treated as a separate accusative case-ending form. In some places, the reading is simply *avinduḥ*. Regarding "the deer-seal" (*mṛgamudrā*): it is formed by joining the tips of the middle and ring fingers together with the thumb.

Furthermore, one should raise the remaining fingers; this is declared to be the *mṛgamudrā*. [The flowers used are: *nṛpabhū* (the royal tree), known in the local dialect as *dhanabahirā*; and *kuraṇṭaka*, known in the local dialect as *kaṭasarai-pā*;
with these, each unmixed [with the others].

A hundred oblations are performed for the fulfillment of desires; one should offer them one by one a hundred times, as seen in other Tantras. With cow's milk—or red cow's milk—and with *śāli* rice grains, one should prepare a sacrificial ball (*piṇḍa*) of clarified butter cooked with the juice of red cow-dung and smeared with ghee.

Based on the observation in the *Prayogasāra* that "it should be mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*) seven times," the phrase "at the time of dawn on the day of [the rite] together with a woman" means that he should be accompanied by his wife (*sapatnīka*). However, others maintain that from this ritual procedure alone, there is no continuous connection to the state of poverty.
"But what is even more than this prosperity? he says: "By Fortune" (*śriyā*). This word does not end in the feminine suffix *tṛc*, but rather belongs to the *vaki* class and so forth;
the sense is that one should live only as long as one is endowed with wealth, and never once liberated from it—thus say the *jvaras*.
The well-known *grahas* are the planetary spirits (*bhūtagraha*) and so forth; my diseases are leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and the like.
Even for one seized by these, whether individually or collectively, life continues to exist for a time;
therefore, [the text says] "having conquered," because their conquest occurs even through the transition to another world as described in the subsequent chapter.

Since it certainly occurs, the phrase "one should live" implies that it is possible even by living for two or three days; likewise, because it is possible [to live] for a hundred years, the intended meaning is that practitioners must necessarily strive in this matter, as such a distinguished fruit belongs to one who is intent upon this practice.
Now, for one who is exceedingly sinful— even more so than the well-known Jāmi and others—

the sequence of bliss arising from the remembrance of that which must be performed immediately after the exposition of the mantra of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of the supreme state, dispels all prior [sins].

Because the author of the root text has not performed the indication of the sun and so forth— due to the desire for brevity and because the investigation of the supreme mantra-attainment occurs precisely through the state of non-reconnection—
he expresses a praise of his own form at the conclusion of the worship.

We display the destruction of Māra; moreover, the manifestation of prosperity for those like us is like the dispelling of darkness, and the accumulation of calamities for those prone to misfortune is surely their end.
Just as the breaking of the stalks of blooming lotuses and the like occurs, let one offer salutation to the Creator.
O lotus, you do not release your fragrance too hastily; rather, you remain thus with your petals closed until the swarm of bees has settled.
As if desiring to fulfill the true purpose of the glances of the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), you have become the very embodiment of those glances and now cause the lotuses to bloom.
"Having sprinkled others with laughter, having caused people to bloom, and having become the lord of light,
the moon becomes blue; yet he becomes full again month after month"—
thus did the swan laugh incessantly.
I bow to you, whose resolve was stolen by Hari; for even the gods,
having first performed the ritual with mantras— both natural and artificial— subsequently find their dwelling here in you alone, O Lord of the Day, as if in a physical image or a yantra.

Vāmana said: "O most beautiful one, if there is indeed doubt regarding the primary form due to uncertainty concerning the variations of mantras and so forth, the ritual procedure for worship remains in doubt; yet, O you who are worthy of praise, it attains perfection only in you.
Let the gods be satisfied by the thousands, and let them all indeed go to you."
All ritual actions arise from this mountain of compassion; indeed, success depends entirely upon you.
Happiness until the end of life depends on you, for even the destruction of poverty and disease is ordained through you. Furthermore, when death has arrived, it too is here dependent upon you, O Son.

"O Lord, you who have destroyed the darkness of the world's eyes, the protector of the virtuous, the adversary of the wicked, and the treasure-house of love—bestow your grace upon me, a wretched man like me, who am destitute.
The meaning of this is: "me, like me"—that is, one who is exceedingly sinful.

The meaning is: "of those things that ought not to be treated with deceit. Regarding "all prosperities"—such as cattle, sons, elephants, horses, and so forth—it refers to all of them collectively, and not to each one individually; nor does it refer to even a single instance of each.
For example, in the manifestation and creation of objects such as pots and words...

Even for those like us, there is no fatigue in opening [the lotuses]; how much less, then, could there be any fatigue for you in bringing about the perfection of the virtuous? In this same way, it should also be applied to the phrase "of the lotuses" (*padmānām*), as it denotes the goddess Lakṣmī.
Since the form [Padmāya] also occurs in the singular dative case,
it is possible for you to bring about the blossoming and gladdening of all lotuses by assuming the form of the eye of the Lord Hari; thus, you have brought her joy.
Intending to show that You assume various forms for the sake of the desired objects of Your devotees who have performed their duties, He says:
"In full bloom. Full bloom (*vikāśa*) is the state of being blossomed due to the excess of satisfaction; however, the moon, becoming diminished month after month, becomes full only through Your rays.

Therefore, [the Veda] says "I am the Moon" (*caṃdramā aham asmi*) with reference to you; the meaning is that "I am the Sun" (*aham saḥ sūrya eva*). Thus, your very name has indeed become "Haṃsa. Now, in response to the inquiry "Where has the letter 'A' gone?", [the text says] "O Hari," and so forth; because it carries away (*haraṇāt*) everything for all beings...
Having attained the state of *Ṛta*, this Viṣṇu, by way of negating the names and so forth [of others] as belonging to the lineage of Bhṛgu,

has avoided the manner of maintaining [those names] for the sake of his own name; the sense is that all worship— whether directed toward an image, a statue, a yantra, or the like— is required only in you.

With the two verses beginning with "devi," [the Lord] says: "The worship of the deities bestows desired fruits; therefore, you alone are to be accepted by all. Since even other deities grant results only through their dependence upon you, why is it that you alone are not to be disregarded?
Thinking thus, [I realize that] you alone are the sustaining cause for the destruction of diseases such as consumption and the like, as well as poverty; in the state of being alive,
happiness is entirely dependent on you, and upon death, since one comes under the authority of Dharmarāja, it is even more so dependent on you.
He said to them, "Do not be afraid," with the words beginning with "jīvana" (living), and so forth; for even one such as me,
who possesses an indescribable state of dejection, has a mother who is most virtuous, and whose father is named Māpati, a lord of the earth whose lineage is renowned for its love.
Rmācala is the birthplace, Sūpāsya is Kṛtavīrya, and Vārāṇasī is the abode of Acyuta;
thus the Mahendra section reached completion in the *Ṣaṣṭhārthacintāmaṇi*.
Now, following the clockwise order from the Sun, he makes a formal promise to extract the Śrī Viṣṇu mantras.

Having said "I shall explain," he speaks [the following] to demonstrate the greatness of this mantra—its superiority over other mantras—by stating "for all purposes" (*sarvārtha*). Generally, the word "purpose" (*artha*) refers primarily to prosperity (*lakṣmī*), such as the attainment of kingdom, sons, and so forth; these are easily accomplished by means of mantras. Thus he says: "for all purposes."
To dispel the misconception that the word "artha" (meaning) might apply here as well because it is possible [to explain it otherwise], he says:

"Of those... *Tāra* is the *praṇava* (OM); *namaḥ* is its own form; *aḥ* follows as the subsequent part, with the word *tāra* to be supplied; *aḥ* is the *visarga*; and after that comes the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra.
At the time of pronouncing the two syllables *vau-ra-ja-pā-dau*, according to the literal hearing,
that single mātrā [of the first syllable] cuts it off— that is, it expels it from itself; thus,
by the rule "there is elision or augmentation of the final mātrā of the Praṇava," the final [mātrā], which is of the form of the letter *a*, is removed.
Only the thirteen vowels remain; because of that, the conjunction with the consonant *na* becomes elevated (*uddhata*) by the vowel *o*. And that is the third letter of the original mantra.
In reality, however, *namaḥ* ends in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhanta*) or the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), [meaning] "of it" or "from it."

The term *paścātpadam* means "lacking one measure," which conveys the previously mentioned sense of *tāra*. Alternatively, it is called *pada* because it gives (*dadāti*) one letter belonging within its own constituent parts; here, the root *dā* has the meaning of "to abandon. Thus, according to the previous logic, by abandoning the final single syllable, there are three [measures].

The attainment of the desired result is as before, provided that ten syllables remain; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of vigor due to the failure to obtain the root [syllable] for the extraction (*uddhāra*) as it was not heard. As for what the author of the *Padārthādarśa* stated—that after the *ru*-substitution of the word *namaḥ*, the vowel *u* arises through *guṇa*-elision—that is utterly devoid of foundation.
By the root [mantra] itself, there is no desire to express an unintended color, because that is understood from it.

The two syllables *na* and *ra* (the letters *na* and *ra*) are joined with the letter *da*, which is long (*dīrgha*) due to its being first encountered; they are properly combined (*saṃsamyakprasekam*) with the letter *da*. That which has the nature of *pavana* is *ṇāya*. Thus is the form.
Thus, this eight-syllable mantra, "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya," has been extracted;
*praṇava* (Oṃ) is its seed (*bīja*), and *āya* is its power (*śakti*). According to the scripture, the first syllable of this eight-syllable mantra is the seed.
From the fifteenth letter, which is made into a pure consonant, the remainder of the mantra follows as *śa*.
This is because it is observed in the *Mantra-tantra-prakāśa* and other works that [the seers] are mentioned for each syllable;
furthermore, in another tantra, the seers are stated as follows: Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, and Kumbha.
"Jaḥ; Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī;

Virāṭ and the Vasus, eight in number, are the deities"—with these words beginning with "Kruddha," he extracts the fifth mantra, preceded by "O Great Hero, enraged, O Day-maker, a thousandfold. Of these...

For those devoted to liberation, at the end [of the mantra] there should be *agnivallabhā* (the beloved of fire), followed by words such as *kruddholkā* and so forth, joined with the [seed-syllable of the] class (*jāti*) ending in the word *vahni* (fire), and so on; in accordance with other tantras, including the word *svāhā* within, [one recites]:
*kruddholkāya svāhā hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *maholkāya svāhā*.

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that the five-limbed placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the mantras beginning with "to the head" (*śirase*). The author of the *Padārthādarśa* also states that the five-limbed placement should be performed with the mantras beginning with "to the head, svāhā" (*śirase svāhā*) and "to the enraged firebrand, svāhā" (*kruddholkāya svāhā*). [He further states] "salutation to the enraged firebrand, salutation to the heart" (*kruddholkāya namaḥ hṛdayāya namaḥ*), and so forth.
The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* considers the usage [of the dative] to be the primary intention of the root;
however, in usages such as *kruddholkāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*, even though *svāhā* or *namaḥ* are not included,
nothing needs to be inferred by them on the grounds that the word ends in the dative case— this is precisely what they intend.
The author of the *Padārthādarśa* has raised the following objection: "Since it is stated that those [mantras] end with 'svāhā' by extracting them with the dative case-ending (*caturthyanta*),

and since a dative ending is impossible due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as 'to the heart' (*hṛdayāya*), the presence of the dative ending must necessarily imply [the addition of] 'svāhā' and so forth."
Having performed the *pañcāṅga-nyāsa* according to the aforementioned method, and having performed the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* with: "Oṃ, salutation to the heart;
Naḥ, svāhā to the head; Moḥ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair; Nāḥ, huṃ to the armor; Rāḥ, vauṣaṭ to the eyes;
Yaḥ, phaṭ to the weapon," one should surround the letter *ṇa* within the belly.

Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the mantra of the wheel that is about to be described—beginning with the words "Furthermore, with the letters" (*bhūyo varṇaiḥ*) and so forth—one should perform the deposition of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*). This is eightfold in every way: one [set] extends from the support (*ādhāra*) up to the nose; therein, the two roots of the two hands, the two shoulders, and the two forms constitute the location.
The two [groups of] phonemes consist of two syllables; the two feet also take the form of two *ūt* (long vowels), which is the location for the two phonemes.
There is one location in the nose, and a second from the throat to the back of the head. Among these, the two locations—breasts and sides—are each twofold; and a third is from the head to the nose.

Here, it is intended that the three locations beginning with the eyes (eyes, ears, and nostrils) consist of two each; for the term "nose" (*ghrāṇa*) and so forth is indicative of the two nostrils. Regarding the phrase "in the joints and fingers of the arms": there are three joints in each arm, and one tip of each finger, thus completing the number eight.

In this manner, having placed the five [syllables] on the directions, feet, joints, and fingers, and the sixteenth [syllable] on the seven dhātus and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—thus in these eight locations—and having placed [the syllable] on the heart, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight syllables should be performed;
this is the sixth [method]. From the head down to the two feet is the seventh; for it is heard [in scripture] that there are two feet.

Although the five locations ending with the two lips (*dadva*) are each produced from two [sounds], they are intended to be the location for each individual phoneme; thus, their number is completed. Furthermore, even though the four locations beginning with the cheeks (*gaṇḍa*) are each intended as a single location, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon them.

One should place the seventh syllable on the upper part of the left arm, which is the location of the conch (*śaṅkha*), and the eighth syllable on the lower part of that same arm, which is the location of the lotus (*kamala*); this is the "eighth placement" (*aṣṭamanyāsa*), according to the author of the *Harṣakaumudī*.
However, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that this is the placement known as the *Vibhūtipañjara*.
Therein, first, there are three nyāsas; each is presented by one half-verse,
followed by another half-verse presenting its subsequent selection,
followed by another half-verse presenting it, and finally presented by one complete verse following that.

The three *canyāsa*s are as before; thus, these six *nyāsa*s have been completed. Regarding the four *nyāsa*s situated between these two triads, they are to be performed on the arms and feet, and so forth, according to some. In that regard, the four joints [of the hands] consist of the four fingers excluding the thumbs.
Due to the distinction between the right and left hands and feet, there are four cycles of placement (*nyāsa*) that remain unimpeded;

however, some explain its eightfold nature by asserting that there are three joints and five fingers [on each limb]. Others, however, maintain that among the joints of the two hands, there is one of such a kind [that completes the count].

They say that the third [placement] is in the joints of the feet, the fourth is on the two toes other than the big toe, and there is a repetition of the placement on such toes of the feet; thus, this number of placements, together with the previously established six, makes four forms in total.
They teach that the tenfold nature of the nyāsas remains entirely unimpeded through their union;

here, for every syllable, one should perform the encasement with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and the addition of the *bindu*. Furthermore, at the conclusion of each repetition, the pervasive nyāsa (*vyāpakanyāsa*) should be performed using the complete root mantra.

One should assign each letter individually, ending with the *bindu* and encircled by the *dhruva* (the *praṇava*), according to the statement in the *Mantra-tantra-prakāśa*: "each letter of the mantra is encapsulated by the *praṇava*"; and also because of the instruction of the teacher Padmapāda that there is a pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) for every cycle. As for the state of being accompanied by the *bindu*...

As for what was stated by the author of the *Harṣakaumudī*— that such a view of Rāmacandra should be disregarded on the grounds that it would lead to the violation of the aforementioned mantra— that is incorrect, because it results in a contradiction with the stated words; for even if there were a specific statement, if one fears abandoning the sequence of the mantra, then [the following applies].

You will even abandon the tying of darbha grass and so forth for the mantras, and you will pour water in the opposite direction at the northern boundary and other points. The eightfold nature consists of the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), the great principle (mahattattva), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the five elements; such is the form of the eightfold nature.

The nature of the *kṛti* [metre] consists in the conjunction of the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the Knowledge-Self (*jñānātman*); it is precisely because of this that it possesses twelve syllables. This is the underlying meaning: for the twelve-syllabled mantra is composed of the eightfold *prakṛti* and has the nature of the four Selves; and although it is eight-syllabled, it likewise consists of the eightfold *prakṛti*.
Since it is said that "one who has been conjoined with Nyāsa will realize his identity with That," Nyāsa must necessarily be performed for the purpose of effecting that identity. Thus,
there are the twelve [deities] beginning with Keśava, accompanied by the twelve syllables, the twelve vowels, and the twelve Ādityas.
The practical meaning is that one should assign the forms (*mūrtis*) to the locations to be described, such as the forehead and so forth.
The ritual application is: *oṃ aṃ dhātre keśavāya namaḥ*. Some maintain the application to be: *oṃ dhātṛkeśavābhyāṃ namaḥ*. [Others say: *oṃ aṃ dhātṛsahitāya keśavāya*.
Some say "yanamaḥ"; others say "oṃ aṅkeśavāya dhātre namaḥ. This [mantra] beginning with "mṇe" pertains to the previous [deity]; that which begins with "kaṇṭha" pertains to Agni.
It is situated on the shoulder—that is, on the right shoulder—and at the throat; it belongs to the southern part of the neck, [and] the portion of the shoulder belongs to Agni.

As for what was stated regarding the posteriority of the left—namely, that one should likewise place [the deities] on the right shoulder, the neck, and the left side of the other [shoulder]—it is connected with the preceding [verse]: "O Hṛṣīkeśa," and similarly with "Tvaṣṭṛ. One should place Nārāyaṇa at the navel; thus it is seen in another tantra, stating that the direction of the back is the region of the neck and the back.

Some maintain that the term "nādatrakukṣipada" should be explained as referring to the navel. Regarding the phrase "the great mantra," it means that one should install two eight-syllabled mantras. The word "again" (punaḥ) implies that it is connected with what precedes; for it is stated that one should install the twelve-syllabled [mantra] together with the eight-syllabled one.

Some say that the term "great mantra" (*mahāmantra*) is an adjective for the twelve-syllable [mantra]; they argue that in phrases such as "the door" (*dvāra*) and "the earring" (*kuṇḍala*), the accusative case is used in the sense of the object of an action, while "the two lights" (*jyotirdvaya*) refers to its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Thus, [the mantra is]: *oṃ kirīṭi keyūra hāra ma...*.
"Salutation to Him who has earrings, a conch, a discus, and a mace, whose hands hold a lotus, who wears yellow garments,
whose chest is marked by the Śrīvatsa, who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, who illuminates with the light of His own two-fold radiance,
and who possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns"— this is the mantra consisting of sixty-seven syllables. Who [should recite it]?
In this mantra, they include the three syllables "cit-kuṇḍalānta-laṅkṛte"; the *tāra* (oṃ); the word "makara" at the end of "kirīṭa-keyūra-hāra"; "kuṇḍalālaṅkṛte";
"śaṅkha-cakra-gadā-abja"; and "śrī-bhūmi-sahita-svātma-jyoti-dvaya-pa".
The statement from the *Mantra-tantra-prakāśa*, "He should show [the weapons]," is cited there as authoritative;
and the weapons are to be meditated upon in this manner: the lotus in the lower right hand, the conch in the hand below that, the mace in the lower left hand, and the discus in the upper left hand.

He explains the meaning of the words beginning with "Vimalā" (the Stainless One) and so forth, which characterize the transformation, starting with the words "Vimalā," etc.: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Self of all beings, the Asura-vāya, the Self of the lotus-throne that is the conjunction of all selves; obeisance. Thus [ends] the thirty-seventh [chapter].
If these *kṣara* (perishable) *koṇa-pīṭha* mantras are said to include incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth,

then since they state that one should perform the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) after offering perfumes and flowers, how will they include incense, lamps, and the rest under the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here? Therefore, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in this context is due to negligence.

We understand that they will certainly accept it as being exactly so; for some maintain that since the worship of each individual syllable— which constitutes the eight-limbed mantra— is prescribed within the filaments (*kesara*) during the subsidiary worship (*aṅgapūjā*) of the *karṇikā*,
the worship of both those limbs [the base and the tip] occurs within the filaments themselves through the distinction between the root and the apex.

The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* maintains that here, as previously, since there is no distinction in the procedure for the six-limbed worship (*ṣaḍaṅgapūjā*)—as it is performed specifically on the filaments (*kesara*)—the root text stated "having worshipped the limbs" (*aṅgānyabhyarcya*). However, if another location had been intended, that would certainly have been specified. Oṃ na.

The application in the worship of the syllables is as follows: "maḥ namaḥ," "moṃ namaḥ," and so forth. According to the observation of other tantras, worship should be performed with the seed-syllables (bījas) stripped of their case-endings upon the filaments (kesara). As for the meditation on the syllables of the mantra, it is as stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra: "One should always meditate upon the syllable Oṃ..."
One should always meditate upon the syllable *ya*, which is filled with garlands of light, cloud-colored, and of gentle form;
upon the syllable *ta*, which bestows fearlessness, water-colored and possessing perfectly blazing splendor; upon the syllable *dhū*, smoke-colored;
and upon the syllable *ya*, the supreme and most excellent, whose form consists of incomparable qualities.
"One should contemplate the syllable *kā* and meditate upon the supreme syllable *ya*, which has a luster like a ruby"—

this is because the worship of the Śaktis is prescribed for the petals at the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the corners, whereas the worship of the weapons, such as the conch and others, is to be performed on the tips of the petals.
Since the eastern direction is defined conventionally as the front portion,

one should worship Garuḍa, Śaṅkha, and the two treasures known as Padma and Makara respectively on the tips of the petals in the east, south, north, and west; then, one should worship Aruṇa, Āryā, Durgā, and Senā on the tips of the petals starting from the southeast (Āgneya).
Having worshipped [the deity] within that, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other weapons, outside of it in a square, as before;
this is the meaning of the complete *pradyadṛk* verse. The application of this is as stated in another Tantra:
"Having meditated upon oneself as the exceedingly terrifying god like Narasiṃha, one should touch [the disciple] with the mantra."
Having conquered the weapon-mantra (*śastra*), one does not retreat; at that time, one should employ the mantra with the *Narasimha* seed-syllable.

Having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should sprinkle water consecrated by the left hand again and again; even one bitten by a serpent will live. Or, [the rosary] may be held in the right hand.
Having touched the water with the right hand,
one should recite the five-syllable mantra consecrated by the left hand, joined with the Gāruḍa [mantra], for the purpose of neutralizing poison;
while meditating upon Viṣṇu, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, one should [place] the two wings upon the leaf of an Aśoka tree.

In the *Khyāśokasaṃhata* [tantra], one should worship the Blessed One with *aśoka* flowers and offer those flowers before him at the three junctions of the day for seven nights; he becomes manifest and bestows the desired boon of the "best of birds. Those flowers are *aśoka* flowers.

Since there is no authoritative evidence for the employment of *nirmālya* flowers— such as *aśoka* blossoms that have become *nirmālya* even without their own inherent efficacy— in a fire sacrifice (*homa*),
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while observing a milk-vow (*payovrata*) in conjunction with the *Gāṇapatya* [mantra], [specifically] the *Mahāgaṇapati*.

One should behold the God here directly; then, having joined the seed-syllable of Bhāratī, one should mutter that mantra—conjoined with the seed-syllable of Śrī and the six-month-born [syllable]—at that time with the mind fixed upon Him. At the beginning of the eight-syllabled mantra, there should be the *praṇava* (Oṃ), which fulfills all desires, both at the beginning and at the end.
When there is an increase in the knowledge of the practitioner, then [the result] shall come to be. Regarding that, this is the sequence from another tantra;
this is the yantra of the sequence from another tantra: an eight-petaled lotus, a hexagon, and a [lotus] with twelve petals (the number of the sun) at its tips;
outside of that, a tooth-patterned petal, a circle, and an auspicious square enclosure (bhūmipura); [this is] together with the object of accomplishment (sādhya).

The wise one should write the first vowel in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Here, at the base, he should write the root-syllable (*mūlārṇa*), and on the petals, he should write the syllables that bring prosperity (*śrīkara*). In the hexagon (*ṣaṭkoṇa*), he should write the twelve syllables of the mantra;
in the circle, the king of mantras consisting of thirty-two syllables, and the seed-syllable of Nṛhari. [He should write] the six mantras...

Having directly invoked the temple of Viṣṇu, which is endowed with the three strides (Trivikrama), and having worshipped it with mantras, one who carries it firmly bound with threads will, in every way, increase his wealth, acquisitions, and prosperity; he shall obtain whatever is desired—be it Sārūpya, Sārṣṭi, Sālokya, or Sāyujya liberation. Thus [ends] the eighth [chapter].
Having written the syllable *ma* with its anusvāra (*m̐*) in the pericarp of the lotus,

and having written the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa mantra on the filaments, one should write the Śrīkara mantra as it will be described hereafter on the petals, and the six syllables of the Sudarśana mantra— excluding the *praṇava*— in the six corners.

Having written the twelve-syllable mantra on the petals outside that twelve-petaled [lotus], and having written the King of Mantras once upon each of the twenty-two petals, one should encircle it with the seed-mantra of Nṛsiṃha;
thus, six mantras of Viṣṇu have been written—this is the meaning. [Twelve...]

Regarding the statement "the perishable is called *praṇava*": since a reading with the visarga (*praṇaviḥ*) of this form is not found in the root text under discussion, the ancient commentators' indication of the reading as *praṇavi* is indeed inappropriate. [The text continues: "joined with the syllable *o*, it is the heart; the heart is *praṇava*..."

The compound *vaścaśrohṛt* consists of the two terms *vaśca* and *hṛt*. The *praṇava* is the *tāra*, whose essential form is the syllable *oṃ*. The word *namaḥ* belongs to the heart; when joined with the syllable *oṃ*, the extraction of the syllables results in *oṃ namaḥ*, ending in the syllable *oṃ*. Indeed, in the sense of the word "heart," when the word *namaḥ* is used, the vowel *ā* takes the place of the *visarga*.

The intended meaning is "let it be cast down. By saying *namasā śiraḥ* ("the head with *namas*"), it is indicated that the word *namaḥ* is used; furthermore, the word ends in a visarga (*namaḥ*), not in the vowel *o* as in *namaḥ*. Therefore, the correct usage is precisely *namaḥ śirase svāhā*. However, in the case of *varṇanyāsa*, [it is] *o*.
In the *rāṃ te vana* mantra, it should be understood that the letter *m* ending in a visarga has entered [the preceding syllable];

however, even in the *numantra*, it is appropriate to recite it precisely as ending in a visarga. Therefore, the meaning of the root does not fail to be established, and in the limb-mantra (*aṅgamantra*) as well, it is recited exactly as the mantra was originally stated.
If it is argued that this will be the case, we say no, because it would entail a contradiction with other Tantras.
As it is stated in the *Mantra-tantra-prakāśa*: "The last two [syllables] should be spoken in the fifth and sixth positions respectively;
the second is joined with the 'mixed' [syllable]. Therefore, the word *bhagavate* follows, along with *sānanta-vāruṇa-vī*."
"If a living being were to be joined with Śiva, [the mantra] would be twelve syllables ending in 'Bhagīrāma' with 'Pañcama' in the fifth position;

this is for women and Śūdras, while for the twice-born it is with 'Satāra'. This is said with reference to the eight groups beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa*; therein, in the fifth group, [the letter] is *aṃ*.

The sixth consonant from the end [of the fifth group] is *ma*; joined with the thirteenth vowel (*miśra*), it is the *vāruṇa* seed-syllable *va*. Joined with the infinite *a*, it becomes *sa*, which is the *jīva*. This very [syllable *sa*], when joined with the fifth vowel by Śiva—since the letter *u* denotes Śiva—becomes *śa*.

From the word *śiva*, the letter *u* is situated as the fifth vowel; the letter *ya* is the third, and the letter *ra* is the fourth. Through its union with the eleventh vowel (*e*), which is its "portion" (*bhaga*), the form *yekāruddha* arises.
Thus, the nature [of the mantra] is *vāye*. Furthermore, this is because of the inclusion of the blending of the letter *ma*.

One should not think that if the state of being a combination were accepted, there would be no disagreement with other systems; for if the letter *o* were taught immediately after the letter *a* in the word *praṇava*, there would be fourteen vowels.
If you say, "It is not recited thus," then you are forgetful; [the correct reading is] *ha* with the *bindu*.

Since this has already been refuted as being untenable during the explanation of the *jīvita* in the second chapter, [the author] describes the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*) with the words "on the head" (*mūrdhni*) and so forth: the weapons are the discus and lotus on the right from the top downwards, and the mace and conch on the left from the top downwards; this is the eight-syllable [mantra].
Having performed the worship of the *kṛtapīṭha* (prepared seat) and having fashioned the form [of the deity] with the twelve-syllable root mantra,

one should worship the principal tutelary deity there with the sixteen and other offerings (*upacāras*). Then, having prayed for the sake of worshipping the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatās*), one should place the limb-forms (*aṅgamūrtis*) upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus, and [the directional forms] in the cardinal petals of the eight-petaled lotus.

In the intermediate petals [of the eight-petaled lotus], Śānti and the others, beginning with Vāsudeva, are placed; outside the eight-petaled lotus, on the twelve imagined petals, are the twelve forms beginning with Keśava and Nārāyaṇa;
outside of that, in the square, are the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons—this is the meaning. [And] Lakṣmī...

He extracts the *sudeva-mantra* with the words beginning "hṛllekhā" and so forth: *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ lakṣmī-vāsudevāya namaḥ*. This is the fourteen-syllabled mantra. Regarding the portion belonging to Ramā, there are the Vidyā-mudrās of the upper [hands] and so forth: the lotus, the mirror, and the jewel-pitcher; [the portion] belonging to the Lord...

To the right of the mace, the mace, conch, and discus should be meditated upon within the lotuses starting from the top; the number of recitations for the primary mantra is equal to the number of its syllables, which is one hundred and forty thousand (lakṣa). He states the mantra of Dadhivāmana as "Tāro hṛd" and so forth.

*Trāpitāraśca u hṛt* is a *dvandva* compound. Joined with the syllable *o*, it becomes *ohṛt*; this is a *madhyapadalopa-tatpuruṣa* compound, as explained previously. "Oṃ namo viṣṇave surapataye mahābalāya svāhā"—this mantra consists of eighteen syllables. *Induḥ* means the moon. *Sa...* [he...]

The Sage (Ṛṣi) is the First Illuminator (Prathamaprakāśaka), the Seed (Bīja) is *praṇava* (Oṃ), and the Power (Śakti) is *svāhā*. Having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the syllables of the mantra in their respective order, one should place the individual mantra-syllables one by one, numbering eighteen, upon the eighteen locations starting from the head and so forth. Thus it is said.

The eight arms of Gajakarṇa, as well as the knees, shanks, and feet— each existing in pairs— are nevertheless counted as single units by virtue of occupying a single location. Therefore, the respective phonemes obtained for each of those locations should be placed in each of the two corresponding positions, even though they are individually unitary, by means of repetition.

The ten locations—namely the head, forehead, nose, palate, throat, back, heart, abdomen, navel, and private parts—attain unity by their very nature; these are the points of placement (*nyāsa-pada*) due to the inherent sweetness of each individual syllable. [The recitation count is] three hundred thousand for the qualities (*guṇa*) and three hundred thousand ending with the Moon (*candrānta*).

Regarding this, some maintain that the worship of the deities of the *pīṭha* extends only as far as the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*), and not beyond it, due to specific scriptural injunctions. In whatever location the worship of the lunar disc is prescribed,
one should omit that [specific] worship there, while performing the worship of all other *pīṭha* deities as usual.

Having performed the worship according to the prescribed sequence, at its conclusion, the worship of the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*) must be performed; it is not to be omitted under any circumstances. This is indeed appropriate, because by the phrase "situated in the moon" (*candrastha*), the lunar disc is established as the abode of the deity currently under discussion, [and thus] for all the deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭhadevatā*).
However, the traditionalists maintain that meditation and worship directed toward him (the Moon) are likewise essential;
thus, according to the *Śrī-sūkta* and the *Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara*, one should perform the worship of the lunar disc with the eighteen-syllable mantra: *Oṃ namo viṣṇave somāya trailokyāpyāyanāya svāhā*.

The specific distinction is that [the mantra] should end with "svāhā," preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *hṛdaya* (namaḥ). According to the statement in another tantra, "One should worship that with this mantra.
As for the claim made by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* that this distinction is indicated by the phrase "according to rule" (*yathāvidhi*), [that is incorrect].

That which was stated is incorrect; for [the phrase] "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*) cannot be construed with either the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-samarcana*) or the worship of the moon (*candra-samarcana*), because that word is absent [there]. Since it is contained within the same half-verse as "one should offer oblations" (*juhu-yāt*), which itself requires the specific manner of the *homa*, the construction [of "according to the rule"] must be with that very term.
And because it is appropriate, having worshipped the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās) on the filaments as before,
one should worship the four deities beginning with Vāsudeva and the four beginning with Śānti in the cardinal and intermediate petals;
then, having worshipped the eight deities beginning with Dhvaja and ending with Śārṅga at the tips of the eight petals.

Having made a twelve-petalled lotus within that [mandala], one should worship the twelve forms beginning with Keśava at the tips of those petals; then, outside of that, having worshipped Indra and the others along with their weapons in the inner and outer quadrants of the square,
one should worship the elephants of the eight directions beginning with Airāvata and Puṇḍarīka.

Furthermore, having written the aforementioned characteristics upon a cloth (*paṭṭa*) made of fine silk (*paṭṭavastra*)— which is well known by the name *śatapuṣpī* in the Śaurasenī dialect— and having established it as one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) through the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and other ceremonies, one should constantly worship it with fragrant flowers, thereby [attaining] great [merit].

Regarding the attainment of the state, he says "with the sādhya," etc.: having drawn an eight-petalled lotus with its filaments, and having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) along with the *sādhya* in its pericarp,
one should write the eighteen syllables of the mantra to be recited in pairs, beginning with the *praṇava*.
Having written the sixteen vowels beginning with *me* (ma, e, ṇa, ṣo, ḍa, śa, va, rṇā), one should then write two other distinguished syllables (*va-ra*) upon that lotus petal.

Above that, having formed two paths by means of three circles, one should encircle the first path with the syllables of the twelve-syllable mantra and the second path with the *mātṛkā* letters. Thus [says] Rāmacandra.
Having written [the mantra] upon the pericarp of the *drāstupraṇava*, one does not perform the act of writing it again; rather,
when the seventeen syllables beginning with "namaḥ" are written there in pairs upon the eight petals, one syllable remains over— this is the elision at the end (*antāllopa*).

Some say that, according to the maxim *vṛddhirvā* (or increase) and the root text stating "the final leaf shines with twice the number of syllables [of the preceding one]," it should be written on the very last petal; however, Harṣakaula refutes this view,
stating that the remaining [syllables] should be written in pairs upon the eight petals.

Regarding the statement that "the pair of syllables remaining from the sound (nāda) is that by which the final leaf shines," this contradicts the root text; for according to the Vṛtti, only a single syllable remains. However, if it is said that Rāmacandra’s view must be reconciled, then listen as follows: [the syllable] *a* remains.
The two syllables "mi" and "ti" are not qualifiers; rather, they are independent.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: having formed a *dvandva* (copulative) compound of the pair of syllables "śi" and "ṣṭa" and the pair of syllables "pa" and "dayoḥ," [the final leaf] shines forth from those two.
Thus, "śiṣṭa" refers to the single syllable written last, while "yugmārṇa" refers to the pair of syllables previously written.

It follows that the pair of syllables obtained in sequence—meaning the three syllables taken together—is to be written on the final petal; thus, there is no contradiction for anyone. Nor does it follow that what has already been written in the pericarp (karṇikā) must be written again without a specific statement, which would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasajya) of redundancy.

It appears as a composition; he states the Hayagrīva mantra with the words beginning "udgira," etc.: "Oṃ, O you who emerge, O Praṇava, O Udgītha, O Lord of all masters of speech, O you who consist of all gods, O inconceivable one, you awaken everything.
This mantra consists of thirty-three syllables; with the Praṇava, the heart [is formed], and with four...

It has been stated that one should worship the deity after fashioning the form with the seed-syllable (*bīja*), beginning from the head and proceeding limb by limb through each of the four feet, including the limbs other than those mentioned in the *tantra*. In that context, since it might be assumed that the *praṇava* (Oṃ) alone serves as the seed-syllable,
he specifies the particular [seed-syllable] with the words beginning "the seed-syllable," etc., [referring to] the letter *sa* and the sixth vowel (*ū*).

One should place the seed-syllable of misfortune, *hūṃ*, joined with the *pariviṃdu* (the nasal bindu), upon the filaments; specifically, on the filaments of the petals starting from the east, one should worship the four Vedas with the mantras: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Ṛgveda," and so forth.
Then, on the filaments of the intermediate petals, one should worship with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Vedāṅgas," "Oṃ, obeisance to the Smṛtis," and "Oṃ..."

Salutations to the Nyāya-śāstra! Oṃ, salutations to all the Śāstras! With these mantras, having worshipped the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga)—namely Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa—as well as the other limbs previously mentioned, one should worship the deities of the heart and the limbs (hṛdayāṅgadevatāḥ) within the leaf, and then outside of that.

In a square diagram, one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Having cooked ghee with four times the amount of *brāhmī* juice, one should drink that essence—remaining only as ghee—which has been consecrated (*abhimantrita*) with the *Śrī Rāma-mantra* one thousand and eight times or more; thereby, one’s poetic skill (*kavitva*) shall become unrestrained.

One should know that the syllable *rāṃ* is the seed-mantra (*bīja*), *namaḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and the first letter is likewise the salutation (*nati*), according to the observation in the *Śaunaka-kalpa*: "The seat and so forth of the fire [mantra] are established by the word 'infinite' (*anaṃta*) and so on; one should know the seed-mantra, the power, and the salutation in that manner. I worship Rāghava, who gazes upon Sītā standing at his side.

This is the connection [of the verse]. However, some, having emended the reading to "rāghavabhadrautu paśyantīti" (the auspicious Rāghava beholds her), state that the connection is "I worship Sītā who is of such a form. Because the particle *ca* (and) is not seen [in the manuscripts], this emended reading is impossible to conceive; for [the text] mentions Sītā only in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) [of the lotus], while Śrī Rāma is [located] in front of the fire.
Having worshipped Śāṅga and Śara in order on the right and left sides, and having requested permission for worship,

one should worship the limbs in the six corners with "Rāṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ," "Rīṃ Śirase Svāhā," "Rūṃ Śikhāyai Vaṣaṭ," and so forth; then, in the eight petals, one should first worship Hanumān in the eastern petal.

Having worshipped Bharata and Śatrughna in the form of the two flanks on the southern and northern petals, Lakṣmaṇa in the western [petal], and Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Aṅgada, and Jāmbavanta in the Āgneyī and other intermediate directions in order; and having worshipped Sṛṣṭi, Jayanta, and the others in the corners starting from the southeast in sequence—
As before, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and other weapons, in the outer square.
Here too, beginning with the limb-deities (aṅgadevatā), the enclosures (āvaraṇas) are as follows: on the left side of the triangle, [one worships] Śā;
on the right, the filaments (keśara); and likewise: "Oṃ, obeisance to the bow (śārṅga)," and "obeisance to the arrows (śara). Oṃ, obeisance to the arrows.

Thus, having obtained permission for worship (*pūjānujñā*), one should worship the limbs with the rays [of light]. Since in another Tantra it is taught that the request for permission (*ājñāprārthana*) occurs at the end of the worship of Sītā and the others, it is certain that the worship prior to that is a primary worship equal in status to the principal [deity] worship; such is the meaning of the words.

Since it has been stated that even the observer [of the ritual] up to this point performs the "principal worship" (mukhyapūjā), by this the *Harṣakaumudī* text—which claims that the first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) is performed with the [five] limbs (*aṅga*) and the second with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*)—is refuted; furthermore, this contradicts the root text which states that the worship extends from the limbs up to the world-protectors. [This concludes the section on] obtaining permission for the worship.

By the detailed explanation of the limb-worship (*aṅgapūjā*) which satisfies the deities, the Blessed One has indicated that everywhere the protective enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) begin precisely from the limbs. With this intention,
we [have established] therein the primacy— which is synonymous with being the principal— of the previously mentioned deities over the limb-deities.

It should be understood that equality [of status] has been stated; indeed, the *dhāraṇā-yantra* itself, which is about to be described, is referred to as the *pūjā-yantra* in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*: "Then one should draw [the diagram] starting from the hexagon and ending with the earth-element as before; then, one should write the *Tāra* (Om) in its center, and likewise in the six corners."

In due order, one should write the syllables of the root mantra at the joints, as well as the *aṅga* mantras; the *mānmatha* and *māyā* mantras should be written on the filaments of the petals. On the petals, the *mālā-mantra* should be written in sequence as before. Then, the consonants beginning with 'ka' should be encircled by the ten-syllable mantra.

One should draw the seed-syllables of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions; this is another yantra here, and one should worship it along with its limbs (aṅgas) and enclosures (āvaraṇas). Having written this very yantra on gold, silver, or birch-bark, one should begin the worship.
The author of the root-text states that this same yantra is to be used as a dhāraṇā-yantra, beginning with the Tāra [Om].

Having written a hexagon with the [mantra] beginning with "tyādi," one should write the Praṇava (Oṃ) containing the name [of the deity] starting with "sadhya" in its pericarp; then, from the front [corner] onwards, the six syllables of the root mantra should be written in the six corners.
Outside the hexagon, that which is to be performed for the sake of the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus should be carried out.

At the junctions of the six corners within the line of the *kavarga* [enclosure], one should place the six limb-mantras beginning with "Oṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ. Then, in sequence, one should place the *māyāvīja* and the *kāmavīja* on the two cheeks of the hexagon. Outside of that, on the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus situated there, one should place the vowels two by two.

Having written the five remaining syllables of the previously mentioned mālā-mantra within the middle of the eighth petal— which corresponds in number to the faces of Kārttikeya, who is renowned as having six faces, though here measured by seven excellent faces in the midst of the petals— one should place it outside of that.

Having surrounded the first enclosure with the ten-syllable mantra to be described hereafter and with the consonants beginning with the second enclosure, one should write the *nṛsiṃha-bīja* in the directions within the *bhūpura* and likewise the *vārāha-bīja* in those directions;
thus he extracts the *mālā-mantra* starting with "namo bhagavate," etc.

Beginning with *mādi* and *praṇava*, [the mantra is]: *oṃ namo bhagavate raghunandanāya nāmarakṣodyūviṃśandāya madhuraprasannavadanāya amitatejase balāya rāmāya viṣṇave namaḥ*. This *mālā-mantra* consists of forty-seven syllables. Thus it is said.
In this context, when the letter *māyā* (the vowel *ī*) is joined with the letter *a* [to form *ai*], the loss of one syllable (*ekākṣara-truṭi*) is not to be observed;

that is to say, the sandhi must be performed. To indicate precisely this, in the eighth [chapter], instead of saying "five letters" (*pañca-varṇān*), it says "eight letters" (*aṣṭau varṇān*), while in the case of sandhi, there are indeed only four.

There would remain nine syllables, not five; thus, there would be no contradiction [with the rule]. "Haṃ Jānakīvallabha Svāhā"—this is the ten-syllable mantra (*daśārṇa-mantra*). As for what was stated by the author of the *Harṣakaumudī*, that "two or three repetitions of this should be performed as a protective enclosure" (*veṣṭana*), that is not correct, because once it has been performed, the requirement of the scripture is fulfilled.

Since no specific statement capable of subverting this established principle is perceived, the recitation of the Lakṣmaṇa-mantra is mandatory here. For it is said: "Those who perform sacrifices without having recited the Lakṣmaṇa-mantra do not attain the fruit of that recitation, even if they are highly skilled."
The extraction of that [mantra] is as follows, according to the *Tantrāntara*: having first extracted the syllable *ripha* (the letter *ra*), joined with a *bindu*, it belongs to Lakṣmaṇa;

this mantra of Lakṣmaṇa begins with *oṃ* and is concluded with *namaḥ*. Bharata’s [mantra] shall be exactly the same, and this same procedure applies to Śatrughna as well. This procedure includes the *bindu* in the name.

Regarding the method of forming a mantra by prefixing and suffixing "oṃ" to a name when it begins with two syllables, the *Sītā-mantra* has been stated in the *Mūla*; the *Hanuman-mantra* is stated in another *Tantra*; or else, a *nāma-mantra* refined according to the previous method should be employed. He extracts the *Varāha-mantra* [beginning] with "tāraṃ" etc.

Oṃ, *Namaḥ bhagavate varāharūpāya bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ pāhi māṃ bhūpatitvaṃ me dehi dāpaya svāhā*. This mantra consists of thirty-three syllables; *huṃ* is its seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is its power (*śakti*), and *analapriyā* (the beloved of fire) is its consort. Now, describe its visualization (*dhyāna*).

Thus, beginning with "āpādetyādi": the *rathacaraṇa* is the wheel; *dara* is the conch; *kṣiti* is the earth, and its *caraṇa* is its foundation. He whose fangs shine there—that is to say, he whose fangs are fixed in the ground—is the one referred to. Among the two [weapons] at the top right and left, the first is the weapon; among those situated below them, it is the other.

Thus, regarding the meditation on the weapons (*āyudha-dhyāna*), since the worship of the heart and other limbs has been taught everywhere for the [deities] starting with Āgneyī, he teaches the procedure for worship in the directions as an exception (*apavāda*) to that, beginning with the words "in the east," etc.
Prior to the worship of the weapon-limbs, which was described in four ways, there is a fourfold [procedure] in the four directions by way of that exception.
He describes that worship in six ways—as the corners, above, and below—by means of the single-footed verse beginning with "Astram.
This worship is performed specifically on the filaments (*kesara*); it refers merely to the directions, not to a location below them.
Outside of those filaments, or outside of the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs], it extends as far as the centers of the petals.

In the outer enclosure (*bhūpura*) as before, one should perform the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and others. Furthermore, another mantra is given: for this mantra, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī meter is the *chaṃdas*, and Śrī Varāha is the deity.
With the syllables "caṃdra-caṃdra-veda-bāhu" (144), and by means of the complete mantra, [one should perform] the five-fold [application] in sequence.

The syllable *gakalpanā* is the *praṇava*; the word *kavaca* is said to end with *oṃ*, and the mantra joined with the letter *ga* is proclaimed as the "Vārāha-mantra," whose application is declared to be like that of the Sun.
Thus, he describes the results of meditation, fire-offerings (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and so forth, in their proper order. *Dhyā*... [text ends]

With the words beginning with "nāditya," he describes the application of *śilā* for the purpose of pacifying afflictions caused by enemies such as lions; and with the words beginning with "ravau," [he notes that] "siṃhe" is also indicative of Aries and Sagittarius. As stated by Nārāyaṇa: "On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, when the sun has entered Leo, Aries, or Sagittarius, one should dig [for the stone]."

Because it has been seen [in tradition], and since the teacher Padmapāda stated that "a stone weighing ten palas, such as one made of crystal or bilva leaves," should be taken, one should face north during the Abhijit muhūrta and, while reciting the aforementioned Varāha-mantra together with the seed-syllable *Bhūḥ*, [perform the rite].
The instruction "one should dig up the forest" refers to a ritual application for the purpose of obtaining land, as stated in the passage beginning with "at the rising of the sun," and so forth.

This application is intended for a specific field one wishes to acquire from a particular plot; however, this ritual is not applicable where there is merely a general desire for land, nor where the desire is directed toward various unspecified plots. [This concludes] the mantra under discussion.

Having recited or not yet finished reciting the mantra, he describes the ritual application for obtaining that very field which is the cause of the dispute, beginning with the words "In the morning" (*prātaḥ*).

He describes a ritual application that brings about all prosperity, beginning with the words "The royal tree" (*rājavṛkṣa*). For it is observed that a single ritual application yields various kinds of fruits.
Based on the observation of such statements as "the path" (*lamityādi*), it should not be understood that two or more fruits can be aimed for simultaneously;

rather, the intended meaning here is that every single desire is accomplished through its own respective performance (*prayoga*). This applies when the specific substances prescribed for each particular desire are unavailable.

Some say that this conceptual construction (vikalpa) is accompanied by the Veda; thus, for that which is specifically designated, there is primacy, while that which is stated by way of a general category is considered a secondary alternative (anukalpa). Some others, however, state that the yantra consists of three thousand according to the previous number—that is, the number previously mentioned.
Having first drawn a hexagon with the words "madhyevījam" and so forth, one should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) in its pericarp,

and within that, the Varāha-bīja which is about to be described; then, having written the *praṇava*— which is the beginning of the seven-syllabled Sudarśana mantra— in the middle of each of the six corners, [one should proceed] with that...

Having written the remaining six syllables, one should write the six limb-mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) of the Sudarśana mantra— since it is present as the five-limbed version of the mantra currently under discussion— within the junctions of the hexagon; then, on the filaments of the four-petaled lotus drawn outside that, one should write them in pairs.
Having written the eight syllables of the *rāyana* mantra eight times each within the middle of the petals,
and having written one specific syllable on the fourth petal,
one should write the vowels two by two in the filaments of the eight petals written outside of that.

Having written four mantra-syllables on each of the petals, one by one, and having written the remaining single syllable on the eighth petal, one should fashion a sixteen-petaled lotus outside of that; then,
having written the thirty-two letters from *ka* to *sa* in pairs upon its filaments, one should likewise write them upon the petals.

Having written the syllables of the Yugmaśoma mantra, one should write the three remaining syllables of the Mātṛkā— namely *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*— along with the syllable *hā* among the mantra-syllables; having written this on the sixteenth petal at the very end, one should place the Praṇava (*oṃ*), the Earth-syllable (*bhūḥ*), and the Vārāha-bīja (*hlīṃ*) one by one in the center of each.

One should encircle [the diagram] in the manner beginning with "Oṃ dattaṃ na rakṣa mo rakṣa bha deva gada ttaṃ va rakṣate," joined with the letters of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (sādhya), and outside of that, in the surrounding path (vīthī), one should place the syllables of the mantra interspersed (vidarbhitam) with the letters of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended. O Deva! Protect this which has been given; protect it, O Bhadra! Protect this which has been given by the gods! O Lord! Protect it!
Having written [the mantra] in this manner, one should write the four seed-syllables of the earth (*bhū-bīja*) in the four corners of the outer *bhūpura* (earth-fortress).

Having written the complete name of the practitioner (*sādhya-nāma*) within each of those seed-syllables, and having drawn a trident in each of the eight directions outside the *bhūpura*, one should [place] on the southern side of the central line therein...
The collective meaning is that one should write the Vārāha-bīja on the left side of the Bhu-bīja.

He extracts the Vārāha-bīja with the words beginning "Sārghīśa" and so forth. Sārghīśa is the sixth vowel (ū). Although this mantra is self-sufficient, its seer (ṛṣi) and other details are stated in another tantra: Hayagrīva is declared to be the seer; the meter is... [the rest of the sentence continues].

The deity is Datriṣṭup, the form is Varāha, and one should fashion the six limbs with the long-conjoined *svana*. The visualization, worship, ritual application, and so forth, are like those of the Vārāha-mantra of Yama. In another Tantra, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of "bhūri" is sometimes given as *glauṃ*, while the seed-syllable of the song is "nābhir vāmaśravāḥ."

The Siddha says: "Having placed the five-syllable [seed-mantra] at the center of the pentagon, [one places] the Viṇdu, the Moon, and so forth, along with the seed-syllable of the Boar (Kroḍa)," according to this observation;

by the words "one should restrict the liquid substance for drawing the yantra" and so on, he restricts the writing instrument; and by the word "made of gold," it is for the purpose of drawing the yantra according to the distinction of one's desires.

By the passage beginning with "He restrains the leaf-protectors upon the golden plate," the specific time [for practice], differentiated according to various particular desires, should be inferred by oneself. When the Vārā [the goddess] has been well-accomplished—having been made intent on achieving the practitioner's goal through the completion of the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*), subsequent recitations (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), and fire-oblations (*homa*)— [The text continues: ...he should perform the rite of piercing (*vedha*). First, having worshipped the *yantra* with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a lotus leaf, he should place that leaf upon the aforementioned vessel. Having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should then recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a copper plate, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a golden plate, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a silver plate, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a lead plate, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a stone slab, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a wooden board, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a cloth, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a wall, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a mirror, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a conch shell, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a skull, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a human bone, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of earth, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of cloth, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of wood, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of metal, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of stone, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of clay, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of paper, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of birch bark, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed the *yantra* within a jar, he should perform the piercing. This is the procedure for the piercing of the *yantra*. Alternatively, having drawn the *yantra* of the desired deity upon a piece of palm leaf, he should place it within a vessel filled with water. Then, having worshipped it with perfumes and the like, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having placed

By the words "Dāvi" and so forth, it is stated that [the rite] is performed at a movable zodiacal sign (*asthira-rāśi-lagna*). Regarding the phrase "with its limbs" (*sāṅgam*): having placed the yantra on the ground and filled it with sand, one should again invoke Varāha together with his limbs (*sāṅga*) therein;

then, meditating upon one's own self as being of the very form of one's chosen deity, Varāha, one should worship him. As for the phrase "the limbs in the directions": [one should place] the ancillary parts in the cardinal directions.

For the purpose of remembering the specific details, it has been said: "The practitioner, having assumed the form of a boar, should bury the yantra at the site of the target; having driven a stake into a fixed zodiac sign, he should duly cast the limbs [of the victim] in the various directions. Furthermore, this region is exceedingly sacred because it is presided over by the yantra.

The meaning is that it cannot be seen even by the lowly through practices such as *uccāṭana* (driving away) or by means of untimely death (*apamṛtyu*) and the like. Now, in connection with Varāha, the *Svapna-Vārāhī-mantra*, which bestows great fruit and was mentioned previously, is described here: "Vāgbhava, Māyā, ending with Prānta—this is the Sū..."

The assembly of *ryya* and *tha*, the long *a* (*ā*) joined with the excellent color (*va*), that which is called space (*vyoma*) joined with sight (*dṛś*), the auspicious *ka* (*śrīkaṃ*), *ṭha*, the rule of creation (*sṛṣṭividhi*), the one enriched by the universe (*viśvāḍhya*), joined with fortune (*bhaga*), fire (*agni*), the syllables of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa, Keśava, and Gopa attached to the side of the Ram; [the letter] standing on *ṭīśa* is declared as the fourfold strength from Kūrma.

"Rddhāsyāt vahnerjāyā"—this is the mantra of Svapnavārāhī, which produces immediate conviction and possesses the color of an elephant; it is the bestower of the grace of Śiva and others. Its meaning is as follows: Sarasvatī is the source of speech (Vāgbhava); Bhairavī is Meṣa (the letter *na*); Sūrya is the letter *ma*; and with "Sadya," [it is joined] with the thirteenth vowel (*e*).

The syllable *Śrīkaṇṭha* (Ś) joined with the first vowel (*a*) is *śa*; the fourth letter from *ka*, which is *gha*, is conjoined with the thirteenth vowel (*au*), whose synonyms are *Viśva* and *Sadyojāta*. Furthermore, the fire (*ra*) is connected with the eleventh vowel (*e*), whose synonyms are *Bhaga* and *Jhiṃṭīśa*. Thus, *ke*.

The first syllable is *śavaḥ*, the side [syllable] is *pa*, from the tortoise [the syllable] *ca*, the seventh is *a* from the immovable [mountain], and the remainder is *ṭha*; thus the eighteen-syllable mantra is extracted as: *aiṃ hrīṃ namo vārāhi aghore svapne ṭhaṭha ṭhaṭha svāhā*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Īśvara.

The meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is declared to be Śrī Svapnavārāhī. The seed-syllable (bīja) is proclaimed as Vāgbhava (Aiṃ), and Māyā (Hrīṃ) is the power (śakti). The kīlaka consists of the syllables "ṭha ṭha ṭha svāhā. The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are formed by the letters associated with the mantra, according to the rule: two, five, three, two, four, and two [syllables].

One should place the six syllables in sequence upon the hips, neck, cheeks, ears, eyes, and head; likewise, one should assign the two limbs according to the stated rotation. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the mantra, he, being composed, should meditate upon the Goddess.
