The meditation is as follows: [She who is] dark like a mountain of blue collyrium...

One should meditate upon the auspicious Mahādevī Vārāhī, who is adorned with jewels, mounted upon a horse, holding a noose and a goad, capable of assuming any form at will, bearing a sword and a shield, four-armed, possessing sharp fangs,
with the earth resting upon the tips of her tusks, and intent on the destruction of the wicked for the sake of practitioners.

"Thus, one should worship the eternal Goddess, the bestower of boons, with uninterrupted devotion. Now, O Nārada, listen to the method for accomplishing this mantra, and how its practice should be performed:
having fasted and become pure, one should worship [the deity] on any single day of the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇa-tithi).

One should offer the *naivedya* (food offering) to the Goddess of the Gods of gods. Although the *naivedya* is already included within the general category of worship (*pūjā*), its specific mention here is for the purpose of indicating its necessity even when other ritual services (*upacāras*) are unavailable; thus, the word "and" (*ca*) implies that the offering may consist of *naivedya* alone.

One should not associate with anyone else; even when offering any other service, one must indeed strive [to do so]. Then, having become composed in mind, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) one thousand and eight times. Once that is accomplished, one should achieve both the past and the future.

And he causes all that which is yet to come to be granted to the one to be accomplished (sādhya), having spoken of his desire in dreams. Now, the ritual application (prayoga): having written the king of mantras on a birch-bark leaf or a betel-leaf, [one should write] "O you who are intoxicated with passion, subdue such-and-such a couple. Amuka...

Having written "syai" and placed it upon one's own heart, and having installed and worshipped it according to the rules with flowers and other offerings, one should meditate upon that leaf as being composed of the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and draw it out from the heart. Having stepped upon it with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Thus, at the three junctions of the day (trisandhya), one should perform [this].

If one performs this seven times with due respect according to the prescribed rite, the entire multitude of people—whether women or men—will certainly come under one's control, even at the cost of their lives or wealth; indeed, they will remain subservient to the practitioners for as long as they live. This is the meaning [of the verse] regarding the birch-bark [manuscript].
Alternatively, having written the previously mentioned mantra on a betel leaf using the juice of dhatura seeds,

and having written the name of the person to be accomplished at its end— such as "Devadatta, subjugate Yajñadatta, subjugate!"— and having placed that leaf upon one's own heart, one should perform the installation of the person to be accomplished.

Having meditated upon that [mantra] as being composed of that [deity], having worshipped it with flowers and other offerings, and having drawn it forth from the heart, one should step upon its petal with one's own left foot and recite this mantra one hundred and eight times. By reciting in this manner three times a day for seven days until the end of the seventh cycle, she will certainly be brought under control.
"One becomes masterful through meditation"—this is another application. One should step upon the form of Mahābhasma with the left foot and recite the mantra while saying:

"Grant [the desired object] to so-and-so," preceded by the words "three jewels" (*triratna*) and "village. Having enchanted the king, one should bring him under control and utter this: [one should fashion] the form of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). Mahā...
Having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in the form of a three-headed elephant, and having stepped upon that form with the left foot,
one should recite this mantra one thousand and eight times,
inserting the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in place of the word "so-and-so" within the twenty-seven-syllable *Kṛṣṇa-krama* mantra.

The meaning is that one should not request [anything else]. There is another application: having fashioned the form of Mahābhasma, one should mutter [the mantra] with the left finger upon the heart one thousand and eight times; then, in a dream, he will grant the desired object, saying, "I shall give this to so-and-so," or "I shall fulfill all his desires. This is the meaning, as before.

Having fashioned a great form of the one to be subdued (sādhya) which cannot be overcome by the speech of gods, having established the vital breaths (prāṇa) of that sādhya therein, and having placed the five fingers of the left hand upon the heart of that form,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, and then [perform] the twenty-seven [rites] as previously described.

One should pray with the *kṣara-mantra*. Thus entreated, the Blessed Lady— having terrified the practitioner in a dream by means of words such as, "If you do not fulfill the desire of me, your worshipper, so-and-so, misfortune shall befall you"— frightens the practitioner.

Since she accomplishes whatever one desires, the mantra for praying to the Goddess after the recitation (*japa*) is as follows: *Namaḥ te svapnavārāhi svapne kathaya me ripoḥ | Sadaiva bhayaṃ ca janaya bhakte mayi kṛpāṃ kuru || Prasādya pīḍaya kṣipraṃ yo yathā...* "Salutations to you, O Svapnavārāhī! In my dream, reveal my enemy; always produce fear in him, and show compassion toward me, your devotee. Having propitiated [him], quickly afflict him so that..."
"O Sādhya, bind me quickly with your noose; draw my mind toward you with your hook. Ward off my suffering, so difficult to cross, with your shield. Cut down death with your sword.
Speak of what is auspicious and inauspicious. Having come here yourself, O Sādhya, bow down and carry out my command."
In this [practice], there is neither the hardship of *puraścaraṇa* nor any other difficulty;

rather, by the very effort described here, the Vidyā grants swift accomplishment—this is the summary. However, in the *Mahodadhi*, cited from another Tantra, certain specific details are mentioned regarding the *Svapnavārāhī* for bringing people under control.

The mantra consists of fifteen syllables: the seed-syllable of the Vedas (the *praṇava*), *māyā* (the letter *ī*), the heart (the letter *hrīṃ*), the two long vowels (*e* and *ai*), the sky (the letter *ha*), the one resembling the moon (the letter *sa*), the pair of *sadyojāta* (the letters *sa* and *ya*), the dreamer (the letter *sva*), the two creators (the letters *ṭha* and *ṭha*), and the beloved of Agni (the letter *ra*) at the end.
The seed-syllable of the Vedas is the *praṇava*; the "long" [vowels] are each joined with the second vowel (*ā*).

*Kaṃ khaṃ* is the letter *ha*; *medyāka* is the fourth letter of the *ka*-group (*ga*). *Resvapnam* consists of three letters ending in an *anusvāra*, referring to their own forms. *Sargiṇau* means "possessing visargas"; the dual suffix *-au* (from *ṭāu*) indicates that there are two of them. The remainder is clear in meaning. Thus, it is: *oṃ hrīṃ namo vārāhi svapnaṃ dyore*.

The fifteen-syllable mantra is *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*. It is proclaimed that Īśvara is the deity, Jagatī is the meter, Svapnavārāhī is the goddess, and the Munis (the Seven Sages) are the seers. *Tāra* (*oṃ*) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Hṛllekhā* is the power (*śakti*), and *ṭhaḥ* is considered the pin (*kīlaka*). The limbs (*aṅga*) of the mantra consist of two, five, two, two, ten, two, and two syllables respectively, assigned to the feet, the genitals, and so forth.

Having placed the letters of the mantra upon the hips, throat, cheeks, eyes, ears, nose, and head, one should meditate on the Supreme Deity. The mantra-syllables correspond in number to the locations, such that the *liṅga*, throat, and head each have one location, while the others have two or two locations; thus one should contemplate her, who possesses a dark, lustrous splendor.
One should meditate upon Vārāhī, who has enchanting breasts, is illuminated by three eyes, has the face of a boar, and is crowned with the moon;
she is adorned with the tip of her tusk, holds a sword, a shield, a noose, and a goad in her lotus-like hands,
is mounted upon a boar, and is beautifully adorned.
One should mutter [the mantra] ten times that many [repetitions], offer oblations with auspicious blue lotuses and sesame seeds, and worship her upon the previously mentioned pedestal.

On the aforementioned pedestal, which is the Vaiṣṇava pedestal, one should likewise worship [the energies]: "Salutation to Vimalā," "Salutation to Utkarṣiṇī," "Salutation to Jñānā," "Salutation to Yogā," and "Salutation to Prhī."

Having worshipped [the directions] starting from the east with "Oṃ namaḥ īśānāya" and in the center with "Oṃ namaḥ anugrahāya," one should conceive of the pedestal as a seat by means of the twenty-eight-syllable mantra: "Oṃ namo bhagavate viṣṇave sarvabhūtātmasaṃyogayogapadmapīṭhātmane namaḥ."
One should offer [oblations] to You; likewise, having worshipped this [deity] in the triangle, one should worship the deities of the limbs in the six corners.

One should worship the sixteen Śaktis in the sixteen spokes, which will be described as follows: Uccāṭanī, her Mistress; Vaśī, Śoṣaṇī, and Śoṣaṇīśvarī; Māraṇī, Māraṇīśī, Bhīṣaṇī, and Bhīṣaṇīśvarī; Trā...
Sanīśā, Sanīśī, Cakrapanī, Īśvarī, Ājñāvivarttanī, and thereafter Ājñāvivarttanīśvarī,
Vastujāteśvarī, and Sarvasampādanīśvarī— these should be worshipped with their names ending in the dative case,
preceded by *Oṃ* and followed by *Namaḥ*. One should worship them for the sake of clarity upon an eight-petaled lotus.

The meaning is that the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, joined with their respective Bhairavas, are to be worshipped on the petals, while Asitāṅgabhairava and the others are to be worshipped at the tips of the petals. One should worship the ten world-protectors (lokapālas) joined with their consorts on the two sets of ten petals;
having performed the general procedure for the protective circle (bhūpura) as obtained from the common scriptures, one should perform it specifically here.
This is the procedure for the *śada* [sixfold] rite; having thus perfected the mantra, the practitioner should employ it for rites of desire (*kāmyakarman*).

He should offer libations with coconut water or even with water from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*). For the sake of attaining all desires and goals, he should honor groups of young women. Having undertaken his vow on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on a Tuesday, or on a Thursday, he should perform the rite.

Having brought earth from a crossroads, from the two banks of a river, and from the house of a potter, and having combined it with the juice of *dhattūra*, bring it; then, feed the beautiful *utpalī* plant, which is provided with the *sādhyā* and *sthāpanā* mantras.
Thereafter, O Lord, one should draw the *yantra* of the foremost of the deceased using the blood of a crow and a goat, mixed with charcoal.
Draw a six-cornered *yoni* within a *bhūpura* (enclosure of earth), and having written the mantra inside it, one should encircle it with this mantra:
"Uccāṭaya" twice, then "Śoṣaya" twice; then "Māraya" twice, then "Vāraya" and "Bhīṣaya" at the end; then "Nāśaya" twice, and finally "Śiraḥkampaya" twice.
"Who shall remain obedient to my command? O you who encompass all directions, make [him] subject to me; let the collection of things be proclaimed, and then bring about the Yuga.
Perform everything, O Yuga, svāhā! This is the seven-syllable mantra of the Sage. A yantra encircled by this, having been consecrated with the Goddess, should be placed in the heart of the effigy.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the path described for the conqueror and the liberated, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times at night while remaining in solitude. Furthermore, one should worship her according to the prescribed rites. By doing so, kings, queens, royal favorites, lions, elephants, deer, and even cruel beings will come under one's control.

"Having firmly resolved upon his own task, he should sleep in a secluded place where he is not observed; then the Goddess, as she has been meditated upon, speaks to the minister in a dream. Regarding this mantra, there are three applications:
libation (*tarpaṇa*) with coconut water, or in its absence, with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as the Gaṅgā, performed one hundred thousand, ten thousand, or ten times.

Since it is prescribed that this should be performed everywhere for the sake of one's desired object without numerical limitation, there is a single application of the rite: the practitioner, while observing the vow of fasting on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
should fetch earth from a crossroads, from the abode of Kailāsa, and from the two banks of a river.

Having fashioned the form of the Goddess by combining it with the resin of *turu*, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of life-force) for the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) therein, and having placed the *yantra* to be described hereafter upon her heart, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* of the Goddess there, and then, having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites according to the previously mentioned method, [one should place] the deity there in the doll (*puttalī*).

Having worshipped [the deity] Vīṃ and standing before him, if one recites this mantra eight thousand and eight times in a secluded place at night, kings and others will certainly become submissive; this is the second application.
As for the construction of the yantra: on a cloth from a corpse, using the three—[the blood of] a crow, a dog, and a ram—...

Having first drawn a triangle joined to a house of thought (cintāgāra), having written the root mantra within it, having made a hexagon outside of that and a *bhūpura* (fortress) outside of that, and having made a circle outside of that,
[one should recite]: "Uccāṭaya uccāṭaya (uproot, uproot), śoṣaya māraya māraya (dry up, kill, kill), ārye bhīṣaya (O Noble One, terrify)."

One should write the mantra consisting of seventy-seven syllables: *bhīṣaya nāśaya nāśaya kampaya kampaya mā kṣāvartinam kuru kuru svāhā*. While observing the vow of fasting and keeping one's desired objective in mind, one should [recite] this mantra one thousand and eight times.
The third application is that she relates her dream to him for the sake of a future event. Now he describes her uncommon *yantra*:
"Now I shall proclaim this great *yantra* of hers, which bestows success upon men; having drawn a triangle, a hexagon, and a sixteen-spoked [wheel]..."

One should draw two beautiful covers with two sets of ten spokes, a fifteen-sided figure, and two outer enclosures (*bhūpura*). Then, one should write the *Vāgbhava* seed-syllable situated within the *Kāmavīja* in the triangle. Furthermore, in the six corners, one should write the *Vāgvīja*, the noose (*pāśa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), *Śrī*, the long vowel, and the armor (*kavaca*). Afterwards, one should write the powers (*śakti*) upon the sixteen petals.

On the eight petals of the previously mentioned sixteen-fold [maṇḍala] beginning with Ābrāhmī, one should place [the syllables] conjoined with the Bhairavas; on the ten spokes, one should place the lords of the directions (dikpati) in sequence, each preceded by its own seed-syllable (*bīja*). Now, the collection of seed-syllables is being described:
*māṃsa* (flesh), *rakta* (blood), *viṣa* (poison), *meru*, *jala* (water), *vāyu* (wind), *bhṛgu*, and *viyat* (ether)—these are joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
One should correctly draw the noose (pāśa), Māyā, Antikā, and Vajra and the others upon the second row of squares;

on the row of lunar days (tithi), one should encircle the root-syllables with the syllables of the Gāyatrī. One should draw the two wind and fire [elements] on the three [squares] of the two earth-palaces. Having drawn this yantra on birch bark or similar material, one should consecrate the yantra.

One should give this, when accomplished and worn on the arm or other limbs, fame, wealth, and happiness to men; what more need be said here? It bestows whatever is desired. This is the meaning: the Kāma-bīja is in the pericarp of the triangle, the Vāgbhava within that, and the name of the person for whom the rite is performed (the sādhya) at its tip; [the mantra is placed] in the hexagon.

One should inscribe the seed-syllables of Śukra, Ātman, Bhava, Pāśa, Māyā, Aṅkuśa, Lakṣmī, Bīja, and Kūrca upon the sixteen petals. One should inscribe the sixteen Śakti-mantras, beginning with "Oṃ uccāṭanyai namaḥ," and so forth.
In the center of the eight-petaled [lotus], one should inscribe "Āṃ brāhmyai namaḥ" and so forth on the petals.
One should write "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya Asitāṅgāya" and so forth on the ten petals;

on the outer ten petals, "Vaṃ Namo Vajrāya" and so forth; and on the fifteen petals outside of that, having written the syllables of the root mantra, one should encircle it with the Gāyatrī of the Vedas.

One should perform the writing by drawing the two *bhūpura*s (enclosures) connected to one another in a double row, or else by writing the *vāyuvīja* and *agnivīja* four times around the eight corners; this yantra, following the general procedure, [is perfected] through the remaining acts of writing, recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and the pouring of offerings.

"It shall be accomplished, bestowing all fruits. Because it shares the commonality of being a means for attaining the acquisition of the earth (*bhūmilābha*), he states the mantra of the Earth (*bhūmimantra*) which has been presented, beginning with "the Heart" (*hṛdaya*). "Heart, *namaḥ*": this Heart-mantra follows after the letter *a* in the previously mentioned mantras; thus, [it is] *oṃ*.
The mantra consisting of nineteen syllables, beginning with *oṃ namo bhagavatyai dharaṇyai uraṇīdhare svāhā*,
has *praṇava* as its seed (*bīja*) and *svāhā* as its power (*śakti*).
With mantras such as *pṛthivyai namaḥ* and *vahnyai namaḥ*, one should worship the four elements— earth and the others— in the four petals of the directions.

In the petals of the directions, one should worship the four *kalās*—Nivṛtti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Śānti—belonging to Earth and the other elements in sequence, according to the formula: "Oṃ Nivṛttyai Namaḥ," "Oṃ Vidyāyai Namaḥ," and so forth; then, as before, one should worship Indra and the other deities. Some, however, [use] *laṃ raṃ vaṃ yaṃ*.

Thus, Rāmacandra teaches the worship of those respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the *kalās* such as Jvalinī and the rest; however, Nivṛtti and the others are also to be worshipped. This is true, but because the author of the root-text mentions them specifically for that particular time, it is understood that [the worship] pertains to the earth.

They say that the application [of mantras] such as "lāyainamaḥ" and "vahnikalāyainamaḥ" is what is accepted in that regard; however, this must be said here: the very purpose of previously stating the names of those respective *kalās* was precisely for their inclusion within the mantras for worship and so forth.

Thus, if one were not intent upon the mantras of those names as they truly are, the labor of designating them by those names would be rendered useless by the author of this root-text. However, it should be understood that their designation as such is merely for the sake of verbal convention and so forth. At the beginning of the day, during the morning time, [one should take] that from the field of the *sādhya*.

Having brought earth from the field intended for acquisition, having placed it in water, and having purified it by removing pebbles and other debris, one should prepare *caru* in a vessel smeared with that [earth] which has been consecrated by the three steps; then, by offering that *caru* mixed with milk and ghee in the fire and so forth, the desired attainment is reached—so says someone. [This is done] in the water.

Having thrown that clay right there into the water and offered it into the fire, some say that one should perform the *caru* oblation together with milk and other substances once [the deity] has been purified; at this juncture, having placed the *caru* in some vessel into which water has been offered, [one should offer] that which is joined with such clay.
Some say that by offering oblations of ghee together with milk and *varu* (barley) which accomplishes speech,
one attains the desired success; his [teacher] was Udyotamati, whose mother was the virtuous Satī, and whose father was named Māpati.

Born in the lineage of Manidhinipaṃtha, whose birthplace was Kūrmācala; who performed great heroic deeds for Sūpāsya and attained the station of Acyuta; and who became a resident of Vārāṇasī—that Śarēndupaṭala reached his fulfillment there.

In the *Jñānapūrtti*, the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*: Now, desiring to set forth the mantras of the venerable Nṛsiṃha, [the author] first extracts the *śloka-mantra*—beginning with "ugram" and so forth—since it is found in the direct Veda and is the king of mantras. Here, in the root text, all the words are [divided] into two...

This King of Mantras, consisting of the verse: "I bow to the fierce, the heroic, the Great Viṣṇu, the blazing one whose face is turned in every direction, the Man-Lion, the terrifying, the auspicious, the death of death," is Vedic; therefore, it begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ). Other mantras [also] begin with the *praṇava*.

Mantras should be recited only when joined at the beginning and end with a *rūpa-setu* (form-bridge). Just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant, so too a mantra without a dam leaks away in an instant for those who perform sacrifices. Therefore, having first established the bridge, one should commence the rite of recitation; [otherwise] the mantras [are lost].

The Praṇava is the bridge; it is remembered as the bridge, the true bridge. That which is the fourteenth vowel, known as the letter *Śeṣa* (*Oṃ*), together with the Anusvāra and the Moon, is called the bridge for the Śūdras.
*Haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Īṃ* is the power (*śakti*); one should know this Māyā to be the seed-syllable of space.
According to the instruction in the *Nṛsiṃhatāpinī*, "māyā" refers to the fourth vowel (the letter *ī*);
"first" refers to the first [vowel] (*a*) which is present before it; "four" refers to the second [vowel] (*i*) which is present before it;
and "six" refers to the sixth [vowel] (*u*) which is present before it. Thus, by means of these four instruments...
In the *Panīya*, however, it is stated that this [mantra] has five limbs (*pañcāṅga*). Its five limbs are as follows:

the four feet are four limbs, and everything together with the *praṇava* constitutes the fifth. Now, one might object: "Is it not more appropriate to perform the practice according to the meaning of a scripture that is directly perceived, rather than performing the practice according to the meaning of a scripture that must be inferred?"

The Smṛti rule stating "the Udumbara post is to be entirely wrapped" cannot be assumed to have a Vedic source because it contradicts the direct Śruti text, "one should chant the Udgītha while touching the Udumbara post.
As long as the Śruti is directly perceived, its authority— characterized by the fact that its subject matter must be put into practice— is superior.

If it is argued: "Since the Mīmāṃsakas have accepted [the Veda as] authoritative, how then can the performance of the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) be justified? [The reply is: Let the position of the six ancillaries not be performed; what loss is there in that? If it is argued: "In that case, the lack of authority—defined as the state of not having the capacity for the meaning to be performed—is incurred regarding the root text."
Nor can it be interpreted as referring to the five-fold division even for the root [mantra],

because the meaning is "with four syllables" (*varṇaiścaturbhiḥ*); since the number two is understood from *vara* and the number five from *viṣama*, the number fifty-two is obtained, and by dividing that by twelve, the result is four.

Because it cannot be otherwise than a number, the meaning of the two words "by four castes" (caturbhir varṇaiḥ) results in the sense of "by eight"; and by the accusative case in the word "syllables" (akṣaraiḥ), the object of qualification is established everywhere as ending in "dā," namely, "the meditator on the womb situated in the dāra-bhāgya-śūla."
Because the numbers four, eight, eleven, and so forth are indicated by the words *caturbhiḥ*, *aṣṭabhiḥ*, *ekādaśabhiḥ*,

and others; however, since in that *Jyotiḥ-sūtra* no number greater than twelve is required for the zodiac signs (*rāśi*), the traditional method (*saṃpradāya*) is that one must perform the division by twelve.

Even if one observes closely that the number three hundred and sixty-one would not be understood from such statements in the Dharmaśāstras as "the nether regions (pātāla) are otherwise vast," there is no harm;
for by means of the word "and" (ca), the number six is added to the number two.
Since it is possible to reach the number eight by combining two with six, those "eight" [syllables]—
like the previous case— are intended to signify the number seven; for, by eliding the letter *a*, the number one is added to the total.

Furthermore, from the repetition, the attainment of the number eight is reached; thus, the meaning of "by six" results in "by eight. Here too, "syllables" (*akṣaraiḥ*) is the substantive, as has already been stated by the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*). In this manner, the placement of the four limbs (*caturaṅga-nyāsa*) is performed with the four words ending with the armor (*kavaca*).

Regarding the five-limbed arrangement (*pañcāṅga-pakṣa*), some say that the placement (*nyāsa*) consists of the eyes alone; they accept the maxim "the elision of *am* [is like the elision of *ā*]" as a supporting principle. For this very reason, Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, in his *Śrī-Kārtavīryārjuna-saparyā*, mentions only the limbs of the eyes as the five.

They teach the four-limbed assignment (cāṅganyāsa); relying on this very opinion, it is said "with so many," meaning with as many syllables as are taught up to that extent for the four-limbed assignment;
[the sense is] "with that many syllables," [and thus] the assignment of the eyes (nayana-nyāsa) is performed with a complete verse.

As long as there is the statement, "In that case, one should abandon the eye among the five limbs of the mind," it is appropriate to apply the abandonment of the eye to the place where the five limbs are located; for such a principle applies only where it is explicitly stated that "one should abandon one limb. Therefore, for us...
Having refuted the opinion of Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa in the *Bhaktitaraṅgiṇī* and established his own position, he says "the weapon" (*astram*), relying upon that very view:
"In the ritual applications under discussion, the King of Mantras which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*)— by means of its constituent syllables (*karaṇākṣaraiḥ*)..."

"Filled with syllables" means, in short, by means of mantras; or rather, by means of verse-quarters (śloka-pāda) characterized by having eight syllables— whereby, due to the use of the plural number, the number four is intended—
and thus the meaning "the placement of the weapon (astra-nyāsa) by means of four quarters" is not difficult to understand.
*Bhaḥ*. Thus, in the view of the five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅga-pakṣa*), the intended meaning of the root text is entirely faultless.

In some Tantras, however, the view of the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) is also mentioned; this is now approved by me, as it may be performed optionally according to one's own guru’s tradition following the direct evidence of the Śruti. This is because [the former] is concise and [the latter] is from the scriptures.

The author of the root text does not incur any lack of elegance by employing such useless and afflicted expressions with the desire that "it may be obtained. In reality, its authority does not derive from being rooted in the Śruti; rather, it derives from the Blessed One, who is omniscient and free from defects.

Precisely because it has been well-composed, the Vedas are understood by those of Nyāya intellect; for just as there are statements such as "the incarnation of the Fish speaks the Veda," here too thousands of words establishing that [this system] was spoken by Śiva are found.
Nor, in this way, does it follow that the Left-hand path (Vāmamārga) would also be accepted as such, since it too was spoken by him.

It must be stated that [the duty] belongs to the Ārya, for this is an accepted conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). For just as the Vedic injunctions, "One should perform the twilight worship" (*saṃdhyām upāsīta*) and "The Aṣṭakā rites should be performed," although authoritative for all,
are to be practiced only by twice-born men who have been initiated (*upanīta*) and whose fathers are deceased— even though they pertain to matters concerning all— so too [is the case here].

Tantric statements such as "having drunk liquor, one should mutter [mantras] while looking at another man's wife who is naked and has had intercourse with five men," although they are all authoritative for everyone, apply in their own context only to Śūdras, outcastes, and twice-born men who have fallen from their status,
and not to all people. Other statements...
Furthermore, because of the determination of those authorized to perform sacrifices, many scriptural statements are found in the *Tantra-śāstra* that both prescribe and prohibit such acts;
thus, for example, there is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "One who practices malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) should sacrifice with the Śyena," which [prescribes] the killing of enemies.

Just as they teach the Śyena sacrifice for the sake of desire, yet it does not prevent the experience of hell and so forth enjoined by the prohibitory scripture "One should not harm any living beings," likewise [it is the same] with those [teachings] that indicate worldly pleasures such as sovereignty,
happiness, subjugation, and attraction.

The words that provide instruction on liquor and so forth do not prevent one from experiencing hell and other such states as taught by the prohibitions; rather, the purpose of the laudatory statements is to induce engagement in those paths by presenting them as leading to the enjoyment of sovereignty and similar rewards, whereas the purpose of the prohibitory statements is [to deter such engagement].

The utility of that path must be explained by all as being solely for the purpose of producing the absence of suffering in hell and other realms through the means of turning away from it; and thus, it should be understood that the fact that such a path generates hell is established by implication. This is not the case with sleeping during the day or eating food at night.
It should not be asked, "Where is there such hatred for you in the path of the wicked, especially toward those who are prohibited from eating meat?

For since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from sin is difficult to discern, the relative gravity or lightness of an act can only be understood through the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). It is for this very reason that it is said: "Better to go to one's own mother; better [to eat] beef."

Although eating on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) has been established as more strictly prohibited than even all the great sins (mahāpātakas) such as violating the Guru’s bed— by such statements as "Eating, killing, and drinking liquor are better than eating on Ekādaśī"—
nevertheless, [eating] on the eleventh day...

Because it is taught as being of minor gravity by the rule of expiation stating, "Having eaten [forbidden food] day and night, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*," it is called "minor" (*alpa*). Therefore, it refers to the drinking of wine (*surāpāna*) which is a constituent part of the path of the Vāma, and which is to be removed by expiations such as the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika-prāyaścitta*).

It is beyond dispute that sins such as sleeping during the day, which are removed by bathing and other rites, are indeed much lighter than [sins like] violating the king's edict or violating the Guru's bed; likewise,
the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is a valid authority even without depending on the postulation of a Vedic text, thereby establishing its efficacy.

The root author’s extreme brevity in employing such an obscure expression is intended to present two alternative views established by their respective guru-lineages, each wishing to proceed according to its own purpose. He states the placement of the syllables (*akṣanyāsa*) beginning with "the head" (*śira*). He says *praṇa*...

Having uttered each letter between the two arms along with a *bindu*, the deposition of letters (*varṇanyāsa*) should be performed on the head and other parts; for it is observed in the instruction that there should be an *oṃkāra* before and after each syllable.
This is to be done according to the method stated in the *Mātṛkānyāsa*, at the locations of the armpits, feet, and the tips of the fingers.

The twenty [fingers] constitute the belly, which is intended as a single location expressed by a singular term; the two sides of the eyes constitute two locations each, making five locations in total. The head, forehead, face, heart, and throat are five [locations]. The "other limb" (aparāṅga) is the back portion; the region below the navel is the "lower limb."

Some say that one should place the letters of the mantra one by one in these thirty-two locations, including the two positions on the back of the *kakut* (the hump). One should perform one hundred thousand recitations for each letter, totaling thirty-two lakhs;
or thirty-two thousand, as an exception to the rule of performing ten-thousandth-part oblations (*daśāṃśahoma*).
This is a specific injunction: according to the rule, having worshipped the limbs upon the filaments, Garuḍa and the others upon the cardinal petals,
and Śrī and the others upon the intermediate petals as before,
one should worship the world-protectors and their weapons in the square [enclosure] for rites such as pacification (śānti) and subjugation (vaśya).

The "gentle form" (*saumyarūpam*) refers to the form described in the passage beginning with "māṇikya" and so forth; the "cruel form" (*krūrarūpam*) refers to the form beginning with "udyatkoṭi" and so forth, used for cruel purposes such as causing hatred, eradication, or battle. "Śrī" refers to the previously mentioned creeper named Lakṣmī; according to the *Amarakośa*, "lavaṅga" is the flower of the gods (*devakusuma*), known by the name "śrī."
Some say that because of the mention of "two," the meaning is "with two clove flowers";

however, in that case, this word "homa" is used figuratively, and the inclusion of the suffix "-svāhā" at the end of the mantra is for the sake of obtaining its specific form. The word "one hundred" (śata) is intended as a small number, whereas in cases of great importance, such a [large] number would be required.

Regarding what was stated by the teachers: "The practitioner, having worshipped with eight thousand blades of *dūrvā* grass, should then offer oblations into the waters; thus the afflictions and calamities of darkness go to peace. 'For [the waters] are purifying and peaceful'—this is the Vedic revelation. Having bathed, one should immediately thereafter [perform the rite for] bad dreams.

In the phrase "one should mutter [the mantra]," the term "one hundred and eight times" is to be supplied. Since this bestows the fruit of pleasant dreams, it means that bad dreams will be cut off by the power of the auspicious [mantra];
it does not mean that one would see a good dream after the mantra-recitation, by which the fruit of the bad dream [would be neutralized].

The meaning is that there would be destruction. Rather than postulating that the attainment of a good dream through the recitation of mantras results in the cessation of the fruit of a bad dream, it is more appropriate to postulate that the cessation occurs from the recitation of mantras alone. "In the form of a lion" refers to one's own self as the venerable Nṛsiṃha.

Having visualized one's own enemy as a young deer pierced by a lion, and having visualized him seized by the neck and cast in all directions, the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of the enemy along with his retinue will occur; this is one application.
Furthermore, this is possible even without a mantra, for the recitation of mantras, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth are not required here.

That which was previously stated regarding the recitation of the mantra (*mantra-puraścaraṇa*) applies only to one who has performed that practice; no one else has the qualification for this, because it is indicated by the root text itself through the subsequent traditional teaching (*āmnāna*).
Having meditated upon oneself as being of the form of Nṛsiṃha, [one should proceed] with the previously mentioned mantra...

In place of the word for "self" (*ātman*) in the mantra, one should employ the name of the enemy to be slain, such as Devadatta; having arranged the remainder as before, one should recite that perfected mantra one hundred and eight times while visualizing the enemy being devoured by [the deity's] sharp claws, fangs, and so forth.
If one should recite [the mantra], then this enemy will go to his own abode even before reaching the circle;

such is one application. He describes the ritual procedure itself with the words beginning "vibhīta" and so forth: having meditated upon Nṛhari, the destroyer of enemies, as devouring the foes with his sharp claws and other weapons.

Having meditated upon a lion, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with a thousand arrows. In that rite, the mantra is [to be recited] while imagining oneself in the form of Nṛsiṃha, as if piercing the enemy with arrows feathered with vultures' plumes; meditating "I am Nṛsiṃha" as if actually cleaving the foes, one should cast the arrows into the fire. Thus it is said:

One should utter [the mantra] as if devouring the enemies and cast the fuel-sticks as if piercing them; having thus offered oblations, one should dispatch the king’s desired army at an auspicious *lagna*—this is the connection. In front of that army, to the east, [one should visualize the deity] slaying—that is, killing—the circle of enemies.
Having meditated upon that Nṛsiṃha, one should perform the practice in the form of recitation and meditation until the army returns;

furthermore, the king should satisfy the performer of the rite with victory, for if he is not satisfied, there will be a fault, even if one has given according to one's capacity. If [he is not satisfied], then...

If it is asked, "What should be done then if the guru is pleased? listen: if he has previously been tested and found to be entirely devoid of concealment (*āvaraṇa*), [that is the course]. But if, even though he was tested, his nature should by chance become otherwise, then how should one proceed? If this is asked:

Since it is necessary to satisfy and carefully attend to his wife, sons, and others, one might ask: "What should be done if they too should become like that? Listen: having meditated upon the Lord himself as the Guru and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, [one should bestow it] upon His devotees.
If those are unavailable, one should offer it to Vaiṣṇavas; if even those are unavailable, one should give it to Vaidikas.

As an expiation for the absence of the Guru’s satisfaction, one should perform at least one of the following: worship of the Lord, offering Tulasī, feeding a Brāhmaṇa, chanting the King of Mantras (the *praṇava*), or chanting the Gāyatrī.

He demonstrates the yantra: having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and so forth, one should write the *nṛsiṃha-bīja*—to be described later—in its pericarp (*karṇikā*), and within that, having inscribed the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) and so forth; then, on the petals, one should arrange the four syllables of the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*).

O King, having surrounded that [central area] with the Mātṛkā letters in a circular form and having constructed two mutually intersecting enclosures of earth (bhūpura), one should write the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha in all its corners;
thus it is said that the two dwellings of earth, consisting of eight squares, are mutually intersecting. Two enclosures of earth...
The term "encircled by that" (*yaṃtenāvṛttam*) is an adjective for the *yantra* known as the *Cintāmaṇi*.
Another [description of this] *yantra* is also stated in another *tantra*: "With a concentrated mind, one should draw a great sixteen-spoked [wheel] on birch bark;
one should write the syllables of the mantra on the petals in pairs of two, [forming] the *Trailokyamohana*."

The wise one should write the seed-syllable in the pericarp, encircle it with the Śrī-bīja, and bind it with the syllable *Kroṃ*. This brings victory in disputes, quarrels, and in royal assemblies; it bestows wisdom, subjugation, and brings men and women under one's control. One should wear it on the crest-lock or on the arm.
Whether worn around the neck or as a waist-thread, one shall become most fortunate in all the world and equal to the Lord of All. This protection named Cintāmaṇi was composed by Siṃha himself.
It should be placed within the jars situated upon the nine-fold maṇḍala, along with milk, barks, decoctions, and water.
The word *ṣikro* (sixfold) should be understood as including all the previously mentioned items to be placed within the jar, such as the gems and so forth;
[the image] should have a peaceful form (*śāntavigraha*) according to the method described starting with "māṇikya" and so forth;
and one should satisfy Tārkṣya and the others—Garuḍa and the rest—as previously mentioned, to the best of one's ability.
Even though he was in need, the king, not deceiving [the preceptor] by manifesting a lesser capacity than he actually possessed,

provided the requisite materials— consisting of perfumes, ornaments, flower garlands, and so forth— as far as his power allowed, acting at that time as the one who performed the ritual application for the Guru.
One should worship a Brahmin of virtuous conduct. Regarding another yantra, [the author] says "marked with seed-syllables" (*bījāṅkam*) and so forth:
having drawn nine lines from east to west, one should draw five lines extending from south to north;
thus says the author of the *Harṣakaumudī*. [Alternatively,] five lines extending from east to west and [five] from south to north...

According to the author of the *Padārthadarśa*, [the squares are formed by] the two [lines] and the five [squares]. However, Rāmacandra says that one should fashion the body of the serpent Śeṣanāga, complete with its long form, five hoods, and tail, and within it, arrange thirty-two squares according to the previous method; thus there are five [squares] in the front line.
The form of the head (phaṇā) should be formed by the five lines at the back; the form of the tail (puccha) should be formed by slightly increasing the outer lines.
According to the middle opinion, this procedure is to be followed on the north-south lines;
according to the first opinion, it is performed there on the hoods (phaṇā), where the seed-syllable (bīja) of Nṛsiṃha will be described.

Having written it five times in thirty-two squares in the form of rows starting from the northeast (īśāna) in sequence, one should write the syllables of the aforementioned King of Mantras one by one; then, having written the name of the person to be protected— such as "Devadatta"— along with the affliction caused by spirits, on each of the five lines located at the tail, [the mantra] consists of the tail.

The traditionalists (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*) maintain that the natural meaning (*svārasya*) of the root word *bhoga*—which follows the phrase "one should write" in the form beginning with *śamaya*—is established precisely by its function of forming the body (*śarīra-nirmāṇa*). The phrase "of whom among the five hoods" is an adjective qualifying the five hoods (*phaṇa-pañcaka*). The previously mentioned yantra is presided over by the *kala*.

It is understood from the root text that this [yantra], when worn, bestows all desired objects through the very act of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Some maintain, however, that the utility of the previous yantra lies in both its being worn and its being used for consecration. Regarding the phrase "marked with the seed-syllable" (*vījāṅka*) and so forth, the "seed" (*vīja*) refers to that which is desired.
The syllable *takāra* (ta) extracts [this mantra]; this also is an independent mantra. As it has been said:
"The seer is Atri, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Lord Śrī Nṛhari; one should fashion the limbs with the long-vowel-conjoined seed-syllable.
The meditation should be as before; one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. Its...

Afterwards, one should perform the oblation and other rites with auspicious milk-rice mixed with ghee, as was done previously for all [other mantras]. One should accomplish its applications just like those of the King of Mantras (Maṃtrarāja).
Its yantra is also taught: one should draw a smooth eight-petaled lotus.

One should write the root mantra joined with the *karṇikā* (pericarp) and endowed with the *praṇava* (Oṃ). Then, the single-syllable Nārasiṃha mantra, together with the object of attainment (*sādhya*), should be placed at the navel. On the eight petals and at the navel within the *karṇikā*, one should place the form of the single-syllable Nārasiṃha root mantra, which has entered within the *praṇava*.

One should draw [the diagram]; however, this is the specific distinction: one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth within that [central] circle. Likewise, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
then, having wound it with a thread, one should enclose it with gold and subsequently wind it with silver, and then with copper.

Afterwards, O beloved, one should diligently smear it with lacquer; then, having consecrated it once more with the root mantra, one should remove it from the fire. One should wear this supreme yantra on the neck, the arm, or the crest-lock.
Thereupon, all women, men, and even kings on earth will come under one's control, and even the wicked shall not harm him.
"By the grace of the Cakrarāja, one shall obtain victory everywhere against thieves, serpents, and rākṣasas.
Another version of this same yantra has also been stated: "The wise man should draw a great twelve-spoked wheel as before;
the learned one should inscribe it upon each petal, conjoined with the twelve mātrās, and place the mantra in the center."
One should encircle the wheel named Kālāntaka—which brings about the destruction of gods and asuras—with the *Śrī-bīja* joined with its power (*śakti*).
One should inscribe this wheel, which wards off all enemies, upon birch bark (*bhūrja*).
By the mere wearing of it, one shall become victorious everywhere; he shall become praiseworthy in the world, just like a deity.

Regarding "from the *vaṃ-kesarī*": having written the aforementioned single-syllable mantra (*ekākṣaramantra*) in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth within it, this also occurs at the end of the *māyāvīja*;
likewise, having written the *māyāvīja* in the pericarp, [one proceeds] in the ten [petals].

The meaning is as follows: having first written the root seed-syllables (*mūlabīja*) joined with the twelve vowels—excluding the neuter vowels—in the order beginning with *ṛ*, one should encircle them externally in the shape of a circle with the *śrībīja* (the syllable *śrīṃ*). He states the *Jvālānṛsiṃha* mantra with the words beginning "the seed-syllable" (*bījam*), etc., starting with *oṃ*.

*Kṣmrauṃ namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya jvālāmāline dīptadaṃṣṭrāya agninetrāya rakṣoghnāya sarvabhūtavināśanāya sarvajvaravināśanāya daha daha paca paca rakṣa rakṣa kuṃ phaṭ svāhā*— this is the mantra of sixty-seven syllables.
If it is asked, "How is this consistent, given that the royal mantra was indicated as having sixty-six syllables by the statement 'with four instruments, indeed with thirteen [limbs],' etc.,
whereas the mantra itself is taught as having sixty-seven syllables?"— this is a delusion.

In the *Timamantra*, within the section on the limbs (*aṅgavidhi*), because the words "agninetraye" are seen as separate and unjoined, there might arise the delusion that the reading in the mantra is intended to be exactly the same; it is precisely to dispel this delusion that it is stated that there are "sixty-seven syllables. By that [statement], the vowel 'a' in "agni" [is shown to be joined with the following word] "daṃṣṭrāye."

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* suggests that a sandhi with the letter *kāra* must be performed so that, through the elision of the vowel *ā*, the mantra results in a reduction of one syllable; this is what is implied. However, the author of the *Harṣakausudī* maintains that even when the mantra is read as "agnī" without sandhi, it is indeed a *mahāmantra*.

The qualifiers are "characterized by sixty-seven syllables" and "beginning with the *dhruvā*"; it is not intended that the quality of having that many syllables belongs specifically to that which is qualified by "beginning with the *dhruvā*. For if that were the case, the *praṇava*, like the *bīja*, would have been extracted even earlier; [the text says] "the *dhruvā*..."
If the specific qualification were given independently [of the context], it would serve no purpose; thus,

since the author of the root text has stated that the mantra consists of sixty-eight syllables by means of the two qualifications— namely, beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and having seventy-six syllables— there is no fault whatsoever.

They say that the latter position is indeed appropriate; for in the case of numerical words such as "thirteen" (*trayodaśabhiḥ*) and so forth, the specific referents are the very words of the mantras themselves. In that context, the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*) should be performed with the eleven mantra-words beginning with "to him whose leader is Agni" (*agninetrāya*). However, this [syllable] 'A' is not a mantra...

If it is argued that the letter *a*, as recited in the mantra, would result in the omission of a syllable when grasping the form of the preceding word— as in the *Prācya-śiro-mantro*— because it becomes *a* somehow through the application of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*),
[we reply: this is possible only by its own inherent natural state (*svārasyena*).
It should be understood that this is because one must somehow resort to a [logical] basis in order to avoid the inconsistency of the argument.

[The Lord is] terrifying—that is, causing fear—with masses of mane (saṭā-kalāpa), meaning clusters of hair on the shoulders, which are scattered and spread out here and there; and [He is] leftward, upward, rightward, upward, and rightward.

The weapons held in the lower right and left hands should be meditated upon as follows: here, the worship—including the ancillary rites (*āvaraṇas*)—should be performed according to the *Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh* mantra on the pedestal described for the eight-syllabled *Nārāyaṇa*. This applies specifically to the various types of minor rites, such as inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and so forth.
This mantra is indestructible due to its swiftness in comparison to other six-syllable mantras.
He demonstrates the Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha mantra with the words beginning with "pāśa," etc. This six-syllable mantra is: *Āṃ hrīṃ kṣrauṃ krauṃ huṃ phaṭ*.
Here, *kṣrauṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*). This [deity] is the eight-armed Nṛsiṃha.
The Lion [statue] holds a wheel and a conch in its two upper right and left hands;

an elephant goad and a noose in the two hands below those; a vajra and a mace in the two hands below those; and in the fourth pair of right and left hands, it displays the two mudrās of rending (*dāraṇa-mudrā*).

As for the *mudrā*: when the fingers are joined together face-to-face, straight, upward-pointing, fierce, and with the thumbs straight in their own positions, this *mudrā* is known as *Dāraṇī*. It is called *Dāraṇī* because by means of this *mudrā*, the heart of Hiraṇyakaśipu was split open. [Six hundred thousand *ṛtus* (seasons)].

One hundred thousand, ten thousand, and six thousand; by this, an exception is made to the general rule of the scriptures regarding the number of repetitions being one-tenth [of the mantra]. Some, however, state that the number sixty—which would result from that tenth part—is intended; or else, [it refers to] the mere vowel following the letter *ta*.

Through the syllable *reṇa*, which is a conventional symbol for zero (*śūnya*), its comprehension signifies the number six; thus, the number sixty is obtained. They say that the oblation (*homa*) is performed by means of this very number, which is a tenth part [of sixty].
Thus, because the numbers sixty-six are understood from the two syllables, it is a tenth part.

Some maintain that because it is an internal [subordinate] element (*antaraṅga*) of the number, it is proper to perform the *nyāsa* with that very same number, as this follows from the natural sense of the word; having worshipped the limbs upon the filaments and the eight weapons, such as the discus, in the centers of the petals, one should worship Indra and the others in the square.

One should worship as before; for even in the absence of another person having a mantra perfected through *puraścaraṇa* and other rites, since one’s own mantra is already perfected, the application [of the ritual] for the sake of another’s welfare should be undertaken without doubt— thus he says, "of another."
When oblations consisting of five substances— *larāja*, *pāmārga*, sacrificial grain (*havis*), and clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—
are offered in sequence, two thousand times for each substance,
then those minor obstacles characterized as previously described are [subdued].
The meaning is that there occurs the pacification of diseases and difficult-to-grasp [afflictions],
as stated in the passage beginning with "sati kta-iṃ" and so forth, in the *Nṛsiṃha*[-tantra].
O Great Hero, that which is pure on this ground is called *heti*.
The individual soul.

Having written the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and having drawn a great trident in its center, one should write the *nṛsiṃha-bīja* in the eastern square and the *māyā-bīja* in the northern square; then, having seated the person afflicted by spirits or planets within both of these, and having touched his head, [one should recite] a thousand times... the six...
One should mutter the six-syllable mantra; the meaning is that one afflicted by spirits or planetary influences shall be liberated from those spirits and planets.

He demonstrates the yantra with the words beginning with "akhila" and so forth: having first drawn a hexagon, and having written the *māyābīja* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) together with the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) and other details within its pericarp, [one should then write it] upon the six...
Having written the six syllables of the six-syllabled mantra one by one in the corners,

and having written the vowels twice in the filaments and the fourfold syllables of the *anuṣṭubh* mantra-king four times on the petals of the eight-petaled lotus fashioned outside that, [one should enclose it] with a circle.

One should surround that earth-fortress (bhūpura) on the outside with thirty-five syllables beginning with *kāreṇaka* and ending with *kṣāntaiḥ*. According to those who follow the inherent intent of the root text, one should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Cintāmaṇi, which is about to be described, in all four corners; however, [others] maintain it should be in two of the front corners.

The author of the *Harṣakaumudī* states that after encircling the seed-syllable, one should place two lion-seed-syllables (*siṃha*) in the two upper corners, and then, by returning in reverse order, place two seed-syllables; however, they have this doubt: having joined the word "nārasiṃham" found in the root-text with what precedes it, they [place it] on the earth.
The meaning is that one should write the Cintāmaṇi and the Narasiṃha [mantras] in the corners;
the word "Cintāmaṇi" is an adjective for the Narasiṃha-bīja,
and therefore the meaning is that one should write the Narasiṃha-bīja itself four times in the corners, as it has been stated regarding Narasiṃha.

In the ritual manual (*kalpa*), one should meditate upon the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) whose pericarp is distinguished by the six-cornered seed-syllable, which is joined with the letters of the Power (*śakti*), surrounded by the four roots and the eight digits (*kalā*), and enclosed within the enclosure of the Mother, the Earth, the House, and the Weapon; the mantra of the Power is: *Āṃ hrīṃ kṣrauṃ kroṃ ca huṃ phaṭ*.

The eight syllables of *kāla*, the even-numbered vowels, *ciṃtā*, *ṛṣabha*, *nṛsiṃha*, *ekākṣara*, and *romanu*— this is the meaning: the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus should be joined with the six-cornered seed-syllable, the *māyā*-seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*), and the letters of the *Śakti-mantra* in the six corners, [and] on the petals.
In the filaments of the *ṣumūla-anuṣṭubha-rāja-mantra*, four syllables each should be written;
the eight *kalās* should be written surrounded by the *jananī-mātṛkā*; and in the corners of the *jagatī-pura* (the outer square), [the syllables] should be placed everywhere without exception.

In response to the inquiry—"Who here possesses the power of the mantra-syllables? What is the group of eight kalās? And what is the Cintāmaṇi?"—the text itself causes one to grasp the power of those terms through the passage beginning with "ĀM," etc., [referring to] the pairs consisting of short and long vowels.

In this context, shortness (*hrasvatva*) is technical (*pāribhāṣika*); therefore, there is no inclusion of *o*. And thus, by the root text, the word *anarasiṃha* results in being a gloss (*vivaraṇa*) upon the word *cintāmaṇi*. Or rather, let the word *cintāmaṇi* itself be of hidden meaning (*gūḍhārtha*) in the root text.

The path refined by those who follow the *Padārthadarśa*— who maintain that the term "Nārasiṃha-pada" refers to a specific type of yantra as presented [in the text]— is untenable; for since individual instances of usage cannot be definitively determined, they must be characterized in a general sense.

He states with the words beginning "by many" that its capacity to accomplish purposes is greater than even those other mantras which have attained a unique status in accomplishing their respective goals; for by this [mantra], all undesirable things are cursed away, and all desirable things are favored.

Regarding the summary of the supplementary applications (*khilaprayoga-saṃgraha*): as for the question, "Since there are many *Nṛsiṃha* yantras, for what purpose is only this much [of them] taken up?", he says, "By many," with the word "by mantra" being understood as the ellipsis.
Thus, among all his mantras, only this much of the mantra [is taken].

The sense is that the inclusion of this much alone [of the mantra] is due to its being the supreme among names; and since the Śrī Viṣṇu mantras are to be described, and because the Śrī Sudarśana-cakra is also Viṣṇu,
there is the writing of the Śrī Sudarśana mantra within the Vārāha mantra.

In response to the expectation regarding this mantra as it has been taught, he says "Tāra" (the syllable Om). Again—that is, once more—he [mentions] that which begins with the letter *Ha*. Because it is taken up again by means of the word *Bhṛgu* (the letter *Ra*), it is said "again. It is accompanied by the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the *Huṃ*-power (*śakti*), and its own nature, which is the form of the arrow (*śara*).
The supreme weapon-mantra consists of [the syllables] ending with *dviṭha* (ṭha), each followed by the word *svāhā*,
and all joined individually with the *jāti*-mantras in the form of *namaḥ svāhā* and so forth;
these are combined at the end with the essential nature beginning with *ācakrāya*, and the supreme heart-word (*hṛtpada*) is likewise [included], because it ends with *namaḥ*.

Because of the observation of [mantras] such as "nyatrahṛdayāya" (to the heart elsewhere), it is thus declared by the Blessed One that even in the case of Agni, the nature of the limb-mantras consists of those ending in the dative case; likewise, there are [mantras] such as "cakrāya svāhā hṛdayāya namaḥ" (svāhā to the wheel,
obeisance to the heart) and "vicakrāya svāhā śirase svāhā" (svāhā to the expanded wheel, svāhā to the head), and so forth— six [in number].
The *ḍaṃga-mantras* have been concluded; beginning with the east and so forth,

although it is stated by this mantra that "one binds even the ten directions," nevertheless, for the binding of the directions starting from the southeast (āgneyī), this mantra containing the word *aindrī* is not appropriate.

Since the purpose [of the mantra] has already been stated, one must perform the modification (*ūha*) of the words "āgneyī" and so forth in their respective places; for it is intended that the status of being a *mantra* belongs only to the portion explicitly recited from the traditional canon (*kaṇṭhataḥ samāmnāta*), and not to the interpolated portion.
Thus, with this *mantra*, the worship of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla-pūjā*) is performed.

In the case of the [deposition] within the object (*viṣaya*), the sequence of directions begins from the east and ends at the zenith; however, in the case of the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the specific distinction is that the sequence begins from the east and ends below. Starting from the eastern direction and ending below, I bind this [direction] called Sudarśana with my disc; salutations!
Having struck the head of the discus with the palm of the hand, one should bind the directions according to the teacher’s instruction;
this is another specific detail. With the palm of the left hand, beginning from the elbow of the right hand and ending at the palm, one recites the Sudarśana weapon mantra: *Oṃ sahasrāra phaṭ*.
In the case of a Vaiṣṇava, one should perform the placement with the *Paśupatāstra* mantra: *oṃ śrīṃ paśupataye huṃ phaṭ*.

In the case of other deities, one should perform the placement with the *Brahmāstra* mantra: *oṃ tapaḥ satyātmane astrāya phaṭ*. In this manner, [one should place it] with the palm of the right hand upon the left [hand].
One should place [the mantra] starting from the *stakūrpa* down to the end of the base. Regarding the *āgniprākāra* mantra, beginning with "Oṃ trailokya...
and so forth: at the end of the word *trailokya*, there are two words for "protection" (*rakṣa*) and the word *svāhā*.
At the beginning is the eternal *praṇava*. Thus, the mantra "Oṃ trailokyarakṣa rakṣa svāhā" emerges from the root.

By stating "for the sake of protecting oneself" (*ātmano rakṣārtham*), the opinion of some who hold that the word *trailokya* (the three worlds) is in the accusative case is rejected; for if that were so, it would be understood that the three worlds alone are the object of the act of protection, and not one's own self as a separate entity—this is the intended meaning. As for what [the opponent] said... [text fragment] ...maṃ.

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* has stated that "the three worlds" (*tretrailokya*) is the second word ending in a noun, because a verb is heard [later in the sentence]; however, this contradicts the root text he cites, for in the absence of a co-occurrence with a specific [verbal] term,
words such as "protection" (*rakṣā*) and so forth— just like the word "we" (*asmat*) and so forth— refer only to the speaker.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the verb *dhakamiti* (it burns) would lack expectancy; for in your own view, the requirement for a verb to expect a subject-word applies even to such cases, as another Tantra has cited the example "He protects the three worlds" (*trailokyam rakṣati rakṣet*), which remains syntactically connected even when read without the vowel *u*.
The secret is that its authority remains doubtful;

however, if the reading *saviṃduke* is determined through methods such as *prāyaścitta*, then this mantra can indeed be restored from its very root. For instance, [the text] beginning with *ādhruvāt*.

The analysis of the words (*padaccheda*) is as follows: *ādyadhruva* means that which has an unstable (*adhruva*) [element] at the beginning (*ādi-mukhe*); *ādikā* means that which has a *ka* at the beginning (*ādi*).

The compound *ādyadhruvādika* is a *madhyamapadalopa-samāsa* (elision of the middle term), meaning "that which has an *ādyadhruva* together with an *ādika*. *Kādinava*, *ṭādinava*, and *pādipaṃca* [are formed similarly].
The five letters beginning with *trya* (t, th, d, dh, n) are conventionally designated as the "ca-group" (*cayādi*) and so forth among the five groups of consonants.
Among them, the letter *ya* belongs to the third group; *kaṃ* refers to the head (*śiras*), and because the nasal bindu is placed there, it is *kaṃ-bindu*.
What remains for you that is desired, once the attainment of the mantra has occurred? Or rather—
Since fire possesses a preeminent form, and because it is remembered that "from space comes air,
and from air comes fire," and because the increase of fire from air is established by direct perception,
its mantra— which consists of the letter *ya* alone— has entered into this mantra here.
However, since it means that the letter *ya*, together with the *bindu*, enters here as having the nature of "this" (*iyam*),
by this [explanation] one understands that "one should construct a rampart with this mantra";
thus, the mention of "Agni" and so forth would be useless for understanding this mantra's status as a rampart-mantra (*prākāramantra*).

It has been stated that this is because it is described as being exceedingly meaningful; some maintain that the mention of its status as a mantra is for the purpose of praising it as superior to all other syllables contained within the "Agni-prākāra" mantra. Therefore...

The *Saṃhitā-saṃvāda* states: "The three worlds are the *praṇava*; the pair of *rakṣas* is the armor; joined with the head of the weapon is the mantra known as the 'Fire-Wall' (*agni-prākāra*). Thus, one should perform the rite while mentally contemplating the fire-wall around oneself and circumambulating clockwise while reciting the water-mantra.

One should cast [the mantra] as previously stated; having established a protective wall of fire around oneself for protection against *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*, the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should thereafter scatter water, flowers,
and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) consecrated with the fire-seed syllable and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) all around to ward off fear and obstacles.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of cessation": the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters should be performed preceded by meditation on each respective letter, and not otherwise.
With this intention, he describes the placement preceded by meditation, beginning with the words "white" (*site*) and so forth;
for the three letters that constitute the *praṇava* (OM) possess, in their respective order, the qualities of being white and so on.

The placement of the seventh and subsequent syllables occurs through six repetitions in the six locations distinct from the two joints and the form of the flame; it will be stated in the context of worship that [the sequence] is "bow, arrow, bow" on one hand and "bow, arrow, bow" on the other, extending across the right and left halves.

Of those two [lips], others [are on] their lips; again, others [are on] their lower parts; and the last two [are on] their weapons. One should perform twenty-four hundred oblations for each of the five substances, such as sesame seeds, numbering one hundred thousand for the sun (arka), twelve lakhs, twelve thousand, and twelve thousand [respectively].

The number [of items] is completed by the count of six; although the order [of the weapons] is obtained from the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the statement "beginning with the discus" (*cakrādīti*) is for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that sesame seeds and so forth are mixed together. Although the weapons are already obtained by the mere mention of "beginning with the discus," they are mentioned again to include the previously stated bow (*cāpa*).

In order to prescribe the additional deities, he shows the powers (*śakti*) to be included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), since Lakṣmī and the others were not mentioned previously, beginning with the words "Lakṣmī... and so on. Likewise, the limbs (*aṅga*) are in the filaments (*kesara*), the weapons (*āyudha*) are in the petals (*dala*), Lakṣmī and the others are at the tips of the petals, and Indra and the others are in the square (*caturaśra*).

The meaning established is that Vajrā and the others are the deities of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), and this is the intended sense of the mantra. Regarding the "two pairs": the first two are yellow; the next two are red; the next two are white; and the final two are the powers (*śakti*) in the form of Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi, which are dark blue (*śyāma*). Thus it is observed.

The fruit—consisting of longevity, health, sons, and so forth—is perceivable by one's own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); whereas the unseen fruit, such as the destruction of evil (*pāpakṣaya*), is not. For the destruction of evil is not accessible to direct perception, since evil itself is imperceptible. [Objection: But is it not the case that fruit is both mediated by a visible means (*dṛṣṭadvāraka*) and mediated by an unseen means (*adṛṣṭadvāraka*)? [Reply: It is not so.
This is because the mere performance [of the ritual] produces the result only by taking the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as its intermediary;

for without the postulation of such an operation, the causal relationship between the performance and the result— which consists in their being connected by immediate temporal succession— cannot be established.
In these applications, even the recitation of the Gāyatrī should be performed as a tenth part of the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Regarding the Gāyatrī, it is threefold due to the differences in the tantras: "Oṃ, we know the Sudarśana;
we meditate upon the King of Wheels; may that Wheel impel us. This is the Sudarśana [Gāyatrī].

"We know the Great Wheel, we meditate upon it; may that Wheel impel us. "We know the Wheel, we meditate upon the one with a thousand flames; may that Anivārita impel us"—thus is the established rule according to the respective traditions of one's own gurus.
For the attainment of long life through the Mṛtyuñjaya-mantra and others, the Śrī-bīja (Hrīṃ) should precede [the mantra];

for the attainment of Lakṣmī or the acquisition of excellent intellect, the Vāgbhava-bīja (Aiṃ) is desired at the beginning. Such is the instruction of the great-souled ones regarding this root-mantra, specifically for the application of warding off calamities.

Regarding "for three days," this refers to the mantra having the *nṛsiṃha* seed-syllable (*vīja*) at its beginning. For the destruction of calamities and for weighty undertakings, this supreme application should be performed for up to four days. As it has been said: "One who is consecrated by mantras should offer a thousand or eight pellets of *guggulu* resin for three days."

If one contemplates [the mantra] for four days, there will be fainting and pain; if one contemplates it until the end of the *maṇḍala* for seven days, death will occur. He describes the ritual application (*prayoga*) for eradication (*uccāṭana*): "beginning with the letter 'A'";
that is, one should encircle the second syllable of the mantra with the sixteen vowels beginning with 'A'.

One should meditate on that [mantra] encircled by the words "go, go outside" (taṃ-tad-bahiḥ-yāhi-yāhi) ten times over the head of the enemy and thus cause the enemy to be driven away, according to the statement: "Ten days after [the meditation], he overcomes the adversary. However, Rāmacandra [interprets] it as "those whose [beginning] is with the letter 'a'."
They say that long vowels alone are to be grasped from the *graha*; by means of the conjunction with the letter *ya*, the state of being a vowel (*svaratva*) must be effected.

Thus, the resultant meaning is that [the mantra] should be encircled by *yaṃ*, *yāṃ*, *piṃ*, *pīṃ*, and so forth. And this is logical, as it is the application of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
The author of the *Gādītipadārthādarśa* states that in both systems, the letter *hya* should be written for the *vāyu-bījas* according to the literal reading;
he says that when this very practice is repeated up to the end of the mandala, it attains the status of a *māraṇa-prayoga* (a rite of killing). By this [he means]:

By such means, having meditated on the third syllable of the mantra—the letter *ha*—as being identical in form to a crow and as remaining upon the head of the enemy for seven days, one should cause him to be driven away (*uccāṭayet*);
this is the application [of the rite] mentioned in another Tantra, which states: "One should [visualize] that which ends in *sa*, having the color of a crow, upon the head of the enemy."

Within seven days, it swiftly causes expulsion or kills; "by its sharpness" (naiśityāt) means by its cruelty (krūratā), such that it should not be employed in rites of killing—this is the sense. He describes the rite of favor (anugraha-prayoga) with the verse beginning "autumn" (śarat), etc. Here...

The term *caṃdranibhatvam* means "resembling the moon" (*caṃdrasadṛśatvam*). Furthermore, it is intended to convey the sense that [the deity] is exceedingly beautiful due to being completely encircled by the moon-related seed-syllable (*bīja*), namely the nectar-seed *vaṃ*, as in *vaṃ vāṃ viṃ vī vuṃ vūm* and so forth.

The implied meaning is that, in this manner, the second syllable of the mantra should also be encircled by the sixteen vowels and the seed-syllable *sudhā* (am). In place of the word "japet" (one should recite),
one should add the verse from the Gītā beginning with "Hṛṣīkeśa," followed at the end of the mantra by "namaḥ sārathinārāyaṇāya huṃ phaṭ."
The meaning is that one should recite the fourteen-syllable mantra beginning with *ṭyaṇāyoṃ*. Regarding the term *sarja*:

it refers to the *śāla* tree; however, because this is a gentle (*saumya*) application, some maintain that the word "gold" (*kanaka*) here refers to the *nāgakesara* flower. Minor diseases include paralysis and the like.
He states the ritual application for warding off injury and malevolent spells with the words beginning "of the *apāmārga*":

having offered one hundred and eight oblations with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, and again having offered that same number with clarified butter, and having offered that same number with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the verse "By Truth, O Varuṇa, Father," and again [offering] with clarified butter...

One should not consume the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) that has been prepared and consecrated individually for each deity without first performing the *samidh* oblations. In the *samiddhoma*, the *sampāta* (the residue of the offering) occurs through the mere contact of the hands with each individual oblation; thus, there is no remainder of the *caru* left over from the *homa*.
Now, if there is no remainder, does it not follow that the consumption of the *caru* cannot take place? Indeed, [it would not].

If it is argued that, since the performance of the rite depends on the expectation of where the remnants are to be used according to the conduct of the learned, the eating is taught [only] when there is no remainder— because in the absence of such a remainder, such an expectation does not exist, and thus there is no fault even in the absence of eating— that is not so. Saṃ...

Since the preparation of the *caru* is traditionally prescribed and because the injunction "one should give the *caru*" is observed, this is indeed an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) for the eating of the remnants, just as in the case of the remnants of a *śrāddha*. Therefore, just as the *caru* might remain after the oblation, so too [the eating of the remnants occurs] through an excess of that [offering] and so forth.

It must be understood that one must indeed exercise restraint. The previously mentioned application for removing minor diseases, when practiced beforehand, maintains their prior absence; however, the application beginning with "soaked in the five products of the cow" (pañcagavya) and so forth, being performed once those [diseases] have arisen, destroys them.
This is a distinction of types or a conceptual differentiation regarding substances such as *nirguṇḍī* and others that are unavailable;
this [remedy] is described as "all-pervading" (*sarvatomukhī*), meaning it pertains to all complications whether mentioned or unmentioned.
Its scope is restricted to those [complications], which is to say its status is defined by being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*) to them.

He describes the practice for pacification with the words beginning "south and north" (*dakṣiṇottaraga*) and so forth: one wheel is to the south of oneself and another is to the north; that [wheel] is hexagonal (*ṣaṭkoṇa*).
Therein, the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is yellow in color and the hexagon is red; the space between them is... [made].

Having drawn the white line for the outer enclosure (vahiḥ-paridhi) denoted by the term *nemi*, and having drawn the lines in the shape of a face outside of that, [one forms] the "black earth-house" (*kṛṣṇa-bhūgṛha*)— this being the form of the entire aggregate; there, upon the wheel situated in the northern portion, one should install the *kumbha* according to the prescribed rule.

It should be filled with red water in the form of a liquid such as lac; there, preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, one should perform the worship of Viṣṇu in the form of Sudarśana as before. Because of the observation that "one should lead those two outside" and so forth, this is not a fire-offering (homa) performed in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on the altar (sthaṇḍila), but rather [it is performed] while laughing.
Likewise, having established the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the wheel situated on the right side of the body,
and having installed the fire in that very place according to the prescribed ritual for one who has been consecrated in the pit,
