[one should offer oblations] consisting of ghee, *āmalaka*, mustard seeds, sesame, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and ghee.

Having offered oblations one by one with twenty-six substances, numbering one hundred and twenty-six each, and having completed the full homa with a count of one thousand and eight, and having performed the collection [of the remnants] into the kalaśa for each oblation, one should prepare *caru* from half a *prastha* of husked rice, and another from half of that.

Having formed a *piṇḍa* (ball of offerings), one should cast it into the interior of the water-pot (*kumbha*). Together with new, clean, and washed garments, and accompanied by the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) who is afflicted by obstacles such as *kṛtyās*,
[the practitioner] should proceed from the south of the fire toward the north, where the fire has been established to the right of the pot.

Having placed [the vessel] in the middle portion between the two jars, and having performed the *nīrājana* rite for the object to be consecrated in sequence with the jar and the fire, one should draw a circle of the zodiac outside the village; then, at that spot where the eighth sign of the victim's [natal] ascendant is situated, one should place the jar and the fire as before, in order from north to south.

Having offered oblations with the previously mentioned substances in the previously mentioned number, and having given sacrificial offerings (*bali*) in the ten directions with the remnants of the *caru* rice, one should feed the Brahmins with food consisting primarily of sweets and other delicacies; then, having satisfied the preceptor with gifts of honorarium (*dakṣiṇā*) and other offerings, one should bring the ritual to completion.

The meaning of "tisamuditvā" (having risen from the three) is as follows: even in the view that [the deity] is established in the right wheel (*dakṣiṇacakra*), the rite of raising up (*utthāpana*) that which resides therein must now be performed. This is because, by observing the rule for moving it [to another place], one gains the conviction that it has indeed been raised up; however, [this applies specifically to] the wheel.
There is no work more magnificent than this, wherein there is the convergence of both [traditions].

The traditionalists (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*) say that at this juncture, the ritual of "entirety-making" (*sakalīkaraṇa*) for the object of accomplishment should be performed with the *Gītā-mantra*; they also say that the "lustration" (*nīrājana*) is performed with the *Gītā-mantra*. As for that which...

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* stated that there is a requirement for another person for the sake of accomplishing the simultaneous *nīrājana*; however, that is to be reconsidered. From the root text, only the *nīrājana* itself is understood, neither simultaneity nor any other tantra demonstrating such a meaning. The locations for the heaps (*rāśi*) have been stated according to another tantra.

The meaning is that they have been demonstrated exactly as before; namely, that one should place the fire on the southern side of the jar, as it was said: "Then one should cast everything, beginning with the fire, onto the southern side of the jar. He now states the mantra for the *bali* offering, beginning with the words "sahṛt" and so forth. In this context:
The meaning is that it is connected according to the *yathāvivīti* [rule], which means not transgressing the euphonic combinations (*saṃdhi*) prescribed in grammar.

Thus, when the word *namaḥ* is employed by such a rule, its ending in the vowel *o* is established; and when the word *abhyopadeśa* is employed, its ending in the visarga (*visargāntatā*) is established. They [the grammarians] hold this view.
"O Viṣṇu’s attendants, who bring peace to all, accept this bali;
salutation to Śānti. This is the mantra for offering the bali, consisting of twenty-four syllables.
He describes another application beginning with the words "having fashioned," etc., [referring to] a cage in the shape of a casket, filled with milk...

Having fashioned a vessel from a single piece of wood from a tree and filling it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should seat the purified person to be treated (*sādhya*) therein with bathing garments and other requisites. Having touched him, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) a thousand and eight times or more. [This is done] in the eight sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) located in the eight directions, beginning with the east.

Or, on sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*), one should perform oblations (*homa*) with each of the eight previously mentioned substances, through the mediation of eight Brahmins, according to the number stated before. The patron (*yajamāna*) should satisfy the officiating priests (*hotṛ*), the chanters (*japtṛ*), and the Brahmins according to his capacity, and he should also satisfy his own preceptor (*guru*). By that [act],...

"One application is that there shall be the pacification of diseases, malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*), and so forth. He states another application with the words beginning "with the five products of the cow" (*pañcagavyaiḥ*): having drawn a nine-petaled lotus mandala and having placed nine jars therein, [one should fill them] with one of the substances such as the five products of the cow, milk-tree sap, or decoctions.

Having filled those [vessels] with water, one should worship the desired deity mentioned in the mantra in the central vessel, as well as the deities of the limbs and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇa-devatās) in the eight jars; then, having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times or more,
one should perform the previously described homa using the eight substances offered into the fire, while pouring the remnants [of the oblation] into the vessels.
One should sprinkle the person to be treated (*sādhya*) with the water from the jar using those [mantras].
The meaning is that the person to be treated, who has been overcome by planetary afflictions and the like, will quickly become healthy through that.
He states another application beginning with "on a Sunday" (*bhānuvāre*), etc.: on a Sunday, one [should perform] a single...

Having established [the deity] in a *maṇḍala* such as the *Laśa-sarvatobhadra* and performed the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should worship [the deity] together with the limbs (*sāṅga*) and the enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*). Then, having touched the water-pot (*kalaśa*) while reciting [mantras] a number of times such as one thousand and eight, and having offered oblations with the previously mentioned eight substances the stated number of times, one should complete the rite.
One should bathe the pregnant woman with the water from that jar; the meaning is that by this, an easy delivery will occur. He states another application beginning with "seven," etc.:
if this rite is performed up to seven times, then all calamities are pacified.
All days are indeed Sundays. He states another application beginning with "pañcagavya" (the five products of the cow):

one should boil the *pañcagavya* with four times the amount of ghee. When only the ghee remains, one should pour it [into the vessel]; the cooking is also preceded by the recitation of mantras. After the cooking, [one should perform] eight thousand [recitations].
The meaning is that it should be recited and performed as a ritual application (*prayoga*). He states another application, beginning with "ucca" and so forth:

when the Sun has reached the sign of Pisces in its exaltation (*uccasthāna*), a copper seal (*mudrā*) consecrated with this mantra according to the method described in the sixth chapter of the *Sādhusādhita*—when worn—yields the aforementioned fruit.

The meaning is that one should give it; he states the application of the sūtra with the words "tad-varṇa" and so forth. This [phrase] "by the number of its syllables" (tad-varṇa-saṃkhyayā) connects with both [cases]. Thus, since there are seven mantra-syllables when the seven sūtras are combined, seven knots should be given preceded by the recitation of the mantras; thereafter, [one hundred and] eight...

Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times and likewise offered oblations, one should place the *sampāta* (remnants) therein; having thus consecrated that thread, one should bind it on the hand or other parts of the body. The meaning is that by this, there shall be the removal of all suffering.
He states another application, beginning with "five," etc.: the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) [should be treated] one thousand times with this mantra.

Having placed [the substance] in a vessel made of *bhīmanta* leaves, a lotus leaf, a *pālāśa* leaf, or a *bilva* fruit, one should bury it in the house of another person—whether oneself or someone else—who is to be protected from evil eyes;
then, by means of the perfection of protection (*rakṣāsaṃpat*), the world shall have confidence [in that person]. This is the meaning.

He describes the application of ashes with the words beginning "palāśa" and so forth: having first recited the mantra for each of the twenty-seven substances, such as the bark of the *palāśa* tree and others, and having thrown them into a vessel filled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should perform the rite in the Vaiṣṇava fire consecrated according to the previously mentioned procedure.

One should cook it until it becomes ashes like fire. Then, having meditated upon the deity of the ashes as one's own form, one should consecrate them ten million times by reciting the mantra ten lakh times.
With that, one should smear all the limbs and also place a small amount on the head; by doing so, one accomplishes the rite.

The meaning is that there shall be peace in all directions, the destruction of enemies, the destruction of sins, the attainment of powers such as subjugation (*vaśyatā*), and especially protection for pregnant women, children, and others. [The materials include] the bark of the *palāśa* tree, and the barks of the four milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*): the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa*.
These are: *mahāyaṣṭi* (liquorice), *śrīkhaṇḍa* (sandalwood), *caṃdana*, *ṛddhi*, *pura* (resin), *guggulu*, *kuṅkuma* (saffron), *dyusṛṇa* (turmeric),
*thayāminī* (another type of turmeric), *haridrā*, *kuṣṭha* (well-known as *kūṭhī*),
*bilva* (the fruit of the *bilva* tree or its bark), *apāmārga*, *sarṣapa* (mustard seeds), and *tila* (sesame seeds).

Dūrvā grass, barley, sahadevī, the two types of tulasī— namely green tulasī and black tulasī— lakṣmī (the aforementioned specific creeper), gorocanā, lotus, and the bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, and roots of the bilva and lotus.
The traditionalists maintain that the five-ingredient formulation (pañcāṅga) should be taken. The twenty-seven medicinal herbs consist of *vacā*, cow dung, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and *arkatvak*.
Furthermore, the cooking process should be performed preceded by the recitation of mantras, precisely because of the great difficulty involved.

Regarding the superiority of this protection (*rakṣā*) over the protection of time (*kālarakṣā*), [the author] describes the *pañcagavya-ghṛta* (clarified butter made from the five products of the cow) beginning with the verse starting "mustā... *Vahni* is *citraka*; *yaṣṭī* is *yaṣṭimadhu*; *vṛṣa* is *vāsaka*;
*dārvī* is *dāruharidrā*; *rohiṇī* is *kaṭukī*; and *phalatraya* consists of *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalakī*.

One *prastha* each of *kīvī*, *bībhītaka*, and *āmalaka* should be prepared according to the method described in the medical treatises (*vaidyaka-śāstra*), as it is stated that the medicinal paste (*kalka*) should be one-fourth the quantity of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Thus, the formulation consists of one *kuḍava* of paste. Furthermore, there are five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), each [weighing] one part relative to the clarified butter.
One should cook it until only a *prastha* measure of ghee remains, and then remove it from the fire; thereafter,
having performed the recitation (*japa*) and oblation (*homa*) as before, one should complete the rite with the *saṃpāta* offering.

The meaning of the verse beginning with *daṃdya* is that what has been eaten and vomited shall become a vessel for the aforementioned fruit. He now describes the yantra for warding off calamities, starting with the words "ending in *rāṃ*" (*rāṃtān*), and so forth: having drawn a hexagon, one should place the letters ending in *rāṃ*—that is, the letter *ṭha*—in sequence within the pericarp and the corners thereof.
Having written the Praṇava within the letter *va* situated in the center, and having written the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) in the middle of that,
one should write the six syllables beginning with *sa* inside the *ṭha*s written in the six corners; this wheel is uniquely effective in destroying asthma and fever.
Based on the observation in the *Nārāyaṇīya* that "it removes asthma and fever," he describes another yantra:

having drawn a hexagon and a circle outside of it, one should write the Praṇava together with the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (the sādhya) in the center; having written the remaining six syllables in the six corners, one should place the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in the junctions.

One should write "nācakrāya svāhā hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth; then, having consecrated this [mixture] through recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and the residue of the oblation (saṃpāta), one should place it in the location to be protected, meaning that protection will be complete on all sides. By the word "according to rule" (vidhivat), the previously mentioned fire-oblation and the residue of the oblation [are implied].

In the phrase "dhiḥ smāritaḥ prajaptam," the word *pra* indicates the excellence (*prakarpa*) of the number one thousand and eight, which was previously established; this is shown to apply to the recitation (*japa*). This is likewise stated in another Tantra: "In the center is the Tāra, followed by the Mantra letter by letter in the six corners, and the Aṅgas on the outside."

Whether written on gold, silver, copper, or stone, that wheel, when consecrated according to the prescribed rite and installed, destroys the fear of thieves, planets, and enemies, and provides protection.
Thus, he describes another yantra beginning with the words "nāram" and so forth; having drawn a hexagon, within it...
Having written the letter *ṭha* within the *ṛṇikā*, having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) inside that, and having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth inside that;

having placed the remaining six syllables in the six corners, the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in the joints, and outside of that, upon a circle drawn therefrom, on sixteen-petaled lotuses, [one should place] each one of the sixteen...

One should write the syllabic mantra (śākṣaramantra) that is about to be described; having written a *bhūpura* (fortress-city diagram) outside of that, it is perfected through recitation (*japa*), oblations (*homa*), and ritual offerings (*sampāta*). When worn on the arm, neck, or other parts of the body, it bestows the fruit of liberation—this is the meaning. He describes another yantra with the words beginning with "in the center" (*madhye*) and so forth, forming a hexagon (*ṣaṭkoṇa*).
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with filaments connected at its center;
above that, a sixteen-petaled lotus with filaments connected in a circle;
then, three pathways (vīthīs) formed by four circles with space between each row; and finally, a square as prescribed by the general scriptures.
One should place the Praṇava together with the name of the person to be protected (the sādhya) in the pericarp; the six syllables of the mantra in the six corners;
the vowels in pairs on the eight filaments;
the eight-syllable mantra of Śrī Nārāyaṇa on the eight petals; and the consonants from *ka* onwards in pairs on the sixteen filaments.

Having written the thirty-two syllables of the mantra to be described hereafter—namely, the sixteen syllables of the mantra—upon the sixteen petals, one should place the remaining syllables between each pair of those [sixteen] syllables, joined with the name of the person for whom protection is sought, such as "Perform the protection of Devadatta! (devadattasya rakṣāṃ kuru kuru). Thus, by means of one's own name, the remaining syllables are to be placed in the middle of each [pair]. The auspicious syllables...

Having filled the first row with the two [syllables], and having filled the second row with the Praṇava— which is denoted by the three words because it is composed of the triad of phonemes in the form of A, U, and M— one should then sequentially draw the noose and the goad.

With those two, one should complete the third [enclosure] ending with the word *kiṃjalke*; here, the word *vītam* (surrounded) is to be supplied. One [enclosure] is by means of the *tāra* alone, and the second is by means of the *pāśa* and *aṅkuśa* joined together; thus, the dual number indicates two enclosures. This refers to the sixteen-syllable mantra.

He demonstrates [the mantra] with the words beginning with "tāram": *oṃ namo bhagavate mahāsudarśanāya huṃ phaṭ*. This is a sixteen-syllable mantra. This mantra is also independent (*svatantra*). For this [mantra], everything from the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] up to the ritual application of worship (*pūjā-prayoga*) is as before. However, the yantra is said to be independent.
In another tantra, it is stated: "One should draw a hexagonal wheel; on its spokes, the Sudarśana [mantra];
on the outer petals, either the eight-syllable or the five-syllable [mantra]; outside that, there should be a twelve-spoked [wheel], upon which one should write the twelve-syllable [mantra];
then a sixteen-spoked lotus, upon which one should inscribe the root mantra."
The most excellent preceptor should surround the supreme Mahāsudarśana yantra with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), and likewise surround it externally with the mantra:
*Tāraṃ namo bhagavate mahāsudarśanāya ca mahācakrāya ca mahājvālaṃ dīptarūpaṃ me sarvato rakṣa*.

Having written the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) in the center, and within its belly the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), this is the yantra that bestows all success; thus the Lord himself declared.
Within the body of the hexagon, one should place the *praṇava*, and inside that, the *sādhya*; and in the six corners, the Sudarśana mantra.

Having written the six syllables of the *namaḥ* mantra on the eight petals situated outside that, the eight-syllable *Nārāyaṇa* mantra on the twelve petals written outside that, and the previously mentioned twelve-syllable *Vāsudeva* mantra on those,
one should then write the present root-mantra on the sixteen petals situated outside that. Outside of that—

Having encircled it with the *māyā*-seed syllable (*māṃ*), one should encircle the exterior with the forty-three-syllable mantra: *oṃ namo bhagavate mahāsudarśanāya mahācakrāya mahājvālāya dīptarūpāya sarvato rakṣa rakṣa mahābalāya svāhā*. This is the *yantra* as before.

The meaning is that it becomes accomplished, granting all attainments (*siddhi*). He describes another yantra consisting of seven squares with the words beginning "having drawn lines," etc. Having made eight lines extending from east to west, each with a large interval between them, and having made them long, he joins the tip of the first line with the fourth [mark] on its own side.
Again, having bound [a line] from the tip of the third line to the tip of its own fourth and sixth lines,
and again from the tip of the fifth line to the tip of the eighth line; furthermore, from the rear, having bound the tips of the first, third,
and fifth lines with their respective fourth-line tips, [one proceeds] solely with the second...

Only the seventh line remains; there too, one should take the eastern end of the second line from its own starting point and lead it toward the north, joining it with its own western end. Likewise, one should take the eastern end of the seventh line from its own starting point and lead it toward the south, joining it with its own western end—this is the meaning.
It should be understood that the word *śruti* is to be repeated; the word *śruti* refers to three, while the other [word] refers to four.
Thus, first the fourth from the previous, then the third from the third, and then the fourth—the tip of the line is obtained. However, the teacher Padmapāda [interprets] *śruti* as three.
This is the meaning;

that is to say, one should connect the tip of each first line and so forth with the tip of its own third line, reaching back to the beginning of the first line. This being the case, no line whatsoever [remains unconnected].
Others say that [the fifth line] remains; however, disregarding the first line which serves as the limit for the sixteenth, twentieth, and twenty-fourth lines of the *anuśruti*,
the binding of the fifth line of one's own *tapa* must be performed by means of the fire-limit (*agni-avaccheda*).

Thus they say: there, in the fourth square which is in the center of all, one should write everything in order, including the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) interspersed with the eight-syllable *Sudarśana* mantra;
and in the first square of the first row, the eight [syllables] of Nārāyaṇa.
In the second square, one should write the first quarter-verse of the mantra to be recited later—"O Hṛṣīkeśa"—interlaced with the *kṣara* syllables;

likewise, one should write the second quarter-verse in the same manner. Then, in the third and fifth rows, one should correctly write the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa mantra by alternating [the syllables].
One should write the sixteen-syllable mantra of Sudarśana, interlaced with [the name], as previously extracted,

in the sixth and seventh rows; furthermore, in those positions, one should write the two feet consisting of the third and fourth quarters of the mantra beginning with "Hṛṣīkeśa," interlaced with the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa.

Regarding this, the author of the *Harṣakaumudī* states that one should draw the wheel; some maintain that in all three [versions], the wheel consists of exactly seven syllables per line. By the phrase "as prescribed," it is indicated that in the third and fifth rows, the *Sudarśana* is interspersed with the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
The author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that the drawing of the mantra is not taught here because it belongs to the wheel (*cakra*) of the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

It is well-established among all people that the natural significance (*svārasya*) of the subsequent words lies in the previously mentioned summary, and not in the summary of the meaning to be explained here; therefore, the *sādhya* [is as follows]: [The text continues with the mantra: *oṃ namo bhagavate āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā oṃ kaṇe kaṇe kumārarūpiṇe svāhā*. This is the mantra for the accomplishment of the deity. One should draw the lotus-wheel (*padmacakra*) on a clean cloth, using saffron, sandalwood, or other fragrant substances. In the center of the lotus, one should place the syllable *oṃ*; in its pericarp, the name of the practitioner; and in the eight petals, the eight syllables beginning with *kaṇe*. Outside of that, one should draw a circle of light rays, and outside of that, a circle of vajras. Then, having visualized the deity, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. By this, one will attain the state of a *kumāra-rūpin* (one who possesses the form of a youth). Thus ends the procedure for the drawing of the mantra.

It must be stated that the name is to be spoken first, followed by the sixteen-syllable *vidarbha*; however, this view from the *Padārthadarśa* is not correct. For how could one speak of a single *cakra* as having sixteen syllables in one place and seven syllables in another? Thus, the mantra would be divided.

In this regard, according to the opinion of the author of the *Ārṣaka-harṣakaumudī*, who states that "the wheel is the mantra," some hold the view that it is the sixteen-syllable mantra alone that possesses the nature of the wheel-mantra;
however, in their view, there is a lack of intrinsic consistency (*asvārasya*) with the root text. Therefore, [this applies] everywhere to the sixteen-syllable mantra.

This is to be accepted based on the inherent force (*svārasya*) of the root text; however, there is this distinction: that which is joined with the *sādhya* in the middle should be written correctly in the third and fifth squares as interlaced (*vidarbhitam*) with eight syllables, because the phrase "interlaced with eight syllables" (*aṣṭārṇavidarbhitam*) has that very meaning. Thus it is understood.

He teaches the *Sthāṇu* mantra with the words beginning "Sthāne," etc. This mantra is indeed the very nature of the Supreme; though independent, it is here proclaimed as having five limbs through its four quarters: "Agni is the head, the eyes are the moon and sun, and the ears are the quarters."

The Vedas are its function; Vāyu is its breath; the universe is its heart; the earth is its two feet; and it is the inner self of all beings—this is the meditation. Reciting this ten hundred thousand times as a preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) results in the destruction of all sins, universal peace, and the removal of the afflictions caused by all malevolent planets. All...
"The ancients have stated that the fruit [of this practice] is the destruction of Rākṣasas. As for the wearing of the yantra:

having made it into a small amulet (*gulikā*), having encased it in lac, and having performed its consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) through recitation (*japa*), oblation (*homa*), and the pouring of the *saṃpāta* [remnants], one should place it in a vessel of gold or other precious materials and then employ it.
This [work] is common to all yantras. It was composed by him whose mother was Udyotamatī, who possessed virtuous qualities; whose father was named Māpati; who was born into the Paṇṭhaka lineage;
whose birthplace was Kūrmmācala; and who made Vārāṇasī—the abode of Acyuta and the site of Cācyuta’s valor—an excellent place of refuge.
[The multitude of kings became that very embodiment in the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*.

Now, desiring to set forth the mantras beginning with *Puruṣottama*, [the author], for the sake of establishing the engagement of the listeners, first demonstrates that [this work] is a means to achieve a desired goal, and addresses the disciples...

He makes a formal declaration (*pratijānīte*) for the sake of achieving concentration (*avadhāna*), characterized by the severance of the mind from other objects, beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth;

the meaning is that immediately after the recollection of this [mantra], by means of the description of the *Śrīviṣṇumantra*, which possesses the nature of a mantra sharing the common attributes of Viṣṇuhood, [he speaks of] Śrī Puruṣottama...

Because of the metaphorical attribution of non-difference [between the mantra and the deity] due to the deity being Śrī Puruṣottama himself, there is the recitation of the mantra as "Śrī Puruṣottama. Its meaning is either "those who possess Śrī (fortune/glory) and are the Supreme Persons (Puruṣas)," or "that by which the worship of Śrī Puruṣottama—the Lord of the worlds—is performed. Śrī-puruṣāḥ means those who possess Śrī; puruṣāḥ means persons; uttamāḥ means supreme or most excellent; and the meaning is that [it is so called] because of that through which His worship is performed. Of Śrī Puruṣottama, the Lord of the worlds...

Since it was established during the occasion of describing the deityhood of this very [Purushottama], here too there is the statement of His being the root of the universe; thus, in the formulation of the mantra and other such utterances, the mention is "the deity Śrī Puruṣottama is the origin of the worlds," and not "the deity Śrī Puruṣottama."

Only this much should be noted: based on the authority of the *Saṃhitās* and other sources stating that "this Kārtavīryārjuna was the god Viṣṇu, the emperor (*cakravartin*)," the venerable Vyāsa of Kāśī employs the expression: "Śrī Kārtavīryārjuna is Viṣṇu, the emperor, and the deity."

The authors of the *Dama-paddhati* accepted this; yet, why is there no mention of the sage Śeṣa’s divine splendor and other qualities? If Dattātreya is declared to be the sage of this twenty-syllable mantra, then [it should be] in the *Saṃhitā*.

It should be stated that this is because the Sage is heard of with such specific qualifications in that very [text]; however, since the Sage is taught in his absolute state alone in the Rudrayāmala, the Uḍḍāmarakavaca, the Stavarāja, and other works, the mention of him there is for the purpose of praise and not for the sake of establishing a formal ritual application.

Otherwise, how could the mention of even a sage—possessing divine splendor like that of a deity, such as Viṣṇu or a Cakravartin—be universally accepted? This can be determined with certainty. However, it should be understood that the application of the ṛṣi and other [limbs] for this mantra occurs precisely in the manner described by the words "of this mantra," and so forth.

Otherwise, if the connection with Puruṣottama— characterized by having Puruṣottama as the deity— is understood through such means as the mention of the *gavākya* (the "cow-sentence") or the mantra of Śrī Puruṣottama,
it would follow that the statement of Agni as the deity is redundant.

The Blessed One has thus declared that this mantra consists of twenty-three syllables; this same principle should be understood to apply to other mantras as well. It bestows enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) through its excellence, its majesty, and its constant practice; it is therefore kept secret from those who lack qualification.
Since no fruit is seen even from this [practice] when it is not properly attended to, there might arise a loss of faith among Vaiṣṇavas;

therefore, this effort at concealment by the Vaiṣṇavas is intended to ensure that those who lack the requisite qualification do not obtain this [knowledge], and not for the sake of fruits such as liberation, lest others [attain them]. Thus, there are two [purposes].

Since hatred toward those of great soul, and especially toward Vaiṣṇavas, is impossible, the remainder [of the mantra] beginning with *nā* and so forth has the meaning already explained; it refers to the essential nature [of the deity]. Thus, *oṃ klīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ puruṣottamāya pratirūpalakṣmīnivāsāya sakalajagad-*.

*trāsaya trāsaya huṃ śirase svāhā*; *pramardaya pramardaya huṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *pradhvaṃsaya pradhvaṃsaya huṃ kavacāya huṃ*; *astrāya phaṭ*.

The five-limbed mantras ending with *phaṭ* are to be placed in sequence upon the eight locations consisting of the head, the two eyes, the throat, the heart, the navel, the two thighs, the two shanks, and the two feet; however, for the pairs beginning with the eyes, only one syllable of the respective mantra obtained by that sequence is to be placed.

One should not forget what was previously stated regarding the "sitting by means of the Vṛtti. Having distributed the quarters of the Vedic mantra beginning with "brāhmaṇo'sya" one by one upon the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet,
and having first displayed their respective mudrās, one should [worship] the fourfold group beginning with the conch using their own respective mantras.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the visualization of the weapons (*āyudhadhyāna*) at the locations of the *nyāsa*. Regarding the visualization of the weapons: in the first [set], they are on the right and left shoulders; in the second, on the two upper arms; and in the last, on the two elbows—so says the *Sārasaṃgraha*.
However, according to the *Lipi-nyāsa*, one should perform the placement on the head, eyes, throat, heart, navel, two thighs, two shanks, and the two feet.

In one's own body, [one should assign] the Brahmins and other castes to the mouth, hands, thighs, and feet respectively; likewise, the discs and other weapons to the hands. Then, having introduced the root mantra, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Brahmins; Ṭaṃ, obeisance to the Kṣatriyas; Śrīṃ, obeisance to the Vaiśyas; Śū..."

They state another method of assignment (*nyāsa*) beginning with "Salutation to the *drebhyaḥ*," and it is possible to connect even the portion [of the text] beginning with "the Brāhmaṇas and others" with the root-text as a single syntactic unit through the mantra portion beginning with "The Brāhmaṇa is yours.
The milk-exuding trees are four: the *aśvattha*, the *udumbara*, the *plakṣa*, and the *tuṭa*.
Having first uttered *raḥ*, one should perform ten thousand *homa* offerings for each of the eight substances, such as *vilva* and others, using ghee;

by this, the requirement of performing a *homa* equal to one-tenth of the recitation (*japa*) is fulfilled. Having projected the form [of the deity] upon the seat described in the *Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara* [mantra] using the root mantra, one should worship the deity with the sixteen and other types of ritual services (*upacāra*).
Having worshipped the *aṅgas* on the filaments, and the four *śaktis* beginning with Śrī on the cardinal petals,
and having worshipped Aniruddha and Viśvakasena on the intermediate petals of the northeast,
one should worship Indra and the other [directional deities] as before in the outer square; thus it is established.

He states Manu’s ritual applications beginning with the words "ḍapūrva" and so forth: having prepared two *carus*, one should offer an oblation with one of those two *carus* and pour the remnants (*saṃpāta*) into the second *caru*.
Furthermore, the oblation is not to be made with the *caru* alone, but rather with it mixed with *dūrvā* grass and clarified butter. Eight [times...]

Having brought lotus-stalk fibers from a famous pond and tied eight knots with this mantra, one should empower them by pouring oblations into the fire until they cease; when this lotus-fiber thread is bound upon the arm, it shall destroy untimely death and other such evils—this is one application. [Now follows] the Gopāla mantra...

He demonstrates [the mantra] with the words beginning with "Kṛṣṇa": *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. This is the eighteen-syllable mantra. Its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *klīṃ*, and its power (*śakti*) is *svāhā*.
As it has been said, we shall explain that the seed-syllable and power of this mantra are the Discus-wielder (*cakrī*) and the Thunderbolt-wielder (*śakrī*).

The seed-syllable *manetrapradīptasapradyumna* is proclaimed; this mantra is Pradyumna, the deluder of the world. *Haṃsa* joined with *medo* and *vaktra*, followed by *potrī* and the rest—this is declared to be the four-syllabled Śakti, who is worshipped by all the hosts of gods, like the fire.

The meaning of *bhākāmadeya* is as follows: it is joined with the letter *ca* (the first consonant), the letter *ka*, and the letter *śa*; it is joined with the left eye, which is the fourth vowel (*ī*); *Pradyumna* is the *anusvāra*;
and because the placement on the head of *Pradyumna* joined with the *anusvāra* is prescribed, it is likewise the seed-syllable of Kāma.
This is a digression: that which has become so arrogant is this Pradyumna, the creator of the world’s delusion; though independent, he possesses a mantra.

*Haṃsaḥ saḥ*, *me do vaḥ*, *vaktra-vṛttam ā*—from the conjunction of these [syllables], there is the attainment of its own form (*svākāra*). By means of the *potrī* (the boar), the letter *ha*; by the eye... [the letter *kṣa*].
Joined by the *syād* prefix and the suffix *nāmukha*, and possessing the power formed by two syllables of the *yuga-aṇa* [mantra],
it is called "that which is to be given by Kāma" (*kāmadeya*); thus, the four preceding limbs were previously stated to have four syllables each,
while the fifth has two syllables— so he says "four."
The connection is that he was "deluding the daughters of the Upanandas by the thousand" through [the ritual] beginning with *rityādi*.

Furthermore, he was one for whom "peacock-feather ornaments"—ornaments made from peacock feathers—were dear; such is the meaning of the phrase *caṭṭāvataṃsapriyam*. By the expression *yathānyāyam* ("in accordance with the rule"), it is indicated that the procedure should follow the method prescribed in other tantras regarding the specific locations.

It has been stated that one should recite the excellent ten-syllable mantra forty thousand times, seated individually in each of these places: on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, at the root of a bilva tree, in water reaching the heart, in a cow-pen, in a temple of Viṣṇu, beneath an aśvattha tree, and on the shore of the ocean.
The eighteen-syllable [mantra] is declared to have a numerical value of two times the Vedas (84) when its individual components are considered;
thus the place has been described, and we shall explain the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) further on.
Having worshipped the limbs (*aṅga*) upon the filaments (*kesara*), one should worship the eight queens of Kālindī upon the petals.
Having worshipped the elephants beginning with Airāvata at the front of the venerable leaves, one should worship Indra and the other [directional guardians] in the square;

he states the ritual applications starting with "with Lakṣmī-flowers" and so forth. Where the number for the fire-oblation (*homa*) is not specified, there, according to the gravity of the task and other factors, it should be performed by the command [of the deity] in numbers ranging from a thousand up to ten thousand (*ayuta*).

This same procedure applies to the *tarpaṇa* (libation) as well. Regarding the *dhāraṇā-yantroddhāra* (the drawing of the retention-diagram), one should write a hexagon according to the instructions beginning with "the *piṇḍa*," etc.;

then, having written the *piṇḍa-bīja* in its pericarp (*karṇikā*), the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) within that, and having likewise encircled that seed-syllable in the pericarp with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*), [one proceeds] to the six corners of the hexagon.

Having written each letter of the six-syllable mantra individually, and having written one syllable at a time from the ten-syllable mantra upon the ten petals of the ten-petalled lotus drawn outside of that, and having encircled it with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), one should [place] the six... constructed above the circle outside of that.

Having written the vowels one by one upon the filaments of a ten-petalled lotus, and the sixteen-syllable mantra letters upon its petals; and having written the consonants beginning with *ka* upon the filaments of a thirty-two-petalled lotus arranged outside that circle—
with all the remaining [consonants] on its filaments and the final [consonant] on its petals— [one should proceed].
One should write the thirty syllables of the mantra one by one; having encircled them with a noose and a goad joined together,
one should draw two city-walls (bhūpura) outside that, joined to each other,
and within their corners, one should write the syllables of the eight-syllable mantra one by one.
The meaning is that it is for the sake of liberation. Furthermore, this yantra has been extracted from the *Gautamīyasaṃhitā* with certain variations here and there.
Alternatively, I shall now describe the Great Yantra (*mahāyantra*), which bestows all desired fruits;
by the mere wearing of which, what on this earth is not accomplished? The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is a triangle.

Having drawn a hexagon, one should write the six-syllable mantra outside of it; there, one should draw a circle and an eight-petaled lotus joined with the eight-syllable mantra. Outside of that, on a sixteen-petaled lotus, one should place the sixteen-syllable Kṛṣṇa-mantra, joined with the ten-syllable mantra on a ten-petaled lotus.

Then, one should draw an eighteen-petaled lotus; within that, [the mantra] of eighteen syllables; outside of that, a thirty-two-petaled lotus known as the *ānuṣṭubha*; and outside of that, one should draw a circle. Therein, one should write the *piṇḍa-bīja* as an encircling perimeter on all sides. Having completed a circle outside of that, [one should draw] a vessel (*pātrī*).
One should encircle the *kānta* [circle]; then, having made two circles, one should encircle them with a noose (*pāśa*) and a goad (*aṅkuśa*).

Outside of that, there is one circle and a square with thunderbolts (*vajra*). O best of sages, out of compassion, this great yantra has been described; it may be written on gold, birch bark, silver, or copper.

Having prepared ink from the eight fragrant substances (aṣṭagandha) mixed with mercury, one should draw [the yantra] with a golden needle. Having established the vital breaths (prāṇas) according to the prescribed rite, one should perform a thousand oblations (homa). At the conclusion of that, having recited the mantra the same number of times, one should indeed wear the yantra. By the mere wearing of this, one becomes a conqueror of cities on earth in person.

One is liberated from impure deeds and even the most terrible sufferings; having attained eternal peace, one reaches that supreme state. For women, what is not accomplished by wearing [this] on the left hand? Even a barren woman obtains a son who lives for a hundred years. Śa[mbhu said:]...
Having drawn a *śricakra* and installed a water-pot as before, one should place the yantra in its center;

by sprinkling [water] from that, one shall accomplish everything. A Brahmin shall become a seer of divine visions, a Kṣatriya shall become a sovereign of the earth, a Vaiśya shall become prosperous, and a Śūdra shall obtain his desires.

"O Sage, listen with devotion to me as I describe the *piṇḍabīja* known as the *gopāla-piṇḍa*, which one rejoices in after death. Having thus begun, the method for extracting this *piṇḍabīja* is stated in the *Gautamasaṃhitā*.

The seed-syllable of Gopāla is the seed-syllable of Kāma (klīṃ), which should be uttered first, followed by "Kṛṣṇa" joined with the fourth case-ending; likewise, "Govinda" is declared with the fourth case-ending. One should then recite the ten-syllable mantra. This eighteen-syllable mantra is remembered as more secret than the secret. (Klīṃ)

The eighteen-syllable mantra, "kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopījanavallabhāya svāhā," is stated in the Devasaṃhitā for one who has released the knots; the six mantras beginning with Piṇḍa will be described hereafter. [In the fire-pit] consisting of a pair of triangles and a hexagon, there is the syllable 'rasa' (sa). The hexagon...
The perishable (*kṣara*) is in the sixteen petals of the *vikṛti* [lotus]; the pair of petals of the *vikṛti* is in the thirty-two-petaled [lotus];
and the four corners of the earth-fortress (*bhūpura*) are in the three [triangles]. Thus, the writing of twenty-eight syllables bears fruit in the two earth-fortresses that are beyond [the lotuses].
Some say that writing the eight syllables in three octagonal corners—two pairs of them interspersed with *sparśa* (stop) consonants, as well as a single *śeva*—is effective.
Now, he extracts the six mantras beginning with the *piṇḍa* in sequence, starting with "pañca" etc.: *dharā*, *laḥ*, *iraḥ*, *yaḥ*.

*Tapo-sthita-pañcāntako gaḥ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā*—this is the six-syllable mantra. *Gopījana-vallabhāya svāhā*—this is the ten-syllable mantra. *Oṃ namaḥ kṛṣṇāya devakī-putrāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—this is the sixteen-syllable mantra. *Glyauṃ klīṃ namo bhaga...* [The text continues].

The thirty-two-syllable mantra is: *oṃ namo nandaputrāya bālavapuṣe śyāmalāya gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. The eight-syllable mantra is: *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya govindāya*. Regarding the Gopāla Piṇḍa-mantra, the procedure for the *tārpya* (offering cloth) and other rites is as follows: [the seer is] the Ṛṣi...

The Vedic meter is Gāyatrī, the deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the seed-syllable and power are for the two throats, and the kīlaka is said to be "Nurpam. One should fashion the six limbs with the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels. [One should meditate on] Kṛṣṇa, who has gone to Vṛndāvana and is seated upon a jeweled throne.
At the base of that Kadamba tree, he beheld the Lord Vanamālī, resplendent with the cowherd women, accompanied by hosts of sages such as Nārada who were eager for the essence of divine song,
shining with jewel ornaments, and his hands radiant with the conch and discus.

O best of sages, having thus meditated upon the flute made of Brahma-wood held in both hands, the self-controlled practitioner should recite the mantra ten thousand times while focusing on the target.
He should perform ten thousand oblations with white milk-rice (pāyasa).
For the practitioner who worships in this manner, all supernatural powers (siddhis) come into his very hands. [With] white...
By performing oblations with *sumana* flowers, one attains mastery of speech before long; by oblations with *karṇikāra* flowers, all forms of prosperity shall arise.
If one drinks pure water consecrated with this mantra every morning, one becomes a poet, eloquent, retentive of what has been heard, and omniscient before long. Of this...

"O Mantrin, what is not accomplished merely by sitting upon this seat? Having enjoyed excellent pleasures here together with sons and grandsons, at the end, the mantrin shall go to that supreme, blissful abode. And among the components of the mantra, the fourth is the fourth [vowel], which is like the nasal sound (anusvāra)."

The *kīlaka* (stake) is the seed-syllable *ga*; the *śakti* is the syllable *la*; and the *śakti* is the syllable *au*. Thus, the established meaning is that [the mantra] is the stake. The six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mantras are: *glyāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *glyīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth. The visualization (*dhyāna*) begins with "Vṛndāvana," and so on.
The number of recitations for the *puraścaraṇa* is one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*); thus, by the words "in this manner" and so forth, three applications have been described.
The remainder is clear in meaning. Here, the method of worship is like that of the ten-syllable mantra;
however, the worship diagram (*pūjā-yantra*) is found in the *Gautamīya*, [which removes] all sufferings arising from defects such as lust and anger.

They call it a *yantra* because of its binding (*yantraṇāt*); in this, the God, being worshipped, is pleased. A lotus with eight petals, auspicious, square, possessing excellent characteristics, endowed with four doors, and having a pericarp containing the seed-syllable (*kāma*)—this is called the general *yantra* for the eighteen-syllable [mantra].

Now, one should draw a square with four doors, provided with an eight-petaled lotus; in the center of the hexagon, one should write the six-syllable supreme mantra encircled by the eighteen-syllable Kāmākhyā mantra within the hexagon. O fortunate one, this yantra has been told to you out of compassion.
In this regard, there is another specific detail: having recited the *piṇḍa-mantra* of Gopāla four hundred thousand times,

and having completed the ritual actions ending with the fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), consecration (*abhiṣecana*), and feeding of Brahmins— each performed one-tenth the number of recitations— one should place Gaṇeśa, Śukra (Bhārgava), Agni, and Brahmā in the four corners of this king of yantras.
Having worshipped the four deities consisting of the [three] jewels and the self with their respective individual name-mantras as taught in the Āgamas,
and following the general procedure for the yantra as well as the other method to be described hereafter, by wearing this consecrated king of yantras, one [attains] all...

One may attain even that which is obscured by delusion; this is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "Adorned with the five ends and the *dhara* [letter], this is declared to be the seed-mantra of the *piṇḍa*, the supreme bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). One should recite this four hundred thousand times, and thereafter perform the *daśāṃśa* [offering]."

One should satisfy [the deities] with a tenth part [of the offerings], perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with a tenth part, and likewise feed the Brahmins with a tenth part, following this sequence. One should worship Gaṇeśa, Bhāskara, Rudra, and Gaurī, preceded by their respective mantras, at the intermediate directions of the King of Yantras.

By merely holding this *sāra* (essence), one will certainly become a knower of the three periods of time; whatever one desires for oneself, all that shall be accomplished here—of this there is no doubt. There is no mantra or yantra equal to this, O lady of virtuous vows; it has been told to you solely out of affection.

The recitation of four hundred thousand [mantras], along with the performance of the *homa* sacrifice consisting of one-tenth of that number as a preliminary part (*pūrvāṅga*) for the sake of attaining mastery (*adhāraṇa*),
is indeed distinct from the recitation performed for the purpose of *puraścaraṇa*; for according to such statements as "when it is performed,
it shall be exactly as declared in the ritual manual (*kalpa*)," the recitation for *puraścaraṇa* also consists of four hundred thousand.
However, regarding the application of specific numbers, the statement beginning with "as stated for the created Kalpa" and so forth does not apply;

this is because such a rule is established only after commencing the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rites), and in reality, as previously stated, the rule concerning the number of recitations according to the age (*yuga*) does not apply to the mantras of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This is the summary. He describes another yantra with the words beginning "prāk" (east) and so forth: having drawn four lines—one from east to west and one from south to north—there are nine squares.
In the four corners, there are four tridents, and in the central square, there is a circle.

The *gaṃcakra* should be constructed as follows: having first written the second quarter-verse, "tameva devaṃ devam," which is located at the end of the first circle within the central square, one should subsequently write the first quarter-verse, "taṃ sakīdevadevetam.
After that, [one writes] the second [quarter-verse] outside of that.

Having first written the fourth quarter, "yavalayetaṃ khyāto devakīsuta iti," and then having subsequently written the third quarter, "taṃ raktarūḍhatākhyātam," how can this meaning be obtained from the root text? For how could there be [meaning] from that which is not obtainable from the root text?

If it is argued that this constitutes validity (*prāmāṇya*), listen: the meaning of the root [of the word *madhyama*] is established as "that which has the middle as its beginning and end. For a verse-mantra (*śloka-mantra*) consists of four quarters (*pāda*); among these, the second and third quarters are the "middle" ones. Thus, [the term] "having the middle as its beginning" (*madhyapūrva*) refers to the first quarter.

The phrase "syamadhyāntam" means "ending with the letter *da* in the middle. Regarding the instruction "one should write," this connects specifically to the word "likhitvā" (having written). Writing starting from the central square is already established by general scriptural authority; therefore, it is not mentioned here as it is merely like the initial writing performed by practitioners.

One should write the first half of the verse in reverse order starting from the second line above; likewise, one should write the second half in reverse order starting from the second line below. Thus, by the transposition of the feet, the hidden meaning of the stated syllables is revealed.

By stating that "one should write the *pikākāka* [syllables] in the first enclosure (*valaya*) starting from the front half in reverse order, and likewise write the second half in the second enclosure," he has taught the very reversal of the two enclosures. Surrounding that, in the eight squares, starting from the front square—

Having written the syllables of the previously mentioned eight-syllable mantra in a clockwise direction, and having written the twelve-syllable mantra individually in each of the four directions outside of that, the authors of the *Harṣadīpikā* state that the mantra is encircled once by repeating it four times. Now, [one might ask]: why?

If it is argued that this view has been refuted by the author of the *Padārthadīpikā* on the grounds that the meaning of the expression "ending with that" (*tadantam*)—namely, "the middle and what precedes it"—is impossible, then what of it? For we have already established the validity of this very meaning in the relevant context; moreover, in his own view, the expression "ending with that" would likewise be untenable.

One should write [the letters] starting from the *lagna* up to the northeast (*īśāna*), because there is no instruction for writing up to the center (*madhya*), because no other action is prescribed, and because it is impossible to connect this [action] elsewhere; and since there is no explicit statement such as "one should cause [him] to recite" regarding that which stands in the middle— either in the middle or within the middle— one should supply the ellipsis by means of the word "recite."
It appears to me that even though the purpose is to state that one should first draw [the figure] with a necklace in the middle and then recite from the center of the elephant,
the author of the *Pādārthādarśa* has combined them as two lines facing east and west,
and two lines facing south and north.
The four corners described at the base are properly arranged;

joined with spikes (śūla) rising from the corners, and by drawing four diagonal lines (karṇasūtra) outward from the corners of the central square, it is fashioned into the shape of a trident (śūla). This is joined with a pair of circles, one inside and one outside.

A second circle, touching the tips of all the lines, must be drawn between that [first] circle and the central square; thus, the central square is "endowed with two such circles. Beginning the writing from the central square and ending there means residing in the central square.
The meaning is "attainment. Regarding that, the sequence for writing the syllables is as follows:

having written the first three syllables in the three central squares starting from the middle and extending toward the east, one then writes two syllables in the two squares on either side of the diagonal line within the space between the two circles in the southeast (āgneyī) direction.

Then, in the two upper compartments to the right, the letters *e*, *ka*, and *ra* are to be read; however, the letter *ta* is to be read as being situated in the middle. This is the first quarter-verse (*pāda*).
Then, by reading the letters from the middle compartment through the two compartments to the right, the three-lettered characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) "taṃ veda" is produced.
In the south-western corner, one should write the two syllables "va-re" on both sides of the middle line;

in the western upper and lower compartments, one should write the two syllables "re-ta," while the letter *taṃ* should be read as situated in the middle. Thus the second quarter is completed. Then, the middle—
Having read the three syllables situated to the west of the central square, those two syllables whose nature is *rata* (joy),
and likewise the syllable *taṃ* situated in the middle— thus is the third quarter. Then,
having read the three syllables situated to the north of the central square, that which is known as *svarūpa*...

Having produced the three syllables [of the mantra], one should write the two syllables "De-va" in the two squares on both sides of the central line in the northeast corner (Īśāna). Then, one should read the syllables written in the east from top to bottom, ending at the central square; this is the fourth quarter, beginning with "parastāt."
Outside the central square, at the end of the first circle, two squares remain on each side of the diagonal line (karṇasūtra) in every corner; thus, when combined across all corners,
the eight corners are established, and therein, in sequence, the eight-syllable mantra of Gopāla...
The meaning is that one should write the twelve syllables. Subsequently, after writing the eight-syllable mantra,

one should write the twelve syllables of Vāsudeva on the outside of the second circle drawn outside that [first circle], by way of being connected to the four cardinal-direction cells of the eight cells produced by the [intersecting] tridents.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the drawing of the eight-syllable mantra, the tridents (śūla) should be placed outside the human form (nṛvat), because they are attached to the base (mūla) precisely by way of achieving the shape of a trident; thus they say that for the twelve-syllable [mantra], there are twelve [tridents] outside the human form. Now, as for the thirty-two syllables of the mantra here...
Otherwise, how would the root text—"one should not write the phonemes (*varṇa*) of the verse"—be consistent?

For this very reason, if [the verse were written out], there would be the undesirable consequence of breaking the writing of all the letters that constitute the thirty-two syllables of the *śloka*-mantra. In cases where the attainment of the fruit occurs solely from the writing of the entire mantra...

From such observations as, "A word lacking its accent, whether by way of accent or syllable, when incorrectly employed, does not convey that meaning," it is implied by the phrase "lacking a syllable" (*varṇa*) that even a mantra deficient by a single syllable does not express the intended meaning; how much less so, then, in the case of a deficiency of many syllables? Therefore, this [position] is rooted solely in recklessness.

If it is argued that this view has been refuted by the author of the *Harṣakaumudī* according to the method of extracting the ritual procedure (*vidhi-yantroddharaṇa*), do not say so; for even when certain letters are written by way of abbreviation (*tantra*), the absence of writing is not thereby concealed. Indeed, what is done by way of abbreviation does not become undone. This, however, is...

In the manner previously described, one should repeatedly write the twelve syllables of my mantra upon the twelve lines that have arisen; this is the inherent intention of the root text. In brief, there is no stronger authority than the *Navāvināvalī* regarding the repetition of the mantra. He describes another yantra with the verse beginning with "śloka," and so forth.

Having prepared sixty-four squares on a birch-bark leaf by means of nine lines extending east-west and nine lines extending north-south, one should [arrange the syllables] in sequence starting from the tenth square of the first decade:
*kṣī*, *ra*, *go*, *ma*, *ya*, *kṣa*, *ra*, *kṣa*, *mā*, *kṣa*, *mā*, *kṣa*, *ra*, *ga*, *mā*, *no*, *mā*, *gā*, *o*, *ya*, *kṣa*.

The meaning is that, having filled four rows of various letters beginning with *gakṣakṣagakṣa* on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*), one should turn it over and write that very same verse-mantra (*śloka-mantra*) in sequence, starting from the southwestern (*nairṛtya*) square;
this is done in order to eliminate any confusion regarding the letters.

The combination of these two is formed as follows: first, the letter *ṇa* followed by *indu* (the moon, i.e., *u*) and *bhṛgu* (Mercury, i.e., *ga*), joined with *śruti* (the Vedas, i.e., four, *ca*) and *khādi* (beginning with the sky, i.e., *ha*), and ending with *dṛk* (the eye, i.e., one, *ka*).

Thus, *ṅkuca* is formed. Then, in the phrase "O God" (*devāte*), when *diśiva* (the ten directions, i.e., *da*) and *bhaga* (fortune, i.e., *bha*) are at the beginning and the end respectively, that three-syllable word [starting with *ṅkuca*] is to be spoken;

thereafter, the word *varapadānta* (ending in the word *vara*, i.e., *ra*) follows, and finally the word *tapas* (*ta-pa-sa*). Thus, the mantra is: **ṄKUCADAVARABHAGĀDĀNTATAPE SA**. (Note: This appears to be a cryptic instruction for constructing a specific Vedic or Tantric mantra through the permutation of syllables and numerical codes.)

The mantra beginning with the first vowel (A), joined with the sixth (Ū) and the letter preceded by the fire-letter (Ra), followed by the three letters in reverse order (Va-Ta-Ka), then the letter preceded by the forest (Na), and ending with the letter preceding the eye (Pha), combined with the final letter of the alphabet (Kṣa)—this is the mantra of Devakī’s son, consisting of eighteen syllables, which has been declared to provide protection for children. (Note: The reconstructed mantra is *Oṃ Ū Va-Ta-Ka-Na-Pha Kṣāḥ Svāhā*.)

The syllables *na*, *na*, *ā*, *kha*, *anta*, *ma*, *rut*, *vi*, *ut*, *krā*, *ntāḥ*, *pu*, *naḥ*, *ar*, *ṇa*, *kā*, *dhu*, *va*, *m*, *a*, *mī*, *ra*, *kṣe*, *tya*, *to*, *mā*, *kṣa*, *yu*, *ke*, *te*, *ve*, *u*, *t*, *kra*, *ma*, *taḥ*, *pu*, *naḥ*, *ca*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *pā*, *dyar*, *ṇaḥ*, *sa*, *vi*, *śvaḥ*, *svaraḥ*, *mā*, *no*, *ge*, *ti*. Then one should utter four syllables in reverse order: *ya*, *kṣā*.
Then, this *drakṣa* mantra, endowed with its sequence,

was taught by Yadunāyaka as being capable of protecting cattle and other purposes; by writing it on birch bark or similar materials and wearing it on one's arm, the pacification of all diseases and other benefits are accomplished.

As it was said, O Gautamī: "Now I shall describe the yantra which bestows both seen and unseen fruits. Having divided the ground from east to north, one should lay down nine lines each way; thus sixty-four squares are produced. From the northeast (Īśāna) to the southwest (Rākṣasa), and from the southwest to the northeast..."
One should draw a diagram consisting of two triangles and the syllables of the mantra originating from the Anuṣṭubh meter;
this yantra, known as Sarvatobhadra, which pacifies all diseases and bestows all human goals, should be inscribed according to the prescribed rules upon birch bark or other suitable materials.

"Always held by Dhṛtabāhu, bestowing the fruits of all desires, fashioned upon a board made of *khadira* wood, and placed in a cow-pen—it provides protection, slays thieves and plagues, and is carried by cows along with their calves. Thus he extracts the single-syllable mantra of desire, beginning with "Brahma... and so forth.

The etymological derivation of this seed-syllable (*bīja*) is stated in the *Gautamīya-tantra*: "The entire universe is devoured by the syllable *klīm*"; thus says the *Śruti-śira*. From the letter *la* arises the earth-element;
from the letter *ka*, the origin of water; from the letter *ī*, fire is produced; and from the *nāda*, wind [is produced].

The birth of the moon arises from space; thus, Manu is said to consist of the elements (*bhūtātmaka*) because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause. He is the one Brahman, the earth, and the water.
Seated upon that seat which is his very form, he is established there; the syllable *ka* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).

According to the statement in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, "The power of the long hook (*dīrghīkora-śakti*) is the fourth seed-power (*bīja-śakti*)," there is a set of four [attributes] beginning with the goad (*aṅkuśa*), extending from the upper left to the upper right. Regarding the seat (*pīṭha*) to be described later, the deity of the seat consists of [the principles] from Maṇḍūka up to Paratattva.
The meaning is that one should worship those aforementioned [deities] and then worship the *pīṭha-śaktis* (seat-powers) to be described hereafter.

[The sequence is: not [starting with] Aśvamohinī and so on, nor Ākledinī and so on, but rather with the *tāna-vak-līṃ-kāma-yoga-pīṭhāya namaḥ* as the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*). Here, the limb-worship (*aṅga-pūjā*) is performed upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Raghavabhaṭṭa maintains that the phrase "the limbs in the same [place] where the pericarp was seen" refers to the pericarp; however, the author of the root text (Mūlakṛt), following his own natural inclination, holds that it refers to the filaments (*kesara*).
This is because the worship of those [filaments] occurs there, whereas the intention regarding worship in another place refers to another location, namely the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

The form [of the deity] would indeed have been shown; since the filaments (*kesara*) are already established by the previously mentioned convention, their omission is appropriate. Likewise, the limbs [of the deity] are [placed] on the filaments, while at the base of the petals—in the four directions starting from the east and in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*)—is the presence of the Deity.

Then one should worship the five arrows with the following mantras: *Taḥ*—obeisance to the one who causes swift drying; *Drīṃ*—obeisance to the one who causes delusion; *Klīṃ*—obeisance to the one who causes inflaming; *Nlūṃ Tānlūṃ*—obeisance to the one who causes burning; *Saḥ*—obeisance to the one who causes intoxication. Thus, with these mantras, one should worship [the arrows] with prostrations and salutations.

Having worshipped the eight Śaktis, beginning with Mudrā Anaṅgarūpā and ending with Anaṅgadīpikā, in the middle of the petals; and having worshipped the sixteen Śaktis, beginning with Yuvati and ending with Māyāvatī, on the petals of the sixteen-petaled lotus constructed outside of that— at the tips of the petals.

Having worshipped the sixteen attendants beginning with Śoka and ending with Mada, one should then worship outside of that, in the eight directions, the eight beloved ones beginning with Parabhṛtī and ending with Bhāva; and [one should worship] the female attendants beginning with Caturasrā and Kausumalatī and ending with Madotkaṭā.
Having worshipped [the deity] within the *ṣkaṃsa*, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as Vajra and the others, in the two square pathways as before;
thus he describes this ninth enclosure (*navāvaraṇa*) through the application of mantras, beginning with the words "In the Aśoka tree," and so forth.
He describes the yantra beginning with the words "Kāma," and so forth, having previously arranged the six-spoked [wheel].
Having drawn a circle preceded by eight petals, then outside that another circle preceded by eight petals, and again outside that another circle preceded by eight petals,

and having drawn a *bhūpura* (fortified city) outside of that, one should place the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), with the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in its center.

One should write the six limbs (*aṅga*) in the six triangles of the day-and-night [lotus]; then, on its petals, the syllables of the *Gāyatrī* mantra three by three; outside of that, on the eight petals, the letters of the *mālā-mantra* six by six; and in the corners of the square, one should write the four *kāma-bījas*. Kāma.
We know the god; we meditate upon the one whose arrow is the flower. May that Aṅga impel us.
Thus [is] the Kāmagāyatrī. Homage to the god of desire, who is beloved by all people, who deludes all people, who blazes, blazes, blazes intensely, O Lord of the heart of all people!

The mantra *yaṃ mama vaśaṃ kuru kuru svāhā*, consisting of forty-eight syllables, demonstrates another yantra for the garland-mantra, beginning with the words "sādhya" and so forth. Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus upon a betel leaf, one should place the seed-syllable of Kāma (*klīṃ*) in its pericarp, and within that—

Having first written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth within the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should encircle it as desired with *kāma-bījas* (the seed-syllables of desire) enclosed by the name of the person to be accomplished; then, one should write the seed-syllables upon the eight petals.
Regarding "Nara" and "Praṇava": because "Nara" consists of three syllables, it possesses a threefold nature.

The authors of the *Padārthādarśa* state that because of this, the vowel *i* (the short form) is not expressible as anything other than that; they further say that this very point is agreed upon by many treatises. According to the teacher Padmapāda, the modification (*vikāra*) is the sixteenth vowel, while in another view it is the second vowel. The word "view" (*pakṣa*) refers to five.

They say that the ten vowels are supreme; "ka" and "pa" [are the consonants]. According to the statement, "Ka" is the designator of Brahman, and the word "ka" is the designator of Vāyu, the letter "a" (makāra) should be understood through the etymological derivation: "What is this Vāyu? He whose companion (sapa) is 'a'. This, however, is the text of the master Padmapādācārya.

The author of the *Padārthadarśa* states that because of contradiction, [the rule] is not to be adopted; among those [alternatives], the nasalized vowel (*ghoṇīyānunāsika*) is intended, and even there, since there is no reason to abandon the first [option], the letter *ṅa* is what is intended. However, the letter *ṛ* contradicts authoritative texts.

The eight syllables— the *dhātu-upekṣya* (the letter *dha*), the sixth vowel (*ū*), the *jhiṃṭī-īśa* (the letter *ṭī*), the eleventh vowel (*ai*), and the fourth of the *ka*-group (*kha*)— should be placed upon the petals and at the tips of the petals. Having completed the worship and recited the hymn, one should ask for forgiveness (*kṣamāpayet*).

In all forms of worship, the *vatāntarapūjā* (worship within the enclosure) must be commenced; in this regard, the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by ritual section) method is to be followed, and not the *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance by individual item).

With the words beginning "ādāya" (having taken), he praises [the vessel] for the sake of purification; as for the praise [expressed] with "yat," it is for the purpose of generating devotion in the disciple.

This statement made by Padārthādarśakṛt is incorrect; for since there would be no engagement at all in hearing the mantra due to the absence of devotion (*bhakti*), the definition [of the mantra] would result in nothing more than "wailing in the wilderness. This has already been stated previously, as the injunctive sentences (*vidhivākya*)—along with the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding the state of being edible (*bhakṣyabhāva*)—[establish the necessity].

Since devotion cannot arise from those [passages] determined to be mere eulogies of the Lord, even if it were granted that praise— by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with an injunctional statement— does indeed generate devotion, nevertheless,
that [knowledge of the Lord's greatness] must be required prior to the hearing [of the injunction], so that faith may arise upon hearing it; this is the essential point.
The connection is as follows: "The station of others is not sufficient for the station of the Asuras.
She whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī, whose father was named Premanidhi, who was born in the lineage of Pataṅka, and whose birthplace was Mount Kūrma.

[The author], whose face is graced by excellent poetry, whose valor is established, who has attained the station of the Imperishable (Viṣṇu), and who resides in Vārāṇasī— having been born there, he, like a mass of moonbeams,
assumed a physical form [to compose] the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*. Now,
in order to describe the mantras of the venerable Sadāśiva which follow in due order, and for the sake of inciting the student's engagement [with the work]:

Having first established that this is a means to attain what is desirable, he introduces the attention of the disciples with the words beginning with "atha" (now), etc.: "The heart is *namaḥ*; the supreme is the letter *śa*;
it is joined with the short vowel *i*; the letter ending in *l* (the letter *va*) is joined with the long vowel *ā*."
"Marut-pakāraḥ śivāya namaḥ"—this is the five-syllabled mantra.
When preceded by the *praṇava* (Om), it becomes six syllables; both forms are to be worshipped by the twice-born (*dvija*).
However, for women and *śūdras*, only the five-syllabled form is prescribed. This very mantra, when ending with "namaḥ," is for the *caṇḍāla*.

Based on the statement "one should initiate [them]," even those such as the *caṇḍālas* have the right [to initiation] through the five-syllabled mantra, "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya. In the five-syllabled [mantra], the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is "Śivāya"; in the six-syllabled [mantra], the seed-syllable is the *praṇava* (Oṃ). In both cases, Umā is the power (*śakti*). Through the six syllables beginning with the *praṇava*, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

Intending to state that the five limbs should be assigned by the five [castes] beginning with the Śūdra, and the sixth limb by all together, he says "by six," etc. Regarding the phrase "by the six castes" in the first alternative, it means by the five castes; in the second, it means by the mantra. He now describes the assignment of the forms (mūrti-nyāsa). Maṃ...

By the passage beginning with "tṛtīya" and ending with "deśika," it is understood that the traditional practice (*sāṃpradāyikī*) regarding the syllables of the mantra is that they begin with *praṇava* (Oṃ), end with the dative case and *namaḥ*, and possess the nasal bindu (*sabiṃdutā*). Since this has been taught as "sāvi," it is thus: *Oṃ naṃta-puruṣāya namaḥ* on the index finger (*tarjanī*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of *oṃ namaḥ aghorāya namaḥ* on the two middle fingers; *oṃ śiṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ* on the two little fingers; *oṃ vāṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ* on the two ring fingers; and *oṃ yaṃ īśānāya namaḥ* on the two thumbs.
One should again project those same form-mantras (*mūrti-mantra*) into the five locations beginning with the *kṛt* [the hands] and ending with the head.

At this point, the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) should be performed; however, the commentator notes that previously only the extraction of the mantras was carried out. Regarding the phrase "endowed with the *jātis*," it is now explained as follows:

Some say: "Why was the extraction [of the mantra] not mentioned previously? Therefore, first there is the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the letters alone in sequence upon the six limbs with *oṃ namaḥ*. Now, however, according to the method of limb-placement (*aṅganyāsa*), it is performed as *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *naṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth."
Those who know the tradition, however, [recite]: *oṃ sarvajñadhāmne hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ naṃ tṛptidhāmne śirase svāhā*; *oṃ namaḥ anādivodhadhāmne śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*;
*oṃ śiṃ aluptaśaktidhāmne kavacāya huṃ*; *oṃ vāṃ svatantraśakti*...

*dhāmnena trāya vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ yaṃ anaṃtaśaktidhāmne astrāya phaṭ*—this is the mantra for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). As it has been said: "One should assign the six limbs to this [deity] using the word 'dhāman' in the dative case; likewise, one should assign 'sarvajña' (the all-knowing), 'tṛpti' (satisfaction), and 'bodha' (awakening), which are devoid of beginning and end and possess incomparable splendor."
By the word "deśika" occurring in the half-verse beginning with "with six syllables," namely "knowledge, sovereignty, and infinite power," this very specific [form of] worship is intended.
Thus, first there is this very *nyāsa*, and afterwards [the worship is performed] solely with the syllables of the mantra, accompanied by the [six] classes (*jāti*).

Regarding this, they say: "The best of teachers should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six syllables of the root mantra according to rule," and so forth. The construction [of the verse] is with the locative endings beginning with "in the heart" (*hṛdi*) and ending with "in the eight petals" (*aṣṭadaleṣu*). Therein, by the first quarter [of the verse]:
The first repetition consists of the six syllables of the mantra; the second is with one and a half quarters;
the third is with one and a half quarters; then there are four repetitions with half a verse each.
Here, the joints of the arms (doḥ-saṃdhi) are to be taken as five, by way of the finger-joints; therein lies the joint of the arms.

Although you were previously abandoned during the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, now, by somehow establishing the state of being joined (*saṃdhitva*) through the union with Durgā, the five joints (*saṃdhayaḥ*) are intended here;
and "one tip" makes six places for a single hand— thus [is it] likewise for the other.
It should be understood that the same method applies to the two verses beginning with "rahas tasya" and the pair of words beginning with "iti.

In this way, seven coverings (āvṛtis) are established. By the first half-verse beginning with "ekāddhaināṣṭamī hṛdi," [the sequence] is completed; the eighth is the axe (paraśu). This placement (nyāsa) is preceded by the display of mudrās. That... [tan mu...]
*Drāyathā*: Joining the fingers of both hands crosswise and keeping them pressed together and extended forms this mudrā.
For the *Paraśu* (axe) mudrā, one should join the tips of the thumbs and middle fingers together;
the remaining fingers should be held upright—this is the *Mṛga* (deer) mudrā.
The *ūrddhvīkṛta* (upraised) gesture is the left hand extended with both fingers [of the same hand] joined;
the *vara-mudrā* (boon-granting gesture) is the right hand extended facing downwards. With this half-verse, the tenth enclosure (*āvṛti*) is performed.
Then, as before, the placement of the forms (*mūrti-nyāsa*) is done for the five [limbs] beginning with the head. Thereafter, having performed the root-mantra (*mūla*)... [sva].
The pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) should be performed with the mantra beginning with "namaḥ" as it is recited in the *Rūpāvatāra*.

He describes the meditation (*dhyāna*) with the words beginning with "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*): the word *avataṃsa* denotes a crown (*mukuṭa*); for it is said, "In the masculine, *utaṃsa* and *avataṃsa* refer to an ear-ornament or a crest."
From the *Viśvakośa*: "The first [mantra] is for the two upper [hands] of Dakṣa and others, and the last is for the two lower ones; these are the weapons to be assigned.
Here, another visualization (*dhyāna*) should be shown, wherein the lotus and the linga-mudrā are displayed.
Then, from the *Prayogasāra*: "Then, the lotus and the linga-mudrā [are placed] in front of that."
One should raise the right thumb and bind it with the left thumb;

one should also bind the left fingers with the right fingers. This is declared to be the *liṅgamudrā*, which brings about the presence (*sānnidhya*) of Śiva. Such is the definition and the essential characteristic of the *liṅgamudrā*.

It is stated that there are twenty-four lakhs [of recitations], and it is said that one should perform the recitation (*japa*) four lakhs of times; thus, those numbers correspond to the number of principles (*tattva*), meaning that the number of oblations (*homa*) to be performed is twenty-four.
Some say that "the numbers of visible portions" means thousands. Herein, *pū*... [text fragment].

The sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the sacrificial substances (jāvastu) should be performed with the root mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*; this is the specific rule.
