This is because it is seen in the *Prayogasāra* and other texts that one should sprinkle [the materials] with the root mantra ending in the armor (*varman*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras, saying, "thus it is prepared. Having worshipped [the deities] from Maṇḍūka up to Paratattva, [one worships] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and so forth.

Having worshipped the nine powers, one should perform the complete worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) with the thirty-nine-syllable pedestal mantra: *oṃ namo bhagavate sakalaguṇātmaśaktiyuktāyānantāya yogapīṭhātmane namaḥ*, beginning with the word *kala*.
Having worshipped Śrī Sadāśiva— the principal deity— in the pericarp with the subsequent verses beginning with "valāya," using offerings such as perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers,
one should then worship the four forms, Tatpuruṣa and the others, in the four directions within that same pericarp.

Having worshipped the form of Īśāna in that very same northeastern direction, and having worshipped Nivṛtti and the others in the four corners of the pericarp itself— concluding with Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, and finally Atītā— one should complete the worship ending with incense,
lamps, food offerings, the waving of lights (nīrājana), the recitation of hymns of praise, and the request for forgiveness.

Having requested permission for the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*), one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*) on the filaments (*kesara*), the eight Vidyeśvaras known as Ananta and the others on the petals, and the eight forms beginning with Umā and ending with Skanda starting from the north and proceeding clockwise on the tips of the petals; and likewise Indra and the other guardians of the directions.

One should worship Tura-srepa as before; or alternatively, having first worshipped Īśa himself in the Īśāna [corner], one should worship Tatpuruṣa and the others in the directions starting from the East. This very alternative is intended by the author of the Mūla; the rest is as before. Thus, this is the mantra with five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇaka).

Three thousand times more is for the fulfillment of desires such as attaining the status of a Pāvaka; one may recite up to a hundred lakhs or even ten million times until the end of the maṇḍala. In another tantra, it is specifically stated that one should recite the excellent five-syllabled mantra during the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) and other such desires.

By joining the word "namas" with the end of the word "śivāya," the mantra "vāyurnamaḥ śivāya" is proclaimed for the purpose of paralyzing (stambhana). Likewise, the recitation ending in "namaḥ śivāya" is considered for the purpose of enchanting (mohana). The mantra ending in "vāya" followed by "namaḥ śī" is declared to be the Saṃhāra-mantra of the five-syllabled (pañcākṣara) [mantra].
Just as the mantras for driving away (uccāṭana) and so forth were previously described,
and those for attracting (ākarṣaṇa) and other purposes grant success through mere recitation a hundred thousand times, so too, for the purpose of attraction,
one should write the five-syllabled mantra— *Ṭa-Śi-na-maḥ-Ya-va*— in sequence within the letter *Ṭa* in the center of the attraction yantra; whereas for paralyzing (staṃbhana), it is a square.
Having drawn [the diagram] and written the letter *la* in the four corners, one should write the letter *na* alone in the center for the purpose of enchantment (*mohana*).
For subduing (*mohana*), having written half a *va*, one should write the letter *ma* in the center.
For eradication (*uccāṭana*), having drawn a hexagon, one should write the two syllables *vā-ya* in its center.
One should consecrate these instruments with their respective mantras as prescribed for each desire.

It should be understood that the mantra for the protection of cows (gorakṣaṇa) is formed by inserting the three syllables "vā-ya-na" between the syllables "maḥ" and "śi. He states another mantra: the six-syllabled one...
By means of the *ṛti* [mantra] and others, Śaktirudra is joined with the *māyā* seed-syllable in its preceding and succeeding parts.

Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Vāmadeva, its meter (*chandas*) is Paṅkti, its deity (*devatā*) is the illustrious Umāpati, its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Oṃ, and its power (*śakti*) is Hrīṃ. The limbs (*aṅga*), the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), and the yantras are exactly as previously stated; [the six limbs are formed by the six long vowels].
Those who know the tradition perform the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the six syllables beginning with *yukta-śakti-bīja* as follows:
*hrāṃ oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ naṃ śirase svāhā*, *hraṃ maṃḥ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*,
*hrauṃ śiṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *hrauṃ vāṃ netrāya vauṣaṭ*, *hraḥ yaṃ astrāya phaṭ*.

In that system, the mantras for the *aṅganyāsa* (limb-assignment) are "yaṃ phaṭ" and so forth. Regarding how one should meditate upon [the deity] as being accompanied by both [Soma and Umā], he says "resembling the Bandhūka flower," and so on.
In the right hand and others, [there are] the upper [weapons] beginning with the discus (*cakra*) and the lower ones ending with the weapon; in the left hand of the Goddess is a red lotus.
"Embracing with the right [hand], her body touched by her own left hand which holds a fresh blue lotus as she sits upon his left thigh"—this is because another mantra is seen [to state this].
"A hundred thousand recitations of the mantra" means one hundred and forty thousand; "mantra" refers to the mantra, and its "lakṣa" (one hundred thousand) is the number of its syllables.
Others explain that "one hundred thousand counted as ten" means eight hundred thousand;
thus, that [number] multiplied by a thousand is fourteen thousand. Here too, there are two meanings as before.
Having worshipped the limbs (*aṅga*) upon the filaments, one should worship Hṛllekhā and the others at the base of the petals in the four directions.

In this manner, having worshipped the five meats before the deity within the pericarp— which constitutes the central element— one should worship the eight deities, beginning with Vṛṣabha, in the middle of the petals.
He describes these very eight along with their meditations in eight verses, beginning with "himālayābham" (resembling the Himalayas), as the meditation on Nandi.
In this verse, [the deities] are: the deer on the tips of the petals, the eight Mothers, and then the four squares;

as before, Indra and the others, along with the Vajra and the rest—these are the deities of the six enclosures (ṣaḍāvaraṇa). He states the mantra of the temple (prāsāda): "Sāṃ" means *ha* (the letter *ha* ending in *sāṃ*), and "sāṃdvayānta" refers to the fourteen [syllables] of the Prāsāda [mantra].

Having bowed according to the rule with a mind characterized by serenity, as prescribed for Manu, that which was spoken within the *Sāṃtānugraha-saṃhitā* is the conventional usage of the *Prastāntrikas* here; thus, this word is profound:
*Haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *Oṃ* is the power (*śakti*). As it is said: "The end is grace... (*sāṃtānugrahasaṃ...*)

The *Yuktavidu* [mantra] with the head adorned is declared to be the machine (*yantra*) named *Prāsāda*; its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is "Haṃ" and its power (*śakti*) is remembered as "Auṃ. Following the word "Vāmadeva," there is a reading of half a verse beginning with "ṣaḍ-dīrgha" in some places, which appears to be an error; everywhere else, it is the installation of the vowels and so forth.

The author of the *Ityapadārthadarśa* states that because [the sequence] was previously mentioned after the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so forth, it shall be the same everywhere; however, some maintain that due to a specific statement here, the placement of the six limbs will occur first. From these five forms, in reverse order...

The five short vowels of the *rādi* [radical] series—namely *o*, *au*, *i*, *e*, and *u*—are likewise used. Thus, the mantras beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger are as follows: *hoṃ īśānāya namaḥ*, *heṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*, *huṃ aghorāya namaḥ*, *hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*, and *haṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ*.
It is understood that one should place [the mantras] upon the five fingers; by the phrase "with those respective fingers," it is meant that one should place them on the thumb and so forth.

By the statement "one should place them on the respective limbs," it is indicated that for whichever specific form (mūrti) a placement on a particular finger is possible, the placement for that form's head and other parts is to be performed with that very same finger.

The meaning is "it should be performed. Thus, the placement (*nyāsa*) with the mouth upon the head, the face, the heart, the private parts, and the feet—starting from the top—is established as follows: with the thumb on the head, the index finger on the face, the middle finger on the heart, the ring finger on the private parts, and the little finger on the region of the feet. He speaks again to describe the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*.
Regarding the placement (nyāsa) of the five *ṛks* beginning with Īśāna as limbs of the Silver [Mantra], he says "Īśānādyāḥ" and so forth;

the meaning is that one should perform the placement of the five *ṛks* in order upon the five fingers beginning with the thumb, and upon the five locations beginning with the head and ending with the feet, which correspond to the five faces. The *ṛks*...
Thus, may He who is the Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the Veda—may that Śiva, the eternally auspicious, be mine.
We know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us.

Salutation to those who are not terrible, to those who are terrible, to those more terrible than the most terrible—to all you Rudra-forms, to every one of them, salutations. Salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Jyeṣṭha;
salutation to Rudra; salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kalavikaraṇa; salutation to Balavikaraṇa.
Salutations to the one who destroys the vehicles of the enemies; salutations to the subduer of all beings; salutations to Manonmanī;
salutations to him who has attained Sadyojāta; salutations to Sadyojāta.
O Bhava, in every birth, transcend existence, favor me; O Bhavodbhava!
Salutation to Vāyana. Thus: "Salutation to the two thumbs; salutation to the two index fingers. || || || || ||

Regarding the statement by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* that [the word] "sattama" in the phrase "ityādiprayogodiśikasattama" is connected with the word "anvita," that is not correct, because such usage is not accepted in works such as the *Harṣakaumudī*. In the root text—
By saying "one should place [the mantras] on the fingers," the fingers themselves are indicated as the locus; thus,
this placement on the thumbs and so forth does not exist for the five-limbed mantras or the six-limbed mantras, by which even the heart and other limbs would be mentioned.
It would be so; thus it has been stated that there is no authority for such a description, and it was said, "One should place [the seed-syllables] in the limbs.

He explains the method of that by means of the verse beginning with *nāra* and so forth: the well-known *vāgbhava* seed-syllable, the *māyā* seed-syllable, the *śrī* seed-syllable, and the *vyoma-bhṛgu-gati*.
On the left side are the letters *ra*, *pha*, *ja*, *ṭī*, *śa*, and *viṃdu* joined together; the fourth is *hsauḥ*.
This is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Thus, the five *Tāras* have been declared in the twelfth chapter, in the section on the visualization of the form (*mūrtikalpanā*).
At the end of this [is]: *sarvajñāya hṛdayāya namaḥ amṛtatejo*.
*Mālinitṛptāya brahmaśirase svāhā*; *Aṅgajvalitaśikhi śikhāyānādivodhāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *Vajriṇe vajrahastāya svatantrāya kavacāya huṃ*; [and] *Bhṛguvaruṇe vyomani* for each [limb].

The three seed-syllables (bījas) joined with the *manusvara* (anusvāra) and the *bindu* are likewise: *sauṃ*, *hauṃ*, and *śrīṃ*. The six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) are: "To the eye of unimpaired power, *vauṣaṭ*; *śrīṃ* to the beast, *huṃ phaṭ*; to the weapon of infinite power, *phaṭ*. Thus, the mantra for the head is applied to the head, and so forth for the limbs.

Rāghavabhadra maintains that the *śikhā-mantra* begins precisely with the word "jvalita" and so forth, and that it also exists here as part of the limbs (*aṅga*) ending with the word "padam. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of these [mantras] on the thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other limbs, one should perform the placement of the *kalās*. In that regard, [the sequence proceeds] from the east, south, and so on.

One should sequentially assign the digits (*kalā*) of the Īśāna mantra to the [five] voids (*kha*). Therein, having divided this *ṛc* into five sections, a connection with each digit should be made in order.
Thus: "Oṃ, Īśāna of all sciences, obeisance to Śaśinī"—this is as before.
At the eastern face: *Oṃ īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām aṅgadāyai namaḥ*. At the southern face: *Oṃ brahmādhipatir brahmaṇo 'dhipatir brahmā dṛṣṭidāyai namaḥ*.
At the western face: *Oṃ śivo me astu marīcaye namaḥ*.

On the gentle face, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the portion of the mantra of Īśāna on the central face with the mantra: *oṃ sadāśiva oṃ aṃśumālinyai namaḥ*. Then, having divided the four sections of the mantra of Tatpuruṣa, one should place them on the faces starting from the east.
The meaning of "pūrva" and so forth is that they shine forth in sequence, one by one, in the directions starting from the east, joined with their respective *kaikakhaṇḍas*.
Thus, at the eastern face: *oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe śāntyai namaḥ*;
and at [the southern face]: *oṃ mahādevāya dhīmahi vidyāyai namaḥ*.
At the western face: *oṃ tat*... *namaḥ*; at the southern face:

*oṃ pracodayāt nivṛttyai namaḥ*; at the northern face: [as above]. Thus he describes the placement of the digits of the Aghora mantra starting from the heart and so forth in the eight locations, beginning with the words "on the heart" (*hṛdgrīva*) and so on.

The meaning is that the placement (*nyāsa*) of this *Aghora-mantra*, divided into eight parts and accompanied by their respective eight *kalās*, must be performed as follows: "Oṃ *aghorebhyaḥ* [to] *tamāyai* namaḥ" in the heart;
"Oṃ *aghorebhyaḥ* [to] *mohāyai* namaḥ" on the neck; "Oṃ *aghora*... [and so forth].

"Oṃ *pādyebhyo namaḥ*" (Salutation to those who receive water for the feet) on the right shoulder; "Oṃ *aghoratarebhyo nidrāyai namaḥ*" (Salutation to the most non-terrible ones and to Sleep) on the left shoulder; "Oṃ *sarvebhyo sarvavyādhibhyo namaḥ*" (Salutation to all and to all diseases) at the navel; "Oṃ *sarvebhyo mṛtyubhyo namaḥ*" (Salutation to all deaths) on the back; and "Oṃ *namaste astu kṣudhāyai namaḥ*" (Salutation to you, salutation to Hunger).

The meaning of the result is that one should place [the mantra] on the head of the *kaparda* (conch-shell) substance with "oṃ rudrarūpebhyas tṛṣāyai namaḥ" and on the chest; having divided the Vāmadeva mantra into thirteen parts, one should [place them] from the secret part (*guhya*) to the left, corresponding to each of those portions and their respective digits (*kalā*).

The meaning of the verse beginning with "guhye" is that the placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed in sequence upon those thirteen locations on the sides. [The mantras are as follows: *oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*, *rajasena namaḥ*—these are for the secret place (*guhya*). *oṃ jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ*, *rakṣāyai namaḥ*—these are for the region of the buttocks (*puṣkara-pada*) and the anus (*daṇḍa-kośa*). *oṃ rudrā...* [and so forth].

*Namaḥ* and *ra-namaḥ* on the right thigh; *oṃ kālāya namaḥ* and *pālinyai namaḥ* on the left thigh; *oṃ kalakāyāyai namaḥ* on the right knee; *oṃ vikaraṇāya namaḥ* and *saṃyaminyai namaḥ* on the left knee; *oṃ*.
"Oṃ *valikriyāyai* namaḥ" on the right calf; "Oṃ *vikaruṇāya* namaḥ, *vṛddhyai* namaḥ" on the left calf; "Oṃ *valasthirāyai* namaḥ" on the right buttock;
"Oṃ *pramathanāya* namaḥ, *rātryai* namaḥ" on the left [buttock].

At the anus: *oṃ sarvabhūtadamanāya namaḥ*; at the hips: *bhrāmaṇyai namaḥ*; on the right side: *oṃ namo mohinyai namaḥ*; on the left side: *oṃ unmanāya namaḥ* and *jarāyai namaḥ*. [Thus, from the sole of the right foot...]

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight *kalās* of Sadyojāta, together with the mantra and its six limbs, in the eight locations ending with the left arm; this is stated by [the author] beginning with the words "feet" (*pāda*), etc. "Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation for the sake of success (*siddhi*)"—thus [one places it] on the sole of the right foot. Oṃ, Sadyo...

"Oṃ jātāyai namaḥ" or "Oṃ vṛddhāyai namaḥ" on the sole of the left foot; "Oṃ bhavad-yutāyai namaḥ" on the palm of the right hand; "Oṃ abhavāyai lakṣmyai namaḥ" on the palm of the left hand; "Oṃ nātibhavāyai medhāyai namaḥ" on the nose; Oṃ.
"Oṃ *bhaja svamāṃ prajñāyai namaḥ*"—thus on the head; "Oṃ *bhava prabhāyai namaḥ*"—thus on the right arm; "Oṃ *udbhavāya namaḥ* [and] *sudhāyai namaḥ*"—thus on the left arm.
Here, the word *praṇava* refers to the *praṇava*, *māyā*, and *prasāda* seed-syllables.

The author of the *Padārthadarśa* states that the application for the placement of all the *kalās* (phonemic units) begins precisely with "Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ īśāna sarvavidyānāṃ śāśinyai namaḥ" and so forth, as this serves as the indicator for the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Furthermore, these placements of the *kalās* are introduced in the context of the *Prāsāda-mantra*.

The traditional teachers maintain that this [rite] pertains not only to this specific vidyā, but rather to all Śaiva mantras. The instruction is as follows: first, the kalā of the mantra is performed with the thumb;
second, the kalā of the mantra is performed with both the index finger and the thumb; third, the mantra...
One should perform the nyāsa with the *kalā* mantra on the middle finger and thumb; with the *turīya* mantra on the ring finger and thumb;
with the *pañcayama* mantra on the little finger and thumb. Regarding the phrase "kalakāme," the portion of the mantra is "kale" and the portion of the mantra is "kāme."
The mantra portion "kriye-ti-kalā vikaraṇāya-nam" is the same in both cases; however,
the mantra portion "kalānusaṃyamanīyavṛddhiśca" is different,
as it serves to preserve the meter (chandas), while the mantra portion "paṃcabrahmaparādikā" is [the other].

The meaning is that those [mantras] which have as their feet (pāda) the *khaṇḍapadas*—the verses (*ṛc*) beginning with the five lords such as Īśāna, which are denoted by the term "dayāvrahma"—are what is meant. It is said, "one becomes Gaṅgādhara";
thus, according to the statement "Śiva should worship Śiva," there is the state of being Śiva.

The sense is that since worship in the form of ritual service (*pūjā*) and so forth is impossible for anyone without identity with Śiva (*śivatādātmya*), all devotees of Śiva must by all means perform this ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the sake of attaining identity with Śiva. He states the meditation (*dhyāna*) beginning with "liberated," etc.
The upper face is white in color; the eastern face is yellow in color;
the southern face is blue in color, which is synonymous with "medya" (fat) and so forth, as it is said here that "at the time of giving rain, the clouds indeed become fat"; the western [face]...
The western face is like the color of the sky, the southern face has the color of a *japā* flower, and the northern face has the color of coral;
it is adorned with three eyes and possesses a crescent moon as its crown.
In each of the right hands, beginning from the uppermost, are held objects ranging from a trident to fire; in the left hand [is held a skull-cup].

According to the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, [the Lord] is the king of serpents, the lord of the nāgas beginning with Ūrdhvādi, the remover of fear, holding the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) mudrā in his right hand; and in his left hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and a blazing fire, while the lord of nāgas, a bell, a goad, and a noose shine in the form of the *bhīti* (terrible) mudrā— as stated in the previously mentioned *Pañcākṣara*.

"Along with the Mūrti and so forth" means together with those [deities] beginning with the Mūrti; "coverings" (āvaraṇas) refers to the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth, which are to be described below. By this, it is indicated that the worship of the Mūrti-deity must be performed prior to the worship of the coverings consisting of the limbs and so forth. [These are] the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās).
It has been indicated that there are no deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*) among those previously worthy of worship, and the result of that has already been demonstrated.

Having worshipped the Lord in the pericarp with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, one should likewise worship the five forms beginning with Īśa in the northeast, east, south, west, and north, as well as the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti in those same directions; then [one should perform] incense, lamps, food offerings, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and hymns of praise.

Having completed the worship with the offering of forgiveness and having requested permission, one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*) on the filaments, the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) such as Ananta and others on the petals, and the [deities] beginning with Upādi in the corners mentioned therein; furthermore, one should worship the directions and the [weapons] such as the vajra and so forth in the four squares in front, as previously described. Therein, Īśāna...
The four-armed Tatpuruṣa has a spear and a boon-granting gesture (varada) in his two upper right hands, and an axe and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in his two upper left hands.
Aghora, however, is eight-armed; he holds a rosary (japa) in his upper [hands].

Holding a garland, a noose, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a trident in their right hands, and a staff, a goad, a human skull, and a garland of severed heads along with a skull-cup in their left hands; Vāmadeva also has four arms, holding a rosary and a lotus in his two right hands, and an axe and a bell in his two left hands; Sadyojāta also has four [arms].
The [deity] has four arms; in the two right hands are a rosary and a boon-granting gesture (*varada*), and in the two left hands are a deer and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
The seed-syllables previously mentioned for these [deities] should also be incorporated into their worship-mantras (*pūjā-mantra*).
For the purpose of wearing this [mantra], the yantra is described: a hexagonal mandala on the outside with *rocanā* and *candana*...

The practitioner should not scratch a *prāsāda* [mantra] joined with a name using a blade of *dūrvā* grass at night; for it will be explained later that the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth are to be placed outside. Within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and outside in the six corners, one should write the six-syllabled mantra preceded by the *praṇava*, totaling thirty-three syllables.

One should write thirty-two syllables on the exterior; then one should write the six syllables of Īśāna, the seven of Tatpuruṣa, the six of Aghora, the seven of Vāmadeva, and likewise the seven of Sadyojāta, ending with "Namaḥ. All these syllables are to be written individually.

One should wear [the yantra] joined with the *yantra* that ends with *namaḥ* and is encircled by the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, as follows: within a hexagon, the *Prāsāda* mantra is joined with the *sādhya*; the root mantra is at the three joints; the limbs (*aṅga*) are on its arms; and here, a five-petaled lotus is located starting from Īśāna.

One should draw the five forms ending with the *hṛdaya* [mantra] upon an eight-petaled lotus, joined with the eight groups of the *mātṛkā* letters written on the outside; this yantra, when perfected through recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and other rites, bestows health, long life, progeny, sovereignty, and the fruits of the four aims of human existence. The root mantra is the six-syllabled one.

The *ānuṣṭubha* mantra and the *vyāpaka-nyāsa* mantra have been previously mentioned. Regarding the number of recitations (*japa*) and so forth, it ranges from one thousand and eight up to ten thousand, depending on the ease of the task and other factors; this also includes the ritual scattering of offerings (*sampāta-pātana*). He now states the eight-syllabled *Prāsāda* mantra, beginning with the word "Tāra" and so forth.

"Oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ namaḥ śivāya"—this is the eight-syllabled mantra. The seed-syllable of Prasāda (pra) is enriched with the six long vowels of Māyā (hrīṃ). Experts in the tradition maintain that the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed by assigning each syllable of the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*) one by one to these three groups. [The attributes are: the Veda, a book, a chisel, and an axe.

The right hand is placed upon the left thigh; the left hand holds a red lotus (raktotpala) or a blue water-lily (kuvalaya). The palm of the lower left hand is turned upward, signifying the granting of boons (varātmaka). On the right [hand], there is a book (vedaṭaṅka); the recitation (japa) consists of eight hundred thousand [times]. Eight.

Having performed a thousand oblations, one should worship the principal deity in the center of the seat described as having five syllables; the limbs (aṅgas) on the spokes, Ananta and others on the petals, Umā and others at the tips of the petals, and Śakti and others with the vajras and so forth on the outer square— thus the enclosure (āvaraṇa) should be worshipped.
The meaning is as follows: the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra is praised by the authors of the *Sthirāñjana* as being "oṃ jaṃ saḥ.
Here, *kārṇa* is the fifth vowel (*ū*), and *bhṛgu* is *s*. Thus, this three-syllabled *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra is "oṃ jaṃ saḥ. The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* also begins with this very same mantra.

In another Tantra, he has praised [this mantra]: "The three-syllabled mantra of Mṛtyuñjaya begins with the *dhruva* (the syllable *Om*), followed by the seventh [vowel] of one's own [alphabet] joined with the ear (*r*) and possessing a half-moon (*ū*), then the *kupaṃca* (the fifth consonant of the gutturals, *ka*) joined with two moons (*i*).

Thus, from the second of the *sṛṣṭi* [group], there is the 'ear' (*r*), the fifth vowel (*u*), and two moons (*i*). *(Note: The reconstructed mantra based on this description is likely Om Hrūṃ Kārim.)*

In the Nandikeśvara-tantra, it is said: "The Tāra (Oṃ), followed by the third letter of the third group (Ḍa) joined with the sixth vowel (Ū), then that same letter (Ḍa) placed below the Tāra and joined with the third letter of the eighth group (Sa), and combined with the vowel Ā—this is the mantra for conquering death. Thus, there are eight [groups]: A, Ka, Ca, Ṭa, Ta, Pa, Ya, and Śa.

Intending [the mantra] as "gām," the third group is the *ca*-group; the first is the *a*-group; the penultimate vowel is the bindu; the initial and final letters are the visarga; the rest is clear. In this way, the status of the letter *ja* as being like the left ear is established. This very root text leads to another alternative view; it is not the primary [view].

It should be understood that [the word] "brought" (lāyātam) is intended for the sake of the preceding [syllable]. In the case of the collision of two [rules], the former prevails by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is subsequently stated takes precedence. Although the word *karṇa* appears to have a fifth vowel [by the general rule], nevertheless, due to this specific statement, the general technical rule is set aside.
The syllable *karṇa* should not be placed at the beginning, but rather at the very end; by doing so, the attainment of the sixth vowel occurs.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The first [syllable] is *veda*, the eighth is *kaṣṭa*, and that *sa* is doubled in the middle of the difficult vowel.
Therefore, some say this mantra is *oṃ jūḥ* with a long vowel in the middle. Others, however...

The syllable *kāra* is the seed-syllable *caṃdra*; by that, the number one is obtained. By the word *karṇa*, the number five is obtained. By two [syllables] looking at each other, the understanding of the number six arises. From the analysis (*vigraha*) "where there is a pair [of *kāra*s] with *indu* [the moon]," the attainment of the sixth with the *bindu* (dot) occurs. Alternatively, *indu* and *caraṃdu* constitute one.
The remainder [of the mantra] is with the first moon (the letter *a*); the second moon (*u*) is not indicated by the vowel sign (*indu*).

Thus, there is the attainment of the desired seed-syllable (*vīja*). And so they say that no paribhāṣā rule is violated: the *praṇava* is the seed-syllable, *saḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and with *bhṛguṇā* (the fifth vowel, *u*), [it becomes] *sīṃ*, as in *sīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

The meaning is that the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the mantras beginning with *śirase svāhā*. According to another tantra, one should sequentially place the root-syllables at the navel, the heart, and between the eyebrows; this refers to their abiding within two lotuses: one lotus facing upward on the head, and a second seated above it.
The meaning of "the lotus which is downward-facing" is that it is at the head. The *mudrā* is the *jñānamudrā*, consisting of the joining of the tips of the index finger and thumb.
Regarding the weapons, they extend from the right upper hand down to the right lower hand.
He states the applications (*prayoga*) as three hundred thousand or one million [recitations] with the words beginning with "dugdhāktaiḥ" (smeared with milk) and ending with "sudhāguḍu".

An oblation consisting of these seven substances— rice, milk, clarified butter, and milk-rice— performed with one thousand and eight repetitions for each substance over the course of seven days, or with the number doubled for each day according to the gravity of the task, is a fire-offering that destroys malevolent spells and other such evils.
O Lord of the Gods, it may be that, due to the gravity of the task, one should perform oblations for seven days with each of the seven substances beginning with nectar (*amṛta*),
and then for another seven days with the next substance obtained in sequence; in this manner,
[the total duration is] forty-nine days.

The oblation of the seven substances (saptadravyahoma) is completed; when the ultimate cessation of life occurs and the homa with the seven substances such as *sudhā* has been performed, death shall not come to men— this is according to worldly renown on each respective day.

The oblation (*homa*) of the seven substances must be performed; thus it should be done for seven days, neither more nor less—this is the instruction. Regarding the three births, when counting starting from the birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*), in whichever constellation that birth-star may fall, there [one should perform it].

Some say that the plural number is used to indicate that the performance [of the rite] occurs at all such times when there is a "sevenfold entry" (*saptāveśa*) in the three asterisms related to birth— namely, the *thīva*, *āra*, and *nakṣatra*—
and that the stalk of both lotuses is composed of the *praṇava*.

In all the petals there is the sound *jū*, and in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) there is the letter *sa*. From that letter, the nectar of immortality (*sudhāmṛta*) flows forth from the pericarp; by remembering it, there is the pacification of all suffering.
He describes the application of absorption (*abhiṣveka*) with the words beginning "in the yantra," etc.; the yantra is the chest.

The mention of gems and so forth once again is for the purpose of indicating that even if one does not obtain all the aforementioned materials, such as gems, the procedure for consecration (abhiṣeka) should still be performed by adopting what has been prescribed here as a secondary alternative (anukalpa), according to the path previously described.

Regarding the yantra, he says "in the center" and so forth: having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should write the Praṇava together with the sādhya in its pericarp; having written the middle syllable on the cardinal petals and the final syllable on the intermediate petals, [one proceeds] to the outer square.

One should write the syllable *syā* in the cardinal directions and the syllables *ṭāṃ* and *vu* in the intermediate directions; having placed the outer *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) marked with *khaḍgī*, *śa*, and *lāṅgalī* in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should place the ritual objects (*padārthas*) within it.

Furthermore, because of the corroboration from other tantras cited in the *Darśa* and because of the subsequent mention of the fruit, this yantra is not intended for use in the ritual of initiation (*abhiṣeka*), but rather [it signifies] that from which the Vedas—those which transcend the senses, meaning they are beyond the range of the eyes and other faculties—are born; such is the meaning. And "transcending the senses" means being outside the scope of the eyes and so forth.

Eternity (*śāśvatatvam*) means being connected with all time. It is indescribable (*anirdeśyaḥ*), meaning impossible to describe, because it is too gross in its coarse divisions; yet it is also impossible to describe even in its subtle divisions because it is too subtle.
It is one by whom all fears, or the fears of all things, have been cast away; thus, it is the death of Time itself (*kāla-apamṛtyu*).
To Him who is the destroyer of worldly existence, whose matted locks (kaparda) are bound by the cord of the Gaṅgā river as its very form;
to Him who is pure, free from both merit and sin, whose disposition (bhāva) is pure and devoid of hatred toward others;
and who manifests as the Self within the inner hearts of such persons alone.
To the one clad in space for clothing; to the one who is the source and progenitor even of the three forms—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
to the abode of the three luminaries—the sun, fire, and moon; to the true bestower of liberation; to the destroyer of rebirth for those who have attained sovereignty;
and to the one whose service is the remedy for the mutual enmity of gods and asuras.
That those who are not in conflict simultaneously fall with their heads at your feet—this greatness of yours is marvelous;
and that your power of generosity is also marvelous, he says with the verse beginning "nija" and so forth:
"The mother of whom was Udyotamatī, virtuous and noble; and the father was named Pṛthivīpati, an ocean of love."
The land of Pañcaka, the tortoise, and the mountain are the birthplace [of the author]; he is well-worshipped by Kṛtavīrya; his feet are like those of Viṣṇu; Vārāṇasī is his place of residence;
and he has completed two and a half chapters of the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*.
Now, all this would be possible if the authority of the mantras were established; however, that is difficult to maintain if their basis is rooted in the Vedas (*śruti*).

The authority of the Śrutis does not arise from their being beginningless sentences or from their being composed by an omniscient Lord; nor is either of these [grounds] present here. For it is not the case that even a single syllable is produced as undesirable by the Śruti mantras; otherwise, there would be the consequence of contradicting [their] status as benefactors of the entire universe.

It has been taught by you yourself that just as one brings about what is desired for oneself, one also brings about what is undesirable for others by means of the mantras of the five-deity (pañcāyatana) system previously determined by the Bhaṭṭas; this is because the authority of mantras such as the Nṛsiṃhānuṣṭubh,
Saurāṣṭrākṣara, and others is established by direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti).
The author of the *Padārthadarśa* has stated that the authority of other [Smṛtis] follows from their similarity to those [Vedic texts];

however, that is not correct, because even though grammatical Smṛtis concerning *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth are authoritative, one still accepts the lack of authority for such rules as *kālāṭṭahavāmadevādrudryāḥ*. Furthermore, regarding the Smṛti on the Aṣṭakā and other rites... [the text continues].

Furthermore, because we do not accept the authority of such Smṛti texts as "The Adhvaryu takes the Vaiśarjanīya garment even at the Mānyas," the mere fact of their general similarity does not establish their authority. Now, one might argue that we shall establish their authority simply by observing the results [of following them]; for indeed, no result whatsoever is seen from that which lacks a basis in the Veda.

If it is argued that [the Veda] ought to be so, it is not thus; for, like a donkey that happens to arrive by chance, mere antecedence does not constitute causality. To this it is replied: in both cases, even that portion of this [Veda] which contradicts the Vedas pertains to specific qualified agents, and through its application to sacrifices and the like—

The authority [of these mantras] can be established just like that of the Śruti. Even for Vedic mantras, rites such as propitiatory ceremonies (śānti) are performed using the most excellent Gāyatrī and other mantras; what then to say of other Vedic mantras? Thus, what offense has been committed by the deities of the five elements (pañcatanmātra-devatās) thus demonstrated?

With the intention of asserting that the authority of these [mantras] is most firm because they are mantras, he begins to demonstrate their application even among the Vedic mantras as being the most excellent of all mantras.

The phrase "atho vadāmi" and so forth is used for the purpose of practical application; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Therefore, it is not [the case that they are superior] by virtue of their intrinsic nature alone.

There is no need for extraction from the three [Vedas]. Since it will be stated here that the phonemes (varṇas) contained therein constitute the nature of the *tattvas*, they possess the nature of the *tattvas* even as the three Vedas. Thus, the sense is that each individual Vedic mantra possesses the capacity for ritual application (*prayoga*). "Truth, consciousness, bliss... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.9.28]... Brahmā.

By the words "He who" (*sa yaḥ*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that even Brahman, whose nature is established by the Vedic revelation beginning with "That" (*tat*), is attained through meditation upon You. "Sat" means truth; "cit" means consciousness;
"ānanda" means a particular kind of bliss. These are its characteristics and its essential natures, but not [like] hands and feet.

Regarding "having *nādi*": there are seven *vyāhṛtis*, and with the *praṇava* at the beginning, there are eight. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the first syllable of the *gāyatrī*; those [syllables] beginning with it have that as their initial. This means that prior to the *gāyatrī*, the *vyāhṛtis* together with the *praṇava* should be recited. In the word *ṇyam*, one should read it as *ṇiyam*.
It has been stated by the author of the *Chandaḥsūtra* that, according to the count of syllables, there are twenty-four [syllables];

thus, "āpo jyotir" and so forth constitute the head (*śiras*). This mantra is employed at the beginning of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other practices. By me, the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other elements of the *praṇava* have been proclaimed.
The connection is with *ṛta*. The phrase "by the sages" (*munibhiḥ*) and so forth is for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding its lack of authority.

If only the words "by the sages" were stated, one might object that this [text] lacks the status of being a statement by a sage and thus contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, the remark "I have spoken after having examined those treatises" was made. [The word] *agniḥ*... or...

The deities of the Vyāhṛtis are Yama, Sūrya, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśvedevas; the meter of the Gāyatrī-mantra beginning with "Devī" is the divine Gāyatrī. As for the Śiras-mantra, its seed-syllable (bīja) is *yaṃ*, its power (śakti) is *īṃ*, and its peg (kīlaka) is *ṇaṃ*. For the Gāyatrī itself, the seed-syllable is *yaṃ* and the power is *īṃ*; *ṇaṃ* is the kīlaka.

This is because of the statement "lakamiti tat-kalpa-vacanāt" (as stated in that ritual manual). He states the *nyāsas*: "the *vyāhṛtis*, etc. By the word "mantra-knowing one" (*mantrajña*), it is indicated that just as the *vyāhṛti-nyāsa* is performed prior to the *gāyatrī-nyāsa*, so too the *praṇava-nyāsa* must be performed prior to the *vyāhṛti-nyāsa*; this is a conventional agreement (*sāmayika-saṃketa*).
It has been stated that there is no distinction [between these]. This is because even the specific secret news (*gopyavārttā-viśeṣa*) is conveyed by means of the mantra-words.

Its method is described in another tantra: "One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) while recollecting their respective forms: *Aṃ* to Brahmā at the navel, *Oṃ* to Viṣṇu in the heart, *Maṃ* to Śiva on the head, and *Namaḥ* to Vichva. *Aṃ* to Brahmā...

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three parts of the *praṇava* thus: "Oṃ namaḥ" at the navel; "Oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ" at the heart; and "Maṃ śivāya namaḥ" at the head; [one should then place: "Oṃ bhūḥ" at the heart;
"Oṃ bhuvaḥ" at the mouth; "Oṃ svaḥ" on the right shoulder; and "Oṃ mahaḥ" on the left shoulder.
*Oṃ janit* on the right thigh; *oṃ tapaḥ* on the left thigh; *oṃ satyam* on the abdomen. This is the Vyāhṛti-nyāsa. Some desire the addition of the word *namaḥ* at the end of each instance.
Then, on the four joints of the right foot, one should place the four syllables of *tat savituḥ*: *oṃ*, *ta*, *ta*, *vi*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner— *maḥ oṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ vi namaḥ*, *oṃ tu namaḥ*— one should again place those same syllables in the same way upon the four joints of the left foot: *oṃ va namaḥ* in the secret place (*guhya*),
*oṃ re namaḥ* in the navel, *oṃ ṇi namaḥ* in the heart, and *oṃ yaṃ namaḥ* in the throat.
In each of the two arms as well, there are four joints; one should place the four syllables *bha*, *r̥*, *ga*, and *de* there according to the sequence:
*oṃ bha namaḥ*, *oṃ r̥ ga namaḥ*, *oṃ de namaḥ*, *oṃ vaṃ namaḥ*. Then, *oṃ sya namaḥ* on the face, *oṃ dhvī namaḥ* on the nose, and *oṃ ma namaḥ* on the left cheek.
With *yoḥ oṃ hinamaḥ*, one repeats over the two eyes; with *oṃ dhvinamaḥ*, one repeats over the two ears;

with *oṃ yonamaḥ*, one repeats over the two eyebrows; with *oṃ yonamaḥ*, on the head; with *oṃ ni*, on the western face; with *oṃ pra namaḥ*, on the northern face; and with *oṃ vo namaḥ*, on the southern face.

Having performed the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*)—*oṃ namaḥ* on the eastern face and *oṃ yātṛ namaḥ* on the upper face—one should then perform the placement of the words (*padanyāsa*). The ancient sages have declared that the ten words of the Gāyatrī are, in sequence, composed of one, three, three, two, three, two, one, one, one, and two syllables. And so: *oṃ tat sa*.
*Maḥ*, on the head; *Oṃ Savitre namaḥ*, between the eyebrows; *Oṃ Vareṇyaṃ namaḥ*, circling the two eyes; *Oṃ Bhargo namaḥ*, on the mouth; *Oṃ Devasya namaḥ*, on the throat;
*Oṃ Dhīmahi namaḥ*, on the heart; *Oṃ Dhiyo namaḥ*, on the navel; *Oṃ Yo namaḥ*, on the feet.

Having repeated "Oṃ Naḥ" at the secret place (the perineum), one should place [the mantra] over the two knees; having repeated "Oṃ Pracodayāt Namaḥ," one should place it over the two feet. He describes the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with the words beginning with "To Brahmā": "To Brahmā, the heart, namaḥ; to Viṣṇu, the head, svāhā," and so forth; these are the mantras for those [limbs]. [The mantra] for the whole self is "Oṃ."

Regarding the statement made by the author of the *Padārthādarśa*— that because the word *astra* is seen in the mantra, the author of the text intended for even mantras composed of [terms such as] *brahmā* and so forth to end with *ātmane*— that is not correct. This is because, following the words *brahmā* and so forth,
the use of the singular dative case (*caturthyekavacana*) indicates that the author of the text intended the status of being a mantra to apply only to that specific portion.

Because it was stated thus; otherwise, he would have said "the heart of a Brahmin" and so forth, or he would have said "all of oneself" and so forth, as he has extensively explained. By the words beginning with "mukta," [it is meant that] the whip is the rope used for striking a horse or similar animal; "white" is an adjective qualifying the skull; and the cord is a quality.
In the two upper hands beginning with *kṣā*, there is a single lotus; in the two below those, a discus and a conch;
in the two below those, a noose and a skull-cup; in the two below those, a whip and a goad;
and in the two below those, the gestures of granting boons and protection—thus she has ten arms. "At the twilights" refers to day and night. "The twilight" [refers to] the transition...

The two *saṃdhyās* are the evening *saṃdhyā* at the end of the day and the morning *saṃdhyā* at the beginning of the day; these constitute the two *saṃdhyās*, namely the morning and the midday *saṃdhyā*. It is with this intention that the dual number is used. The meaning is "of the evening *saṃdhyā* and the morning *saṃdhyā*. Regarding the statement "having performed *prāṇāyāma* during the time of *saṃdhi*," that refers to this.

Regarding the desire for the procedure [of *prāṇāyāma*], he says "seven," and so forth. Here, there is the application of the *praṇava* (oṃ) to each of the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and the *praṇava* to the *śiras* of the *gāyatrī*; thus, there are nine *praṇavas*. Alternatively, when the *śiras* is at the end, it is a single *prāṇāyāma-mantra* consisting of ten *praṇavas*. This is the complete *prāṇāyāma-mantra*.

Regarding the possibility that one might recite only the *gāyatrī* alone during the two twilights—as in such injunctions as "one should recite"—the author states a specific qualification beginning with "the *vyāhṛtis*, etc. "That [number] by the hundred-thousand" means twenty-four hundred-thousands.
"According to the rule" means according to the procedure prescribed for the *puraścaraṇa*. Even if sprinkled, it is proper.

According to the desire of people, there is the attainment of whatever object they wish for by means of that particular state; having become a conqueror of the senses, one should practice begging for alms here and there and be habituated to eating only what is obtained.
Even if it is not specifically prescribed, if one’s own desired object is attained, then we do not forbid even that food.

Milk-rice, rice cooked with milk, sesame seeds, and dūrvā grass—these are the four [primary offerings]. For fuel sticks (samidh), there are eight substances: one each from the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa trees. When the oblation is performed with these individually three thousand times each, the total number of oblations results in twenty-four thousand. Pū...

He demonstrates the ritual procedure with the words beginning "having performed" (*vidhāya*) and so forth: having constructed the previously mentioned *Sarvatobhadra* mandala, having drawn an upward-pointing triangle outside of it, and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus there,
[one should worship] from Maṇḍūka onwards in due order, ending with the nine throne-powers (*pīṭha-śakti*) of the Sauriya [tradition], beginning with Dīptā.

Having worshipped as before with the root mantra and having visualized the form [of the deity], one should worship the Goddess Gāyatrī with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers. Then, having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara in the corners of the southeast (Agni), northwest (Varuṇa), and northeast (Īśāna) within the triangle, one should likewise worship Indra, Nairṛta, and Vāyu in the corners of the outer part of that very [triangle].

One should worship the powers (śaktis) known as Suvrahmāṇī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī. Some say that the objects of the powers are Harṣadīpikā, Akṣatā, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī; however, this designation is contradicted by various tantras, as it is stated [elsewhere] that Gāyatrī resides in the sun and Śatamakhi in the one born of night-stalkers (the moon).
One should worship Sāvitrī in the northwest (pavana-gata), Sarasvatī in the north, Brahmā in the southeast, Viṣṇu in the west,
Īśa in the sixth direction (the northeast), and likewise Īśānī in the northeast; for although by this statement one should first worship the powers of the three forms (Trimūrti-śaktis),
according to the words of Ārya, one should indeed worship from Brahmā onwards, beginning with Brahmāṇī and the others in their respective directions.

Although worship [of these] is understood [from the text], nevertheless, following the root source, there is a sequence of priority and posteriority; for those who stand apart, this option is established through the oral tradition of the Guru. Thus, the first enclosure consists of Āditya, Ravi, Bhānu, and Bhāskara, located outside the pericarp (karṇikā) in the four directions.

The meditations on the light of wisdom (*vidikṣuḍakhāprajñāprabhāsandhyāḥ*) constitute the second enclosure. On the filaments (*kesara*) are the six limbs; this is the third enclosure. At the bases of the petals, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, the eight powers (*śakti*) beginning with Prahlādinī and ending with Śānti are to be worshipped; this is the fourth [enclosure]. In the middle of the petals, [Kāma...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly at "kāṃ". The translation reflects the available portion.*

The fifth [stage] is that the eight Śaktis beginning with Tārā and ending with Vimalā are to be worshipped. The sixth is that at the tips of the petals, those beginning with Tamopahāriṇī and ending with Padmarūpā are to be worshipped. Then, on the outer petals in the eight directions, one should worship the deities of the nectar, beginning with Brāhmī and others, in the place of Mahālakṣmī. Some...
Even if Aruṇā were not present, she would still be worthy of worship there in the presence of the principal deity;

however, even the abandonment of Mahālakṣmī is not possible, for the word "with" (sa-) is capable of including Mahālakṣmī as well. Furthermore, the statement that "Brahmāṇī and the others are accompanied by Aruṇā" also maintains its own internal consistency, since the word "with" cannot possibly exclude Mahālakṣmī who is being carried along.

Huḥ! This is the seventh [enclosure]. Furthermore, the planets beginning with the Moon (Candra) are to be worshipped outside of that; however, the Sun (Āditya) has already been worshipped in the second enclosure. Alternatively, the Sun is placed in the center of the Goddess, and then the Moon and the others are placed in the eight directions—this constitutes the eighth [enclosure]. The ninth is with Indra and the other [guardians], and the tenth is with the thunderbolt (vajra) and the other [weapons].
[Objection: But surely, in all cases, the enumeration of the retinue (āvaraṇa) was previously stated beginning with the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatā);
how then can there be a different arrangement here? To this he says: "by ten enclosures" (daśabhirāvaraṇaiḥ).
Thus, according to the fundamental statement beginning with "the Great Goddess (Maheśvarī) is to be worshipped together with the deities of the ten enclosures," it is different here.

The implication is that even those deities who are to be worshipped prior to the limb-deities (aṅgadevatā) possess the status of being enclosure-deities (āvaraṇadevatā). In reality, however, those worshipped prior to the limb-deities are indeed equal in rank to the principal deity; their status as enclosure-deities is merely nominal, like Gaṇeśa in the section on the Mahāgaṇapati [Paṭala].

This should be meditated upon according to the method taught in the *Trikalpa*. As for the fruit: after the principal worship with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and the prayer for its permission (*ājñā*), one begins.

In the intervals between these principal worships, there is the washing of the hands, the principal worship, the offering of that worship, and so forth; he describes the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) starting with the words "there" (*tataḥ*) and so on, in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.

He states the application for longevity in twenty-four measures, beginning with "For the sake of longevity" (*āyuṣe*) and so forth. [The substances are]: first, *havis* alone; second, clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) alone; likewise, third, *havis* mixed with clarified butter (*sājya*); fourth, pure *havis*; fifth, pure clarified butter; sixth, the three liquids (*dravyatraya*); and seventh, sesame seeds (*tilāḥ*).

The meaning is that by means of these five substances, each offered three thousand times in the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), one's lifespan shall become very long. As it is stated in another Tantra: "One desiring long life should offer milk-rice oblation, clarified butter alone, and *dūrvā* grass with sesame seeds."

Since it is impossible to state the applications of every mantra individually, numbering three thousand, he speaks of all the applications by means of general terms. By using the word "many" (*bahu*) and so forth,
he indicates that there is no restriction here regarding the eligibility of Śūdras and others, and thus [the author] mentions the twice-born (*dvijana*).

Regarding this, the yantra described in another Tantra is as follows: [A lotus] with a trikoṇa (triangle) outside the Śakti, possessing six excellent pericarp-petals beginning with Bhūḥ; having pairs of vowels as filaments; with the mantra *kraṃ* and the three-syllable mantra on each petal;
encircled by the Cūḍāmantra and its fourth part; and marked with the syllable *kṣmā*, the corners, and the Tārā (Oṃ).
That [yantra] of Gāyatrī, whose greatness has been described, is marked with the directions starting from the east.

This is the meaning: within the pericarp of an eight-petalled lotus is a triangle; in its center is the Māyā-bīja; inside that, in the corners, are the three heart-mantras beginning with Bhūḥ; and on the filaments, [the syllables] two by two... [sva].

In the three corners of the *rāndala*, one should write the syllables of the *gāyatrī*. Outside that, on two circles, one should write the *cūḍā-mantras* beginning with "āpo jyotī raso'mṛtaṃ," followed by the eight-syllable mantra "parojase sāvadom.
Outside of that, in the corners of the *bhūpura*, one should write the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) in rotation, and in the cardinal directions, the worlds *mahaḥ* and *janaḥ*.

"The four *vyāhṛtis*, namely *tapaḥ*, *satyam*, *ṛtam*, and *mṛtyuḥ*, should be written. However, some say that the diagram for this is the aforementioned diagram multiplied twelve times. To demonstrate the application of the *āgneya* weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), he describes the method for accomplishing the *āgneya* mantra, beginning with the words "The *āgneya*... and so forth.
No. I shall explain it by means of describing those respective applications, such that it accomplishes all purposes;
or rather, I shall define it as being the basis for various applications, so that there is no harm even if its mantras are not extracted. Marīci is Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.

The specific sage (muni) is [indicated by] its name. According to the authors of the *Sārasaṃgraha*, "huṃ" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), "hrīṃ" is the power (*śakti*), and "raṃ" is the peg (*kīlaka*). Alternatively, in this mantra, the consonants (*hal*) situated therein are the seed-syllables, and the vowels (*svara*) situated therein are the powers. [The mantra begins: "jātavedase sunavāma somaṃ arātī... [and so forth].

"Since Agni, who knows all things, carries us across all difficulties as if in a boat, he leads us beyond all sins"—this mantra consists of forty-four syllables and is for the purpose of purification (*upamṛj*).
Now he states the mantras for the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), beginning with "by nine," etc.: *oṃ jātavedase sunavāma...* (Oṃ, let us press the soma for Jātavedas).

*Dayāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Dayā); *somamarātīyato'śirase svāhā* (To the head of him who hates Soma, Svāhā); *nidahāti vedas śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (May he burn away the knowledge, Vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair); *sanaḥ pariṣadat kavacāya huṃ* (May he protect us from all sides, Huṃ to the armor); *durgāṇi viśvā nāveva netrāya vauṣaṭ* (As with a boat across all difficulties, Vauṣaṭ to the eyes); *siṃvuṃ duritāty agniḥ astrāya phaṭ* (May Agni carry us beyond all misfortunes, Phaṭ to the weapon). Thus is the sixfold [application].

The *gaṇyāsa* mantras have been explained. Now he describes the *varṇanyāsa* (the ritual placement of the letters) with the verse beginning "aṅguṣṭha" and so forth. The term "aṅguṣṭha-pada" refers to the big toe of the foot. [The sequence of locations is: the big toes, ankles, calves, knees, thighs, sides, breasts, shoulders, elbows, forearms, wrists, hands, palms, back of the hands, nose, eyes, ears, and so on.
Since each of the fifteen locations is intended to be considered as two locations, thirty locations are produced. Furthermore, since the ten locations—
namely the hips, the private parts, the navel, the heart, the back, the neck, the mouth, the forehead, the chest, and the head—
are each treated as a single location, there are forty locations in total.

The two armpits (*bāhumūla*), the two upper arms (*upabāhu*), and the two thighs (*ūru*)—these four constitute forty-four locations; one should place one mantra-syllable upon each of these. Because of the association with the two shoulders, the middle word [of the mantra] also refers to that which is between them, thereby resulting in the inclusion of the neck (*grīvā*).

Between the root of the arm (*vāhumūla*) and the elbow (*prakūrpara*), that portion belonging to the upper arm is called the *upavāhu*; by the term *prakūrpara*, the second joint-portion of the arm well-known in the vernacular as *kudbhaṇī* is described;
and by the term *maṇibandha*, the third joint-portion of the arm is designated. [The text continues with] *maṇibandha-prakūrpara*.
The middle portion between the two [shoulders] is designated by the term *prakoṣṭha*. *Masta* refers to the junction of the forehead and the hair; *mastiṣka* refers to the hair above that.
The word *mūrdhan* (head) refers to the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture at the crown). He describes the placement of the feet with the words beginning with "crest" (*śikhā*) and so on;
here, there are two feet for the eyes and two feet for the ears, whereas elsewhere there is only one foot for each.

It has been stated by Īśānaśiva: "In this system, the locations for the syllables are remembered as follows: the forehead, eyes, ears, upper lip, tongue, throat, arms, heart, navel region, hips, thighs, shanks, and feet; these are one for each [syllable], while the other is for the head, ears, and eyes."
The eighteen-word *mantra* consists of eighteen steps: [the first] with two, five, one, one, two, one, one, and five;
[the second] with two, three, two, three, two, and two syllables. This is because it is taught that there are eighteen steps.
Thus: "To Jātavedas" is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); "O you who are bright" is for the forehead (*lalāṭa*); "To Soma" is for the right [eye].
*ṇa* on the right eye; *arātīyataḥ* on the left eye; *ni* on the right ear; *iha* on the left ear; *ati* and *ā* repeated on the two lips; *siti* on the tongue; *naḥ* on the throat;
*pari* repeated on the two arms; *ṣata* on the heart; *ati durgāṇi*.

Thus, having recited "iti," one should place [the mantra] on the two stomachs; "nāve" on the private parts; having recited "siṃdhuṃ," on the two thighs; having recited "duri," on the two knees; having recited "ati," on the two shanks; and having recited "agniḥ," the placement should be performed on the two feet—this is the resultant meaning. Ha.
The author of the *Rṣadīpikā*, however, maintains that one should conceive of the two flanks of the horse as two separate locations;

this contradicts the aforementioned statement of Īśāna. Furthermore, the placement of two syllables on the private parts and four syllables on the two shanks, which has been taught by him, is also contrary to the previously cited verse that divides the words.

This is contradictory. Regarding the meditation: [the author] says "lightning" and so forth; the trident has a cord like a conch-shell. The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* states that the noose is the object of the category of qualities (*guṇapadārtha*). That contradicts the statement of Dakṣa-Māṇava. This [deity] has eight arms; therein, by the right hands, she holds a wheel, a sword, an arrow, and a trident.

In the left hands, there are the conch, the discus, the bow, and the raised index finger; likewise, in the right hands, there are the discus and the conch in the upper two, the sword and the shield in the two below them, the arrow and the bow in the two below those, and the trident and the raised index finger in the two below those. As it has been said: "The [attributes] called the discs, the arrows, and the tridents..."

"With right hands [holding] the conch and the bow, and with left arms [displaying] the index finger," thus it is said "of the nature of fire" (*analātmikā*). Accordingly, in the previously cited statement establishing the deity, Durgā herself becomes the presiding deity here; thus, even the word "fire" (*agni*) in that context refers to one who is of such a nature.

It should be meditated upon as being solely the supreme fire of Durgā; and according to the method of initiation (*dīkṣā*), this method of worship of this mantra occurs only after that initiation, and not otherwise. As it has been said: "First, initiation is duly performed by the most excellent teachers;
thereafter, the arrangement of the weapons (*astra*) is proclaimed, and following that is the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vidhi*)."
Elsewhere it is said: "One should speak of the ointments only to one who is initiated; he shall accomplish [the rite].

Citra, citraka, white mustard, the root of citraka, aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa—these ten substances, together with well-kindled fuel, ghee, milk-rice (pāyasa), and boiled rice, amount to forty [units].

Some say that the oblation should be performed with a number of four thousand offerings; however, others maintain that since the sacrificial materials consist of food-grains alone, there are only nine substances for the oblations. According to this latter view, the oblation results in a total of four hundred and ninety-four offerings for each substance.

Thus, according to the former view, the oblation for each substance results in a number of forty-four; that is, the number forty-four is obtained. The remainder of the number four remains, and that too must be completed by four individual offerings. This is [the point].

The natural consistency of the former opinion—that the fulfillment of all numbers is not achieved by all the aforementioned substances—is thus refuted; therefore, the latter opinion alone is more correct. It demonstrates the procedure for worship beginning with the words "in the mandala" and so forth. By the term "six-cornered," the previously mentioned yantra multiplied sixfold is indicated.

Regarding the *lakṣmī* [yantra], it has been stated by the Teachers (*ācāryas*): "First, surround with power (*śakti*) the syllables known as those of the initiator (*dīkṣaka*); then, having made the yantra sixfold, [surround it] with beautiful lines of excellent letters;
outside, an eight-petaled lotus," and so forth. Some [make] only a hexagon, [and others] the *sarvatobhadra*.

In the pericarp (karṇikā), they prescribe the final syllable of the mantra, which is *agniḥ* (fire). That which has this as its first syllable constitutes the first quarter-verse (*pāda*). In this sequence, the eight forms (*mūrti*) that are about to be described, arising from those [eight quarters], are to be worshipped in the middle of the petals. This is the further description of the forms.

Since a difference in form would follow from a difference in meditation (*dhyāna*), for the purpose of precluding such forms, the worship-mantras (*pūjāmantra*) are exactly as before, beginning with *oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ* and so forth. However, some maintain that by the force of the repetition, the abandonment of the previously mentioned mantras is understood; therefore, only the name-mantras (*nāmamantra*) in the dative case [are used].

If [the forms] were to be produced here again preceded by the word *mūrti*, then, since such a form of the group (*vṛnda*) has already been mentioned previously, its re-mention would not be appropriate. In our view, however, because those characterized by such qualifiers are not to be grasped here, the absence of tautology is consistent. Regarding the forms (*mūrti*):

They teach that it is appropriate to state that there is no tautology because it serves the purpose of excluding other forms, as expressed in the *Padārthādarśa*; furthermore, they explain that this can properly be construed as being for the sake of this very meaning:
"Then, on the tips of the leaves, [one should offer] *namaḥ* to the self of water, *namaḥ* to the self of fire, *namaḥ* to the self of earth."

Having worshipped with "Nenama" in the four directions, one should worship the tetrad consisting of the kalās (subtle powers) of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, and Śānti at the tips of the petals in the corners. As for the application [of the mantra] "Vātātmane namaḥ," the usage mentioned in the Harṣakaumudī is not correct; [this is because it involves] the abandonment of the root [mantra].

Because it would entail the improper application of non-synonymous offspring [terms], or else it would lead to the necessity of seeking out the ultimate root for the application of each specific term dependent upon its retention; therefore, the usage "vāyvātmanā" (by means of the wind-self) is appropriate, since such a word has been introduced in the Vāyu-mantra itself. [This applies] to the east and so forth.
On each of the [four] directions, eleven forms are to be worshipped in sequence, making forty-four forms in total.
Some say that after worshipping those in the eight directions in groups of five,
one should again worship four [forms] in the east and so forth, or specifically in the northeast.
Some say that after worshipping those [deities] in the ten directions by groups of four, the remaining ones should be worshipped as before.
Others hold that *parā* is the name of the energy (*śakti*) of the letter *ṣa*, and that *parā* is an adjective qualifying the energy;
thus the application is: *Jāṃ Jāgatāyai namaḥ*, *Taṃ Tāpinyai namaḥ*, and so forth.

Regarding the statement by the author of the *Harṣakaumudī* that "the mantras of the power of the letters (varṇa-śakti-mantra) are preceded by each individual letter, such as the mantra *gaḥ* [for the letter *ga*], *yatrujājāgatāmainamaḥ*, *tanapinyainamaḥ*, and so forth," the source for this must be sought.
In the passage beginning with *jāṇam āpo yāsām iti*, the rule of being preceded by the letter *ya* applies everywhere.

The meaning extracted from the root text is as follows: "The state of being preceded by the phonemes beginning with *ja* and *na*" (pyetanatujādivarṇapūrvakatvam); therefore, "that which arises from the phoneme *ja*" (*jārṇodya*) refers to the first power named *jāgatā*. She is the primordial [power] among those phonemic powers beginning with *jāgatā*. Thus, "those beginning with *jā" (*jārṇādyāḥ*) refers to the mantra-syllables beginning with *jā*.
Even the statement that the meaning of the word *dyāiti* is like a mirror is established only by accepting its excellence;

for if the original author had recited it as *dyājāprabhṛti-mantrākṣarādya-ādyāiti*, or if the author of the *Chandaḥsūtra* had likewise recited it so that there were no defects in the meter, then perhaps that [objection] might have some utility.

The meaning of "cow's root" (*gomūla*) is that [the name] must be preceded by the first letter together with the *bindu* (anusvāra); this is obtained from the general scripture and is not contradicted by anyone. Therefore, the actual application is as follows: "Oṃ Jāṃ, obeisance to Jāgatī," and so forth. The worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and others is as before within the square (*caturasra*), and likewise in the case of the six-fold enclosure (*ṣaḍāvaraṇa*).

The question "Who is this [person]? is resolved by the aforementioned principle: only one who has mastered the mantra through the practice of nyāsa, japa, homa, pūjā, and so forth, possesses the authority (adhikāra) over the Agneya Astra-mantra to be described hereafter, and no other.
As stated by the author of the root-text: "When this [mantra] has been perfected through such practices as japa, one becomes authorized for the Astra-mantra; otherwise, it is the reverse."

The previously mentioned mantra is the Vajra-weapon (Vajrāstra) mantra, which is as follows: *agniḥ tyatāri dudhuṃsiṃcavenā śvāviṇirgādutidaṣvaripanaḥ sadaḥ vetihādanitīyatīrāmamaso mavānaśusedave tajā iti*.
This mantra consists of forty-four syllables and is recited in reverse order (*viloma*).
In response to the doubt that [the mantras] might be something other than those previously recited—such as the human [mantras] and so forth—he says, "These are indeed those previously mentioned.

He asks, "Are they then only the previously mentioned six-limbed mantras? and answers with the words beginning "pratiloma" (in reverse order), referring to the numbers stated as nine, seven, six, and so on; and thus, seven...
The ritual for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-vidhi*) is thus established by means of seven, six, seven, and nine syllables, as stated:

"By those [syllables] numbering the elements, the worlds, the limbs, and the Dhātus and Nandas, which are reversed and placed upon the three seed-syllables beginning with *Tārā* (Oṃ), the first phrase is: *Māṃ rakṣa rakṣāgnaye trāya ca*."

"With the syllables *phaṭ* joined [to the end], one should fashion the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Fire-Weapon (*dahanāstra*) together with the seed-syllables (*jāti*). This is the meaning: the seven stones, the eight serpents, the seven worlds, the six limbs, the seven fires, and the nine Nandas—this is the number of the previously mentioned mantra in its reverse order.

The syllables beginning with *agniḥ* and so forth consist of the three seed-syllables starting with *TĀRĀ* (OM), the *Praṇava*, and the seeds of *Māyā* and *Durgā*; these are the "head-located" (*śirogata*) elements that constitute their prior components—this is the qualification of the syllables.
The first word is *jātavedase*, while the other is their own essential form (*svarūpa*), used for the purpose of completing the meter.

Because the seed-syllables (*bīja*) are said to reside at the head [of the mantra], and because these [syllables] are associated with their respective classes (*jāti*), it has been explained by the commentators hundreds of times that they occupy the final positions when joined with their classes. Thus: *oṃ hrīṃ duḥgniḥtyanāridudhuṃsi jātavedase māṃ rakṣa rakṣa astrāya phaṭ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hrīṃ duḥ va venāśva avi-nirgād u jātavedase imāṃ rakṣa rakṣa astrāya phaṭ śirase svāhā. Oṃ hrīṃ dva duḥ tiṣṭha ṣat ripataḥ sa jātavedase imāṃ rakṣa rakṣa astrāya phaṭ. Oṃ hrīṃ duḥ daḥ veti hādana ija jātavedase imāṃ rakṣa.

*Rakṣāstrāya phaṭ kavacāya huṃ | Oṃ hrīṃ duḥ toyatīrā mama so jātavedase māṃ rakṣa rakṣa astrāya phaṭ | Netratrayāya vaṣaṭ | Oṃ hrīṃ duḥ mavā nastrasedave tajājātavedase māṃ rakṣa rakṣa astrāya phaṭ*— thus is the mantra for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Some conclude with *trāḥ*, while others say that the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) consists solely of the syllables of the mantra.

Regarding the "assignment of syllables" (*varṇanyāsa*) and so forth: one should perform the assignment of the syllables of the fire-mantra and the others, which are the reverse order of the preceding mantra-syllables, sequentially at the locations starting from the big toe up to the head. In the same way, the words [of the mantra] are to be assigned as before.
The division of these eighteen [syllables] is indeed according to the previously mentioned method of five, four, two, and so forth.

Furthermore, the locations such as the *śikhā* (topknot) and others are the same; however, the specific distinction is that by the statement "in reverse order," the words are to be uttered according to the reverse order of the phonemes (*varṇa*). Thus it is said in the *Sedavetajā*.
The placement of words (*pada-nyāsa*) is thus accomplished in the manner beginning with "on the crest" (*tiśikhāyām*), "on the left ear" (*vāmaśrutau*), and "on the forehead" (*lalāṭe*).

However, some say that one should perform the placement according to the sequence starting from the crest by dividing this very mantra—which is in reverse order—into eighteen parts through divisions of five and so forth. Others, however, [perform it] by the division of words...

Others, however, relying on the reversal of even the words that divide the *padas*, and having devised a division of the *padas* ending with the fifth by means of the sequence two, two, three, two, three, two, prescribe the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras in locations beginning with the tuft of hair (*śikhā*).
Furthermore, others rely on the reversal of both the words that divide the *padas* and the locations themselves.

In those very locations, there is the placement (nyāsa) of the respective phonemes and the respective words; for even in the Saṃhāra-mātṛkā-nyāsa, some teachers instruct that the locations are the same as in the Sṛṣṭi-mātṛkā-nyāsa, though they differ in their arrangement, citing differences in visualization (dhyāna). In that regard, [there is] the Āgneya-astra...
On the path of the deities, as if in the midst of a grove of palm trees, like a mass of fire upon the earth,
near the base of a great palmyra tree, in the southeast corner where the shoulders of lions shone,
she stood with her feet firmly planted, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning and glowing like the fire at the end of an aeon.
Lāṃ! She whose mouth possesses natural, fierce fangs; whose waist flashes with garlands of bells; who holds a trident, a lordly serpent, and a *ḍamaru* drum;
whose radiant splendor blazes like a lion; who resounds with her own skull-drums;
adorned with fierce ornaments consisting of serpents and other creatures fashioned by the lords of serpents; Ā.
"One should meditate on the Goddess, who consists of three colors and whose nature is consciousness," according to the previously mentioned number.

Regarding this, there is a specific detail in another tantra: "The practitioner of mantra, devoted to the vow of silence, pure in conduct, with senses subdued, seated upon the previously mentioned seat, facing east in the svastika posture, should mutter the Agneya weapon-mantra."

For the sake of accomplishing the two [goals], according to the previously stated number; these applications apply to both types of mantras when they have been mastered, and not when only one or the other has been mastered. Having accomplished this Vidyā—ending with the *pratiloma* and *anuloma* sequences—the preceptor should begin the application of these weapons according to the path described.

From the statement of the *Tītikā* [text]: "Indeed, those divine weapons and deities destroy one who desires to perform these rites that are properly incurable," and because of the prohibition, "O fierce one!
as before, there is the performance of *japa*, *homa*, and so forth, with a number [of repetitions], and the offering of *caru* cooked with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

This is the distinction regarding the materials for the oblation (*homa*). As for the worship (*pūjā*), it is also exactly as before; however, the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with Jāgatī and the others are to be worshipped in reverse order (*vilomataḥ*).
The point is simply that [the sequence] from Niḥsaṃpannā onwards up to Jāgatī is to be worshipped.
This is the distinction in the worship. By this, the eight [powers] mentioned in other Tantras—[are also included].

By teaching that even the worship of the power of the word (*padaśakti-pūjana*) is superior here, the *Padārthādarśa* treatise is refuted; for the author of this [work] intends only that distinction which is made by the mere reversal of power (*śakti*), whether in every case of the direct method (*anuloma-vidhi*), the inverse method (*pratiloma-vidhi*), or the mere application (*prayoga*).

Whatever number of mantra recitations the yogi performs, twice that amount of Gāyatrī recitation should be performed as stated at the beginning of this chapter. For acts such as inciting hatred or killing, the practice should be done with the mantra in reverse order (*pratiloma*); however, for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) or nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), the practice should be done with the previously mentioned mantra in forward order (*anuloma*).

First, even a mere portion of the eight-footed recitation (*pādāṣṭaka-japa*) of the mantra should be performed for the pacification of all defects such as instability in the mantra, and because of the injunction that one should recite the eight-footed mantra against those [defects] caused by malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). This extends from the root-recitation up to the end of the eight-footed recitation.

From the collection of questions, its excellence is established; in this [text], it demonstrates the eight feet beginning with "Agni" and so forth. The seven constituents (dhātus) are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; their corresponding forms are the seven colors, beginning with "tya," in sequence.

Hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death are the six enemies; the trunk, bones, marrow, skin, flesh, and intestines are the six sheaths. Although these have already been mentioned as constituent elements (*dhātu*), their re-selection here as "sheaths" (*kośa*) is not a fault, due to the distinction in their functional properties (*dharma-bheda*). Sound and the other [objects] are... [the rest of the sentence is truncated in the source].

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; speech, grasping, walking, excretion, and sexual pleasure—these and others arise from the sense organs (*indriya*). Those produced by the first two quarters [of the verse] are not so produced; those arising from the final two quarters are born from the objects of the senses (*indriyārtha*). [The objects are: the form of a woman, below, and horizontally...
There are also other deities who possess neuter forms (*klība-rūpa*).

It is taught that the commencement of propitiation (*ārādhana*) should take place under human asterisms (*nakṣatra*), the application (*prayoga*) under demonic asterisms, and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) under divine asterisms; this is demonstrated following the determination of those specific asterisms in the passage beginning with "the weapon" (*astra*).
