By the passage beginning with "one should commence," [the author] demonstrates that the day, lunar mansion, weekday, and ascendant must be favorable for the commencement and so forth; having prepared all the necessary materials and performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and others,
one begins the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the primary rite, which involves the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other acts, starting with the *astra-mantra*.

The objects such as cleansing (*marjana*) and so forth are synonymous with the ritual application (*prayoga*). Following the attainment of the desired goal, there is purification (*iddhāsana*), withdrawal (*saṃharaṇa*), and dissolution (*maṃhṛti*);

in both of these dual-natured states, [the breath] moves through the right nostril by means of the great fire (*analena*) and through the left nostril by means of the great moon (*śaśinā*), while the sun (*bhānu*) acts as the sun itself.

The meaning of this, as explained by Patayādhyātana, is as follows: having meditated upon the nature of the Self as the Sun, the processes of emission (*visarjana*) and withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) are to be performed during the dark fortnight when the breath flows through the right nostril, or during the night;
whereas during the bright fortnight, they are to be performed when the breath flows through the left nostril. However, some [hold] otherwise...

Having meditated on a triangular fire-maṇḍala with its seed-syllable, and having contemplated one's own solar nature, they say that this should be practiced during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). However, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), having meditated on a lunar maṇḍala with its seed-syllable and contemplated one's own solar state, it should be practiced; so say others. Furthermore, others... [text truncated]

In some other tantras, the same meaning expressed by the terms "nakṣatra" (asterism) and "tithi" (lunar day) in the phrase *laśaśipade* is also stated using terms such as "analādi" (fire, etc.); it is nothing more than this.
Thus, the author indicates that his own work is in agreement with those [other texts] by expressing the intended meaning through such terminology.

This is a restatement of that very point, whereas the passage beginning with "Bhāskara" (the Sun) is an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*). Thus, the meaning is as follows: having meditated upon one's own self as being of the nature of the Sun, one should perform liberation (*mokṣa*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) during the previously mentioned lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and lunar days (*tithi*) in both fortnights. As it has been stated by the Teachers: "The Fire is the soul of the lunar mansions."

It is most appropriately taught that the Sun performs the acts of emission and withdrawal through those two—the lunar day (tithi) and the moon (indu)—which are brought forth by the self. Furthermore, this correction of the asterism, lunar day, and weekday applies to matters that allow for flexibility; however, in matters that admit no room for deviation, this rule does not apply.

Because of the statement, "In times of great fear and the like, when there is intense form, no restriction of time is to be understood for the applications at any time," the practitioner should face westward in all cases— at the commencement, the dismissal, and the conclusion. He states the applications [beginning with] the asterism, and so forth.

Having struck forty earthen jars, each measuring one span in size, which were prepared under the enemy’s birth asterism, one should write upon each of them with a needle made of iron or copper the mantra syllables containing the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) along with the ritual action—such as "Kill! Kill! (*māraya māraya*)—using the juice of the *dhattūra* plant.

Having joined each [syllable] one by one, beginning with *reṇagrya* and ending with *anta*, and having written them down and established the deity of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) therein, one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) of each individual segment according to the order of writing.
Although it is understood that the name should be joined at the end of the mantra because of the rule "joined" (*saṃyuta*), [the procedure remains as described].

Nevertheless, since the mantra ending in *astobha* is characterized as "sprouting" (*pallava*) for the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*), its application is appropriate in the case of "sprouting," because the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) consists of killing; furthermore, the term *saṃyutān* can be justified even by the sense of mere conjunction (*saṃyuktatva-mātra*). [Regarding] the goal (*sādhya*)... [text ends].

From the statement regarding the letters of the mantra immediately following, the intention of the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*) is likewise inferred. However, in the view of those who maintain that the entire mantra should be written out,
the author of the root-text, having set aside the phrase "endowed with the mantra" (*mantropetāni*), [uses] the phrase "endowed with the syllables of the mantra" (*mantrākṣaropetāni*).

One should not think that there is a lack of efficacy [in this practice]; he states another application beginning with "on the eighth day of the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*) and so forth. *Viṣavṛkṣa* is the *kāraskara*, well known in the vernacular as *kucilā*;
*akṣa* is the *vibhītaka*. [The rite is performed] every day with each of these, such as the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *dhattūra* and others, individually.

The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed according to the number of days; thus, in a homa lasting up to seven days, the sacrifice of each individual substance culminates in a total of seven thousand repetitions. However, in cases where there is a decrease or increase in the number of days, the daily count of the homa should be increased or decreased accordingly.
Having accepted the reduction [of the duration], he states another application beginning with "for seven nights" (*saptarātram*), etc.

It is not the case that "any [period] of seven nights" is intended here—as was previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "the eighth day of the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*)—because the status of being "seven nights" therein is not fixed. This is established by the section beginning with "on a palm leaf" (*tālapatre*) and ending with "is produced" (*jāyate*).

Another application is as follows: by the word "vidhvī" (in the manner prescribed), writing [the mantra] while harboring the desire for killing should be performed; this is the instruction that "all [is done] with the juice of *dhattūra*.

The meaning is that one should give [it away]. *Visarga* is the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). *Ādāna* is the acceptance of the mantra immediately after its application. By the phrase "in tanks and so forth," ponds, wells, and the like are included. However, rivers are not included because, due to their powerful current, it is impossible for sand to remain in one place.
Otherwise, it would have been more appropriate to say simply "in the river" (*nadīṣu*).

Having recited the mantra for the ashes of the deceased (*pretabhasma*) as many times as there are syllables in the mantra, and having mixed it with buffalo ghee (*mahiṣājya*), one should form pills (*guṭikā*) exactly equal in number to the syllables of the mantra. Thus it is done.
One should offer oblations into a fire that has increased in size with fuel-sticks of *śviti* wood for the goddess Prāṇapratiṣṭhā.

With the words beginning "In the cremation ground," he describes another ritual application; the use of buffalo-derived *pañcagavya* is a figurative (or exceptional) application. He states another ritual application with the words beginning "On the seven Sundays."

Starting from Tuesday and continuing until Monday, during the *kulika* periods, one should take sand from the dwellings of the seventeen Durgās, beginning with Agneyī and ending with Śaivī; on the seventh day, during the *kulika* period, after taking that [sand], those...
The meaning is that one should take all seven types of sand together, touch them, and recite this mantra.
Regarding the phrase "as before," it means one should burn [the substance] in a fire of poisonous wood using a ladle made of poisonous wood.
He states another application beginning with "brahmadaṇḍī" and so forth; *brahmadaṇḍī* is *vijayā*. *Makaṃ*... [text fragment].

The *ṭikākākapikacchra*, *karakrośanikā*, and *vajrakanda* are for eradication (*utsāda*). Furthermore, he describes another application for a specific type of exorcism (*uccāṭana*) characterized by the absence of returning, beginning with the words "six dots" (*ṣaḍbindu*), etc. *Ṣaḍbindu* is a particular kind of insect, another name for which is *paṃ*.

Regarding the *pañcakūṭa* [insect], there are five white spots on it, and one other color which appears during the first fall of rain in the monsoon season. As it has been said: "Of the *pañcakūṭa* insect, there are five white spots; likewise, there is one of a different color, very glossy, and white in hue."
"At the commencement of the rainy season, there occurs that which is celebrated as 'the six drops' (*ṣaḍbindu*);

[this is to be performed] upon a doll made from the wood of the tree belonging to the birth-star (*janmarkṣa*) of the person to be acted upon—this is the remainder of the sense; [it refers to] pieces of the heads of great animals, such is the meaning; [this applies to] 'fragments of skulls' (*kapāla-śakala*)," beginning with these words, [this is] another application.
He describes another application for the restoration of life (*prāṇasthāpana*) for one who is to be healed, beginning with the word "snake" (*ahi*).

[One should] touch a living black cobra (*kṛṣṇasarpa*) while reciting [the mantra]; then, having performed the recitation (*japa*) over it, one performs a complete fire-oblation (*homa*) of that very [snake].
Another application is described by the words "for the person to be healed" (*sādhya*), etc., [beginning with] a black cat (*viḍāla*), i.e., a black *mārjāra*, [and] worship (*pūjā*), etc.

By taking up a cloth that has been dyed red and covered with a lid, and by igniting it preceded by the recitation of the *kṛtyā* weapon-mantra, the fire becomes permeated with the essence of the *kṛtyā* weapon. Following the oblation of wound-oil (*vraṇataila*) and *bhallātaka* oil, the subsequent rite of the cloth (*paṭakarma*) is most excellent.

The meaning is that, by means of such [verses] as "tyādi," one should perform another ritual application (*prayoga*) consisting of ten thousand oblations (*ayuta-homa*) with *rājī* leaves, complete it, then perform ten thousand oblations with *bhallātaka* fuel-sticks, and finally perform ten thousand oblations with sesame oil; here, the word "oil" (*taila*) is to be connected with each [of the preceding items].

"One should recite"—the sense is that by doing so, self-protection indeed occurs, and thus the omission of it is not appropriate. In connection with the *triṣṭubh* mantra, the *indra-triṣṭubh* mantra is also written here:
Gṛtsamada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), *triṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Indra is the deity (*devatā*). [The mantra begins: "Indra, the best..."

"Place the heart in the south; may there be auspiciousness for us in the south; [place] the head for nourishment; [place] the armor for the invulnerability of the bodies; [place] the crest for the sweetness of speech; [place] the eye for the excellence of the days;
[place] the kavaca with the complete mantra; and the weapon with the [concluding] mantra. Thus is the five-limbed assignment (*pañcāṅganyāsa*). [The assignment] on the head... [etc.]

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the hair, ears, eyes, the two nostrils, cheeks, teeth, lips, hands, feet, and the tips of the fingers; then, having thus placed them, one should further place the deity upon the *ādhāra*, navel, belly, breasts, sides, back, heart, and head.

In these eighteen locations well-known for their nature as "thou" (tvam), the practitioner of mantra should place the desired number of stars and so forth: on the head, the two ears, the two cheeks, the two eyes, the right side, the forehead, the private parts, the left side of the hip,
the two shoulders, the two arms, the lower jaw, the sacrificial ladle, the base, the navel, the heart, and the mouth.
Having thus arranged the syllables in their proper sequence, one should meditate [on the deity] as follows:
seated upon a beautiful throne of emerald, surrounded by celestial trees such as the Kalpavṛkṣa and Mandāra which are pleasing to the mind,
praised by gods and sages, possessing the luster of refined gold, and holding a multitude of golden jars raised in his hands.

"I bow to the Lord of the gods, who is well-pleased, who rains down streams of the nectar of nectar, and who bestows all desired objects. Now, the worship: *Oṃ Ṛdhyai namaḥ* (Salutation to Ṛddhi) *Oṃ Mṛdhyai namaḥ* (Salutation to Mṛddhi) *Oṃ Sukhadāyai namaḥ* (Salutation to the Giver of Happiness) *Oṃ Manojñāyai namaḥ* (Salutation to the Beautiful One) *Oṃ Kāntyai namaḥ* (Salutation to Splendor) *Oṃ Kāmadāyai namaḥ* (Salutation to the Giver of Desires) *Oṃ Surūpāyai namaḥ* (Salutation to the One of Excellent Form)

Having worshipped the eight powers of the seats (*aṣṭapīṭhaśakti*) with "Oṃ Kāmarūpāyai," one should worship the pericarp (*karṇikā*) with "Oṃ namo bhagavate ratnamayāya siṃhāsanāya namaḥ. Then, on the left side of Indra, [one should worship] with "Oṃ Pulomanaṃdanāyai namaḥ," and in front with "Oṃ Mātalaye namaḥ. Ta...
In the filaments for the worship of the deities of the stalks, the first enclosure [is as follows]:

"Salutation to Mandāra," "Salutation to Saṃtānaka," "Salutation to Kalpavṛkṣa," and "Salutation to Haricandana" in the four directions starting from the east; "Salutation to Pārijāta" at the front of the principal [deity].
At the second whorls (kesara), outside the limbs (aṅga), at the bases of the eight petals:
*ādityebhyo namaḥ*, *viśvebhyo devebhyo namaḥ*, *marudbhyo namaḥ*, *prajāpatibhyo namaḥ*, *vasubhyo namaḥ*, *aśvibhyāṃ namaḥ*, *rudrābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
"Salutation to the Drebhyaḥ, salutation to the Sādhyas"—thus [is the third]; in the middle of the petals:
"To Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Yuñjisthalā, Tilottamā, Citralekhā, and Uttatā"—thus [is the fourth] at the tips of the petals; [this is for] the Guru.
To the [deities] beginning with Brahmā, to Nārada, to Tuṃburu, to Citrastha,

to Abhramuvallabha, to Vājipati, to Aditi, to Jayanta— [these are placed] on the fifth square; and to Indra as before, along with the thunderbolt and others thereafter— thus are the six enclosures for the purpose of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).

One should perform one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*) and an oblation (*homa*) with skull-bowls smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*) at a tenth part of that number; the remainder is as previously described. Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*): he who offers oblations for seven days, numbering one thousand, with *dūrvā* grass and the three [sweet substances] soaked in milk, shall live for a hundred autumns, freed from diseases along with his circle of kinsmen.

Another application: having meditated upon this Lord of the Six Continents at midnight upon his bed— seated on a lotus, wearing red garments, ointments, and garlands, holding in his hands the noose, the goad, the wish-granting gem, and the gesture of fearlessness— one should recite the mantra empowered with the seed-syllables of the noose, the goad, and the spear (Pāśāṅkuśa-śakti).
Reciting this one thousand times, one brings Urvaśī—who has adopted a conduct fashioned by the god of love—onto one's own lap.
Thus, the Śakti-bīja is flanked by the Kāmamudrā, Varadamudrā, Pāśa, and Aṅkuśa;
likewise, there is the Ṛg-verse beginning with "aṃ hrīṃ kroṃ indraśreṣṭhāni draviṇāni... and so forth. This is the thirty-seventh [chapter].

The meaning is that by reciting the six-syllable mantra one thousand times, there will be the subjugation and attraction of Urvaśī and others. Another application: having meditated upon Him—deep red in color, with a serene lotus-face, holding in His hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a spear, or even a thunderbolt—and having recited [the mantra] within the orb of the sun, one should offer oblations.

For the sake of prosperity, at the beginning of the day—that is, in the morning—one should perform another ritual application: one who is wise should offer a large cluster of *śāli* rice blossoms mixed with honey into the fire. Having consecrated the householder’s home with mantras, he should do so before three maṇḍalas are completed, using those [blossoms] sprinkled with the "three sweets" (*trimadhu*).

The meaning is that for a person who offers oblations by the thousands, tens of thousands, and so forth, measured in *jarī* units, there will certainly be an abundance of rice within a radius of three *maṇḍalas*. However, the gods and Indra say that the limit of three *maṇḍalas* applies only to the duration of the sacrifice and not to the fruit [of the ritual]; yet the inherent force of the root text does not support this interpretation.

If you ask how long the duration of the ritual application (*prayoga*) is according to your view, understand that it lasts exactly as long as it takes to complete the number of one thousand or other counts established for the light and heavy tasks.
Furthermore, the principle that "the accomplishment [of the goal] occurs within seven days" is to be respected by everyone alike.

Another ritual application: the householder who offers oblations with the *vaiśvadeva* hymn composed of eight verses and accompanied by *mandhas* [soma-juice], to him the Thousand-eyed Lord daily bestows most delicious food.
Another ritual application: even when uttered but once, the Lord of the Immortals [bestows] upon this best of men...

The meaning is this: for a Brāhmaṇa who, though possessing a family, gives excellent and succulent food daily to those born from the mouths of the [four] directions, Indra certainly bestows food upon that Brāhmaṇa and his family even if he recites this mantra only once in the morning. Now, as for the yantra, [it contains] the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), the action (karman), and...
One should write the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ) in the pericarp of the lotus containing the pair of fire-purifiers (*śikhipura*); the seed-syllable in the corners;
the vowels arising from the filaments in the eight-petalled lotus; the letters representing the sense organs (*indriyārṇa*)—numbering six—in the petals of the directions;
and subsequently, the consonant letters surrounding the corners of the petals.
This is the Aindra Yantra, joined with the *nipura* (the syllable *laṃ*). The *praṇava* (*oṃ*) is in the pericarp of the six-cornered [lotus];
in its center is the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth; in the six corners, the seed-syllable of Indra (*laṃ*) is repeated;
outside of that, on the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus, the vowels are placed two by two in the four directions starting from the east.

The meaning is that on the petals, five by five, there are six sets of mantra-syllables in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (āgneya); outside of that, there is one circle, and outside of that, a square. Regarding its fruit, it is stated in that very same source: "Having written this on a copper plate, having well-recited [the mantra] and offered oblations into the fire..."

One should perform protection by sprinkling with *dhūpa* (incense) smoke; that which has been established in a temple or other place is protected from *rakṣas*, *bhūtas*, *pretas*, thieves, and the like. Thus, "Whatever today, O Indra, you have struck down, all that is under your control"—this is the *gāyatrī* verse of Indra, consisting of three triplets of syllables, as before.
"One should write 'dbhupureva lekhya' and the three syllables 'sūryyaputra sūriyam'; this is to be understood.
Now, he promises to demonstrate the applications of the salt-mantra (*lavaṇamantra*), beginning with "atha" (now).
Even though recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and other such rites may be performed independently of one another, [the following is prescribed].
Although the proof for the distinction between the *ṛc* and others is not [otherwise] required,

nevertheless, because it is useful for the application to be described later— beginning with "one should offer with each one, starting with the *ṛc*"— he says, "The *ṛc*s and so forth are declared," in order to establish that distinction.
Here, in this treatise, the letters of the *ṛc*s and so forth are declared, but they are not complete...
This is the meaning of *ṛṇā*. He clarifies that very point with the words beginning "pūrva" and so forth;
the meaning is that there is a verse (*ṛc*) first, at the beginning. Therefore, its application occurs prior to [other rites] such as *japa* and *homa*.
And that [verse], having emerged in its entirety, was [placed] by the Teachers on the earth...

*vīmudakam* (waterless), *utkāṇām* (of those who have gone up), *ambhasi* (in the water)—after that, *tīkṣṇo'si* (you are sharp), *ugro'si* (you are fierce), *hṛdayam* (the heart), *te* (your). The word of Lavaṇa is *pṛthvī* (the earth); thus Mātālavaṇa’s father is Varuṇa.
*Prathameyam* (this first one), *pṛthvī* (the earth)—thus, following the fourth vowel, there is a confusion of the diphthong (*saṃdhyabhrama*) produced by shortening.

If one reads "pṛthvī" (earth) with a long vowel at the end (*pṛthvī*), as in the *Rasāyanamūla*, then there would be a contradiction with what was previously stated— that the *lavaṇa* mantra consists of thirty-two syllables— since reading it as *pṛthivī* with three syllables would result in a discrepancy. By this [explanation], the previous statement that the *lavaṇa* mantra is "ambhasī" (in the waters), as mentioned in the *Ṛgveda* and other texts, is also addressed.

Regarding the root text, even where certain passages had fallen due to the negligence of scribes, the teachers— considering them authoritative— refuted those who taught that the first Ṛk begins with "lavaṇa" etc., rather than "pūrva lavaṇa" etc.;
for they maintain that the first Ṛk begins precisely with the letter *la*, which constitutes the color of the earth.

Because the reading of the preceding word is not seen anywhere at all, it indicates the second [case]; "the second [word] beginning with *lavaṇa*," that very [term] being raised by those [very words]. The introduction is "in *lavaṇe*" for the second case; but as for "when being offered" (*hūyamāne*), from what does sleep arise, and from what does delight? "He cooks salt" (*lavaṇaṃ pacati*).

Having said, "Thus he purifies," and having said, "He cuts the salt," he speaks as follows: "I burn his limbs; I burn his flesh; burn his skin! Thus he indicates the third [verse]. "May another burn it"—this other is the third; by these, that purity is attained.
The third [letter] after *ha* (i.e., *i*) becomes the beginning; knowing that it arises from *la* and *asthi*, one should burn the word *asthibhyaḥ* and the marrow (*majjikā*).

Then, having addressed [it] with "if" (*yadi*), one should utter the word "dwells" (*vasati*). With the conjunction "and" (*ca*), there are eight syllables, or within a hundred [syllables] of the vowels; thus he indicates the fourth [letter].

Regarding the phrase "having burnt" (*daṃdagdhvā*), it has been stated by the teachers as follows: in cases such as the dative case (e.g., *tam dagdhvā*), the word *yama* should not be used immediately; rather, the word *agni* should follow *daṃ*. In the case of salt (*lavaṇasya*), they become red like copper in color through its brilliance, while in the case of black sesame seeds (*tila*), they become black in color at the end of the word *sarpa*.
In this very context, the syllables of the *lavaṇa-mantra* are preceded by "māyā" (the syllable Hrīṃ);

thus he indicates the fifth verse, "yā te pūrve. This verse also has been extracted by them as "yā te rātriḥ," which is proclaimed for one who is pierced by an arrow or placed upon the tip of a stake.

One should utter "mahārātriḥ"; having said "sā rātriḥ mahā," the fifth [syllable] is "niśā. Then follows the Praṇava (Oṃ), the Pāśa (Hrīṃ), the Āpeca (Hūṃ), and this Aṅkuśa-bīja (Kroṃ). After that are the Vāk (Aiṃ), Indrā (Hrīṃ), and Amṛta (Svā) seeds, followed by Yaṃ and Laṃ. At the end is the Ciṭi-mantra (Phreṃ), and in the middle is the five-verse Ṛk.
Thus, having combined them, this mantra consists of twenty-one syllables:

*oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ laṃ vaṃ lavaṇāṃbhasi tīkṣṇe syugro si hṛdayaṃ tava lavaṇaṃ sya pṛthvīmātā lavaṇasya varuṇaḥ pitā lavaṇe hūyayāne*. In this way, the mantra is formed by uniting these elements: *oṃ* (the seed-syllable), *āṃ* (the heart), *hrīṃ* (the head), *kroṃ* (the tuft of hair), followed by the five great elements (*yaṃ* for air, *laṃ* for earth, *vaṃ* for water, *laṃ* for salt, and *vaṃ* for the ocean). Then follows: "O sharp one, in the fierce ocean, O heart of the terrible one! Salt is the mother of the earth; Varuṇa is the father of salt. In the salt, [I offer] with the *hūyayāna* [mantra]."
Sleeping on a couch, sleeping in a bed, delighting in pleasure; salt he cooks, salt he causes to be cooked; salt he cuts, salt he splits;
"May I burn the limbs of such-and-such a person! May I burn his flesh! May I burn his skin, bones, and marrow!
From the bones, may I burn the marrow! For as many *yojanas* as he dwells [in that state], [so long does it last].
Within a hundred *dīna*s, he shall be swiftly consumed by the brilliance of this *lavaṇa* [salt] mantra;
he will fall into subjection right there in a city surrounded by iron walls, with bolts made of black serpents,
while being attended by the *lavaṇa* mantra— just as one pierced by an arrow suffers when placed upon the fire of a stake throughout the night.

And of that journey, the night is the "Great Night" (mahārātri); that night is the "Great Midnight" (mahāniśā). *Oṃ ciṭi ciṭi cāṇḍāli mahācāṇḍāli, bring [so-and-so] under my control, svāhā!* This mantra consists of two hundred and thirty-two syllables. Thus is the meaning of the conclusion. [Now for] the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.

By the words beginning with "Who is said to be Aṅgiras," etc., the teacher Padmapāda has indeed stated that the seed-syllable (bīja) is *māyā* (the letter *m*), while the power (*śakti*) is the syllable *kroṃ*, which is called the "hook" (*aṅkuśa*). It is thus stated [in the tradition].
For this great garland-mantra (*mahāmālāmantra*) consisting of two hundred and thirty-two syllables, Aṅgiras is the seer (*ṛṣi*) and Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*).
The *devatās* are Agni, Rātri, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī; the *bīja* is *hrīṃ*; the *śakti* is *kroṃ*.

For the attainment of the mantra, the application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation (*japa*), and so forth—this is the *saṃkalpa* formula. *Oṃ*, salutation to Aṅgiṣṭha the *ṛṣi*; salutation to Anuṣṭubh the *chandas*; salutation to the illustrious Agni, Rātri, Durgā, and Kālī.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers and other elements as follows: "Obeisance to the Bhūta-devatās; obeisance to the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*; obeisance to the power (*śakti*) *kroṃ*. Then:
"Oṃ *ciṭi ciṭi*, obeisance to the heart; *cāṇḍāli*, svāhā to the head;
*mahācāṇḍāli*, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); [the name] *amukaṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*)."

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantras *huṃ vaśamānaya netrāya vauṣaṭ svāhā astrāya phaṭ* on the thumb and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other parts of the body. Then, he describes the meditation (*dhyāna*) to be practiced, beginning with the words "nine saffron... and so forth; the visualization of the weapons is such that the first [weapon] is on the two upper [hands] starting from the right, and the last is on the two lower ones.

In the meditation on day (namagni-dhyāna), there is a skull in the lower left hand, a noose in the upper left, a goad in the upper right, and a trident in the lower right. In the meditation on night (rātri-dhyāna), from the upper right hand down to the lower left hand, the weapons beginning with the mouth [of Durgā] are arranged in sequence; specifically, in the lower right hand of Durgā.

In her lower left hand is an axe (*ṭaṅka*), in her upper left hand a skull-cup (*kapāla*), in her upper right hand a *ḍamaru* drum, and in her lower right hand a trident (*triśūla*). Regarding the number of recitations for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) of Bhadrakālī,
[the text] says "ten thousand" (*ayuta*) and so forth, meaning ten thousand recitations of the mantra together with the *ṛk*, the *pañcaka*, and the rest, performed correctly.

With reference to this purpose, for one who is incapable [of the full practice], the number of recitations is three thousand, as stated by the Teachers: "The practitioner, when successful, should worship ten thousand [mantras] endowed with the mantra-well; or, being properly composed, he may worship three thousand, according to the gravity or lightness of the task. Thus is the recitation.
Regarding the numerical weight [of the recitation], there is a certain distinction in another tantra:

one who has mastery should recite this previously mentioned *ciṭi-mantra* three thousand times, or by the count of ten thousand, at a self-arisen abode of Durgā situated on the banks of principal rivers such as the Gaṅgā.
One skilled in the application [of mantras] should perform the recitation four times that amount; this is the requirement for one capable of performing the ritual application (*prayoga*).

Just as there is a specific duration for the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*), so too is daily worship (*nityapūjā*) necessary for that same duration, and it has been described in almost the same manner. In some cases, there are specific details found in other tantras, such as in the *Bhīṣaṇa* and *Vahurūpā*.
The powers of the *loṇa-mantra* are: Kṣṇadaṃṣṭrā, Madotkaṭā, Māraṇī, Mohanī, Kāntā, and Kamaṇḍaludharā; and Abhicārakarī. These are the *pīṭha-śaktis*.
[Om] salutation to the seat of all powers, marked by the noose, the goad, the axe, and the spear. Om.

The mantra for the pedestal (pīṭha) should begin with *dhruva* and so forth: *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*; this is the mantra for the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*). Having invoked the deity into the image, one should fully worship the deity with perfumes and other offerings.
First, the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) is performed with the limbs (*aṅga*), and secondly, with the forms of the fires (*vahnimūrti*); outside of that—

The fourth [veneration] is impelled by the Śaktis such as Śūlahastā and others, while the fifth rotation is said to be by Utkaṭā and others. This is proclaimed as the ritual procedure for the mantra of the Lord of the World (Lokeśa).
The forms of Fire, beginning with Jāta-vedaḥ and so forth, have been previously mentioned; likewise, [the forms] beginning with Śūlahasta and others [are to be understood].
Kṛti said: "The eight Śaktis of Tāmasa are Śūlahastā, Vikeśī, Dāruṇā, Lavaṇapriyā, Varākarā, Līvā, Atiyugrā, and Tāmasī. Regarding Utkaṭa and the others:
Utkaṭa, Vikaṭākṣa, Śūlahasta, Mahābala, Agnijahnu, and Khaḍgadhara."

The world-protectors (lokapālas) are indeed stated to be Kapālī, Tāraṇa, Priya, and Viti; furthermore, the Vajra and others are also to be included here by the very term "world-protector," because of their constant association (sāhacarya). However, as for their status as the eighth enclosure (aṣṭāvaraṇatva), it is said that "the fifth enclosure is proclaimed [to consist of these]," and thus they constitute the fifth enclosure.

Because only one side is worshipped, just as it is clearly stated in the Rudrayāmala and other texts that in the three-fold enclosure authorized by Dattātreya for the illustrious Rājarājeśvara, Indra and the others share a single enclosure together with Vajra and the rest, so too here those two share a single enclosure.

It should not be thought that this is impossible to state; for while four deities have been mentioned for this mantra in the context of *puraścaraṇa* and the like, in the specific application (*prayoga*) for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), Agni and Rātri are the deities, and not those four. Likewise, in the application for killing (*māraṇa*), Durgā and Bhadrakālī [are the deities].

He states that those four are brought about by that deity with the words beginning with "Agni," and he describes the ritual application (*prayoga*) with the words beginning with "jānu. Standing in water reaching up to the knees during the night, one who recites [the mantra] one thousand and eight times or more becomes a virtuous person under control; this is one method.

The application: standing in water reaching up to the navel and reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eight times at night, this same result is obtained; this is the second [method]. Standing in water reaching up to the neck and reciting it that same number of times, one will become even more completely subjugated; this is the third alternative. As before...

Since the states of lightness and heaviness exist even within the two *yogas*, the distinction between an ordinary person and a superior person as the object [of the practice] should be inferred from the sequence [of the syllables]. Indeed, it is impossible even for a Brahmin to state that the fruit is the same for both the light and heavy categories; for [the fruit] is determined by the specific letters of the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Another application is as follows: having written the mantra on a palm leaf (*tāḍapatra*) and boiled it in water mixed with milk, the person to be subdued becomes submissive. Furthermore, by writing the mantra on a palm leaf and burying it in the temple of Bhadrakālī, the same result as previously mentioned is achieved; this is indicated by the phrase "having thus written."
It has been stated that here too, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (the *sādhya*) must be interwoven [with the mantra].

Having thus interwoven the name of the *sādhya* into the mantra and written it on a palm leaf (*tāḍapatra*), one should heat that leaf for one month in a fire kindled with *khadira* wood; the result will be as follows: [one should offer] cow’s milk into a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having thoroughly powdered rock salt (*saindhava-lavaṇa*) that has been purified by washing and removing gravel and other impurities, one should offer it as a burnt oblation (*homa*). From this practice, for a period of seven days, the result will be the subjugation of people;
such is another application. [One should perform this] in a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with rock salt mixed with curd, honey, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Another application is as follows: thinking, "By offering oblations with these [five] salts, the lord of the earth shall surely become submissive," one should take one *prastha* measure of pure rock salt (*saindhava*) after cleansing it by washing and so forth, divide it into five parts, and offer each part respectively with each of the five Ṛg-verses in their sequential order.

Another application is as follows: for one day at a time until the end of the fortnight, whichever person the mantra-practitioner intends to bring under control, he should write that person's name in place of the two words [of the mantra]; that person will certainly become submissive.
As before, one should offer pure salt into the fire forty-nine times.

The accomplishment of the fruit established by the topic is as follows: for the subjugation of enemies, there is the oblation of pure salt alone; another application is that through oblations of salt combined with the "three sweets"—consisting of ghee, honey, and sugar—there arises the subjugation of men and others. Previously, there was the inclusion of curd; now...

The opinion of those who say that there is no repetition because *śarkarā* (sugar) is a distinct variety [of sugar-candy] and thus there is no insistence on including it within the "three sweets" (*madhuratraya*) is understood not to be supported by the root text; otherwise, the fault of redundancy (*paunaruktya*) would arise. He states another application: *maṃ...*
By the words "tram" and so forth, [it is taught that] that very eighth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇāṣṭamī) is complete with all its primary and secondary limbs.

The summary of the parts is as follows: the hands, heart, sides, hips, shoulders, neck, arms, back, belly, thighs, and shanks; "kaṃ" refers to the head, "pāt" to the feet, "kaṃdharā" to the neck, and "hasta" to the hand.
The wrists, the forearms, and the upper arms; the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) are the two eyebrows,
the two cheeks, the nose, the two lips, the teeth, the tongue, the chin, the mouth, the navel, the hips,
the vulva, the private parts, the two knees, the two wrists, the sixty toes, and likewise the two ankles.

In the hands and feet, [one should place] the syllable *tūl*. Thus, the five beautiful limbs, each twelve finger-breadths in length, consist of all the major and minor parts as previously described. The yantra formed by the *prāṇamantra* is as follows;
the specific procedure for the installation of life (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*) will be explained in the chapter on the fire-ritual (*agnipaṭala*) in another tantra.
Touching the heart of the effigy, one should recite the mantra until the end of the "abiding of life" (*jīvasthiti*).

Touching all the sense organs—beginning with speech, mind, eyes, ears, and nose, up to the end—one should touch the entire body. Beginning from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should touch the entire head.
"One should offer oblations with *nsvāhā* and *iti*"— this refers to the previously mentioned *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.

By the words "beginning with *niṭī*" and so forth, the terms "pair of breasts" (*stanayugma*) and "pair of eyes" (*dṛś-dvaya*) are stated here with the intention of indicating two locations each, due to the use of the dual number for the ears and the eyes.

The understanding that there is an intention to express the state of having the same location arises because the nose is singular and because the formation of a *dvandva* compound with two words expressing a single location establishes the intention to express sameness of location; likewise, it is unimpeded that the two cavities (*kukṣi*) possess that same nature precisely by virtue of being two locations.

The twenty positions beginning with *camūrdhā* and ending with *yāmva* are established. This section is commenced again with the words "the remainder" (*śiṣṭam*) and so forth, so that there may be no confusion regarding the fact that even for [plants] such as *durvā*, each occupies one, two, or three positions. [The rite is performed] with wood from the tree associated with the *sādhya*-constellation, which is harsh (*dāruṇa*).
One should dig and bury [the image]; for each of them, the digging is two finger-breadths below [the surface].

The phrase "facing downwards" is intended with reference to an effigy made of dough (*sikyamayī-puttalī*), because in the murderous ritual (*māraṇa-prayoga*) to be described later, one must take care that all of them face downwards.

In the present application, however, all three puppets must be buried face upwards and not face downwards; as it is said: "One should bury the wooden image face upwards at a depth of two finger-breadths below the edge of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus, one should bury the wooden [image] in the pit face upwards.

The teachers state that it should be consecrated with mantras; while being touched by smoke from above, one should ignite a lamp made of *mayanaja* (flax) and hang a doll made of beeswax (*sikthamayi*) from the ceiling with its feet half-way down and its head facing downwards, as established by such scriptural injunctions regarding the downward-facing beeswax doll.
By means of burying and establishing [the following items]: a wooden one beneath the *khītvāṅku* vessel; a sweet-scented one beneath his own seat;
a clay one made of potter’s earth in the place where his feet rest, near his own seat;
and a golden one in the space above the vessel in the atmosphere.
He demonstrates the application of the fifth [ingredient], which has been set aside, with the words "with salt," and so forth.

According to the rule, having performed the previously mentioned six-limbed mantra-installation (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) upon the effigy—which has become a deity—one should install the limbs; likewise, one should install them upon the image as well by means of one's own limbs.

Based on the statement from another *tāntra*, one should recite [the mantra] together with the *citimant* and the previously mentioned "five-fold *ṛk*" (*ṛkpañcaka*). Regarding the word "having withdrawn" (*saṃhṛtya*), it means starting from the thumb and ending at the top of the head.
Furthermore, because of the mention of "of that effigy" (*puttalī*) in the dual number, [it refers to] oneself previously in this manner.

The sound produced by the stretching of the strings consists of six positions, calculated by counting each of the fingers from the thumb to the little finger as they rest individually upon the strings; however, in two other positions, there are only two notes.
As stated by the Teachers: "Below the secret place (the navel) there is non-differentiation; above it, when the two [fingers] are present, there is differentiation."

This is the meaning: the "secret" (guhya) refers to the region of the anus; it is so designated because, like the others, it possesses the specific quality of being concealed. "Below that" means from the positions previously mentioned, up to the toes of the big toes.
Here, although the thighs, knees, and so forth each consist of two locations, they are treated as non-distinct [as a single unit].

The intended meaning is precisely that there is a single location; the practical implication is that the placement (*nyāsa*) of the two [groups], such as the *ūrdhva* and so forth, should be performed by repeating each individual syllable. Regarding the "above" (*ūrdhvam*), immediately after the location of the anus (*pāyu-sthāna*), there is a distinction because they occupy two locations; thus, two syllables are to be placed in those two locations.

As for the claim that [the ritual] is performed by the repetition of only a single syllable, one might ask: "Should this be done in the same way for each individual location, such as the *liṅga*, the navel, and so forth? To this he says: "When there are two" (*dvike sati*). Thus, it is only in the case of locations belonging to a single individual (*ekavyaktika*) that [the rule] applies; it is not so in the case of the breasts, ears, and other [locations].

Or it may be accepted that, having performed the installation of the fire according to the previously mentioned procedure by saying "having established the fire," one kindles it with wood from the tree corresponding to the asterism of the person for whom the rite is intended; then, preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, one should worship the deity of the mantra— the present deity in the form of Agni-Rātri— along with his retinue and enclosures, using the sixteen and other types of offerings.

Having worshipped him with hymns and praised him, and having asked for forgiveness, one should fill a silver vessel— also known as *kuśīta*— with red sandalwood, black mustard seeds (*rājikā*), flowers, and water; having consecrated it according to the procedure prescribed for the placement of the *arghya*,
and having offered the *arghya*, one should prostrate with the fire-mantras beginning with "Thou art he" (*tvam anena*) and so forth.

The *Ṛgvedic* mantras of Bhadrakālī should be used for the prostration at the beginning; it should be understood that they are not employed here in the ritual application (*prayoga*) for killing (*māraṇa*). The worship, the offering of the *arghya*, and so forth, belong to both [the practitioner and the victim] as well. As for what was stated by the author of the *Padārthādarśa*: "Having established the fire and kindled it with wood belonging to the birth-star (*nakṣatra*) of the victim..."
The meaning of "in that" (*tasmin*) in the root text— "the deity mentioned in the mantra having been worshipped in that"—
is "on the seat described in another tantra," because since worship in the fire has already been stated in the fourth chapter,
there would be no purpose in repeating it; thus, [the deity is worshipped] on the seat described in another tantra.
The statement that one should worship her with the preliminary rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and then offer the *arghya* is not correct;

for the seat (*āsana*) mentioned in other tantras is irrelevant to this context, and because it would result in the subversion of worship performed elsewhere in fire or worship based on fire as its locus. Furthermore, this is not even accepted by [the author of] the *Tattva-vāpy-āvalī*.
Why would one not state that [the ritual] beginning with "The worship of the deity Thāgnau is described in the fourth chapter" and so forth?

Therefore, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that this is not the primary meaning of the root text. Now, if it is argued that even a meaning stated in another tantra should be accepted provided it does not contradict the meaning stated in one's own tantra—then [we respond]: [This is not so].

Oṃ. Having thus worshipped the foremost [deities], one should then, in the eastern direction, construct a beautiful altar (*vedi*) measuring one cubit square, raised from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by a measurement of four, twelve, or some other number of finger-breadths, with its corners dyed red with lac. Therein, [one should prepare] a cord (*sūtra*) seven cubits long...
Having spread out a fresh white cloth folded fourfold, one should further spread a red cloth upon it;
each of these cloths being seven cubits in length and folded fourfold both internally and externally.

Therein, one should worship the deity under discussion, preceded by the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth, along with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the attendants (*sāvaraṇa*).
Having worshipped the sacrificial pit (raṇa), one should offer the arghya; this specific rule is also to be followed here, as is established by the following statement from another source:
"In the eastern direction of the pit, there should be a new square, elevated mound, one cubit in length, with its base and other parts reddened with lac; upon that, a very pure cloth..."
Having spread a very beautiful, fine cloth, four times [the size], seven cubits long, and new;
and having again spread two red cloths over it— broad, fine, multiplied as before, and new—
one should worship the deities of the fire-altar seat (pīṭha) upon this seat according to the previous method and invoke them.

Having first worshipped the deity not currently under discussion along with its limbs and retinue, the offering of *arghya* (water for honor) is prescribed; this means that the offering of *arghya* must be performed at the beginning and at the end of the application of this mantra. Regarding the statement "having split the doll sevenfold," one may cut it as desired therein.
Regarding that, he states the rule for those not yet engaged [in the practice] with the words beginning "first," etc.

The realized meaning is as follows: having divided each of the aforementioned single sections—such as the right foot and so forth—into seven parts according to one's desire, one should offer that many oblations using forty-nine parts (*bhāgas*). This is the [rule].

The position that there should be more oblations is primary because of the greater number of offerings; furthermore, the position that each part should consist of eleven parts is also primary, as it has been stated by the best of mantrins: "Having divided each of the seven limbs into eleven parts or into eleven portions of Rudra, one should offer them."

The phrase "beginning from the right foot" is intended for the subjugation of men; for the enchantment of women, it will be stated that one begins from the left foot; and for the ritual application of killing men, it will be stated that one begins from the left foot.
Therefore, in the ritual application of killing women, the cutting of the flesh must be performed starting precisely from the right foot.

In order to explain the specific details regarding the application of the rite of killing (*māraṇaprayoga*), he demonstrates that the distinction lies in every previously mentioned component by stating "that which was previously proclaimed," and so forth. Thus, one should fashion four effigies (*puttalī*) using the respective materials such as the constellations (*nakṣatra*) and trees, and likewise [arrange] the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the lower regions, and so on.

One should perform the ritual of burying the needles; this fifth [rite] should be performed with salt. However, for the boar and the pigeon [rites], one should prepare a mixture consisting of sesame, ginger, long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marīca*)—these being the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*)—as well as *rāmaṭha* (also known by the synonym *hiṅgu*), seeds of *bhṛṅgarāja*, seeds of *nīvāra*, and mustard seeds. This is the procedure to be accomplished.

This [preparation] is to be performed by combining eleven substances, including the previously mentioned sea salt (*lavaṇa-sāmudra*), which should also be added there; these are to be ground together with buffalo urine and water—
thus there is a requirement for thirteen substances here, according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*.

They say that only the oil of *labha*, *llātaka*, *viṃcavīja*, and *siddhārtha* should be taken, because of the teacher’s statement: "With [the substances] including *niṃba*, *siddhārtha*, and the wound-oil (*vraṇataila*). However, others argue: even though a resolution is possible through internal consistency, how can there be a natural force (*svārasya*) in the original statement?
It appears, however, that "riharjavyam" means "to arrange correctly"; for it is stated in another treatise:
"The span of her two feet is four finger-breadths; the waist is one and three-quarter finger-breadths;
the belly is likewise [one and three-quarter] finger-breadths; and the region of the neck is two finger-breadths from the mouth."
The measurement of the head and face should be one and a half *aṅgulas* here;

according to another [source], having made the face five parts, the neck again with half of that, and all the other limbs with the remainder— one should fashion the images of the goddesses, whether Durgā or Bhadrakālī.
By the word "līṃ ca," it is indicated that there is no divinity for both [deities] simultaneously;

and this is logical, because it is impossible to perform the worship of two different forms, including their respective seats (*pīṭha*), deities, and retinues (*āvaraṇa*), through distinct meditations on each simultaneously. This is due to the absence of the word "ca" (and).
Some maintain that, due to the sequence of the recitation, it is possible for both types of worship to occur according to their respective order;
however, in reality, in all these positions,

since the worship of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth— introduced by the present mantra— is what must be performed, the properties such as being of the nature of fire (*agnitva*) and so on [apply to them].

Some say that this is for those who have attained [the state] through the *skāra*. The author of the root text has made each of the four terms—*agni* and so forth—end in the nominative case in order to indicate that the status of being a deity is sufficient for each one individually, and not for all four together, nor even for two. Thus, worship should be performed [for each].

Each individual deity is to be instructed in their respective ritual duties according to the instruction of their own guru; by this, it is implied that even in the previous option, there is no single performance involving the worship of both deities. The secret is that even when offering the *arghya*, it is for only one deity; thus it is said, "for three weeks."

Thus, it is established that for one who follows this ritual application during the seven days occurring within the three-month period, beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth, the attainment of the desired goal shall not be impossible; furthermore,
regarding the specific sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the rite of killing (*māraṇa-karman*), it is stated in another Tantra:

In the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), one should give as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) a red cow with horns adorned with gold and pearls; specifically, one should give seven *karṣas*. Here, "red" (*śoṇā*) means crimson; "of uniform color" (*savarṇakām*) means having a single consistent appearance throughout all its limbs; and *karṣa* is a specific measure of weight for gold, also known by other synonymous terms.

There is another specific detail: one should perform rites of sorcery (*ābhicārika*) in a cremation ground or a desolate place where the practitioner performs the fire-oblation of sorcery; there, for the sake of his own success, he should have the area guarded by soldiers on all sides. Likewise, he should perform it during a border conflict with his own kingdom, and not when [the kingdom] is at peace.

"If the practitioner, deluded by ignorance, should perform [the rite] on the wrong day through negligence, he will certainly afflict that kingdom and the king gradually. There is also another specific detail in the *Sudarśanasaṃhitā*: "One performing cruel rites should examine the lifespan of the enemy. lā.

A wise person should carefully examine the omens from the *gnā* spirits or birds, the positions of the planets, the piercing diagrams (*vedhacakra*), or the *vāmaka* [diagrams], and then perform the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*). Otherwise, one will be overcome by them oneself; for if one performs a malevolent rite while seized by unfavorable planets, one will suffer misery oneself.

One attains death or encounters it; likewise, when the ascendant is occupied by an enemy planet and is devoid of strength, while the lord of the ascendant possesses strength and is joined by benefics in the eighth house, unobserved by malefics, and the lord of the night (the Moon) is situated in the eighth house of the enemy, or when other planets are so positioned.

If one's own natal ascendant, the *iṣṭalagna*, or the *jīvita* (ascendant at birth) are endowed with strength and are favorable to the yoga of "good death" (*sumṛtyuyoga*), then the initiated king may undertake the effort of slaughter when entering [the enemy's territory]. If it is objected:
"In that case, since the enemy's death would occur from those very factors, what is the use of the ritual application (*prayoga*)?", we reply: No; for their death... [is not certain].

The presentation [of the reason] is precisely by way of being a non-obstructer; thus, its absence results in the absence of an obstructer. For a result does not arise from the mere absence of an obstructer.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing the cause, a formal argument (*prayoga*) must indeed be pursued, such as the apprehension of one's own [self], and so forth.
Furthermore, the suitability of the application (*prayoga*)—whether for the sake of its completion without obstacles or for the sake of enjoying the fruit of that application—is required;
thus it is said: "Even by a thousand causes, the fruit does not arise if there is even a single obstacle. Therefore, one should examine the lifespan of the enemy, and so forth.

The statement regarding the enemy’s liberation (*kamukta*)—the requirement for a planet that causes death—is stated according to the logic of the "staff and the wheel" (*daṇḍacakra*), for the purpose of bringing about their conjunction (*sāmagrī*).

For this very reason, it was said [in the previous verse] that [the condition applies] to those that are beneficial (*upakārin*), but not to those that are non-contributory (*anādhāyaka*). Indeed, the nature of being beneficial (*upakāritva*) is defined as the state of being necessarily required by another for the production of a result.
Thus, everything regarding their cooperative action is consistent; there is also another distinction mentioned in other systems:

"Having fasted during that night, on the following day the practitioner, having become liberated from sin through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the like, as well as by the recitation of the Gāyatrī and burnt offerings (homa), shall once again wander as one who has attained self-mastery."
Now, it was previously stated that one should fashion a *puttalī* (effigy) from the tree corresponding to the asterism of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), and so forth;

since it is impossible to know which trees correspond to the asterisms of those to be acted upon without a specific mantra for that purpose, [the author], in response to this inquiry, shows all the trees corresponding to the asterisms beginning with Āśvinī. [He says: *Kāraskara*...
By the phrase beginning with "rityādi" [it is meant]: *kāraskara* (the *kuvila* tree), *dhātrī* (the *āmalakī*), *khadira*,
*śvetasāra* (a specific variety of *khadira*), *kṛṣṇa* (a specific variety of *khadira* known as *kṛṣṇasāra*),
*nāga* (the *nāgakesara*), *rohiṇī* (the *vaṭa* tree), *plakṣa*, *karkaṭī*, and *ambaṣṭha*.
The *mrāta*, *arjuna*, *kakubha*, *sarja*, *śāla*, *vañjula*, and *aśoka* trees—

since there is a prohibition stating that "one should never cut the tree of one's own *nakṣatra*," if the tree of one's own *nakṣatra* is to be used as the target tree (*sādhyarkṣavṛkṣa*), then its cutting must be performed by means of another person, or else [the target] is a doll made from the wood of a tree already cut down.
Regarding the preparation of the medicinal ingredients, even the trees are mentioned in other treatises as follows:
sandalwood, kucandana, agaru, camphor, uśīra, water, saffron, kaṅkola, jasmine, yāṃsī, muracorā, the root of piṃpala, granthi, rocanā, patra, long pepper, bilva, graha, and aruṇa.
Tṛṇakalaṃvaka, āhuka, miñjikā, candinī, sauduṃvarikā, āśmarikā, asthirā, udajada, puṣpikā, mayūraśikhā, plakṣa, agnimantha, sindhu-nabha-eda, tiṇa, ṣayā, hrī,
kuśā, hrada-darbha, kṛṣṇa-darapuṣpī, rohiṇa, huṅgira, and mālā.

*Ḍu*, *kavṛhatī*, *pāṭali*, *citrā*, *atulasi*, *apāmārga*, *śatamūlā*, and *vibhṛṅgarāja*; *repha*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *muśalī*, and *aśvagandhā* with joined palms (*añjali*); *durvā*, *śrīdevī*, and likewise *lakṣmī*, *sadābhadra*, and so forth—these are declared to be the eight [plants] according to the sequence of the letters.

Herbs are of various types, such as pills (*guḷikā*), decoctions (*kaṣāya*), and ashes; they grant all accomplishments (*siddhi*). This application of herbs is also stated in another Tantra: "Whichever mantra [is used], pills made from the herbs corresponding to its syllables, prepared according to the number of those syllables, grant the accomplishment of that mantra. Likewise, there is consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and wearing [the herb]."

"The taste of that, the smearing with that, the worship with that, and likewise the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) through that—could such a thing possibly occur? No, for activity toward an object does not arise when there is knowledge that it is followed by a powerful undesirable consequence;
since this [attainment of powers] is universally loathed as being the very cause of hell."
Because there is no engagement [with such things] as they truly are, this moment is entirely devoid of essence; however, its investigation is even more so.

Thus he says "Ātmā" and so forth: by means of the recitation and fire-offerings (*homa*) of the *Gāyatrī*, one accomplishes self-protection and the destruction of the sins arising from those actions, resulting in the cessation of falling into hell and other such states, just as before through the application [of the ritual].

The meaning is that one should perform the self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*) exactly as previously described by its characteristics, even after the ritual application (*prayoga*). Furthermore, the intention is that through this expiation (*prāyaścitta*), everything will become as it was before, and not even a trace of sin (*pāpāṃśa*) shall remain. Alternatively, [it refers to] death within the previously mentioned mantras such as *jñeya-astro* and so forth.

The meaning is that just as self-protection and the performance of remedies through the recitation of the *Jayagāyatrī* have been prescribed as duties, so too must they be performed here. [He whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī, whose father was Māpati, whose lineage was named Premanidhi, whose birthplace was Kūrmācala, and who was well-approachable and of undiminished prowess...]
The one whose feet have fallen [in grace], who dwells in Vārāṇasī, and whose chest is broad like an elephant, has reached completion regarding the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*. Now,

since it was stated that "one should indeed perform self-protection," and in response to the inquiry as to by what method that is to be practiced, he teaches the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra with the words beginning with "atha" (now), thus indicating protection itself.

The sense is: how could one who is incapable of even looking at the Three-Eyed Lord (Tryambaka), who is consuming [the world], ever bring him under his own control? Likewise, what remains for him to protect? Thus, with thirty-two syllables, [the mantra says]: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may he release us from death, as a cucumber from its stem, [and lead us] to immortality."

Regarding this mantra: although it might seem inappropriate to say "whatever mantra I shall declare" because this specific mantra has not been extracted by its own vocal utterance, nevertheless, by defining the injunction of the phrase "I shall declare," the meaning is that "I shall make it fit for worship. Therefore, having set aside [the use of] "vakṣye" (I will speak) and so forth, the prefix "abhi" is employed.

The sage is Vasiṣṭha, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Tryambaka, the seed-syllable (bīja) is Śrīṃ, and the power (śakti) is Hrīṃ. As it is said regarding the Śrīdevīs: "In the worship of Śiva, the conjunction of the two Praṇavas is the seed and the power.
Thus, the conjunction of the two Śrīdevīs is joined non-differently with the Praṇavas; [this is done] by means of the six mantra-syllables that are divided.
The conceptualization of the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) has been stated; what then?

Regarding the statement in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*: "The six rites and so forth are to be performed in a single season; or else, there is no fixed rule for the mantras," this refers to the seasons such as spring and the rest, which are well-known to occur at specific times and are described [in the text] starting with "at sunrise" and so on.

In the case of [the rites] beginning with *śyena*, these [times] are to be adopted. However, regarding other necessary activities—such as the employment of royal wrath, poison, or [medicines for] childbirth—at whatever time [one is] engaged in those respective actions, the rite must be performed without waiting for that specific [prescribed] time; this is the meaning [of the rule] when there is a secondary (*gauṇa*) interruption.

In the case of a secondary (gauṇa) application, one should simply say "it is to be performed. However, some maintain that the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is the summer (*grīṣma*), the midday (*madhyandina*) is the rainy season (*prāvṛṭkāla*), and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is the twilight (*saṃdhyā*), while they do not recognize the cool season (*śiśira*). This is because there is no authoritative evidence for the other [seasons]. Nor is there a hexad.

It should not be said that "let there be only the eight-petaled lotus" or "let there be only the encirclement by the mantra-syllables beginning with *ya*," for that would result in a contradiction with the root text which states, "by the syllables beginning with *ra* written upon the petals. "The wheel of letters" (*varṇavṛtta*) means the wheel of the Mātṛkā letters. Thus [ends] the hidden [meaning].

This [view] of the author of the *Arthadīpikā* contradicts the text of the venerable Padmapāda, who states, "one should wrap it with what remains outside. This is because [the text] implies that the purpose of making the yantras and so forth "possessed of life" (*prāṇavat*)—the word "by means of" (*vāreṇa*) being understood—is not that their direct result is subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Indeed, such a direct result is not taught for this [process].

The reality of knowledge (*mititattva*). Having thus concluded the exposition of the mantra through this extensive treatise, he makes a formal promise (*pratijānīte*) to explain the mudrās that are useful for the worship of all mantra-deities, beginning with the words "āvāhanyādikā" and so forth. He demonstrates the etymological derivation of the term *mudrā*.

By the verse beginning with "yābhiḥ" (by which), the etymological derivation of *mudrā* is demonstrated as follows: they are called *mudrās* because through them one attains (*rānti*) joy (*muda*). As it has been said: "The elements, such as earth and the rest, exist in the form of a sequence from the lowest [element] upwards; their state of clarity [is attained] through the modes of their mutual interpenetration."

"During the time of secret recitation (japa), meditation, and indeed in every ritual action, those respective mudrās which cause the presence of the deity should be employed. However, these mudrās are to be kept strictly secret;
as it is said: 'One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one's guru. Furthermore: 'Not [to others]..."

One should display the mudrās in a gathering of great people; O best of sages, this is secret, therefore one should employ them in private or elsewhere. One should not reveal the characteristics of the mudrās to one who has not been initiated; the deities become agitated toward him, and his efforts will become fruitless.

Thus, even here, the *mudrā* known as *mudrāsya* (the face of the seal), which is essentially a single closed fist, generates anger, joy, or excessive delight among people due to slight variations; in the same way, this *mudrā* bestows joy upon all the gods. The *añjali* (palms joined) filled with flowers is the *āvāhana* (invocation).

Regarding the mudrās: some say that having formed a *añjali* with both hands, one should place the thumbs upon the navel and the root-joint [of the little fingers]; for it is seen in the statement, "This mudrā is known as the *āvāhanī*," that the *āvāhana-mudrā* consists of an *añjali* formed by first placing the thumbs upon the navel and the root-joints.

They say this: that very *āvāhanī* mudrā is declared to be displayed in the rite of installation (*sthāna-karman*); it is not called "the installer" (*sthānī*) because it is employed for the rite of invocation (*sthāpana-karman*). This is clearly understood from what is stated there: "In the raised [mudrā]," meaning the pair of thumbs is held upright.

The meaning is that this very mudrā, being of such a nature, is described by those learned in the *tantra* scriptures as that which is to be displayed during the rite of bringing [the deity] into proximity (*sannidhāna*). That very [mudrā] is the *sannidhāna-mudrā*. The mention of "placement of the six limbs" (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) is also an elliptical expression for the placement of five limbs (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*); therefore, it refers to the ritual procedure involving the five limbs.

There is the consequence of the failure to accomplish the seizing, drawing, and releasing [of the weapon]. Having performed the nourishment (*puṣṭi*) with the right hand, one should extend the forefinger (*tarjanī*) long and upward-facing, and rotate it from the left side along the path behind the back; this is specifically for the Brāhmaṇa. Or rather, it is the forefinger alone.

The *guṇṭhana-saṃlagna-mudrā*. He defines the *dhenu-mudrā* with the words beginning "anyonya" and so forth: the right ring finger and little finger should be joined face-to-face and interlocked with the left ring finger and little finger; [the right] little finger...

Having passed over the tips [of the fingers], it should be joined from the front with the ring finger (*anāmikā*) when it has come to the left side of that; this is the meaning of the root text beginning with "the left little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), the right ring finger (*anāmikā*), and the right little finger," and so forth. In that regard, the left little finger remains as it is, while the tip of the right ring finger [is joined].

Then, having joined them from the middle of the index fingers in that same manner, they should be embraced facing one another; there, the left index finger, having crossed over the back of the left middle finger, should be joined with the right middle finger on its right side, and the right index finger, remaining as it was, should be joined with the left middle finger.

He demonstrates the Mahāmudrā. By the words "mutually entwined" and so forth, the meaning is that one should extend all the fingers without exception after having bound them by entangling the two thumbs of the downward-facing hands with one another. Regarding the phrase "one should employ": it refers to the object of desire other than liberation.

This [is the case] for those seeking liberation; however, for those seeking liberation, the wise know that *mudrā-dhyāna* is performed by the mind alone, as it is said: "For others, however, [the performance of *mudrā*] with both hands is prescribed. Although there are various kinds of *mudrās*, nevertheless, in all cases...

It should be understood that because there is an absence of [specific] yoga, it was indicated in general terms as "the deity of the *dhvananāpada*. Now, he shows the rosary useful for the recitation (*japa*) of all mantras, beginning with the words "first," etc., [referring to] a rosary made from the letters starting with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa'.

Although there is no distinction in their being counted as gems on the rosary of the *lākṣā* garland, their entry into the state of Meru is indeed obstructed. As it is said in another Tantra: "Having visualized the letters from 'A' to 'KṢa' situated within the Brahma-nāḍī, and having joined each letter with the Bindu, one should then recite one's desired mantra."

"O Goddess of the World, one should then fashion Meru there from the syllable *Kṣa*. That rosary (*akṣamālā*) shall consist of a count of fifty beads. By means of this, the recitation (*japa*) of all mantras becomes the accomplisher of all goals. The phrase "fifty" (*śatārdha*) is an elliptical indication; [it implies] a rosary of one hundred or one hundred and eight beads.
From the letter *a* up to the letter *la*, preceded by the utterance of each respective syllable along with the *bindu*, one should recite the mantra according to the direct order (*anuloma*).

Without performing the recitation of the *kṣakāra* mantra, one should remember it and then recite again from the letter *la* up to the letter *kṣa*. This is the "hundred-beaded rosary" (*śatākṣamālā*). If, however, [the sequence] begins with the letter *a*...

After reciting that [mantra] in reverse order, one should also recite the mantra by uttering each letter starting from the first of the eight groups—*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*—one by one; then the rosary of one hundred and eight beads is perfected.
As it has been said: "The fifty-bead string begins with the letter *a* and ends with the letter *la*."

In the position of the syllable *kṣa*, starting from *la* and proceeding in reverse order through the division of the eight groups (*varga*), there shall be one hundred and eight [beads]. Regarding the specific fruits according to the distinction of the *paṇikā*, he says with the words beginning "Rudrākṣa": *rudrākṣa*, *padmākṣa*, *kuśa-granthi*, *putrajīva*, silver, gold...

By means of garlands made respectively from coral, crystal, pearl, conch, and gem— these ten substances— one attains, in sequence: the fulfillment of all desires, the destruction of enemies, the diminution of evil, the acquisition of sons, the attainment of all desired objects, and the gaining of good fortune.

It is said that deeds in the form of attaining fame and so forth are accomplished by means of five jewels for each [deity]; however, by means of a rosary made from the ten previously mentioned substances, the attainment of liberation occurs. Thus he says, beginning with "These," etc., that according to the difference in the number of jewels, there is a difference in the fruit, as stated in the Tantra.

Liberation is attained with twenty-five [recitations], the perfections of speech with thirty; all goals are achieved with twenty-seven, and salutations with fifteen. The accomplishment of rites for specific desires occurs with fifty, and with four more (fifty-four), there is success in all matters. It is said that by reciting one hundred and eight times with red [saffron] threads, all things are accomplished.

Regarding the daily recitation (*nityajapa*), there is a specific rule in another Tantra: "The recitation common to all [practitioners] is performed with a rosary (*mālā*) consisting of one hundred and eight, fifty-four, or twenty-seven beads made of crystal, coral, pearl, gold, or *putrajīva*. However, there is a further distinction according to Piṅgalāvatī: [the beads may be] made of crystal, coral, pearl, gold, or *putrajīva*.

The practitioner of mantra should fashion a rosary with one hundred and eight *tamaṇi* beads; this sequence of recitation is to be employed for liberation, sorcery, pacification, subjugation, and attraction. One should place the rosary on the middle finger and rotate it in order on the thumb; this bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

This is the sequence for counting with the *maṇika* beads: likewise, one should recite with the thumb and the navel [finger] in rites of pacification (*śānti*). Through the union of the index finger and the thumb, there is victory in rites of subduing, driving away, and subjugation.
One should recite with the little finger and the thumb in the rite of killing (*māraṇa*). Likewise, [with] the tips of the fingers...

That which is recited without following the method (naya) is as if it were not recited at all; that which is recited without counting is fruitless. Likewise, one should recite the mantra over the rosary that has been consecrated;
the wise should never perform the recitation of another mantra with it. One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor should it tremble.

Furthermore, one should not touch [the rosary] with the left hand, nor allow it to fall from the hand; nor should one touch another bead with the thumb while moving the beads. These and other such specific rules should be learned from our own works, such as the *Bhaktimadaṅgiṇī* and others. This has been stated.

In the absence of [a rosary], one may perform the recitation even with the fingers; or, having placed the mantra-beads upon the intervals between the strings, one should fashion them from the joints of the fingers. Having fashioned the *meru* (the central bead) from the two middle joints of the middle and ring fingers, one should begin at the root joint of the ring finger while circumambulating it clockwise.

One should count from the base of the middle finger up to its tip in sequence; Meru is to be assigned to the pair of joints at the base of the middle finger. One should then count from the middle of the ring finger up to the base of the index finger. This method of counting the garland of joints (parvamālā) for recitation is stated to be of two types, or alternatively, of five counts.
The recitation performed by turning back with two fingers at a time, counted by the number of finger-joints, is called *aṅgulimālājapa*.
In the same manner as described, the recitation performed by counting with lines is called *rekhājapa*. As for their specific fruits, they are stated in the Tantras.

"The fruit of counting on the fingers is remembered as having a single-fold merit; one should know that on the lines it is eight-fold, and by means of the joints it is a hundred-fold. This fourfold rosary is considered for the practitioner. Regarding this, there is a specific detail in another Tantra: "Not [using] the fingers..."

One should recite while the palms are slightly contracted; for when the fingers are separated, the mantra flows out through the gaps. Now, the rites of pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and so forth have been previously mentioned; it must be understood how many there are, so that one may perform each respective rite accordingly.

Incorporating those respective actions within the intellect, one should perform each specific rite according to the manner described for that particular rite. For it is not heard in other tantras that the desired result is obtained merely by performing what has been stated;
rather, [the attainment of results] depends on the color of the garments, flowers, and so forth used in the worship of the deity of each respective rite.

Due to its divisions it is Mahānāḍa; due to its divisions it is Mahānāḍaṃvara. Regarding the characteristics such as "Is he self-controlled? and so forth, this has been stated in the *Jñāna* [section]. Fearing that people might become confused by thinking that what is taught there must be practiced when there is a desire for liberation, [the author] intends to describe everything, including the deities and their respective divisions.

He makes a formal promise with the words beginning with "atha" (now). He says "in all tantras," etc., to indicate that even what is heard in other tantras has already been stated here as necessary; thus, one should not look to other tantras, nor should one entertain any notion of lack of authority. This was spoken following the method that will be explained below.
To indicate this very point—that the fruit of those applications does not arise at all, and thus their investigation is purposeless—the author states "prayoga" and so forth.
The removal, destruction, or pacification (*śānti*) of diseases and the like while they are being experienced by oneself [is the result]. Of these...

Gain, which consists in the preservation of what was previously absent, or which consists in the continuous succession of its absolute non-existence, will be included within *stambhana* (paralysis) or *vaśīkaraṇa* (subjugation), but not within *śānti* (appeasement). For this very reason, the warding off of an enemy army, which consists in the non-arrival of the hostile force, is included within *stambhana*.

We are experts in the Tantras. Even by the Blessed Śiva, in the *Saṃhitā*, yellow garments, garlands, and so forth were prescribed for the employment against an enemy army.
