Now, when a thief has reached the path, one should recite [the mantra] at night during the appropriate time; standing with his face toward the fifth [direction], that thief...

If it is argued that this contradicts the *Stavarāja* which states "one should not protect [the deity] here," because it is impossible for the deity to face westward for the sake of pacifying the thief-like Tārā, we reply: no, because a specific statement is more authoritative. Furthermore, if what is intended is protection in the form of remaining present, then that is indeed pacification (*śānti*).

The "stopping" (*saṃstambhana*) of the arrival of what is undesirable consists in the continuous succession of the absence of that which is undesirable; thus, one must certainly not entertain doubts regarding its distinctness [from mere non-existence]. The relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is expressed by the words "of all people. However, it is for the sake of slaying the wicked *daityas*.

Just as in the case of "of Śumbha and Niśumbha" and so forth, the term "of people" (*janānām*) is intended to indicate all [people] (*sarveṣām*) in order to suggest their predominance; likewise, "subjugation" (*vidheyatvam*) means being under one's own control (*svādhīnatvam*). Thus, the meaning of the word *vaśya* (subdued) is precisely the bringing of all [beings] under one's own control. Therefore, it does not refer merely to [the subjugation of] wealth, sons, or wives.

There would be a contradiction regarding the number of actions being six, due to the predominance of gains such as those involving the heart and so forth. Furthermore, the interpretation found in the *Padārthādarśa* and other works—that it is "subservience to another" (*avaśyatva*) or "acting according to the word of another" (*vacanakāritva*)—is also refuted, because it fails to apply to cases such as the acquisition of wealth and the like. Now, if this were so, what of the case where one is carried away by a flood?

If one were to recite it seven times at night while facing the western direction for the sake of wealth such as white cattle and the like, there would be a contradiction with the words of the *Śrīrājarājeśvarī-kavaca*:
"In your presence, by the power of this application, [I shall obtain] the command of the regions," and so forth, as will be stated later.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement [that the practice] must be performed specifically in the direction of the Moon, the following statement from the *Saṃhitā*— namely, "In the subjugation of a great king,
one should recite twenty-seven times over the course of twenty-one days while standing facing the eastern direction"— would be contradicted in every school of thought.

Indeed, no one, even in their mind, can claim that this practice for bringing a great king under control lacks the quality of being a "subduing" (vaśya) practice; for through it, one may attain results such as the ritual of paralyzing (staṃbhana) or the granting of boons (diśā). Nor is what is called "bringing under control" (vaśīkāra) merely a matter of intoxication.
It must be stated that everything is indeed a binding and a bending, or "all is equal.

In that case, however, there arises the contingency of the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) being expectant of further application during the act of making [the object] submissive (*tadāyattīkaraṇe*). Immediately after the description of this procedure, it is said that in the acts of attraction and subjugation (*ākarṣaṇa-vaśīkāre*), [it is done] by means of the single [mantra].
Nor is there any sublation of the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā*.
For it is not reasonably possible for the injunction regarding the ear to be identical with the procedure for immobilization (*staṃbhanavidhi*) characterized as previously described;

this is because they are absolutely contradictory, being mutually exclusive by virtue of their respective counter-correlates (*pratiyogi*). Nor [can it be established] through the principle of "presumption from the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*).

If it is argued that "since the text [states] 'facing east,' one can indeed say that the injunctions are identical," we reply: "Not so. For while it is possible for the text to refer primarily to the principal [act], there is no lack of justification [for this interpretation]. Indeed, it is precisely because of the specific [injunction] that the facing eastward is restricted to the act of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

It is said that because it is possible for this [rite] to be adopted, there is no possibility of its being a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*). Even according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, since facing westward is possible precisely because of the specific statement,
the inclusion of this ritual act within [the established rite] is established without obstacle.
He indicates the cause [of this] by means of the passage beginning with "pravṛtti" (activity).
For every effect—characterized by coming, going, anger, speaking, victory, and so forth—is dependent upon activity;
therefore, for those who possess yoga, anger arises from the obstruction of that [activity], just as it arises from the obstruction of wealth. In that regard:

In this regard, there is the possession of the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇasamanvaya*). Nor should it be argued that, in such a case, there would be no cessation of eating and so forth; for we do not prescribe the performance [of the rite] with reference to the general category of "paralysis" (*stambhana*), but rather to specific instances of paralysis, such as the arrival of an enemy army and the like.

There is no fault in this, because the application [of the rite] is directed toward the commonality of enemies; even in the case of eating together and so forth, it is accepted as a desired outcome. "Mutually" (*mithaḥ*) means those who have attained mutual affection;
"enmity-removal" (*vairasādana*) refers to causing hatred [between them]. Nor is there hatred toward a neutral person.

The production [of hatred] would not be included here; for it is not said that "those two have hatred at their end" merely for the purpose of describing the greatness of the act of hating, as in the case of the phrase "of those who are affectionate. For even one who is affectionate generates hatred, how much more so one who is not such?

Regarding the word "not": since the definition [of hatred] as "that which enters into the production of aversion" cannot avoid the fault of being under-extensive (*avyāpti*), [the opponent's response] is ineffective. Furthermore, the phrase "mutually" merely refers to the observation of greatness;
for even in the case of an action that produces aversion toward one of two parties, it remains included within the category of hatred itself.
This is because that part [of the definition] cannot be included, as it would result in under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Although "expulsion" (*uccāṭana*) consists in driving someone out from one's own country, city, village, house, and so forth, once they have been expelled from the country and such places, their expulsion from the house is already accomplished as a matter of course.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) can indeed be formulated as follows: "If [the term] *namita* were to mean 'one who has been excessively tormented,' then the primary word *ādi* (and so forth), which serves to include the city and other such places, would be redundant. Nevertheless, even in that case, it refers to one for whom the expulsion from the city, the house, and so forth is intended.

This statement is made in order to indicate that even the expulsion of one's own [enemy] is included within *uccāṭana* (eradication); otherwise, since the expulsion from a specific location would itself be [that], there would be the undesirable consequence of the expulsion from a city or similar place being a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).
O Brahmins, one should avoid killing brahmins and others who are very righteous. One should employ [the means of death] against enemies of the king, excluding women.
One may act for the sake of the blood of people according to one's own will, but a minister should not do so out of greed.
The term "killing" (*māraṇa*), which might be misconstrued from such statements as "battle" (*raṇa*) and so forth, is defined by the passage beginning with "of living beings" (*prāṇinām*).

To avoid the consequence that even the taking of life from Prajñā and others—whose vital breaths have not been established through ritual—by means of fire-offerings (*homa*), digging, and so forth, would also constitute killing, he says: "of living beings" (*prāṇinām*); [meaning those who possess] life inherently.

The meaning is: "of those who possess perfected vital breaths" (*siddhaprāṇavatām*). Now, an objection: for one engaged in the construction of a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and so forth for the purpose of performing rites such as pacification (*śānti*), if by chance a tree falls or a sculptor dies during the cutting and other operations, would it not follow that he becomes an agent of the practice of killing (*māraṇa*)? To this [it is replied]:...

If it is argued that this is not the case because even there [in those instances], the defining characteristic [of the act] is present due to the presence of the sense of sight, and that such an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) is not accepted—[the opponent replies: "If that were so, then since the fear of death exists everywhere, the unshakable engagement of the learned (śiṣṭas) in activities such as the construction of a pavilion would be impossible. We say: do not say so; for what is called 'taking' (haraṇa) is that which has 'taking' as its intended object (uddeśaka).

There is no such activity here; for this [action] was not undertaken with the destruction of the artisan's life as its aim, whereby his status as a "killer" (māraka) might be suspected in this case. Nor is it the case that one who recites the hymn at the three junctions of the day becomes a killer in that way, for even so, [the charge] is unavoidable, since he recites that hymn specifically with the intent to kill.
It must be stated: if death is inevitable, then [the rite] takes place in the Gaṅgā;

for it is the specific location itself that is the intended object (uddeśya). Nor does this mean that even when a performance is undertaken with the intent of dying there, if it is not completed due to a powerful obstacle, the performance is still considered to have occurred in that place.

It should not be argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established there because the application of a lighter expiation is desired and impossible to perform; for if that were the case, then the meaning of the word "stealing" (*haraṇa*) would simply be an activity conducive to stealing with the intent to steal, and yet this definition would still over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to the Śyena sacrifice and similar acts.

It should not be argued that there is pervasion (*vyāpti*) [of the definition] because both components are present therein—since the death of the enemy is indeed the intended object (*uddeśya*), and since [the act] is the instigator of the meditation on death and the brandishing of one's own sword;
for such an operation must be qualified by the absence of such an intervening agency (*dvāraka*). For it is not [the case that...].

Does the operation consisting of the Śyena sacrifice and so forth become the cause of the enemy’s death without making the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) its medium? Or rather, is it that from the Śyena sacrifice an *adṛṣṭa* arises, by which [the act of] striking with a sword and so forth is accomplished, and from that, death [occurs]? And yet, even among the learned (*śiṣṭas*), there is no engagement in this [Śyena sacrifice].

It should not be said that [the Śyena sacrifice] is the cause of hell; for while it is true that "from the Śyena comes killing, from killing comes hell," thus it produces hell through a causal chain, the sacrifice itself does not produce hell in any of its fivefold aspects. If you argue that this is because of the prohibition, "One must not kill," which constitutes its object, then [we reply]: in that case, [let us consider] with an animal...

"Even a sacrifice enjoined by such [injunctions] as 'one should sacrifice'—would it not be the same? It is replied: In the animal sacrifice, when it is performed with heaven as its objective, the injunction compels one to carry out even the act of killing; however, the Śyena and other such [sacrifices] do not have killing as their objective, for they are undertaken with the intent to kill [the enemy].

Thus, there is a great disparity between the two. [Objection: Even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyā*), and likewise, there is the consequence of an improper extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to dying at Prayāga and other such places.
For in those cases, death does not occur by means of a Vedic prior action (*pūrvakriyā*) as seen in the example; rather, it occurs through the mediation of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
One should not be confused; for such an action is a means specifically toward the primary fruit of death characterized by that [action].

Now, one might object: is there not a mutual relationship of cause and effect between the action and the death? Indeed, it is precisely through the aforementioned method, such as entering the fire, that such a death occurs.

If it is argued that [the action] is not [the cause] because another action in its production is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), do not say so; for the operation (*vyāpāra*) must also be qualified by being something other than what is enjoined (*vihitānyatvena*). Indeed, existing actions such as going and the like are not enjoined. [Objection:
But if this were the case, then even in the absence of a son, the *putrīya-homa* and other [rites] would [be valid].

If it is argued that even the practices for killing—though universally agreed upon as being applications of killing—are nonetheless prescribed by the Tantric scriptures, this is true; however, there are indeed two types of injunctions. One concerns worldly results, such as the desire for subjugation of kings or the death of enemies; the other concerns the hereafter, such as heaven.

The second [type of action] is performed out of a desire for liberation (*mokṣa*). Even the first [type] is of two kinds: that which contains elements such as approaching the wives of others, drinking intoxicants, and violence—each of which is prohibited by other scriptural injunctions—and that which does not contain such elements.
Thus, that which is prescribed here by the term "enjoined" (*vihita*) refers specifically to that which is not prohibited by other scriptural injunctions.

For there is no possibility of non-occurrence [of the injunction] because it is easily established that it is distinct from what has been enjoined— such that our stated position would be contradicted by another procedural statement (prayoga-vacana) like the *puttalī-homa* and so forth; thus,
the objection regarding death is avoided if it is understood through the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) and the like.

It is intended as being of the nature of the destruction of the destruction of the respective times qualified by their producing death; or, if what is intended is the continued existence of the connection with the vital air known as *jīvana* for a time other than its end, then it is necessarily [the result of] karma.

If what is intended is merely the non-arrival of the time of death, then there is paralysis (*stambhana*). Likewise, the destruction of snakes, thieves, and so forth is the cessation of the possibility of undesirable events arising from them;
this consists in the non-perception of those [objects], followed by their persistence in subsequent times and in that same location.

Due to the distinction of the intention (*vivakṣā*) regarding non-arrival, this should be understood as being included within pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and immobilization (*staṃbhanā*). Thus, even in the three nights, if the destruction of recitation (*japa-nāśa*) is intended, then it consists of the protection of the state prior to the victory over enemies through pacification and so forth; or else, [it is] the recitation itself.

The absolute non-existence [of an enemy] consists in the attainment of successive recurrence; therefore, if there is no coming or going [of the enemy], then there is paralysis (*stambha*), but not the destruction of the enemy. O Goddess, when the enemy is subdued, it is by means of a hundred lamps, yet even with those, one suffers defeat if they are devoid of feet.

In the *Saṃhitā*, the separate mention of the destruction of enemies and the defeat of enemies [is sufficient]; therefore, enough with this prolixity. Furthermore, the practice of killing is not fit to be performed, because it produces rebirth in hell. Nor is this [text] to be considered authoritative merely because of its description of such practices.
Or rather, explaining that rebirth in hell for all occurs due to the arising of hatred, [the author] describes the yantras associated with the letters of the alphabet;
compared to other yantras, these letter-yantras are easily mastered,
and according to the Saṃhitā, the letter-yantras for women shall yield results immediately.
It has been established that the mantras of base men yield only meager results;
therefore, the author begins with the words "Now," etc., to reveal a few previously mentioned seed-mantras (*bījamantra*) from among the tantras. However, [he does not do so] in [all] the tantras...

By this much, it has been indicated that the authority (*prāmāṇya*) [of the work] and the fruitfulness of the effort expended by the author [are established], as well as the purpose of this *yantra* which was taught through the words "those who accomplish...
and so forth; and all this *yantra* is perceived as being favorable to oneself.
One should not employ the entire mind in meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and other such practices; rather, one should know how to act in accordance with that [knowledge].
Thus, having performed the daily obligatory duties such as bathing, and having worshipped the chosen deity while practicing celibacy, one should eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) on an auspicious day.
Having propitiated one's own family deity, having written [the mantra] there, and at night...

"Oṃ! This yantra has been drawn by me; O Lord, what kind of auspicious result will it yield? Having asked this, one should sleep for three days. Then, when knowledge favorable to the attainment of the desired object arises, one should consecrate that divine yantra through rites such as *pratiṣṭhā* and wear it for the removal of suffering.

If, due to one's own prior habituation, a dream, or adverse circumstances, this [mantra] is not understood, another yantra should be followed, and not that [mantra]. This is stated in the Yantracintāmaṇi: "Having bathed and become pure, one should worship the deity of the bank; with effort, one should draw the yantra."
O beloved, one should perform worship for three days according to the prescribed rules for enjoyment.

For three days, one should sleep on the ground, remain pure, and be devoted to celibacy. After three days, a dream will undoubtedly arise for the practitioner—whether it be of a Siddha, a Sādhya, or an enemy. It is truly auspicious.

Whether it be auspicious or fixed, this presiding deity of the machine (yantra) speaks necessarily in the dream. When a dream occurs, one should predict its fulfillment; or rather, one should predict exactly what was heard in the dream as it was heard from the mouth of the deity. Having heard the fruit of the dream from the mouth of the deity...
Success is achieved through the prescribed ritual. When one's dreams are unimpeded, then another supreme yantra must be employed;

for even though many mantras have been taught by me, O Lord of Creatures, whichever yantra brings success for whichever specific mantra, that [yantra] alone should be adopted, and others are prohibited.
One should strictly avoid [impure] substances; having written [the mantra] in this manner, whatever one performs, success (*siddhi*) is proclaimed.
This procedure has been proclaimed for any and every application. Also, in the *Mantramahodadhi*:
"On an auspicious day, having propitiated one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), being self-restrained, one should sleep..."
For three days, one should subsist on sacrificial offerings (haviṣya) and remain restrained;
one should worship one's own deity every day, asking: "O Lord, what is this that has been written here? What is your desired form?
On the third night, the person shall obtain in a dream [the deity] as perfected, as yet to be accomplished, or as well-disposed.

If this [enemy] has indeed become an enemy, then one should not draw this "enemy-yamtra" at all; rather, having abandoned that, the wise person should draw another yamtra even in the absence of a dream.
The word "third" (tṛtīya) is used with the intention of referring to the first and second [cases], but not...
It is restricted to the three [classes], as it was previously stated that it begins from the third day. There is a distinction elsewhere:

a straight line indicates prosperity (*lakṣmī*), while a curved line indicates poverty (*daridratā*). If, at the time of constructing the diagram (*yantra*), the lines have gone astray elsewhere, it will certainly not bear fruit despite long effort and victory.

Furthermore, if one should, out of delusion or other causes, write a letter in a place where it is not prescribed, even if it occurs in a dream, the wise man should abandon that and write another letter in its place. Otherwise, he incurs failure, whether in the waking state or even in the body; for among the prescribed clusters of letters, even a single one may be omitted.
If a syllable is missing, one does not attain full perfection, nor even proximity to Śiva himself.
Through the omission of a mantra-syllable, the practitioner’s lifespan shall diminish. Through the omission of a vowel, there is lethargy;
through the omission of the objective (the goal), there is the loss of ritual efficacy. Through the contraction of the yantra-seat, the syllables become indistinct.

"By means of writing, all yantras become effective, just as the word of Śiva himself; therefore, having become composed, one should write all the yantras. Now, the letters to be written in all the yantras are demonstrated, specifically regarding the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and other parts.

That which has not been mentioned [elsewhere] is written here: one should write in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) the seed-syllable (*bīja*) produced in accordance with each respective rite. These are the fivefold-compounded seed-syllables: *hrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hyaiṃ hauṃ*. This was stated by the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. These are the uncompounded...

Having performed these [preliminaries], one should write a single seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the middle of that [mandala] for the purpose of the rite; then, one should write the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of practice (*sādhya*), and so forth, in the directions starting from the east. Furthermore, one should write another seed-syllable in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), or else within the respective elemental circles (*bhūta-maṇḍala*) beneath that seed-syllable.

Alternatively, one should write a single seed-syllable outside each of those; the wise man should place the seed-syllables of the five unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛta*) in the center according to the requirements of the rite, as seen in the *Arjunārvāpārijāta*. One should assign the letters of the elements to the four corners of the *bhūpura* (the protective square). Of the *bhūpura*...

O Goddess, one should draw three sets of eight syllables each—corresponding to the eight rasas, the eight directions, the eight vital breaths (prāṇas), and the Gāyatrī—as well as the fivefold syllables (*apañcīkṛtārṇaka*), according to the observation of the *Saṃhitā*. These [syllables] are extracted in the *Pārijāta* commentary on the *Arjunopaniṣad*: "The vital breaths, together with the long vowels, [beginning with] 'pu' and 'ru'... (prāṇāḥ saddīrghāḥ puruhutapā...).

The seed-syllables (bījas) known as the "uncompounded" (apañcīkṛta) consist of the letters *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, *na*, *ja*, *pa*, *pra*, *ṇa*, *ya*, *u*, *tāḥ*, *sa-daṇḍāḥ* [the letter *ṃ* with the *daṇḍa*], and the void-state (*riktabhāva*) excluding the final vowel. Furthermore, the four vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*),
joined respectively with the letters *la*, *va*, *ra*, and *pa*, are combined with the long vowels of the second, fourth, and sixth [classes].
Being joined with the twelve vowels, they should be combined with the "staff" (the letter *m*), which is the anusvāra;

and the fifth, which is the vital breath (*praṇa*), being devoid of—that is, excluding—the final long vowel, it means that [the syllable] is accompanied by that [fifth vowel] and possesses the staff. Thus, the seed-mantra (*bīja*) of Prāsāda is finalized. These...

The meaning is that all five are denoted by the term "uncompounded seed" (*apañcīkṛtabīja*). Likewise, the individual soul (*jīva*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), power (*śakti*), vision (*dṛṣṭi*), and subjugation (*vaśyādi*) [are included]. For the mantra and yantra, there is the mantra for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*) according to the *Gāyatrī*. Furthermore, the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the elements (*bhūta*) and the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) are located within the yantra.

The phrase *gānivaidaśeti* refers to another tantra. Its meaning is as follows: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is said to be joined with the letters *sa* and *ṣa*, conjoined with the vowel *u* (the sound of the world), pervaded by *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, and accompanied by the *visarga*. This specific phoneme, characterized by these aforementioned qualities, is designated by the term *jīva* within the yantra.

The meaning is that the letter *ha*, which is at the end of *saṃ* (the letter *s*), conjoined with the letter *u*—which is the vowel of the world (*bhuvanasvara*) and the first of the vowels (*nārādi*)—becomes known as the "life-force" (*jīva*). Its writing should be performed below the central seed-syllable within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that [lotus]; for this *oṃ* is the life-force of the yantra.

It should be placed below the middle seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*), according to the statement in the *Itikāmika-tantra*: "In the middle of the seed-syllable of the individual soul (*jīvabīja*) is 'Saḥ'. Thus, the *Bhṛgu* [syllable] with the *visarga* is well-known as the vital breath (*prāṇa*); another [reading] states that it is to be written as such, according to Bhāskarāya in the *Tribhāskara*: "The vital breath is *ahaṃsaḥ*; I am that (*so'ham*)."

The four syllables [of *haṃsaḥ so'haṃ*] should be written in the four intermediate directions starting from the northeast (īśāna). According to the statement, "One should write the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the order beginning with the northeast as 'haṃsaḥ so'haṃ'," one should write the *ajapā* [mantra] according to the sequence of the letters in both direct and reverse order, starting from the direction of Śambhu (the northeast).
And because of the statement in the *Tisaṃhitā*: "One should write the mantra of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) in the four directions above.

As for what has been said by some—that this very injunction is what establishes the northeast and so forth, since the word "direction" (*dik*) refers to the intermediate points (*vidiś*), that is incorrect; for such a term [does not apply here].
If it is argued that such [a sequence] is accepted because there is no evidence for the Saura calculation and it serves to harmonize the aforementioned statements,
[we reply]: "On both sides of the middle seed-syllable,

there is the letter ending in *sa* (ṣa), then the vowel *u*, then the letter ending in *śa* (śa) joined with the visarga, then the letter ending in *śa* (śa) joined with the thirteenth [vowel], then the letter ending in *sa* (ṣa) with the anusvāra."

In passages such as "one should recite *raṃ*," since there is no mention of writing the *ajapā* mantra on the sides in the descriptions of Śiva’s dance (*śivatāṇḍava*) and so forth, why would one not prefer a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) even there, in order to ensure syntactic unity with that [context]? Nor can it be argued that the word "sides" (*pārśva*) must be figurative when referring to Īśāna and the other [faces].

It cannot be argued that the word *diś* (direction) alone is used figuratively for the two sides (*pārśva*), nor can it be said that there is no possibility of generating [the meaning] by following the deficient [textual tradition]; for you too must assume that the words *diś* and *pārśva* have meanings such as "northeast" (*aiśāna*) and so forth, which results in a lack of elegance (*asaurasya*) across numerous instances.

Because it would also be possible [to interpret] it as referring to the sense-organ (*akṣa*). Nor does the word "direction" (*dik*) denote the sun and so forth in the context of the *Vidhiśeṣa*; otherwise, your own text would be contradicted by the fact that the word "direction" here refers to the intermediate directions (*vidik*). Since the existence and non-existence of the word "direction" are equal [in both cases], in all instances...

The inclusion of the word "pada" (foot) would be entirely purposeless. Furthermore, even if one were to abandon the natural sense of the words to maintain a single unified sentence, it would still be sublated by the alternative view; therefore, this argument amounts to nothing. As for the term "śakti," it refers to the power of the seed situated in the middle, as described in its respective Kalpa.

This is illustrative. By this, those who claim that in the case of the absence of the *śakti-bīja*, the *jīva-bīja* alone occupies the middle position are refuted; for it is generally taught that in almost all instances, the non-writing of those *bījas* is prescribed. Even in the absence of such a specific instance in some cases, [the rule holds].
Since the writing of the unquintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*) seed-syllables has been taught by you with supporting authority,
it follows by this same method that you must also establish the tenfold nature (*daśāṅgikatva*) of the general yantra;
otherwise, your own justification for the presence of such a nature in cases where the *śakti* is not written would be difficult to maintain.

Even those who claim that the seed-syllable of power (*śaktivīja*) must be written everywhere, their intellect is mistaken; for since this [rule] is sufficiently explained as being merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no authoritative evidence for writing the seed-syllable of power in every instance. This statement, however, is [based on] other statements belonging to various specific ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
It might be argued that this can be interpreted as referring to various specific seed-syllables (*bīja*) through the use of the particle *api*;
however, it is not capable of being authoritative by way of a simultaneous conjunction (*sahasamuccaya*).

In reality, O Great-minded One, where one recites the limbs (*aṅga*) and the mantras in their proper sequence, [the syllable] *Āṃ* is the seed-syllable, and *Śiru*, *Dvati*, and *Prāṇa* are the deities.

The seed-syllable (*bījaka*): the mouth-seed (*mukhabīja*) is *Śrīṃ*, and the sight-seed (*dṛṣṭibīja*) is *Māṃ*. Since this is demonstrated in the context of extracting the Gāyatrī mantra from the *Viśiṣṭasaṃhitā*, it follows that not only the Māyā-seed (*Hrīṃ*) is necessary everywhere, but rather both the Pāśava-seed (*Klīṃ*) and the Śrī-seed (*Śrīṃ*) as well.

The term *dṛṣṭi* refers to the two eyes; it is also indicative of the two ears, since the intention is to include the following of both as being conveyed by the word *dṛṣṭi*. Their placement is on the sides of the central seed-syllable, according to the sequence of right and left.
One should draw these two eyes on the sides;
likewise, according to the traditional instruction, one should draw the ears from the root-seed syllables written at the corners.
One should also place the seed-syllable of breath (praṇava) below the mountain (the forehead), repeating "I am that which is to be known."

And because it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: first from the right eye, then from its south, then from the north, then from its left, and then from the right; in this sequence, the right and left [eyes] should be drawn. Furthermore, one may proceed according to one's own preference, following either the traditional order (*āmnānakrama*) or the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), since both are well-established. However, some... [bhṛ...]

Those who reside in the six syllables of the *gum-ru-dana-lā-nā*, holding the *dhata* [syllable] upon their heads and possessing the nature of a single seed-syllable—this is renowned in the world by the name *yantra-jihvā*. They teach that it should be placed without fear directly below the central seed-syllable. *Jihvā*.

Some cite the statement, "One should place the seed-syllable in front," and the statement from the *Maṃtrasāra*, "The tongue [is touched] with 'Spraṃ'"; they present these as authoritative evidence in that regard. Others, however, maintain that all the letters [of the mantra], joined together, are found in the *Drāmarādrau* and in the compendia composed by humans.
How could there be consolation for the multitude of hands of the gods, who are agitated by doubts such as, "Is this not the tongue that sleeps? Is it not the tongue that speaks here?"?
Therefore, wherever the tongue is spoken of, what is written and remembered is precisely that [same] poison of the yantra.
They say that the state of the cognition of the commonality [of the object] is [the result]. Regarding "subjugation and so forth":

by the phrase "and so forth," there is the inclusion of other rites to be accomplished, such as pacification up to destruction, as well as the actions of the practitioner and the words [of the mantra].
For example, when Caitra performs a mantra for the purpose of subjugating Devadatta...

In the sentence "Make Devadatta, who belongs to Caitra, subject to my control," which is written there, Caitra is the agent (*sādhaka*), Devadatta is the object (*sādhya*), "subject to control" (*vaśam*) is the object (*karma*),
and "make do" (*kurviti*) is the verb (*kriyāpada*) repeated twice. The writing of these [elements] is declared in the *Saṃhitā*.
One should place the name of the practitioner, ending in the sixth case (dative), above the central seed-syllable;
one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (the *sādhya*), ending in the second case (accusative), below the central seed-syllable;
and one should place a pair of *kuru*s on both sides of the central seed-syllable in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Alternatively, [one may write] the name repeatedly or as a single line.
"The wise man should write it in its proper place"—thus it is said. "Reduplicated" means stated twice. "Pallava" (the sprout) refers to *vaśa-vaśaya* and so forth;

this is also found in the *Rāmapūrvatāpanīya*: "One should write the object of attainment (*sādhya*) ending in the accusative case, and likewise the practitioner (*sādhaka*) ending in the genitive case; one should place the two words 'kurū' at its sides. Thus [it is said]. Ṣa...

"The word of the practitioner (sādhaka) ending in the sixth case (genitive) is remembered above the central seed-syllable; the word of the object to be accomplished (sādhya) ending in the second case (accusative), along with a pair of *kurus*, is to be placed on both sides of the middle. This is from another Tantra. Regarding that, the specific method for the placement of the *māyā* seed-syllable in the center of the yantra is found in the *Padārthādarśa*.

The name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) is placed in the portion following the seed-syllable *vīja* and the letter *ra*; the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is placed above the fourth vowel.

Between those two, the name of the person to be acted upon is written again, followed by the verbal phrase "perform the rite" (*kuru*) such as "subjugate" (*vaśam*), etc., which is to be written above the person to be acted upon. As it is said in the *Saṃhitā*: "That is its power..."

"In the fourth part of the vowel-segment, one should write the syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*); in the fourth part of the vowel-segment, one should place the person to be subdued (*sādhaka*) under their control; one should write this joined above the *sādhya* for the sake of all success.
Thus also says the Teacher: "The *sādhya* is situated within the circle of the *Hṛllekhā*..."
In the two palms; then, one should write the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the north of the practitioner (*sādhaka*);
and within the space between *agni* (fire) and *śrī* (fortune), one should write the portion of the means for accomplishing the rite (*karmasādhakāṃśa*). This is the meaning:
the *sādhya* is the word expressing the action of the object to be accomplished, such as "do, do," and so forth. That...

On the two cheeks (kapolau) of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) drawn in a circular shape suitable for the entry of the name of the deity and so forth, [the letters] should be written. On the lower lip, in the portion of the letter *ra* within the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the syllables of the practitioner’s (*sādhaka*) name should be written below. Above that, [the letters of the name of the one to be protected should be written].
This means "the head of the letter *ṛ*. Thus, it follows that the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should be written in the upper portion of the fourth vowel-syllable.

Between the letters *ra* and the fourth vowel—the two syllables of fire and splendor (*agni-śrī*)—the word for the action, such as "subjugation" (*vaśa*), and so forth, should be placed in the middle portion within the part belonging to the practitioner.

"It should be drawn slightly above," [it is said]. Furthermore, regarding the reading of some that "one should draw another name of the object of meditation (sādhya) in the portion of the letter *repha* (*r*) of that [syllable]," even there, because it is intended to provide space for the interior [of the syllable], there is no disagreement whatsoever on this point. She...
Between the two, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), that which is intended here is as follows:
since it is possible to understand the meaning that one should draw [the syllable] on the cheek— an alternative term for the upper part of the practitioner—
and above the object to be accomplished, the [syllable] within the seed-syllable...

The statement that "that which is to be accomplished by *dhak* is *dhaḥ*, denoting the action" is also contrary to this meaning, because the fourth portion of the vowel (*svarabhāga*) is the nature of the end of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and because it is clear that the letter *ra* is posterior to the seed-syllable. Therefore, the five-syllabled [mantra] "caitrasya mama" is... [sā].
The name of the practitioner (*dhaka*) should be written above the portion containing the vowel *ī*, and below the portion containing the letter *ra*.

Between the fourth vowel (*ī*) and the letter *ra*—within the four-syllable sequence such as "Dhyāna-nāma-devadatta"—the two syllables "va-śaṃ" should be placed in the middle; and above the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should place the syllable *moha* on both sides of the line.
The established doctrine is that the *kurukurvi* mark should be written on the cheeks— which are synonymous with the *yoḥ*—
and this same method is indeed observed even in the case of the *kāma-bīja*, the *cāmuṇḍā-bīja*, the *śrī-rājarājeśvara-bīja*,
and others; however, writing them in the upper or other parts according to one's own preference is mentioned elsewhere.
Since it is appropriate [to refer] only to that which is being grasped (*upādāna*), what is the proof for the usage "this one" (*ayam amam*)?

If you argue that it is for the purpose of distinguishing [the speaker] from those many people named Caitra, do not say so; for the word *ayam* (this), when uttered with its three morae (*mātra*), has as its denotation only that which is being uttered, and thus there is no need for exclusion (*avyāvartana*). Where it is written...
If it is argued that this [formula] should be recited as "I desire to perform," then that other [formula],
"Enough, this is done for me," would not be possible; therefore,
one should say "for me" (*mahyam*) in the dative case after one's own name, followed by the word "pada" (step), and then the name of the fruit in the accusative case, followed by "dehi" (grant).
If it is argued that because of the observation of the statement "one should practice," such usage occurs even in instances where the genitive case ending is present;

[we reply: there is no confidence in this statement, as it is not seen in various authoritative texts such as the *Padārthādarśa* and others. Or, let it be granted that this statement occurs in the context of the *yantra* (diagrammatic arrangement).

If it is argued that "it should be *mamaiva tathā* [mine alone thus]," let it not be so; for according to the works of Bhāskara Rāma, this [word *mama*] is accompanied by the word *iti*, and since the word *sādhaka* appears in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) in the root verses, the word *asmad* (we/us) is likewise indistinguishable from the word *sādhaka*. Therefore...

Since the inclusion of both [the agent and the instrument] is intended, even in cases such as "the designation of the accomplisher (*sādhaka*) ending in the sixth case," the term "designation" (*ākhyā*) and so forth refers to the denoter (*vācaka*); thus, it is easy to include both of them. This is the direction [of the argument]. Furthermore, all that is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is... [end of fragment].

The multitude of ritual actions and mantras should be written in sequential rows within the seed-syllable (*bīja*), as it has been said: "The entire application [of the mantra] is to be written within the seed-syllable. Furthermore, even in the *saṃhitā*, one should write the root-seed-syllable again at its end, and within that, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).

Regarding the phrase "endowed with ritual action" (*karmādiyuktam*): for a mantra-diagram (*mantrayantra*), the Gāyatrī of that mantra must be written; for a mantra-diagram, the Gāyatrī of that mantra—such as "We know that [the essence] of that Person, we meditate upon the Great God" (*tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi*) and so forth—as prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for that specific mantra, should be written. This refers to the deity of the diagram.
In that context, the Gāyatrī of Tārayasi has been specifically stated as follows: "We know the King of Mantras;
we meditate upon the Bestower of Boons; may that Mantra inspire us. This is the Gāyatrī to be written.
Wherever the Gāyatrī is of this very form, by the substitution of the syllable *yaṃ* in place of the syllable *maṃ*, [the mantra is formed]. Where...

In the case of a [diagram] with eight petals and so forth that is empty, or according to a specific instruction, one should write the syllables of the *gāyatrī* mantra in the first row in groups of three; then, in the second row, one should write the syllables of the *yaṃtra-gāyatrī* in groups of three. However, in the specific case of the eight-petaled [diagram] and others, [the procedure for] the *gāyatrī*...
The syllables are traditionally remembered as being on the yantra, because of the statement that there are thirty-three [syllables] on each petal of the Gāyatrī;

the term "yantra" here is also indicative of the mantra. However, in the case of an eight-petaled [lotus] and other such [diagrams], it is specifically taught that the letters of the other [mantras] alone are the "lines" (linam); therein, the *bhūpura* (fortress-city) belongs to these [letters].
The following method for drawing the *aṣṭakāsuta* [diagram] should be performed, as stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
"The city of the earth is pervaded by the corners of the *kakubh* [triangle] divided threefold by the *gāyatrī* measures of the diagram.
Regarding that, where the specific drawing of the *mantra-gāyatrī* is prescribed elsewhere than in this context, there it should be applied.

Only the *gāyatrī* of the yantra is to be written on the outside, and not the *mantra-gāyatrī* as well; for even the previously cited statement intends only the writing of one or the other, not the writing of both together in a single place. However, where there is a discrepancy in number, in the absence of a specific rule, the general [rule applies].

Having written the [mantra] syllables starting from *triśādi* on the final leaf and so forth, one should perform the writing of the remaining [syllables], whether they are more or fewer, according to the maxim "there is elision or there is vṛddhi.
As for that which begins with *va* on the third petal and *vya* on the fifth petal...

Regarding the statement by some that "even in cases where there is a deficiency or excess of syllables, one should not be confused [by the discrepancy], provided there is no contradiction with the rule 'Dhīma' on the eighth petal and so forth," this must be said in reply:
in the case of twenty-four syllables, on such petals, such...

Even if there were a restriction that [the rule] applies only to those of the same class (*śavarṇa*), there is no evidence for such a restriction. And as long as it is possible, the absence of evidence means that the general rule does not apply;
for in such a case, where the scope has been attained, the maxim of "the abandonment of what was already obtained" (*antyalopa*) would apply by default.

Now, regarding the *nanu-saraṇa*: furthermore, if one accepts the previously stated rule, one should again write the syllables of the root *gāyatrī* beneath them, according to the number of syllables in the Vedas, Vedas, Vedas, three, five, three, two, two, and Vedas— this being the interpretation of the statement from the *Keralatantra*, in the chapter on the extraction of the *Tāraṇī* yantra.

Otherwise, a contradiction would arise; for in this case, since the twenty-seven syllables of the Gāyatrī—namely *vidmahe*, *dhīmahī*, and *pracodayāt*—would be written on the eight petals, the writing of the syllables themselves would be established. Now, even if that aforementioned objection were raised here, it is not accepted.

If it is argued that the word *teti* (in the phrase *tetitavāpi*) is supplied [as an ellipsis], then let it be so supplied; for I have already stated previously that the phrase "in the absence of a specific [qualification]" (*asati viśeṣe*) is intended precisely to exclude such cases. Furthermore, I too, having supplied the phrase "in the absence of specific statements" (*viśeṣavacanānām asattve*) within my own treatise...

If it is argued that [the term] should be excluded, let it be excluded; for what purpose would it serve? This is because the fault of *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis) has already become the primary defect, and because the previously mentioned faults—such as the lack of authoritative evidence (*niṣpramāṇatva*)—are as unalterable as a vajra-strike. This applies even in cases where there is an absence of eight petals and so forth.

Being distressed by the failure to find a place for writing the *gāyatrī*, some have instructed that one should write it within a square grid (*caturasra*) with paths (*vīthī*) in between; in the absence of such [space], one should perform a mental visualization of an eight-petaled lotus and then write it upon the support of the yantra.

The non-observation of the *Dukta-saṃhitā* reveals that the mantra for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*) is the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*. One should write it within two specific verses in the shape of a circle; outside of that, one should write the mantra of the Goddess Prāṇa everywhere.

"One should move it," because of the statement in the *Saṃhitā*; and because the construction of the ghee is clearly taught in the *Kavacapaṭala* section of the *Saṃhitā*, stating, "Having drawn [the design] with that ghee, one should move it with the *prāṇa-mantra*. And this mantra is to be recited twice, as stated in that very same place.

From the instruction [in the Kevalī-tantra]: "One should write four letters of the breath and mind on the tooth-leaf (daṃtapatra), and the remaining letters, five each, on the filament-leaves (timapatra)";
since this specific rule is seen there, and in the absence of such a specific rule, the Mātṛkā [is placed] only on the line of the circumference (vṛttarekhā).

However, those who have seen much [in the tradition] maintain that the writing of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and other mantras should be done within the pathways (*vīthī*) formed by the two layers of powder; this applies everywhere in the same way. Even the statement, "One should write the *pratiṣṭhā* and *prāṇa* [mantras] in the spaces of the fire-lines," refers to this very point: in the spaces of the fire-lines.

The meaning of the phrase "in the intervals between these" is not that the writing of the mantras of the world-protectors (dikpālas) will take place in the spaces between the eight petals and the two outer drawn circles;
rather, it refers to the encirclement by the Mātṛkās, having drawn the two circular lines.

Whatever is performed within that interval should first be done by means of the movement of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra. One should cause it to be surrounded on all sides and enveloped with the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *gha*, according to the *Saṃhitā*; thus says the *Mantrakalpa* regarding those beginning with *dra* and *ma*.
Because of the observation of a specific statement regarding a particular location, there is no further drawing [of the diagram] there; for it is stated in another mantra:

"The seed-syllables of the elements (*bhūtabīja*) and the letters of the elements (*bhūtavarṇa*)—which are described in the second chapter—should be installed according to the distinction of the ritual, as there is a distinction of the elements. Thus, one should install the syllables of the elements (*bhūtārṇa*). [End of section: *Udrāmare*.

One should draw the elemental syllables (*bhūtavarṇa*) in the four corners of the ground-pur (*bhūpura*); O Goddess, one should assign those respective syllables according to the requirements of each specific rite.
Regarding the phrase "in the corners of this *bhūpura*" and so forth, since no distinction was made there, it is stated in the first half [of the verse] that one should draw the elemental syllables.

"When all [the syllables] have been written," and so forth, regarding what is to be done there: the intention is that in rites such as pacification (śānti) and subjugation (vaśya), one should write exactly ten syllables of the respective element that has arrived, and not all of them. Regarding the question of where these are to be written, in response to that requirement for a location:

"Syetyādi" and so forth; one should likewise assign the elemental colors (*bhūtavarṇa*) to the other four corners of the ground as well. According to the requirements of each specific rite, one should assign those respective colors.
As for Kāśī-vyāsa, at the time of performing the application of the six rites (*ṣaṭkarmaprayoga*), he [describes] the maṇḍala of each respective element...

Regarding the ten syllables to be written, the traditional instruction is as follows: starting from the southeast corner of the square and proceeding clockwise, one should divide the four corners in the sequence of one, two, three, and four, and write the ten syllables as they have been described. This is the teaching of Nārāyaṇabhadra.
They say that one should divide the syllables of the *bhūta* [mantra] into four parts and write them in the four directions.

As for the passage beginning with "tattatkārya," Nārāyaṇa maintains that it is not redundant, because it is an analysis of the meaning of the half-verse "bhūmikoṇe" (in the corners of the ground) by means of a verse and three-quarters of another verse.
What was stated by Bhadra is incorrect, because it must be explained according to the direction already given;

nor is it possible for it to be a "vicaraṇa" (explanation/elucidation), for a vicaraṇa consists in stating that very same meaning through a different synonym, as for example, explaining "he cooks" (*pacati*) by the word "cooking" (*pāka*).

It is not so here, because of the addition of the phrase "tattatkārya" (for each respective effect) and so forth; thus, by this incidental discussion, since these locations have not been stated, one might ask: is there a drawing at the site of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath), or rather, what is the seed-syllable of the respective world-protectors (*dikpāla*)?

Regarding the objection raised by some that, because the sense of conjunction (*sāhitya*) is understood through the dual compound (*dvaṃdva*), there would be a requirement to write the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*)— which consist of the letters *va* and *bha*— in all ten directions, it is answered that such a requirement does not arise because there is no expectation for further spatial placement (*sthala-ākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, [this applies] to the elemental mandalas (*bhūta-maṇḍala*) in their respective...

Regarding the statement that even those [mantras] obtained through differences in desire should be written here: it is said that for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), one should write everywhere within a water-maṇḍala; for subjugation (*vaśya*), in a fire-maṇḍala; for paralyzing (*stambhana*), in an earth-maṇḍala; for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), in an ether-maṇḍala; and for eradication (*uccāṭana*), in an air-maṇḍala or in a fire-house.

"One should draw [the diagram] for one desiring death and worship it as well; at the time of the rising of each respective *bhūta*, one should remove that particular *maṇḍala*. Some authorities maintain that this means one should draw *maṇḍalas* within the corners (vidiś) inside the square on the exterior of the *yantras*. Furthermore, beyond the square...

Some say those [letters] should be placed in the four corners; others say they should be in the center. This dual opinion—that they should be in the corners of the ground or elsewhere—is contrary to the *Udrāma*. Furthermore, even when writing the letters of the elements (*bhūtavarṇa*) within mandalas drawn in the corners, writing them in the corners is contradictory.

The first opinion stated that this does not encounter any contradiction; therefore, they say that the writing of the constituent letters (*bhūtavarṇa*) of all mantras occurs within the mandala drawn in the corner.
And as it has been said regarding this: "By virtue of possessing qualities such as subjugation (*vaśyatva*) and so forth, [this applies] to all mantras..."
Furthermore, since the writing of letters is also prescribed specifically in those places designated for the attainment of the petals (*dalas*),

and because it is observed in the *Uḍḍāmareśvara* during the section on the *Ḍuṃdubhi* yantra that one should write the letters of the elements (*bhūtas*) belonging to the external mandala, [the letters] are joined with their respective mandalas.
One should write [the letters] according to the *Taittirīya-saṃhitā*, as seen in its introductory section; elsewhere, their writing is indeed impossible.
In the circles of elements (*bhūta-maṇḍala*), for the sake of each respective ritual action, all the elemental letters determined by the desired rules must be written down, ten in number for each.

As for what was stated by Itikāśī, Vyāḍi, and others—that [the mantra] should be divided [and applied] by revolving through the ten directions—this is not correct, because it would contradict the *Saṃhitā* introductory to the *Śrīrājarājeśvara-kavaca*, which states: "one should offer the letters of the elements [by revolving] in the ten directions. For this [text] does not prescribe the writing of the letters of a single element.

Because the fulfillment of the ten directions occurs simply by the placement of each individual syllable (*raṃ*), a second enclosure would be redundant; furthermore, since it is specifically observed in this ritual procedure that all desires are fulfilled by repeating [the process] twice, the mandalas of all beings should be drawn in the ten directions with a double repetition.

In that view, there is no contradiction whatsoever in writing the complete colors of each respective element within its own mandala in the ten directions, and performing the repetition twice during the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*). Thus, by the previously cited statements, [the colors] of each single element alone [are to be placed] in the four corners.

If it is argued that, because they have been obtained [as applicable] throughout the ten directions, a specific rule is enjoined; and likewise, because of the maxim that "when [an action] has been performed once, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled," they are written down in only one place, while their repetition is enjoined as a specific rule when they have already been obtained— if this is the case, then there would be the acceptance of two distinct things to be enjoined.

Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). In our view, when only "delimited by the ten directions" (*daśadigavacchedena*) is written down, this alone is what is enjoined (*vidhīyate*).

However, since writing [the word] five times in the ten directions is otherwise inexplicable (*anupapadyamāna*), it implies (*ākṣipati) a repetition twice; thus, that part is not the object of the injunction (*vidheyatā*), but rather—

This is merely a restatement of what has already been established. By this same line of reasoning, the injunction for sacrifice (*yāga-vidhi*)—conveyed by the very word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—being untenable without a substance, implies all substances whatsoever.
Since rice (*vrīhi*) is also thus obtained, [injunctions] such as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) function as restrictive rules (*niyama*).

The Mīmāṃsakas establish the conclusion that [the suffix] *dhāyeṣa* follows the previously mentioned rule. Here, the writing of the ten vowels—*a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ*—beginning with *a*, should be performed according to their respective desires in the manner: *aṃ āṃ namaḥ*, *aiṃ aiṃ namaḥ*, and so forth. Thus, each ritual action (*karman*) is associated with two vowels.

Regarding the statement by the teachers that "five mantras of each of the three purified letters are accomplished," it is said: "By ten [syllables] at a time, preceded by *namaḥ* and *oṃ*, joined with the *dvandva* and the *bindu*.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "The previously mentioned elemental letters (*bhūtavarṇa*), ten by ten, [are joined] with the *rāya* group and the *bindu*."

"Yuktānnamotān"—therefore, those *bhūtas* of the respective classes who have arrived according to their desires should be depicted as having attained the state of the fifth mantra as described; they are not to be depicted otherwise than as heard [in the scripture].
Furthermore, in any *bhūta-maṇḍala* that serves as the locus for the mantras to be depicted, there is a triangle (*trikoṇa*).

Having performed the meditation, the practitioner of mantra should inscribe the five mantras, beginning with the first, in due order within the central, eastern, northern, southern, and middle sections; he should worship them according to his own preference in the three corners of the center of the *yoni* and in its middle,
as well as at its tip and center, repeatedly.
The two statements of the Ācārya, "the letters [should be] established as having become the object" and "it is said," show the remainder [of the teaching].

This is the summary according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. Furthermore, the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the guardians of the directions have also been stated in the context of the mantras of those respective directional guardians;
they should be inscribed in their corresponding directions—this is the specific detail.

Since the writing of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the [eight] guardians of the directions is established by implication through the mention of the writing of the mantras of the guardians of the directions, their writing should also be performed.

However, in cases where they are not explicitly mentioned, one should write these very seed-syllables within squares at the respective directions; one should offer the seed-syllables of the respective guardians of the directions in those respective directions.

One should write "tyādi" (and so forth) outside of that, adorned with the mantras of Indra and the other [guardians] in the directions, as well as a square [mandala] with four doors and provided with three lines; this is because it is seen in the *Saṃhitā* and other texts.

As for the statement in another tantra that one should place the syllables of the lords of the directions, beginning with the one called "Hṛdaya," outside of those eight directions—that is [also valid].
In that context as well, the word *vāhya* (to be carried out) has the same meaning as *saṃhitā* (collected/combined).

Indeed, it is not possible even for the mind to interpret *vāhya* in the *saṃhitā* as having the sense of "four-sided" (*caturasra*); rather, it refers to being outside (*bahiḥ*) from the previously mentioned machine (*yantra*).

Dārṭāntika said: "In this case as well, by this [statement], the objection of some who claim that the 'Heart' is the name for the heart-machines (*hṛdayayantra*) of the seed-syllables of the Guardians of the Directions (*dikpāla*), and that these should be drawn in the outer portion in their respective directions, is refuted; or rather, it is resolved by the intention that they belong to the outer part starting from the enclosure (*vṛta*)."

The intended meaning is that these ten limbs have been collected here, while others not included must be taken from other tantras; otherwise, because the colors, the fivefold elements, the seed-syllables, and so forth are not mentioned, the number would be less than ten.

Regarding the *tāpatraya*: since another Tantra states, "The syllable of Agni (*ra*) is projected outside the mantra for protection," the seed-syllable of Fire (*ra*) should also be written outside the yantra in the eight directions. All of this has been shown in its entirety by Bhāskararāya in the *Ṛgbhāskara*, beginning with the words: "The life-force (*jīva*): prā..."

The *jīva-mantra*, the *ātman-mantra*, *śakti*, *netra*, the pair of *śrotras*, and the *jihvā*; the *sādhya*, the *kartṛ*, the *karma*, the *etad-kriyāvat-vega*, and the two *gāyatrīs*—these are distinguished by the *mantra*, the *yantra*, and the *prabheda*. [Therein are] the *prāṇakṣepa*, the *mantra-hṛd-bhūta-bīja*, the *rakṣā-varṇas*, the *mātṛkā-bhūta-varṇas*, and so forth. Thus...

Twenty syllables are to be written; this mantra is according to the tradition (*saṃpradāya*), as stated by Jīva. *Hsauḥ* is the aggregate of the five specific Mātṛkās; *Prāṇa* with the *visarga* is *Bhṛgu*. The *Jīva-mantra* is *Haṃsa*, consisting of two syllables; *Dhaka* is their agent (*kartṛ*).

The "projection of the vital breaths" (*prāṇakṣepa*) refers to that by which the vital breaths are projected into a doll or similar object; this is the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra. It consists of the mantras of the heart, the world-protectors, the seed-syllables of the elements, and specifically the seed-syllables of the unevolved (*apañcīkṛta*) elements, for even when there is an addition of mere ornaments, there is no loss of their essential nature.

Therefore, the discrepancy and the deficiency or excess—namely, that those items mentioned as things to be adopted in the *Padārthādarśa* and other works are not discussed here as such, nor conversely, that the "seeds of the elements" (*bhūtabīja*) mentioned here are not mentioned there—is hereby removed. [Objection: But what about the description of the colors of the elements (*bhūtavarṇa*)...?
If it is argued that the *Khanādevamātṛkā* mantra should also be written [therein], it would not be so;

for according to one's specific desire, only the letters corresponding to each individual element (*bhūta*) are to be written. The rest is clear in meaning. Herein lies this great secret: the seed-syllable *hsauṃḥ* is the life-force (*prāṇa*) within the middle of the mantra.
One should not perform the visualization; rather, one should write the letters of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of practice (*sādhya*) within the center of the seed-syllable.

It should be understood that the *sādhya* is the deity, while the *sādhaka* is one who is eager for the task. In the diagrams (*yantra*) mentioned by me, such as those in the *Śivatāṇḍava* and others, the name of the *sādhya* should indeed be written separately, and so forth.

Since the term *sādhya* (the one to be accomplished) is also conventionally designated for the deity, and since it is established that the deity must be written in the center [of the yantra], the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the deities of the yantra must necessarily be written there as well; for this very reason, the action expressed by the verb "one should do" (*kuryāt*) requires a subject.

The *Vṛtti* states that, according to the previous view, this sentence— "Bring Devadatta under the control of Caitra"— would be incomplete (*sākāṅkṣa*), as it would require the repetition "bring, bring" or "do, do. It is argued that rather than accepting such a defect of incompleteness, it is more appropriate to accept the inclusion of another system (*tantrāntara*) based on mutual requirement (*apekṣā*).

Within that [triangle], one should again write the root seed-syllable (*mūlabīja*), and within that, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*), joined with the ritual action (*karman*) and so forth; for even in the *Saṃhitās* and other texts, the term "the object to be accomplished" (*sādhya-pada*) can be explained as referring to the deity.
Precisely for this reason, it is made explicit there, in the first section (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*), in the context of the *Hanumat*-yantra.

The syllable *muktaṃ* (the *muktikāra*) should be written with *hsauṃḥ* in its center, followed by the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), namely "Hanumat. The meaning is that the name of the one to be accomplished is non-different from Hanumat.

This statement of non-difference is intended to indicate that even in other instances where the word "sādhya" (the one to be accomplished) is used, it should be understood as referring to the deity itself, as we shall explain elsewhere when discussing the writing of the *sādhya*. Other... [text truncated]

One should say, "The name Hanumān must be written," and that [name] should indeed be in the vocative case, because it conforms to the imperative endings of the verbs such as "do" (*kuru*) and so forth, and because it is seen accordingly in the half-verse beginning with "O Hanuman, write in the six corners of the hexagram" (*hanumannakṣatre ṣaṭkoṇeṣu likha*). O Bhobho! Pa... [text truncated]

Since we observe the form *saṃbuddhyaṃta* even without the suffix *dam*, there is no insistence on our part regarding the use of that specific term, nor is there any aversion to it; for this is authorized in such instances as "O, O! (*bhobhoḥ saṃbodhanāt param*) and so forth. Furthermore, in the verse beginning with "the agent of the goal" (*sādhya-kartā*), [it refers to] the practitioner (*sādhaka*).

Although the word *pada* is well-known [in this context], the reason the traditionalists (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*) have included the word *kartṛ* (agent) is as follows: wherever there is the inclusion of the agent—
even though he is like an instrument (*sādhana*)— it is because of the agent’s own desire, such as the necessity [to act] or the like,
which occurs when the deity is also included in the drawing of the yantra.
The letters beginning with *śa* (the moon), which are prescribed as the seed-syllables (*yantra-bīja*) of this [mantra] to be recited,
and which were previously mentioned at the root of the work in the passage beginning "the moon, water, earth," etc., are to be written all around;
and all these letters should be written facing the primary seed-syllable inscribed in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

According to the written instructions, they may be made favorable at will, or they may be turned away in suppression; for it is said that "the castes [should be employed] in the yantras for rites such as these. Here, "favorable" refers to pacification (*śānti*) and subjugation (*vaśya*), while "suppression" refers to killing (*māraṇa*). "Turned away" refers to paralyzing (*stambhana*), causing hatred (*dveṣaṇa*), and driving away (*uccāṭana*); herein, subjugation and the others are intended.

There is a certain rule of application: in the *saṃhitā*, one should bring [the mantra] under control (*vaśa*); for subjugation (*vaśya*), it should be written accompanied by repetition (*āmneḍita*). For causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), repetition is proclaimed; for paralyzing (*stambhana*), repetition is declared; and for killing (*māraṇa*), "kill" (*māraya*) is used with repetition.

"Mudīritam" means repeated; "mohana" means delusion, and "mohane" means manifested as delusion. "Āmneḍitam" means "mokṣayet" (one should liberate); it is proclaimed that [this] is for liberation from bondage. "Āmneḍitam" refers to a sprout (*pallava*), or it means one should inscribe it in the place of *vāk* (speech).
This is also the meaning of what has been stated regarding the other [mantra]. And herein...
"Make Devadatta tremble! Make him come under my control! Strive, strive! Cause mutual enmity between these two! Cause it, cause it! Paralyze the movement of the enemy army!
Paralyze it! Bring about his death! Bring it about!"—in such applications as these, one should employ [the mantra] accordingly.

The *cchika* [suffix] is prohibited; however, there is also usage such as "make Devadatta submissive," "create mutual enmity between these two," "perform the paralyzing of the army," and "perform the *māruṇa* of this person. This is because of the statement: "Place a pair on both sides."

Since yoga is prescribed, one should infer the ritual applications (prayoga) accordingly, such as: "O Peace, pacify this disease," or "Perform the pacification of the disease of Śama," and so forth. Furthermore, the diagrams (yantras) intended for wearing should be drawn by following the well-known directions starting from the East.
It is not otherwise; as it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "O Goddess, if one should draw [the diagram] for the purpose of worship, then one should draw it starting from the southeast (Svāgra);
O Maheśānī, for the purpose of wearing it, one should draw it starting from the pure east.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "O Mahādevī, for the purpose of wearing it, one should draw this yantra starting from the pure eastern direction."

Regarding worship, it is said that by means of the "earth-script" (*bhūtalipi*) worshipped at the beginning of one's own ritual arrangement, the worship of the *yantra* becomes essential for the practitioner through the attraction of the phonemes (*varṇākarṣaṇa*), which is like the wind for the worship of Bhairava; this has been stated in the *Mantramahodadhi* and other works. Therein, the method of worshipping the earth-script is as follows:

The method of worship for Svarṇākarṣaṇabhairava was stated in the *Pṛthvīmūla*; however, the details regarding the mantra should be understood from sources such as the *Mantramahodadhi*. This is the general direction.

Furthermore, this collection of yantras should specifically be drawn on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) or similar materials at the prescribed locations; having fashioned them into pills (*gulikā*), they should be [bound] with silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*).
Having wound it three times with lac and covered it, one should place gold, silver, or copper inside a mirror;

having worshipped that [mirror] by means of the root mantra of the respective deity, preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and having performed the extraction of the fire (*agnyuttāraṇa*) within the seed-syllable (*bīja*) written in its center;

Having warmed [the image] with medicinal herbs, decoctions, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) a thousand times or more; having offered oblations according to a specific portion of that number, one should pour the residue of those oblations onto the respective yantras. Then, having consecrated it with the root mantra a hundred times or more, one should [invite] the Guru and the Brahmins.

Having satisfied them with food, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth, and by their command, one should first prostrate before this yantra and its presiding deity; then, after mentioning the guest and other details, and stating the specific desire, one should form the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) saying, "I shall wear this yantra," and [thus receive] this yantra which has been fashioned for the sake of protection.

For the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the rite of retention (*dhāraṇa-karma*), one should give abundant food for Brahmins, liberal sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth; then, having performed the dedication of the rite to the Lord of Karma (*karmeśvara-arpaṇa*), one may rest at ease. As it is said in the *Mantramahodadhi*: "When no specific material is mentioned, the yantra should be drawn upon birch bark, linen, or palm leaf."
Having wrapped a small pill with a thread, one should enclose it— covered with lac— in gold, silver, or copper.
Having worshipped the deity with the central seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*) or with the *mātṛkā*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*),
one should sprinkle it with the remains of the oblation (*huta-saṃpāta*) and then apply it either to the head, the vehicle, or the neck.
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing the desired object, it is said that by one devoted to the service of the *yantra*, the supreme *Bhūtalipi* (the alphabet of the earth) is to be worshipped;

through its worship, the perfection of all *yantras* arises. Now, [one might ask]: "O Great Lord, even without mantras, recitations, fire-offerings, or ritual attachment, does success arise at that very moment? [The answer is: Yes.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the statement, "O Goddess, this Yantra is a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) that grants all desires and is perfectly perfected," because such Yantras have not been mentioned [previously], then their subsequent mention would be illogical;
whereas if they have been mentioned, then the worship described therein would be illogical—[we reply: do not say so, for when the Mantra is primary...

The intent here is that while there is an increase in affliction (*kleśa*) in formal worship (*upāsanā*), such affliction does not exist in the case of those [mantras] which serve as ancillaries (*aṅga*) to a mantra; for this very reason, the injunctions for the worship, recitation (*japa*), and fire-oblation (*homa*) of yantras mentioned in various places are properly consistent. In the phrase "without affliction" (*akleśena*), there is no [intended] negation.

The meaning is precisely this: the inclusion of that [mantra] is as follows. One should take one's own desired name ending in the vocative case, the intended name of the deity ending in the genitive case, and the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as the accusative case.

Then, joined with devotion, one should append the six syllables—*dṛk*, *japa*, *śrauta*, *ātma*, *bhūta*, and *aṇavaḥ*—followed by the mantra of action (*kriyā-manu*) together with the individual soul (*jīva*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is the heart of the yantra; furthermore, [one should recite] the Gāyatrī.

In the respective elemental circles (*bhūtārṇamaṇḍala*), the six components of the Yantra are traditionally known as: the Tryausaka-lipi, the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the vital mantra (*prāṇamanu*), and likewise the tongue, mouth, head, nose, and the syllables for protection (*rakṣārṇa*).
These are to be written according to the specific time prescribed for each.

The written document should be as follows: having taken the words of all the Tantras, regarding the desired grace, the destruction of disease, and so forth, as well as subjugation and other such goals, one should cause the deity to be brought to a state of accomplishment; even Devadatta is subdued. In writing "vaśaya" (subjugate) and so on, the desire is included within the action itself.

Therefore, the phrase "it is said" (*uktam*) is merely general and not universal; this is the summary. Now, because protection is desired by all, he first demonstrates the deities of the *mātṛkā* [syllables] for that purpose, beginning with the words "the letter *ma*" (*mārṇam*), etc., after having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus in its pericarp.

Having written the letter *sa* together with the nasal (*anusvāra*)— which is another synonym for Bhṛgu— and having written within it the fifth letter of the *pa*-group (*ma*) together with the nasal, and having further written within that the form of the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) such as "protect, protect Devadatta from evil deeds" (*sakarmakṛt devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa*), one should place the vowels two by two on the filaments and [the consonants] on the petals.
Having written the six groups of consonants (*svara*) consisting of *ṣa-ka-va-ṭa-ta-pa-śa-la*,

one should surround them with the seed-syllables *hāṃ* and *hīṃ* within a circle; this is stated following the *Harṣadīpikā* as "protect, protect Devadatta," but in reality, it should be "perform, perform the protection of Devadatta."

Yoga has already been established as such by the statements in the *Saṃhitā* and other texts. For this very reason, it should be understood that what the author of the *Padārthādarśa* calls "the goal" (*sādhya*) is accompanied by the identity of the means and the end (*sādhyasādhakakarmya*).
In that context, the word for one's own name is in the genitive case, denoting the fruit that has become the object of attainment (*sādhvībhūtaphala*).

Having written the words ending in the accusative case in sequence, one should then repeat "kurviti" (do it) twice; thus they say according to the traditional instruction (*saṃpradāya*). As for the remainder, that which was prescribed by the general procedure for yantras should be adopted here as well.
This [mantra], joined with the letters and the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*), is to be read with the accusative case endings.
