This was stated following the opinion of Harṣadīpikākāra and others, who maintain that one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) together with its own vowel in the seventh case-ending followed by the letter *sa*. However, according to the view of the authors of the Padārthādarśa, who follow the second *sa* and the letter *ka*, the meaning is as follows: [the letter] *ma*...
One should write Bhṛgu within the *rasa* (sixth) [triangle], and within that, the *Sādhya* and so forth; this is to be written in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
The remainder is entirely as before. He describes the *vaśya* yantra with the words beginning "having made into a city" (*purīkṛtya*), etc.:
having written the *māyā-bīja* in the center of two mutually intersecting *bhūpura*s (circles), one should write [the name] within that.

Having written [the mantra] in the manner described by Dhyānāsādhaka and others, one should write the letter *va*, which is the seed-syllable of water along with its *anusvāra*, within the eight corners; then, having constructed a *bhūpura* (fortified city) outside of that, one should inscribe the eight *vajras* in its eight directions—so says the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. However, [others say it is] *mahī*...

The syntactical connection is: "in the pair of earth-purīs joined together with the pure [element]. Regarding "joined together" (*puṭīkṛte*): when two things are joined (*puṭīkṛte*), they are situated within one another. In that regard, having first drawn a square, one should draw another square inside it, with its corners touching the cardinal directions of the lines of the first square.

Then, having formed a third square whose corner-tips touch the intermediate corners of the second square, one should write the *māyā-bīja* in its center; within that, having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth in the previously mentioned directions, one should write the letter *va* in the eight corners.

As it has been stated in the *Apekṣitārthayojanikā*: having drawn a terrestrial mandala, one should draw another terrestrial mandala within it toward the east, south, west, and north, so that its corners are not distorted; then, once again, one should draw [another] within that in the same manner.
Having said "khityādi" and so forth, the authors of the *Harṣadīpikā* state: one should produce a square formed by two such diagonal corners joined to each other and make it the form of a *saṃpra*.
Having written the *māyā* and so forth in its center, [one should place] the outer [elements] within the *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) at the diagonal corners.

It is said that one should write the letter *va* with an *anusvāra* in the corners of the third outer enclosure (*būpura*) surrounding the *nāviṣṭya*; furthermore, the drawing of a thunderbolt (*vajra*) should be performed in all the corners.
Here, the deity of the *māyāvīja* is indeed Bhuvaneśvarī, the protectress against *rakṣas*, *jvara*, and so forth.

He describes a single yantra for both pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the attainment of prosperity (*śrīprāpti*), and so forth, as well as for subjugation (*vaśya*), beginning with the words "in the center" (*madhye*) and including the three qualifiers of the name. The letter *kṣa* should be written in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the eight-petaled lotus; within that, [the mantra] "protect Devadatta, do so, do so" (*rakṣī kuru kuru*) [should be placed].

Having first interwoven (*vidarbhitam*) the name of the object to be accomplished— which is characterized by the syllables *saṃ*, *da*, *saṃ*, *da*, *saṃ*, *ta*, *saṃ*, *sa*, *ra*, *saṃ*, *kṣāṃ*, *saṃ*, *ku*, *saṃ*, *ruṣṭaṃ*, *ku*, *saṃ*, *ha*— in their regular order, then in reverse order, and finally in a mixed sequence; and having encased (*puṭitam*) this with the previously mentioned three-syllable *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, one should write [it].
The meaning is that one should enclose this yantra by writing the vowels in pairs upon the filaments (kesara) and then drawing a lotus with its face upward below;
however, since the syllable *sa* is a single mantra-syllable, one should write the syllables of the name of the person to be protected situated between two mantra-syllables.

The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* has stated that because the characteristic of being "twofold and *vidarbha*-like" is impossible here, the two syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) themselves constitute the two mantras; however, even that is not correct,
as the flaw of the definition’s lack of pervasiveness (*avyāpti*) remains, for neither of the two mantras consists of two syllables of either the mantra or the person to be accomplished.

As for the statement that "the two syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) are situated within one mantra-syllable"— that is, the characteristic found in the Tantras where it is said that [the name] has entered into the middle of a single mantra-syllable— since this would result in the pervasion (vyāpti) being sublated, this is of no consequence. However, others [hold as follows]:

Based on the observation that "the name with its vowels" (*sārṇavidarbhitām iti*) indicates that the completion of the name's syllables occurs by means of two vowels, one should perform the *vidarbha* (interlacing) by repeating each syllable of the name up to the end. Even for those who maintain that the performance of *vidarbha* is done with only a single syllable, the repetition must still conform to the name to be accomplished (*sādhyanāma*).

Since it must necessarily be followed, what offense have I committed by following it first? This is indeed the intention of the author as well; otherwise, had it been composed in the middle [of the work], he would have simply said, "the *mṛtyuñjaya* with three syllables," rather than having interwoven it [in this manner].

Regarding this, they say "tamiti" (this). Intending to show that even for one who accomplishes all desires, there is the power to immediately overcome poison, fever, and the like through the rites described here with ease, he says "viṣa" and so forth. The deity is Mṛtyuñjaya, [who grants] the destruction of fever.
He describes the yantra for destroying that [fever], which has the Cintāmaṇi deity as its presiding divinity even beyond [ordinary] association,
beginning with the words "sā dhyā" and so forth: having constructed a triangle with its apex pointing upward and marked with a svastika,
one should write within it the previously mentioned Śaiva Cintāmaṇi seed-syllable (bīja), and inside that, the fever of Devadatta.

Having aimed at the object to be accomplished (sādhya) in the form "pacify [him]" (*paśamaṃ kuru*) and so forth, one should surround it on the outside by means of another [mantra] according to the previously mentioned method; that is to say, one should encircle it with the eight-syllable mantra *saḥ-plava saḥ-plāvaya* outside of that. This alone is [the procedure].

The meaning is that even this *Ṣṭāṇa* mantra, when practiced, becomes a destroyer of poison and a destroyer of fever; however, in reality, it is understood as a constant destroyer of fevers arising from the course of poison. By sprinkling water consecrated with its recitation, or by [the sound of] a conch or a drum consecrated with it, one should raise up what has been seen [fallen].

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, by hearing the sound of the *Diti* [mantra], one sees the fruit of the mere measure of the poison-remedy; for when there is doubt regarding the meaning, it is proper to determine that meaning through another treatise (*tantrāntara*). In the context of the poison-remedy, [the author] states the serpent-destroying yantra in the *Tāra*.

By these [words] and so forth, here the mantra of the deity Kurukullā consists of seven syllables: *tāre* (the first word), followed by *vara-mate-svāhā* (the second word), and in the middle, the four-syllabled word *kurukulle* ending in the vocative case. All of this combined constitutes the seven-syllable mantra. Of that [mantra], the first syllable is to be placed in the center of the six corners (*ṣaṭkoṇa*).
The meaning is that one should draw the six syllables many times in their respective places. This yantra should be drawn with *rocanā* (yellow pigment) on a birch-bark leaf;

for it is seen in another tantra that "one should draw the snake-destroying yantra, which has six corners, on a birch-bark leaf with *rocanā*. Regarding the phrase "it destroys," this refers to its placement within the house.

The meaning is that by extracting [the seed-syllable] from that cavity and establishing this yantra within that same cavity, one causes [the target] to be expelled from that cavity; therefore, this is not a practice for killing (*māraṇa*), but rather for expulsion (*uccāṭana*). Consequently, only those elements such as air (*vāyu*), form (*rūpa*), and the phonemes (*varṇa*) that are conducive to that [expulsion] should be employed here. Is it not the case, however, that the meaning of the root text is exactly as it was heard?

If it is asked, "From where [is this] abandoned?", accept that it is for the sake of consistency with other tantras. For it is stated in the *Nāradīya*: "One should cause snakes to emerge from holes after having placed them in a pit, and likewise one should expel them by means of an *uccāṭana* [rite].
He states another snake-killing yantra beginning with the words "Oṃkāra" and ending with "mekhalāt."

The deity is addressed with the seven-syllable mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ mekhale svāhā*. The meaning is that it removes the serpent (*nāga*) or snake that has arisen as an enemy; the sense is that one should employ this yantra specifically when there is a threat from an enemy-serpent, but not for the removal of all serpents indiscriminately—this yantra is not for that purpose.

Regarding the phrase "the remover of even mother-nagas who have become enemies," its intended meaning is as follows: having drawn a hexagon, one should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center and the syllables beginning with *māyā* (hrīṃ) in the corners starting from the front.
Here too, as before, one should follow the procedure previously described using birch bark and gorocana.
Based on the observation of other tantras and in the context of the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of serpents,

[the author] describes a general yantra for eradication beginning with the words "marked by a trident" (*śūlāṅkita*), etc.: having fashioned a hexagon for the deity Dhūmāvatī, one should write the two seed-syllables *dhūṃ* and *dhūm* in its center.

In the remaining six corners starting from the northeast, one should write the [six] syllables minus [one]. Outside of that, having fashioned a wind-maṇḍala consisting of a circle marked with six spokes, one should surround it on the outside with the fire-seed-syllable (*raṃ*);
the meaning is that one should likewise surround it on the outside with the *dhūmāvatī*-seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*).

He extracts the mantra with the words "dāntau" and so forth. Regarding "dāntau," there are two *dhakāra*s; when each of these is joined individually with its presiding vowel—the sixth vowel (*ū*)—and the *bindu*, one obtains "dhūṃ dhūṃ," which signifies the attainment of the desired object; this is the view of other commentators. However, Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that [the reading] is "dāntau."

The reading beginning with "dikaḥ" is more correct, however, as it contains the letter *ga*, which is another synonym for "pañcāntaka"; by this, the attainment of the seed-syllables *dyūṃ* and *dyūṃ* occurs, because such is seen in the Nārāyaṇīya [Tantra], so they say. Regarding the passage beginning with "kanaka," etc., this [is done] on a cloth of the deceased (*pretavastra*) with poison smeared by the juice of the *dhakkūra* plant.

The meaning is that by writing *traṃ* and reciting it in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), the enemy is driven away (*uccāṭita*). Following the context of the cremation ground and the *preta*, he describes the *yantra* for seizing the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* who have ascended to the memory [of the practitioner], beginning with the words "having offered oblations" (*hutvāśa*) and so forth, ending with "the deity of Vaivasvata."

Starting from the tip of one corner of that hexagon and proceeding to the middle and then to the end of the opposite side, one should write the mantra "tathāsyāstathācaivasvatāya svāhā" according to the sequence of each individual syllable; the meaning is that one should then encircle it with a lunar disc (candrabimba). [End of section on] the cremation ground (śmaśāna).

In this context, as a related matter, he describes the yantra for burying and piercing: having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with "noṃ me" and so forth, and having written the syllable *ma* in its pericarp,
one should [place] the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and the means of action (*sādhana*) respectively within those same circles and squares.

Having written the form "kanāmanīvidveṣaṇaṃ kuru kuru caitrayoḥ," one should write the letter *ma* four times in the four corners starting from the northeast (īśāna) of that very [diagram], each accompanied by a *bindu* and the syllable *ṅa*, and then [place] the previously mentioned *dhūmāvatī* mantra upon the leaves.
Having written the syllables many times, then, within the space between two drawn circles, [one should write]:
*arghughuṭikeṣu ghuṛghuṭike markaṭike ghore vidveṣakāriṇi vidveṣodvegakāriṇi ghorāghorayoḥ amukāmukayoḥ vidveṣaya*.

One should write the fifty-three-syllable mantra "dveṣaya huṃ phaṭ" in a circular form; outside of that, one should encircle it with three wind-mandalas. In the phrase "amukāmukāṃ yoḥ," the names Devadatta and Yajñadatta are to be inserted [in place of amuka]; this is the deity Dhūmavatī.
In connection with the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), he teaches the *yantra* for killing which leads to that [result], beginning with the words "In the east" (*prāk*) and so forth.

This has already been explained according to different traditions in the seventeenth chapter; the only difference here is that it involves a different mantra. Here, Yama is the presiding deity (*devatā*).

By the word "vadit" (saying), the procedure mentioned in another tantra is recalled, which states that one should draw the heads of a buffalo and a horse on both sides and write this yantra in their middle.
For it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīdīpa*: "Having drawn [the figures] from the limbs and the eyes, [one should place them] between the heads of the buffalo and the horse."

To avoid confusion regarding the change of phonemes (*varṇāntara*), the extraction of the verse-mantra (*ślokamantra-uddhāra*) is performed: "At the end of *Yama* (ma) there should be *Rāja* (ja); then *Bhṛgu* (sa), followed by *Viśva* (la) and *Atri* (u); *Udita* (na) at the end; *Māruta* (ya); then *Vāyu* (sa) in reverse order; these three are thus stated;
then *Marut* (ya) joined with *Mitra* (sa) and *Karṇa* (ra); then at the end of the foot, *Nitya* (sa)—this is the meaning."
At the end of that [time], when the body of the Lord was endowed with the supreme wind that had been closely embraced by fire,
the Lord— the King who is the extinguisher of the three fires and the one whose breath is the wind— having reached his final end, burned away the state of being subject to rebirth,
just as the Blessed One, Nṛsiṃha, burns at the edge of the forest of worldly existence.
It is not said by me that this [mantra] is for the letter *na*; it was spoken by the enemy of Tripura (Śiva) for the sake of Āruṇa on the cloth of the corpse (*pretapaṭa*).
Thus, the eight poisons have been shown. Now, he describes another yantra for killing, beginning with "eighty-one" and so forth: ten lines extending east-west and ten extending south-north.

Having drawn the lines so that they intersect one another to form eighty-one squares, and having completed them, one should write the seed-syllable *ram* (the fire-seed) in the center, together with the name of the deity and the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) such as "Kill Devadatta! Kill! Then, from that central square, [one proceeds] toward the east and so forth.
In the four squares starting from the west, in the square without the letter *ra* (the northeast), one should place the seed-syllable as stated in the root-text; likewise,
in the four squares starting from the south and the four squares starting from the north, combining them all together,
there are sixteen seed-syllables of Nṛsiṃha produced from the sixteenth vowel and the bindu, beginning with the letter *ka*.

Having written the four seed-syllables (*bīja*) consisting of the collection of eight *aṭaviṃdu*s (the nasal bindu) in the thirty-second square, one should then write the *Kālī* mantra in the form of verses sequentially in the remaining squares, starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and proceeding clockwise, and then again starting from the southwest (*naiṛtya*).

One should write the *meṇakālī* mantra itself; having first encircled it on the outside with the *ṣaḍaṃta-tvaritā* mantra, one should then encircle it starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) with the *Yama* mantra to be described hereafter,
and again encircle it starting from the southwest (*naiṛtya*) with that same *Yama* mantra to be described.
The meaning is that one should encircle [the mantra] with the seed-syllable *ram* and then encircle it with the seed-syllable *yam*.
This has been made clear in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"One should write the six-limbed *Tvaritā* vidyā as before on the outside; at the end of the *Yama* mantra, one should place the fire-seed (*ra*) all around, radiant."
"One should draw that seed-syllable made of *jan* around the exterior," according to the *Harṣakaumudī*;
however, [others] maintain that one should encircle it with the *Yama-mantra* in each of the four directions, one by one.
But the *Ācāryas* [state] that thereafter, starting from the south-west (*nairṛtya*), one should write the *Kālī-mantra*.

Some teachers instruct that the word *khe* [stands for] the letter *ya* (the seed-syllable of Yama) and that it is also the vow (*vrata*); others maintain that by the words *agni* and *pavana*, the respective mandalas are intended. In this latter view, there is a clear contradiction with the statement "the seed-syllable of fire" (*vahnivīja*) and so forth. [The author] now extracts the mantra of Kālī and the mantra of Yama in their proper order.

With the words beginning with "Kālī," everything concerning the essential nature [of the mantra] is stated for the purpose of dispelling confusion regarding the phonemes; thus, the word *kālīmāra* is joined in both direct and reverse order, followed by the four phonemes dissolved from the end, then the pair [of phonemes] transcending liberation, and finally the two vowels of the universe joined separately.

This group of forty-four syllables, beginning with *detapadaṃtatotraṃ* and joined with *mayutaṃ*, is indeed a collection of Vedic verses; saying "protect me" (*rakṣa*) at the end of the description of the letters of the reality of the syllables, and then again in reverse order, this supreme Kālī-mantra is an exceedingly perfect means for accomplishment through its practice.
From the wind (*vāyu*), from the city of the wind (*vāyupura*), then from that mouth, [the syllable] *ta*; the void (*vyu*), the liberated one (*vimau*).

In forward order, she is with him, and he too is Śiva; thus they are spoken of. Or again, in reverse order, these vowels and consonants, having reached the state of being joined in reverse, form a multitude whose nature consists of pairs of letters—both in sequence and out of sequence—which is the abode of many states. This multitude, consisting of the reversal of the sequence, is one's own self.

This mantra has not been recited [elsewhere], yet it is declared to belong to this [deity]. To establish the independent status of these two mantras—namely, "The Night of Destruction for Enemies" (*vairiṇāṃ kālarātriḥ*) and "The Destroyer of Enemies" (*vairivināśanaḥ*)—one should, in this context of the Ārūḍhā-vidyā, offer one thousand and eight oblations of buffalo-ghee into the fire. In the yantra...

The specific instruction is that one should bury it after performing the *sampāta* (the ritual pouring of offerings). One should recite the root mantra until success is achieved, accompanied by eight thousand oblations of buffalo ghee. This method of writing the mantra, however, is intended for the purpose of killing a man, [not] a woman.

The experts of the tradition maintain that one should perform the encircling with the *kālī-mantra* within the compartments of the diagram used for killing, as taught in the *Yamāntaka-tantra*. [The materials required are: charcoal, charcoal from a funeral pyre, a human skull-bowl, human fat and the like, and a wick made from the cloth of a corpse impaled on a stake.
The material for this [lamp] is the soot produced from a burning lamp;
one should place it upon a corpse’s garment hung on a trident, or in the hollow of a *vibhītaka* tree,
or in an anthill, or at a crossroads, or in a cremation ground— according to the observation of other tantras.
In this regard, if it is buried at a mechanical device (*yantra*), the enemy’s death occurs; if buried at a crossroads, there will be great diseases;
if buried in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), he falls from a great tree or similar object; and if buried upon a stone—that is, a washerman’s stone prepared for washing clothes—or upon a brick.

When [the goddess] is stationed in a temple of Śiva, one should smear [the ground] with these three— Daṇḍī, Brahmadaṇḍī, and [the third substance]— and having turned it face downwards, wherever a wheel inscribed on stone or other materials is buried,
in that very place, such as a region or a village, there shall be repeated misfortune; thus [it is said] regarding the stone.
The "direct application" (direka-prayoga) is that wherein one should deposit the yantra in villages, cities, and so forth, in the regions of the mantra-practitioner;

this is understood from the observation of other tantras. It follows from the essential meaning [of these texts] that the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should not be written in place of the village, city, or other location. This is stated in connection with the writing of the Kālī-mantra.
Regarding the mantra for writing on a leaf (*lekhyakālīmantra*), which causes expulsion (*uccāṭana*), he states another method beginning with the words "one should write" (*likhet*).

The phrase "with that which consists of Yama" (*yamātmakena*) is to be connected with the word "having encircled" (*saṃveṣṭya*). On a stone slab or a brick (*iṣṭakā*), using the previously mentioned substances such as the eight poisons (*aṣṭaviṣa*) and so forth, and with a pen made of a crow’s wing (*kākapakṣalekhinī*), [one should write] nine...
Having drawn lines extending east-west and north-south, one should form sixty-four squares. Then, having written the previously mentioned Kālī-mantra in sequence starting from the northeast (Īśāna),
and again having written the Kālī-mantra starting from the southwest (Nairṛta) using the same grid, [one should write] "Vaṣaṭ" outside.

After encircling it with the *Ḍaṃtvaritā* mantra, one should encircle it with the *Yama* mantra; outside of that, according to tradition, one should encircle it with the seed-syllable of Fire (*vahnivīja*) together with the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the ritual action (*karma*), and the rite (*kriyā*);
thereafter, one should encircle it with the seed-syllable of Wind (*vāyuvīja*) in the eastern and other directions of the central square, as per another Tantra.

The writing of the previously mentioned *hrūṃ*, *ghra*, *bhṛti*, and *vīja* is prescribed. Having placed the sixty-four squares, the *Kālī*, the *Īśa*, the *doṣāvara*, and so forth, one should place the four syllables beginning with *hrūṃ* in the center; by the word "and" (*ca*), there is an inclusion of the syllables of the *Kālī-mantra* as they occur in sequence. In the center, all around—

There are three squares [on each side], making nine squares in total; the outermost ring consists of three squares, while the middle consists of four squares. In that central area, which serves as the locus for the syllable *kāra*, one should place the name and the action (*karma*) of those to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within the intermediate spaces between those seed-syllables, according to the available space, in the middle portion.
With the *khet* mantra ending with the *śikhā-vidyā*, and with the fire-mantra (*vahni*) ending with the *śikhā-vidyā* followed by *vaṣaṭ*,
one should quickly perform the burning. Having encircled the seed-syllable *raṃ* with the wind-mantra (*vāyu*),
this well-prepared rite accomplishes actions such as killing (*māraṇa*) and eradication (*utsādana*).

"One should accomplish it well"—this also refers to the expulsion (*uccāṭana*) of men; for the expulsion of women, this is the mantra of Yama. Regarding the encircling within the squares twice over with the *Kālikā* mantra, this is the consensus of the Tantrikas. The ink is as previously mentioned, using lamp-soot (*kajjalī*). [The plants] *daṇḍī*, *brahmadāṇḍī*, and *marka*...

The *Ṭīkapikaccha* [states]: Now, regarding both of these [yantras] just mentioned, as well as the yantra of the goddess Tvaritā, [the author], following the context of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), demonstrates the yantra for their removal with the words beginning "I shall declare" (*ākhyāmi*).
Here, according to the author of the *Harṣadīpikā*, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus and within it...
Having written the *tuṃvuru* seed-syllable upon a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*), with the *kāma* seed-syllable inside it, and within that,

having written the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the target (*sādhya*) along with the ritual action (*karman*) in such a form as "Bring Devadatta under the control of Yajñadatta," and so forth;
then, on the petals starting from its own front, one should write in sequence the *vidyā* beginning with *Jambha*, which will be described hereafter.
Having written the *kāmabīja* on the intermediate petals, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth within it.

Some say that the word "goddesses" (*devīḥ*) is a qualifier for Jambha and the others; however, that is incorrect, because the words "Jambhādikām" and "vidyām devīḥ" are distinct syntactic units and thus cannot function as a qualifier [in that manner].

Because the relation of qualifier and qualified is impossible when there is no proof of existence, the requirement that the words for the qualified and the qualifier possess identical case endings is the very factor that determines their identity in number; this is established by the use of the word "asati" (when not existing), as in the case of "The Vedas are authoritative, [and so are] the Smṛtis."

Furthermore, since the word "atha" (now/then) excludes connection with what precedes it, how could there be a prior connection for that which was intended [by the opponent]? It is precisely for this purpose that the suffix is employed;
thus, the objection raised by the author of the *Padārthādarśa* is of no consequence. Karṇi... [text truncated]
In the center of the *tuṃvuru* [diagram] of the body, one should write the *kāmabīja*, and within that, the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of attainment (*sādhya*),
and the ritual action (*karman*) as previously described; having written the well-known *vidyās* of Jambhā and the others starting from the east on the cardinal petals,
one should write the goddesses Jayā, Vijayā, and Ajitā as prescribed in the *Kalpa* on the intermediate petals.

They say that one should write the Aparājitā seed-syllable (bīja), and within those seed-syllables, one should write the Kāma seed-syllables; and within those, one should write the names of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka), like the pericarp (karṇikā). Why is it said that this refers only to the seed-syllable at the end of the word, as in the case of Jambha and others, but not also for Japa and others?

Even when the complete writing of the mantra has been achieved with its fundamental excellence (*mūlakharasya*), we do not know from where their mutual hostility arises. *Tuṃvuru* is the deity of the yantra; in this very context, he shows eight yantras that produce different results through the application of various specific modifications, beginning with the word "hi" (*hitā*).

Having removed the five [syllables] of desire from the middle and the diagonal petals, one should write the syllable of peace (ŚĀM), the fourth vowel, in that place; then it will be necessarily powerful and exceedingly effective. This diagram should be drawn on a human skull at the three junctions of the day, beginning with morning, and heated.

Having removed the five *śānti* syllables located at the beginning and middle of the four *dicatuḥ* seed-syllables, and having inserted the *varma* seed-syllable in their place, this [mantra] becomes the *māraka*. This is to be written upon a cloth for the deceased (*pretapaṭa*) or on human skin with a crow-feather pen, using a mixture of the eight poisons and the juice of *dhatura*. This is its procedure.

One should surround it externally with a fire-pentagon (*tri-kona*), and outside that, one should encircle it with a wind-pentagon in the form of a circle marked with six dots. Regarding this, Harṣadīkṣita states: "There is no digging of the mouth [of the pit] in the cremation ground, nor is there the movement [of the cord] with the noose and goad; this is according to the *Mūla*. This is what is intended.

On the contrary, it is obtained; indeed, it is obtained, because the act of wrapping (*veṣṭana*) alone is enjoined as the root of the avoidance of the mere seed. For wrapping with fire, houses, and so forth does not perform the function of wrapping the seed, nor is it a contradictory conjunction (*viruddha-samuccaya*), such that fire, houses, and the like would be enjoined [as alternatives].

By implication, the covering of the seed-syllable (bīja) may be understood; thus, those who have not seen the meaning of the words do not teach its prohibition—this is the summary. Regarding the phrase "the armor of the directions" (digvāvarmma):
having omitted the fivefold armor-seed syllables, one should write the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) in their place, namely the fire-seed syllable and the wind-seed syllable.

Regarding "traivalikhet": the writing of the names of the sādhya, the sādhaka, and so forth, preceded by the letter *ra*, is exactly as previously stated; however, it is distinct here in that the encirclement by the fire-house (*vahnigṛha*) and other elements is also obtained here. Here, on a board made of *vibhītaka* wood, with a crow-feather pen, together with the eight poisons—

The drawing on the yantra is made with the blood of a black owl. Chanted in a courtyard or a cluster of houses with a count of one thousand and eight or more, it is consecrated with the *vahni-bīja* (the seed-syllable of fire).
Having removed the letter *pi* from the five previously mentioned locations, the letter *la* is placed in the position of the middle *ra*, and [the letter *ka*] in the intermediate directions.

One should write a single letter *ya* in the place of the *tārakāra*; however, as previously stated, there is one *yakāra*, and thus two *yakāras* are effectively present in the petals of the directions. This is precisely what is meant by the phrase "two *yakāras*.
By the phrase "with the city of earth" (*dharāpureṇa*), it refers to the aforementioned inner city consisting of the abodes of fire and wind.
There is no exclusion of the encircling [mantras], because their conjunction is impossible due to their performing a single function,
and because they are prescribed for use in the *stambhana* rite within the *dharāmaṇḍala*.
Thus, between the syllables *kāra*, *kāra*, and *kāra* in the central space, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth, according to the available space.
Having completed the majority [of the work], one should write with turmeric between two bricks; [this is] the "hi-tvā-laka-āra" [mantra].

Having omitted the letter *la* situated in the center of the previously mentioned yantra, and having omitted the letter *ya*, one should insert the letter *pa* in its place, and there [insert] the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth.
Having written this yantra, one should prepare it on a cloth from a banner, a garment from a corpse, or a cloth from a crow;

using a crow’s wing as a pen, with eight kinds of poison, and with ink made from the aforementioned substances mixed with blood, crow-dung, and excrement, having drawn this yantra, [one should place it] face down...

The meaning is that by burying [the object] in a cremation ground (śmaśāna), there shall be the destruction of the enemy's clan; or alternatively, having written the *sra* mantra in the place of the wind-seed (*vāyu-bīja*), one should discard the wind-seed entirely and perform everything else as before. With the blood of a crow on a garment of a corpse, using a crow-feather as a pen...

Having written [the letters] in their desired positions, one should bury them at the meeting point of the two who are to be made hostile, in such a way that there is no overstepping of the "machine" (yantra); by this, the accomplishment of enmity shall occur. However, the author of the *Harṣadīpikā* says that one should omit only the letter *ya* situated in the middle.

They say that the four *tu*-shaped [lines] situated at the intermediate corners exist exactly as they are; however, the author of the root text—who, having omitted the seed-syllable of air (*vāyu-bīja*) from the center of the *muktā*, provides the general designation "consisting of air"—does not intend this [interpretation]. Thus [ends] the commentary on the root text.

One should meditate on [the mantra] beginning with "Potrāvyāhatā" as the *astra*. Regarding the five *astra*-seed syllables (*astrabīja*), one should also expel and remove them; in this place of the *astra*, one should write the letter *sa* (which is the first letter of the *bhṛgu* group) joined at the beginning and end with the vowel *u* and the fifth vowel (*ū*) along with the *bindu*. [Thus, one writes] the letter *sa*.
One should write the name of the person for whom protection is desired, such as "Devadatta, perform protection for me," using the *sādhya* (the name of the person) and other designations;

one should enclose this in the three metals of gold, silver, and copper. Written on birch bark with white sandalwood paste, its wearing on the hand or elsewhere results in the attainment of fruits such as the destruction of malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*). Having thus described it...
In the pericarp of the previously mentioned yantra, one should write the syllable *u* in the center of the *tuṃburu* seed-syllable;

having omitted that *u*, one should write the earth-seed-syllable *glauṃ* in its place. In the middle of that, one should write the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) as "paralyze the army of Devadatta, paralyze! (*devadattasya sainyaṃ staṃbhaya staṃbhaya*), upon the removal of the *u*.

Therefore, there is also the cessation of the *sakāra*s at the beginning and end of those [words]; for those two are not written or recited independently, but rather as qualifiers of the vowel *u*. When the qualified object is negated, the negation of the qualifier follows by implication—this is the hidden meaning of the *Dīpikā*.

The letter *ka* [is used] by Glamiti Harṣadīkṣita; however, in case of doubt regarding the reading, it is more appropriate to adopt the *bhū-bīja* (the syllable *laṃ*). This is because, for the rite of immobilization (*staṃbhanam*), one adopts the color and other attributes of the earth element itself. On the outside, beyond the eight-petaled lotus, one should encircle [the diagram] with the letter *kṣa*; that is, with the letter *kṣa*.

Because the mention of "six enclosures" (*ṣatoveṣṭana*) might lead to the misconception that the previously established encirclement by the noose (*pāśa*) and goad (*aṅkuśa*)— which is obtained through general application— is thereby sublated,
the phrase "encircled by the noose and goad" (*pāśāṅkuśavṛta*) is stated again to dispel such doubt. Thus,
there is a second encirclement formed by the combined noose and goad, and beyond that, by the subsequent letter *ṭha*.

Then, one should encircle it with a third enclosure, a *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) consisting of the eight directions joined by eight *vajras*. Beyond that, one should encircle it with the root letter *la*, which is the color of the earth and accompanied by a *bindu*. Furthermore, beyond that, one should encircle it with the fifty-one *mātṛkā* letters together with the *visarga*. Beyond even that...
The meaning is that one should wrap it with inner bark. Having drawn this yantra on a cloth,
having consecrated two bricks by placing them one above the other,
and having inserted the yantra between them, one should cast it upon the path where the approaching enemy army is expected to arrive.

It is not certain that the paralysis of the enemy's army will necessarily occur; likewise, because there is the contingency that a *tuṃvuru* yantra— which is divided into nine types, possesses a deity, and is made of silver— might, by its very fruitfulness,
remove fear from one's desired house and so forth through the destruction of snakes, [the following is stated regarding] the house...
He describes the *yantra* that removes fear and has Garuḍa as its presiding deity, beginning with the words "In the center" (*madhye*) and so forth.
Intending that one should utter the names of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the guru, and those worthy of honor preceded by the syllable *Śrī*,
he likewise places the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Nṛsiṃha in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the eight-petaled lotus, with the object of attainment (*sādhya*) situated in the middle.
Having written the vowels in pairs upon the filaments (*kesara*),

one should write one syllable each from the five-syllabled *rudra-mantra*— which is to be spoken in the words "Varīndra-candra-yama-indra"— upon the petals in the west, north, south, and east respectively; [ending with] the syllable *hā*, [the syllable] *nṛsiṃ*.

Having written *havīja* below, one should write the vowels from *a* to *au*, along with the *anusvāra*, in order within the petals of Vāyu, Agni, Nirṛti, and Īśāna; having surrounded that on the outside with the consonants beginning with *ka* and those remaining inside, one should surround it further on the outside with the letter *kṣa* together with the *visarga*.

Regarding the reading "veṣṭayed aṣṭadikṣu catuś-catur-vargāvṛtam," the *Harṣakaumudī* explains it as "surrounded in the eight directions by the eight groups beginning with 'ka'. However, others consider that [explanation] untenable; for this yantra is said to be "protected from the serpents by the six groups of consonants starting with 'sa' (the sibilants)."
Because it would result in a contradiction with the statements of the Rāyaṇīya-tantra,

and because it would contradict the explanatory texts (*arthavivaraṇa*) which clarify the intended meaning by showing that one should "move [the letters] like a garland with written characters and write the final letter with a *visarga* in the eight directions," [the author] extracts the Garuḍa-mantra according to Saṃvarta.

By the words "kavityādi" and so forth, he introduces the five-syllabled mantra "oṃ svā heti. It is stated that this mantra possesses independence even in destroying the two types of poison—those of stationary and moving origin—in the act of bringing them down;
this very point he has now made manifest by means of demonstrating its practical application, beginning with the words "smaran" and so forth.

By means of the application of poison-destroying [mantras], he demonstrates the yantra for removing minor ailments, those created by others, hatred, expulsion, and diseases, beginning with the word "in the center" (*madhye*) and so forth; here, according to Harṣadīpikākṛt, having written the syllable *sa* (representing Bhṛgu) in the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, in its center—

One should write the four-syllable letter of the previously presented Garuḍa-mantra before the central seed-syllable consisting of the *praṇava*; having written that which is distinct from it—namely "svāhā"—one should then write the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in the middle of that, saying "make the restoration of Devadatta, make [it]! (*devadattasya saṃjīvanaṃ kuru kuru*).

Having written the vowels two by two upon the filaments, having written the Praṇava in the middle of each of the eight petals as the central seed-syllable, having drawn a circle outside that, and having fashioned a sixteen-petaled lotus attached to it,
one should write the letters from *ka* to *sa* two by two upon its filaments.

Having again written the *praṇava* (Oṃ), which serves as the seed-syllable in the center of the sixteen petals, one should surround it on the outside with the water-maṇḍala; they say that Garuḍa is the presiding deity here. However, the authors of the *Padārthādarśa* state that the syllable *va* is situated within the letter *bha*, and the syllable *ka* is situated within the letter *sa*; thus, by means of those, the seed-syllable *svam* is formed at the corner.

One should write [the mantra] on the body along with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) according to the prescribed rule; the meaning is that it is "interlaced" (vidarbhitam). This is because the *Nārāyaṇīya-tantra* states: "One should write the life-force (jīva) and the name interlaced in the center of the lotus. Thus: *devasvaṃ dattasvaṃ sya saṃ svajī*.

Having written *vanaṃ*, *ku*, *svaṃ*, *ru*, *ku*, *svaṃ*, *ru*, *dī*, *svaṃ*, *mi*, *ti* in this sequence, one should place the central seed-syllable *svaṃ* in the middle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and write [the remaining syllables] upon the petals— whether eight or sixteen— in the manner previously described. The presiding deity of the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra is Sañjīvana.

They say that for this mantra, both [the interpretations] are established from the beginning. Regarding the term "madhyabīja" (middle seed), in the first opinion it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, while in the second opinion it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
According to the maxim that a *karmadhāraya* is superior to a *tatpuruṣa*, this is the "ringing of the bell" (*ghaṇṭāghoṣa*) in all the scriptures. Or.

Regarding the statement "one should write the name of the debtor situated in the syllable *ṛ* (the *bhṛgu*), joined with the letters [of the mantra] and the object of the rite (*sādhya*)," and so forth—one should follow this either by placing it outside the circle or by its being conjoined with the *bhṛgu*. This is intended to dispel the doubt as to which method should be followed; thus, one should consult other tantras, for those who do not rely on such authorities would be at fault.

It follows that because the root mantra was already present previously, there is no lack of elegance in the statement that one should write that syllable situated in *bhṛgu* (the letter *s*) with four syllables; for the number four is not understood through the letter *va*, nor is it anything other than what the author of the root [text] intended, as seen in passages such as "laṃ gau ra pi" and so forth.
Furthermore, since that number has already been understood by the word "and" (*ca*) in the second chapter,

and because the Garuḍa-mantra was not written in the previous and subsequent yantras, it follows from the root text that another mantra alone should be written in this middle yantra, and the Garuḍa-mantra is certainly not intended there.
It appears that this *nārāyaṇīya* [yantra] teaches a yantra distinct from the one described in the root text (*mūla*). In connection with the writing of the Garuḍa-mantra,
he states another yantra for the writing of the taught Garuḍa-mantra, beginning with "In the center, the *piṇḍa*" (the *parā* mantra).

In connection with the discussion on the disease-removing yantra following the view of Arthadarśa, and specifically regarding the ancient disease-removing yantras, there is a thematic link between these two concerning the pride of the disease-destroying yantras that bring about health and so forth. Within the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus is the *piṇḍabīja*.

Having drawn [the diagram], one should place the Vāruṇa seed-syllable in the center for pacification (śānti); for subjugation (vaśya), the seed-syllable called the noose (pāśa) along with the Vidarbha; for eradication (uccāṭana), the Krodhana seed-syllable; and for attraction (ākṛṣṭi), the Āgneya seed-syllable—this is stated according to the *Nārāyaṇīya-tantra*. Thus, [the seed-syllables] are applied according to the specific desire.

Having written the mantra beginning with "divījavidarbhitvasvasādhyasādhakakarmanāmadevadattasya rakṣāṃ kuru kuru" and so forth, one should write the vowels (*svara*) twice upon the filaments (*kesara*) situated at the initial parts of the petals— that is, the leaves— of the lotus. Then, having worshipped...
Having cast the arrows upon the petals located in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Varuṇa, and the Lord of the Western Star (Nairṛta), as well as the directions of Candra,
the Lord of the Pretas (Yama), and Śakra,
he should place the four syllables of the previously mentioned mantra upon the arrows of the sword and Garuḍa.
Without writing the final syllable in the pericarp— which constitutes the central meaning—
one should write the subsequent vowels on the petals in the northwest, southeast, southwest, and northeast directions;
having written those along with the *bindus*, one should then write outside of that the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*, together with the subsequent *la* and *sa*.

Having performed a single movement with them, one should perform a threefold encirclement with the *bindu* and the fourth vowel, which is denoted by the term "left eye. According to the observation of the *Nārāyaṇīya-tantra*, "one should encircle the lotus with the *māyā* [syllable] and the *bindu* three times," and according to the *Harṣadīpikā*, "Garuḍa is the presiding deity."

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* maintains that the deity is indeed the body itself (*piṇḍātman*). He extracts the seed-syllable of the body with the words beginning with "thinking" (*matvītyādi*). The letter *ū* is the fourth of the *ca*-group and the Lord (*īśa*) who is unborn (*aja*).

The letter *ja* is the third of the *ca*-group and the four-faced one (*caturānana*), according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. The letter *ja* is the third of the *ca*-group and the four-faced one.

Thus, the authors of the *Harṣadīpikā* and the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* maintain that when the fourteenth vowel (*au*) is joined with the nasal (*ṃ*), the moon (*u*), the bindu (*ṃ*), and the letter *ra*, these two letters (*sa* and *ka*) attain the state of being the *piṇḍabīja*. This [mantra] protects the fetus for a pregnant woman, and for one who is not pregnant, it results in a son.

By the statement, "It bestows sons upon the illustrious [practitioner] and grants the accomplishment of all goals," it is indicated that its application exists independently as well. And this is stated in another Tantra: "When the *piṇḍa* (syllable) situated in the house of Candra and Indra (the letter *i*) is visualized as brilliant, yellow, and shaped like a thunderbolt (*kuliśa*), it causes the immobilization of an army, such as horses and so forth."

Likewise, one should meditate upon the supreme form [of the weapon] as having the moon, Indra, Agni, and the city (Pura) upon its head; it is shaped like a trident, wards off all enemies such as intoxicated elephants and buffaloes, and possesses a brilliance equal to the gods and fire.
One should contemplate it within the enemy army so that the host of foes is scorched by the flame of the massed [weapon], just as if they were turned away in retreat.

Having drawn this [mantra] upon a cloth or other surface, wherever it is worshipped, thieves, malignant diseases, serpents, and the like abandon it and hide away. Likewise, even those who are rising up [to attack] are paralyzed by the flowers;
thus one should likewise [visualize] the Piṇḍa-mantra ending with the syllable *va* (vāruṇa), which is devoid of the grace of fire (*tejas*), and having seen it, one should place it upon the head.

"That which effects the destruction of poison" refers to *teja* (the syllable *ra*). "Favor" (*anugraha*) is the syllable *au*. Devoid of these two, it is the Vāruṇa [syllable] joined with the Navakāra at the end; this is the meaning of the "poison-destroying seed-syllable" (*piṇḍabīja*).
Some say it is joined with the letter *śa*, the final letter of the Vāruṇa [group]. [The word] *mṛga* is...

Ghraḥ. Regarding "subjugation" (*vaśya*), there is a specific detail in another *tantra*: one should write the *piṇḍabīja* in the center of a lotus, with the name placed within its mouth according to the previously stated method; the remaining syllables are likewise written three times.
One should encircle the lotus with Mahāmāyā joined with the *bindu*, using cow-dung water at the beginning and the end.

One should write [the mantra] on birch bark with a golden stylus, or enclose it in copper or silver; one should accomplish it through recitation (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), and fire-oblation (*havana*) using gold. One should always recite the *piṇḍa* [mantra], which is enclosed by the *pāśa* and ends with the *śikhā*, for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*). Through following this alternative method, [one achieves] eradication (*uccāṭana*).

Its agency is also stated in another Tantra: "The wise man, having placed the enemy's yantra—which has been brought by the winds—upon a crow’s wing feather, should recite the mantra for the expulsion (uccāṭana) of the foe, which is split by the fire of wrath;
[the mantra] is Ā-KĀ-ŚA-SĀ-GNI-KAR-ṆĀ-RDHA-CANDRA-KRO..."

It is said that Agni is called "the one who holds. When Vāta has brought his own [seed] forward, one should write this yantra at some place where there is the logic of the "crow's wing" (ekākapakṣalekhanyāya). Therein, the drops (*bindu*) and *anusvāras* previously extracted from the yantra—those which are the internal stops (*antaḥstha*) such as *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*—are his desire.
The seed-syllable of the fettered state (*pāśabīja*), which constitutes the meaning of this word, has not been taught here as something to be explicitly written down;

therefore, even this triad is not to be employed here in the *uccāṭana* (eradication) yantra. Rather, the meaning is that one should recite the *piṇḍabīja* enclosed by the seed-syllable *huṃ*, which consists of the fire of wrath (*krodhāgni*).
In connection with the destruction of diseases and so forth, he describes another yantra for performing such tasks as the destruction of diseases,

beginning with the words "in the center of the water" (*madhyetoya*). Having drawn the water-mandala— the "house of water" mentioned in the first chapter— within the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should arrange its internal ornaments.
Having written the letter *sakāra* (sa) at the end of the name [of the deity], and having written "protect the deity, protect" (*devatāyā rakṣāṃ kuru kuru*) within that as well,
one should write the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and so forth. Then,
having written the mantra *haṃsa* eight times upon all eight petals, one should encircle the lotus on the outside with that *haṃsa* mantra.

One should encircle that with a *bhūpura* (fortified city). Regarding the mantra-deities such as Yaśas and Saṃpat, and so forth, in connection with this yantra, he describes the *vaśya-yantra* which bestows wealth and other benefits, beginning with the syllable *ī*.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should place the fourth [syllable] in its pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Having written the vowel [Oṃ] and within it the names of the practitioner and the target— such as "Devadatta, bring Yajñadatta under your control"— and having written the fourth vowel eight times upon the eight petals,
one should draw a lotus outside that with the same fourth vowel accompanied by the bindu.

"Enveloped by the earth-puram" means that one should surround it with the earth-puram. In the *Harṣadīpikā*, however, the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava is prescribed in place of the fourth vowel; since the deity Māyā brings about subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), fear of her ceases to exist—thus, in the context of Nivṛtti, [the text refers to] that which removes the fear of enemies.

The text says: "In the middle of the petals," and so forth; having written the letter *ma*—ending with *bha* (i.e., *mbha*)—within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of an eight-petaled lotus, one should surround it on all sides with the letters of the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), such as "O God, effect the removal of fear for Devadatta from Yajñadatta."

The meaning is that one should enclose [the seed-syllables] within the eight petals, together with the letters *ṭa* and *la*, and having combined the two syllables consisting of *ṭa* and *va*, one should encircle each of them individually upon the eight petals with the *bhūpura* (the outer square enclosure).
According to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*, the presiding deity of this *mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra] is [the letter] *ma* and *sa*.

The author of the *Harṣadīpikā* states that the status of the Sun and Moon as deities arises from their connection with the letter *ṭa*; this truth resides only in Śiva. In connection with the discussion of the *yantra* that removes fear, he describes the *yantra* that removes the fear of fever, beginning with the words "surrounded by syllables" (*varṇāvṛtam*), [in an] eight[-petalled diagram].
Having written the letter *ṭa* in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should write the letter *sa* at its end, and within that, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).
This *sa*, together with the name, is then to be made to enter into the interior of the letter *va*. Then, having written the two syllables *haṃ si* on each of the eight petals, one should proceed.
One should encircle that with a circle of water; then, one should encircle it even further at the end of the fire [circle] with the syllable *kṣa*.

Alternatively, having joined the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) and so forth with the letter *sa*, and having surrounded it on all sides with the letter *va*, one should cast it into the middle of the letter *ṭa* and place it within the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Eight...

Having written "haṃsa" on each petal and having enclosed them with the letter *la*, one should then enclose that with a circle (*maṇḍala*) outside. Here, in connection with the *haṃsa*-deity fever-destroying yantra, he demonstrates the sorcery-destroying yantra, beginning with "ṭāṃ".
In the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus, one should first write the letter *kṣa*; at its end, the letter *ṭa*;
within that, the three-syllable *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra; and above that, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*), etc.

It has been stated that "obstruction" (*rodhana*) consists of placing [the letters] at the beginning, middle, and end of the name; this characteristic of obstruction applies here to the petals as well.
One should write the three-syllable *Mṛtyuñjaya* Rudra mantra; then, having made a surrounding circle, one should fashion a sixteen-petaled lotus.

On its filaments, one should place the vowels one by one, and on the petals, as before, the three-syllable *Rudra* mantra along with the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) and so forth. Having made another surrounding circle outside of that—
Having fashioned a thirty-petaled lotus and having written the letters beginning with *ka* one by one upon its filaments,

and having written the remaining letters on the central filament, one should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) and so forth— conjoined with the three-syllabled *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra— as before, upon the petals, [ending] with the fourth [syllable].

One should encircle [the syllable] externally with the vowel *s* (ś) and the bindu; however, in reality, it is proper not to write the letters *ṭa* and *kṣa* repeatedly once they have been written in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). As for the letter *la*, since it is already written as equal to the letter *pa*, it should not be written again.

The intention of the root *vam* is as follows: or rather, since the status of being a suffix ending in *ṭa* (ṭāntitva) does not apply to the name [of the letter], it enters into the category of letters ending in *kṣa*; by that, one obtains the designation "in the *kṣa*" (*kṣakārānte*). However, it is not so; rather, the meaning obtained is "in the opening of the letter *kṣa*" (*kṣakāravivare*), which refers to its occurrence at the end of a word ending in *ṭa*.

The meaning is that after first writing the letter *ṭha* and then writing the letter *kṣa* there, one's name should be written in the middle of it; this is the sense of "the fruit. According to this view, there is also agreement with the previously mentioned diagrams (yantras), such as "the name of one desiring victory should be placed within *kṣa*," and so forth. This is the meaning.

Regarding the deity Mṛtyuñjaya, in the context of writing the *rudrākṣara* (the eleven-syllable mantra), he describes another yantra for writing the *rudrākṣara* with the words beginning "glauṃ rudra... and so on. The word "likhet" (he should write) implies that it should be written within a circle (*vṛta*). Thus, having first drawn a circle, one should place "glauṃ oṃ oṃ" inside it.
Having written two *praṇavas* conjoined with the seed-syllable *glauṃ*, and having written the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) within them,

one should draw a *bhūpura* (fortress diagram) outside of that; then, having drawn a line of vajras in the eight directions outside of that, one should write eight *praṇavas* in the middle of those lines and the letter *laṃ* in the intermediate directions.

Having written [the syllable] with a bindu, one should surround it with the three-syllabled mantra of the noose and goad (*pāśāṅkuśa*), which consists of the three syllables containing the *māyā-bīja* interspersed with the noose and goad;
the meaning is that one should further encircle that with the eight ears of the *vidyā* beginning with *juṃ*. As it was said by the Noble One herself: "The *praṇava*..."
One should draw a pair of winds situated within the seed-syllable of the Earth (la), followed by a human (na) and that [same] syllable situated within the eight (aṣṭau) and the thunderbolt (kuliśa).

In their midst, one should place the Pole Star (dhruva—ha) between the Earth (la) and the Lord of the Immortals (amarapati—the eastern direction, i.e., ka); then, between the noose (pāśa—pha) and the goad (aṅkuśa—ña), one should encircle it with Māyā (ī). Then, one should draw a lotus (o) and the eight beginning with Bhadra (bha); thus one achieves victory.

The path following the *Padārthādarśa* holds that the mention of a name by a single part of its designation— such as "Vṛttagata" for "Vṛttagatā"— is intended here; furthermore, since stabilization (*staṃbhana*) is the primary fruit [of this rite],
one should first establish a square (catur-asra) appropriate for it, and therein place the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth upon the earth.
Having enclosed [the syllable] with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) at the joints of the thighs, one should write it;
then, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus attached to the surrounding circle, one should write the *praṇava* upon each petal.
Outside that, within the circle, one should write the letter *kṣa* in the corners and the letter *laṃ* in the cardinal directions. Beyond that—
The path followed by the author of the *Harṣadīpikā* is that the wrapping (*veṣṭana*) is as before;

even in the reading "on eight petals" (*aṣṭapatra*), it must necessarily be understood that "having performed the wrapping" (*vṛtaṃ kṛtvā*) is an ellipsis (*śeṣa*). Thus, it should be noted that these [authors] needlessly endure contradiction with the words of the Teacher (*ācārya*). Aṣṭa...
Although this interpretation— reading it as *vajre*— is plausible, since the deities of the grounds are involved here in the context of immobilization (*stambhana*),
he describes the yantra for immobilizing speech, beginning with "LĀM" and so forth. Having drawn a square, one should write the letter *KṢA* inside it, and within that, the letter *LAṂ*.
Outside of those [mantras] interwoven with the *kāra* syllables, having made an inner square,
one should write that same form in the eight directions; in the center of that are the two who are lords of men,
belonging to the Kṣatriya caste as previously mentioned, named Pāśupata and Śaṅkhapāla.
Having written the *rasa* (taste) [letters] in the non-joined (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*) form, one should write the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) once in each of those two mouths.

In this way, having enclosed the letter *kṣa* as well, the threefold writing of the *sādhya* is completed. This yantra is made from the fruit of the *vibhītaka* tree and [anointed with] red ochre (*gairika*).

Having written [the mantra], one should bury it again at a place where the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of Śiva has been placed; one should cause it to be trampled by a stone slab. According to the author of the *Harṣadīpikā*, however, the original reading is "at the end of 'tu'"; therefore, the letter 'na' should be written in the middle of the letter 'la'. Thus, "lāṃ".
They say that even in the *Pāṭhapañcalakṣaṇa*, it is possible for the name to be written after the writing [of the mantra];

however, this is contradicted by other tantras, for it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Aindra [mantra], which consists of eight parts of meat and the letter Ṇ at the end, interwoven with the names of the meats, and possessing eight directions and the thunderbolt (vajra), belongs to the Earth."

"One should draw a serpent encircled by a *vāhi* [wind] within its mouth; when placed upon a *vibhītaka* leaf with *gaurika* [red chalk], and pressed down with a stone, it becomes a pillar for *nirmālya*.
Regarding this, the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* explains that "*nirmālya*" refers to the *nirmālya* of Śiva.
The Earth is the deity here as well. Regarding the mantra for paralyzing speech (*vāk-stambhana*), he states another mantra beginning with "sādhyāyyam" and so forth:

having written the armor-syllable (*kavaca-bīja*) consisting of the letter *huṃ*, joined with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and others, in the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, and having likewise written that same armor-syllable on the petals in the cardinal directions—

Having written *Ṛddhāṃ* in the other intermediate petals, one should write the seed-syllable of the earth, *glauṃ*, and then construct an outer square (*bhūpura*) adorned with eight vajras. In its corners, one should write the forms *gaṃ*, *glam*, and so forth, accompanied by *lāṃ*; and upon each of the eight vajras, [one should likewise write].

Having written [the mantra] within the armor (*varma*), one should surround it externally with a water-mandala (*jalamandala*), and from there, surround it further with an earth-fortress (*bhūpura*). This yantra, thus drawn with turmeric powder, one should fashion into the form of Gaṇapati using turmeric and place it inside that [image]. One should then place that image in a shallow vessel (*śarāva*).

Having placed it between two [objects], one should keep it in a secret place; by worshipping it daily, one will accomplish tasks such as paralyzing the speech of enemies—this is the meaning. According to the *Harṣadīpikā*, the mantra of Gaṇapati with turmeric should be used to wrap it on the outside, and the mantra is as follows: [Mantra omitted] The meaning is that by performing this, one achieves the desired effect.

In another tantra, after the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should state the armor-syllable (*varmabīja*) and the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati; at the end of the earth-seed syllable (*bhūbīja*), one should utter Gaṇapati preceded by turmeric (*haridrā*). It is proclaimed that the mantra of Niśā-Gaṇapati consists of a pair of "boon-granters" (*varadvandva*), the heart of all people, and a pair of "paralyses" (*staṃbhadvaya*), ending with two *ṭa*-consonants. Thus: Oṃ huṃ.
Some say that the practical meaning is that the wrapping should be performed with the mantra *gaṃ glauṃ haridrāgaṇapataye vara-vara sarva-jana-hṛdaya-stambhaya stambhaya stambhaya svāhā*,
which consists of thirty syllables and extends over three nights; however,
others [disagree].

This is indeed appropriate, for by such a fundamental intent, it would follow that even the mantra of the *Rātrivināyaka*—just like the *Jaṃbhā* and other vidyās—would have to be extracted [from the source]. Therefore, in the passage beginning with "of the army-leaders" (*senārīnām*), terms such as "without dispute" (*avivāda*) and so forth are understood.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should write... (*likhed va*).
Having placed the image made of flour within the belly of a pestle,
one should place it in a pair of earthen bowls and worship it with yellow flowers; there will then be a paralysis [of effects] regarding rain,
armies, speech, disputes, arrivals, and so forth— thus is the deity Vināyaka worshipped.

Having described the application for the immobilization (*stambhana*) of fever— which is included by the first term even in its future state— he now states, beginning with the words "having made" (*kṛta*), the appropriate application for its destruction once it has reached the state of arrival: [one should draw] eight lines extending east-west and eight lines extending north-south.

Having divided the six *khāṣas* (rows) so that they intersect one another, one should produce thirty-five squares. Within the twenty outer squares, one should place the letter *kṣa* along with its *bindu*.
Then, in the twelve squares situated around its interior, one should likewise place the letter denoted by the word *dharaṇī* (the earth), namely *la*, together with its *bindu*.

The meaning is as follows: having written the letter *la*, one should write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) inside it—specifically within the three remaining squares situated there—after unifying them by erasing the dividing lines, with the words: "O Devadatta, effect the removal of this fever without harm to this body. *Sa* refers to that [name].

"Having worshipped" (mabhyarcya) means having performed the sixteenfold offerings and so forth, preceded by the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Alternatively, it refers to the practice for those who are exhausted, terrified, afflicted, or ill, and so on, even through a concise method.

The worship performed by those who are not authorized for it is not to be accepted here, because that [latter] is the subject matter of daily obligatory worship (*nityapūjā*); whereas this is optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*), according to the scriptural injunction: "One should perform it whenever one is able. Thus, there is the offering of all the ritual materials to Him.

Having first performed the purification (*viśuddhi*), the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, and so forth, which constitute the preliminary limbs of all those respective mantras employed for the day, one should offer the *bhūtabali*—the oblation to the spirits—with five-colored rice and the mantra: *oṃ sarvabhūtebhyo namaḥ*. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: having drawn eight straight lines and formed six squares, one should write the name in three word-units (*pada*) within two concentric circles on the mountain-like [central] square; having offered a *bali* of five-colored grains, one should meditate upon the worshipped wheel which [overcomes] fever occurring every third day, fevers caused by deities, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "for the pacification of appearances" (*rābhāsapraśāntaye*), the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* explains that this refers to an offering of five-colored substances and an offering of five-colored rice. Here, the deity of the ground is [the subject].
He now states another fever-destroying yantra beginning with the word "Tāra," within a pair of fire-fortresses (*vahnipura*).
In a hexagon intersected by the *rasas* (six), that is to say, having drawn the syllable *praṇava* (*oṃ*) in its center,
and having written the syllable of Earth (*laṃ*) on the eastern and western sides,
one should write the fire-seed-syllable *raṃ* in all six of its corners. Then, [having written] that...
One should encircle the inner square-path with nooses and goads;

having performed the worship and other rites with the three-syllable mantra *oṃ āṃ kroṃ*, the author of the *Harṣadīpikā* and the author of the *Padārthādarśa* state that this [preparation], once accomplished, should be worn on the hand, the head, or the throat to destroy old age.
One should draw two fire-purans (vahni-puras) separately in the south and north;

the drawing for both of these should be identical. In the center is the Praṇava (Oṃ). On the sides of the Praṇava, the seed-syllable *laṃ* is written twice. In the corners of both fire-purans as well, [the syllables] are likewise [to be placed].

In each of the three corners, as well as in the two directions situated outside the eastern and western [sides], a noose (pāśa) and a goad (aṅkuśa) should be drawn in sequence; this reading is corroborated by other tantras, which state "surrounded by a string of goads" (guṇāṅkuśāvītam). [This applies] to each of the three fire-walls (vahnipura).
The meaning of this is that [the letter] should be written on each of the left and right sides; this is stated in the Nāradīya:
"One should write the star facing north or south within two fire-houses (triangles);
Indra on the two sides of the star, and Agni in the corner squares; outside, one should mark the wheel in the east and west."
They say it is adorned with the *śakti*. Here, the specific deity is the one whose nature consists of the *praṇava*, the noose (*pāśa*), and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).

Now he describes another *yantra* for the destruction of fever, beginning with the word "in the *piṇḍa*": in the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) is preceded by the syllable *ṭa* (the last letter of the *ṭa*-class) together with the *visarga*, and is interlaced (*vidarbhitam*) with it.
Having written the seed-syllable of Kṛtapiṇḍa in the center, one should write the vowels in pairs on the filaments;

the eight letters ending with *ṭa* (the *ṭa*-group) are to be written on the eight petals. The meaning is that this [diagram] should be encircled by a *bhūpura* (fortress of the earth) on the outside. And this [yantra] not only destroys diseases through mantras, but also increases one's luster.

He does not accomplish the fever-removing yantra; rather, in connection with the *urudviṣāharaṇa* (poison-removal) yantra, he demonstrates it beginning with the syllable *tāra*. Having written the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) in the center and having written the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) and so forth within it, [he consecrates it] with the six-syllable mantra: *oṃ laluvam svāhā*.

Having surrounded that with the outermost limit by means of the syllable *ṭa*, and having encircled this entire [diagram], one should further construct two circles outside of it—also known as the moon-mandala—and bind them together by surrounding those two with downward-facing half-moons (*ardhacandra*). Regarding the word "sādhya": it exists within the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished).
Thus, having stated [the mantra] beginning with *sādhyāśaṃā* and ending with *at*, this very [yantra] is described in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:

"The *Tāra* (Oṃ), followed by two *Laya*s (Hrīṃ Hrīṃ), and the *Udaka* (Jal) along with the *Śiras* syllables (Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ); surrounded by the powers (*śakti*) and the group of vowels (*vṛtta*), and the name of the child;
encircled on the outside by half-moons and downward-facing triangles—this is the yantra that quickly bestows [success]."
Regarding the explanation that "one should raise the Śūrodaḷa," one should draw the Goddess from the *Aryakṣitārthadyotanikā*,
draw a child in her midst, encircle her with the mantra "Oṃ lu lu vaṃ svāhā," and outside of that, a lunar disc.

The authors of the *Padārthādarśa* state that one should write two *la*s, each facing downward, and bind them together by adorning them with crescent moons (*ardhendu*s). Having written the *māyā*-seed syllable (*hrīṃ*) on birch bark or similar material, and having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within it, one should enclose all of this with "Oṃ lulu... [and so forth].

The meaning is that one should encircle [the diagram] with the seven-syllable mantra "Jvalasvāhā," then encircle it again with the second letter of the labial class (va), and outside of that, one should perform an encirclement with half-moons connected to the mouth, culminating in the *pāśa* seed-syllable (*phaṭ*). Thus ends the *Harṣadīpikā*.

Regarding the syllable *kā*: some, however, state that the seven-syllable mantra is *oṃ lulupa dānte vāri paryāya jalapadānte svāhā*. The reading *jvala* does not exist in the root text, as it would result in a metrical defect (*chanda-bhaṅga*). How then [is it] *vajakāra-vakāra-mor-mili*?

We do not know whether the inclusion of these two mantras within those [others] was intended by the authors of the *Harṣadīpikā*, even though they are the authors of the *Ṭīṣyaṇa*. In both systems, Śakti is the deity here.
Furthermore, he states another yantra for the destruction of fever, beginning with the words "The letter of space" (*vyomārṇa*).
Although it would have been appropriate to describe the fever-destroying yantras immediately following one another without interruption,
rather than requiring the separation by the *ruru-diṣāpahāri* yantra, nevertheless,
compared to a yantra composed of three *lu*s, [the merit of] a yantra composed of two *lu*s—

Intending that its very primacy is required, he describes this same syllable of space—the letter *ha*—as "with the bindu" (*sabiṃdu*), and so forth; for it is the syllable of space accompanied by both the *bindu* and the *nāda*. Thus, it is "with the bindu."
The remainder [of the definition] is that the seed of memory is ultimately established as being written in the middle; furthermore,

he states another qualification for this very [seed] in the passage beginning with "akhyā" (non-apprehension), etc., [referring to] the verbal expression (*ākhyāta*) of the action of the means and the object, such as "Devadatta, perform the destruction of fever," "do it," and so forth.

The meaning is "that which is not interlaced" (*avidarbhitam*). Consequently, the *karmadhāraya* compound of the two words "with the *bindu*" (*sabiṃdu*) and "interlaced" (*avidarbhitapadayoḥ*) is as follows:
*itthaṃvadabrahmyaṃ*, *dattahmyaṃ*, *syajvahmyaṃ*, *ranāhmyaṃ*, *kuruhmyaṃ*, *rukuhmyaṃ*, *śaṃkuhmyaṃ*. In this manner, one should write [the letters] in the middle.
Having drawn two square enclosures (bhūpura) outside of that, with their sides intersecting one another, one should write three *la* syllables in each of the eight corners in the order of each row;
this perfected yantra, when bound upon the hand or other parts of the body, bestows the aforementioned fruits. In its corners, one should place three *luṃ* syllables.

The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that according to the *Nārāyaṇīya* [section of the *Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa*], this yantra—consisting of the syllable *yaṃ* interspersed with the names of the six [directions] and the sky (*viyat*) in the center—is the remover of all fevers.

[The layout is as follows: two earth-circles (*bhūgṛha*), with [the syllables] at each intermediate direction (*vidik*), and at each corner (*koṇa*), with the syllable *saṃ* and the thunderbolt (*vajra*) outside in the eight directions.

Having written the letter of space (ha) with a bindu (ṃ) in the center, thinking "I shall produce [the desired effect] within this," one should write three *ḷ* sounds—each in the form of the ninth vowel—in each of the four corners of the earth-house (*bhūgṛha*).
Thus says the author of the *Harṣadīpikā*. Furthermore, by this alone, there is the destruction of fever and other ailments.

He describes the yantra with the words beginning "sārṇam" and so forth: having written the syllable *bhṛ* (the seed-syllable of Bhṛgu) in the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus, interspersed with the name as before, and having likewise written the letter *sa* on all eight petals, one should construct a thirty-petaled lotus above the circle drawn outside of that.
One should write the thirty letters from *ka* to *śa*, one by one, on the eight petals;
although this much alone would suffice for consistency, because of the mention of "externally" (*vāhya*),

it is understood that something must be written within that [lotus], since the writing of the *ka*-series is prescribed in the southeast (the fire-quarter), and thus the vowels [must be placed elsewhere].

It is determined that they are to be drawn; specifically, the vowels are to be inscribed upon the filaments (kesara) themselves. Thus, the distilled meaning is that two vowels each are to be written upon the filaments of the eight petals.
And one should surround that with a circle of water; such is the nature of the Mātṛkā.

Regarding the section on the fever-removing *vata* [mantra], he states "in the mouth" (*vaktre*) and so forth. Having drawn nine lines extending both east-west and north-south, one produces a *vajra*-shaped grid of sixty squares;
within those, one places the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) consisting of the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*.

One should draw sixteen bindus in the sequence beginning with *śa* and so forth; one should also fashion tridents at the heads of all the lines. By the very act of writing the letters corresponding to the deities of air, fire, earth, and water for this yantra, [the purpose is accomplished].

"This [remedy] removes fever caused by cold (śītajvara), but it does not remove ordinary fever"—this is the opinion of Harṣadīkṣita. The author of the *Padārthādarśa* states that "by this sequence" (*anena krameṇa*), a specific order is intended here;
thus, in the first recitation, the letter *ya* together with the bindu (the *anusvāra*) is [the eighth].

In the twenty squares of the second enclosure, the letter *ra* with a bindu; in the twenty squares of the third enclosure, the letter *la* with a bindu in twelve squares; and thereafter, in four squares, the letter *va* with a bindu—[these should be drawn] using substances that possess forms identical to their respective elements.
