One should draw thirty-six tridents on that ground, each one individually produced by means of those lines; for one who sleeps there, all fevers are destroyed.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "In a field of sixty-four squares, [one should draw] thirty-six tridents..."
One should write the letters *pi*, *te*, *ja*, *rā*, *nā*, *rī*, *tra*, *yī*, *bhā*, *nu*, *ko*, and *ṣṭe* in sequence within the enclosures;
then, one should write the vowels with their nasal bindus inside that, and upon that, the syllable *svet*.

By this procedure, all fevers of one who lies down [after drawing] on the ground with the appropriate colored substances will perish. Thus it is said. One should draw it on the ground using those respective colored materials.
Having reached the bed there, as explained in the *Vyākhyāna* which illuminates the intended meaning,
with reference to the convention stated as "nine days" and "nine jars," the numbers twenty-eight, twelve, and four are indicated respectively by the four words *jarā*, *nārī*, *trayī*, and *bhānu*.

In this very manner, by means of the two terms "anārī" and "rājyapada," which were mentioned previously, the numbers twenty and twelve are obtained. They say that these are indeed the deities praised.
He now states another fever-removing yantra, beginning with the word "puṭita": [it consists of] the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Having fashioned two *gaṃbhu* squares, having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and others in their center, and having written the *praṇava* (Oṃ) on each of the corners and the backs, this is the *yantra* for warding off the affliction of fever by the deity Bhuvaneśī; it follows as a corollary to the section on subjugation (*vaśya*).

He demonstrates the protective diagrams (*yantras*) for warding off afflictions such as the fever of desire (*lakāmajvara*) and others, beginning with the word "varṇe" and so forth: having drawn a square outer enclosure (*bhūpura*), one should inscribe the syllable *va* within it; inside that, having inscribed the moon-like syllable *ṭa*, one should [inscribe] the name of Caitra within that as well.

Having written the letters of the target [person] such as "bring her under the influence of my friend" (*maitraṃ vaśam ānaya*), one should encircle them on the outside with the letter *ṭa*; the meaning is that one should draw a circle outside of that. The deity is the Moon; this is a yantra for subjugation (*vaśya*) by prioritizing its feminine nature, which is mentioned here in connection with the topic of subjugation.

He demonstrates [the procedure] by means of the Truths and so forth: having drawn a hexagon upon an unbroken leaf of the *bṛhannaranāga* creeper, having fashioned svastikas attached to its corners from the outside,
having written the *māyā-bīja* within the corners with the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, and having written [the name] Devadatta of Caitra inside that.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth with the words "vaśam ānaya mānaya" (bring under control, bring under control), and having encircled it with a six-pointed star using a noose and a goad, one should, at night,
while reciting the three-syllable mantra consisting of the noose and the goad, [use] this aforementioned yantra with the flame of a lamp.

One should install [the mantra]; her woman, who is to be accomplished and brought under control, will herself, even without any other means, become submissive and approach—that is, go toward—the practitioner.
This is stated in the *Pravāsara*: "In the middle of the *hṛllekhā*, at midday, one should place *yam* or *hrīṃ* outside, and *kroṃ*..."

Then, having drawn that yantra on a leaf with *nāgavalī* paste— marked with fire-tridents, pairs of triangles, and svastikas— one should recite the mantra of Śakti, accompanied by the noose (*pāśa*), goad (*aṅkuśa*), and hand-gestures (*mudrā*),
over a lamp-fire for one hundred thousand times with devotion; she, her body bent low, overcome by the arrows of Love, will become filled with love.

Regarding the attainment of the three powers (*śaktitraya*), he describes another yantra for subjugating women with the verse beginning "ṣaḍ" and so forth. Here too, the deity is indeed Śakti herself. Having drawn a hexagon on a betel leaf using *kokilākṣa* thorns, one should place the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) in its center and [the name] within that.

The meaning is as follows: having first written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth within the corners, and having written the *māyā* syllable (*hrīṃ*) inscribed with those names of the person to be accomplished and others in each individual corner, one should then construct a square enclosure (*bhūpura*) with vajras on the outside, and within it, write the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*, *klīṃ*) four times in the corners.

The reading "likhen madhyatiṣṭhāne likhec ca smaram" (one should write [the seed] in the central position and write Smara) is the authoritative version following the *Prapañcasāra*, according to the author of the *Padārthādarśa*. Thus, the practical meaning is that the seed-syllable of Kāma (*klīm*) should also be written within the six triangles. [Recited...]

Regarding what was stated by the Teachers concerning the enclosure of the thousand [petals] and so forth: one should first place the seed-syllable (bīja) situated within the Śakti, inside the cavity formed by the pair of fire-palaces (the two triangles), surrounded by the name through interlacing (vidarbha), and outside that, the Earth-element (pārthiva) [square], with the Smara [triangle] in its corners. Furthermore—
With the desire for [her] eyes and speech, one should again write her name upon a betel leaf with thorns, consecrated by mantras;

this is the "Charm that Enchants the Mind of Women. However, according to the author of the *Harṣadīpikā*, one should write the name of the Śakti surrounded by the [five] arrows, the noose, and the goad, and outside of that, within the six corners.

The first half of the root text is seen as: "vidarbhitāmathalikhecchaktiṃ svasādhyākhyayeti. Its meaning is as follows: one should write the *māyā* (Hrīṃ) seed-syllable, which contains the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), within the *kāma* (Klīṃ) seed-syllable, inside the pericarp of the six-cornered [diagram]. These two, *kāma* and *śrī*, [are to be written] in the center.
One should draw [the diagram] and surround it with the four seeds known as Kāma, Śrī, Pāśa, and Aṅkuśa;

then, in the six corners starting from the east, one should write Māyā interlaced with the name of one's own sādhya, just as before. They say that the *troṣa* should be written as previously described; this, however, is a secret for the sake of the sādhya.

It is understood that what is given for the purpose of bringing me under one's control is not required; this same principle should be understood to apply everywhere regarding subjugation (*vaśya*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), inciting hatred (*dveṣaṇa*), killing (*māraṇa*), and so forth. When the practitioner is unknown to the target (*sādhya*), the ritual application (*prayoga*) brings about the result; however, when he is known, the result desired by him [the target] does not occur.
Regarding the path of those who know the tradition of universal certainty,

he states an alternative for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*) starting with the words "In Śakra": having written the seed-syllable *Māyā* (Hrīṃ) in the center of the heart of the person to be accomplished, who has been fashioned from flour in the likeness of Indra, one should [place] Caitra’s [name] within it for the purpose of subjugation.
Having written the name of the person to be subdued (sādhya) and so forth with the word "namānaya" (subdue), one should enclose it with the four seed-syllables; then,
having surrounded it with the four seed-syllables consisting of Śakti, Manobhava, Aṅkuśa, and Pramathana,
one should consecrate it therein through the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, worship, and so on, [and offer] the three sweets (*trisvādu*).
The meaning is that by worshipping that form with the three sweets consisting of ghee, honey, and sugar,

the practitioner who partakes [of it] will have his object of attainment become submissive for as long as he lives, like a servant. Regarding the phrase "with the four seed-syllables," according to the tradition of oral instruction, [one should meditate on] Nṛsiṃha...
Regarding this, some say that the seed-syllables of Tāra, Aṇimā, Śakti, and Durgā should be taken;

others say that because of their proximity, only the four seed-syllables of Śakti should be used. Still others, however, maintain that it is stated one should "envelop with four," and when the question arises as to what those four are, [the answer is] the seed-syllables...
Having performed one round of encirclement with the four [syllables] beginning with *jam* and so forth, such as *śakti* and the rest,

they say that one should encircle it again with these very same [syllables]. Others, however, read *marut* in place of *manu*, and [encircle it] with the five seed-syllables (*bījas*)— *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *krāṃ*, *yaṃ*, and *pro*— as the outer seed-syllable.

You [the author] cite [the view]: "This [mantra], having the name of the object to be accomplished situated within its power, is surrounded on all sides by four seed-syllables"—but this should be disregarded due to its contradiction with other tantras. Therefore, the path shown in the *Padārthādarśa* is [correct]; as for Harṣadīpikākṛt, however, [he says] "peace."

The reading "nobhavāṅkuśamarudbhiḥ" refers to the four seed-syllables previously shown in the alternative reading for the killing rite (*māraṇa*) from the preceding verse; thus, it pertains to the tetrad of seed-syllables consisting of the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*). Likewise, [there are] ghee, honey, and sugar.

Having prepared a dough made from parched rice flour, one should draw an image of the person to be subjugated (sādhya) within the heart of that image; having surrounded it with the four seeds beginning with *kāma* (the seed-mantras *klīm*, etc.), and having further surrounded that with the fourth vowel (the letter *ī*), which is denoted by the word "peace" (*śānti*), as well as the *manobhava* (heart-born), *aṅkuśa* (goad), and *vāyu* (wind) seeds.

Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) and other rites, the practitioner necessarily brings the target under control; this is what they say. Now, he describes another yantra for subjugation (*vaśya*) beginning with the word "Kāma": having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should place the seed-syllable of Kāma in its pericarp.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth at the center, one should write the vowels twice in the filaments and the eight groups of consonants beginning with 'ka' on the petals; thus, according to the Kāma-kalā, the deity resides there. In this manner, forty-five yantras have been obtained from the root texts and explained here according to various traditions.
This is the summary regarding the basis and so forth. Regarding the substances for drawing the yantra, he says "kāśmīram" and so on:

*kāśmīram* is saffron; *rocanā* is gorocana; *mṛgamadaḥ* is musk; *drabhamadaḥ* is the ichor flowing from the temples of an elephant. With these six—[the preceding four and these two]—[one should draw].
Regarding what was stated in another [text] concerning drawing with mixed substances:

"One who desires all success should draw the yantras with a golden stylus, using a mixture of elephant ichor, saffron, and fragrant gorocanā, consecrated three times, along with lac and juice, in a beautiful manner. Thus, [it is done] with a golden stylus.

This refers to the domain of auspicious actions performed at night; for it has been stated that auspicious rites such as *vaśya* (subjugation) and others arise from one's own caste and recitation (*japa*), whereas inauspicious ones arise from iron, charcoal, and so forth.
Just as these, all these machines (*yantras*) must be kept strictly secret by you, my son.
That collection of yantras which brings great prosperity must be given to one who is not a disciple, nor one who is sinful, nor one who is unpeaceful, nor one who is disliked;
it should be given to a disciple who is devoted to the mantra, pure, faithful, and virtuous, and to one who bestows the weapon-mantra (astra). Otherwise, one would go to hell—thus says Hiraṇyagarbha.
Based on the statement in the *Rbhasaṃhitā*, even in other cases, if someone out of greed gives [this] to an unworthy disciple,
he incurs the sin of killing a cow, a child, a woman, or a Brahmin;
this is shown by the passage beginning with "He shows an unretentive yantra that has touched the ground," and so forth.

Tactile contact and auditory perception are precluded; for example, when a birch-bark leaf or similar substrate is partially burnt, even though the written characters are not burnt, the support itself is destroyed. Since there is no manifestation of the burnt yantra as it was originally heard, even that which is partially burnt results in the disappearance of the lines and letters that constitute the body of the yantra.

Since there is no possibility of maintaining [the image] due to the absence of a manifest mechanical device (*yaṃtra*), and since the prohibition [of maintenance] would otherwise be impossible, the prohibition—

"one should not maintain [an image] that has fallen apart over several days, such as when its support is likely to break"— merely demonstrates the lack of attainment of the fruit; it is not [a prohibition against the act of maintenance itself].
The word *yantra* has the sense of "awakening" (*bodhana*). Its meaning was explained in the *Śitāṇḍava*:

"In the *yantra*, indeed, the state of being a *yantra* is proclaimed; for the supreme pacification (*śamana*) occurs through restraint (*yamana*). That wherein the entire universe is restrained (*yantryate*) is called *yantra*. It protects (*saṃtrāyate*) from that which is not protected (*atrāta*); such is the meaning of *yantra* as it has been declared."
This is the meaning: the word *iti* has the sense of "thus"; the phrase "the pacification of the impermanent" (*yamanityasya śamana*) is the explanation.

Likewise, because he is intent upon the pacification—that is, the supreme restraint—of the wicked, he is therefore called *yamana*. Thus, the meaning is "in whatever [restraint] he restrains. For this very reason, the commentary explains: "He restrains (*yamayati*), that is, he subdues the unrighteous."

The meaning of the word *yantra* is as follows: it is that by which one is restrained (*yantryate*) from diseases, malevolent rites (*kṛtyā*), and so forth; or it is that which is held fast (*ātaṅka*) by no means whatsoever through its application; or it is that which protects (*trāyate*) the good (*sat*). Thus is the meaning of the word *yantra*. Alternatively, it signifies excellence (*utkarṣa*).

The summary is this: some [terms] are said to be derived through *yoga-rūḍhi* (etymological-cum-conventional derivation), while others are said to be derived by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone. Furthermore, because there is a binding (*niyaṃtraṇā*)—in the form of a restriction—of the syllables of the mantras, which are of the nature of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), upon their respective locations such as the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and filaments (*kesara*) of the yantras, they are called *yantras*.
Recalling that [the goddesses] bestow the fruits of their grace upon practitioners without fail,
he begins to praise the Goddess who consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahma), his heart overflowing with the surge of devotion:
"O Mother, [I bow] to the hand of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, which bestows [these fruits] upon me."
Since I am not even fit to be an instrument for Your praise— beginning with the act of sprinkling water and so forth—
and have entered into a lineage of births produced by You, I have become unworthy; therefore, by the spear of performing Your praise, I shall purify my own speech.
He states that even the three-eyed Lord Śiva cannot be praised because [his greatness] is impossible to fathom, using the verse beginning with "ādyām" and so forth.

He further states, using the verse beginning with "pṛthvī" and so forth, that even the majesty of Śiva—who possesses the eight forms consisting of earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the sacrificer, the moon, and the sun—is dependent upon you alone. Three...

He states with the verse beginning "trisrotasi" that even the excellence of the triple-streamed Gaṅgā— its superiority over all else and its particular capacity for purification— is produced by You alone;
likewise, even the moon, the sun, and so forth, each possesses individually that power which is well-known in the world.
He says that because You are composed of everything (*sarvamayī*), You are indeed the most excellent of all, by means of the passage beginning with "You delight" (*ānandayi*).
He further states that even various contradictory attributes reside in You alone, by means of the passage beginning with "You are water and so forth" (*apādyāpīpī*).
Regarding worship and other such rites, it is only human beings who possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) therein.

He says that even those qualified persons who possess a refined faculty of perception, though they worship [the Lord], fall back down once again after having ascended the human body and so forth— which serves as a staircase to heaven and other realms—
and go instead to the lower worlds such as hell, the animal kingdom, and the realm of ghosts. Thus he speaks of "āsām" (of these).

With the words beginning with "dyeti," [the author] says that those who worship you even with sandalwood, flowers, and so forth—which are very easy to obtain—they, moreover, attain the state of being the Lord of the World (*bhuvanādhipatya*), which is extremely difficult to attain, O Lord of the World (*bhuvanātha*). He states this with the verse beginning with "karpūra... and so on; thus ends the pair of verses in the first [chapter].
In the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, the serpent Śeṣa— who is like a sleeping king— remains coiled like a flash of lightning; creating the illusion of its likeness,
she enters the central path, the *suṣumṇā*, and [traverses] the five lotuses, beginning with the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
Having ascended through the spaces known as Mūlādhāra, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, Ājñā, and Vidyullatā,
which are difficult to traverse, and having reached the Brahma-randhra, she resorted there to the nectar flowing from the union with Brahman;
then, becoming Gāyatrī, she returned again by way of the five lotuses to the Mūlādhāra.
The meaning of the pair of verses is that for those who remember her as she has departed, the destruction of their essential afflictions (*sāra-cheda*) is accomplished.
She is depicted with the *cintā-jñāna-mudrās* and four hands holding objects such as the *cintāmaṇi*;
this refers to her form as Sarasvatī. One should meditate upon her as the identity (*aikya*) of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Relying upon yoga— defined as the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (cittavṛttinirodha)— which is proficient in the application of the *gaṃ* [mantra],
one should conquer the six enemies consisting of lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and arrogance, thereby casting off their mastery,
and likewise [subdue] the group of senses, the five beginning with the eye.

The meaning is that yogis, whose minds have not yet transcended the objects of their own senses, perceive You as being obstructed by nooses, goads, and the like; thus they meditate upon You as possessing attributes (*saguṇa*). Yet, even this form with attributes is to be meditated upon by those who have already accomplished their purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*); how much more so [the formless one]!

The intention is that for those such as the *smadā* (the lowly), there is only the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). He states that she is indeed the very nature of Lakṣmī with the words beginning "heated" (*uttapta*), and he states that she is indeed the nature of Durgā with the words beginning "with eight" (*aṣṭābhiḥ*).
[She is] one whose heat (*dharma*) manifests through fatigue from activities such as moving her feet, starting from the appearance [of perspiration].

Wearing garments of leaves and bark, she is free from the languor of passion; yet, burdened by the fullness of youth, she is overcome by an excess of desire for you. Here, the word *tandrā* signifies being under the sway of another. By this much, it is stated that you alone are her wanderer, her dweller in the home, and her mover in the arena.

The name "haṃsa" for an anklet is indeed well-known from the phrase *vati haṃsaiḥ*. In that context, it is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that even the *haṃsa*, a specific type of bird, comes to the anklets due to the delusion of their being of the same species, because of its gait— its movement— and its *kvaṇita*— its particular sound.

Those very objects—substances and so forth—are determined to be both the swans and the words; thus, there is a determination of the feet as lotuses and the shanks as stalks. Since every person has only two eyes, how could Śambhu have three? [This is the rhetorical objection.]
The cause for this [comparison] is imagined by the two verses beginning with "dvābhyām" (by the two). "Karāvaleya" refers to the trunk of the elephant;

"haṃkāra" refers to the plantain pillar (raṃbhā-kadalī-staṃbha). Because of their heaviness, even the two thighs were like pillars capable of supporting her weight; thus, they were as if bestowed by her youth in its middle stage—that is, by her adolescence.

The sense is that it has become as if it were a fire that has not yet arisen. By the verse beginning with "śroṇyau" (the hips), he offers a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) for the reason why the middle part is so exceedingly slender: through the word "simultaneously" (*yugapat*), he describes the natural state (*svabhāva*) in which both [the hips] possess heaviness together, while the middle possesses thinness.

Regarding the question, "What is the proof for the existence of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-sattva*) since its perception has not been established?", he says: "Because of the emergence of body hair. The meaning is this: that which is implied as the very substratum (*āśraya*) by that [emergence of hair], which would otherwise be inexplicable without a substratum, is precisely what we term the "intermediate state" (*madhyapada*). This is not a mere recollection of the navel.

He imagines [the ash] as being like a friend, a youth, and one who is not empty of affection, by means of the words beginning with "friend" (*sakhi*). The ash (*bhasita*) is a "hint" (*piśuna*), that is, an indicator, of the embrace (*upagūha*);
it is the father (*tāta*) arisen first, and then the father arisen from behind; it is that which has emerged from the neck (*kaṇṭha*) and surpassed it.

Alas! From the neck of the Lord, which is worthy of being bound, a binding by anything inferior to the curd-like [substance] is not possible. And those brilliant splendors that flow and stream forth serve as the very means [of binding], acting like the edge of a blade attached to the side of the noose;
for indeed, at the end of the noose, there is the edge of a blade somewhere.
In the *Purāṇa*, it is stated that there is no [other] caste; following that, "kaṃbu" means a conch-shell.
"Abhijātam" means beautiful. "Daram" means a fang. Because he was born from that [conch], his birth alone is fruitful—this is the meaning.
"Āviriteḥ" means the line of the frost-maker (the moon), that is, the lunar digit, has become manifest or revealed.
And because her mass of hair was bound with a particular ornament in the shape of the moon,

there was no distinction between the fragrance of the flowers situated upon that mass of hair— which possessed no other scent— and the fragrance wafting from above; for the blackness [of the hair] was identical to the [dark] color of the bees.

That ancient noose, characterized by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), although it possesses the capacity to produce results merely through its existence as one's own nature—even when recited as a hymn of praise—it is not [effective] as something known for the purpose of bestowing specific fruits; for it is said: "Even when remembered with wicked thoughts, Hari removes sins, even if he does not desire it."

Just as fire indeed burns even that which merely touches it, it is not established by experience for anyone that its touch— which occurs immediately after the cognition of its burning nature— is something other than that which possesses the capacity to burn; nevertheless,
since the commencement of recitation is impossible without the knowledge of the result, [the result must be understood].
Intending to show the fruit [of this practice] by asking, "How could there be no hope? he says, "By the Veda," and so forth.
The meaning is: for the wise, those possessed of intelligence, it is one whose ears have undergone a well-performed ripening, which takes the form of the fruit of bliss born from hearing.
To him whose mother was the virtuous Udyotamatī, whose father was named Māpati, who was born into the lineage of Paṃtha, whose birthplace was Kūrmācala,
and who made Vārāṇasī his residence— there, the Creator attained perfection in his work, as did the Lord of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) at the feet of Kṛtavīrya.
In the *Śabdārthacintāmaṇi*,

[the author] now demonstrates, by means of the passage beginning with "atha," the means for accomplishing the yoga that is useful for the previously mentioned piercing (*vedha*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), and so forth, which are attainable solely by yogis; he indicates the fruit [of this practice] with the word "saṃvit" (consciousness).

That is to say, it is the specific state of perfect knowledge of the Self (saṃsamyakcit-jñāna-viśeṣa), which is the experience of eternal bliss (nityānandānubhava) and is synonymous with liberation (mokṣa). Thus, it is stated that the fruit of yoga is liberation.
According to the Vedāntins, yoga is the knowledge of the non-difference between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).

O Auspicious One, for us, the authors of the *Pratyabhijñā* and other treatises maintain that yoga is the knowledge of the identity of Śiva with His power (*śakti*), which is characterized as the cause of saṃsāra. By the inclusion of the word "characterized" (*viśiṣṭa*), [it is implied] that there is also identity of Śiva with the effect (*kāryya*).
Some partial proponents of the Tantras maintain that the knowledge of that [reality] is what is included within the scope of its defining characteristics;

however, the Naiyāyikas and others, who are proponents of dualism, declare that yoga is indeed the perfect thorough knowledge of the Ancient Puruṣa. He [the author] demonstrates all four of these views as follows: ai...
With the two verses beginning with "kyam" (what?), he explains the means for attaining yoga. Regarding the words "having conquered," etc.:

desire and the other [afflictions] are the enemies of the self because they repeatedly produce the experience of various sufferings such as those in the hells; among these, "desire" (*kāma*) refers to the longing for objects such as women and sensual enjoyments.

Desire (*kāma*) is the wish for [objects] such as sentient beings; anger (*krodha*) is a particular mental modification (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*) conducive to such a wish to kill—so some say; greed (*lobha*) is thirst for wealth, kingdom, and so forth;
delusion (*moha*) is the misconception regarding a real entity, such as thinking "I am wealthy," "I am happy," or "I am learned."
Intoxication (*mada*) is a specific state of inflation characterized by vanity and so forth, having synonyms such as arrogance (*avajñā*).

Envy (*matsara*) is aversion toward other auspicious objects. "They say" means that they strive [to describe] these six internal enemies (*ari-ṣaḍ-varga*), beginning with desire (*kāma*), which cause suffering to oneself; the meaning is that they declare this to be their conquest.
By the words "Pāpamāha yogāṣṭāṅgaiḥ" and so forth, [the author] indicates that the yogis— who possess a longing for yoga—
merely name the eight limbs; and by the words "yadyam" and so forth,
he states that they were spoken by the yogis in order to dispel any suspicion regarding their lack of authority.
Since it is established by experience that what has been taught by those yogins who have attained yoga is indeed true,
it follows that the attainment of yoga occurs through these eight limbs beginning with *yama*.
Therefore, the intention is that those desiring the attainment of yoga must certainly strive in these [limbs] beginning with *yama*.

He who observes the first duty mentioned there, namely non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), and so forth— firmly resolving in accordance with reality that "I shall not kill even a single living being"— and who possesses the firm resolve, "I shall not speak untruth through greed and the like," is a *brāhmaṇa*.

Some maintain that even speaking untruth for the sake of protection and so forth is indeed truth; however, this is to avoid the charge of over-extension (*avyāpti*) in those cases. Others, however, hold that even such speech is not truth, but is indeed untruth (*anṛta*), and from it there certainly arises transgression (*pratyavāya*), as stated in the injunction: "One should not speak untruth."

Because even that [prohibition] is included within it; however, since there is also an excellence of merit produced by acts such as saving a Brāhmaṇa, the destruction of the demerit arising from that falsehood is further increased,
and thus its [resulting] prosperity is brought about.

If the learned do not abandon such a falsehood out of greed, then the *Harṣadīpikā* text— which states that "truth" consists in the practice of speaking what is pleasing to others when one is overcome by greed and the like— would be contradicted; for [the term] "overcome by greed and the like" would have to be understood according to your interpretation.
If it is argued that [the definition] applies to the middle state of a corpse, what of it? It is indeed true;

however, the author of the *Padārthadarśa* has established that the definition of greed (*lobha*) and so forth consists precisely in the habitual resort to improper means, joined with falsehood, and is not constituted by [other factors such as] deceit (*māyā*) and the like. Thus they say. *Samakṣa*.

Theft (*steya*) is the appropriation of another's property in their presence, without [the owner's] consent, except through acceptance, victory, purchase, and so forth; non-theft (*asteya*) is the opposite of that. Unchastity (*abrahmacarya*) is the desire for women at improper times, as well as the lack of enjoyment even with one's own wife [at such times].

Celibacy (*brahmacaryya*) is prescribed by the injunction "one should approach [one's wife] for sexual enjoyment limited to the period of her season" (*ṛtukālāvacchinna-ihabhogah*); likewise, the injunction "one should establish the sacred fires" (*vasante 'gnīn ādadhīta*) and others are fulfilled by approaching one's wife during the season (*ṛtau upagacchet*), as prescribed by the injunction "one should approach one's wife during her season" (*ṛtāv upeyāt*). Thus, it is through this single primary performance that both requirements are met.

Since the purpose is accomplished even by approaching [the woman] only once, the word "only once" (*sakṛt*) is used; otherwise, approaching her more than once would result in a deviation from the meaning of the vow. Furthermore, because of the boon granted by Indra, although the fulfillment of women's desires occurs, there is no deviation from celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Thus it is established.

By being expressed through the letters beginning with *kṣa*, that which is stated up to the end [of the alphabet] is as follows: for living beings, there is the cessation of cruel intent; compassion (*kṛpā*), which is synonymous with mercy (*dayā*), is the desire to eliminate the suffering of others without ulterior motive;
and [the absence of] causing suffering to others through even a slight degree of greed or other such passions.
Some say that even one who is merciless performs [this act], and therefore it is unconditional (*nirupādhi*).

Rectitude (*ārjava*) is the cessation [of crookedness] through mental dishonesty (*cittakauṭilya*). Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the state of the mind being inclined toward non-anger even toward an oppressor. It is the absence of mental agitation (*khacintā*) induced by the desire for a desired object.

*Āhārayama* is the gradual reduction of food until one takes only that amount of sustenance necessary for the maintenance of the body; *mātrāhāra* is eating in moderation. *Śauca* is the performance of the aforementioned purifications that produce mental clarity.

The *yamas* are the restraints that turn back desire and the other passions; they consist of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*).
Because they are derived from the verbal root *me* (to restrain), the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: "those which restrain or turn back [the senses] are *yamas*.

Among these, the conquest of desire is achieved through non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*); the conquest of anger through compassion (*kṛpā*) and forbearance (*kṣamā*); and the conquest of greed through contentment (*asaṃpad*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), truthfulness (*satya*), and uprightness (*ārjava*).

The conquest of delusion (*moha*) is to be achieved through the grandfather’s [qualities of] purity and restraint; the conquest of pride (*mada*) through forbearance and straightforwardness; and the conquest of envy (*matsara*) through non-violence, compassion, straightforwardness, and forbearance.
Thus, the characteristics of all of these have been declared in the *Saṃhitā*.
That which does not cause suffering to living beings through speech, mind, or action is indeed designated as *ahiṃsā* (non-violence).
Furthermore, the truthful description of things exactly as they have been seen or heard is certainly called *satya* (truth);
by this, it is established as being based on reality.
If the statement of the object as it is were not true, then even a person who, while himself experiencing the delusion of silver in mother-of-pearl and the like,
deceives another by saying "this is mother-of-pearl," would have to be considered a speaker of truth; this is what was emphasized there.

One who says "this is silver" is indeed a speaker of truth, because he speaks of an object exactly as it was perceived; however, let it be granted that the definition [of truth] is not merely "that which exists in reality," for even a deluded person or a deceiver who speaks falsely might say, "Let there be silver here."

It should not be said that [the speaker] is a liar simply because he utters a sentence that produces a successful activity; for in such cases, the learned (śiṣṭas) regard even a deluded deceiver as being the one who is a liar, since it is the aforementioned [absence of contradiction] alone that serves as the decisive factor.

Furthermore, it is not the case that a non-corresponding uttered sentence is the motivator for an action; rather, it is only a sentence that, by the nature of things, conveys what possesses that property [the object] which is the motivator. Thus, even from a false statement of a speaker, a corresponding action may indeed be accomplished.
The truth is that even from sentences such as "this," activity may be non-concordant;

likewise, the non-taking even of grass and the like, and the taking of another's property as one's own, is called theft— addressing him as "O you whose wealth is penance" (tapodhana), the grasping of only what is one's own is non-stealing (asteya).

It has been stated that even when one takes kuśa grass and kāśa reeds standing in a forest, or water from a river, a pond, and so forth, there is no attachment to them because one does not take possession of them as one's own;
therefore, it is said that "taking possession" (*sarasvatādāna*) is required for [the sin of theft] to occur. This is just as it happens in other cases.
Since taking what belongs to another does not constitute theft if it is not one's own, there is no contradiction with the rule;

likewise, regarding all states of life, the Smṛti declares: "The abandonment of association with women through action, mind, and speech is known as celibacy (brahmacarya). Thus, [the rule applies] to all states.
This is also indicated by the word "api" (even);
for even when sexual union with a woman is permitted by scriptural injunctions during specific seasons (*ṛtu*) or other states,
such union must be abandoned— how much more so in other circumstances?

Just as in such passages as "one may even kill one who seeks to kill a knower of the Vedanta," the purport is the necessity of killing anyone other than a knower of the Vedanta, and not that one should kill a knower of the Vedanta;
likewise here too, the purport is the attainment of the supreme state, and not [the attainment of] other states.

Even when one is in such a state [of suffering], there is no movement away from it, because the masters of yoga and others have authorized the endurance of that very state; likewise, having observed the suffering of others as if it were one's own,
the pursuit of its remedy is compassion, just as it is for oneself.

Having reflected upon some form of greed and so forth through three examples, it was stated that there is a desire to eliminate that suffering; for indeed, the activity of eliminating one's own suffering is not carried out by means of greed and the like.
Thus, in all worldly dealings involving mind, speech, and body...

The experts in the Tantras maintain that *ārjava* (straightforwardness) is known as the absence of crookedness in all matters; likewise, *kṣamā* (forbearance) is the conduct of treating those who cause harm at all times, in every way, and everywhere exactly like one's own kinsmen; and [the state of] being devoid of desire and effort regarding things already produced.

"Steadfastness even toward sense objects" means that one maintains restraint even toward objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women that have been obtained quite unexpectedly— how much more so toward those not yet obtained;
for since desire arises subsequent to effort, the absence of desire is itself the result of that very effort.

The meaning is that it is described by the term *dhṛti*. Likewise, they declare that food which is pure, wholesome, well-oiled, and consists of eating only a fourth part of what is fit to be eaten is beneficial for one of clear mind;
likewise, they say that excrement is that which has emerged from the nails, hair, and the nine apertures.
Purification by means of earth and water for the exterior is called *śauca*;

alternatively, internal purification is desired through the previously mentioned rites such as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Thus, purification is twofold: external and internal. The external is properly performed three times with earth and water.

The meaning is that by means of washing, internal purification (*āntarbhūtaśuddhi*), the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters (*mātṛkānyāsa*), freedom from distraction, and so forth— for the sake of that [practice]— the ten categories beginning with austerity (*tapas*) are called "observances" (*niyamas*) because they must necessarily be performed by Yama; this also applies to these [other practices].

In the *Saṃhitā*, austerity (*tapas*) is held to be that which is performed according to rule; it is intended here as that preceded by the prescribed method through the practice of vows such as fasting and the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*), on the other hand, is said to be contentment arising from what is obtained by chance (*yadṛcchā-lābha*).

They declare that *āstikya* (faith) is the conviction in what is taught by the Vedas (*śruti*) and other authorities; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the *Smṛtis*, the *Śāstras*, the *Āgamas*, and other treatises. However, the definition stated in the *Upadārthadarśa*—that faith is the practice of *dharma* and so forth based on the conviction in the existence of the next world—is not mentioned here.

The meaning of the words in this compound is as follows: *āstikya* (orthodoxy) should be understood as the very conviction regarding the truthfulness of the meanings declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and so forth. The etymological description of the term is: one who possesses faith (*āstika*) is so called because he has conviction (*āstikya*); thus, *āstikya* is the state of being such a person. This is the intended meaning.

The *Padārthādarśa* author would have contradicted his own work had he not demonstrated that very statement— beginning with "It is said in the *Saṃhitā*" and so forth— which was indicated by the Blessed One in the *Muktasaṃhitā*, though not stated there in exactly those words,
but rather its definition was shown. Otherwise, the text of the *Padārthādarśa* author would be inconsistent.

If it is argued that it is inappropriate to demonstrate that [meaning], because the meaning of the *Saṃhitā* is not established by the non-acceptance of what was stated by oneself as a support for that [meaning], we reply: this is not our fault.
For instance, if one were to meditate upon one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and offer [the merit] to them daily, and then give [alms] to a worthy recipient (*satpātra*), [it would be appropriate].

That which is called *dīta-dharma* (the dharma of shame) is as follows: when one refrains from engaging in that which is utterly condemned by the Vedas (*śruti*) and other such authorities as well as by worldly convention, that very state of shame is designated as *hrī*.
For if one were to engage in such acts, the mind would become defiled, and through that defilement, knowledge itself would not arise; therefore, [one should avoid] what is condemned.

The meaning is that it does not proceed merely according to its own course, but rather it must be guided so that cessation occurs through the force of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and so forth. Likewise, the thorough investigation (*anusandhāna*) of the various [objects] by means of the ears, which is also the correct reflection on words and smiles, is "reflection" (*manana*); and the ascertainment of that [reflection] is "reasoning" (*tarka*), which is manifold.

The meaning is that *mati* (intellect) arises from the contemplation and reflection upon the meaning of the scriptures as heard through the medium of sound, established by the authority of the Word (*śabda*). Likewise, *japa* is the constant repetition of a mantra received from the Guru. Similarly, *homa* is the offering made with substances prescribed in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
Thus it is said; he demonstrates the postures with the words beginning with "the lotus posture" (*padmāsana*) and so forth.

Regarding the fatigue that arises during the practice of standing, one who has fallen like a staff upon a bed or similar surface is overcome by sleep; therefore, the practice should be performed only while seated in these postures.

The sense is that one must necessarily adopt at least one of those [eight] postures (*āsana*). Furthermore, the destruction of disease is accomplished through the practice of *āsana*, as it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*: "By means of *āsana* one destroys diseases, and by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)..."

The practitioner of yoga always attains purification from mental transgressions through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), steadiness of mind through concentrations (*dhāraṇā*), and supreme sovereignty through sounds; then, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, he attains liberation in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). As for the phrase "upon the thighs," it is used here because of the inversion [of the usual order].
The same [rule] applies here as well; thus, having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and the left foot upon the right thigh,
and having crossed the two arms behind the back,
one should grasp the big toe of the left foot with the right hand and the big toe of the right foot with the left hand.
One should bind the thumbs; such a posture is called *padmāsana*. The meaning is that this is dear to yogins. This is the path of the authors of the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* (or *Sārasaṃgrahadīpikā*).
However, the author of the *Padārthādarśa* [states] "due to the inversion," etc., and [mentions] "from behind" and "only a cubit," and so forth.
They say that the binding of the thumbs is not done out of sequence; rather, each thumb is bound with its corresponding Brahman. Regarding "the knees and thighs":
having placed the sole of the left foot between the right knee and thigh, and the sole of the right foot between the left knee and thigh, one remains straight.

The meaning is that one should sit down in such a way that it takes the form of a *svastika*, thus becoming the *svastikāsana*. Although the state of having a straight body (*ṛjukāyatva*) was required even for the previous posture, here it is specifically so because of the traditional instruction regarding the binding of the big toes; therefore, [the body] is straight there as well.

Because the goal of the body has been attained, it is designated here as "the seam" (*sīvanyā*). The *sīvani* is the vertical line between the anus and the penis; on its right side is the ankle of the left foot, and on its left side is the ankle of the right foot, below the testicles.

The remainder [of the sentence] is that it occurs by inversion beneath the *ḍaka* (the perineum); the meaning here is that, as in the *padmāsana*, one should bind the two big toes with both hands. Having placed the ankles on either side of the suture of the self's body, [one places them] upon the feet.

Having placed the left ankle upon the right, and the right [ankle] upon the other (the left), and having placed the right hand upon the left foot, one should bind the two big toes with both hands in reverse order; thus, with arms raised,
[one should place them] facing backward over one's own raised arms.

Placing the toes of one foot against the thighs and the toes of the other foot against the shanks, one should place the knees upon the hands; this is what is meant by the statement that it is called *vajrāsana*. "One" means that one should place one foot beneath the thigh of the other.
Having pressed one foot down, one should place it upon the thigh; this is what is meant by *vīrāsana*. He describes the definition of *prāṇāyāma* with the words beginning "by the *iḍā*" and so forth:
the retention of the movement and return of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is likewise *prāṇāyāma*.

Thus it has been declared by those expert in the Yoga-śāstra. In that regard, the *Gautamīya* states that "of the *prāṇa*"—this is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound—and that [term] is a synonym for *prāṇavāyu*.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *āyāma* is the restraint of movement according to one's will; and that is exclusively... [gamana].

With the intention that [the restraint of breath] is not possible merely by the act of filling [the body] nor by the simultaneous cessation of both inhalation and exhalation, he explains the previous verse;
therein Gautama states: "The vital breath (prāṇa) is known as air (vāyu); its restraint..."

"Prāṇāyāma is said to be the wealth of the yogis and the means for accomplishing yoga. Regarding this, the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā* in the *Harṣadīpikā* states: "The time required for the utterance of a single long syllable of the Guru—neither too fast nor too slow—is traditionally known as one *mātrā* according to the sound."

Having performed a circumambulation clockwise around the knee, one should perform the snapping of the fingers neither too quickly nor too slowly; this is proclaimed as the *samā* measure. Through the *iḍā*, the left channel, one should draw the breath from the external state into the interior for a duration of sixteen *mātrās*.

This is indeed the *pūraka* (inhalation); one should perform the retention of the drawn-in breath for up to sixty-four *mātrās*, remaining motionless. This is called *kuṃbhaka* because, like a water-pot (*kuṃbha*), it is devoid of the actions of [exhalation and] inhalation. Then, slowly, for a duration of twenty-two *mātrās*...

One should exhale the air that has been filled to its limit; because it is exhaled from the navel, this is truly named *revaka*, as its name is etymologically significant (*anvartha*). In this manner, by the performance of these three types of breath-control (*vāyuniyama*) consisting of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), one [attains] a single...
"Prāṇāyāma is accomplished when one properly holds the air previously filled [within] as it moves through the center of the *suṣumṇā*";

this is the connection with what precedes. Then, by means of repeated practice in reverse order—through the sequence of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kuṃbhaka*)—the twelve *prāṇāyāmas* [are completed].

The meaning is that one should perform sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. When this is done, the destruction of sin occurs, as it has been said: "O Vaśī, if a twice-born man performs sixteen *prāṇāyāmas* accompanied by the *praṇava* every morning, he thus dispels his sin day after day."

"That which purifies even one who has committed the murder of a fetus or the drinking of liquor—like rising fires for the cotton of evil—is this breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which is twofold: with seed (*sagarbha*) and without seed (*vigarbha*).
That which is preceded by the simultaneous recitation of the *praṇava*, root-mantras, and so forth, is [the former]."
Prāṇāyāma preceded by [japa] and preceded by both [japa and dhyāna] is "with seed" (sagarbha);
however, where there is merely the silent restraint of the breath, that is "seedless" (avigarbha) prāṇāyāma.
The accomplishment of prāṇāyāma is inferred through three types of effects: when it is being practiced, when it has been mastered, and when it is perfected.

Doubt, delusion, and deceit are the indicators of that [mastery’s] attainment; when a trembling of the body arises, through that [trembling], the attainment of the *arghya* state is to be inferred. For a superior person endowed with that attainment, as long as there is practice—that is, during the time of its cultivation—[the result persists].

The ultimate meaning is that there occurs the abandonment of the earth element and the quality (guṇa) exists in the form of abiding in the intermediate space (ākāśa). He defines *pratyāhāra* with the words beginning "of the senses" (*indriyāṇām*), etc.;
[the five] consisting of breath, taste, sight, hearing, and touch are the five organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*).

The meaning is this: when the senses proceed without obstruction or hesitation toward their respective objects—smell, scent, taste, form, sound, and touch—the withdrawal from those various objects by means of their power is what is designated by the term *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). From that follows cessation, which is the means for attaining those respective goals.

That [aversion] arises from ignorance or hatred; and that [ignorance] arises from the apprehension of a sign (liṅga) that indicates an object grasped as a means to what is desired. And that [aversion] is possible only when the mind is directed toward the apprehension of something as a means to what is desired; for it cannot exist without the mind.
The sense is that since it is established that some of the senses possess the capacity to grasp their respective objects,

there is the withdrawal (pratyāhāra) of the senses. He states the definition of concentration (dhāraṇā) with the words beginning "aṅguṣṭha" [the thumb], regarding the vital air (prāṇavāyu) which has been brought under control through the practice of breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma).

The meaning is that "retention" (dhāraṇā) refers specifically to the concentration [of the breath] upon the sixteen locations beginning from the big toe and ending at the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta). The term *laṃvikā* refers to the base of the palate, which is synonymous with the *ghaṇṭikā*; the region above that, comprising the head, forehead, and the junction of the hair, is the referent of the word "head" (*mūrdhan*). The two... [end of fragment]

He describes the characteristic of meditation on the state of the *brahmarandhra* at the end of the ten [stages] with the words beginning "by one who is concentrated" (*samāhitena*). This means by one who is concentrated— that is, not distracted by other objects—
and by one who abides within another consciousness, situated in the midst of the consciousness of the Supreme Brahman, being attached to the Supreme Brahman.
The meaning is that whatever meditation upon one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) occurs within one's own self, that is what is designated by the term "meditation" (*dhyāna*).

He concludes [the section] with the word "proclaimed" (*prokta*); the meaning is that the characteristics of the eight limbs of yoga have been proclaimed by this much of the treatise. Now, [he describes] the *mūlādhāra*.

In order to explain the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) within the locations of the channels (*nāḍī*), he demonstrates the nature of the body along with its measurements, beginning with the word "six" (*ṣaḍ*): the body of all beings consists of both [elements], being composed of fire and moon, or alternatively, composed of semen and blood, measured by one's own fingers.
It is ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length, and its center is the navel.
Within that body, in the space between the genitals and the anus, there is the Mūlādhāra, which is two finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width;
it is circular at its opening and is called "Mūla" because it is the root of all the channels (nāḍīs).
They declare that which sustains [the body] to be the *dhārakā* [channel]; from it, infinite channels have arisen.

Among these, three are principal, known by the names *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumṇā*. Therein, they say that the *suṣumṇā* channel is situated within, resting upon the backbone (*vaṃśa*) and the spinal column (*pṛṣṭavaṃśa*). It is that which is called *muṇḍā*.
Situated between the two channels (nāḍīs) within the central column of the body is the Suṣumṇā;
it originates from the big toes of the feet and extends up to the Brahma-randhra, remaining fixed in the head.

Regarding the phrase "by the two channels" (*śiphābhyām*): if this were not stated, then even though [the Suṣumṇā] arises from the big toes, its state of being "originated" (*pravṛttatvam*) would still be understood as such.

"Attainable from that"—this is what was stated; therefore, it is understood that [the attainment] arises from and proceeds from that. Since it would be possible to attain that from a single thumb alone, the dual number is used.
This very Suṣumṇā consists of the forms of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni; within the center of that Suṣumṇā, one should enter.

The channel of consciousness (saṃjñā-nāḍī) revolves within that very [channel]; for there exists a place called the Brahma-aperture (brahmarandhra), resembling a lotus fiber and as subtle as a lotus stalk-thread. Furthermore, the channel of consciousness is connected to the Mūlādhāra; according to the various traditions regarding the Ādhāra, it is of many kinds.
Some say it is one, others twelve, and still others sixteen; thus they speak.

This channel called Citrā, situated within the Suṣumṇā, is designated by the term "divine path" because it is the conduit for the exit of the immortal, divine substance. Indeed, through this door, Brahman [is attained].

The nectar (*amṛta*) that has flowed from the aperture (*raṃdhra*), which is the cause of bliss, enters the body of the living being through the channels of *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, and exits from the body; due to the exit of this [nectar], which is synonymous with *vīrya*, various conditions such as the destruction of longevity and health arise. Of that...

Just as there is no external means for men to escape from their state, so too the means [of liberation] is to be accomplished only through the instruction of the venerable Guru, O Yogin. In that regard, if the movement of the Moon is in the *iḍā*, then there is success in rites such as pacifying (*śāntika*); if the movement of the Sun is in the *piṅgalā*, [there is success in] fierce rites (*krūra-karman*).

Success occurs when there is the upward movement of both the moon and the sun within the *suṣumṇā*; this is the auspicious time for the practice of yoga. This distinction can be known only by yogis and not by others—this is the meaning of the passage beginning with "Parāta" and so forth. Now, as for the *kuṇḍalī*...
He indicates the location of Kuṇḍalinī with the words beginning "ādhāra" (the support), etc.
There exists within the previously mentioned support, in the center of the *da* (vulva), a triangular mandala; therein resides the power Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is like a sleeping serpent.
And she sustains both the individual self (*ātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). She... [is that].
In what manner does she come to have a connection with the Supreme Lord? To this he says:
"Haṃsam" (the swan). She has resorted to—that is, she supports—the *jīvātman* (the individual soul);
having taken hold of the individual soul, she has arrived at the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā) by way of the *suṣumṇā* path. Thus [it is said].

This power then becomes a union with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); for the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) is indeed the abode of the Supreme Self, and the sense is that when [the power] is united there, its union with that which resides therein becomes even more complete. He demonstrates the refuge and other attributes of the *haṃsa* in the verse beginning with "haṃsi."
"By day, [it is] the support of the vital breaths"—the meaning is that it has the *prāṇa* wind as its substratum;

for the *prāṇa* wind is one whose substratum is the channels (*nāḍīs*). To the question, "How is there the state of being the *prāṇa* for that which has the channels as its substratum? he says: "The support," and so forth; and thus, at the time of departure...
The meaning is that by qualifying the wind with the term "external region" (*bāhyadeśa*), it is indicated that "prāṇa" is a name for the wind;

for since it is stated that the *prāṇa* moves within the channels (*nāḍīs*), it circulates throughout the entire body, and by means of that, it is also implied that the Kuṇḍalinī energy likewise exists there. [It extends] twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*).
In the phrase "it goes out through the mind," the words "in the left and right parts" are to be understood as the ellipsis.

This has been stated in another Tantra: "One should perform eating, sexual intercourse, battle, and likewise the gathering of fruits and flowers, as well as cruel deeds, when [the breath] is situated in the left or the right; [so too for] journeys and marriages."
"Whatever auspicious actions there may be,

let him perform them all when the left wind is established," thus he describes the manner of practicing yoga with the words beginning with "in a pleasant place" and ending with "not [in a place] that causes distraction of the mind"; by this, a solitary location that does not cause mental distraction is designated.
He abandoned that place because mental seclusion cannot be achieved there— since it is crowded with many people and filled with contemptible things— and thus the practice of yoga is impossible;
furthermore, even if the seat is firm, mental distraction may still occur, and for that reason he avoided it.
However, for one whose mind is not interrupted due to the firmness of practice in *kṣā* (patience), this is permitted:
among the five postures previously mentioned, such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and others, one should adopt any one of them;
this is the meaning of the injunction "having taken a single posture," and then one should mutter the *bhūta-mantra*.

Thus, the nature [of these elements] is that the five elements, beginning with earth, flow through the iḍā and piṅgalā channels. However, when, by the power of practicing the retention of breath (prāṇadhāraṇā), the movement of those very elements is accomplished solely within the prāṇa, then their recitation (japa) occurs; such is the meaning. From each respective element...

Regarding what was stated there, in response to the inquiry as to which [element] has arisen at the time of sunrise (*udayakāla*), he says "staff" (*daṇḍa*) and so forth. When the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs in a straight line for twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*) while touching the staff-like form of the *prāṇa-daṇḍa*, then the rising of the earth (*bhūmi*) is to be known; this is the lower portion of the *prāṇa*.

When the breath flows downward, touching eight finger-breadths below, there is the emergence of water; when it flows upward, touching four finger-breadths above the tip of the nose and facing upwards, there is the emergence of fire;
and when it flows outward, touching eight finger-breadths at the side, [there is the emergence of air].

When the breath flows straight upward at that time, it should be known as the rising of air (vāyu); and when, while touching all around in the four directions, it flows through the center, then the rising of space (ākāśa) occurs—this is the meaning. Incidentally, [the following is] the application of the respective elemental risings to their respective effects.
He demonstrates the nature of yoga with the verse beginning "mā darśayit dharaṇeḥ" (Do not show the earth), which has been largely explained;

he further indicates the instruments— the senses consisting of the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth— with the verse beginning "aṅgulībhiḥ" (With the fingers), stating that they should not be held too tightly.
Even when there is only a slight opening for the path of one's own exit,
a powerful wind might force its way out through any available passage;
therefore, contemplating the unity of the individual self (jīvātman), the vital breath (prāṇa), and the mind, one should gradually retain the prāṇa-vāyu.

By practicing this, one attains steadiness of mind or firmness of body. It has been stated in general that the sense organs are [constrained] by the fingers; in response to the inquiry as to which organ is to be bound by which finger, he says "by the two thumbs," and so forth. Thus it is.
For a man who practices for a long time, first a sound arises resembling the song of a swarm of intoxicated bees; immediately after that, a sound like that of a flute filled with wind arises;
and thereafter, a sound like that of a jar arises.
From that, a sound arises which is produced from the cessation of [mental] activity; for them, a sound equal to that [inner resonance] arises.
Thus he says with the words beginning "nāda" (sound). In this way, through the intensity of practice, knowledge arises; for daily, those cognitions which have sense objects as their domain...

To the question, "Do they arise and dissolve [only] through the attainment of knowledge? he says, "The end of saṃsāra," meaning that because it destroys saṃsāra, this knowledge is superior to other forms of knowledge; therefore, one should strive for such knowledge in every way.
Since the nature of cognition is necessarily bound to having an object, [the question arises] "what is the object of that cognition?
To this he says: "Haṃsa," meaning it has Śiva and Śakti as its object. It will be stated later that in such a state, yogis should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *praṇava* itself.
Desiring to dispel the inquiry as to how the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) arose within the *mastita* and *kośa*, he describes its origin with the words beginning with "puṃ" and so forth:
"The bindu is the male (*pumān*), and the sarga is nature (*prakṛti*); from those two, the bindu and the sarga, [arise] the two sounds 'ha' and 'sa'. Thus ends the section on the bindu and the sarga.

The letter *kā* marks the end of creation (*sarga*), and the letter *sa* arises from both the male (*puṃs*) and nature (*prakṛti*). One might ask: "Are these two, being of that very nature, not identical and thus lacking distinction? To this he replies with the words beginning "ha," and so forth. Here, the letter *ha*, which was previously mentioned as ending in the bindu (*visarga*), possesses the form of the male (*puṃrūpa*).

Because it must be spoken [with a vowel], the *ha* is stated as being accompanied by the *bindu*; however, in the previous [context], since the state of ending with the *visarga* was mentioned separately, its reading here as being accompanied by the *bindu* appears to be due to the error of a scribe. These two alone are also designated by the term *ajapā*. Regarding the *haṃkāra*...
Because of the word *ruṣat* (shining) and by the prior insertion of the letter *a*, everyone perceives their own self as "I.
Thus, by means of that very mantra, the individual soul (*jīva*), performing its utterance through the inhalation and exhalation of breath, attends upon the Supreme Person, the Self.
As for how the individual soul (jīva) performs the worship of the Supreme Self, he says:

"as if it were its own" (*svāprāyam*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "considering [the body] to be its own support," because it is by nature (*prakṛtyā*) that the soul—which is of the same nature as *māyā*—[acts].
Since the individual soul (jīvātman) is conceived as distinct from the Supreme Person (puruṣa),
it is stated that primordial nature (prakṛti) constitutes the very being of the individual soul;
and since primordial nature rests upon the Puruṣa, the worship of that which is the support of one's own self follows.

The meaning is that it is indeed appropriate for the individual self (*jīvātman*) to worship the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). When this *prakṛti* reaches the state of oneness with Brahman through the excellence of the practice of yoga, then, due to the non-difference between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
Through the realization of the identity of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), the firm conviction "I am He" arises.
In this expression "so'ham," when the *sa* and *ha* are elided, it becomes "so'ham," which is pronounced as "so'ham" (like *eṣo 'ham*).
Regarding those two [vowels], there is the rule for the single substitute of *eṅ* in place of a word-final [vowel] and the following vowel (*eṅaḥ padāntād ati*).
The intention is that when the *pūrvarūpa* sandhi is applied by the rule *nādinyākrośe putrasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.130), the form *om* is established;
thus, for one who practices the recitation of *oṃ*, the attainment of the state of *so'ham* occurs because of the relationship of cause and effect between those two. [The letter] *ha*...
There is the elision of the two [final] vowels; there is the elision of the masculine base [of *bindu*]. From the vowel *a* and from the vowel *u*, the thirteen vowels are established.
Therein, when the prior form of *bindu* (Śiva) is united with Brahmā, and when non-duality is realized in the intellect, the yogi becomes the *praṇava*.
[This is] Brahmā-Viṣṇu...

One attains identity with the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is Śiva; this very point he expresses as "this supreme bliss. Bliss is that which transcends all other streams of bliss; its essence is such that, unlike primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it is not produced through modification (*vikāra*). He states "eternal" (*nityam*) to indicate that it is not something created. Thus ends the commentary.

Then, one should contemplate— that is, practice— the single quality called *nāma* (name), which consists of that [quality] but is not its substratum, which exists as non-different from the self of the yogi, and which, through the power of the intensification of yoga practice, has reached its culmination according to the previous method; this should be done continuously until—

The intention is that as long as the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra have not been completely severed, one is not qualified for [the performance of] injunctions and prohibitions; consequently, having attained the nature of Brahman, one will become a wanderer according to one's own will. By this much of the treatise, [the author has established] his intended subject matter...

Having performed at the end of the book an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) in the form of praise to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), etc., in accordance with the instruction of the great traditionalists (*mahāsāṃpradāyin*) that "actions which begin with an auspicious rite and end with an auspicious rite are praiseworthy," [the author] composes [the following] for the instruction of his disciples, beginning with the words "The Tradition" (*āmnāya*).

By day, through the words of the *āmnāya*—the declarations of the Vedas—it is established that [Brahman] is beyond description as a quality, for the Śruti declares: "From whence words return, not having attained Him.
How much more so, then, is it unattainable by the words of men who know but little? It is eternal consciousness (*nitya-vijñāna*).

The meaning is that even such scriptural passages as "Nanda is Brahman" do not take as their object a [Brahman] devoid of qualities, but rather establish [Brahman] as qualified by attributes such as eternity and the possession of eternal knowledge.
For it is said in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, in the hymn to the Vedas: "In some places, while You move about as the unconquered Self..."

The meaning is as follows: "The scripture (Nigama) would proclaim You"—that is, the Veda would describe You as being associated with the *māyā* which is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and through that association, as one who has accepted its qualities such as *sattva* and so forth;
it does not mean that You are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). [This refers to] that which is self-evident...

The meaning is that those whose mental modifications (*mano-vṛtti*) are fixed upon the Self— having made it an object through self-luminous knowledge (*svaprakāśa-jñāna*) which is not an object of the senses (*anindriyavedya*)— behold Him.

The meaning is that they do not perceive it as real; however, that which is different from it does not exist as a reality, but rather only that which lasts until the end of ignorance (avidyā) is perceived as real, just like an elephant or other objects perceived in a dream—this is the sense. Why [would there be] a cause in that which is devoid of a cause?

The meaning is that it is devoid of specific attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not made an object of perception, or else, it is devoid of causes. The consciousness residing within is the consciousness whose nature is the Self;
thus there are seven manifestations: *a*, *ā*, *u*, *ū*, *m*, *bindu*, and *nāda*.

The seven parts consist of the digits (kalās) beginning with Kṛti and Śāntā; it is indeed encompassed by them as well, yet it is not even described. The meaning of the statement "unattainable through songs" is that it cannot be established by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); it is to be sought within the *Śrutimaulis*, that is, the portions of the Upaniṣads.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "four-faced" is that [the Lord] has resorted to— that is, presides over— the navel-lotus which is attainable through practice by the four-faced Brahmā. Furthermore, it was stated that it is impossible for that which is contained in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) not to be expounded, and likewise impossible for that which is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) not to be expounded.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "May the body of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), which is the root of bliss, protect you before the *bindu*. Regarding that body, its head consists of the *praṇava*;
he describes the origin of that *tāra* [the *praṇava*] with the words "from the *bindu*," meaning from the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and from the *nāda*, the *tāra*. The world... [is produced].
Because it causes one to cross over, the movement [of the breath] is swift; the face of that body consists of the twenty-four principles.
The body of the Lord Bhava is well known as being surrounded by the elements;
this too is surrounded by the phonemes (varṇas) produced from the elements, such as earth and the rest.

The four Vedas are the conduct that constitutes the very body of this [Being]; from the crescent moon of his forehead, a stream of nectar flows forth in abundance, and by that mass of ambrosia, he has become one who is most thoroughly saturated— such is the description of his body.

The "piṇḍa" (body) of the six [syllables] refers to the fact that the praṇava itself constitutes the piṇḍa by way of its forms as the vowels *ā*, *u*, and *m*. That very [piṇḍa] is the body; Śivā, in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, is the self (*ātman*). The two phonemes *ha* and *sa* are the place of the *pada* (word), while the *bindu* is the place of the *rūpa* (form).
"O Yoginī, [attain] that which is such—possessing a state of *samarasa* (equal flavor) with Śiva that is thus constituted—and which is something ineffable;

[attain] that which has passed and is coming," is the ellipsis. This is the verb in the second person plural, derived from the root *i* preceded by *ati*. "The body and so forth" (*piṇḍādīti*). Piṇḍa...

The *ḍayoga* is that yoga previously described as being preceded by the recitation (*japa*) of the *praṇava*; the *piṇḍayoga* is the acquisition of the supreme seed-mantra (*bījamantra*) and mantra through the aforementioned characteristics, and it is called the "yoga of the seed-syllable whose nature is Śiva," because the syllable *vī* is the seed— that is, the cause— of the nature of Śiva.

Union occurs; however, the seed-yoga is supreme because it consists of *sāmarasya* (homogeneity). Indeed, *sāmarasya* is merely the state of having the same form. But that yoga which is performed without regard for the fruit is [the yoga] with qualities (*saguṇa*) in the case of Śiva.

The meaning is that the proximity of that Supreme Brahman—which is devoid of qualities and is the agent of that identity—becomes the cause of liberation. Regarding the passage beginning with "mūle" (in the root): from the root, that is, from the *mūlādhāra*, she who consists of the states of sleep and waking goes toward Śiva residing in the *brahmarandhra*.

Having properly visualized and meditated upon the collection of channels— the six chakras beginning with Svādhiṣṭhāna— and the sky-lotus, which is the sphere of space located above the space between the eyebrows and extending as far as the Brahma-randhra; one should then [withdraw] the Haṃsa, the individual soul, from one's own abode, the Mūlādhāra.

The distinction from the preceding verse is that [the soul] comes having seized that living *haṃsa*; the distinction in the subsequent [verse] is that it comes having seized its own unmanifest self (*avyakta-svātmāna*). Regarding the phrase "in the two winds," [it refers to] greed arising from the suppression of both the *apāna* wind and the *prāṇa* wind.

The "clashing" (*saṃghaṭṭa*) of the two downward-flowing winds, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, refers here specifically to the mere transcendence of the sound born from that clashing. The term "jāṃyikī" means capable of movement with speed.
Regarding "the support" (*ādhāra*) and so forth: the "support" is the *mūlādhāra*; "vakra" is the channel situated there, and the "power" (*śakti*) is that which resides therein.
The meaning is that its triangle has the *bindu* (point) in the middle region as its abode and place of residence;

or rather, because in another tantra it is stated that she resides in the *bindu* associated with the *kāmabīja* (seed-syllable of desire) situated in the *mūlādhāra*. The "middle of the bow" refers to the space between the eyebrows (*bhrūmadhya*).

This refers to the *jñānacakra*. Here, the specific distinction is that meditation (*dhyāna*) itself—situated in the center of this wheel—is like the rising sun, dispelling darkness with its ruddy brilliance; such is the connection. By means of each individual verse, [the practice is applied] to three locations according to the division of time.
Regarding the statement "at the root," he describes the simultaneous abiding in three locations for stability and liberation.
If it is asked how a single entity can abide simultaneously in three places, one should understand that this is due to the excellence of its power (*sāmarthya-viśeṣāt*).
Some, however, having accepted a division of the *kuṇḍalī* based on a division of the wheels (*cakra-bheda*), [proceed as follows].
They recognize the six *kuṇḍalīs*. From the restraint of the *apāna* wind arises the *ādhārabandha*;

the word "foremost" (*pramukha*) signifies the primary meaning, by which the restraint of the *prāṇa* wind is included. The connection is that they worship the threefold seed-syllable Śiva with nectars. The *Anaṅga-tantra* is primarily concerned with desire (*kāma*).

Regarding the phrase "naṃ dīrghādīrghaiḥ": the author of the *Padārthādarśa* explains that "long" (*dīrgha*) refers to the act of casting a sidelong glance, while "not long" (*adīrgha*) refers to the contraction of that [glance]. However, in reality, the analysis of the compound is as follows: "long" (*dīrgha*) means long objects, and "not long" (*adīrgha*) means those things which possess only a small degree of length; thus, it means "excessively long" (*atidīrgha*). This is the meaning.

The literal meaning (*litārtha*) is as follows: the Supreme Deity (*aparadevatā*), who pierces through the centers of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakramadhyāt*) with the tips of the crests (*koṭīrāgraiḥ*)—that is, the frontal parts of the crowns—of the gods who have bowed down specifically, may she bestow joy upon the minds of the three worlds; such is the connection [of the words]. This is a specific description of the center of the wheel.

Regarding the triad of mantras there, the first begins with "varṇaiḥ" and so forth. With the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a', and with the consonants beginning with 'sa' and ending with 'ka', the four-petaled lotus of Varuṇa and the [deities] Ceta and Bhṛgu are to be placed in the first wheel; therein also, they are arranged according to the sequence starting from Varuṇa.
Intending that [the sequence] is not otherwise, but rather follows the order of Bhṛgu and the rest, it was stated that they begin with the letter *sa*;

this is connected to the phrase "by the letters joined with *kṣa*. Furthermore, the fact that *da* is placed at the end also indicates that the placement (*nyāsa*) is indeed by way of reverse order, as shown by the mention of Ḍākinī and so forth, up to Rākiṇī.
