The phrase "accompanied by Ḍākinī and Śākinī" and so forth includes Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva, as stated in another Tantra: "This Mūlādhāra is the station of Brahmā; it has the luster of gold and is presided over by Ḍākinī."

The deity here is Svādhiṣṭhāna, declared to be the abode of Viṣṇu; it has the luster of the rising sun, and the goddess there is Rākinī. Maṇipūra, however, is blue, the station of Rudra; Lākinī is there, and the red Anāhata is said to be the house of Īśvara, where Śākini also resides. This is the division of the stations of Sadāśiva.

Even here, there is a pure *kākini* who is smoke-colored; the city of the Command (*ājñāpura*) is as beautiful as the autumn moon. Then *ḍākini* is said to be this abode of Śiva. From the *ādhāra* onwards, it consists of a triangle with a pericarp, composed of the three qualities (*guṇas*) whose nature is *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

"Outside of that" refers to the nature of the support (*ādhāra*) being thus situated; "from that," meaning quickly—desiring to emerge swiftly—the lotuses (*kamala*) and wheels (*cakra*) previously mentioned [are seen].

He who consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), whose nature is pure awareness (*saṃvit-svarūpa*), is the Bliss (*ānanda*) which is dense and unbroken (*nibiḍa-akhaṇḍita*). The light (*dyota*)... [is]... bliss.

Śiva is the self-born, devoid of qualities; his awakening is the act of turning toward the creation of the universe. In that regard, he possesses anklets—ornaments for the feet—whose tinkling is beautiful, most excellent, and subdued. Such is he.
"Even half [of it] is unbroken"—this is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*). Regarding the phrase "space, time," and so forth:
because it is devoid of spatial location, it is impossible to ascertain that "it is situated in this place and not in that place";
and because it is impossible to ascertain that "it exists at this very time and not at that."

By that [statement], its being devoid of time is indicated; by the word "beginning" (ādi), the inclusion of its own essential nature is intended. Because it is impossible to determine whether "this is red" or "this is white," it is devoid of essential nature.
In that void, the fivefold cause is equal, being free from the latent impressions (vāsanā) of sin, merit, and so forth.

Alternatively, when the dissolution of the fivefold causes— consisting of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyin*), the efficient cause (*nimitta*), the instrumental cause (*prayojaka*), and the absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhakābhāva*)— is accepted as the locus of destruction (*vināśasthāna*), then for those who do not perceive any further entity, the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) is considered the primary cause (*mukhyakāraṇa*). Or else:

The cause is the mud, namely the five elements beginning with earth; or alternatively, the cause of the elements is the five subtle essences (*tanmātras*). Having fixed the self—the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—in the supportless, which is devoid of a foundation, with an unwavering mind, one attains the fruit of yoga. He further specifies that fruit:

"Root-elephant" (mūlebha) means that, in the manner described above, once yoga is accomplished, it is easily obtained because it does not depend on any other cause. For its fruit is not produced by yoga, nor is it brought about at that time from any defect; rather, it is eternally manifest at all times.
He says "eternally arisen" (*nityodita*) and so forth, [meaning] even including the acts of taking away, bringing near,
and so on. Furthermore, for as long as his own lineage of texts continues to exist throughout all spatial and temporal limitations,
for that long he himself maintains the lineage of the name previously celebrated by his predecessors.

Desiring to recount the names of many of his ancestors, he begins the description of his own lineage with the words "To Mahāvana," and so forth; Mahāvana was a certain eminent scholar, the great-grandfather of the author of this work. Vanamapi... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
Since it becomes cool through being embraced, he too, being embraced by that creeper in the form of a specific knowledge, attained a state of coolness by abandoning the heat arising from saṃsāra;
even the forest, filled with various fruits, [became] his own.

Just as one bestows fruits upon those who have taken refuge in the branches of a tree, so too does He grant the fruit in the form of liberation— by means of the instruction on the six-fold categories of Vedānta— to His own disciples who have taken refuge in the branches of the Veda, that is, those who study the various recensions of the Veda.
He bestows the supreme goal of human endeavor. The son of the great forest-scholars became a scholar worthy of being sought after;

he was an ocean in the six rites beginning with pacification (*śānti*). His status as an "ocean" is stated because of the common characteristic of being difficult to cross due to their difficulty of performance; however, this [other] one possesses the six [rites] that are easy to perform.
He was able to dwell at will and move freely within the ocean of the Mahāyāna;
he was the son of the learned Ācārya named Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and by his grace, the disciples attained great prosperity. His son was Lakṣmaṇa.
The author of the present work was one whose wealth consisted of the appropriate sciences among the Ācāryas— or rather, whose very wealth was knowledge; for even among the sciences, the Vedas,
which rest upon the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the Aṅgas, are the primary foundations.

Although the fourteen sciences (*vidyās*) and the sixty-four arts (*kalās*), which are thus subsumed under *dharma*, are included within the [sixty-four] arts, they are mentioned separately because they are superior to other arts such as weaving with a shuttle, cooking, burning, carving, and the construction of pavilions.

The plural form "in the sciences" (*vidyāsu*) is used to indicate the predominance of excessive attachment toward the arts that have the nature of knowledge as their defining characteristic; this is done so that, according to the logic of the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*, the number three might not be understood as the intended limit, and thus [the term] refers to all [sciences] without exception.
In the verse beginning with "The manner of his excellence in the arts... and so forth, he states [the following] by means of the words "fame" (*prathām*) and so on:
it is not merely that knowledge of those [arts] is real, but rather that there was also renown and fame in the world due to his being the knower of them;
thus he speaks of the fruit of the knowledge of all sciences.

"Taking up the *Lamādarśamati* and so forth"—by these names, [it refers to] all the *āgamas*, not just two or three; that which has come from the mouths of Śiva and gone to the mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain (*Girisutā*) is considered the *mata* of the venerable Vāsudeva, and therefore it is called an *āgama*. Thus it is said.
All of this is the essential core of those treatises rooted in the moment [of realization], and not merely that which was composed by ordinary persons;
it is the essence, and not some triviality resulting from the practice of abbreviated texts. It has been compiled with prior wisdom, not haphazardly or adventitiously, and not merely as it was heard.

However, he states that it is not merely bound to the literal meaning, but rather that a determination of one specific meaning was reached after investigation by means of Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and other sciences; the word "prājña" (wise) is to be supplied as the subject, meaning one who is renowned in all branches of knowledge.
For such a person does not adhere to a meaning exactly as it appears like a mere physical object.
The sense is that it is destroyed, and not by those that are non-numerical; rather, by those numbered as twenty-five.
In this regard, in the first [section], under the guise of describing creation (*sṛṣṭi*), *prakṛti* along with its manifestations (*saprapañca*) is defined.
In the middle, by the twenty-three chapters, however, both *prakṛti* and its transformations (*vikṛti*) are defined. At the end...

Under the guise of explaining the application of the *timenu* [the *timira* eye disease] chapter, it is established that the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) is distinct both from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*); thus, the meaning is that there are chapters equal in number to the principles (*tatva*). This concludes the purpose for composing the treatise.

She who creates speech that is venerable because it is honored by all as being "of the wise" and so forth, and which is worthy of worship by everyone due to its faultlessness— she alone is the one who brings forth such speech, whose meaning is accepted by the virtuous and the traditionalists; she is also the one who sustains my own work.
The intention is that it is entirely appropriate to remember Him at the conclusion of the book, as He has become speech itself.

What is there for me to conceive of that has not already been definitively established with great difficulty by the foremost scholars such as Ādyabhaṭṭa and others, who are like elephants among the most learned, in their treatises? In every land, there are wise men.
O you who have abandoned the faults of envy through your dwelling and your assembly, for what reason, for what purpose,

and by which deluded men— those few humans who have not looked upon you with respect on this long and vast surface of the earth— have you been made weary by them while searching for the objects deposited by yourself?
Since it is not possible to conceive of a limit [to its duration], let there be the river of devotion,
the light of the lamp,
the father who has prescribed the rules for atonement, and the illumination of the word "Mallādarśi," which is the first term of the ritual application.

May that Śabdārthacintāmaṇi (The Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Words and Meanings), the elder brother of Śiva, be victorious— he who is a mine of jewels known as the *Rvā* [Ṛgveda], and who, though devoid of feet, goes further than the furthest distance; and oh,
how he satisfies the wise with his own words while leaving the proponents of fallacious logic far behind!

And by those very [qualities], he who is included among the virtuous here rightly destroys even the one devoid of virtue; may that son, whose fame for excellence is well-established, live long—may he be studied [by you]!
For he is naturally deluded by the absence of practice and is exceedingly full of self-doubt.
Since there is no attainment of association with the gods who are lords of [liberation],
why should the wise not compose such a work that is exceedingly pleasing to the mind?
For when compassion does not prevail toward the Lord of Śrī, where is this ocean of love, and where is this harsh lord of the dull-witted?
Where indeed, or where is that [person] who, for the sake of corrupting the multitude of objects esteemed by others, has come?
